This session invites multidisciplinary contributions addressing the different components of natural hydrogen systems: water sources, circulation and access to reactive rocks; geometry and dynamics of ultramafic source regions; serpentinization mechanisms, reaction kinetics and H₂ generation; structural controls and migration pathways; geochemical and biological sinks; gas–water–rock interactions and gas mixtures; reservoir properties, trapping and sealing mechanisms; and H₂ accumulation and preservation. We particularly welcome studies integrating geology, structural geology, petrology, geochemistry, microbiology, laboratory experiments, numerical and reactive-transport modelling, and geophysical imaging, including seismic, electromagnetic, gravity, magnetic and multiphysics approaches. A central objective is to connect processes with observable signatures: What transforms an H₂-generating geological environment into a functioning natural hydrogen system? Which observations can constrain its source, activity, migration pathways and potential accumulation? By connecting fundamental understanding with subsurface observations, this session aims to advance both the science and exploration of natural hydrogen.
title: Bridging Fundamental Science and Exploration of Natural Hydrogen Systems

description: Mining moves more material each year than all natural terrestrial processes combined, while crushing and refining the extracted ores consumes some 2% of global energy production. The energy transition sharpens this paradox, as replacing fossil infrastructure with renewables demands a many-fold increase in the supply of copper, lithium, rare earth elements and other critical raw materials, which secondary supply cannot deliver on the timescales involved. Europe, notably, has one of the world's longest mining histories, yet limited investment and low public acceptance due to environmental and social costs have left the geology of many districts unexplored by modern methods. This session convenes the technical and conceptual advances needed to explore differently in Europe and worldwide. We thus invite contributions on non-invasive, low-impact exploration for societally acceptable resource sources: novel geophysical acquisition and inversion, including passive, airborne and drone-borne methods; remote sensing from satellite through UAV to drill-core scales, including hyperspectral imaging and rapid geochemical characterisation; and mineral-systems or knowledge-driven frameworks that turn sparse observations into testable targets. Innovative approaches to holistic data integration and prospectivity mapping are equally relevant, as a fusion of diverse legacy and new data is needed to generate predictive targets. We especially encourage submissions that take this interdisciplinary approach even further: to integrate societal and environmental licence to operate into target prioritisation, monitoring tools that ensure accountability across the exploration and mining lifecycle, and work identifying overlooked primary and secondary resources in legacy mining areas.
title: Next-generation mineral exploration: from non-invasive technologies to holistic data integration and targeting

description: Deep-seated and concealed mineral deposits represent a major opportunity for securing the sustainable supply of critical raw materials required for Europe’s energy, digital and industrial transitions. However, exploring mineral resources at greater depths and beneath geological cover remains technically challenging, costly, and uncertain. Reducing these uncertainties requires a new generation of exploration approaches capable of integrating geological knowledge with advanced sensing, geophysical imaging, geochemistry, Earth observation, automated data processing, and predictive modelling. This session invites contributions presenting innovative technologies, methodologies and integrated workflows for the exploration of mineral resources, from early-stage geological targeting to field validation and demonstration. Particular attention will be given to approaches that combine complementary datasets and technologies across different spatial scales and improve our ability to identify indirect geological, geochemical, geophysical and spectral expressions of mineralisation at depth. We particularly encourage contributions linked to recent advances in remote and proximal sensing, passive and active geophysics, UAV-based measurements, hyperspectral imaging, robotics, artificial intelligence and multi-source data integration are creating new possibilities for detecting, characterising and assessing deep mineral systems. These technologies can improve exploration targeting while reducing drilling requirements, operational costs, environmental disturbance and the time needed to move from regional-scale prospectivity assessment to deposit-scale investigation. This session is promoted by DEXPLORE project entitled Recognising European potential for hosting deep land primary CRM by combining new mineral models and advanced exploration and visualisation techniques (Grant Agreement: 101178897), funded by the European Union. Views and opinions expressed are, however, those of the author(s) only and do not necessarily reflect those of the European Union or European Health and Digital Executive Agency (HADEA). Neither the European Union nor the granting authority can be held responsible for them.
title: Integrated Geoscience and Emerging Technologies for Critical Raw Material Discovery

description: The transition towards sustainable and resilient raw materials supply requires improved monitoring and characterisation across the entire mining lifecycle, from exploration to closure and post-mining management. Earth Observation (EO), combined with in-situ measurements, geospatial technologies and advanced data analytics, is opening new possibilities for the continuous characterization and monitoring of areas of raw material potential, as well as active, inactive, abandoned and legacy mining sites, This includes the exploration of prospective areas, open pits, underground mining areas, waste rock dumps, tailings storage facilities and surrounding environments, supporting a comprehensive understanding of mining activities and their environmental impacts throughout the full mining cycle This session brings together innovative EO products, sensor technologies, and modelling approaches for developing integrated monitoring frameworks that transform heterogeneous multi-source observations into actionable knowledge across the full raw materials and mining lifecycle. We particularly welcome interdisciplinary contributions addressing the characterization, monitoring, management, and risk assessment of prospective areas, mine waste sites, including tailings facilities and waste-rock deposits The session welcomes contributions on • Earth observation, geospatial approaches and sensor technologies across the full mining life cycle • Ground deformation, dynamic hazard and geotechnical and risk monitoring and assessment of mining sites, tailings facilities, waste-rock deposits, and other mining-related infrastructure • Environmental and sustainability monitoring, including land-use change, water, vegetation, contamination, and ecosystem impacts associated with mining and mine waste • Multi-scale and multi-source data integration, combining satellite, airborne, UAV, and ground-based observations with geological, geochemical, geotechnical, and historical data for exploration, mine monitoring and post-mining assessment • AI, ML, data fusion, and predictive modelling for automated, continuous, and near-real-time monitoring and assessment • Data scalability, interoperability, and practical uptake of monitoring approaches, including their transferability across sites and regions and implementation by industry, authorities, and environmental managers
title: Earth Observation for Sustainable and Resilient Raw materials supply: Multi-Scale Monitoring of Mining Sites and Facilities

description: Climate change is increasingly interacting with rapid urbanization, socioeconomic transformation, environmental degradation, and uneven development across Asia. Floods, droughts, tropical cyclones, sea-level rise, salinity intrusion, landslides, etc., and compound extremes are affecting communities, ecosystems, infrastructure, livelihoods, and economic development. These challenges are particularly significant in emerging and developing regions, where high exposure often coincides with limited resources, institutional constraints, and social inequalities. At the same time, communities, governments, researchers, and other actors across Asia are developing diverse ways to anticipate, absorb, adapt to, and transform in response to climate risks. Understanding which approaches are effective, under what conditions, and how they can support long-term climate-resilient development remains a major scientific and policy challenge. This session brings together interdisciplinary research on the assessment, mechanisms, practices, and pathways of climate resilience in emerging and developing Asia. We welcome contributions that connect climate hazards and environmental change with social, institutional, technological, and policy responses, including:  Measurement and assessment of climate resilience and climate-resilient development  Innovative technologies, modelling approaches, and nature-based solutions for climate adaptation  Empirical case studies, best practices, and lessons from successful and unsuccessful resilience initiatives  Governance, institutional capacity, and policy mechanisms for climate resilience  Community resilience, socio-cultural dimensions, equity, justice, and local knowledge  Methodological advances in climate resilience research, including GIS, remote sensing, participatory methods, and data-driven approaches  Adaptation pathways, transformative resilience, and opportunities for scaling up effective solutions  Theoretical, conceptual, comparative, and review studies on climate resilience in emerging and developing Asia.
title: Climate-Resilient Development in Emerging and Developing Asia: Risks, Responses, and Resilience Pathways

description: Micromorphology is an irreplaceable tool that provides access to multiple characteristics of soils and sediments to deepen our knowledge on both long- and short-term soil and landscape dynamics in time. W. Kubiëna, who introduced the method of micromorphological analysis, stated that “a crushed or pulverized soil is related to the soil formed by nature like a pile of debris to a demolished building”. In fact, the micromorphological analysis of undisturbed samples is fundamental for a holistic architectural approach to the study of soil genesis and soil functions, and recently it is increasingly advocated as an advanced framework in studies of soil genesis, behavior and functions. Moreover, this method uniquely enables the detection of faint traces of initial and/or weakly developed soil processes and the direct reconstruction of sequences of both natural and anthropogenic soil and sedimentary processes over time. After more than 80 years of method’s application it retained its key role in studies of soils diversity, soil genesis and behavior in space and time, but also has advanced to new methodological and technological frontiers. During last decades, micromorphology evolved from a primarily descriptive method into an increasingly quantitative technique, allowing wider application, shorter analysis time and higher replicability. Possibilities of working with stored digital images without access to a microscope further increases the accessibility of micromorphological analysis, while collections of thin sections preserve records of sites and samples that may no longer be accessible. The session is open to but not limited to contributions on the application of micromorphological analysis as one of the proxies for paleoenvironmental reconstructions in soil-sedimentary archives, studies of soil genesis, and, most importantly, as a tool to identify and understand human impacts in modern and archeological contexts. We particularly welcome contributions highlighting methodological innovations in micromorphology.
title: Micromorphology as a Tool for Reconstructing Natural and Anthropogenic Processes in Soils, Sediments and Landscapes

description: Pedology provides a framework for understanding the formation, distribution, and evolution of soils within landscapes. Sitting at the intersection of the geosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, and atmosphere, soils and the landscapes within which they reside represent useful proxy records for understanding the complementary influences of time, topography, biota, climate, and mineralogy on the evolution of planetary surfaces. This session brings together research exploring soil–landscape relationships across spatial and temporal scales, from individual pedons to regional landscapes and across a diversity of environmental settings, including modern, past, extreme, and extraterrestrial environments. We welcome contributions focused on soil genesis, soil geomorphology, paleopedology, soil mapping, and astropedology that address questions related to soil and landscape evolution, paleoenvironmental reconstruction, and related phenomena. The session aims to highlight novel and diverse approaches for using soils to understand environmental change and the history of terrestrial and planetary surfaces.
title: New Perspectives in Pedology and Soil-Landscape Systems

description: Climate change is reshaping the interactions among land use, ecosystems, human activities, and spatial development, creating interconnected risks that extend across administrative and geographic boundaries. At the same time, land systems provide a critical arena for climate mitigation, adaptation, ecosystem restoration, and sustainable development. Strengthening climate resilience therefore requires moving beyond sectoral and place-based interventions towards integrated approaches that connect land-system dynamics with spatial planning and governance across scales. This session explores how land systems can be understood, managed, and transformed to strengthen climate resilience and sustainability. We particularly welcome research examining the interactions between land-use and land-cover change, climate risks, ecosystem services, human well-being, and spatial development, as well as studies investigating how planning and governance can mediate trade-offs, enhance synergies, and support resilient development pathways. Contributions may address urban, peri-urban, rural, regional, and coupled human–environment systems and employ empirical, modelling, remote-sensing, spatial analytical, participatory, or comparative approaches. Topics of interest include, but are not limited to: • land-system responses and vulnerability to climate change and extreme events; • land-use and spatial planning for climate mitigation, adaptation, and resilience; • interactions and trade-offs among climate resilience, ecosystem services, biodiversity, and socio-economic development; • nature-based solutions, ecosystem restoration, and multifunctional land management; • cross-boundary, multi-level, and regional governance of climate and land-system risks; • spatial inequalities, environmental justice, and differentiated adaptive capacities; • Earth observation, spatial modelling, GeoAI, and decision-support tools for climate-resilient land governance; • pathways for translating land-system science into planning, policy, and implementation. By bringing together geoscientists, land-system scientists, planners, social scientists, practitioners, and policymakers, the session aims to strengthen dialogue across disciplines and scales and advance place-sensitive, evidence-based approaches to climate-resilient spatial governance.
title: Land Systems for Climate Resilience and Spatial Governance

description: Glaciers and ice caps around the globe are responding rapidly to climate change, with significant consequences for the environment and society. Advancing our understanding of glacier change requires an integrated approach that combines field observations, remote sensing, modelling, and emerging technologies to quantify glacier evolution, improve process understanding, and project future change. At the same time, glacier retreat is driving a wide range of environmental and societal impacts, including contributions to sea-level rise, changes to meltwater availability and resource security, evolving and cascading hazards, and consequences for downstream ecosystems and communities. Changes to glaciers also feed into socio-cultural pressures that modify the ways in which people interact with and benefit from polar and mountain environments. This session welcomes contributions spanning all aspects of glacier and ice cap research, from observations and modelling of glacier processes, dynamics, and mass balance to studies of past, present, and future glacier change and its environmental and societal impacts. We encourage contributions that explore innovative and integrated approaches to glacier monitoring and modelling, including emerging datasets, data assimilation, machine learning, and other new technologies. We particularly welcome research that spans disciplinary boundaries, linking glaciology with climate science, hydrology, ecology, hazards, risk, and resilience. Contributions addressing communication beyond the scientific community, co-production of knowledge, and strategies to support mitigation, adaptation, and decision-making in glacierized regions are also encouraged.
title: Glaciers and ice caps in a changing climate: from observations and modelling to impacts and risks

description: Rapid changes across the global cryosphere, including snow cover, glaciers, ice sheets, and permafrost, are reshaping the Earth system. These changes affect climate, sea level, hydrology, freshwater resources, ecosystems, and communities from mountain regions to polar coasts. Reducing uncertainties in future projections and supporting adaptation requires stronger integration of observations across scales with advanced modelling approaches. This session invites contributions that improve understanding of snow, inland ice, and permafrost dynamics by bridging observations (satellite, airborne, and in situ) with numerical models, including ice-flow, hydrological, regional and global climate models, and AI-based emulators. We particularly encourage studies exploring interactions within the Cryosphere-Atmosphere-Hydrosphere system and translating scientific advances into actionable knowledge for climate resilience. We welcome abstracts addressing: - Data-Model Integration: Improved representation of snow, ice, and permafrost processes through assimilation of Earth observation, remote sensing, and field data into models. - Coupled System Dynamics: Physical and geochemical Cryosphere-Atmosphere-Hydrosphere interactions and feedbacks across glaciated and snow-fed catchments, critical cold spots, and polar regions. - Earth System Impacts: Effects of changing snow regimes, land ice loss, and permafrost degradation on water resources, ecosystems, ocean circulation, and sea-level rise. - Methodological Innovation: Novel modelling tools, machine learning frameworks, and AI approaches that connect cryosphere observations and prediction. - Upscaling and Global Initiatives: Studies linking local observations with regional and global models, including contributions to CMIP, ISMIP, CORDEX, Copernicus, and other international climate assessments. Contributions associated with Horizon Europe projects such as LIQUIDICE, CryoSCOPE, ICELINK, and SnowPI, as well as other relevant international initiatives, are strongly encouraged. By bringing together observational, modelling, and impact-focused perspectives, this session aims to strengthen interdisciplinary collaboration, improve predictive capabilities, and provide robust evidence for climate adaptation across the cryospheric sciences.
title: The Cryosphere in Transition: Linking observations and models of snow, inland ice, and permafrost impacts on the Earth system

description: The increasing availability of remotely sensed observations, combined with advances in computational capacity, is driving modelling and observational glacier studies towards increasingly large spatial scales. Such large-scale perspectives are of particular relevance, as they impact cross-country policy decisions and shape public discourse. Glaciers play a key role in present-day sea-level rise, seasonal water availability, natural hazards susceptibility and in touristic attractiveness. To tackle the spatial challenge, AI-informed techniques have become of particular interest in terms of computational feasibility, both for data processing and modelling. This session focuses on advances in observing and modelling mountain glaciers and ice caps at the regional to global scale. We invite both observation- and modelling-based contributions, which may include, but are not limited to, the following topics: • Observation and modelling results that reveal previously underappreciated regional differences in glacier changes or in their dynamics. • Large-scale impact studies, including glacier contribution to sea level change, susceptibility to natural hazards or changes in water availability from glacierised regions. • Advances in large-scale modelling (reconciling machine learning (ML) with classical approaches, including physical processes, improving/extending strategies for data assimilation/inverse approaches, refining climatic downscaling, increasing representativeness, etc.) • Advances in large-scale monitoring (ML-boosted monitoring and interpretation, multi-sensor homogenisation, meta-analysis of ground-based data, process inferences, etc.) • Development and dissemination of regional to global glacier datasets.
title: Observing and modelling glaciers at regional to global scales

description: Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs)—the sudden release of water from lakes dammed by moraines, ice, or bedrock—are among the most dynamic perturbations of Earth’s surface. Their geomorphic signatures can persist for hundreds to thousands of years, while recent events in mountainous regions have demonstrated their potential to cause damage and loss of life when floods reach downstream communities that may be unprepared. Major uncertainties remain in understanding where and when GLOFs occur, how they are triggered and propagate, how landscapes respond, and how these processes may change in the future. This session explores links between glacial-lake evolution, outburst-flood processes, geomorphic legacies, and societal impacts, with the aim of advancing our understanding of landscape evolution and future hazard and risk. We particularly welcome contributions using sedimentary and geochronological evidence to reconstruct paleo-lakes and paleo-GLOFs, constrain their magnitude and frequency, quantify sediment fluxes, and investigate how outburst floods establish, reorganise, or abandon drainage systems. Contributions addressing the processes controlling GLOF initiation are also encouraged, including ice–lake interactions, dam failure, and triggering and preconditioning mechanisms. A particular focus is the changing abundance and size of glacial lakes, and potential feedbacks on GLOF frequency and magnitude, as well as downstream geomorphic and ecological impacts. We invite studies examining the role of anthropogenic climate warming in GLOF activity, as well as approaches for incorporating dynamically evolving lake populations into flood, hazard, and risk models. We therefore welcome new insights from field observations, remote sensing, and process-based modelling that can improve lake monitoring, early warning, risk management, and assessments of downstream vulnerability. This session seeks to cover the full breadth of glacial-lake research, spanning paleo-lake and paleo-flood reconstruction, state-of-the-art glacial-lake mapping and remote sensing, field observations, process-based modelling, and assessments of the geomorphological, hydraulic, and ecological impacts of GLOFs. We therefore aim to synthesize studies connecting observations across timescales and spatial scales, from individual lake and flood processes to regional and global changes, in order to provide new perspectives on the future evolution of glacial lakes and GLOF hazards.
title: Glacial lakes and outburst floods: formation, processes, impacts, and projections

description: Long-term, large-scale monitoring using multiple observation techniques is necessary to establish historic glacier distributions and their changes over time. Such observations – ranging from seasonal mass balances of individual glaciers to decadal volume changes within entire regions – are vital to understanding underlying processes and projecting future changes. We thus invite contributions targeting all aspects of glacier monitoring (e.g., of area, length, volume, temperature, velocity, mass), as well as method comparisons and uncertainty assessments.
title: Glacier monitoring from in-situ and remotely sensed observations

description: Earth’s cryosphere demonstrates itself in many shapes and forms, but we use similar geophysical and in-situ methods to study its wide spectrum: from ice-sheets and glaciers, to firn and snow, sea ice, permafrost, and en-glacial and subglacial environments. In this session, we welcome contributions related to all methods in cryospheric measurements, including: advances in radioglaciology, active and passive seismology, geoelectrics, acoustic sounding, fibre-optic sensing, GNSS reflectometry, signal attenuation, and time delay techniques, cosmic ray neutron sensing, ROV and drone applications, and electromagnetic methods. Contributions can include field applications, new approaches in geophysical or in-situ survey techniques, or theoretical advances in data analysis processing or inversion. Case studies from all parts of the cryosphere, including snow and firn, alpine glaciers, ice sheets, glacial and periglacial environments, alpine and arctic permafrost as well as rock glaciers, or sea ice, are highly welcome. This session will give you an opportunity to step out of your research focus of a single cryosphere type and to share experiences in the application, processing, analysis, and interpretation of different geophysical and in-situ techniques in these highly complex environments. This session has been running for over a decade and always produces lively and informative discussion. We have a successful history of PICO and other short-style presentations - submit here if you want a guaranteed short oral!
title: Geophysical and in situ methods in the Cryosphere

description: Recent advances in sensing technology have resulted in the development of a range of ground-based methods which can “sense” cryospheric environments at high spatial (millimetre to centimetre scale) and temporal (minutes to hours) resolutions. Such close-range sensors can be used to observe rapidly evolving processes (e.g. iceberg calving, glacial lake outburst floods, supraglacial lake drainage events, snow accumulation/melting) as well as cryospheric environments at small spatial scales (e.g. small glaciers, glacierets, snow patches, rock glaciers). Such processes and environments cannot be observed using satellite Earth Observation techniques due to their coarse spatial resolution and long revisit times. In particular, close-range sensors are flexible in their deployment in the field and can observe cryospheric phenomenon from a range of viewing angles which is particularly beneficial in environments with complex topography, which are commonplace across the cryosphere. Close-range sensors are therefore critical for improving process understanding but also for monitoring cryospheric hazards and the development of hazard warning systems. In this session, we welcome contributions related to a variety of close-range sensing methods, including, but not limited to, uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs), radar, time-lapse photography, TLS and LiDAR. Contributions may include field-based applications, laboratory experiments, development of new systems (e.g. payloads, sensors), novel sensing networks, and new approaches related to the processing and analysis of these data. We strongly welcome case studies from all parts of the cryosphere, including glaciers (both land-based or calving), ice sheets, snow and firn, glacial and periglacial environments, and sea ice. The focus of this session will be to share experiences of developing and applying close-range sensors for cryospheric research in order to showcase the latest developments in this evolving field of research.
title: Close-range sensing of the cryosphere: Sensors, methods, and applications

description: Remote sensing in the ‘Big Data’ era is characterised by the availability of petabytes of satellite data, facilitating observations of the cryosphere at increasingly high temporal and spatial scales. These datasets are invaluable for understanding past and contemporary changes to the cryosphere, which is particularly crucial as climate change continues and extreme events become increasingly frequent. To fully utilise the wealth of satellite data available, the last decade has seen reliance on new approaches for accessing, processing, interpreting, and distributing results from large-scale datasets. These approaches include: • new technologies for data access including cloud-optimised datasets; • cloud geoprocessing platforms and on-demand data products; • data fusion methods that combine coincident satellite observations and assimilate them into numerical and physical models; • machine- and deep-learning approaches; • large-scale, automated data pipelines to understand and monitor entire ice sheets, ice shelves, or glaciated and snow-covered regions; • and a widespread philosophy of open data and software sharing to enable rapid dissemination of new approaches. This session seeks contributions from anyone working on remote sensing of any element of the cryosphere. In particular, we welcome submissions from those researching the cryosphere using large-scale remote sensing data pipelines, machine and deep learning, cloud processing, open-source code/data, and other contemporary approaches.
title: Advances in Remote Sensing of the Cryosphere

description: Climate is inherently geographical. Climatic processes vary across space and time and interact with topography, land cover, water bodies, ecosystems, urban environments and human societies. Geographical climatology provides an integrative framework for understanding these interactions and for bridging atmospheric processes with their spatial expression and environmental and societal consequences. This session invites contributions addressing the geographical dimensions of climate variability and change across a broad range of spatial and temporal scales. We particularly welcome studies dealing with: • synoptic, regional and local climatology; • spatial and temporal variability of temperature, precipitation and other climatic variables; • heat waves, droughts, floods, storms, cold spells and other climatic extremes; • urban climatology, urban heat islands and thermal environments; • topoclimatology and microclimatology; • land–atmosphere and ocean–atmosphere interactions; • climate variability and long-term climatic trends; • geographical patterns and regional manifestations of climate change; • climate hazards, vulnerability and risk; • interactions between climate, landscapes, ecosystems and human societies; • climate-related impacts on health, agriculture, water resources and urban environments; • adaptation to climate change at local and regional scales; • remote sensing and GIS applications in climatology; • spatial climatological databases, reanalysis products and observational networks; • statistical, geospatial and modelling approaches to geographical climatology. The session particularly encourages research that crosses traditional disciplinary boundaries and demonstrates how geographical approaches can contribute to understanding climate processes and their environmental and societal impacts. Contributions integrating observations, remote sensing, reanalysis data, climate modelling and spatial analysis are welcome, as are comparative studies from different climatic regions of the world. The session aims to strengthen interaction between climatology and the broader geographical and geoscientific communities and to highlight the continuing importance of geographical perspectives for understanding climate variability, extremes and climate change.
title: Geographical Climatology in a Changing World: Spatial Patterns, Extremes and Human–Environment Interactions

description: Marine sedimentary archives provide crucial information about past climate conditions and biogeochemical processes in the polar oceans. These records help constrain the range and underlying mechanisms of natural environmental variability and provide an essential long-term context for understanding ongoing changes at high latitudes. This session invites contributions focused on reconstructing Quaternary polar environments from marine sediment archives, as well as methodological developments that expand and refine the proxy toolbox available for studying these records. We welcome a broad range of approaches, including, but not limited to, sedimentology, micropaleontology, organic and inorganic geochemistry, isotope geochemistry, and sedimentary ancient DNA (sedaDNA).
title: Quaternary Polar Environments Inferred from Marine Sedimentary Archives

description: Machine learning (ML) is increasingly advancing cryospheric science, offering new ways to extract information from the rapidly growing volume of satellite, airborne, and in situ observations and to accelerate numerical modeling. Deep learning has proven particularly effective for computer vision tasks such as calving front detection, glacier outline delineation, mapping of permafrost landforms, sea ice classification, and snow cover mapping. Beyond image analysis, ML-based emulators can reproduce the behavior of computationally expensive physical models. This enables large ensembles and the inversion of poorly constrained parameters. Hybrid and physics-informed approaches further promise to combine the flexibility of data-driven methods with physical consistency. More recently, foundation models pretrained on large Earth observation archives have raised expectations of strong transferability across regions and sensors, particularly for applications where labeled training data are scarce. However, their benefit for cryospheric applications has yet to be demonstrated, as they have not consistently outperformed task-specific architectures trained from scratch. Systematic evaluation on shared benchmark datasets is therefore essential to measure real progress. We invite contributions on all aspects of machine learning for the cryosphere, including but not limited to computer vision and remote sensing, model emulation and hybrid modeling, benchmark datasets, as well as trust and interpretability. We also welcome critical perspectives, such as barriers to adoption, computational costs, and cases where ML approaches did not outperform physics-based methods.
title: Machine Learning and Data-Driven Methods for the Cryosphere

description: Earth Science is a compulsory component of many European school curricula and plays a critical role in understanding major global challenges. However, it often receives limited visibility and attention within school education. This concern is also reflected in the declining number of students enrolling in Earth Science degree programmes at university level. The session will showcase projects, teaching strategies, educational resources, and innovative approaches designed to engage students and strengthen the role and relevance of Earth Science in the classroom. Contributions addressing the development, implementation, or evaluation of Earth Science curricula are also particularly welcome, including experiences related to national education policies, curriculum frameworks, and legislative reforms. Comparative perspectives from different countries are encouraged, particularly where curriculum changes or policy initiatives have highlighted effective practices, opportunities, limitations, or critical issues that may be transferable across different educational contexts. Participants are invited to share their experiences, research, and ideas to strengthen international collaboration and build a broader network supporting Earth Science education, including its relevance for policy and governance.
title: Supporting Earth Science in school education

description: The tropical Atlantic exhibits significant ocean variability from daily to decadal time scales, driven by complex ocean dynamics and air-sea interactions. This session is devoted to advancing the understanding of these dynamics and their climatic impacts on both adjacent and remote regions, including their interactions with other tropical basins. Relevant ocean processes include upper and deep ocean circulation, eddies, tropical instability waves, mixing, and upwelling. We further welcome studies analyzing marine heat waves, mechanisms related to climate modes such as Atlantic, Dakar and Benguela Niños, the Atlantic Meridional Mode and the South Atlantic Ocean Dipole, effects of climate change, extratropical as well as interbasin teleconnections, and local biological impacts of ocean variability. Finally, we seek for studies that explore the causes and impacts of systematic model errors in simulating the local to regional Atlantic climate variability. Submissions based on direct observations, reanalysis, model simulations and machine learning techniques are welcome.
title: Tropical Atlantic Variability and teleconnections

description: Coastal oceanographic processes present important differences with deep water oceanography, resulting in higher prediction errors, where topo-bathymetry in shallow areas exerts a strong control on hydrodynamic fields, further modified by stratification, land boundaries and coastal infrastructure. Predictability is limited by strong non-linear interactions (e.g. breaking waves, nearshore circulation and sediment fluxes), choice of numerical strategies (e.g. nested meshes, finite-elements or smooth-particle simulations) or modulations typical of restricted domains (e.g. seiching or vegetation filtering). Coastal observations (in-situ and remote) are therefore necessary to enhance numerical models, where the advent of new satellite capabilities (e.g. Sentinel resolution and sensors) and modelling advances (e.g. coupling or unstructured grids), together with enhanced coastal observatories, are leading to qualitative advances for coastal oceanography applications. Coastal analyses under future scenarios become even more challenging, since transitional areas are more strongly impacted by changing climates (e.g. changing domains due to sea-level rise). For these reasons, it is timely to discuss recent advances in: a) coastal coupled hydro-morpho-ecological modelling at different scales; b) coastal aggregation of in-situ/satellite/numerical data from different sources; c) knowledge-based coastal applications, including the assessment of nature-based interventions; d) use of novel approaches, such as data assimilation or machine learning; and e) uncertainties in coastal decision-making. Building on these challenges, we invite presentations on coastal modelling, data assimilation, boundary effects or operational coastal predictions with/without interactions with Nature-based or traditional interventions. Contributions tackling open questions on non-linear response functions, artificial intelligence or big data for coastal applications are welcome. These coastal topics should conform a fruitful session for discussing coastal oceanography applications, including conventional and nature-based interventions under climate change.
title: Oceanography at Coastal Scales: Modelling, Coupling, Observations and Applications.

description: The ocean’s Biological Carbon Pump (BCP) plays a pivotal role in the oceanic carbon cycle by transporting organic carbon from the surface to the deep ocean, thereby regulating atmospheric CO₂ levels and long-term climate. A critical, yet poorly constrained component of the BCP is the velocity at which marine snow particles sink in the ocean. Various observations, imaging, laboratory experiments, and modeling have revealed significant variability in marine snow sinking velocities, influenced by factors such as particle composition, size, density, ballast minerals, but also hydrodynamic conditions such as vertical currents. The oceanic vertical currents are extremely difficult to assess since very variable and up to several orders of magnitude smaller than their horizontal counterparts. Nonetheless vertical velocities about 1 mm/s (~100 m/day) can have strong influences on sinking velocities. This session invites contributions, , based on models or observations, exploring the physical, chemical and biological controls on marine snow sinking velocities as well as their biogeochemical feedback and parameterization. We welcome studies assessing sinking velocities using novel methodologies and biogeochemical models investigating the role of particle composition on sinking rates, examining the impact of environmental drivers (e.g., temperature, currents, internal tides, turbulence) on particle sinking rates and studies integrating observational, experimental, and modeling approaches to improve parameterizations of sinking velocities in global biogeochemical models. By bringing together interdisciplinary research, this session aims to advance our understanding of the BCP’s efficiency and its representation in Earth system models, ultimately contributing to more accurate projections of ocean long term carbon sequestration.
title: Marine snow sinking velocities: Controls, models and biogeochemical feedbacks

description: Advanced remote sensing capabilities have provided unprecedented opportunities for monitoring and studying the ocean environment as well as improving ocean and climate predictions. Synthesis of remote sensing data with in situ measurements and ocean models have further enhanced the values of oceanic remote sensing measurements. This session provides a forum for interdisciplinary discussions of the latest advances in oceanographic remote sensing (using electromagnetic or acoustic waves) and the related applications and to promote collaborations. We welcome contributions on all aspects of the oceanic remote sensing and the related applications. Topics for this session include but are not limited to: physical oceanography, marine biology and biogeochemistry, biophysical interaction, marine gravity and space geodesy, linkages of the ocean with the atmosphere, cryosphere, and hydrology, new instruments and techniques in ocean remote sensing, new mission concepts, development and evaluation of remote sensing products of the ocean, and improvements of models and forecasts using remote sensing data. Applications of multi-sensor observations to study ocean and climate processes and applications using international (virtual) constellations of satellites are particularly welcome.
title: Ocean Remote Sensing

description: Laboratory experiments enable us to isolate, reproduce, and investigate cryospheric processes and to develop and test new measurement techniques under controlled conditions. By complementing field studies, remote sensing, and numerical modeling, they provide a powerful approach to address pressing and complex questions about the fate of the cryosphere. This session explores both the strengths and unique challenges of this laboratory approach, from experimental design and practical implementation to translating findings to the field. We welcome laboratory studies covering all components of the cryosphere on Earth and other planetary bodies, such as permafrost, sea ice, snow, and glaciers. We invite contributions across methods and scales, from microscale to large-scale experiments, such as physical analogue experiments, mechanical testing, tomography, and the development and testing of new measurement methods. This includes testing of materials, infrastructure, in situ sensors, and technologies for engineering applications. We encourage studies explicitly linking laboratory experiments with field observations, numerical modeling, and remote sensing. By bringing together researchers working across different cryospheric disciplines and at different experimental scales, this session will provide a unique opportunity to discuss the methods, strengths, and challenges of laboratory approaches.
title: Laboratory Experiments in the Cryosphere

description: Droughts, characterized by precipitation deficits and high evaporative demand, are becoming increasingly frequent, prolonged, and intense under global environmental change. Climatic drivers (such as altered precipitation regimes and rising temperatures) and land surface modifications (including vegetation greening, deforestation, land-use transitions, and wildfires) interact in complex ways to shape ecohydrological responses to droughts across spatial and temporal scales. This session invites contributions that explore how ecosystems and hydrological processes respond to droughts, aiming to uncover both underlying mechanisms and broader consequences. We welcome studies based on observational, modeling, and conceptual approaches. Topics of interest include, but are not limited to: 1. New insights into drought responses based on emerging in-situ and satellite observations of soil moisture, evapotranspiration, and vegetation dynamics. 2. Process-based understanding of ecohydrological responses to droughts of varying severity under changing climate and land surface conditions. 3. Long-term trends and resilience of ecohydrological systems under recurrent droughts, with a focus on resistance, recovery, and key environmental drivers. 4. Advances in modeling frameworks (process-based or AI-based) and observation-constrained approaches for improving the representation of drought responses. 5. Social and ecological impacts of evolving droughts, including implications for ecosystems, agriculture, water resources, and human well-being. By integrating hydrology, ecology, and remote sensing, this session seeks to advance our understanding of ecohydrological drought responses and to inform sustainable adaptation strategies in a changing environment.
title: Ecohydrological responses to droughts in a changing environment: Mechanism, trends and impacts

description: Catchments are spatially heterogeneous because of topography, soils, vegetation covers, and climate. These features shape the redistribution of water, energy, carbon, and nutrients in the landscape, influence hydrological connectivity, and create biogeochemical hotspots. This session explores how the spatial organization of landscapes, soil, and vegetation cover shapes coupled water, energy, carbon, and nutrient processes in heterogenous landscapes. We welcome observational, experimental, process-based modelling, and AI/ML-driven studies that identify the mechanisms organizing the spatial patterns of ecohydrological processes and feedbacks. Relevant topics include simulated and observed spatial patterns of water, carbon, and water quality and underlying mechanisms; hydrological connectivity and lateral transfers; the emergence of biogeochemical hotspots; propagation of local dynamics to catchment-scale carbon, nutrient, sediment, and pollution export; and spatially heterogeneous responses to climate change. We also encourage cross-catchments studies that compare contrasting landscapes, explicitly consider spatial heterogeneity, and larger-scale study that develop approaches for representing sub-catchment and sub-grid heterogeneity at regional and continental scales. This session potentially brings together hydrologists, biogeochemists, and modelers that improved the process understanding and modelling ability of coupled water, energy and elements in spatially heterogeneous catchments.
title: Spatial heterogeneity from plot to continental scale: ecohydrological and biogeochemical processes and feedbacks

description: Water may be present in soil, groundwater or surface storage yet remain inaccessible because it is hydraulically disconnected, too saline, too tightly retained, or stored on timescales mismatched with biological or human demand. We define water accessibility as the capacity of stored water to enter ecologically or societally relevant fluxes, with that capacity varying with hydrological state, connectivity, salinity, biological demand and human intervention. This session asks when, where, for whom and for how long stored water becomes accessible in human-modified critical zones. We welcome studies of mobile and less-mobile domains, preferential flow, soil hydraulic structure, root access, groundwater depth, salinity, wetting-drying transitions, irrigation, drainage, pumping, land-use change, restoration, hydrological memory, water age and transit times. Contributions may use field or laboratory experiments, stable isotopes and other tracers, geophysics, remote sensing, water-age and transit-time analyses, and a broad range of modelling approaches. We encourage studies addressing accessibility and functional outcomes for transpiration, recharge, runoff, ecological resilience, crop production, water security and other major ecohydrological or societal fluxes. We particularly encourage work from agricultural systems, wetlands, deltas, drylands, forests, restored landscapes and other human-modified critical zones. Comparative and negative-result studies are welcome, including cases where connectivity or tracer contrasts strengthen, collapse or shift with hydrological state. The aim is to identify measurable indicators, thresholds, trade-offs and management timing while avoiding the assumption that more stored water necessarily means more accessible water.
title: Water Accessibility, Storage and Connectivity in Human-Modified Critical Zones: Mechanisms, Thresholds and Functional Outcomes

description: Vegetation change in mountainous regions is often treated as an outcome of changing hydro-meteorological regimes, yet its feedback to those regimes remains poorly resolved. While it is known that vegetation has significant effects on water partitioning, and shifts in species distributions may actively alter the distribution and temporal availability of water in the regions, these latter dynamics remain poorly represented in the scientific discussion and existing Earth-System-Models. A consolidated understanding of the effects has been hampered by their apparent global heterogeneity: While the European Alps have experienced intensive greening rates, other systems like the North American Rocky Mountains and Sierra Nevada face widespread forest degradation and disturbance driven mortality with varying hydroclimatic impacts. This session focuses on the underlying and resulting snow-water-vegetation interactions in seasonally and perennially snow-dominated mountain regions across the globe, where runoff generation heavily depends on the seasonality of snow and glacier melt and its interaction with vegetation, surface- and groundwater bodies. We invite contributions addressing the process interactions between snow and glacier melt, surface- and groundwater, evapotranspiration, primary production, soil moisture distribution and runoff generation, welcoming field work as well as modelling studies. We especially look forward to the integration of novel monitoring techniques into modelling frameworks, inviting case studies as well as comparative and scenario studies across space and time. We want to connect scientists across disciplines to advance ecohydrological understanding of mountain systems and investigate the role of vegetation in these diverse and complex landscapes.
title: Vegetation as Active Agents in Mountain Water Partitioning: Snow, Water and Ecosystem Interactions Across Elevation Gradients

description: Hydrological extremes, water abstraction and reservoir operations are driving many lakes and reservoirs through low water, fragmented, dry and reflooded states. These transitions alter more than surface area and storage: they change residence time and connectivity, expose sediments to oxidation and desiccation, and reorganize exchanges among catchments, sediments, water and the atmosphere. Their sequence and duration can therefore generate thresholds, delayed recovery and persistent legacies in water quality and ecosystem function. During contraction, solutes and contaminants may concentrate while littoral and bottom sediments become exposed. Drying changes redox conditions, microbial activity and organic matter processing. Reflooding can remobilize nutrients, salts, metals, suspended sediment and organic contaminants, trigger oxygen demand and greenhouse gas pulses, and reshape habitats and food web interactions. In managed reservoirs, the timing and rate of drawdown and refilling may amplify or reduce these effects. The session will bring together hydrology, limnology, aquatic biogeochemistry, water quality, ecology, Earth observation and reservoir management. We invite field and experimental studies, in situ observations, water and sediment analyses, remote sensing, process based and data driven modelling, and regional or global assessments. Relevant topics include detection and attribution of state transitions; thresholds, hysteresis and recovery; sediment exposure and rewetting; carbon, nutrient and contaminant dynamics; ecological resistance and resilience; and monitoring, restoration and adaptive reservoir operation. By treating contraction, drying and reflooding as a connected trajectory, the session will examine when responses are reversible, when legacies persist, and how observations and management can reduce risks to water quality and ecosystem function.
title: Hydrological state transitions in lakes and reservoirs: water quality, biogeochemical and ecological responses to contraction, drying, and reflooding

description: Lakes are sentinels of climate change and human pressure, yet harmful algal blooms, loss of aquatic vegetation and water-quality deterioration are intensifying worldwide. Recent progress in satellite and UAV remote sensing, high-frequency sensor networks and artificial intelligence opens new opportunities for "smart" lake monitoring and operational early warning. This session invites contributions on: (1) retrieval algorithms for water-quality parameters (chlorophyll-a, cyanobacteria, turbidity, CDOM) and aquatic vegetation from multi-source remote sensing; (2) integration of in-situ, optical and physiological measurements for calibration and validation; (3) long-term (multi-decadal) reconstruction of lake ecosystem change; (4) data-driven and hybrid models (e.g. deep learning, KAN) for short-term forecasting of bloom events; and (5) cloud platforms (e.g. Google Earth Engine), open tools and management applications. We particularly welcome comparative studies across lakes and regions, as well as contributions from early-career scientists.
title: Smart Lake: remote sensing, in-situ networks and AI for monitoring and early warning of aquatic ecosystems

description: How do soil-plant-atmosphere interactions shape hydrological and vegetation responses to climate extremes? How do antecedent soil-water and vegetation conditions influence the pathways through which droughts, heatwaves and floods affect agricultural and natural systems? Which approaches can explain contrasting responses and improve predictions? This session explores soil-plant-atmosphere processes and hydrological pathways during the onset and development of climate extremes and subsequent recovery. We examine links between meteorological forcing, antecedent system states, plant water use, land-atmosphere exchanges and hydrological responses, from field to catchment scales. We welcome studies of contrasting responses under dry and wet conditions, drought-heat interactions and transitions between extremes. Topics of interest: 1. Soil-plant-atmosphere responses and feedbacks. Root water uptake, plant water regulation, evapotranspiration, canopy energy balance and vegetation stress during droughts, heatwaves and excess water, including soil-water supply and atmospheric demand interactions. 2. Antecedent conditions and hydrological pathways. How soil moisture, root-zone water storage, vegetation condition and groundwater connectivity shape responses to extremes; how water storage and partitioning among evapotranspiration, drainage, recharge and runoff link plant water availability to broader hydrological behaviour. 3. Contrasting extremes, event sequences and recovery. Contrasting responses under different initial conditions; drought-to-flood transitions; compound hot-dry conditions; and hydrological and vegetation recovery: timing, thresholds and legacy effects. 4. Observation-informed process understanding and prediction. Combining observations and models to identify response pathways, test process explanations, link spatial scales and assess predictive performance across events and environmental conditions. We welcome research using satellite and uncrewed aircraft system (UAS) remote sensing, field experiments, process-based models, data assimilation and interpretable or hybrid machine learning, especially integrating soil-water, vegetation, surface-flux and hydrological observations. Studies may examine single extremes or processes or compare events and systems. We link soil-plant-atmosphere and hydrological extremes research to explain how initial conditions and interacting processes shape responses and recovery.
title: Soil-Plant-Atmosphere Interactions and Hydrological Pathways Across Climate Extremes

description: Integrating hydrological, biogeochemical, and ecological perspectives is essential to understand spatial and temporal dynamics of biogeochemical processes and ecosystem functioning in freshwater, and their emergent responses and sensitivity to a rapidly changing climate. Hydrological processes shape terrestrial-aquatic connectivity within catchments, with cascading effects on aquatic ecosystems through the mobilization and transport of chemical elements and organic compounds, as well as the dispersal of organisms. On the other hand, biota influences hydrological processes through mechanisms such as tree transpiration and ecosystem engineering, while regulating the biogeochemical cycling of carbon, nutrients, metals, and pollutants. This session aims to advance understanding of these multifaceted processes by integrating perspectives at the terrestrial-aquatic-atmospheric interface. We welcome contributions that integrate hydrology, biogeochemistry, and ecology across different organizational and spatial scales, from organisms and communities to stream reaches, lakes, river networks, and catchments. Relevant topics include carbon and nutrient cycling and associated fluxes in soils and inland waters, ecohydrological dynamics, riverine metacommunities, food webs, greenhouse gas exchange, and ecosystem responses to anthropogenic and environmental pressures, including land-use and climate change. We particularly encourage submissions that develop or combine innovative methods, including remote sensing, machine learning, mathematical modeling, and novel laboratory or field approaches, to address current spatial and temporal data limitations. We also welcome studies that apply concepts, tools, or methods from one discipline to generate new insights in another. By bringing together scientists from diverse backgrounds, this session seeks to foster interdisciplinary dialogue, promote methodological exchange, and stimulate new collaborations in hydrological, biogeochemical, and ecological research.
title: Bridging hydrological, biogeochemical, and ecological processes in freshwater networks and catchments

description: Forest ecosystems interact strongly with hydrological processes across a wide range of spatial and temporal scales. Their interactions with soils, groundwater and topography, together with often extensive root systems, create complex pathways for water movement through forest ecosystems. These include the interception, storage and redistribution of water in forest canopies before it reaches the soil, the infiltration and redistribution of water in the soil and subsurface, interactions with groundwater, and the uptake of water by roots and its subsequent transport to the atmosphere. Understanding these often-hidden connections is essential for quantifying forest water use and the role of forests in the water cycle. Our ability to detect these processes is expanding through new approaches, including geochemical and isotopic tracers, geophysical and remote sensing techniques, high-resolution measurements and process-based modelling. These approaches provide new and sometimes surprising perspectives on water fluxes in forested ecosystems. The exceptional drought and heat experienced across large parts of Europe in 2026 further highlight the importance of understanding how forests access, redistribute and use water. This session welcomes contributions that provide new insights into forest ecohydrological processes or demonstrate novel approaches to observing and modelling water fluxes in forest ecosystems. We particularly invite studies addressing how forest canopies modify water availability and fluxes, including interception, throughfall and stemflow; water movement through the soil and subsurface; root water uptake and water sources; and the transport and use of water within trees, as well as forest water stress, drought responses, and the links between forest hydrological processes and the water, carbon and nutrient cycles.
title: Forest Ecohydrology

description: Evapotranspiration (ET) is the key water flux at the interface of soil, vegetation and atmosphere. Methods to derive this flux or its individual components from in-situ measurements have been developed in various research disciplines, covering different scales from e.g. point scale sap flow or soil heat pulse measurements, via pedon-scale of lysimeters, ecosystem scale of eddy covariance footprints to the landscape scale via drones or scintillometers. In-situ-measurements are necessary for calibration, validation and comparisons with larger scale estimates from remote sensing and modelling, but scaling procedures and uncertainty estimations are required for meaningful comparisons. Additionally, the support of these processes by AI methods holds much promise, but usually depends on large well-described data sets. This session will mainly focus on the variety of in-situ ET estimates such as from sap flow or soil heat pulse sensors, lysimeters, eddy covariance stations, scintillometers and other (possibly new) methods. We would also like to address the challenges in comparing the different in-situ estimates while dealing with scale-dependency, uncertainty and representativity. We welcome contributions that (1) assess and compare established and new in-situ measurements, (2) address error sources and uncertainty considerations of the respective methods, (3) bridge scales between different in-situ measurements and modelled and remotely sensed ET, (4) demonstrate the value of in situ ET measurements to improve modelling of ET or characterizing large scale ET in combination with remote sensing; (5) evaluate challenges and opportunities of using AI for in-situ scaling and comparisons.
title: In-situ ET – still a challenge: Estimating, scaling, assessing and comparing evapotranspiration measurements

description: Hydrology and soil science originated from water-management needs for ancient civilisation and agriculture, but since then have developed into many specialised disciplines. While irrigation and yield management remain prominent research topics, agricultural fields as soil-plant-atmosphere systems are rarely seen as an integrated hydrological system, despite the pressing challenges posed by intensifying climatic extremes, degrading soils and declining water resources. This session therefore refocuses attention on agricultural fields as coupled soil-plant-atmosphere systems in which hydrological, biogeochemical and ecological processes interact. Interdisciplinary approaches are crucial to improve process understanding for enhancing agricultural practices and making agricultural landscapes more resilient. Given the contrasting temporal and spatial legacies of the processes involved, we need to consider agricultural landscapes under change. How can we prospectively manage systems with different process turnover scales? Moreover, which system-stabilising processes exist to make the landscapes more resilient, not only through “isolated” measures such as retention basins or hedges, but by enhancing characteristics and properties across entire fields or landscapes (e.g. improving soil structure to increase infiltration capacities)? We invite contributions investigating soil-plant-atmosphere interactions, water, carbon and nutrient cycling, crop responses to environmental stress, and other processes shaping agricultural landscapes across temporal and spatial scales. We particularly encourage contributions addressing how fundamental process understanding can inform agricultural management practices and modelling approaches. It is important to us to strengthen the connection between different scales – for example, linking small-scale and/or short-term observations and large-scale and/or long-term system responses, and translating them into management strategies/practices and applications. This session aims to foster exchange between fundamental and applied research, and discussion about transforming interdisciplinary collaboration to impactful solution prospects.
title: From fundamental to applied process understanding for resilient agricultural landscapes

description: Wetlands and their associated wetlandscapes are strongly controlled by hydrological processes that determine water availability, connectivity, inundation patterns, and other key dynamics. These processes in turn are recently driven by climate change and human pressures, affecting ecosystem services such as water quantity and quality regulation, carbon storage, and food provision. Linking changes in water availability with pressures and services can therefore provide a stronger basis for wetland management, restoration, protection and conservation. This session aims to address the following question: How do climatic and human pressures alter hydrological, geomorphological and ecological processes in inland and coastal wetlands and wetlandscapes, and what are the consequences for communities and society? We welcome studies using remote sensing, hydrogeodesy, hydrological modelling and field observations to understand water-related changes in both water quality and quantity (represented by water surface area, depth, connectivity and storage). The processes seeking to be understood include hydroperiod, inundation dynamics, carbon and nutrient cycling, pollution, socio-hydrological interactions and how changes in ecosystem condition influence ecosystem services and livelihoods. Contributions that combine multiple data sources or connect understanding of wetland processes with management and decision-making are also encouraged.
title: Wetland Hydrology and Societal Benefits under Environmental Change

description: Environmental DNA (eDNA) has become a popular biological survey tool, but its potential as a tracer of water and sediment transport remains underexplored. Understanding how eDNA signals are generated, mobilized, degraded, and preserved in water is essential not only for tracking biodiversity, but might reveal flow paths, residence time, sediment origin, and connectivity across hydrological and geophysical systems. This session is dedicated to exploring eDNA as a tracer of transport, discussing it alongside the established toolkit of hydrological tracers, including stable water isotopes, hydrochemistry, and particles such as fluorescent microspheres, bacteriophages, and spores. Recent work has demonstrated the feasibility of using eDNA to characterize flow paths and catchment response in Alpine and urban systems, and of incorporating eDNA sampling directly into hydrological monitoring and time series studies. Our primary focus is on recent-time eDNA signals in freshwater and surface waters, but we also welcome contributions that link present-day eDNA patterns to longer-term records preserved in sediment archives. Beyond rivers, we are interested in studies from wetlands, groundwater, and even lakes, coastal waters, and oceans. Presentations in this session will address the methodologies, applications, and implications of eDNA for understanding the movement, persistence, and transformation of genetic tracer material within hydrological and geophysical systems. We encourage contributions that investigate how eDNA distribution is shaped by transport mechanisms, degradation kinetics, and environmental drivers such as flow, sediment, and biogeochemistry and what that knowledge can reveal about the underlying physical processes. Studies that integrate laboratory analyses, modeling, or sediment archives to connect scales and processes are particularly welcome. We also seek contributions that push the boundaries of how eDNA is observed. This includes innovative sampling strategies such as custom-built sensors and passive samplers, automated or distributed collection networks, and citizen science approaches that expand the spatial and temporal characterization of eDNA signal transport, concentration, and decay. By bringing together diverse systems and approaches, this session aims to advance eDNA as a tool for tracing physical transport processes, fostering new interdisciplinary collaborations between hydrology, sedimentology, and molecular methods.
title: Environmental DNA as a Tracer of Water and Sediment Transport

description: Plant hydraulics, which studies the capacity of plants to extract water from the soil and transport it up to the aerial organs, and ecohydrology, which studies the bidirectional interaction between the water cycle and ecosystems, share substantial conceptual overlap. Yet, communication between the two research communities remains limited. This session aims to bridge this gap by soliciting contributions that present case studies that have benefited, or could benefit, from an interdisciplinary approach. Relevant topics include, but are not limited to: • Ecohydrological processes in complex landscapes, including ecological studies at sites with significant lateral water fluxes, groundwater-dependent ecosystems, and landscape evolution contexts • Vegetation-water interactions under environmental change, encompassing drought studies and forest hydrological research in both urban and natural catchments • Plant hydraulic traits and ecosystem functioning, focusing on the ecohydrological implications of plant hydraulic strategies across scales • Linking plant and catchment water dynamics through observations and modelling, including the use of isotopes and other novel measurement techniques, scaling approaches and integration of plant hydraulics into ecohydrological models To facilitate meaningful exchange between the communities, contributors are encouraged to explicitly highlight the realised or anticipated benefits of integrating concepts, methods, or perspectives from the complementary discipline, for example through advances in theory, improved interpretation of observations, or the development of modelling approaches.
title: Bridging plant hydraulics and ecohydrology: mutual insights across scales

description: Ecohydrology, i.e., the study of the interactions between water and ecosystems, has expanded rapidly as a field of research, beyond traditional discipline boundaries in terms of questions and approaches. This session aims to draw examples from this wide field, portraying the current diversity and common features of research frontiers in ecohydrological studies, as well as the range of methods employed. We thus encourage contributions showing novel results or methods when tackling questions related to the coupling of ecological, biogeochemical and hydrological processes, at scales ranging from the single organ or organisms to whole ecosystem/catchment. Contributions relative to all terrestrial and aquatic systems are welcome, including those relative to managed ecosystems, showing how human intervention alters the interactions between water and ecosystems.
title: General Ecohydrology

description: Stable isotopes are powerful tools for tracing water fluxes and associated nutrients in the soil-plant-atmosphere continuum. Because subsurface water and nutrient fluxes, plant water uptake, and atmospheric processes are tightly interconnected, advances in field methods, laboratory techniques, and modeling are critical for capturing these dynamics and their drivers with greater temporal and spatial resolution, precision, and accuracy. At the same time, ecohydrological models are expanding our ability to integrate these observations and assess fluxes in the soil-plant-atmosphere continuum. This session welcomes experimental and modeling contributions that apply isotope tracers to advance process-based understanding of water and nutrient fluxes across the subsurface, vegetation, and atmosphere, spanning scales from individual plants and forest stands to catchments. In our session, we aim to discuss i) innovative process-based interpretations of stable isotope data; ii) bridge ecophysiological and hydrological perspectives through field-based approaches; iii) development of novel modeling applications and frameworks or data analysis techniques; and iv) current methodological developments. We aim to foster interdisciplinary exchange among researchers investigating ecohydrological processes with natural tracers, spanning groundwater and vadose zone hydrology, plant physiology, and ecology. By linking subsurface hydrology with ecophysiological process studies, the session will showcase cutting-edge methodological advances and stimulate discussion to deepen our understanding of water and nutrient dynamics across the soil–plant–atmosphere continuum.
title: Stable isotopes to study water and nutrient dynamics in the soil-plant-atmosphere continuum

description: Peatland hydrology is a key control on peatland vegetation, carbon cycling and greenhouse gas exchange. Peatland hydrology can change substantially following drainage, restoration, permafrost thaw and other disturbances, as well as in response to changes in precipitation and evapotranspiration. These changes affect not only water-table depth but also peat hydraulic properties, groundwater and surface-water exchange, runoff and hydrological connectivity. This session brings together studies of hydrological processes in peatlands across tropical, temperate, boreal and subarctic regions. Studies from tropical, permafrost and other regions where peatland hydrology remains poorly observed are particularly encouraged, as are studies evaluating hydrological responses to disturbance, climate change and restoration. We welcome contributions from pristine, drained, degraded, managed and restored peatlands. Topics may include: - water-table dynamics, - peat hydraulic properties, - groundwater–surface water interactions, - aquifer–peatland connectivity, - evapotranspiration, - runoff and streamflow, - as well as interactions between hydrology, vegetation, biogeochemistry and greenhouse gas exchange. We particularly welcome studies that consider hydrological processes below the near-surface peat layer and interactions between peatlands and the surrounding groundwater and surface-water systems. We invite field and laboratory studies, long-term observations, remote sensing, geophysical methods and modelling approaches across scales from pore and individual peat profiles to catchments and continental regions.
title: Peatland hydrology: Groundwater and surface water from tropical to subarctic latitudes

description: Held regularly since 2005, the session has established itself at the EGU as the primary platform for advancing limnology within the geophysical community. As confined water bodies, lakes and inland seas are particularly vulnerable to climatic and human impacts accumulated over broad catchment areas. Hence, they mirror both the global change effects and anthropogenic pressures stronger than any other aquatic objects. Research of lakes and inland seas admits many common approaches and techniques. Oceanographic methodology and instrumentation are often applicable to limnological studies. Reciprocally, insights obtained from lakes can also be instructive with respect to marine systems. Lakes and inland seas also play an important role in ecosystem services such as fisheries, aquaculture, tourism. These multifunctional roles require careful governance measures to avoid hydrological and environmental deterioration. The session brings together specialists in limnology, hydrology, boundary-layer meteorology, and oceanography of inland seas to discuss the role of lakes in the land-atmosphere interaction, the response of lakes and inland seas to global change, the physical and biogeochemical interactions within the enclosed aquatic systems. The session offers an interdisciplinary forum for discussing novel advances in observational, modeling and remote sensing studies on lakes.
title: Lakes and Inland Seas under Global Change

description: This session invites contributions that advance the observation, understanding, and modelling of ecohydrological processes across spatial and temporal scales. We particularly welcome studies of vegetation–water interactions, including root water uptake, evaporation and transpiration, canopy interception, soil moisture–plant feedbacks, and ecosystem responses to climatic and environmental changes. Contributions combining experiments, in-situ observations, remote sensing, data-driven approaches, and process-based modelling are encouraged, with particular emphasis on identifying mechanisms, understanding their variability across scales, and improving the representation and prediction of ecohydrological processes. A particular focus is placed on scaling, data-model integration, and transferability: how can observations and process understanding obtained at fine spatial and temporal scales be translated into reliable predictions across heterogeneous landscapes and under climatic, ecological, and land-use change? Contributions addressing model evaluation, uncertainty, parameterization, scaling, and transferability across contrasting environments are especially encouraged. We also welcome work that connects improved predictive capability to challenges in ecosystem, water resources, and land management.
