Topics of interest include, but are not limited to: (1) ecohydrological mechanisms and feedbacks among hydrological, ecological, and biogeochemical processes; (2) multi-scale observation and modelling of ecohydrological processes; and (3) scaling, model evaluation, uncertainty, and transferability across heterogeneous landscapes and changing climatic, ecological, and land-use conditions. The session aims to bring together approaches that advance fundamental process understanding and the predictive capability of ecohydrological models, fostering new perspectives on how ecohydrological knowledge can be translated across scales and environmental conditions.
title: Advancing Ecohydrological Process Understanding and Modelling Across Scales: From Mechanistic Insights to Actionable Predictions

description: Dynamic bidirectional exchanges between groundwater and surface water systems give rise to critical transition zones - including the hyporheic zone, the benthic layer, riparian corridors, wetlands, and lake sediments - where unique hydrological, biogeochemical, and ecological processes converge. These transition zones regulate the transport and transformation of nutrients, microplastics, and pollutants across hydrological copartments and associated aquatic ecosystems. They also control the availability of heat, oxygen, and organic matter within sediments, shaping habitat conditions for microorganisms and macroinvertebrates. Despite intese research, further investigation is needed to establish a comprehensive understanding of the physical, biogeochemical, and ecological processes occurring at groundwater-surface water interfaces, and their implications for fluvial ecology and limnology. Furthermore, it is essential to consider how exchange fluxes respond to environmental and climate factors associated with different spatial and temporal scales, spanning the sediment layer, river channel, alluvial aquifer, and regional groundwater scales. Upscaling and downscaling of a general conceptual framework, as well as enhancing process comprehension, are identified as the most significant challenges in this field of research. We invite contributions that focus on the development and application of novel experimental methods for studying physical, biogeochemical, and ecological conditions at the groundwater-surface water interfaces in rivers, lakes, riparian zones, and wetlands. One of our main interests lies in investigating the role of hyporheic processes in the retention and natural attenuation of nutrients and pollutants, and their influence on surface and groundwater quality. Additionally, we encourage research involving hydrological, biogeochemical, and ecological modeling approaches (e.g. transient storage models, coupled groundwater-surface water models, etc.). Finally, we welcome presentations that investigate the impact of groundwater-surface water interactions on management and risk assessment in view of the European Water Framework Directive.
title: Groundwater-surface water interactions: physical, biogeochemical and ecological processes

description: Forest hydrological processes have been extensively studied in temperate, tropical, and semi-arid ecosystems, yet remain understudied in snow-dominated forests. In high-latitude boreal forests and high-altitude Alpine forests, snow interception, snowmelt dynamics, frozen and cold soils, xylem freeze-thaw, and short growing seasons create fundamentally different and complex hydrological conditions. These regions are experiencing amplified warming, with rapid shifts in precipitation seasonality (snow-rain), snow cover, growing season length, and drought frequency, making it urgent to understand the forest hydrological processes in these regions and their responses to climate change. A persistent challenge in forest hydrology is connecting processes at different spatial scales. Tree-level observations of water use and transport, ecosystem-level measurements of evapotranspiration and other water fluxes, and catchment-level analyses of streamflow and water yield are typically conducted independently, while processes at one scale often depend on those at another. This challenge is compounded in snow-dominated cold environments, where snow tightly couples processes across scales. This session brings together researchers working at and/or across spatial scales in snow-dominated forests. We welcome contributions on forest-water interactions in snow-dominated cold environments, including: - Tree level: root water uptake, sap flow dynamics, transpiration regulation, xylem transport and freeze-thaw responses, and stem water storage - Stand and ecosystem level: evapotranspiration partitioning, canopy interception of snow and rain, forest water balance, and the role of forest structure in snow accumulation and melt - Catchment level: effects of forest cover and disturbance on streamflow, snowmelt-driven runoff generation, and forest management impacts on water yield - We particularly encourage studies that bridge two or more scales, e.g., linking tree-level observations to stand or catchment predictions, or using catchment-scale patterns to inform tree-level process understanding. Contributions based on field observations, experiments, remote sensing, and modelling in boreal or high-mountain forests are welcome. We aim to foster dialogue between field-based researchers and modellers, and between researchers working at different scales, to advance integrated understanding of forest-water interactions in snow-dominated environments under climate change.
title: Forest-water interactions in snow environments at different scales: from trees to catchments

description: X-ray and neutron imaging are transforming experimental geosciences by allowing processes occurring inside opaque Earth materials to be directly observed in three dimensions and through time. Beyond increasingly detailed 3D characterization, advances in synchrotron and neutron imaging now make it possible to follow dynamic geological processes in situ, under controlled and increasingly realistic thermo-hydro-chemo-mechanical conditions. This transition to 4D observation has opened a fundamentally different window on experiments. Many processes that are difficult or impossible to infer from conventional bulk measurements or before-and-after observations can now be observed as they occur: where deformation first localizes, how fractures nucleate and propagate, how fluids invade and redistribute through pore networks, and how dissolution, precipitation or phase transformations interact with transport and mechanics. X-rays and neutrons offer particularly complementary information. Their different interaction mechanisms provide sensitivity to different phases and elements, opening opportunities for correlative, multimodal and increasingly simultaneous observations of complex geological systems. This session aims to bring together the growing X-ray and neutron imaging communities in geosciences, from instrumentation and methodological developments to fundamental and applied discoveries. We welcome contributions on deformation and fracture, fluid flow and multiphase processes, reactive transport, mineral reactions, CO₂ storage and mineralisation, geothermal systems, volcanology, soils, ice and planetary materials, as well as new experimental, analytical and multimodal approaches. By bringing together users of synchrotron and neutron facilities, Large-scale infrastructures or university benched scanners, we hope to encourage exchanges across techniques and applications and discuss the next generation of 4D experiments in geosciences.
title: X-ray and neutron imaging in geosciences: unveiling processes in 4D

description: Composite indicators for vulnerability and resilience — SoVI, ND-GAIN, INFORM, national climate risk indices — have proliferated across research and policy communities over the past decade. Yet the pathway from indicator to institutional action remains under-theorised. Which indicators actually enter governance processes? At which scales are they legible? Where do they reshape decisions, and where do they merely accompany them? This session invites contributions that trace this pathway across scales, from household and neighbourhood measurement to municipal, regional, and national adaptation planning. We are particularly interested in ageing societies, where compound climate–demographic pressures — heat exposure, social isolation, care-system strain, mobility loss — expose the limits of conventional indicator frameworks and demand new integrations across environmental, health, and social data. Contributions are welcome on: • Methodological advances in composite vulnerability and resilience measurement, including uncertainty quantification, sensitivity analysis, and integration of qualitative evidence • Governance case studies where indicators demonstrably shaped adaptation policy, risk allocation, or resource distribution — and where they did not • Cross-national comparisons of indicator uptake across governance systems (EU, East and Southeast Asia, Global South) • Participatory and community-based measurement approaches that bridge technical and lived-experience knowledge • Applications focused on ageing populations, long-term care systems, and intergenerational climate risk • Institutional and knowledge-brokering mechanisms that translate indicators into decisions The session welcomes both quantitative and qualitative work, single-country deep dives and comparative studies. By bringing measurement scientists, governance scholars, and practitioners together within GS, we aim to build a shared vocabulary for the indicator–institution link and to support the emerging Climate Resilience and Sustainability subdivision as a durable interdisciplinary platform.
title: From indicator to institution: climate resilience governance in ageing societies across scales

description: Rapid urbanization, land-use change, environmental degradation and socioeconomic vulnerability are increasingly interacting with hydroclimatic hazards, resulting in complex risks that cannot be solved with conventional hazard mapping or gray infrastructure alone. Nature-Based Solutions (NbS), ecosystem restoration and integrated risk management are powerful means to reduce hazards and build socioeconomic resilience. Advances in GIS, Earth Observation, hydrological modeling, machine learning and GeoAI enable the accurate identification of risks, mapping of vulnerabilities and spatial targeting of adaptation interventions. This session convenes interdisciplinary researchers working across hydroclimatic hazards, geospatial science, GeoAI, NbS and community resilience. Key scientific themes include: 1. Hydroclimatic variability and hazard dynamics (extreme rainfall, flood generation, catchment processes) 2. GIS, Earth Observation, GeoAI, and spatial modeling (machine learning, decision-support tools) 3. Nature-Based Solutions (NbS) and ecosystem-based adaptation (wetlands, green infrastructure, spatial prioritization) 4. Socioeconomic vulnerability and community resilience (adaptive capacity, local coping mechanisms, governance) 5. Integrated climate resilience and sustainable development (risk-informed planning, science-policy links) Existing studies typically address hydrological modeling, NbS, vulnerability and community resilience separately. This session builds on discussions of how to embed these dimensions within coherent and actionable climate resilience frameworks. We are seeking global case studies from cities, river basins, wetlands and rural landscapes to link technology innovation with ecosystem-based adaptation and evidence-based decision making.
title: GeoAI and Nature-Based Solutions for Hydroclimatic Risk and Socioeconomic Resilience

description: Across Europe, a wide range of geoscience-relevant legislation is currently moving through the policy pipeline — from critical raw materials and deforestation regulation, to the Climate Resilience Framework, the Soil Monitoring Law, and the Nature Restoration Law. For many researchers, these processes and how to engage with them remain opaque. This session explores how geoscience can inform policy, regulation and decision-making, and how researchers and other stakeholders in science can engage effectively with policy processes to deliver societal benefits beyond academia. We welcome contributions from researchers, policymakers, practitioners, industry and NGO representatives, and others working at the science–policy–society interface. We particularly encourage presentations that share concrete examples of how engagement happened in practice: what pathways were used, what worked, what did not, and what can be learnt from these experiences. This may include engagement at different stages of the policy-decision cycle, such as responding to public consultations, contributing to advisory groups, participating in national delegations, providing formal or informal science advice to decision-makers, or contributing to the design and implementation of legislation, directives, strategies and regulations. We also welcome highlights of current and recent policy developments relevant to the geosciences where the research community can engage. By bringing together perspectives from both science and policy, the session aims to foster an open exchange on how science–policy engagement works in practice, where it falls short, and how it can be improved. We seek to create a space where researchers and policymakers can share experiences, ask questions and learn from one another, including through the proposed associated Splinter Meeting during the EGU 2027 week.
title: Strengthening Policy Through Science: Insights from the Interface

description: Agriculture is the largest consumer of water worldwide and at the same time irrigation is a sector where huge differences between modern technology and traditional practices do exist. Furthermore, reliable and organized data about water withdrawals for agricultural purposes are generally lacking worldwide, thus making irrigation the missing variable to close the water budget over anthropized basins. As a result, building systems for improving water use efficiency in agriculture is not an easy task, even though it is an immediate requirement of human society for sustaining the global food security, rationally managing the resource and reducing causes of poverties, migrations and conflicts among states, which depend on trans-boundary river basins. Climate changes and increasing human pressure together with traditional wasteful irrigation practices are enhancing the conflictual problems in water use also in countries traditionally rich in water. Hence, saving irrigation water improving irrigation efficiency on large areas with modern techniques is an urgent action to do. In fact, it is well known that agriculture uses large volumes of water with low irrigation efficiency, accounting in Europe for around 24% of the total water use, with peak of 80% in the Southern Mediterranean part and may reach the same percentage in Mediterranean non-EU countries. North Africa region has the lowest per-capita freshwater resource availability among all Regions of the world. Several studies have recently explored the possibility of monitoring irrigation dynamics and by optimizing irrigation water management to achieve precision farming exploiting remote sensing information combined with ground data and/or water balance modelling. In this session, we will focus on: the use of remote sensing data to estimate irrigation volumes and timing; management of irrigation using hydrological modeling combined with satellite data; improving irrigation water use efficiency based on remote sensing vegetation indices, hydrological modeling, satellite soil moisture or land surface temperature data; precision farming with high resolution satellite data or drones; farm and irrigation district irrigation management; improving the performance of irrigation schemes; estimates of irrigation water requirements from ground and satellite data; ICT tools for real-time irrigation management with remote sensing and ground data coupled with hydrological modelling.
title: Irrigation estimate and management from remote sensing and agro-hydrological modelling

description: Remote sensing products have great potential to support the monitoring and modelling of water resources. Nevertheless, their uptake by water managers remains limited because of concerns related to data quality, spatial and temporal resolution, trust, accessibility, and technical expertise. In this session, we look for contributions on new developments that support the use of remote sensing data for water-management applications, from local to global scales. We welcome research aimed at improving the quality and usability of remote sensing products, such as higher spatial and/or temporal resolution mapping of land use and agricultural practices; improved assessments of river discharge, lake and reservoir volumes, and groundwater resources; drought monitoring and modelling and its impacts on water-stressed vegetation; and the monitoring and modelling of irrigation volumes. We are also interested in studies assessing the quality of remote sensing products through uncertainty analysis or validation against independent data sources. Contributions that combine different techniques —such as physically based models and artificial intelligence—or integrate multiple data sources from different sensors, including remote sensing and in situ observations, are particularly welcome. Studies using different types of imagery, including satellite, airborne, and drone data, are also encouraged. Finally, we invite presentations on the development of user-friendly platforms that follow the FAIR principles and provide smooth access to remote sensing data for water-management applications. We are particularly interested in applications of remote sensing to characterise human–water interactions and assess the impacts of climate change across the entire water cycle, including the connections between inland and sea (coastal) systems.
title: Innovative technologies using remote sensing data for water management applications

description: The water cycle or hydrological cycle involves the continuous movement of water on, above, and below the surface of the Earth. In general, hydrological cycle components (e.g., precipitation, evaporation, water storage, and runoff) are characterized by large temporal and spatial variability. Accurate monitoring of various hydrological cycle components and developing hydrological models are important for improving our understanding of hydrological processes. With significant development of sensor technology and sharply growing platforms in past decades, remote sensing offers enhanced capability to monitor various hydrological cycle components at different temporal and spatial scales to complement conventional in situ measurements. Considerable efforts have been made to explore the potentials of remotely sensed data from a vast range of different platforms (e.g., satellite, airborne, drone, ground-based radar) and sensors (e.g., optical, infrared, microwave) in advancing hydrology research, particularly in poorly gauged and ungauged regions. The application of remote sensing in hydrology is expected to increase with enhanced recognition of its potentials and continuous development of advanced sensors (e.g., new satellite missions) and retrieval methods (e.g., innovative machine learning and data assimilation techniques). The session aims to present and discuss recent advances in the remote sensing of hydrological cycle components as well as the application of remote sensing in hydrological modeling. We encourage studies to investigate the performance of remotely sensed data in multi-variable calibration and spatial evaluation of hydrological models. The added-value of spatially downscaling remotely sensed data in improving hydrological modelling is also particularly welcome.
title: Application of remotely sensed water cycle components in hydrological modelling

description: This session concentrates on extreme rainfall events, surface water dynamics, and flood events, exploring innovative remote sensing, AI, and digital twin technologies for real-time monitoring, risk assessment, and mitigation. It invites submissions on advanced data integration, modeling approaches, early warning systems, and decision-support tools to improve understanding, forecasting, and management of flooding and related surface water hazards. The integration of AI with digital twin improves the analytical and operational capabilities of geospatial systems, which through the analysis of historical data and the integration of real-time information (IoT) are able to highlight even “hidden patterns” in the data, identifying new models capable of improving forecasts with greater control over the quantification of uncertainty and the variability of the phenomenon analysed. This session aims to focus on flood hazard and risk assessment, monitoring, and management. This Topic invites the submission of articles focused on, but not limited to, the following areas: • Monitoring of extreme rainfall events and flood hazards for risk assessment and communication. • Digital twins (DTs)/prototypes of DTs in flood hazard forecasting, early warning, monitoring, and supporting tools for urban governance. • DSSs to extract meaningful information in the artificial intelligence era, eventually serving to reduce risk and provide support tools to mitigate flood hazards. • The role of AI and digital twins to assess the economic impacts of flood hazards and the cost-effectiveness of various mitigation strategies. • Novel techniques to analyse big data coming from Earth observation platforms, drones, and other geospatial data in order to provide timely information related to the extend, exposure, and impacts of flood hazards.
title: UAV, Remote Sensing, AI, and Digital Twin Technologies for Next-Generation Flood Risk Monitoring, Modelling and Management

description: Climate warming poses a significant risk to seasonal snow water storage, which impacts over a billion people worldwide. Snowpack shrinkage results in a drastic reduction in meltwater supply, a temporal shift in runoff, and a decrease in its seasonal predictability. Therefore, understanding seasonal snow dynamics, the potential changes, and their implications is crucial for effective water resource management. Remote sensing of seasonal snow is a key tool in this regard, as it provides a wide range of techniques and data across various spatial and temporal scales. This session focuses on studies linking remote sensing of seasonal snow to hydrological applications. The works presented will aim to (i) monitor, model and understand snow-related processes and dynamics (snowfall, melting, evaporation, wind redistribution and sublimation), (ii) quantify the snowpack characteristics (e.g., snow water equivalent, snow grain size, albedo, light-absorbing particles, snow cover area, snow depth and snow density), (iii) assess hydrological impacts of the snowpack dynamics. We welcome contributions that integrate methods and data from traditional or from emerging technologies, including time-lapse imagery, laser scanning, radar, passive microwave, optical photography, photogrammetry, thermal and hyperspectral sensing. All types of platform and all spatial and temporal scales of studies are welcome, from UAV plot-level studies to global multi-year time series of satellite observations.
title: Remote sensing of seasonal snow

description: We invite presentations concerning the past, present and future of soil moisture estimation, including remote sensing, multi-sensor data fusion, field experiments, land surface modelling and data assimilation, machine learning, and Cal/Val activities, in particular concerning the establishment and use of Fiducial Reference Measurements (FRMs). Microwave remote sensing has made tremendous progress to provide robust estimates of surface and subsurface soil moisture at different scales. From local to landscape scales, several field or aircraft experiments have been organized to improve our understanding of active and passive microwave soil moisture sensing, including the effects of soil roughness, vegetation, spatial heterogeneities, and topography. At continental scales, a series of passive and active microwave space sensors, such as SMMR (1978-1987), AMSR (2002-), and ERS/SCAT (1992-2000) provided information on surface soil moisture. Current investigations of L-band passive observations with SMOS (2009-) and SMAP (2015-), active C-band observations with the Metop/ASCAT series (2006-) and Sentinel-1 (2014-), L- and S-band observations from the NISAR mission (2025-), and bistatic L-band radar observations from GNSS-R missions such as HydroGNSS (2025-) enable an accurate quantification of the soil moisture at regional and global scales at ever higher spatial resolution. Operational programmes like Copernicus but also novel developments, such as the upcoming CIMR and ROSE-L, will further enhance our capabilities to monitor soil moisture, and they will ensure continuity of multi-scale soil moisture measurements from agricultural to climate scales. At the same time, research has put a new focus on establishing rigorous guidelines for the installation, calibration, and operation of in situ soil moisture measurements that are informed by metrological practices, as well as on the development of advanced quality control procedures for an ever growing suit of global in situ soil moisture measurement networks to obtain so-called Fiducial Reference Measurements (FRMs) for soil moisture. Lastly, machine learning has opened up new opportunities for soil moisture retrieval, downscaling, data fusion, gap filling and data assimilation. For example, data assimilation systems have been complemented with machine learning-based observation operators to assimilate remotely sensed soil moisture using techniques such as neural networks and gradient boosting trees.
title: Remote Sensing of Soil Moisture

description: Remote sensing is a critical tool for data collection and observation of floods and surface water dynamics, especially in regions where field surveys and gauging stations are limited, such as remote or conflict ridden areas and data-poor developing nations. The integration of dynamic variables derived from remote sensing (e.g. water extent, depth and width, river slope and cross sections, flow velocities, land cover and land use) into hydraulic models offers the potential to significantly enhance our understanding of hydrological processes and improve predictive capabilities. Case studies from the Global South are strongly encouraged, as are contributions from ungauged and transboundary basins where satellite observations are the primary record. This session invites cutting-edge presentations on advancing surface water and flood monitoring and mapping through remotely-sensed data, focusing on: -Flood and surface water mapping from satellite and airborne sensors, including commercial constellations and emerging observation concepts -Machine learning, deep learning and foundation models for water body detection and flood segmentation -Flood mapping in challenging environments such as urban, vegetated, arid, and cloud-persistent regions -Multi-sensor and multi-frequency fusion for consistent flood extent retrieval -Flood hazard, risk and impact mapping from Earth observation -Assimilation of satellite-derived flood extent and inundation maps into hydrological and hydraulic models -Calibration and validation of hydrological and hydraulic models using remotely sensed observations and field measurements, as well as the creation and use of benchmarks, uncertainty quantification methods, and standards for this purpose -Monitoring surface water dynamics and change such as seasonal water body variation, wetland extent, river planform -Operational rapid mapping and emergency response, and the path from research product to sustained service or tool -Multi-satellite data products and services for improved monitoring of surface water dynamics including floods Early career and underrepresented scientists are particularly encouraged to participate.
title: Remote Sensing for Surface Water and Flood Dynamics Mapping and Modelling

description: Water is our planet’s most vital resource, and the primary agent in some of the biggest hazards facing society and nature. Recent extreme heat and flood events underline the significance of water both as a threat and as an increasingly volatile resource. The accurate and timely measurement of streamflow is therefore more critical than ever to enable the management of water for ecology, for people and industry, for flood risk management and for understanding changes to the hydrological regime. Despite this, effective monitoring networks remain scarce, under-resourced, and often under threat on a global scale. Even where they exist, in-situ observational networks are increasingly inadequate when faced with extreme conditions, and lack the precision and spatial coverage to fully represent crucial aspects of the hydrological cycle. This session aims to tackle this problem by inviting presentations that demonstrate new and improved methods and approaches to streamflow monitoring, including: 1) Innovative methodologies for measuring/modelling/estimating river stream flows; 2) Real-time acquisition of hydrological variables; 3) UAS and satellite remote sensing techniques for hydrological & morphological monitoring; 4) Measurement in extreme conditions associated with the changing climate; 5) Measurement of sudden-onset extreme flows associated with catastrophic events; 6) Strategies to quantify and describe hydro-morphological evolution of rivers; 7) New methods to cope with data-scarce environments; 8) Inter-comparison of innovative & classical models and approaches; 9) Evolution and refinement of existing methods; 10) Guidelines and standards for hydro-morphological streamflow monitoring; 11) Quantification of uncertainties; 12) Development of expert networks to advance methods. Contributions are welcome with an emphasis on innovation, efficiency, operator safety, and meeting the growing challenges associated with the changing climate, and with natural and anthropogenically driven disasters such as dam failures and flash floods. Additionally, presentations will be welcomed which explore options for greater collaboration in advancing riverflow methods and which link innovative research to operational monitoring.
title: Advances in river monitoring and modelling, including UAS and satellite based methods

description: The Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) satellite mission, launched in December 2022, has marked a significant advancement in hydrological sciences. SWOT uses novel Ka-band radar interferometry to deliver, for the first time, simultaneous, high-resolution measurements of water surface elevation and inundation extent in rivers, lakes, reservoirs, and wetlands globally. SWOT is fundamentally transforming our ability to understand the movement of water across landscapes globally. The hydrology and remote sensing science communities have worked for over a decade to develop new methods and scientific understanding that will allow SWOT data to advance global hydrology. For this session, we solicit abstracts presenting recent advances using data from SWOT to unlock new frontiers in hydrology, inland cryosphere, and estuaries. We also welcome presentations of improved algorithms for extracting hydrologically relevant information from SWOT data, as well as new modeling and data science techniques leveraging data from SWOT combined with other satellite data.
title: The Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) Mission: New Frontiers in Hydrology

description: Surface water bodies are critical resources, yet face pressure from environmental changes across scales, ranging from widespread pollution and overexploitation to climate change and land use shifts such as urbanisation. They are further impacted by historical legacies often associated with local human activities (e.g. flood control measures, land cover changes driven by human needs, local pollution). These dynamics operate and interact at different spatio-temporal scales, from local (water quality, flood management, etc.) to global (biogeochemical cycles, etc.). Remote sensing, especially in combination with in-situ data and modelling approaches, is a powerful tool to analyse this complexity, but its integration with governance or policy strategies remains poorly understood and implemented. This session invites submissions that highlight the potential of approaches combining remote sensing with in-situ data and/or modelling approaches to detecting, assessing, and tracking human impacts within and across watersheds. Submissions highlighting the value of remote sensing for water management and governance at multiple scales are particularly welcome. This can, for example, include studies on: - Data, methods, and tools for multi-scale analyses of watersheds (combining field data and remote sensing; data or sensor fusion; time series; visualisation approaches) - Critical appraisals of remote sensing approaches in river science and management (e.g. evaluation of global data products for their suitability for supporting decision making) - Past, present and future human pressures and their impacts on floodplains and alluvial corridors, notably addressed at large or multiple spatial scales - Governance, political strategies and regulatory frameworks interacting with remotely sensed data or derived products, which address or facilitate solutions for watershed management and resilience.
title: From pixels to policies: bridging the gap between remote sensing and governance strategies to foster surface water bodies resilience under global environmental changes

description: With the proliferation and wide accessibility of remotely sensed information, data from remotely piloted aircraft (RPA), piloted airplanes, and satellite missions such as Landsat, Sentinel, NISAR and VIIRS are being increasingly used to better our understanding of hydrological processes on the earth’s surface. This understanding is a crucial prerequisite to ameliorate resource management, optimise the development of infrastructure, and adjust land use practices to changing climate conditions and hazards such as floods and droughts. However, many analyses incorporate remote sensing data by default without a thorough critical examination of their applicability and limitations. In-situ data, though expensive to collect and therefore often less readily available, provide a valuable layer of information and a benchmark for methods relying on remotely sensed data. This session invites contributions that highlight innovative approaches to synthesizing remotely sensed and in-situ data at local-to-regional scales. We welcome contributions that focus on combining multi-scale remote sensing and/or remote sensing with in-situ information and that critically engage this intersection to better understand: * Processes such as evapotranspiration, infiltration, (Monsoon) inundations, water abstraction for agricultural use * Hydrological extremes such as floods and droughts * Improve monitoring and science in poorly gauged and ungauged basins * Developing novel methods of gathering in-situ benchmark data to combine with remotely sensed approaches
title: Synthesising Multi-platform Remotely Sensed and In-Situ Data to Understand Hydrological Processes at Local-to-Regional Scales

description: The Tibetan Plateau and surrounding mountain regions, known as the Third Pole, cover an area of > 5 million km2 and are considered to be the water tower of Asia. The Pan Third Pole expands on both the north-south and the east-west directions, going across the Tibetan Plateau, Pamir, Hindu Kush, Iran Plateau, Caucasian and Carpathian, and covering an area of about 20 million km2. Like the Arctic and Antarctica, the Pan Third Pole’s environment is extremely sensitive to global climate change. In recent years, scientists from around the globe have increased observational, remote sensing and numerical modeling research related to the Pan Third Pole in an effort to quantify and predict past, current and future scenarios. Co-sponsored by TPE (www.tpe.ac.cn), this session is dedicated to studies of Pan Third Pole atmosphere, cryosphere, hydrosphere, and biosphere and their interactions with global change. Related contributions are welcomed.
title: The Third Pole Environment (TPE) under Global Changes

description: The RS-ET community continues to advance the monitoring and understanding of water use and availability across diverse landscapes. These developments increasingly support operational applications in agriculture, water management, climate adaptation, ecosystem monitoring and environmental services. This session provides a forum to share advances, address challenges and explore future directions in remote sensing of ET. This session focuses on methodological advancements in the use of remote sensing (RS) to improve the quantification of ET across a range of climates and environments. We invite contributions that demonstrate how RS techniques can enhance ET assessment, validation, uncertainty quantification, and prediction in diverse settings including agricultural landscapes, riparian zones, urban areas and forest ecosystems. The session aims to provide an overview of recent developments in RS-based ET estimation from regional to global scales. By applying innovative approaches, we seek to address the challenges of ET quantification and deepen our understanding of water and vegetation dynamics across different landscapes. With growing societal attention to climate change, drought and flood early warning systems, ecosystem monitoring, biodiversity conservation, and the pursuit of a sustainable future, the demand for accurate estimation, modelling, mapping and forecasting of ET has expanded. We welcome contributions that leverage physically-based and hybrid models, data assimilation and fusion, sharpening algorithms, empirical and statistical methods, as well as artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML). New spaceborne and airborne sensors are creating opportunities to quantify ET across scales and ecosystems. Cloud computing platforms enable scalable, reproducible analysis through access to large datasets and computational resources. By combining advances in observations, modelling, algorithms and computing, this session aims to advance next-generation ET products and applications for sustainable water management and understanding of the terrestrial water cycle. We welcome research, commentary and debates on: • recent developments in RS-based ET estimation • application of AI, cloud computing and other technological advancements • Integration of RS, modelling, data assimilation and ground measurements • validation, calibration, uncertainty quantification and upscaling - challenges & solutions • future directions in RS of ET.
title: Remote Sensing of Evapotranspiration

description: Increasing climate variability and water scarcity are placing unprecedented pressure on agricultural systems worldwide. To address these challenges, the agricultural sector is rapidly adopting precision technologies that combine remote sensing capabilities with artificial intelligence to optimize crop water management. This session focuses on cutting-edge applications of remote sensing technologies and AI-driven analytics in transforming agricultural water management practices. We welcome research that demonstrates innovative approaches to monitoring, predicting, and managing agricultural water resources by integrating datasets from Earth observation satellites, unmanned aerial systems, Internet of Things (IoT) sensors and using advanced computational methods. Key topics include: Multi-platform remote sensing applications (satellite, UAV, hyperspectral, SAR, thermal infrared) for estimation of soil moisture and crop water requirement. Deep learning and AI-driven detection of crop water stress and yield prediction. Precision irrigation systems and automated water management technologies. Multi-sensor data fusion combining space-based, airborne, and ground observations. Real-time monitoring systems and subseasonal-to-seasonal water demand forecasting models. Digital agriculture platforms and decision support tools for sustainable water management. LLM-augmented modeling and digital twin of the agri-climatic or agri-weather landscape. This session aims to showcase practical solutions that bridge the gap between technological innovation and real-world agricultural applications, emphasizing scalable approaches that support both productivity and environmental sustainability.
title: Toward Climate-Resilient Agriculture: Integrating Remote Sensing and Artificial Intelligence for Precision Water Management

description: Accurately capturing the glacial surface mass balance (SMB) and surface energy budget (SEB) is essential to reconstruct the past and reliably project the future mass change of glaciers, ice sheets and ice shelves, and their contribution to global sea level and freshwater supply. Changes in accumulation and surface melt affect glacier mass balance through fluctuations in equilibrium line altitude, snow/ice albedo and extent, surface elevation, rain and meltwater retention in firn. However, adequately accounting for all glacial surface processes and for their associated feedbacks over various spatiotemporal scales remains challenging. Combining observations and simulations across scales is thus crucial to better understand the SMB of glaciers, ice sheets and ice shelves. We invite observational and model-based presentations on past reconstructions and future projections of the SMB and SEB over glaciers, ice sheets and ice shelves. We promote research that identifies drivers and further explores changes in rain/snow accumulation and redistribution, meltwater production, retention and refreezing in firn, and subsequent surface runoff, sublimation and blowing snow erosion. We welcome studies using global/regional climate models, SMB-SEB and positive degree day (PDD) models, or machine learning techniques that enhance our understanding of glacial surface processes from local to regional scales. Works combining SMB models with in-situ or remote sensing observations to quantify glacial mass change are also encouraged.
title: Surface mass balance of glaciers, ice sheets and ice shelves

description: Ice sheets and the surrounding polar oceans and atmosphere form a tightly coupled system whose evolution is central to global sea level, ocean circulation, and the overall climate. This session focuses on the interactions of ice shelves and tidewater glaciers with the ocean, atmosphere, and sea ice on the continental shelves around Greenland, Antarctica, and the Arctic. We welcome contributions addressing any scale and aspect of this physical system or of any of its approximations, simplifications, or analogs. This session aims to bridge observational, laboratory, theoretical, modeling, and data-science perspectives to improve understanding of ice-ocean-atmosphere interactions and their relevance in the climate system. We welcome work from both polar regions or any other planets and across disciplines, including fluid and solid mechanics, glaciology, oceanography, or atmospheric and climate sciences. We propose an interactive PICO session format to encourage in-person dialog and random human interactions with the hope of fostering in-depth discussions and future scientific collaborations.
title: Ice shelves and tidewater glaciers - dynamics, interactions, processes, and climate implications

description: The increasing availability of in-situ and remote sensing observations provides new opportunities to constrain glacier and ice sheet models and improve the representation of model parameters and states. In this session, we aim to bring together researchers who develop observational products and those developing new approaches in calibration, inverse modelling and data assimilation to better inform models and uncertainties in the predictions. We invite studies developing direct and indirect observations, including, but not limited to, mass balance, surface elevation, ice thickness, velocity, glacier geometry, transient snowlines, albedo, snow cover, and firn properties. We also welcome contributions on model calibration, parameter estimation and inverse modelling, including optimisation, Bayesian methods, automatic differentiation and multi-objective approaches. Contributions on data assimilation and state estimation, including ensemble, particle-filter and variational methods as well as machine-learning-assisted approaches, are also encouraged. We also welcome studies addressing observational, parameter and model uncertainties and their propagation through calibration and data assimilation.
title: Observation-informed glacier and ice sheet modelling: calibration, data assimilation and inverse modelling

description: Dynamic subglacial, supraglacial and englacial water networks play a key role in the flow and stability of glaciers and ice sheets. The accumulation of meltwater on the surface of ice shelves has been hypothesized as a potential mechanism controlling ice-shelf stability, with ice-shelf collapse triggering substantial increases in discharge of grounded ice. Observations and modelling also suggest that complex hydrological networks occur at the base of glaciers and ice sheets and these systems play a prominent role in controlling the flow of grounded ice. This session tackles the urgent need to better understand the fundamental processes involved in glacial hydrology that need to be addressed in order to accurately predict future ice-sheet evolution and mass loss, and ultimately the contribution to sea-level rise. We seek contributions from both the observational and modelling communities relating to any area of ice-sheet, ice-shelf, or glacier hydrology. This includes but is not limited to: surface hydrology, melt lake and river formation; meltwater processes within the ice and firn; basal hydrology; subglacial lakes; impacts of meltwater on ice-sheet stability and flow; incorporation of any of these processes into large-scale climate and ice-sheet models.
title: Hydrology of ice sheets, ice shelves and glaciers

description: Ice rheology and basal sliding properties are among the primary modulators for glacier and ice sheet’s response to climate change -- yet they are also among the least-well constrained. This session invites lab, theory, field, and modelling studies that pertain directly to improving our understanding of ice rheology and basal sliding, alongside quantification of error terms inherent to their imperfect understanding. Examples of the type of work we look forward to platforming include laboratory, field, and computational studies regarding the following: ice rheology (constraints on Glen’s flow law parameters, damage, anisotropy, the influence of impurities and water content, and indeed alternative formulations for representing ice rheology), basal sliding over a diverse range of bed properties, snapshot/transient methods for deriving ice rheology and basal sliding relationships, and sensitivity/error quantification studies considering what happens when we turn these dials. Extensions to the influence of hydrology on basal sliding are explicitly welcome. We hope to use this session to promote conversations for practitioners within and between these two strands, to bridge the different communities working on those topics, and to foster the generation of ideas that advance progress to better quantify and reduce uncertainties.
title: Progress and uncertainties in ice rheology and basal sliding

description: The ice-ocean boundary is an important interface in global climate system, both due to the ocean’s ability to impact ice sheet mass balance and the cryosphere’s influence on global ocean circulation. Processes at the ice-ocean interface play a crucial role in the dynamics of tidewater glaciers and ice shelves, and associated fjord and cavity circulation. However, a complete understanding and accurate representation of these processes in models remains a major challenge and a source of uncertainty for projections of ice mass loss and sea-level rise. Recent work to understand ice-ocean interactions has led to significant progress in theory, idealised models, and coupled ice-ocean models. New observations of processes such as seawater intrusion at grounding lines and channelised ice-shelf melting can provide further insights into our understanding of this important climate interface. These continued efforts are essential for improving projections of future sea-level rise contributions and freshwater fluxes from the Earth’s cryosphere under climate change. In this session we aim to bring together the most up to date work on ice-ocean interactions across all latitudes, covering in-situ observations, remote-sensing, modelling and theory. We seek a bi-directional perspective, investigating both the impact of the ocean on the cryosphere and vice-versa, from small scale physical processes to global impacts. Topics for submission include but are not limited to: coupled ice-ocean models, ice shelf cavity and fjord circulation, ice mélange, subglacial meltwater plumes, basal and submarine melting and freshwater fluxes into the ocean. New observational datasets and methodologies are encouraged. We welcome and encourage submissions from groups who are underrepresented in the cryosphere community and will endeavour to provide reasonable adjustments to any presenter who requires them.
title: Advances at the Ice-Ocean Interface

description: Ice sheets play an active role in the climate system by amplifying, pacing, and potentially driving global climate change over a wide range of time scales. The impact of interactions between ice sheets and climate include changes in atmospheric and ocean temperatures and circulation, global biogeochemical cycles, the global hydrological cycle, vegetation, sea level, and land-surface albedo, which in turn cause additional feedbacks in the climate system. This session will present data and modelling results that examine ice sheet interactions with other components of the climate system over several time scales. Among other topics, issues to be addressed in this session include ice sheet-climate interactions from glacial-interglacial to millennial and centennial time scales, the role of ice sheets in Cenozoic global cooling and the mid-Pleistocene transition, reconstructions of past ice sheets and sea level, the current and future evolution of the ice sheets, and the role of ice sheets in abrupt climate change.
title: Ice sheet - climate interactions

description: The Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets are the primary sources of uncertainty in sea-level projections through 2100 and beyond. This session focuses on recent progress in ice-sheet modelling and its implications for sea-level rise across timescales – from paleo-climates to future projections. We invite contributions linked to international coordinated ice-sheet modelling efforts, such as the Ice Sheet Model Intercomparison Project for CMIP7 (ISMIP7), the Tipping Points Modelling Intercomparison Project (TIPMIP), the Paleo Ice Sheet Modelling Intercomparison Project (PaleoISMIP), and other model intercomparison projects. Together, these initiatives aim to advance our understanding of ice-sheet trajectories across timescales by projecting the ice-sheet contributions to sea level over the coming decades and centuries, systematically assessing the long-term ice-sheet stability and tipping risks, and investigating the ice-sheet response to past, warmer than pre-industrial climates. We welcome multi-model and single-model analyses of simulations following the coordinated protocols, as well as following other approaches. We particularly encourage submissions that explore and quantify uncertainties in the past and future ice-sheet evolution, including those arising from model physics, parameterizations, and climate forcing. Studies disentangling the role of initialization approaches, and the sensitivity of ice-sheet trajectories to initial conditions are highly welcome. We also seek contributions that examine coupled ice sheet-climate interactions, including feedback processes between the ice sheets, atmosphere, and ocean, and their impact on ice-sheet stability and sea-level rise. Through this session, we aim to foster collaboration and advance a more robust, community-based understanding of the past and future ice-sheet trajectories.
title: From past to future ice–sheet evolution: Sea-level projections and tipping dynamics

description: The Antarctic Ice Sheet is a critical component of the global climate system, and its margins are particularly vulnerable to atmospheric and oceanic forcing. The retreat and dynamic instability of these margins pose one of the largest uncertainties in future sea-level rise projections. Understanding the past and future evolution of the Antarctic Ice Sheet requires an approach that brings together direct observations, paleo-environmental reconstructions, and numerical modeling. This session invites contributions focusing on understanding the dynamics of Antarctic ice sheet margins through data and models across various timescales, from paleo and Holocene retreat to near- and long-term future projections. To bridge the gaps between empirical data and physical models, we strongly encourage (1) field studies incorporating different empirical datasets that help constrain numerical models, (2) modeling-based studies that help interpret observations and paleo reconstructions, and (3) combined studies involving data-model comparisons over different timescales. Topics of interest include processes driving grounding line migration across timescales; reconstructions of past ice margin retreat/advance from marine and terrestrial geological archives; observations or reconstructions of ice dynamics and mass balance changes; the identification of tipping points and conditions, and projections of future ice-sheet contributions to global sea-level rise. By bringing together observation and modeling, this session aims to foster cross-disciplinary discussions and improve our predictive capability regarding the fate of the Antarctic Ice Sheet.
title: Past and Future Evolution of Antarctic ice sheet margins

description: As glaciers retreat globally under climate warming, ice-marginal lakes are expanding rapidly in both number and area, and an increasing number of glaciers and ice sheet margins now terminate in freshwater. The presence of a lake alters glacier boundary conditions by enabling calving and subaqueous melt, which can destabilize glacier termini, modify ice motion, and decouple glacier retreat from direct climatic forcing. However, the physical processes governing lake-terminating systems and their representation in numerical models remain poorly constrained compared with marine-terminating systems. This session aims to advance our understanding of the interactions between glaciers and ice-marginal lakes across diverse spatial and temporal scales. We invite contributions addressing, but not limited to: (1) the dynamics of lake-terminating glaciers, including calving, frontal ablation, subaqueous melt, flotation, and terminus stability, (2) the dynamic response of glaciers to lake-level changes and drainage events, including the filling and draining of ice-marginal lakes and their effects on basal conditions, ice velocity, and terminus position, and (3) the transition from land- to lake-terminating conditions (or vice versa) and its effects on glacier dynamics. We invite contributions based on field observations, remote sensing, numerical modelling, laboratory experiments, and theoretical framework, covering mountain glaciers, ice caps, and ice sheet margins across all glaciated regions. Studies comparing lake-terminating and marine-terminating systems, and palaeo perspectives on ice-lake interaction are also encouraged.
title: Lake-terminating glaciers: processes, dynamics, and environmental drivers

description: This session welcomes a broad range of contributions on the modelling of glaciers and ice sheets, spanning methodological and applied studies, with an emphasis on their use in practice. We particularly encourage contributions on ice dynamics and higher-order mechanical models, data assimilation and inversion, uncertainty quantification, and the representation of coupled Earth-system processes within glacier and ice-sheet models. Contributions addressing key physical processes and parameterizations, including basal processes, grounding line and calving dynamics, ice-ocean interactions, and novel constitutive relationships, are especially welcome. We also encourage applications of machine learning, differentiable programming, surrogate modelling, and other data driven methods to glacier and ice-sheet modelling. Applications may address glaciers and ice sheets in both past and present climates, with specific interest in rapid ice dynamic change, ice streams and outlet glaciers, grounding line migration, glacier and ice sheet response to changing environmental forcing, and projections of future evolution and sea-level contribution. Model intercomparison, benchmarking, verification, and studies exploring model sensitivity and uncertainty are also strongly encouraged. The session aims to bring together researchers developing modelling approaches and those applying them to observations and societally relevant questions, fostering exchange between the modelling and observational communities.
title: Modelling ice sheets and glaciers

description: This session seeks advances in the mathematical and numerical foundations of physics-based models of glaciers and ice sheets. We welcome new numerical methods and discretization frameworks, as well as mathematical analysis of the underlying continuum equations, including results on well-posedness and solution behavior. Contributions on the analysis of numerical methods, including consistency, stability, convergence, accuracy, and robustness, are particularly encouraged. We welcome advances in solvers, computational libraries, and coupling techniques. Methodological advancements for the treatment of challenging components and boundaries, such as grounding lines, calving fronts, subglacial hydrology, and ice–ocean interactions, along with inverse problem methodology, are aligned with the session's scope. Theoretical and methodological developments in machine learning, including new architectures for glaciological applications, are also welcome, as are contributions that connect mathematical analysis to practical glacier and ice-sheet simulation.
title: Advances in numerical methods and mathematical theory for glacier and ice sheet models

description: The Critical Zone (CZ), encompassing the Earth's surface from the top of the vegetation canopy to the bottom of the circulating groundwater, is essential for sustaining life and maintaining environmental health. Understanding this region of complex intersections within the natural world, and between the environment and society, requires a collaborative, multidisciplinary approach that transcends disciplinary and national boundaries, bridging gaps between short-term and long-term environmental processes. This session will highlight CZ science, CZ methodologies, and the collaborative efforts of CZ research sites and networks from around the world. Topics of interest include, but are not limited to: Innovative techniques in CZ research and monitoring, such as integrated observation and modeling approaches or hybrid methods; Advances in understanding soils, hydrology, and biogeochemical cycling within the CZ; Intersections of society and the CZ; Policy or management implications of CZ research; Development of CZ science networks; And case studies of successful national and international CZ collaborations.
title: Critical Zone Science Around the World: Innovations, Insights, and Collaborative Efforts

description: Hydrological connectivity governs the transfer of water, sediment, solutes, and energy across forested catchments. It is strongly influenced not only by topography, vegetation cover, and climate, but also by managed infrastructure elements and proxies that create, enhance, or interrupt flow pathways. These include roads and skid trails, drainage ditches, culverts, embankments, drainage networks (including surface and subsurface systems like tile drains), reconnection measures, wetlands, beaver-related structures, and other land and water management interventions. This session focuses on how such elements modify surface and subsurface connectivity, runoff generation, infiltration, groundwater–surface water exchange, erosion, nutrient and sediment delivery, flood wave propagation, and drought buffering in forested catchments. We particularly welcome studies that quantify connectivity through field observations, remote sensing, LiDAR, GIS, indices, modelling, or proxy-based approaches, and that translate these insights into management, planning, or decision-support frameworks. We invite contributions across hillslope to catchment to regional scales, and across hydrology, geomorphology, ecohydrology, remote sensing, and landscape management. Of particular interest are studies that show how altering connectivity can reduce flood risk, enhance drought resilience, support sediment control, and improve catchment adaptation under climate extremes.
title: Water resilience in Forested Catchments. How managed landscape elements create, interrupt, or reroute hydrological connectivity

description: Cold cloud thinning covers proposed climate interventions that looks to seed ice clouds with efficient ice nucleating particles, so they trap less outgoing longwave radiation. With cirrus cloud thinning, seeding aims to shift ice formation away from homogenous to heterogenous freezing nucleation, producing fewer but larger ice crystals that fall out faster, giving thinner, shorter-lived clouds. More recently, mixed-phase cloud thinning has sought to target supercooled clouds over the polar oceans in the winter, where cloud glaciation could reduce longwave radiation from reaching the surface and so help slow sea ice loss. Model estimates of the resulting cooling varies from net negative to net positive when clouds are overseeded, and much of this spread comes from processes that are difficult to constrain, such as the competition between nucleation modes, pre-existing ice, small-scale updrafts, and gravity waves. This session focusses on work that helps improve our understanding of the ice cloud processes that decide whether cold cloud thinning could work, and what its side effects might be. We welcome laboratory studies of ice nucleation and possible seeding particles, field experiments including targeted glaciogenic seeding, in situ and satellite observations of cirrus and mixed-phase clouds (including early results from EarthCARE), and modelling from process- to global-scale climate models. Natural analogues are of interest, since mineral dust, volcanic eruptions and aviation all perturb ice clouds in ways that let us test seeding hypotheses in the atmosphere. Contributions on detectability, attribution, risks, and wider impacts are also welcome, and we encourage early career researchers to submit.
title: Cold cloud thinning: ice cloud microphysics, modification, and climate impacts

description: The accelerating growth of atmospheric CO2, CH4, and N2O poses major threats to the Earth system and climate, having moved the world closer to breaching international climate targets, such as the Paris Agreement and the Global Methane Pledge. In recent years, evidence is accumulating that warming is driving increased greenhouse gas emissions from natural systems. This emission-driven warming will likely continue and intensify due to climate feedback mechanisms. These biogeochemical feedbacks involve not only well-known processes in the atmosphere, ocean, and cryosphere, but also land-based systems such as permafrost, boreal–tropical forests, dynamic vegetation, wetlands, fire, and inland waters, many of which are tightly linked to one another. However, large uncertainties remain in the quantification of these processes for both warming-induced emissions and the associated temperature implications. Understanding these underlying mechanisms will help us address our remaining questions, such as: 1) Which feedback processes are most relevant for mitigation strategy planning (e.g., via the Transient Climate Response to cumulative Emissions of carbon dioxide (TCRE) or non-CO2 contributions to carbon budgets)? 2) What drives nonlinearity in the future climate trajectories? 3) Is the future climate (ir)reversible? 4) When will the climate be irreversible? 5) How will the climate respond to “overshoot, peak, and decline” scenarios? 6) What are the associated uncertainties across regional to global scales? This session aims to gather and integrate work that tackles the impacts of warming-induced emissions on the Earth system and the mechanisms underlying them, thereby providing clearer guidance for sustaining human society within the remaining carbon budget. All community efforts (e.g., WIEMIP) toward these goals are strongly encouraged. We welcome all contributions spanning laboratory-based experiments, satellite and field observations, machine-learning emulators, and modeling approaches, including fully-coupled Earth system models and stand-alone models.
title: Warming-Induced Emissions and Earth System Feedbacks: Overshoot, (Ir)Reversibility, and the Carbon Budget

description: Solar Radiation Management (SRM) refers to climate intervention technologies which propose to temporarily modify Earth’s radiative budget to offset climate risks associated with climate change. These include stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI), marine cloud brightening (MCB), and cirrus cloud thinning (CCT), among others. In all cases, the tightly coupled complex interplay between chemistry, radiation and dynamics especially with respect to aerosol-cloud interactions, make the regional and global impacts of these proposals highly uncertain. These uncertainties cascade into assessment of human and ecosystem relevant impacts, including but not limited to our understanding of the agricultural, ecological, or socio-political ramifications of large-scale adoption. This session focuses on advances in the natural science of SRM and seeks to identify or reduce sources of uncertainty. This may include climate modeling studies, idealized process investigations, experimental results, or observations of natural analogues. We welcome submissions from across the natural sciences as well as the social sciences, including impacts assessment or governance related to SRM strategies. We are particularly interested in work which focuses on understanding and constraining uncertainty related to regions or communities that are especially vulnerable to climate change, and we encourage early career or new members of the research community to consider applying.
title: Advances in Understanding Solar Radiation Modification Technologies and their Impact on the Earth System

description: Running Earth system models, downscaling outputs and driving process-based impact models are computationally expensive tasks that hinder the exploration of climate change impacts. New generations of statistical, physical, and hybrid climate change emulators reduce these bottlenecks by mimicking global, regional and extreme-event responses to generate projections of climate change and its associated impacts more efficiently. This capability transforms the assessment of climate change impacts and risks by enabling rapid policy-relevant analyses for sectors such as natural systems, agriculture, water resources, economics, energy systems and human health. This session invites contributions on the developments and applications in climate change emulation, highlighting opportunities and challenges for robust and computationally efficient climate risk assessments. This includes simple climate models, probabilistic emulation techniques and machine learning approaches, including traditional pattern scaling, as well as benchmarking efforts that aid in interpretability and consistency between emulation methods. To foster interdisciplinary exchange, we also encourage submissions regarding approaches for climate impact projections.
title: Climate emulators in the causal chain from scenarios to impacts

description: Large-scale atmospheric dynamics and synoptic systems are key drivers of near-surface variables (e.g., air temperature, precipitation), their variability and their extremes such as heatwaves, floods, and droughts. To be prepared for potential future extreme weather events, we need to further study the link between regional extremes and features of the large-scale atmospheric circulation (e.g., circulation patterns, weather regimes, blocking patterns, extra-tropical cyclones, teleconnection indices) and if and how these dynamics are changing. Various linear and non-linear approaches of synoptic climatology (e.g., multiple regression, canonical correlation, neural networks) can be applied to relate the circulation dynamics to diverse climatic and environmental elements and extremes. This session focuses on understanding regional extremes, their link to atmospheric dynamics, and their future evolution under climate change while welcoming contributions from various methodological approaches. We welcome contributions that explore: - The links between large-scale atmospheric circulation features (e.g., circulation patterns, weather regimes, blocking patterns, extra-tropical cyclones, teleconnection indices, NAO) and various types of regional extreme weather events (such as heat waves, heavy precipitation, floods, droughts) - Past, recent and future trends in frequency, intensity, and variability of regional extremes or surface environmental variables and their associated atmospheric features under climate change - The influence of internal climate variability on the occurrence of regional extreme events associated with large-scale atmospheric circulation features - The use of innovative methods, including large ensembles, and AI for circulation type classification This session invites contributions that explore the connections between different types of regional extremes and the atmospheric circulation, as well as studies from general synoptic climatology that focus on the relationship between atmospheric circulation dynamics and near surface environmental variables, their variability, and changes. The aim is to enhance our understanding of the dynamic drivers behind regional extremes in the context of climate change.
title: Synoptic and Large-Scale Circulation Dynamics: Impacts on Regional Extremes, Climate Variability, and Change

description: Kilometer-scale models provide new opportunities to understand how weather systems respond to climate change by explicitly representing convection, mesoscale organization, complex terrain, and coupled processes. Regional convection-permitting simulations and emerging global storm-resolving models offer complementary approaches, ranging from targeted event studies to multi-decadal climate simulations. This session focuses on how kilometer-scale modelling can advance our understanding of weather in a changing climate. We particularly welcome studies using event attribution, storylines, pseudo-global-warming experiments, extreme-event boosting, and other process-oriented approaches to investigate the mechanisms driving changes in individual events or classes of weather systems. We invite contributions that: 1. use regional or global kilometer-scale simulations to investigate climate change effects on weather and extremes; 2. use attribution, storylines, pseudo-global-warming, extreme-event boosting, or targeted experiments to investigate the effects of climate change on weather systems and the mechanisms involved; 3. examine the physical mechanisms and cross-scale interactions that control changes in the intensity, frequency, duration, or organization of extremes; 4. compare regional and global kilometer-scale modelling approaches, including their respective strengths, limitations, and complementarity; 5. evaluate the added value, biases, uncertainties, and computational challenges of kilometer-scale modelling. Studies of heavy precipitation, severe convection, tropical cyclones, heatwaves, windstorms, compound extremes, and other high-impact weather are encouraged. Contributions from regional and global modelling communities, including those involved in CORDEX, DYAMOND, nextGEMS, Destination Earth, and EERIE, are particularly welcome.
title: Kilometer-Scale Modelling of Weather in a Changing Climate

description: Deltas and estuaries are dynamic landscapes shaped by interactions among river flow, tides, waves, sediment transport, and biota. Their hydrology and geomorphology support ecosystems and human activities, while interactions with ecological and biogeochemical processes influence their physical evolution. Accelerating sea-level rise, changes in river discharge and sediment supply, extreme storms and floods, subsidence, and human interventions are reshaping the delicate balance of processes that sustain these environments. Understanding how landscapes respond to these pressures, including nonlinear responses and thresholds of change, is essential for assessing their future trajectories and developing effective adaptation and management strategies. This session brings together research on the biophysical processes shaping deltaic and estuarine landscapes and on strategies for their adaptation, restoration, and sustainable management. It aims to connect understanding of hydrological and biogeomorphological responses to climatic and anthropogenic pressures with the assessment of management interventions. We welcome research on the hydrology, morphodynamics, and biogeomorphology of deltas and estuaries, for example addressing river–marine interactions, sediment transport and budgets, feedback between biota and sediment dynamics, and morphological change. Contributions may address the effects of sea-level rise, changing river discharge, storms and floods, subsidence, and human activities, including nonlinear landscape responses and the implications of crossing thresholds. Contributions on adaptation, restoration, and management are equally welcome, including studies of nature-based solutions and conventional engineering approaches grounded in an understanding of physical processes, biogeomorphological interactions, and landscape dynamics. The session embraces theoretical, numerical, and data-driven approaches, including AI, as well as field observations, remote sensing, and experimental studies. We encourage interdisciplinary contributions that connect understanding of physical and biogeomorphological processes with decisions about the future of deltas and estuaries.
title: Deltas and estuaries: linking physical processes to adaptation and sustainable management

description: The Planetary Geomorphology and Surface Processes session brings together scientists studying the formation, evolution, and erosion of landscapes on Earth and other planetary bodies in the Solar System. Our session will provide a platform for cross-planetary discussion of the processes that generate and erode landscapes, create stratigraphy, and couple planetary surface dynamics to climatic and tectonic drivers. Considered processes could include aeolian, volcanic, tectonic, fluvial, glacial, periglacial, or as-yet "undetermined" ones. We welcome contributions on Mars, Venus, Mercury, the Moon, icy satellites of the outer solar system, comets, and/or asteroids, to submit to our session. We believe that an interdisciplinary approach through sharing and discussing ideas across planetary borders is key in answering current problems and for the formation of new ideas. We particularly welcome contributions from early-career scientists and geomorphologists who are new to planetary science.
title: Planetary Geomorphology and Surface Processes

description: Worldwide, disturbances modify the interactions and feedbacks among hydrologic, geomorphic, biogeochemical, and ecological systems, thereby reshaping the hydrological functioning of landscapes. Wildfires, deforestation, volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, and other disturbances alter water partitioning, flow paths, the transport of solutes and sediments. Although their immediate impacts may be spatially or temporally constrained, their hydrological consequences can persist and propagate across landscapes. This session explores how disturbances reshape hydrological processes across spatial and temporal scales, with particular interest in the mechanisms controlling the system response and recovery. We welcome observational, experimental, and modeling studies addressing individual, sequential, or interacting disturbances. We especially encourage contributions examining multiple or overlapping disturbances and their implications for predicting hydrological change and informing watershed and land management.
title: Disturbance Hydrology

description: Currently arid to sub-humid regions are home to >40% of the world’s population, and many prehistoric and historic cultures developed in these regions. Due to the high sensitivity of drylands to also small-scale environmental changes and anthropogenic activities, ongoing geomorphological processes under the intensified climatic and human pressure of the Anthropocene, but also the Late Quaternary geomorphological and paleoenvironmental evolution as recorded in sediment archives, are becoming increasingly relevant for geological, geomorphological, paleoenvironmental, paleoclimatic and geoarchaeological research. Dryland research is constantly boosted by methodological advances, and especially by emerging linkages with other climatic and geomorphic systems that allow using dryland areas as indicator-regions of global environmental changes. This session aims to pool contributions dealing with past to recent geomorphological processes and environmental changes spanning the entire Quaternary until today, as well as with all types of sedimentary and morphological archives in dryland areas (dunes, loess, slope deposits, fluvial sediments, alluvial fans, lake and playa sediments, desert pavements, soils, palaeosols etc.) studied on different spatial and temporal scales. Besides case studies on archives and landscapes from individual regions and review studies, cross-disciplinary, methodical and conceptual contributions are especially welcome in this session, e.g., dealing with the special role of aeolian, fluvial, gravitational and biological processes in dryland environments and their preservation in deposits and landforms, the role of such processes for past and present societies, methods to obtain chronological frameworks and process rates, and emerging geo-technologies.
title: Dryland evolution: Paleoenvironmental, geomorphic and geoarchaeological perspectives
