description: This session focuses on the small-scale transport processes of plastic pollution (macro, micro- and nano-plastics) across aquatic environments and groundwaters. While we aim to place special emphasis on laboratory experiments and modelling approaches, we also welcome presentations employing field work, and contributions focused on theoretical concepts. The presentations will revolve around understanding and characterising plastic movement and distribution, considering governing factors like particle physical characteristics, including size, shape, density, and surface chemistry, as well as environmental conditions such as flow, turbulence, temperature, salinity and suspended sediment. Relevant biological and chemical processes will be taken into account such as biofouling, aggregation and fragmentation, as well as plastic's role as transport vectors for other emerging contaminants, adding to their transport complexity. Beyond the presentation of research findings, this session will also focus on advancements in laboratory and numerical techniques, highlighting improvements in accuracy, complexity, and spatial-temporal resolution. Cutting-edge modelling approaches tailored to simulate the transport dynamics of plastics in the environments will be showcased. Through engaging discussions, the session aims to enhance our comprehension and predictive capabilities, while also identifying unresolved questions and paving the way for future research in this field.
title: Small-scale transport processes of plastics in aquatic systems

description: Aeolian processes operate across a myriad of spatial and temporal scales both on Earth and other planetary bodies. Interactions among geochemical, atmospheric, hydrologic, biological, cyrospheric, and soil processes shape aeolian dynamics and landforms, generating feedbacks that influence evolution across scales. Yet the controls governing aeolian transport, soil erosion, dust emission, and the resulting landforms are complex, interconnected, and remain incompletely understood. Bridging observations and understanding across spatial and temporal scales is therefore critical to advancing our understanding of aeolian systems and their evolution. This session brings together research traversing the spectrum of scale, from long term landscape evolution modelling to small-scale process studies. It will be of interest to researchers that study wind-driven processes and associated bedforms in a range of environments, including, coastal, arid and hyper arid regions, vegetated landscapes, icy beds, and planetary environments. Contributions employing novel instrumentation in field or laboratory studies, remote sensing, innovative numerical modelling, theoretical approaches, or combinations of these methods are encouraged.
title: Aeolian processes and landforms

description: Interactions between tectonics, climate, and surface processes govern the evolution of mountain belts and sedimentary basins, yet the strength, timescales, and consequences of these couplings remain poorly constrained. Robust first-order quantitative constraints are therefore needed. These can be derived from geomorphic and sedimentary archives such as longitudinal river profiles, fluvial and marine terraces, landslides, downstream fining trends, growth strata, sediment provenance, sequence stratigraphy, and shifts in depositional environments. Complementary insights can be gained from geodetic analyses (e.g., GPS, UAV, satellite imagery) and innovative geoinformatic approaches. Increasingly, the integration of geochronological methods for quantifying erosion rates and source-to-sink sediment fluxes with landscape evolution, stratigraphic, climatic, and tectonic models is advancing our understanding of how these systems interact across scales. We invite contributions that use geomorphic, geochronologic and/or sedimentary records to understand tectonic deformation, climate histories, and surface processes, and welcome studies that address their interactions and couplings at a range of spatial and temporal scales. In particular, we encourage coupled catchment-basin studies that take advantage of numerical/physical modelling, geochemical tools for quantifying rates of surface processes (cosmogenic nuclides, low-temperature thermochronology, luminescence dating) and high resolution digital topographic and subsurface data. We invite contributions that address the role of surface processes in modulating rates of deformation and tectonic style, or of tectonics modulating the response of landscapes to climate change. We encourage contributions from researchers with diverse expertise, backgrounds, and career stages. We particularly welcome interdisciplinary approaches that bring together different fields, methods, and research communities.
title: Interactions between tectonics, climate and surface processes from mountain belts to basins

description: Coastal and submarine environments are among the most dynamic landscapes on Earth, continuously reshaped by the interplay of hydrodynamic processes, sediment transport, tectonics, land subsidence, sea-level change, climate variability, and anthropogenic activities. Understanding the evolution of these interconnected systems is increasingly important in the face of accelerating climate change, growing coastal populations, and expanding offshore development. Recent advances in remote sensing, marine geophysics, bathymetric mapping, LiDAR, InSAR, unmanned aerial systems (UAS), numerical modelling, and field observations have substantially enhanced our ability to investigate geomorphic processes and landscape evolution across the land–sea continuum. This session welcomes contributions investigating the evolution, morphodynamics, and sedimentary processes of coastal and submarine environments across a wide range of spatial and temporal scales. We encourage studies focusing on beaches, deltas, estuaries, tidal flats, coastal dunes, rocky coasts, cliffs, barrier systems, continental shelves, submarine canyons, submarine landslides, and other coastal and marine landforms. Contributions addressing shoreline evolution, land subsidence, relative sea-level rise, sediment budgets, coastal erosion and accretion, sediment connectivity, and interactions between terrestrial and marine geomorphic processes are particularly encouraged. We especially welcome multidisciplinary studies integrating field observations with remote sensing, satellite data, LiDAR, InSAR, bathymetric surveys, seismic reflection, magnetic and other geophysical datasets, GIS analyses, machine learning, and process-based numerical modelling to improve our understanding of geomorphic evolution and sediment dynamics. Contributions exploring climate change impacts, coastal hazards, ecosystem resilience, nature-based solutions, and sustainable coastal management are also encouraged. The session aims to provide a platform for coastal geomorphologists, marine geologists, geophysicists, remote sensing specialists, natural hazard scientists, and numerical modellers to exchange ideas, foster interdisciplinary collaborations, and advance our understanding of the processes shaping coastal and submarine landscapes across the land–sea continuum.
title: Advances in Coastal and Submarine Geomorphology under Climate Change: Integrating Field Observations, Remote Sensing, and Geophysical Perspectives

description: While African mountain terrain above 2000 m represents only 1% of the continent, it is highly diverse, extending across the Northern and Southern Hemispheres and spanning a wide range of climate zones, from tropical rainforests to arid deserts. These mountain environmental refuges signify some of the continent’s most dynamic geoecological and socio-ecological systems, encompassing important water towers, complex geomorphologies, and local communities that depend on high-altitude ecosystem services. The long- and short-term geo-ecological evolution of African mountain areas has received limited scientific attention, including from the European geoscience community. Past and present landscape evolution and climatic change, including cryosphere development, soil processes, vegetation shifts, and slope geomorphological dynamics, have reshaped Africa’s high mountains. These changes in high-elevation environments have influenced the socio-ecological services and resources available to populations now facing increasing climate change related risks under ongoing global warming. In this session, we invite contributions on these and related topics in African mountains, particularly those addressing past and recent landscape evolution, including millennial-, centennial-, and decadal-scale changes. We also welcome datasets from experimental areas, chronological databases, climate and environmental modeling, community-based approaches, remote sensing (satellite, InSAR, UAV) studies, and other multidisciplinary approaches that integrate the topics outlined above.
title: Past and present environmental evolution in African mountains

description: Artificial intelligence is changing the way geomorphologists observe and interpret landscapes. Its role is no longer limited to speeding up the identification of landforms. Data-driven methods are now being used to reconstruct incomplete surfaces, follow rapid environmental changes, estimate process dynamics, and explore how landscapes may evolve under future conditions. This session focuses on the use of artificial intelligence to investigate both geomorphic forms and the processes that create and modify them. We seek contributions dealing with terrestrial, coastal, submarine and planetary environments, including rivers, slopes, badlands, karst areas, deserts, glaciers and periglacial regions. Studies may address landform recognition, surface and sediment characterization, topographic or bathymetric reconstruction, environmental monitoring, palaeolandscape analysis, susceptibility assessment and the prediction of geomorphic change. We are particularly interested in research that combines information from different sources, such as satellite imagery, UAV surveys, digital elevation models, LiDAR, photogrammetry, geophysical data, field measurements and video observations. Contributions based on machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, generative approaches, foundation models and physics-guided methods are welcome, especially when they provide new ways of linking observations with geomorphic processes. The session will also provide space for critical discussion. High predictive accuracy alone does not necessarily guarantee that a model is reliable or scientifically meaningful. We therefore encourage studies examining uncertainty, spatial dependence, model interpretation, transferability between regions, data limitations and unsuccessful applications. Comparisons between data-driven methods, traditional statistical approaches and process-based models are equally relevant. By bringing together geomorphologists, remote-sensing researchers, modellers and data scientists, the session aims to discuss how artificial intelligence can help us move from the automatic description of landscapes towards a deeper understanding of their behaviour and evolution.
title: From Landforms to Processes: Artificial Intelligence in Geomorphology

description: We are looking herein for new methodological, new techniques, new processing and new applications using UAS / drones to study any Earth Science processes. We would like first to share our various knowledge, techniques, processing, methodologies, and experience in the use of UAS. Then we would like to illustrate the so many applications existing nowadays in Earth Sciences. Moreover, we would like to insist on the importance to get a whole high resolution - pluri centimetric Ground Resolution – multitemporal dataset of aerial photographs coverage of a studied area at a so low price. An UAS acquisition provides after processing orthophotos as well as a high resolution Digital Surface Model from which we may process a high resolution Digital Terrain Model with many applications. Consequently, we would expect various examples and applications from very different field in Earth Sciences such as geological and geomorphological mapping, geomorphometry, geodesy, natural hazards such as volcanic and seismic hazards, or landslide monitoring, floods, or other applications such as neotectonics and active tectonics, structural geology, tectonics, sedimentology and mapping of inaccessible outcrops, monitoring of fluvial or marine terrasses in order to get their evolutions, climate changes, and so on... Finally we hope by this session and with time to create an « UAS community of the different colleagues who use UAS with applications in Earth Sciences » in order to optimize our practise, our results and our knowledge.
title: Inputs of multiplatform UAS/drones to study Earth Science processes

description: Imaging the Earth’s surface and reconstructing its topography to study the landscape and (sub-)surface processes have advanced rapidly over the past two decades, sometimes separately within different geoscientific disciplines. Developments in satellite, airborne, uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV), and ground-based sensing, alongside advances in photogrammetry, Structure-from-Motion (SfM), LiDAR, computer vision, and automated processing, have transformed our ability to reconstruct and monitor the Earth’s surface in 2D, 3D, and 4D (time series). The spatial, temporal, and spectral resolutions of current measurements offer the opportunity to study the surface evolution from local to regional scale at unprecedented detail. Equipped with optimized workflows, either digitizing analogue data, such as historical aerial photographs, or processing near-continuous records of topographic change, geoscientists now have a variety of tools to better understand our rapidly changing environment and disentangle anthropogenic from natural drivers. Yet, challenges still exist at both methodological and application levels. How can reliable data be acquired in harsh, remote, or non-ideal environments? How can observations from different time periods, scales, and platforms be reconstructed, co-registered, and compared? How should measurement precision, systematic errors, and uncertainty be quantified and propagated into estimates of surface change? And how can computer-vision, machine-learning, and automation extract meaningful information from large and complex 3D and 4D datasets? In this session, we invite contributions from across the geosciences (e.g., geomorphology, glaciology, volcanology, hydrology, soil sciences) on the opportunities, limitations, and challenges of surface imaging, topographic reconstruction, and change analysis across diverse environments. We especially welcome contributions addressing (1) novel data acquisition in complex, remote, or rapidly changing environments; (2) image and point-cloud processing, including image matching, reconstruction, co-registration, and correction of sensor distortions; (3) precision and uncertainty assessment, including systematic errors; (4) construction and analysis of multitemporal and 4D datasets, from historical records to high-frequency and near-continuous observations; (5) automated processing, analysis, and information extraction from large and complex datasets; and (6) innovative applications in geosciences.
title: From historical images to modern high-resolution topography: methods and applications in geosciences

description: Assessing multi-temporal coastal evolution across contrasting morpho-dynamic settings remains a central challenge in reconstructing how coastal landscapes have responded to environmental change over the long term, shaping in turn the patterns of human occupation they supported. Relative sea-level history, sediment supply, and shoreline dynamics have varied considerably from one coastal context to another, and disentangling these trajectories provides the long-term perspective needed to interpret both the coastal changes observed today and those anticipated as sea level continues to rise. The study of past coastal environments requires the integration of different types of evidence, including sedimentary archives, geomorphological features, palaeoecological proxies, archaeological remains, historical sources, and instrumental data. These records provide complementary information on the evolution of coastal systems and allow us to investigate environmental changes over a wide range of temporal scales, from millennial and centennial timescales to more recent and historical periods. Combined, these records also document how coastal landscapes have influenced human occupation, particularly for earlier periods, and how populations have in turn modified these landscapes through their activities. This session aims to bring together work on the palaeoenvironmental evolution and human occupation of coastal areas, at whatever temporal or spatial scale, from a single stratigraphic sequence to an entire coastal system. We welcome contributions that cross disciplinary lines, drawing on geoarchaeology, geomorphology, Quaternary science, palaeoecology, and archaeology. The main topics include: - Reconstruction of past coastal environments and landscapes from sedimentary and geomorphological records; - Human occupation and transformation of coastal environments through time; - Geoarchaeological approaches to coastal landscape evolution; - Interactions between relative sea-level change, coastal dynamics, and human societies; - Evolution of deltas, estuaries, lagoons, wetlands, and other coastal environments; - Palaeoenvironmental reconstruction of ancient harbours and coastal settlements; - Coastal responses to climatic variability and extreme events at different timescales; - Multi-proxy and interdisciplinary approaches to reconstructing past coastal environments; - New methodological approaches for investigating long-term human–environment interactions in coastal areas.
title: Coastal environments and human occupation: a long-term perspective

description: Over the past several decades, topographic measurement techniques have undergone significant advancement, evolving toward increasingly sophisticated instruments capable of higher precision and spatial resolution. This technological progression has enabled diverse applications across Earth sciences, particularly in territorial analysis for monitoring and quantifying geomorphological processes and their associated changes at varying temporal and spatial scales. The intersection between geomatics and geomorphology represents a fundamental pathway for quantifying landscape evolution, assessing geohazards, improving cartographic representation, and informing land management decisions. From debris flow channel activation to glacial retreat monitoring, and from geomorphic signature of active tectonics to landslide hazard mapping, integrated geomatics approaches provide critical insights into surface processes. This session invites researchers to present work employing integrated methodologies across diverse environmental settings. We encourage submissions utilizing topographic surveying, GPS/GNSS data analysis, photogrammetry (including UAV-based approaches), remote sensing imagery, geomorphometric analyses, InSAR data analysis, and machine learning applications. Contributions demonstrating multi-scale and multi-temporal approaches are particularly welcomed.
title: Monitoring strategies of geomorphic processes: where geomatics applications quantify landscape changes

description: Landscape evolution models (LEMs) have matured into powerful and widely used tools in the geomorphologist’s toolbox. Increasingly robust representations of weathering, erosion, sediment transport and hillslope processes allow LEMs to function as digital laboratories in which hypotheses about landscape dynamics can be explored across spatial and especially temporal scales that are impossible to directly observe. LEMs have been used to investigate a wide range of questions, including the response of landscapes to climate and tectonic forcing; river incision and sediment transport; hillslope evolution and landslide dynamics; glacial and periglacial processes; soil formation and weathering; drainage-network development; interactions between geomorphic processes and ecosystems; and the propagation of disturbances through coupled Earth-surface systems. Their ability to represent interacting processes also offers opportunities to explore cascading natural hazards, from landslide–river interactions to chains of sediment, flooding and slope instability, making LEMs increasingly relevant to a key societal concern. At the same time, the field is entering an exciting period of methodological tension. As process-based models, LEMs seek to encode physical mechanisms and study their emerging interactions explicitly, while AI and data-driven approaches offer powerful alternatives for identifying patterns and emulating processes. Rather than treating these approaches as competing paradigms, this tension raises fundamental questions about what we expect models to represent, how we evaluate them, and how process understanding can be combined with emerging computational methods. This session welcomes contributions from researchers who use, modify, or develop landscape evolution models, as well as those whose research questions could benefit from the application of LEMs.
title: Landscape evolution models as digital laboratories for studying coupled Earth-surface systems

description: Karst areas and cave networks represent both dynamic systems and palaeoenvironmental archives, preserving records of palaeoclimate, geomorphological evolution, geodynamics, and broader palaeoenvironmental change across timescales ranging from decades to millions of years. Cave sediments, speleothems, endokarst morphologies, and associated biological and archaeological material collectively constitute a uniquely diverse and durable repository of Earth surface history. Yet karst systems are inherently heterogeneous and complex environments. Their present-day hydrological functioning and their response to environmental change depend on this long-term evolution, which affects connectivity and flow paths within these systems. Furthermore, interpreting karst archives in terms of palaeoenvironmental reconstruction relies on understanding modern and ancient karst system processes and behaviour. Karstological and geomorphological analysis is therefore essential to decipher the complexity of the functioning and evolution of these systems, and the external forcings that control them (climate, tectonics, cryosphere, among others). This session invites contributions that consider karst systems both as palaeoenvironmental archives and as dynamic systems, with particular attention to studies linking external forcings to karst system response. This session is explicitly interdisciplinary and welcomes contributions from palaeoclimatology, geomorphology, karst hydrology, palaeoanthropology, cryosphere research, and geodynamics. Relevant methodological approaches include, but are not limited to spatial analysis, cave monitoring, geochronology, geochemistry, geophysics, sedimentology and stratigraphy, and numerical modelling.
title: Karst geomorphology, dynamics and archives: from process to paleoenvironmental record

description: Fractured-porous media and karst systems remain among the most challenging geological media to investigate due to their high heterogeneity and scale-dependent flow and transport properties. Given their abundance, they are important for various research fields such as hydrogeology, geothermal energy, CO₂ storage and nuclear waste repository management, as well as petroleum and mining engineering. Decades of research have explored a broad spectrum of methods, including field experiments, laboratory-scale approaches, analytical techniques and numerical modeling. However, the multiscale nature of these systems requires bridging micro- and macro-scale processes in order to accurately represent flow and (reactive) transport processes. In this session, we therefore welcome contributions that focus on flow and (reactive) transport in karst systems and fractured-porous media. Topics include, but are not limited to: (1) advances in field methods and laboratory techniques to characterize flow and transport from pore to field scales; (2) numerical and analytical modeling approaches for multiscale process understanding; (3) studies targeting the management and efficient use of geothermal, mineral and petroleum resources; and (4) studies targeting water resources management and environmental risk assessment.
title: Multiscale characterization of structure, flow and transport processes in fractured-porous media and karst systems

description: Groundwater is one of the largest stores of freshwater on Earth. Yet, it remains one of the least directly observed components, with its dynamics often inferred from sparse observations, indirect measurements, models, and satellite and remote-sensing products. This limited observability contributes to persistent uncertainties in how groundwater interacts with other components of the hydrological cycle and regulates hydrological variability across spatial and temporal scales. Groundwater is not an isolated component. Through recharge, storage, subsurface flow, and exchanges with surface water and ecosystems, it can buffer or amplify hydrological variability, sustain river and ecosystem flows, influence drought propagation and recovery, and redistribute water across catchments and regions. Understanding these processes is essential for a complete picture of the water cycle under a changing climate. An emerging challenge is to move beyond viewing the terrestrial water cycle primarily as individual stores, fluxes and water-balance terms toward understanding its integrated connectivity and redistribution structure. Quantifying groundwater contributions and connectivity is important for understanding how the water cycle is organized, where uncertainty is concentrated, and how changes propagate through the wider hydrological system. We welcome contributions addressing, but not limited to: • Groundwater dynamics and connectivity, including contributions to terrestrial water storage, streamflow, evapotranspiration, coastal discharge, and groundwater–surface-water interactions; • Observing and quantifying groundwater using in situ measurements, remote sensing, geophysical and tracer-based methods, and integration of heterogeneous observations; • Modelling groundwater within the hydrological cycle, including large-scale and Earth system models, precipitation/runoff partitioning, groundwater representation and uncertainties; • AI-powered, data-driven and hybrid approaches, including data assimilation, machine learning, reconstruction, prediction and scaling; • Groundwater roles in hydrological variability, change and extremes, including drought and flood onset, propagation, persistence and recovery, and responses to climate variability, climate change and human interventions; and • Scaling and implications from local and catchment to continental and global hydrology, including ecosystems, water availability and resilience.
title: Seeing the Unseen: Groundwater’s Role in the Hydrological Cycle

description: Groundwater resources face increasing pressures from climate change, abstraction, pollution and other human activities, requiring integrated approaches to assess groundwater quality and quantity and to support sustainable management. While monitoring provides the essential evidence base, heterogeneous monitoring networks, methods and assessment criteria still limit comparability and integration across Europe. This session will explore how monitoring data, indicators, modelling and mapping tools can be harmonized and integrated to move from observations towards decision-making. A particular focus is on translating heterogeneous observations and scientific knowledge into robust, spatially explicit information that supports ground water management across scales, from water bodies to national and European assessments. Contributions may address groundwater levels and storage, recharge and abstraction, natural baselines, trend assessments, anthropogenic pressures, uncertainty assessment, data harmonization, and the development of indicators and decision-support tools. The session welcomes approaches supporting the implementation of the Water Framework Directive and Groundwater Directive, as well as broader European initiatives such as the EU Water Resilience Strategy and the Geological Service for Europe (GSEU).
title: From groundwater monitoring to decision-making: Indicators, data and tools across scales for water quality and quantity

description: The strong nonlinearity of the governing PDEs, coupled with the spatial heterogeneity and anisotropy of the subsurface media parameters, continues to pose significant challenges in mathematical and numerical modeling of subsurface flow and transport processes. These challenges become pronounced under changing climatic conditions, where increasing hydroclimatic variability and extreme events can induce rapid transitions in soil moisture and phase dynamics, flow regimes, and freshwater availability within subsurface environments. The conventional modeling approaches may struggle to adequately resolve these highly transient and nonlinear processes across multiple spatial and temporal scales. In parallel, increasing natural and anthropogenic influences are introducing a wide range of emerging contaminants, such as microplastics, PPCPs, PFAS, and other persistent pollutants, into soil and groundwater systems, whose transport, retention, transformation, and fate in variably saturated subsurface environments have yet to be studied properly. Simulating the complex interactions among these emerging contaminants, soil particles, pore-water chemistry, air-water interfaces, and biological processes further challenges the existing modeling frameworks. Besides, certain complex flow and transport phenomena in subsurface hydrology require problem-specific mathematical formulations and robust numerical strategies to obtain stable, accurate, and physically consistent solutions. This session invites contributions that advance the mathematical, numerical, analytical, statistical, and data-driven modeling of subsurface flow and transport processes. Contributions addressing methodological developments, model applications, laboratory- or field-scale investigations, and multiphysics and multiscale modeling approaches are particularly encouraged. Contributions related to the following topics, and beyond, are welcome: ● Microplastics in vadose zone – insights into pore-scale complexities and modeling strategies. ● Advanced mathematical modeling approaches for transport dynamics of emerging contaminants in variably saturated subsurface environments. ● Coupled modeling of flow, solute transport, and exchange processes between surface and subsurface systems. ● Numerical and analytical modeling of seawater intrusion in coastal aquifers. ● Numerical modeling of non-Darcian flows through subsurface media. ● Development and application of AIML modeling surrogates in subsurface hydrology.
title: Advances in Mathematical and Computational Modeling of Subsurface Flow and Transport Processes under Emerging Hydrological and Anthropological Challenges

description: Multiphase flows play a central role in a broad range of natural and engineered processes, such as nutrient cycles and contaminant remediation in soils, and geological storage of carbon dioxide and hydrogen in deep reservoirs. Understanding multiphase systems across scales is therefore fundamental for water resources management as well energy and climate concerns. The presence of multiple fluid phases enhances heterogeneity at the level of flow, mixing, and reaction in structurally heterogeneous media. This impacts the transport of dissolved substances and fundamentally changes mixing patterns and effective reaction rates, posing major challenges for predictive modeling. Recent theoretical and experimental advances provide unprecedented insights into the pore-scale mechanisms governing these processes and open new opportunities to tackle these challenges. This session aims to bring together researchers working on fundamental and applied aspects of flow, transport, mixing, and reaction in multi-phase systems across scales. In particular, we encourage submissions relating to experimental, numerical, and theoretical contributions pertaining to the following topics: - Impact of medium heterogeneity on multiphase flow, from the pore to the continuum scale. - Impact of multiphase flow patterns on mixing and reaction rates across scales in heterogeneous media. - Biogeochemical processes in multiphase systems. - Applications to vadose zone hydrology and geological storage.
title: Flow, transport, mixing, and reaction in heterogeneous multiphase systems across scales

description: Extreme hydroclimatic events are expected to increase in both frequency and intensity as a result of climate change. Groundwater systems are particularly vulnerable to these events, yet their medium- to long-term responses remain insufficiently understood. Consequences such as reduced aquifer recharge, sustained groundwater depletion, and groundwater quality degradation can induce cascading impacts including land subsidence, threats to freshwater availability and food security, and saltwater intrusion. It is therefore essential to advance our understanding of the full spectrum of these processes and their impacts, as well as to improve our ability to represent them through physics-based numerical modeling and machine learning approaches. Such knowledge can foster the implementation of effective mitigation and adaptation strategies to safeguard groundwater resources and ensure their sustainable use. These strategies can vary from improved forecasting and modeling of the impacts of extreme events on aquifer systems, to targeted engineering interventions and sustainable management practices. This session invites contributions that provide insights into innovative methodologies, field case studies, or novel perspectives investigating the qualitative and quantitative impacts that extreme hydroclimatic events exert on groundwater systems, and their cascading environmental and socio-economic effects. In particular, we welcome studies that address: (i) evaluation of the combined effects of climatic extremes and anthropogenic stresses on groundwater quantity and quality; (ii) comparative analysis of field observations and methodologies unraveling system responses across different spatial scales and climatic contexts; (iii) development and application of physics-based, machine learning, or hybrid modeling frameworks for simulating past, present, and projected aquifer responses under extreme hydroclimatic events; (iv) characterization and modeling of system memory and recovery dynamics; (v) identification and evaluation of potential management, mitigation, and adaptation strategies to enhance groundwater resilience.
title: Unraveling the impacts of extreme hydroclimatic events on groundwater security

description: Human-induced climate change has increased the frequency and intensity of many weather and climate hazards, including heatwaves and humid heat, droughts, floods and heavy precipitation, windstorms, tropical cyclones, and wildfires, often with severe societal impacts. Yet the confidence with which observed changes can be attributed to anthropogenic influence still varies between hazard types, as does climate models’ ability to reproduce observed extreme events. Both limit our ability to project future risks at different warming levels. Understanding and projecting changes in these emerging hazards, including unprecedented, compound, consecutive, flash-change, and seasonally-shifting extremes, as well as their interaction with exposure, vulnerability, and adaptation, is a challenge that spans the physical sciences, statistics and machine learning, climate risk modelling, geography, and the socioeconomic sciences. The sheer number of recent extreme events underlines the urgency of improved understanding and modelling capacities for better adaptation, policymaking, and early warning systems. This session highlights recent progress on understanding, modelling, and projecting weather and climate hazards across these disciplines and aims to identify open research questions and form new collaborations. Which hazards receive too little attention compared to, e.g., heat and drought, and which regions remain under-studied? Which sectors should work more closely with weather and climate scientists to make progress? We invite contributions on changing weather and climate hazards and their impacts from all regions of the world. Studies on floods, storms, humid heat, and other hazards less represented in the literature are particularly welcome, as are contributions including, but not limited to: - Understanding physical processes associated with weather extremes, including unprecedented, compound, consecutive, flash-change, and seasonality-related extremes - Teleconnections and natural modes of variability as well as their links to hazards and impacts - Advances in hazard and impact modelling, including bias-adjustments and data-driven approaches - Detection and attribution of weather and climate hazards and their impacts - Storyline and other approaches to low-likelihood, high-impact events - Trends and projections of hazards on decadal to centennial timescales - Changing exposure and vulnerability; interactions between hazards, local socioeconomics, & adaptation
title: Understanding and Modelling of Weather and Climate Hazards in a changing climate

description: Emerging contaminants (e.g., PFAS, pharmaceuticals, microplastics) and climate change pose new challenges to our already fragile ecosystems. The vadose zone is a dynamically changing heterogeneous system, which plays a key role in regulating water and solute exchanges between atmosphere, vegetation, and groundwater and hosts a large portion of subsurface biochemical reactions. Understanding the interrelation between hydrological, physicochemical, and biological processes in the unsaturated zone is paramount to developing sustainable management strategies. This can solely be attained by translating novel experimental insights into well-validated modeling tools, which can benefit from recent advances in machine learning. This session welcomes research that advances the current understanding of the vadose zone hydro-biogeochemical functioning across multiple scales, including experimental or modeling approaches, and field or simulation studies. In particular, we encourage researchers to participate with contributions on the following topics: • Monitoring of water flow, solute transport, and biochemical reactions from the pore scale to the field scale • Experimental investigation and numerical modeling of the reactive transport of emerging contaminants in variably-saturated porous media • Influence of static and dynamically changing soil structures (e.g., heterogeneity) on water flow and reactive solute transport • Transport of water and contaminants in/from the rhizosphere into the plant • Development of novel modeling approaches to predict water and chemical transport in the vadose zone • Novel techniques for model appraisal, including calibration, sensitivity analysis, uncertainty assessment, and surrogate-based modeling for hydro-biogeochemical vadose zone modeling.
title: Hydrological processes and contaminants transport in the vadose zone: Recent developments and novel insights

description: Tsunamis can be generated by a variety of mechanisms, including earthquakes, landslides, volcanic activity and atmospheric disturbances. They can cause widespread damage and fatalities in coastal areas including lakeshores, highlighting the need to advance tsunami science towards implementing effective disaster risk reduction measures and developing early warning systems. Since the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, the tsunami science has evolved significantly, expanding into new research areas and regions. However, recent events, such as the 2022 Hunga Tonga - Hunga Hapai and the 2025 Kamchatka tsunamis, have challenged the progress in tsunami science and warning, and raised further questions on modeling, hazard assessment and warning capabilities at different scales. They particularly underscored the importance of closer collaboration between different research fields and operational communities, especially in: - Analytical and numerical modelling of tsunami generation, propagation and inundation from various triggering mechanisms, including single or multi-causative sources (from large subduction to more local earthquakes generated in tectonically complex environments, from subaerial/submarine landslides and glacier collapses to volcanic eruptions and atmospheric disturbances) - Deterministic and probabilistic tsunami hazard, vulnerability, and risk assessments, including a multi-hazard perspective - Forecasting tsunamis using emerging technologies, such as artificial intelligence and satellite altimetry (e.g. SWOT satellite) - Early warning and monitoring, emphasizing innovative marine and seafloor observation methods, sensors and data processing techniques to improve the early characterization of tsunami sources and detection - Societal and economic impacts of tsunami events on coastal communities - Hazards perceptions, communication and engagement - Present and future challenges related to global climate change (e.g. the impact of sea level rise) The overall goal of this session is to enhance our understanding of the tsunami phenomenon and to strengthen our capacity to build safer and more resilient tsunami communities. The session welcomes both specialized and multidisciplinary contributions covering any of the topics mentioned above, including observation databases, real-time networks, numerical and experimental modeling, hazard-vulnerability-risk assessments, and operational tools and procedures for more effective warnings.
title: Tsunami science and warning: advances in modelling, disaster risk reduction, forecasting and hazard communication

description: Recent decades have seen widespread increases in daily minimum temperatures across regions and seasons, with many projections showing that minimum temperatures will continue to increase at a faster rate than daily maxima in many regions. But low temperatures and cold extremes remain a significant source of environmental and societal risk. Cold spells, frost events, and cold-air outbreaks continue to affect human health, agriculture, transportation, energy systems, ecosystems, and infrastructure. Although the frequency and intensity of cold extremes are expected to decrease in a warming climate, such events may still produce substantial impacts, especially as natural and human systems have already started adapting to warmer conditions. Furthermore, important questions remain regarding the physical drivers, predictability, attribution, future evolution, and impacts of cold extremes and cold temperature-related phenomena across different temporal and spatial scales. This session aims to bring together researchers from various disciplines, including climatology, meteorology, hydrology, ecology, biometeorology and impact-focused disciplines, to advance our understanding of cold extremes and their role in the changing climate. We welcome contributions addressing observational, modelling, mechanism, and impact-based perspectives on cold temperatures and cold extremes. We invite contributions related to: - Past and future trends and variability in cold extremes at global, regional, and local scales - Changes in frost occurrence, duration, timing, and seasonality - Cold-air outbreaks, cold spells, and extreme cold weather events - Physical drivers of cold extremes, including atmospheric circulation, Rossby wave breaking, blocking, jet-stream variability, stratosphere-troposphere coupling, and teleconnections - Compound and cascading cold-related events (e.g., cold and snow, cold and wind, cold and energy-system stress) - Attribution of cold extremes and assessment of underlying drivers - Representation of cold extremes in numerical models - Ecological and environmental impacts of cold temperatures, frost damage, and winter stress - Impacts on agriculture, forestry, water resources, transportation, infrastructure, and energy systems - Human health impacts and societal vulnerability to cold extremes - Adaptation, resilience, and risk management in a changing climate - Paleoclimate and future long-term perspectives on cold extremes and cold-related events
title: Cold extremes in the warming climate: changes and impacts, processes and attribution

description: Climate change is reshaping hydro-climatic extremes by disturbing the long-term stability of hydrological systems, a pattern known as non-stationarity. This non-stationarity is far more pronounced wherever watersheds are physically disturbed. Wildfire is one of the most rapid forms of such disturbance. It strips vegetation, alters soil properties, and reduces the land's ability to absorb water. When heavy rainfall follows, floods expected once every 100 years can become up to three times larger in the first year after a fire. This risk is intensifying. Warming raises the likelihood of severe fire seasons followed within a year by extreme rainfall. Compound climate hazards are also becoming more frequent in fire-prone regions such as the Mediterranean. Most models, however, evaluate hazards one at a time. They rarely capture how hazards interact and cascade. This leaves the added complexity that a warming climate brings to post-fire hazard planning largely unaccounted for. This leaves the added complexity that a warming climate brings to post-fire hazard planning largely unaccounted for. This session aims to bring together researchers exploring how Earth observation, machine learning, and deep learning methods can model and monitor these compound and cascading hydro-climatic extremes under climate change. It welcomes hydrologists, remote sensing specialists, climatologists, and machine learning researchers to discuss practical approaches for understanding and predicting these evolving fire-to-flood extremes. By fostering interdisciplinary discussions, we aim to form new collaborations and identify outstanding research questions like: Which climatic regimes and conditions foster this fire-to-flood interaction? What role do geographical and anthropogenic influences play in this? What role can explainable AI play in detecting and providing early warnings for these non-stationary compound hydro-climatic extremes? How can data-scarce regions be better modeled using deep learning and Earth observation?
title: Fire-to-Flood: Earth Observation and Machine Learning for Compound Hydro-Climatic Extremes Under Climate Change

description: In the current context of global change, a better understanding of our large-scale hydrology is vital. For example, by increasing our knowledge of the climate system and water cycle, improve assessments of water resources in a changing environment, perform seasonal predictions, and evaluate the impact of transboundary water resource management. We invite contributions from across hydrological, atmospheric, and earth surface processes communities. In particular, we welcome abstracts that address advances in: (i) understanding and predicting the present and future state of water resources worldwide and within large-scale systems, including hydrological extremes and uncertainty assessment. (ii) the use of global Earth observations and in-situ datasets for large-scale hydrology and data assimilation techniques for large-scale hydrological models, including machine learning and hybrid modelling approaches. (iii) the representation and evaluation of various components of the terrestrial water cycle fluxes and storages (e.g., soil moisture, snow, groundwater, lakes, floodplains, evaporation, river discharge) and atmospheric modelling. (iv) providing syntheses that combine knowledge gained at smaller scales (e.g. catchments or hillslope) to increase our knowledge on process understanding needed for further development of large-scale hydrological models and to identify large-scale patterns and trends. (v) understanding interactions and feedbacks between hydrological processes, water management, and human intervention activities (e.g. reservoirs, dams, irrigation) across large-scale systems.
title: Large Scale Hydrology

description: Water moves continuously between the atmosphere, the land surface and the subsurface, yet models are usually built for one compartment at a time. Atmospheric models simplify land and groundwater processes, hydrological models treat precipitation as fixed input, and groundwater models often reduce recharge to a boundary condition. Human interventions such as reservoirs, irrigation, pumping, land-use change and grey–green infrastructure further alter these connections. The gaps matter most during extremes: floods, droughts, landslides, subsidence and seawater intrusion often arise from processes that cascade across compartments, and models that miss these links can underestimate hazard and misjudge risk. This session welcomes process-based, data-driven and hybrid modelling studies, from plot to global scale, on topics including: (1) atmospheric water, such as precipitation downscaling, extreme rainfall, land–atmosphere coupling and moisture recycling; (2) land-surface and subsurface water, such as runoff, soil moisture, evapotranspiration, snow and glacier melt, recharge, groundwater flow and surface water–groundwater exchange; (3) coupled frameworks linking compartments across scales; (4) human interventions and their feedbacks on the water cycle; (5) hydrological hazards and risk, including compound and cascading events, hazard, exposure and vulnerability assessment, and impact-based early warning; (6) machine learning, physics-informed and explainable AI, data assimilation and digital twins; and (7) uncertainty, scenario analysis and decision support. We particularly welcome studies from data-scarce, Mediterranean and monsoon-dominated regions, work that tests models against observed events, approaches that link hazard modelling to risk reduction and water management, and model intercomparisons or benchmark datasets that help the community move forward. Early-career scientists are strongly encouraged to submit.
title: Modelling water from atmosphere to ground and back: integrated approaches for water management, risk and hazards under change

description: Different approaches, including global models, data-driven approaches, and machine learning, are used to assess water balance components at the global, continental, and regional scales. By making use of in-situ as well as remotely sensed observations, they attempt to quantify water fluxes (e.g., evapotranspiration, streamflow, groundwater recharge) and water storage on the terrestrial part of the Earth as a whole (e.g., from GRACE/-FO and future missions such as MAGIC and NGGM) or in separate compartments (e.g., water bodies, snow, soil, groundwater). Increasing attention is given to uncertainties that stem from forcing datasets, model structure, parameters and combinations of these. Recent advances also include hybrid approaches that integrate machine learning with process-based models and assimilate Earth Observation data for improved water balance closure. Current research shows that flux and storage estimates differ considerably due to the methodology and datasets used, so a robust assessment of global, continental and regional water balance components remains challenging. This session is seeking contributions, including: 1) past/future assessment of water balance components (fluxes and storages) such as precipitation, freshwater fluxes to the oceans (or inland sinks), evapotranspiration, groundwater recharge, water use, changes in terrestrial water storage or individual components at global, continental and regional scales, 2) application of innovative explorative approaches undertaking such assessments – through better use of advanced data-driven and statistical approaches, mechanistic models, machine learning and approaches to assimilate (or accommodate) in-situ and remote sensing datasets for improved estimation of terrestrial water storages/fluxes, 3) analysis and quantification of different sources of uncertainties in estimation of water balance components, 4) examination and attribution of systematic differences in storage/flux estimates between different methodologies, and/or 5) applications/consequences of those findings, such as sea level rise and water surplus or scarcity. We encourage submissions based on different methodological approaches that estimate and analyse water balance components individually or integratively on global, continental, or regional scales. Assessments of uncertainty in past/future estimates of water balance components and their implications are highly welcome.
title: Recent advancements in estimating global, continental and regional scale water balance components

description: Reducing tropical cyclone (TC) risk requires an integrated view that connects large-scale circulation and storm physics with nearshore processes, impacts, and the effectiveness of risk-reduction measures. This session invites studies that advance understanding across the full cascade: climate drivers and variability; TC genesis, track, and intensity-frequency change; atmosphere–ocean coupling (winds, waves, storm surge, rainfall); wind impacts, precipitation footprint, storm surge and wave dynamics; compound flooding, erosion, and other TC-related impacts; consequence modelling for people, health, ecosystems, the built environment, and critical infrastructure; and the appraisal and implementation of risk-reduction and adaptation options. We particularly welcome contributions on modelling and downscaling (from global to local), ensembles and probabilistic methods, data assimilation and remote sensing, model evaluation, uncertainty quantification under climate change, and storylines or event attribution. The scope is global and includes unprecedented or record-breaking TCs, Medicanes or post-tropical transitions. Submissions addressing multi-hazard interactions, cascading and compounding effects, social vulnerability and exposure, as well as decision-support—such as early warning systems, risk communication, risk assessment, and appraisal of structural, nature-based measures and public policies—are encouraged.
title: Integrated advances in tropical cyclones: linking physics, impacts, risk and adaptation

description: Climate change and urbanisation increase climate risks and the negative consequences of extreme events. For instance, floods cost billions of euros of losses and result in thousands of fatalities every year. Accelerated adaptation by societies, including governments, insurance companies, households and others is urgently required. However, there are limits to the adaptability of societies. For instance, social vulnerability factors (e.g. income, education, etc.) may reduce households’ adaptation efforts. When societies stop implementing additional adaptation, risk may become ‘intolerable’, and adaptation limits may be reached. At such point, people may have to migrate to safer locations. However, very little is known about the extent to which societies can adapt, which factors drive these limits, and where and when limits to adaptation will be reached. This session welcomes abstracts considering how to conceptualise, assess, project and avoid adaptation limits. The session aims to facilitate discussions and cooperation about interdisciplinary research on adaptation and its limits by bringing together experts in climate, natural hazards and the social sciences. Relevant topics include, but are not limited to: • Where were soft or hard limits of adaptation reached already? • Which social and physical vulnerability constraints can lead to adaptation limits? • How to conceptualise and measure intolerable risk • Motivation for and hindrances of adaptation efforts • Simulation of adaptation and migration decisions • Quantification of adaptation effects
title: Limits of Adaptation

description: Floods and droughts have major impacts on society and ecosystems and are projected to become more frequent and severe with climate change. This session seeks to unite the flood and drought research communities by studying the similarities in their processes and study approaches to identify synergies. We aim to deepen understanding of the processes governing these hydrological extremes and their interplay, develop robust methods for data analysis and modeling of floods and droughts and their transitions, assess the influence of global change on hydro-climatic extremes, and study the socio-economic and environmental impacts of both types of extremes. We seek studies where: - (new) methods advance process understanding - the inclusion of that understanding advances indicators, analysis, and modeling. - methods are demonstrated to be fit for purpose, transparant, and robust. We welcome submissions that present insightful flood and/or drought research, including case studies, large-sample studies, statistical hydrology, and analyses of flood or drought non-stationarity under the effects of climate-, land cover-, and other anthropogenic changes. Studies that investigate both extremes, or their interplay, are of particular interest.
title: Hydrological extremes: from droughts to floods

description: Assessing the impact of climate variability and changes on hydrological systems and water resources is crucial for society to better adapt to future changes in water resources, as well as extreme conditions (floods and droughts). However, important sources of uncertainty have often been neglected in projecting climate impacts on hydrological systems, especially uncertainties associated with internal/natural climate variability. From one model to another, or one model realisation to another, the impact of diverging trends and sequences of interannual and decadal variability of various internal/natural climate modes (e.g., ENSO, NAO, AMO) could substantially alter the impact of human-induced climate change on hydrological variability and extremes. Therefore, we need to improve both our understanding of how internal/natural climate patterns affect hydrological variability and extremes, and how we communicate these impacts. We also need to understand better how internal/natural variations interact with various catchment properties (e.g., vegetation cover, groundwater support) and land-use changes. Developing storylines of plausible worst cases, or multiple physically plausible cases, arising from internal climate variability can complement information from probabilistic impact scenarios. We welcome abstracts capturing recent insights for understanding past, present, and future impacts of internal/natural climate variability on hydrological systems and extremes, as well as newly developed probabilistic and storyline impact scenarios. Results from model intercomparisons using large ensembles are encouraged.
title: Understanding and predicting the impact of climate variability on hydrological regimes and extremes

description: Large-sample hydrology (LSH) is essential for understanding and predicting hydrological variability and change across spatiotemporal scales. The field has advanced significantly in recent decades, supported by the growing availability of datasets including a large variety of hydrological systems. The session highlights recent advances in LSH, with a focus on understanding hydrological variability by making use of large-sample datasets, developing and improving these datasets, and working towards catchment classification and characterization. We welcome abstracts that contribute to these topics, particularly (but not exclusively) related to the following sub-topics: 1. Enhance process understanding based on LSH: How can we use large-sample datasets to improve and synthesize hydrological process understanding and to transfer knowledge obtained in well-monitored catchments to data scarce regions? How can we bridge and consolidate findings from large-sample analyses with our understanding of hydrological processes from well-monitored or experimental catchments? 2. Develop and improve large-sample datasets: How can we address current challenges, e.g., uneven spatial coverage, representativeness of catchment descriptors, dataset harmonization, and uncertainty quantification? How can we expand large-sample datasets by, e.g., including data at higher spatial and temporal resolution or real-time data? How can we ensure data quality? What new, unconventional data sources might be exploited? How can we (systematically) represent anthropogenic influences in large-sample datasets? 3. Advance hydrologic modeling: How can we improve process-based and data-driven modeling by using LSH? How can functional knowledge obtained from large-sample studies be transferred to ungauged basins or data-scarce regions through modeling? How can we develop new models and workflows to evaluate hydrological response under change, also with regard to human impacts? How can processes that extend beyond the topographic catchment boundaries, e.g., groundwater or water quality, be integrated into large-sample hydrological models? 4. Improve catchment classification and characterization: How can we use static and dynamic catchment descriptors available in large sample datasets to derive groups of catchments with similar hydrologic behavior? How can we improve catchment characterization, e.g., by developing and including new descriptors or replacing static with dynamic attributes?
title: Large-sample hydrology: Enhancing process understanding, advancing dataset development, and unifying insights through modeling

description: The space-time dynamics of floods are controlled by atmospheric, catchment, riverine and anthropogenic processes, and their interactions. The natural oscillation between flood-rich and flood-poor periods is superimposed on anthropogenic climate change and human interventions in rivers and catchments, such as the construction of reservoirs, alterations in river morphology, water retention capacity and land use. In addition, flood risk is further shaped by continuous changes in exposure and vulnerability. In this complex setting, it remains unclear what is the relative contribution of each factor to the space-time dynamics of flood risk. The scope of this session is to report when, where, how (detection) and why (attribution) changes in the space-time dynamics of floods occur. The session particularly welcomes presentations on attributing different drivers to observed changes in flood risk. Presentations on the impact of climate variability and change, land use transitions, morphologic changes in streams, and the role of pre-flood catchment conditions in shaping flood risk are also welcome. Furthermore, contributions on the impact of socio-economic factors, including adaptation and mitigation of past and future risk changes are invited. The session will further stimulate scientific discussion on the detection and attribution of flood risk change. Specifically, the following topics are of interest for this session: - Long-term changes in rainfall patterns and flood occurrence; - Process-informed extreme value statistics; - Interactions between rainfall distribution and catchment conditions in shaping flood patterns; - Detection and attribution of flood hazard changes, such as atmospheric drivers, land use controls, natural water retention measures, reservoir construction, and river training; - Changes in flood exposure: economic and demographic growth, urbanisation of flood prone areas, implementation of multi-scale risk mitigation measures (particularly structural defences); - Changes in flood vulnerability: changes of economic, societal and technological aspects driving flood vulnerability and private precautionary measures; - Multi-factor decomposition of observed flood damages combining the hydrological and socio-economic drivers; - Future flood risk scenarios and the role of adaptation and mitigation strategies.
title: Space-time dynamics of flood risk: processes, controls, and attribution

description: Research on changes in the pace of the water cycle dates back to the 1970s. In the last few decades, leveraging a number of new regional and global datasets, research has highlighted changes in the water cycle and distribution attributed to secular trends in relevant processes and/or to anthropogenic activities, such as irrigation, groundwater pumping, dam and reservoir operations. For example, studies have investigated changes in the rate of exchange across terrestrial water storages and land-atmosphere interactions using different datasets, including remotely sensed, modeled, or data-assimilated, and reanalysis products. Past studies have also differed in their period of analysis, regional focus, and methods for change detection, attribution, and uncertainty assessment. This session aims to provide a platform to present and discuss studies that seek to understand: (i) The current state of knowledge regarding the role of climatic change and human water management in influencing land-atmosphere interactions. (ii) How these factors result in accelerating or decelerating water cycle processes, with implications for droughts, floods, and other hydroclimatic extremes. (iii) Attribution of changes in water fluxes, storages, and land-atmosphere interactions to climate variability, long-term climate change, and human water and land management. (iv) Uncertainties and open questions related to this critically important research topic. Studies focused on change analysis of individual or integrated water cycle components and land atmosphere interactions using one or more of the above-mentioned data types and conceptual, coupled, or impact modeling techniques are encouraged, with either a regional or global focus. Contributions utilizing emerging observational capabilities, including gravity-based observations, surface water monitoring, and flux measurements, are particularly welcome. We also encourage studies that quantify and attribute changes in water fluxes, storages, and land-atmosphere interactions, highlight associated uncertainties, and disentangle the relative roles of climate variability, long-term climate change, and human water and land management. This especially includes interdisciplinary studies that improve our understanding of Earth system feedbacks and inform sustainable water management under global change.
title: The Beat of the Water Cycle: Measuring and Attributing Changes in Water Fluxes and Storage Across Scales, from Climate Feedbacks to Human Water Management

description: Global warming has fundamentally altered the statistical behavior of the Earth’s climate system, introducing non-stationarity across the atmosphere, oceans, and land. Variations in atmospheric circulation, such as shifts in monsoon systems, jet streams, and subtropical highs, have induced changes in oceanic dynamics, including sea surface temperature anomalies, altered circulation patterns, and marine heatwaves. These coupled atmospheric-oceanic processes, in turn, drive evolving hydroclimatic patterns on land, directly influencing precipitation regimes, streamflow variability, and the frequency and intensity of extreme events like floods, droughts, and compound extremes. This session aims to foster interdisciplinary discussion on detecting, modeling, and understanding non-stationarity across the interconnected Earth system. We invite contributions that assess or model non-stationarity in atmospheric, oceanic, or hydrological domains, along with its cascading impacts on hydroclimatic variability. We highly encourage research addressing individual and compound extremes, large-scale teleconnections, or regional climate responses. We also welcome submissions employing observational data analysis, climate and hydrological modeling, statistical and dynamical frameworks, and machine learning to explore how non-stationarity propagates across Earth system components. By integrating diverse perspectives from hydrology, atmospheric sciences, oceanography, and the broader geosciences, this session seeks to advance our understanding of evolving hydroclimatic extremes and support improved prediction, adaptation, and resilience strategies under a changing climate.
title: Hydroclimatic Variability and Non-Stationarity under Climate Change: Bridging the Atmosphere, Ocean, and Land Systems

description: Recent droughts in Europe (e.g. 2018 and 2022) have highlighted the vulnerability of temperate and subarctic regions to drought, and the threats it poses to ecosystems, agriculture, energy production, water resources and societies. However, much of the research body on drought focusses on hotter and drier regions, potentially under- or misrepresenting colder and wetter regions, and their complex behavior under droughts – including systems dominated by snow and glaciers to systems without, systems with shallow soils to systems with large groundwater bodies. This session aims to gather knowledge about droughts in cold- and temperate regions across the full chain from meteorological to hydrological drought, spanning water vapor, precipitation, soil moisture, streamflow, and groundwater. We especially welcome submissions related to the following topics: 1. Drought monitoring and forecasting, hereunder work related to drought indices, drought drivers and climate change 2. Drought impacts on society and ecosystems, including water resources, risk assessment, management, and governance. 3. Groundwater drought, including aquifer vulnerability, quality and quantity issues and anthropogenic impacts from abstraction and irrigation 4. Related hazards such as heatwaves and wildfires typical for cold- and temperate regions.
title: Droughts in temperate and subarctic regions: Cold, wet and vulnerable to droughts

description: A large number of micropollutants, also known as trace contaminants or emerging contaminants, and their transformation products (veterinary and human pharmaceuticals, pesticides and biocides, personal care products, organic pollutants such as PFAS or chlorinated compounds) and heavy metals pose a risk for soil, groundwater and surface water. The large diversity of compounds and of their sources makes the quantification of their occurrence in the terrestrial and aquatic environment across space and time a challenging task. Regulatory monitoring programs cover a small selection out of the compound diversity and quantify these selected compounds only at coarse temporal and spatial resolution. Carefully designed monitoring, however, allows to detect and elucidate processes and to estimate parameters in the aquatic environment. Modelling is a complementary tool to generalize measured data and extrapolate in time and space, which is needed as a basis for scenario analysis and decision making. Mitigation measures can help reduce contamination of groundwater and surface water and impacts on water quality and aquatic ecosystems. This session invites contributions that improve our quantitative understanding of the sources and pathways, mass fluxes, the fate and transport and the mitigation of micropollutants in the soil-groundwater-river continuum of catchments. Topics cover: - Novel sampling and monitoring concepts and devices - New analytical methods such as new detection methods for micropollutants, non-target screening - Experimental studies to improve process understanding and to quantify diffuse and point source inputs - Biogeochemical interactions and impact on micropollutant behaviour - Fate studies on parent compounds and transformation products - Modelling approaches (including hydrology and sediment transport) to simulate pollutant transport and fate at several spatial and temporal scales - Spatial and temporal monitoring to elucidate transport processes and to support modelling - Modelling tools for decision support - Setup of mitigation measures and evaluating their effectiveness. - Methods to evaluate water quality modelling uncertainty, and/or combining data and modeling (data assimilation)
title: Water quality at the catchment scale: measuring and modelling of micropollutants

description: Water temperature is crucial for ecosystems and society, and is strongly driven by climate, environmental and human factors. Extreme water temperature and variability can severely impact these systems by altering physical processes (e.g. lake evaporation and stratification), biological functioning (e.g. deoxygenation and fish mortality) or limiting the usefulness to humans (e.g. drinking water quality, cooling water use and power generation potentials). Water temperature is also used as a tracer for hydrological processes, enabling us to understand interactions of different hydrological components such as groundwater recharge, runoff processes and lake in- and outflow. This session aims to bring together freshwater temperature researchers from both the surface (i.e. springs, rivers, streams, lakes and reservoirs) and subsurface waters (i.e. soil and groundwater) communities, to shed light on the natural and anthropogenic processes governing freshwater temperature, and the resulting implications for ecosystem health, water resources management and sectoral uses. We are interested in spatio-temporal patterns and historic or future trends of water temperature and its extremes, their impact on aquatic biogeochemistry and ecosystems, as well as different types of water temperature modelling approaches (e.g. process-based, machine learning). We welcome submissions that investigate water temperature dynamics across various temporal and spatial scales (local to global) in any inland water bodies using field and lab experiments, large-scale and -sample analyses, and modelling approaches.
title: Freshwater Temperature: Local to Global Scales

description: Session Description The Anthropocene is characterized by unprecedented human pressures on aquatic environments, with rapid urbanization, industrialization, intensive agriculture, mining, and climate change increasingly affecting the quality and availability of water resources. Emerging and persistent contaminants—including pharmaceuticals, pesticides, heavy metals, nutrients, microplastics, pathogens, and other chemical pollutants—pose complex challenges to freshwater and coastal ecosystems and may create significant risks to human and environmental health. Understanding the sources, transport, transformation, fate, and impacts of these contaminants is therefore essential for safeguarding water security and ecosystem integrity. This session, “Safeguarding Water Quality in the Anthropocene: Contaminants, Health and Sustainable Management,” will bring together interdisciplinary research addressing contemporary and emerging challenges in water quality. Contributions are invited on contaminant monitoring and assessment, advanced analytical and sensing technologies, pollutant fate and transport, exposure pathways, ecological and human health impacts, risk assessment, and innovative approaches for water and wastewater treatment. The session will also explore nature-based solutions, circular approaches, remediation strategies, and data-driven and integrated frameworks for sustainable water-quality management. By connecting environmental science, hydrology, engineering, public health, ecology, and policy, the session aims to foster knowledge exchange and identify science-based pathways for protecting water resources and supporting resilient, healthy, and sustainable aquatic systems in the Anthropocene.
title: Safeguarding Water Quality in the Anthropocene: Contaminants, Health and Sustainable Management

description: This session advances modern water quality science by multi-platform observation, process-level understanding and intelligent governance. It highlights climate and human impact analysis, hybrid process–machine learning modelling, updated assessment standards, and smart digital management. We welcome cross-disciplinary work linking observation, simulation and governance, including transboundary water quality cooperation, to build more resilient, adaptive solutions for global water quality challenges. This session invites cutting-edge abstracts spanning the following priority research areas (topics are not restricted to the listed items):  Space–air–ground integrated monitoring systems for water quality assessment;  Novel monitoring technologies for the detection of pathogens and (micro)biological parameters;  Transport and transformation processes of nutrients, contaminants, and emerging pollutants  Impacts of ecological processes, climate change and human activities on water quality
title: From Sensors to Systems: Space–Air–Ground Integrated Monitoring, Hybrid Modeling and Digital Water Quality Management

description: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are persistent contaminants increasingly detected across terrestrial environments, from contaminated source zones and soils to the vadose zone, groundwater, and urban subsurface systems. PFAS persistence, mobility, complex sorption behaviour, precursor transformations, and interactions with air-water and soil-water interfaces in heterogeneous subsurface environments present challenges for understanding and predicting their long-term environmental fate. This session aims to bring together experimental, field-based, modelling, and remediation studies addressing PFAS as well as other emerging or traditional contaminants in terrestrial systems. We welcome contributions that: • Advance understanding of PFAS retention and mobilisation, source-zone behaviour, mass flux, transformation processes, and the performance and longevity of remediation technologies • Explore the influence of hydroclimatic variability, including changing recharge, drought, snowmelt, and extreme precipitation. • Map new contaminant pathways to soil and groundwater, including transport through urban subsurface environments and bedrock, where heterogeneous geological structures, preferential flow, infrastructure, and complex recharge conditions can influence contaminant migration. • Investigate soil-bedrock-groundwater interactions and emerging approaches for identifying and quantifying these pathways By connecting process understanding, field observations, modelling, and remediation, the session seeks to identify lessons learned, emerging challenges, and new pathways for predicting and managing persistent contamination in vadose zone and groundwater systems.
