Topics include: • PFAS/Contaminant fate and transport in vadose zone and groundwater systems, including surface water interactions • Sorption, interfacial processes, precursor transformations, and PFAS mass flux • Remediation technologies and long-term performance, including in-situ and on-site methods for stabilization, separation and destruction • Hydroclimatic and hydrogeological controls on PFAS mobilization and groundwater contamination • Model development and modelling studies • Urban and bedrock transport pathways connecting contaminated terrestrial environments to groundwater • Site characterization
title: PFAS contamination in terrestrial systems – fate, transport, remediation and modelling

description: Groundwater provides about 40% of all human water abstractions and is an essential water source for terrestrial ecosystems and freshwater biota in rivers, lakes, and wetlands, as well as a keystone ecosystem in itself. Aquifers span political and natural boundaries, connecting people, ecosystems, and different parts of the hydrological cycle. However, our large-scale understanding of groundwater processes and the connection between ground and surface waters is still limited. The development of global groundwater models and big-data assessments of groundwater monitoring data have helped to push the boundaries of our large-scale understanding of groundwater processes. In particular, knowledge of the exchange between surface and subsurface waters is essential for determining the water balance at larger scales. Surface and subsurface water exchanges and inter-catchment groundwater flow affect water, pollutant, and nutrient fluxes, bio-organisms in streams, and the groundwater itself. Additionally, human activities (e.g., pumping/irrigation) increasingly affect groundwater flow processes and the exchange between surface and subsurface waters. In this session, we want to highlight the increasing interest in the large-scale study of groundwater availability, quality, and processes (including groundwater recharge) and discuss current obstacles related to data availability and model design. Therefore, we seek contributions that address issues including: • Continental to global groundwater-related datasets • Regional to global big-data assessments with models and machine learning • Transboundary and inter-catchment assessments of groundwater processes • Identification of dominant controls on groundwater processes across large domains • Recent methodological developments for inclusion of small-scale hydrological processes into large-scale estimates • Surface-subsurface water exchange and its effects on hydrological extremes (drought/flood), water availability, and solute and pollutant transport • Effects of climate change, land use change, and water use change on global groundwater • Implications of large-scale groundwater understanding on monitoring design, integrated water management, and global water policies • Feedbacks between large-scale groundwater processes and groundwater users • Large-scale groundwater assessments related to the fulfillment of the UN sustainable development goals (SDGs)
title: Large-scale groundwater

description: Interactions between plants and their environment shape terrestrial fluxes, biochemical cycles, and agro-ecosystem productivity. However, we still lack detailed knowledge of how these interactions impact plant access to soil resources and, hence, plant growth, particularly under deficit conditions. The main challenge arises from the complexity inherent to biophysical and biochemical processes in soil and plants across multiple scales. To address these knowledge gaps, an improved understanding of soil-plant-related transfer processes is needed. Quantitative approaches that integrate across disciplines and scales constitute stepping-stones to foster our understanding of fundamental biophysical processes at the interface between soil and plants. This session targets research investigating soil-plant-related resource transfer processes across different scales (from the rhizosphere to the global scale) and welcomes scientists from multiple disciplines encompassing soil and plant sciences across natural as well as agricultural systems. We are specifically inviting contributions on the following topics: - Hot topics 2027: Heat and drought interactions, hybrid process-based and data-driven models - Bridging the gap between biologically and physically oriented research in soil and plant sciences - Measuring and modeling of soil-plant hydraulics and gas exchange, water, solute, and carbon fluxes through the soil-plant-atmosphere continuum across scales - Identification of plant strategies to better access and use resources from the soil, including under abiotic stress(es) - Experimental techniques such as non-invasive imaging and three-dimensional root system modeling tools - Novel experimental and modeling techniques assessing belowground processes such as root growth, root water, and nutrient uptake, root exudation, microbial interactions, and soil aggregation - Mechanistic understanding of plant water use and gas exchange regulation under drought and their implementation across scales (from cell to organ to single plant to agro- ecosystems, Earth system)
title: Soil-Plant Interactions

description: Sustainable groundwater management is becoming increasingly important as growing societal demands, environmental pressures, and climate change place unprecedented stress on water resources. Ensuring the long-term availability of groundwater requires an integrated approach that considers water quantity, water quality, ecosystem preservation, and society's needs. Effective management strategies must therefore account for both natural processes and human impacts, while enhancing the resilience of groundwater-dependent systems under changing climatic conditions. This session aims to bring together case studies and scientific contributions addressing the sustainable management and protection of groundwater resources. Contributions are invited on topics including, but not limited to: (i) the application of environmental tracers, hydrochemical methods, and isotopic techniques to investigate groundwater processes and anthropogenic impacts; (ii) groundwater and hydrogeological budget assessments for evaluating water availability and sustainability; (iii) approaches for preventing, managing, and mitigating groundwater degradation caused by overexploitation, contamination, competing water demands, and climate change; and (iv) the identification of key challenges, emerging pressures, and innovative solutions for groundwater governance and protection; and (v) studies applying the concept of regional groundwater flow systems to improve the understanding, assessment, and sustainable management of groundwater resources and groundwater-dependent ecosystems. Contributions covering local, regional, and continental-scale studies are welcome. The session is co-organized by the Regional Groundwater Flow Commission (RGFC) of the International Association of Hydrogeologists (IAH).
title: Sustainable Groundwater Management Through Integrated Hydrogeological Approaches

description: This session invites contributions that advance the understanding of groundwater in cold-climate hydrosystems. Groundwater in high-latitudes is controlled by prolonged cold winters, warm summers with intense vegetation growth, and precipitation distributed year-round. In these regions, atmospheric water is stored over winter as snowpack, soil frost commonly occurs, and permafrost may be absent, discontinuous, or temporary. Temperature plays a dominant role in cold-climate hydrogeological dynamics, making these systems particularly sensitive to global warming. In addition, these regions have recently experienced climate extremes, including unusually high temperatures and prolonged dry spells imposing new stresses. Land use and land cover are also climate-dependent, further exacerbating global change impacts. Across these regions, common hydrogeological patterns emerge: strong groundwater–surface water connectivity, widespread presence of wetlands, seasonality in groundwater recharge, short aquifer memory, typically low groundwater mineralization, and pronounced freeze–thaw impacts on infiltration and storage. Rapidly changing climate conditions are altering these dynamics, with implications for water resources, ecosystems, carbon and nutrient fluxes, and the resilience of communities and infrastructure. Despite the widespread anthropogenic and ecosystem reliance on groundwater in cold-climates, there remains a gap in understanding how groundwater systems will evolve under climate change. In response, this session invites topics on the characterization of hydrogeological processes and their seasonal variability, cryohydrogeological mechanisms, northern groundwater vulnerability, ecosystem and biogeochemical linkages, droughts and floods, post-wildfire hydrogeological responses, and the quantification of environmental and climate-change impacts on cold-climate groundwater resources. We also welcome studies addressing groundwater management, adaptation measures, and interactions with ecosystems and society. The session will provide a platform to exchange ideas on field methodologies (including geophysics), challenges of long-term and year-round monitoring (in situ and remote), advances in data-driven and modeling approaches (including coupled hydro-climate models), and strategies for mitigating the impacts of global change. All scales of investigation are of interest, ranging from laboratory and field scale processes to regional and sub-continental systems.
title: Groundwater in cold-climate hydrosystems : processes, changes, and adaptation

description: Observing soil moisture at the ground is essential to assess plant available water, manage water resources and calibrate, validate satellite products or environmental models and conduct climate impact studies. Unfortunately, the availability of in situ observations is very limited in space and time. Whereas the spatial distribution is biased towards the global North, the temporal availability of soil moisture time series is on average 10 years as can be seen from the largest archive of in situ soil moisture, the International Soil Moisture Network (ISMN). Apart of the data availability issues, a substantial amount of the in situ observations face data quality issues that might result from sensor deployment, sensor calibration, data processing or other error sources. This session will address issues in the development and deployment of state-of-the-art soil moisture observation networks, the financing of their long-term operation, data quality assurance, data imputation, and data scaling as well as sensor deployment and assessments of differences between these deployments. We further encourage contributions presenting developments of novel measurement techniques including citizen science initiatives and studies utilizing (primarily) in situ soil moisture to understand and assess hydrological processes, water availability, land-atmosphere feedbacks and soil moisture dependent hazards.
title: Advancing the monitoring, maintenance and utilization of in situ soil moisture

description: Blue and green water management is vital for sustainable and resilient food systems around the world. This is true not only in drylands, where any productive activity is deeply related to the understanding of soil hydrological behaviour, and irrigation and green water management are key for agroecosystems’ health (e.g. being a defence against desertification), but in every socio-ecological ecosystem. Also temperate or humid climates are, in fact, increasingly subjected to variations in the hydrological cycle, as well as to water scarcity and/or mis-management. Improper practices, which are not able to cope with climate-induced threats, may contribute to soil degradation and depletion of the available water resource. For example, incorrect irrigation techniques may lead to soil and groundwater salinization, with dramatic fallout on agricultural productivity. Irrigation expansion, and paradoxically -through complex socio-hydrological dynamics- also irrigation efficiency improvements, could lead to increasing water consumption and water scarcity conditions . On the other hand, the role of irrigation goes beyond the technological aspects: traditional irrigation is a cultural heritage, which is often structurally resilient, and which needs to be faced with an interdisciplinary approach involving humanities. This session welcomes contributions with a specific focus on: - The understanding of the soil hydrological behaviour and of the mass fluxes through the soil in both drylands and environments under actual or projected water stress conditions (e.g. water shortage and/or mis-management, compaction, salinization) - The understanding of the sociohydrological dynamics linking irrigation, green water, and soil management - The interaction between irrigation, soil hydrology (including deep drainage) and socio-economic impacts. - The analysis of the bio-geo-physical and social dynamics related to rainfed and irrigated agriculture in both arid and non-arid areas and oases, including rainwater harvesting, and managed aquifer recharge systems - The management of rangeland areas, including their restoration - The management and conservation of traditional irrigation systems, including the provision of co-benefits and ecosystem services This session is co—sponsored by the International Commission on Irrigation and Drainage (ICID - https://icid-ciid.org/home); and by the International Center for Agriculture Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA - https://icarda.org/).
title: Soil hydrology, soil sociohydrology and irrigation for sustainable and resilient food systems

description: The continuum approach is a classical framework to describe and understand the soil--water dynamics and the soil effective--stress state in unsaturated soils. This approach is robustly rooted in the definition of the soil--water constitutive laws (soil--water retention curve, soil hydraulic conductivity, Kirchhoff potential, etc.). They link the real soil and its model. Advancements along their development and the comprehension of their role stand at the intersection of experimental measurements, mathematical representation and modelling, numerical solutions, theoretical understandings and practical applications. This session aims at stimulating an interdisciplinary discussion about the state of the art and recent advances about soil--water constitutive laws and soil physical and hydrological properties, in the framework of a continuum approach and contributing to define its limits. Experimental, theoretical and numerical contributions are encouraged about, but not limited to, (1) scaling of soil--water constitutive laws and their changes in time and space as a consequence of seasonality, climatic changes, anthropogenic changes and pedogenesis; (2) physics of water--repellent soils, and of swelling, dispersive and collapsible soils; (3) constitutive laws for extremely dry conditions and for nearly saturated soils; (4) nonequilibrium and hysteretic behaviours; (5) limits of the Darcian approach in the presence of macroporosity; (6) heat transfer and dispersion; (7) freezing and thawing processes in permafrost; (8) mechanisms of incipient erosion; (9) mathematical functions of constitutive laws and their physical implications; (10) pedotransfer functions and database analysis. Advancements along those lines will have major implications in many fields, ranging from hydrology, to soil science and soil physics, agriculture and geotechnics.
title: Back to the soil--water constitutive laws: Where modeling meets Physics

description: The Critical Zone (CZ) encompasses natural and anthropogenic environments where air, water, soil and rock interact with ecosystems and society. Water connects these components through the transfer of matter and energy across a wide range of spatial and temporal scales. Although groundwater is a major reservoir within this integrated system, its role in linking surface and subsurface processes and in shaping the evolution of the CZ remains incompletely understood. The slow and heterogeneous dynamics of groundwater in particular make it challenging to identify how processes operating at different spatial and temporal scales interact and respond to environmental change. This session welcomes contributions exploring groundwater processes and their interactions with other CZ components, from local to regional scales and from short-term dynamics to long-term evolution. We encourage observational, experimental and modelling studies, as well as approaches combining these perspectives, including data-driven methods and insights from long-term observatories. Contributions may address natural processes, interactions within ecosystems, or anthropogenic influences, including the effects of climate and land use change on groundwater and CZ dynamics. Topics may include, but are not limited to: groundwater–surface water interactions and hyporheic processes; recharge, evapotranspiration and root-zone dynamics; groundwater-dependent ecosystems; weathering, solute and contaminant transport; mining-impacted and other human-modified systems; cold-region, coastal, karst and crystalline aquifers; and the use of tracers, isotopes and geophysics to constrain CZ processes. By connecting processes, observations and models, this session aims to foster a more integrated understanding of groundwater within the CZ. We particularly welcome studies that bridge disciplines and scales, and we strongly encourage early-career researchers to submit their work.
title: Groundwater in the Earth's critical zone: Connecting Processes, Observations and Models

description: This session focuses on the use of geophysical methods for characterising subsurface properties, states and processes in hydrology, hydrogeology, Critical Zone, contaminant transport, ecology and beyond. Topics of particular interest include groundwater flow and storage, aquifer and soil heterogeneity, soil moisture and vadose zone dynamics, transport processes and surface water–groundwater interactions, as well as the influence of subsurface heterogeneity on biogeochemical processes and microbial biodiversity. Geophysical methods can provide subsurface information at exceptionally high spatial and temporal resolution in a non-invasive manner. However, the interpretation of these measurements remains far from straightforward in many applications and a number of challenges persist. These include improving the quantitative use of geophysical measurements for hydrogeological model conceptualisation and parameterisation, resolving structural and hydraulic heterogeneity and extending quantitative hydrogeophysical investigations beyond laboratory and field scales towards the catchment scale. We therefore welcome submissions addressing advances in the acquisition, processing, analysis and interpretation of data obtained from geophysical and other minimally invasive methods applied to hydrogeological, hydrological, biogeochemical and contaminant-related problems. In particular, we encourage contributions on innovative experimental and numerical methods supporting model–data fusion, new concepts for coupled and joint inversion, and advances in petrophysical understanding of the relationships between geophysical properties and hydrogeological parameters, states and processes.
title: Hydrogeophysics: a tool for hydro(geo)logy, contaminant transport, ecology, and beyond

description: Information on groundwater residence times and flow paths can be used to understand the hydrological and biogeochemical functioning of aquifers including impacts of subsurface heterogeneities, seasonal and long-term changing climatic conditions, groundwater-surface water interactions and many other processes. Tracer and model based estimates on residence times and flow paths are valuable tools to protect groundwater dependent ecosystems, to estimate vulnerabilities and recovery times of aquifers impacted by pollution, to define drinking water protection areas and for planning sustainable groundwater use. The session wants to bring together experiences of applied resource management and advanced research using a wide range of different techniques including new tracers and advances in modelling techniques in variable aquifers at various spatial scales. Especially, welcome are presentations with new or not so frequently used tracers of long or short half-life.
title: Groundwater residence times and flow paths

description: Groundwater quantity and quality assessments traditionally rely on periodic observations, long-term trends, and threshold-based indicators. While these approaches underpin monitoring and regulatory assessment, emerging data and analytical capabilities raise a fundamental question: are we assessing groundwater through the wrong lens? Groundwater observations can provide information not only on system status, but also on aquifer dynamics and functioning. Aquifers receive climatic and anthropogenic forcing and transform these signals through their hydrogeological properties, storage, connectivity, memory, and characteristic response times. Understanding these dynamics can reveal how groundwater systems respond to pressures, whether their behaviour is changing, and how they recover from disturbances—information that may remain hidden when assessment is limited to trends, averages, or threshold exceedances. This session invites contributions exploring new ways to characterize and assess groundwater quantity and quality through the analysis of aquifer dynamics. We welcome studies using continuous and high-frequency records, multi-source observations, time-series analysis, dynamic indicators, response and recovery metrics, change detection, and other observational or analytical approaches. Particular interest is given to studies that characterize aquifer response, identify climatic and anthropogenic controls, detect changes in system behaviour, assess resilience, or translate dynamic information into meaningful indicators of groundwater condition. The aim is to explore how a better understanding of aquifer dynamics can complement conventional groundwater assessment and support more diagnostic and anticipatory approaches to monitoring and management. Ultimately, the session asks: what can groundwater dynamics tell us about the condition and evolution of aquifers that snapshots, averages, trends, and thresholds cannot?
title: Rethinking Groundwater Dynamics Beyond Trends and Thresholds

description: Groundwater recharge is a key component of the hydrological cycle and is essential for sustaining groundwater resources, ecosystems, agriculture, and water security. Climate change, land-use change, urbanization, and changing water-management practices are altering the magnitude, timing, and spatial distribution of recharge, creating new challenges for groundwater assessment and sustainable management. This session brings together researchers to advance understanding of recharge processes under changing environmental and anthropogenic conditions. We welcome contributions on climate impacts, land-use and agricultural effects, natural and managed aquifer recharge, groundwater–surface water interactions, and recharge estimation using field observations, tracers, remote sensing, geophysics, and modelling. We also invite studies using data-driven and machine-learning approaches to quantify and predict recharge. Contributions addressing uncertainty, scaling, emerging methodologies, and implications for groundwater sustainability and water security are particularly encouraged. The session aims to foster interdisciplinary discussion on how improved understanding and quantification of recharge can support resilient groundwater management in a changing world.
title: Groundwater recharge in a changing world

description: Coastal aquifers, pivotal freshwater reserves for millions worldwide, are increasingly vulnerable to seawater intrusion due to the joint impacts of climate change and intensive human activity. Rising sea levels, changing precipitation patterns, over-abstraction, land use change, and population growth intensify the stress on these valuable but fragile resources. As salinization threatens groundwater-dependent ecosystem health, agriculture, and urban water supplies, integrated approaches to monitoring, modelling, and managing coastal aquifers are urgently needed. This session invites contributions that advance understanding, prediction, and management strategies for minimizing seawater intrusion and ensuring sustainable water resources in coastal regions. We aim to foster interdisciplinary discussion on innovative concepts, methods, and policies that support resilience under global-change scenarios. We encourage submissions related to, but not limited to: -Field and modelling studies of seawater-intrusion processes in coastal aquifers -Impacts of climate change, including sea-level rise, extreme weather, and shifting recharge patterns, on groundwater salinization -Effects of groundwater pumping, land-use change, and urbanization on aquifer vulnerability -Advances in observation techniques, including hydrochemical and isotopic tracers, remote sensing, and geophysical methods -Integrated management strategies and decision-support tools for sustainable groundwater extraction and adaptation -Case stdies of coastal-aquifer restoration -Nature-based solutions and managed aquifer recharge (MAR) to enhance coastal-aquifer resilience -Socioeconomic, legal, and policy dimensions, including water quality, stakeholder involvement, and governance -Multi-scale approaches, from local to global perspectives
title: Integrated Water Resources Management in Coastal Aquifers: Seawater Intrusion in a Changing Climate and under Human-Impacted World

description: Groundwater is a crucial source of water that underpins, supports, or sustains entire habitats and biocoenosis, ranging from wetlands, riparian zones, caves, aquifers, springs, forests, grasslands, and coastal environments. Conversely, ecosystem processes can significantly influence groundwater quality and dynamics. These interactions involve a diversity of ecological and hydrological processes such as groundwater uptake by vegetation, stream–aquifer exchange, biogeochemical reactions in aquifers, bioturbation by groundwater resident fauna, and soil–plant–atmosphere interactions. As these feedbacks are tightly connected to land surface, GDEs can be highly sensitive and vulnerable to anthropogenic pressures such as land use (change), water withdrawal, and climate change. Conversely, GDEs can provide important buffering capacities to environmental variability and extremes, and present important forms of Nature-based solutions. Further, GDEs often support human activities, from supporting pastoral livelihoods to underpinning cultural values. Thus, understanding groundwater-ecosystem interactions is not only important for the field of ecohydrogeology, but moreover to inform management policies and strategies that holistically integrate ecological, hydrological, and social outcomes. This session seeks contributions that: highlight the role of groundwater in sustaining ecosystems; examine the impacts and feedbacks linking diverse ecosystem processes with groundwater quality and quantity; the detection and delineation (i.e., mapping) of GDEs across local to global scales; and introduce of new methods to analyze interactions between groundwater and dependent ecosystems. Submissions that advance data acquisition methods; local-scale in-situ studies; empirical data analysis; ecohydrogeological model simulations; scaling of processes and their detection from the plant to regional scales; the resilience of GDEs and their connected systems; socioeconomic and cultural interactions and meanings of GDEs; and analytical developments are equally welcome. The session seeks to include work on GDEs across a wide range of physiographic and social contexts, including surface, unsaturated, and saturated zones; urban, rural, and coastal environments; and a wide range of socioeconomic and sociocultural contexts.
title: Groundwater-Dependent Ecosystems: Processes, Feedbacks, Adaptations, and Resilience in a Changing World

description: Data-driven modelling continues to gain momentum within the groundwater research community, reflecting strong interest in machine learning, AI and innovative approaches integrating data-driven techniques with physical process understanding. Data-driven approaches, including time-series models, statistical methods, machine and deep learning techniques and emulators, are transforming how we study, manage and forecast groundwater systems. By learning from observations and other sources, these methods can complement or even substitute detailed process-based models. Advancements in physics-informed methods, spatiotemporal deep learning, probabilistic machine learning, foundation-model approaches and generative AI are rapidly expanding possibilities for groundwater science. We welcome novel methodological developments and practical applications addressing real-world groundwater management problems along the following topics: Methodological Advances -Modelling techniques and data-driven methods for predicting groundwater quantity/quality in space or time, such as machine learning, deep learning, statistical methods and time series models -Hybrid approaches combining machine learning with conventional physical based models, including physics-informed neural networks -Machine learning-based emulation of physical based models for enhanced modelling and data assimilation -Applications of generative AI and large language models for synthetic data generation, knowledge extraction and model development for groundwater research and management workflows Uncertainty and Interpretability -Uncertainty quantification and sensitivity analysis using machine learning techniques, including probabilistic forecasting, quantile regression and deep ensembles -Explainable and interpretable machine learning approaches to improve hydrogeological system understanding Data Handling and Transferability -Approaches for analysing big data and complex datasets from groundwater systems - Solutions for data scarcity, multi-source/scale/fidelity data integration, non-stationary time series and irregular time steps -Transferability and regionalization methods for spatial transfer to ungauged sites and temporal extrapolation to unseen conditions In session you will engage with researchers working at the intersection of data science, process-based modelling and groundwater quantity/quality. Join us to share your research and advance this dynamic field through knowledge exchange and discussion.
title: Data-driven, AI and hybrid groundwater modelling: methods, applications and challenges

description: Sustainable groundwater use depends on reliable estimates of groundwater recharge—a critical but difficult-to-quantify flux. Before water reaches the aquifer, surface inputs, vegetation, and vadose zone processes alter both its quantity and timing. Climate and land use changes, along with extreme events such as droughts and intense rainfall, further complicate the spatial and temporal dynamics of the recharge. Now more than ever, refining our understanding of recharge is critical to informing decisions and managing groundwater sustainably. This session offers a platform to exchange concepts, expertise, and methods related to groundwater recharge estimation across disciplines and application contexts. We invite contributions focusing on the estimation of groundwater recharge across multiple temporal and spatial scales, including studies that compare or combine different methods. Estimation approaches may be based on: • Field-based measurements from various compartments of the hydrological cycle: o Land surface water balance components o Vadose zone measurements (e.g. soil moisture) o Groundwater heads (water table fluctuations) o Discharge measurements (baseflow separation) o Environmental tracers for recharge estimation and model calibration (e.g., stable isotopes, radioisotopes, dissolved gases) o Including suggestions for improved monitoring concepts • Model-based approaches (local to global scale), such as: o Water balance models o Land surface models o Physically-based vadose zone or groundwater models o Hybrid or machine learning-supported methods o Groundwater time-series models • Upscaling strategies from point-scale to landscape-scale assessments • Varying temporal scales from short-term recharge quantification to long-term recharge trends (past or future scenarios) We welcome studies addressing recharge estimation for various purposes, including (but not limited to) agricultural water management and irrigation, forest management and ecosystem transition, groundwater resource planning, and sustainable management.
title: Multiscale Perspectives on Groundwater Recharge: From Field Observations to Integrated Models

description: Particles (inorganic particles, biocolloids, plastics) in environmental systems are of great concern because of their potential adverse effects on ecosystem functions, wildlife and human health. They may also alter the transport properties of dissolved contaminants and change the hydraulic properties of subsurface systems. On the other hand, engineered particles and biocolloids play an important role in site remediation and aquifer restoration. This interdisciplinary session fosters the exchange among scientists from hydrogeology, microbiology, ecotoxicology, engineering, and analytical chemistry in order to provide a general picture of the occurrence and fate of natural and engineered particles in aquatic and terrestrial systems. We are expecting contributions in the following fields: • occurrence, fate and transport of biocolloids, nanoparticles and other particles (microplastics, soot, ...) in aquatic and terrestrial systems • methods to detect, characterize, and quantify particles in aquatic and terrestrial systems • advanced experimental methods to test the behaviour of particles in aquatic and terrestrial systems (mesocosms, non-invasive imaging, ...) • interactions between biocolloids, particles and solid surfaces • biocolloid biodegradation in the presence of solids • toxicity of products generated from biological disruption of pollutants in the presence of biocolloids • adverse effects of nanoparticles on microorganisms • effects of climate change on biocolloid and nanoparticle migration • public health risks associated with water and air polluted with biocolloids and nanoparticles.
title: Emerging particles and biocolloids in terrestrial and aquatic systems

description: Society faces immense challenges when natural hazards and disease outbreaks co-occur. For example, in the midst of the COVID-19 pandemic, the immediate response after natural hazard events was often complicated, because of travel restrictions and local lockdown measures. This arguably led to increased exposure to other hazards such as earthquakes or tropical cyclones (e.g. the 2020 Zagreb earthquake, tropical cyclones Eta and Iota in Honduras). Natural hazards can also trigger the outbreak of diseases, such as cholera and outbreaks following the devastating floods in Pakistan in August 2022. The co-occurrence of natural hazards and diseases creates cascading effects that worsen the overall impact. Consequently, natural hazards can be associated with public health emergencies. A limited understanding of these cascading impacts creates operational, ethical, and decision-making challenges for society, disaster management, and humanitarian organisations. Building on the RiskKAN working group on disasters and diseases and the NHESS special issue "The convergence of disasters, diseases and health impacts", this session invites contributions on: - the probability and dynamics of (climate-sensitive) disease outbreaks following natural hazards; - health and health-system impacts as components of disaster risk; - the compounding of hazard exposure and disease burden under climate change; - integration of health metrics into multi-hazard risk frameworks; - new measurement approaches, including remote sensing combined with public health and socio-demographic data; - disease risk modeling for early warning systems and anticipatory action; - and the synergies and trade-offs of disaster risk reduction measures in outbreak contexts. This session focuses on hazard events and their interaction with disease dynamics and health systems, and the consequences for disaster risk management. We welcome quantitative, qualitative and mixed-methods work at any scale, and particularly encourage submissions from epidemiology, public health and humanitarian practice.
title: The convergence of natural hazards, health, and diseases

description: This session focuses on innovations in methods, tools and technologies for climate and multi-hazard risk assessment. The increasing interconnections between socio-economic, technological, and natural systems have increased risk complexity, raising the likelihood and impact of multi-hazard events, which are further amplified by climate change. This highlights the urgent need to develop and apply these innovative technologies and methodologies (such as Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML), digital twins, remote sensing, decision-support tools, early warning systems, stress testing methodologies) to effectively assess these interconnected and evolving risks. Unlike single-risk assessments, multi-risk approaches offer a holistic understanding of risk interactions and compounding effects, providing the evidence base for better-informed adaptation and management decisions. We particularly encourage submissions of research, case studies, and practical applications that showcase how these technologies provide valuable insights into the complexities of multi-risk dynamics under a changing climate, and optimise decision-making. We also welcome critical discussions of implementation challenges, barriers, and lessons learned from both successful and unsuccessful deployment experiences. Potential research topics include, but are not limited to: Examples of collaborative research efforts addressing implementation needs for real-world applications for climate and multi-hazard related risks AI/ML and other advanced methods for projecting multi-hazard risk dynamics under climate change scenarios Novel data collection technologies including LLMs, remote sensing for vulnerability and exposure mapping, and forensic assessment of past multi-risk events Resilience stress-testing for multi-hazard and high-impact low-probability events Innovative approaches in communications, knowledge-sharing, and capacity building across multi-hazard risk assessments and early warning systems Best practices for transferring innovations across different contexts and hazards Decision-support tools, open source software and novel risk assessment methods co-developed with stakeholders to enhance the preparedness of first responders and decision-makers to multi-risk.
title: Innovations in climate and multi-hazard risk assessment

description: Multi-risk events, intensified by climate change, environmental degradation and increasing human pressures, pose growing challenges to societies and ecosystems worldwide. The interaction between climate and social-environmental hazards, exposure and vulnerability can amplify impacts on food and water security, infrastructure, ecosystems, livelihoods and socio-economic development. While substantial advances have been made in understanding and modelling multi-risk events, applications remain relatively limited. Multi-risk approaches remain only limitedly integrated into disaster risk management, which continues to be largely organized around individual hazards, sectors and institutional mandates, limiting the ability to address interconnected and systemic risks. This session aims to bridge science, policy and practice by exploring how multi-risk knowledge can be mainstreamed into disaster risk management policies, planning processes and decision-making. We invite studies that explore how multi-risk concepts, methods, tools and evidence can inform disaster risk management across the cycle, from mitigation and preparedness to response and recovery. We particularly welcome contributions that explore the usability and uptake of multi-risk research in practice, as well as challenges and enabling conditions that shape its implementation. Contributions may address, but are not limited to: ● Real-world applications, evaluations and lessons learned from integrating multi-risk knowledge into disaster risk management; ● Development, evaluation and application of multi-risk early warning and early-action systems and preparedness strategies; ● Community-driven and participatory approaches to multi-risk disaster risk reduction and resilience building; ● Translation of multi-risk assessments, indicators, models and scenarios into actionable policies, plans and decisions; ● Risk awareness and communication approaches for making multi-risk information understandable and actionable beyond scientific communities; ● Integration of disaster risk reduction, adaptation, humanitarian action and development planning; ● Multi-risk-informed priority-setting, resource allocation and risk financing; ● Monitoring and evaluation approaches for assessing the effectiveness and outcomes of multi-risk approaches/systems in disaster risk management.
title: Bridging Science, Policy and Practice in Multi-Risk Research

description: Hazard interactions are becoming more frequent and consequential globally. Climate warming is increasing the chances of compound and cascading climate hazards, including extreme rainfall, storms, heat, and droughts. Risks can become further intensified when they interact with inland/coastal flooding, landslides, earthquakes, tsunamis, and volcanic eruptions. When hazards interrelate, impacts on people and infrastructure can exceed extremes, deepen disruption and slow recovery. While understanding of compounding and cascading disasters has advanced, these events continue to expose weaknesses in how risks are communicated, understood, and acted upon. Forecasts, probability statements, impact matrices and alerts are organised around single hazards - failing to represent interactions, overlapping impacts, evolving conditions, and spatiotemporal dependencies. Although many sectors have developed capabilities to assess multi-hazard impacts, impact-based operations and communications are not universally applied, requiring stronger coordination of user-centred practices. The challenge, therefore, lies in producing and translating knowledge to practice in ways that can enable greater understanding and action. Communication, a key determinant of behavioural response during disasters, remains a bottleneck in effective risk reduction. The gap between hazard forecasts and loss-minimising action lies in the failure to account for how warnings are received, understood, and acted upon. Alerts especially are a critical link in the chain of rapid response and can fail in complex scenarios of multi-hazards and divided attention. This session focuses on communication and alerting as central components of multi-hazard risk management, with the aim of exploring how interacting, compounding, and cascading hazards can be represented to make complex risk information more accessible, understandable, and practical for decision-making. We welcome contributions examining communication across the full chain - technological advances in alerting, risk assessment, trust and sense making to scientific underpinning of the local and community-level actionability. We encourage submissions that examine a) how uncertainty in the timing of cascading hazards can be communicated, b) how evolving impacts can be conveyed when the consequences of one event alter subsequent hazards, and c) how multi-hazard warnings and alerts can be made coherent and actionable while reflecting interconnected risks.
title: Multi-hazard risk communication: interactions, understanding, protective action, and challenges

description: This session will showcase innovative approaches to multi-(hazard) risk assessment and management, focusing on advancing the understanding of risk components (hazard, exposure, vulnerability, and capacity) in multi-hazard settings, as well as applications of multi-hazard thinking in disaster risk reduction (DRR) and climate change adaptation. Effective DRR and the translation of research results into practice require considering multiple hazards and their interactions as highlighted in international frameworks and reports, including the Sendai Framework, the IPCC’s AR6, and the EUCRA. Multi-(hazard) risk assessment examines how interactions among hazards shape exposure and vulnerability through hazard impacts and adaptation measures, particularly in the context of climate change and slow-onset hazards (e.g., droughts). Yet, conventional frameworks still often overlook interrelated hazards and risks, opening the door to unintended consequences. The session will highlight a spectrum of approaches to multi-(hazard) risk, from analysing hazard interactions and vulnerability dynamics to characterising multi-hazard exposure. It will also discuss good practices and persistent challenges in managing multi-(hazard) risk across spatial and temporal scales. Finally, the session will engage with work on societal implications of multi-hazards, including societal impacts and resilience to multi-hazards. By addressing the full risk management chain, this session will identify research gaps, synergies, and opportunities for collaboration across disciplines and hazard types. We welcome abstracts presenting original research, case studies, and critical reflections across the DRR cycle. Suggested topics include: - Multi-(hazard) risk methodologies addressing interacting hazards, exposure, vulnerability, and impacts; - Tools and frameworks for multi-(hazard) risk assessment and management; - Cross-sectoral approaches that integrate physical, social, economic, environmental, and institutional dimensions; - Implementation of DRR measures from a multi-hazard perspective, with attention to synergies and trade-offs between hazard-specific measures; - Multi-hazard early warning systems; - Societal implications of multi-hazard risks; - Resilience in the context of interacting hazards.
title: Multi-(hazard) risk assessment and management: innovative approaches for disaster risk reduction and climate change adaptation

description: Natural hazards rarely occur independently. Earthquakes can trigger landslides, landslides can dam rivers and generate floods, volcanic eruptions can induce mass movements and tsunamis, wildfires can alter hydrological and sediment transport processes, and changes in glaciers and permafrost can initiate sequences of slope failure, debris flow, and flooding. In such cascades, an initial process modifies the physical state of the system and controls the initiation, magnitude, timing, or propagation of subsequent hazards. Risk evolves with these cascades, as exposure and vulnerability are reshaped by each successive event. Damaged infrastructure, depleted response capacity, displaced populations, and altered land use can amplify the consequences of later hazards, so that dynamic vulnerability becomes a first-order control on cascading risk. Despite increasing attention to multi-hazard risk, the mechanisms governing these interactions remain poorly understood. Key questions concern how energy, mass, water, sediment, and stress are transferred between processes; how these processes interact; how antecedent conditions and event history influence subsequent hazards; and how feedbacks, nonlinearities, and differences in spatial and temporal scales control whether a disturbance attenuates or develops into a cascade. Answering these questions requires long-term observations to capture the slow preconditioning, relaxation, and recovery phases that link successive events, and allow rare but high-impact cascades to be placed in a meaningful statistical and process-based context. This session brings together research on the physical processes governing cascading natural hazards. We welcome observational, experimental, theoretical, numerical, and data driven studies addressing topics including: •Multiphysics modelling of triggering, coupling, amplification, and attenuation between hazard processes; •Transfer of mass, momentum, energy, stress, water, and sediment between interacting processes; •Reconstruction and analysis of well documented cascading events across different environments and spatial and temporal scales. •Field observations, Earth observation, geodetic, seismological, hydrological monitoring, and other measurements used to resolve process interactions; •Methods for identifying causal relationships and separating triggering from coincident or common forcing; •Effects of environmental and climatic change on the physical conditions controlling hazard cascades;
title: Cascading Multi-Hazards: Physical Processes, Interactions, and Dynamics

description: The increasing frequency, complexity and interconnectedness of disasters require a shift from hazard-specific approaches towards integrated multi-hazard disaster risk reduction and resilience. Interactions among hazards, exposure, vulnerability, capacity and changing climatic conditions can generate compound, cascading and systemic risks that challenge conventional risk assessment and disaster management approaches. This session will explore how geospatial intelligence, Earth Observation, Remote Sensing, GIS, Geospatial Artificial Intelligence (Geo-AI), machine learning, digital twins, cloud computing and real-time geospatial analytics can strengthen the understanding, assessment and management of multi-hazard risks. Contributions are encouraged across the disaster risk management cycle, including hazard and risk assessment, prevention and mitigation, early warning and impact-based forecasting, preparedness, emergency response, recovery and resilience building. The session welcomes research on multi-hazard and multi-risk assessment, hazard-exposure-vulnerability-capacity modelling, compound and cascading hazards, urban flood and drainage resilience; heatwave and climate-risk assessment, geophysical and geological hazard monitoring including landslides, permafrost and high-mountain hazards, geospatial approaches for environmental health risk assessment, multi-source Earth Observation and geospatial data fusion, multispectral, hyperspectral and InSAR-based monitoring, AI/ML and explainable AI, digital twins and decision-support systems, impact-based early warning, rapid disaster mapping and damage assessment and operational applications supporting disaster risk governance and decision-making. The session aligns with the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015-2030, EU Disaster Resilience Goals and the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, promoting science and technology-enabled approaches to understanding and reducing disaster risk, strengthening resilience, enhancing early warning and preparedness, and supporting risk-informed and sustainable development globally. The session aims to connect researchers and practitioners from natural hazards, geoinformatics, Earth observation, AI/data science, climate science and disaster risk management, with emphasis on translating scientific advances into actionable, risk-informed decision support for resilient communities and infrastructure.
title: Geospatial Intelligence for Multi-Hazard Disaster Risk Reduction and Resilience: From Risk Assessment to Early Warning, Preparedness and Response

description: Urban areas increasingly face interconnected challenges from heat, flooding, biodiversity loss, and ecosystem degradation, intensified by climate change and rapid urbanization. Green infrastructure and nature-based solutions can address these challenges by regulating urban temperatures, managing stormwater, providing habitats to species, and supporting ecosystem services. However, their effectiveness depends on vegetation characteristics, spatial configuration, environmental conditions, and interactions among ecological, hydrological, and climatic processes. This session invites contributions that use quantitative frameworks to assess, predict, and optimize the benefits and trade-offs of green adaptation. Contributions may address: 1. Modelling interactions among urban heat, flooding, biodiversity, and ecosystem processes under different green adaptation scenarios. 2. Computational modelling, machine learning, remote sensing, field observations, and data-driven approaches for hazard prediction and resilience assessment. 3. Effects of vegetation characteristics and spatial configuration on microclimate regulation, runoff reduction, habitat quality, and ecosystem functioning. 4. Synergies, trade-offs, uncertainties, and unintended consequences associated with green adaptation. 5. Planning, optimization, and spatial prioritization of nature-based solutions under climatic, ecological, social, and economic constraints. 6. Comparative studies across cities, climate zones, ecological settings, and adaptation strategies. 7. Social, governance, and equity dimensions, including the distribution of adaptation benefits and residual risks among communities. By bridging urban climate science, hydrology, ecology, and computational innovation, this session will advance understanding of how nature-based solutions can support multifunctional, equitable, and climate-resilient cities under global change.
title: Quantitative approaches to green adaptation for urban heat, flood, and ecological resilience

description: Despite rapid advances in compound-extreme research, the global evidence base remains geographically uneven. Many studies rely on long-term gridded datasets and reanalysis products, while observationally constrained regions, including South and Southeast Asia, Africa, the Middle East and North Africa, Central Asia and other parts of the Global South remain comparatively underrepresented. This session seeks to advance understanding of compound climate and hydrometeorological extremes in data-scarce and observation-limited environments. We welcome studies based on meteorological and hydrological observations, remote sensing, field campaigns, historical records, disaster databases, health and agricultural records, citizen science and other innovative sources of evidence. Particular emphasis will be placed on the observed impacts and local manifestation of compound events, rather than solely their statistical characterization or future projection. Contributions addressing observational challenges, uncertainty, scale mismatch, data reconstruction, exposure and vulnerability, cascading impacts, risk assessment and locally relevant adaptation are encouraged.
title: Compound Extremes Where Data Are Scarce: Observations, Impacts and Evidence from the Global South

description: Fieldwork is an essential component of geographical research, providing opportunities to test hypotheses, observe real-world phenomena, and measure natural in-situ process-interactions that are essential for calibrating and validating theoretical and physical models. However, even with the best planning, the reality of capturing real-world phenomena can prove challenging, with unforeseen failures with technology, inclement weather, and broken or missing hardware threatening to halt further data collection. As such, fieldwork often requires technological or methodological innovation on a limited budget with minimal resources in short timeframes. This interactive session seeks to pool the diverse fieldwork experiences from researchers working across the full range of geographic environments to empower the next generation of field researchers and build resilience into their field expeditions, thus maximising the potential for data capture and strengthening confidence in the field. We specifically seek solutions to common or unanticipated challenges, as well as challenges that are less well broadcast in the field and ultimately develop an online community case book. We invite researchers and technicians from all career stages with experiences spanning the full spectrum of geographic research to contribute to the session and particularly encourage contributions from early career scientists, teachers, those who lead or plan educational fieldtrips, and those from diverse backgrounds.
title: Field Fails: Building resilience against the unanticipated challenges of geographic fieldwork

description: 'In this session we encourage contributions of general interest within the Higher Education community which are not covered by other sessions. The session is open to all areas involving the teaching of geoscience and all related fields in higher education with a particular interest in current innovations and trends in geoscience education research. Examples might include describing a new resource available to the community, presenting a solution to a teaching challenge, pros and cons of a new educational technique/technology e.g. generative AI and chat bots, linking taught science content to societally relevant challenges/issues, developing critical thinking skills through the curriculum and effective strategies for online/remote instruction and/or hybrid/blended learning. Our intent with this session is to foster international discourse on common challenges and strategies for people teaching in higher education - let's share, discuss, reflect and develop effective practice and educational scholarship.
title: Open session on Teaching and Learning in Higher Education

description: Storylines, defined as “physically self-consistent unfoldings of past events, or of plausible future events or pathways,” can be used to describe risks and impacts of climate-driven trends or extreme events while making uncertainty, assumptions and decision relevance explicit. They provide a powerful framework to investigate short- to long-term climate risk pathways driven by the interplay of hazard, exposure, vulnerability and response capacity, including compound and cascading risks, stress testing of systems, and intervention options in uncertain futures. As boundary objects across climate science, disaster risk reduction, adaptation, social sciences and operational decision-making, they can support dialogue across disciplines, but also reveal that communities do not always share the same definitions, evidence standards or expectations of use. This session brings together researchers and practitioners working across climate science, impacts and risk assessment, disaster risk reduction, social sciences and decision practice to advance the physical understanding, methodological development and application of climate risk storylines. We welcome contributions that span the full chain from physical climate modelling and event attribution to impact analysis, participatory co-production, and the translation of scenarios into real-world decision contexts. We invite abstracts that address, among others: a) Physical and impact-based climate storylines, including past events, attribution studies, downward counterfactuals and plausible future extremes b) Methods for integrating quantitative and qualitative knowledge, and linking climate and non-climate risk drivers across scales c) Conceptual models and frameworks for combining hazards, exposure, vulnerability, response capacity and cascading impacts d) Applications of storylines and scenarios for stress testing, impact and risk assessment, early warning systems, adaptation planning and policy support e) Participatory and co-production approaches that enhance relevance, transparency, robustness and uptake for decision-making f) Reflections on terminology, quality criteria and responsible translation of storylines across scientific, policy and practice communities By bridging physical modelling, socioeconomic pathways and stakeholder-driven approaches, this session aims to strengthen the role of storylines as shared, transparent and actionable tools for managing climate risks in a rapidly changing world.
title: Climate Risk Storylines: From physical modelling to co-production for decision-making

description: Recent advances in physical and statistical modeling based on seismicity patterns provide new insights into the preparation of large earthquakes and the temporal, spatial, and magnitude evolution of seismicity. Improvements in monitoring technologies now deliver seismic data of unprecedented quality and quantity. Earthquake catalogs are more complete and accurate than ever, and many are now publicly available, enabling analysis of understudied regions and expanding global knowledge. New-generation catalogs, sometimes compiled with machine learning, reveal seismicity structures in ways not previously possible. Additionally, geodetic, geological, and geochemical data, fluid analyses, laboratory experiments, and earthquake simulators generating synthetic catalogs help refine models and test hypotheses. Integrating these multidisciplinary perspectives enhances our understanding of earthquake generation. To exploit these datasets, statistical approaches and machine learning are essential. These tools uncover hidden relationships and clustering and address challenges of data inhomogeneity, paving the way for deeper understanding and more robust forecasting. We invite contributions on developments in physical and statistical modeling and machine learning, including: • Spatial, temporal, and magnitude properties of earthquake statistics • Earthquake clustering analyses • Earthquake forecasting, including related software and methods • Effects of fluid diffusion and geodetic deformation on seismicity • Applications in understudied regions (e.g., Africa, Southeast Asia) • Quantitative testing, data requirements and validation of models • Machine learning and pattern recognition applied to seismic data • Model uncertainty quantification • Reliability and completeness of catalogs • Time-dependent hazard assessment
title: Machine Learning and Statistical Models Applied to Earthquake Occurrence

description: Changes in the natural and/or artificial electric, magnetic and electromagnetic fields have been observed during the past few decades in relation with the earthquakes and with the tectonic processes. For example, disturbances in the ground electric currents, in the geomagnetic field, in the VLF-LF-MF radio signals as well the appearance of electromagnetic emissions in the frequency range from ULF to VHF have been revealed. Usually, these effects take place before the occurrence of earthquakes, so that seismic precursors can be pointed out. In particular, a clear lithosphere-atmosphere-ionosphere coupling (LAIC) appears. This session will focus on: (1) electric/magnetic signals and electromagnetic emissions related to seismic-tectonic activity; (2) disturbances in the electromagnetic wave propagation in the lithosphere, atmosphere and ionosphere related to the previous activity; (3) underlying mechanisms of lithosphere-atmosphere-ionosphere coupling; (4) seismic electric/magnetic and electromagnetic precursors revealed by ground/satellite data; (5) laboratory experiments and theoretical models. Reviews of the past worldwide results as well presentations of future research plans are welcome. Likewise results on different precursors of earthquakes observed in ground and atmospheric parameters as well by mathematical-statistical analysis are welcome.
title: Electromagnetic phenomena related to seismic/tectonic activity, seismic precursors and lithosphere-atmosphere-ionosphere coupling during earthquakes/atmospheric events

description: Mitigating earthquake disasters involves several key elements, from hazard assessment to impacts quantification and reduction. Core components are: a) The analysis of hazards– assessing ground shaking and cascading effects on natural/built environments; b) The assessment of vulnerability and exposure to hazards, for buildings, infrastructures and people (including social vulnerability); c) Risk management – from short-term emergency response and recovery, to long-term governance and preparedness actions. Given the complexity of earthquake related hazards and their impact on different systems, diverse seismic hazard and risk models are needed at multiple spatial and temporal scales. These rely on multi-disciplinary data, and require testing and validation of all components to ensure effective mitigation. We therefore invite contributions on seismic risk research and assessment, covering: - Development of physical/statistical models, including AI and machine learning for hazard, exposure and vulnerability; - Assessment of earthquake hazard and risk across scales, as well as their validation against observations; - Time-dependent hazard and risk assessments, including the impact of aftershocks; - Assessment of cascading hazards (e.g. earthquake induced landslides and tsunamis) and development of multi-risk scenarios; - Development of systems providing post-event information, such as early warning and alerts for effective emergency management; - Social vulnerability and mitigation challenges, from assessment to governance, along with advances in communication, citizen-science and risk awareness research. This interdisciplinary session aims to foster knowledge exchange, share best practices, highlight current gaps, and outline future research directions.
title: Advances in seismic risk assessment and mitigation

description: Assessing the time-dependent probability of earthquakes and anticipating their cascading effects—including earthquake-generated tsunami waves and volcanic unrest—remain major challenges in Earth sciences. Recent advances in ground-based and spaceborne observations, laboratory experiments, numerical modelling, statistical analysis, computational methods and data-driven approaches offer unprecedented opportunities to investigate preparatory processes and evolving hazards by integrating heterogeneous observations across the different domains of the Earth system. The session aims to foster interdisciplinary discussion on earthquake-related processes and to assess critically how multiparametric observations, physical knowledge and advanced data-analysis methods can improve our understanding, forecasting and time-dependent assessment of seismic and volcanic hazards and their impacts. Particularly welcome are studies addressing: - Ground-based and satellite observations of electric, magnetic, electromagnetic anomalies potentially associated with impending seismic and volcanic activity; - Multi-parametric seismological, geodetic, geological, geochemical, hydrological, atmospheric and ionospheric observations; - Lithosphere Atmosphere Ionosphere Coupling (LAIC) and related measurements; - Transient deformation, fluid-related processes, seismicity patterns, earthquake-generated tsunami waves and other coupled phenomena; - Possible relationships between seismic processes, Earth tides, lunar forcing, solar–Earth interactions and Space Weather; - Theoretical models, numerical simulations and long-term data-analyses; - Artificial intelligence, machine learning and deep-learning methods for anomaly detection, data integration, forecasting and uncertainty assessment. Contributions presenting results from new instruments, innovative observational infrastructures and current or forthcoming satellite missions investigating atmospheric, ionospheric and electromagnetic disturbances potentially related to seismic and volcanic activity are especially encouraged. Further contributions may focus on real-time monitoring, multimission and multiplatform data integration, open-data services and interoperable platforms supporting the development of integrated Earthquake Observing Systems.
title: Short-Term Earthquake Forecasting (StEF) and Time-Dependent Assessment of Seismic Hazard (t-DASH) through Earth Observations and Data-Driven Approaches

description: Why do soils that appear similar in properties respond so differently under cyclic loading? The answer lies in processes at the grain scale: changes in particle contacts, fabric, and pore structure that govern pore-pressure build-up, strain accumulation, and strength degradation. While engineering predictions are typically made at the scale of laboratory specimens, soil deposits, slopes, or geotechnical systems, bridging these scales remains a challenge, especially for soils containing fines or exhibiting complex gradation and fabric. This session examines cyclic soil behaviour from various angles. We invite contributions involving laboratory and physical modelling, advanced imaging techniques, discrete element (DEM) and particle-based methods (SPH, MPM, etc.), constitutive and continuum modelling, and field observations and case histories. Special emphasis is placed on studies that use observations at one scale to better explain or improve predictions at other scales. Relevant topics include stiffness degradation, pore-pressure buildup and dissipation, cyclic mobility, liquefaction, strain localisation, post-cyclic strength, settlement, lateral spreading, slope stability, and large deformations. Contributions may concentrate on a specific method or scale, as long as they enhance understanding of how soil behaviour evolves from grain-scale mechanisms to ground response and failure.
title: From Grain-Scale Mechanisms to Ground Response and Failure: Bridging Scales in Cyclic Soil Behaviour

description: This session focuses on the hydrogeodetic measurement of water bodies such as rivers, lakes, reservoirs, floodplains, wetlands, and groundwater. The measurements relate to estimating water levels, extent, storage, discharge and runoff through the combined use of remote sensing and in situ observations, and their assimilation in numerical models, data-driven and machine learning approaches, leading to both hindcasts and forecasts. Detailed monitoring of water bodies plays a key role in assessing water resources, understanding water dynamics, characterising and mitigating water-related risks and enabling integrated and sustainable water resources management of aquatic ecosystems. While in situ measurement networks play a central role in the monitoring effort, remote sensing techniques provide homogeneous spatiotemporal measurements in near real-time with great spatial coverage and long time series. The combined use of in situ observations, remote sensing, machine learning approaches, and numerical modelling can provide new insights into the impact of climate change on water bodies from local to regional and global scales. During the past three decades, a large number of satellites and sensors has been developed and launched, allowing to quantify and monitor the extent of open water bodies (passive and active microwave, optical), the water levels (radar/laser altimetry), the global water storage and its changes (variable gravity). River discharge, a key variable of hydrological dynamics, can be estimated by combining space/in situ observations and modelling, although it remains still challenging with available spaceborne techniques, particularly in poorly gauged and ungauged regions. Additionally, we welcome studies developing multi-mission integration, data fusion, uncertainty characterisation, calibration and validation, data assimilation, machine learning, and forecasting approaches for water body applications. Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) is also commonly used to understand wetland connectivity, floodplain dynamics and surface water level and extent changes. We also welcome submissions on maturing recent technologies like fully-focused SAR Altimetry, and on the growing exploitation of SWOT observations, providing remarkable hydrology-related opportunities, as well as submissions of pre-launch studies for CRISTAL, Sentinel-3C/3D/3NG/6NG, MAGIC/NGGM, Guanlan, HY-2 and SmallSat constellations e.g., the SMASH concept now called REVALTO.
title: Water Level, Extent, Storage, Runoff and Discharge Integrating Remote Sensing, In Situ Observation and Numerical Modelling

description: Chemical reactions between fluids and minerals continuously reshape porous and fractured rocks. Dissolution, precipitation, cementation, and mineral replacement alter pore geometry and connectivity, changing the pathways through which fluids and solutes reach reactive sites. The resulting feedbacks between reaction and transport can amplify or suppress heterogeneity and generate recognizable structures across a wide range of spatial and temporal scales. This can be illustrated by acidization wormholes, karst networks, reactive melt channels in magmatic rocks, and diagenetic features such as concretions, reaction fronts and precipitation and/or dissolution patterns. The underlying challenge is common to all of them: how reactions in individual pores become expressed as large-scale patterns and as changes in porosity and permeability — a question shared across sedimentology, geochemistry, hydrology, petrophysics, and geophysics. It matters wherever reactive flow must be predicted or engineered: carbon storage and mineralization, hydrogen production, geothermal energy, hydrocarbon recovery, nuclear waste repositories, and contaminant transport and remediation. This field covers approaches, methodologies, and scales of a wide variety. X-ray imaging, microfluidics, and other in situ methods now resolve local mineral reactions as the geometry of the medium evolves. Computational advances bridge pores, fractures, laboratory samples, and field systems. Rock record study shows how these processes accumulate and interact over geological time, on timescales no experiment can reach. Thereby, we invite contributions on reactive transport and diagenesis from experiments, field observations, theory, and computation. Studies may address dissolution, precipitation, cementation, mineral replacement, authigenesis, water-rock interaction, or biogeochemical transformations. They should investigate the consequences of these processes on porosity, permeability, flow localization, and pattern formation. Work at any scale is welcome; from single pores and table-top experiments to hydrogeological systems and sedimentary basins.
title: Reactive transport and diagenesis: from pore-scale reactions to large-scale patterns

description: This session pays tribute to Hannes Flühler - a scientific leader and mentor, and the 2004 EGU John Dalton Medalist. The session celebrates Hannes’s many contributions to soil physics and vadose zone hydrology. His creativity and optimism in addressing flow and transport processes in unsaturated porous media were always guided by the cautionary principle of “digging deeper”. Meaning that we must revert to physical fundamentals and question incomplete explanations to observations. His approach is even more relevant today where artificial intelligence and computational capacity transform data analysis and modelling, enabling consideration of increasingly complex scenarios across hydrology, land-surface science, plant physiology and agronomy. Meanwhile, societal expectations concerning soil health, ecosystem resilience and food security create new demand for rigorous soil physics offering new opportunities, but also a risk that sophisticated computations may obscure fundamental gaps in understanding. An illustrative example of these contemporary challenges is taken from work of Hannes Flühler (Flühler et al., 1976). Field measurements of unsaturated hydraulic conductivity differ markedly from laboratory measurements and model predictions, which naturally raise questions about the transferability of hydraulic descriptions from laboratory to field conditions. The example motivates us to take a deeper look at the physical basis and applicability of our description of soil processes. In the spirit of Hannes Flühler’s approach, we invite contributions that dig deeper into fundamental questions in soil physics and hydrology. We encourage early career scientists and students to submit their work to this session. We welcome experimental, theoretical and computational studies that investigate discrepancies between observations and predictions, examine how soil structure and moisture history affect flow and transport, and test the transferability of hydraulic descriptions across scales and changing environmental conditions. Flühler, H., Germann, P., Richard, F., & Leuenberger, J. (1976). Bestimmung von hydraulischen Parametern für die Wasserhaushaltsuntersuchungen im natürlich gelagerten Boden. Ein Vergleich von Feld‐und Laboratoriumsmethoden. Zeitschrift für Pflanzenernährung und Bodenkunde, 139(3), 329-342.
title: Frontiers in hydrology and soil physics

description: Water in the snowpack and in glaciers represents an important component of the hydrological cycle in many regions of the world and is crucial to sustaining life during dry seasons. Predicted impacts of climate change in catchments with snow and/or glacier cover (i.e., shifts from snowfall to rainfall, modified total precipitation amounts, earlier snowmelt, and shrinking glacier cover) will affect water resources availability for environmental and anthropogenic uses at multiple scales, with implications for energy production, agriculture, drinking water provision, as well as for water water management and ecosystems. Runoff generation in catchments that feature snow or ice profoundly differs from purely rainfed catchments. Yet, our knowledge of snow/ice accumulation and melt, meltwater flowpaths, meltwater contribution to runoff, and the evolution of these catchments' hydrological regime in a changing climate, remain highly uncertain. This is due to both limited availability and inherently high spatial variability of hydrological and meteorological data. This session welcomes contributions on the following topics (but is not limited to these): - Experimental research on the physical processes determining snow and ice melt runoff and their potential implementation in hydrological models; - Development of novel strategies for snow and ice melt runoff modelling in diverse and/or changing climatic and land-cover conditions, including glacier retreat - Evaluation of remote-sensing or in-situ snow products and application for snow and glacier melt runoff calibration, data assimilation, streamflow forecasting or quantification of the physical properties of snow and ice - Studies exploring glacier and snow meltwater through stable water isotopes, including experimental investigations and development of isotope-enabled snow and hydrological models - Studies addressing the impact of climate change and/or extreme events, e.g., droughts, on the water cycle of snow and glacier affected catchments - Studies targeting snowpack, snowmelt, glacier, ice melt or runoff time series reconstruction or reanalysis over long periods to fill data gaps
title: Snow and glacier hydrology

description: The behaviour of ice sheets, ice shelves, and glaciers is strongly influenced by the geology, structure, and evolving boundary conditions of the solid Earth beneath and around them.
