From mantle dynamics and crustal architecture to subglacial topography, geothermal heat flux, and basement geology, these boundary conditions influence ice-sheet and ice-shelf dynamics and their response to climate change. However, their representation in the numerical models used to project future sea-level rise remains subject to significant uncertainties. Growing amounts of geological and geophysical data from Antarctica, Greenland, and other ice-covered regions have improved our understanding of these solid Earth–ice interactions, yet many connections between geological boundary conditions and ice-sheet, ice-shelf, and glacier behaviour remain poorly constrained. This session seeks to bring together research spanning mantle-to-crustal-scale processes, tectonic and geodynamic controls (e.g., rifting, uplift, exhumation), and surface and subglacial boundary conditions (e.g., subglacial topography, sub-ice shelf bathymetry, geothermal heat flux, subglacial geology, basal sediment and water distribution) that together provide critical constraints on ice behaviour. This session aims to link deep Earth processes with the boundary conditions that govern ice-sheet and ice-shelf behaviour, thus aiming to foster dialogue across the solid Earth, geodynamics, and cryosphere communities and to explore implications for past, present, and future ice stability. While we anticipate particular interest in the Cenozoic evolution of the Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets, contributions addressing older glacial events and the deeper-time geological drivers of glaciation are equally welcome. Contributions addressing solid Earth-ice interactions across a range of spatial and temporal scales are encouraged, and we invite studies using geophysical measurements, geological and geochronology data, and/or numerical geodynamic/landscape-evolution/ice-sheet modelling approaches.
title: Geological and tectonic controls on ice sheets and ice shelves: boundary conditions from mantle to surface

description: The evolution of glaciers, ice caps, and ice sheets can have a profound impact on the Earth system. Ice mass growth and decay results in the fluctuation of sea levels, alteration of global air and ocean circulation patterns, sculpting of the landscape, and reorganisation of continental drainage. Landforms and sediments provide important information about the dimensions, distribution, and dynamics of former ice masses. This record can be used to understand ice dynamics, reconstruct climate, and refine our understanding of the future response of ice masses to variations in climate. The glacial geological record is also often compared with observations of the modern-day processes at work on Earth. The aim of this session is to bring together researchers focused on reconstructing past glaciations and understanding glacial processes at all spatial scales and from all parts of the world. We welcome studies of all relevant aspects, for example (i) glacial landforms and sediments, (ii) glacial reconstructions and chronologies, (iii) glaciologic and climatic interpretations, and (iv) numerical modelling. While the focus of the session will be Quaternary glaciations, studies from any geological period are encouraged to fully address the diversity of the topic.
title: Deciphering the record of glaciations through space and time: lessons for the future

description: The marine-grounded basins of East Antarctica hold many metres of sea level potential. Some of their outlet glaciers are exhibiting signs of thinning and retreat, and in one case, an ice shelf has collapsed. Projections of the region's future have reduced confidence due to uncertain boundary conditions, among other factors. The understanding of regional natural climate variability remains low, and uncertainty on basin ice-mass balance is high. Change in this basin will impact sea level, ocean circulation, and regional marine ecosystems. This session will focus on evidence from the past, observations from the present, and new projections to, together, advance our understanding of the East Antarctic Ice Sheet's future. The session expects to receive work presenting existing and newly collected data from regions of East Antarctica where the ice sheet is grounded below sea level. Topics of interest include holistic studies on processes regulating ice dynamics, like subglacial hydrology, ice sheet grounding, ice shelf melt, ice shelf cavity regime transition, water stratification and circulation, dense water production and sea ice change. Data and models aimed at reconstructing ice mass and subglacial topography changes as well as continental margin and ocean circulation at regional scale are also included in this session, as ice-ocean-bedrock interactions strongly depend on the evolution of the basin’s geological boundary conditions.
title: Past, present, and future of East Antarctic marine-grounded basins

description: Recent changes across the Antarctic atmosphere–ocean–cryosphere system have been profound, and projections suggest that many of these changes will continue or even accelerate. These changes arise from interactions spanning scales from turbulent boundary-layer exchange and individual weather systems to basin-scale ocean circulation and large-scale atmospheric variability. These components are often studied separately, despite forming connected physical pathways. Large-scale circulation and storm tracks modulate cyclones, katabatic winds and air-mass intrusions; atmospheric heat, moisture and momentum fluxes affect sea-ice formation, drift, export and polynya activity; sea-ice changes modify air–sea exchange, ocean stratification, mixing and continental-shelf circulation; and ocean heat and freshwater exchanges influence ice-shelf basal melting, cavity circulation and downstream climate feedbacks. Resolving these multiscale pathways is essential for understanding recent Antarctic change and improving future projections. We invite contributions based on in situ observations, field campaigns, satellite remote sensing, reanalyses, theory, process studies, regional coupled models and Earth system models. Topics include multiscale atmospheric forcing of sea ice, polynyas and ice shelves; interactions among katabatic winds, cyclones, large-scale circulation and surface fluxes; feedbacks from leads and open water to the atmospheric boundary layer; sea-ice–wave–ice-shelf interactions; upper-ocean buoyancy forcing, stratification and convection; continental-shelf circulation, dense-water formation and export; ice-shelf meltwater and coupled feedbacks; and emergent behaviour under future climate change. We particularly encourage studies that connect two or more components through testable physical mechanisms, quantify interactions across weather-to-climate scales, assess observational or modelling uncertainties, or identify priorities for future observing systems and coupled-model development.
title: Multiscale Atmosphere–Sea Ice–Ocean–Ice Shelf Interactions in a Changing Antarctic Climate

description: Understanding hydrological processes in drylands, from hyperarid to semi-arid regions, is a major research challenge, particularly under increasing pressure from climate change, land-use change, and water scarcity. These regions, which span over 40% of the Earth’s land surface and support more than two billion people, face complex hydrological challenges due to their high climatic variability. Their limited water resources are characterized by strong climatic variability, intermittent flows, and complex interactions between rainfall, soils, vegetation, surface runoff, and groundwater. This session welcomes contributions that improve our understanding of key hydrological processes in drylands (such as semi-arid zones in the Mediterranean or hyperarid ones in the Sahara and other desertic areas), including rainfall variability, infiltration and runoff generation mechanisms, antecedent soil moisture controls, hydrological connectivity, transmission losses, evapotranspiration, and groundwater recharge. We particularly encourage studies addressing the episodic and threshold-driven nature of hydrological responses, surface–groundwater interactions, and the challenges of monitoring and modeling water fluxes across scales. Given the scarcity of long-term observations in many dryland regions, notably in the Global South, we also welcome approaches combining field observations, remote sensing, novel monitoring techniques, citizen science, and modeling. Studies examining how climate and land-use changes may alter hydrological processes and water availability are especially encouraged. By bringing together observational, experimental, and modeling perspectives, this session aims to improve process-based understanding of dryland hydrology and identify pathways towards more resilient water systems in dryland regions.
title: Hydrological processes in dryland catchments

description: Advances in hydrological science and technology are transforming water resource management and mitigating water and food insecurity challenges that are being intensified by climate change across Africa. Emerging methods in artificial intelligence, machine learning, including foundation models and transfer-learning approaches for data-scarce basins, and digital innovations are being combined with process-based hydrological models. These approaches are improving provision of information on water availability, and enhancing early warnings of floods, droughts, and water stress. This session aims to bring together communities working on different strands of African hydrology, climate risks, environmental risks, and Water-Energy-Food-Ecosystem nexus. We invite contributions across three key areas: (1) understanding and monitoring hydrological processes, groundwater-surface water interactions, low-cost innovative measurement and monitoring systems, remote sensing and AI-driven modelling; (2) Prediction and assessment - drought/flood forecasting, seasonal to decadal forecasting, climate change impact assessments including compound and multi-hazard risks, and operational early warning systems for anticipatory action; and (3) Management and solutions - water resources management and climate change adaptation strategies. Studies that utilize interdisciplinary approaches are particularly encouraged. By fostering collaboration among researchers, practitioners, and policymakers, this session aims to bring to the forefront the advances in understanding African hydrology and climate while promoting practical solutions. Science-for-solutions initiatives contributing to the IAHS HELPING decade are welcome.
title: Advances in African hydrology and climate: methods, innovations and applications

description: Stable and radioactive isotopes and other natural and artificial tracers are useful tools to (i) fingerprint the sources of water and solutes in catchments, (ii) trace flow pathways, and/or (iii) quantify exchanges of water, solutes and particulates between hydrological compartments both in the natural and simulated environments. We invite contributions that demonstrate novel applications and recent developments of isotope and other tracer techniques in hydrological field studies and data driven or physical modelling in the areas of surface water-groundwater interactions, unsaturated and saturated zone, rainfall-runoff processes, cold-region hydrology, nutrient or contaminant transport, ecohydrology or other catchment processes.
title: Isotope and tracer methods: flow paths characterization, catchment response, and transformation processes

description: Hydrological information is more available than ever, but substantial knowledge gaps remain which limit our ability to coherently explain and connect hydrological phenomena across spatial and temporal scales. Hydrological synthesis represents efforts to combine components or elements of existing knowledge to form a connected whole. These connections may be across geographic locations and scales, or across temporal windows and scales. This session will focus on the investigation of similarities and patterns among catchment hydrological responses and processes. We welcome contributions that, e.g., focus on: - Synthesis across places: using field observations across multiple sites or large sample hydrology datasets, to synthesize process-based explanations of hydrological phenomena - Synthesis across timescales: connections between characteristic timescales of catchments, e.g., residence time and catchment response time - Synthesis across processes: theoretical explanations of hydrological phenomena across multiple places or scales, e.g., what is the link of event recession timescales to seasonal streamflow patterns? - Synthesis across signatures: connections among hydrological signatures at different time scales, e.g. connection of the streamflow seasonality to the long term mean flow - Synthesis across models: new approaches to use modelling tools to make process and pattern interpretations - Synthesis across data: new methods to identify hydrological patterns in data
title: New Developments in Hydrological Synthesis

description: A multitude of processes contribute to the hydrologic functioning of catchments. Traditionally, catchment hydrology has been centered around surface runoff, which is readily observable. But at the same time, invisible below ground processes entailing the storage dynamics and flows of water are still underexplored. This includes subsurface runoff, as well as feedbacks of subsurface processes to the surface and the specific role of soil moisture in shaping these fluxes. This session aims to bring together contributions on the following topics and to address gaps in observations, models, and understanding of hydrologic systems: - Identifying, tracing, and modeling subsurface runoff generation at the catchment scale. - Factors and mechanisms controlling subsurface water storage and fluxes - How soil moisture measurements at different scales can be used to improve process understanding, models, and hydrologic theory - Interactions of surface and subsurface hydrologic processes
title: The invisible controls of catchment hydrology: storage, flows and interactions in the subsurface

description: Understanding and representing hydrological processes is the basis for developing and improving hydrological and Earth system models. Hydrological observations, experiments, Earth observations, and new data products are becoming increasingly available across spatial and temporal scales, opening new opportunities to improve the representation, parametrization, evaluation, and understanding of hydrological processes in models. In this session, we welcome contributions that advance hydrological modelling through new approaches to process representation, model development, parametrization, and evaluation across spatio-temporal scales. We particularly encourage contributions that use new observations, experiments, or modelling concepts to improve our understanding and representation of hydrological processes, and that provide insights or approaches that can be transferred beyond individual study sites or applications. Potential contributions could (but are not limited to): 1. Advance seamless modelling of spatial patterns in hydrology and land models using new data products and Earth observations, particularly where these data provide new constraints on process representation; 2. Improve model structure by representing often neglected or insufficiently represented processes in hydrological models, such as human impacts, river regulation, irrigation, and vegetation dynamics; 3. Provide novel concepts for improving the characterization of internal and external model fluxes and their spatio-temporal dynamics, including approaches that enable better representation and understanding of hydrological processes across scales; 4. Introduce new approaches for model calibration and evaluation, especially approaches that diagnose deficiencies in process representation, improve understanding of model behaviour, and/or improve model predictions under changing conditions; 5. Upscale experimental and process-based knowledge from plot, hillslope, or other small scales to catchment, regional, or larger-scale models; We particularly encourage contributions that go beyond the application of established models to individual study sites and instead provide new insights, methods, or frameworks for improving process representation. Contributions demonstrating how observations, experiments, or novel modelling approaches can lead to improved and transferable process understanding and model representation are especially welcome.
title: Advancing process representation for hydrological modelling across spatio-temporal scales

description: Hydrologic data have traditionally been sparse in space and time, requiring process-based models to interpolate observations and predict fluxes under limited data availability. Rapid advances in observation technologies are now enabling near–real-time monitoring of complex hydrologic processes across a wide range of spatial and temporal scales, fundamentally transforming hydrology from data scarcity to data abundance. Fully exploiting these emerging observation systems requires parallel advances in digital tools for data processing, integration, modeling, and visualization. New digital solutions—including digital twins, real-time data platforms, and interactive visualization environments—play a critical role in translating novel observations and scientific insights into actionable information for water resources research, multi-sector management, and decision-making. Under accelerating environmental change, two-way data exchange between models, observations, and stakeholders is increasingly essential for responsive forecasting and intervention. This session invites contributions on next-generation hydrologic observation systems and multi-scale digital solutions that advance process understanding, modeling, and application. Topics of interest include, but are not limited to: - Novel observation techniques enabling improved parametrization of hydrologic processes - Integration and fusion of next-generation hydrologic observations into modeling frameworks - Digital twins and other advanced digital representations of hydrologic systems - Real-time forecasting, early-warning, and decision-support systems for water resources and hydrologic hazards - Case studies demonstrating the operational use and societal impact of hydrologic digititalization Hosted by the Digital Water Flagship (https://digitalwaters.fi)
title: Data-driven insight into hydrological processes and hydrologic digitalization

description: All hydrology is local, and no catchment behavior is average. Yet as a community we often gravitate toward generalization — universal frameworks, transferable methods, and broad conclusions — sometimes at the cost of engaging seriously with what makes catchment response genuinely unique. This session therefore invites contributions that place the modelling case study and its uniqueness at the center. What is hydrologically special about your study site? What made modelling it challenging? Which solutions did you find? And what does that tell us about the limits of the one-size-fits-all thinking? By bringing together a diverse collection of modelling case studies, this session celebrates hydrological diversity and argues that careful examination of the specific is one of the most powerful ways to advance our general understanding of hydrology.
title: The Devil is in the Details: Hydrological Modelling Case Studies and What We Can Learn from Them

description: Land use and climate change as well as legal requirements (e.g. the EU Water Framework Directive) pose challenges for the assessment and sustainable management of surface water quality at the catchment scale. Sources and pathways of nutrients and other pollutants as well as nutrient interactions need to be characterized to understand and manage the impacts in river systems. Additionally, water quality assessment needs to cover the chemical and ecological status to link the hydrological view with aquatic ecology. Models can help to optimize monitoring schemes and provide assessments of future changes and management options. However, insufficient temporal and/or spatial resolution, a short duration of observations and the widespread use of different analytical methods limit the potential for model application. Moreover, model-based water quality calculations are affected by errors in input data, model errors, inappropriate model complexity and insufficient process knowledge or implementation. In addition, models should be capable of representing changing land use and climate conditions to meet the needs of decision makers under uncertain future conditions. Given these challenges, there remains a strong need for advances in water quality modeling. This session aims to bring together scientists working on both experimental and modelling studies to improve the prediction and management of water quality constituents (e.g. nutrients, organic matter, algae, sediment) at the catchment scale. Contributions addressing the following topics are welcome: - Experimental and modelling studies on the identification of sources, hot spots, pathways and interactions of nutrients and other, related pollutants at the catchment scale - New approaches to develop effective water quality monitoring schemes - Innovative monitoring strategies that support both process investigation and improved model performance - Advanced modelling tools for integrating catchments and/or simulating in-stream processes - Observational and modelling studies at the catchment scale that relate and quantify water quality changes to changes in land use and climate - Measurements and modelling of abiotic and biotic interaction and feedback involved in the transport and fate of nutrients and other pollutants at the catchment scale - Catchment management: pollution reduction measures, stakeholder involvement, scenario analysis for catchment management
title: Water quality at the catchment scale: measuring and modelling of nutrients, sediment and eutrophication impacts

description: Quantifying and understanding how global change, such as climate change and extremes, land use change and socio-economic developments affects clean water availability across space and time is essential. This knowledge is key to ensuring sufficient water of suitable quality to meet both human and ecosystem needs at present day and in the future. Recent work has highlighted the importance of considering water quality as a key factor in limiting water supply for sectoral uses. Hence, there is an urgent need for tools such as models that span a gradient from purely statistical (e.g., machine learning) to process-based approaches, anticipating the combined impacts of climate and socio-economic changes on water quality and addressing the resulting environmental and societal consequences. Some of these tools, within both Bayesian and frequentist paradigms, enable consideration of prediction reliability, relating uncertainties to a decision makers’ attitudes and preferences towards risks, all while accounting for the uncertainty related to our system understanding, data and random processes. We seek contributions that apply modeling and data-analytic approaches to: • investigate the combined impacts on water quality and quantity from climate change and/or extremes across local to global scales, including climate impact attribution studies; • investigate the impacts of present and future socio-economic developments on surface and/or groundwater quality; • investigate the implications of compound and cascading extreme climate events (e.g., wildfire and floods, drought and heatwaves) on water quality; • analysis of drivers and impacts of water quality, including agricultural and other diffuse sources, point-source inputs, and water quality effects on aquatic ecosystems and human health; • quantify and couple supply and demand in support of water quality management including vulnerability assessment, scenario analysis, indicators, and the water footprint; • project future water scarcity (combining water quality & quantity) supply and demand in the context of a changing climate; • interpret and characterize uncertainties in machine-learning, AI and data-mining approaches that are trained on large data sets; • address the problem of temporal and spatial scaling in water quality modelling; • test transferability and generalizability of water quality predictions; • application of remote sensing and/or citizen science in water quality estimates at multiple scales.
title: Water quality and clean water availability modeling under current conditions and future global change scenarios

description: The growing availability of large-sample and large-scale water quality datasets creates new opportunities to understand how water quality varies in space and time across diverse natural and human-influenced settings. Although homogenizing heterogeneous data remains challenging, such datasets move research beyond site-specific studies towards comparative, multi-catchment analyses that reveal emergent patterns in water quality responses. They also help identify the drivers of these patterns, including climate, geology, soil, land use and human activities, together with their interactions and evolution over time. Large-sample analyses support robust statistical and machine learning models and improve the transferability of findings across sites, ecosystem types and regions, thereby deepening our understanding of water quality controls and informing management under changing environmental conditions. We invite contributions from scientists compiling and exploring large water quality datasets to unravel the natural and anthropogenic drivers shaping water quality patterns. Studies on any solute, such as major ions, nutrients, carbon, metals, emerging contaminants and other pollutants, in inland water ecosystems (streams, rivers, lakes, groundwater) and soils are welcome. Early career scientists are especially welcome. Topics include, but are not limited to: 1. Development and improvement of large water quality datasets •Dataset compilation and harmonization across regions; data platform development •QA/QC, treatment of data gaps, censored values and uncertainty •Integration of high-frequency sensor, remote sensing and citizen science data 2. Innovative approaches to handling big datasets •Machine learning and deep learning methods, explainable AI methods •Process-based modelling and statistical approaches beyond machine learning •Empirical and mechanistic analyses of concentration-discharge (C-Q) relationships 3. Spatial patterns, temporal trends and controls •Regional contrasts and multi-scale trend analysis •Driver-response relationships, including lagged responses to changing management and pressures •Influence of hydrological regimes, climate variability, land cover, soil and geology, and human activity 4. Hot spots and hot moments •Event-based or threshold-triggered changes during extremes (floods, droughts, heatwaves) •Spatial clustering of high-impact areas and sources •Seasonal timing of pollutant loading and retention
title: Water quality analysis across large-samples and scales: Datasets, Patterns and Drivers

description: Our understanding of water pollution sources and their ecological impact has significantly advanced in the last decades. Major advancements have been possible thanks to automated water quality sensing techniques, novel separation techniques such as field-flow-fractionation, inferring ecological function from stream metabolism metrics and eDNA, and developments in modelling tools driven e.g. by the increasing access to high-resolution DEM data and satellite imaging. Further advancements are likely to emerge from the fusion of these datasets and techniques. This session will bring together examples of application of these novel tools for improving scientific understanding of dynamic freshwater ecosystems and their catchments, specifically for detecting water quality and stream ecology change over time and in response to natural and anthropogenic drivers such as global change. We also welcome contributions presenting examples of knowledge transfer to freshwater monitoring and management and freshwater-oriented collaborations between scientists, stakeholders, citizens, and authorities.
title: Challenges and opportunities with improving freshwater quality and ecology in an era of global change

description: Reliable hydrological information is essential for water-resource management, disaster risk reduction, ecosystem protection, and climate adaptation. However, hydrological prediction remains challenging in many regions due to sparse monitoring networks, limited observations, and rapidly changing hydroclimatic conditions. Advances in Earth observation, artificial intelligence (AI), digital technologies, and computational methods are transforming the field, enabling a shift beyond traditional Prediction in Ungauged Basins (PUB) toward a broader concept of hydrological intelligence that integrates observations, process understanding, modelling, and data-driven approaches. This session invites interdisciplinary contributions that advance hydrological prediction and intelligence in data-scarce and poorly monitored catchments. We welcome methodological, observational, and applied studies that improve predictive capability, transferability, interpretability, uncertainty characterisation, and operational utility. Topics include hydrological prediction and forecasting, early-warning systems, regionalisation and transfer learning, AI and machine learning, foundation models, explainable and trustworthy AI, hybrid and physics-informed modelling, digital twins, data assimilation, model calibration, uncertainty analysis, climate-change impacts and adaptation, groundwater-surface water interactions, ecohydrology, socio-hydrology, citizen science, and open hydrological science. Particular emphasis is placed on integrating Earth observation products, environmental data streams, and emerging computational techniques to improve prediction, enhance process understanding, and support decision-making under uncertainty. Contributions spanning local to global scales are encouraged. By bringing together researchers from hydrology, hydro informatics, Earth observation, and environmental data science, the session aims to foster collaboration and accelerate the development of next-generation hydrological intelligence systems for robust prediction, adaptive water management, and climate resilience in an increasingly uncertain and data-constrained world.
title: Hydrological Intelligence and Prediction in Data-Scarce Catchments: Integrating Earth Observation, AI, Digital Twins and Process Understanding

description: Land-use and land-cover changes can substantially modify hydrological processes, erosion and sediment dynamics in catchments. This session welcomes studies investigating the effects of past, ongoing and projected land-use and land-cover changes, including their interactions with climate change. Contributions may focus on hydrological or sediment-related processes, or their interactions, using different methodologies: distributed and semi-distributed models, remote sensing, machine learning, data-driven approaches or hybrid modelling frameworks. We particularly encourage studies that work on scenario analysis, model uncertainty, scale effects, process understanding and future projections.
title: Changing Landscapes, Changing Waters: Land-Use Change Impacts on Hydrology and Sediment Dynamics

description: River basins are increasingly affected by compound, sequential, and spatially clustered hydro-climatic extremes. At the same time, many basins have interconnected reservoirs, diversions, and regulated river reaches. These systems can change how extreme events move through a catchment. Reservoir storage and operational decisions can amplify, reduce, delay, or transfer these effects. Therefore, studying individual reservoirs or isolated extreme events may not fully capture the response of the entire basin. This session aims to advance understanding of cascading hydrological extremes and basin-scale responses in regulated river systems. We welcome observational, theoretical, statistical, and modelling studies addressing the interactions between hydro-climatic extremes, catchment processes, reservoir storage and releases, and downstream hydrological responses. Topics of interest include: compound and sequential floods and droughts; dependence structures and spatial propagation of hydrological extremes; hydrological connectivity in regulated basins; multi-reservoir and basin-scale hydrological modelling; reservoir storage, yield and reliability under climate variability and change; forecast-informed and adaptive reservoir operation; real-time hydrological forecasting and flood routing; and interactions between extreme precipitation, snowmelt, glacier melt, reservoir inflows, and downstream discharge. We welcome contributions using remote sensing and Earth observation, hydroinformatics, telemetry, data assimilation, machine learning, and hybrid physics–data-driven approaches to improve monitoring, prediction, and understanding of cascading hydrological responses. Studies from a wide range of hydro-climatic and physiographic settings, including mountain, snow- and glacier-fed, monsoon, temperate, tropical, arid and semi-arid basins are encouraged, as are comparative studies across different hydro-climatic settings and regulated and unregulated river systems. The session seeks to bring together researchers working across hydrological observations, process-based and statistical modelling, forecasting, Earth observation, and water-resources management to identify common mechanisms controlling cascading hydrological responses and to develop improved approaches for understanding and managing extremes in regulated river basins.
title: Cascading Hydrological Extremes in Regulated River Basins: From Compound Events to Multi-Reservoir Responses

description: While water plays a critical role in sustaining human health, food security, energy production, and ecosystem services, factors such as population growth, climate, and land use change increasingly threaten water quality and quantity. The complexity of water resources systems requires methods integrating technical, economic, environmental, legal, and social issues within frameworks that help design and test efficient and sustainable water management strategies to meet the water challenges of the 21st century. System analyses adopt practical, problem-oriented approaches for addressing the most challenging water issues of our times. These include competing objectives for water, multi-stakeholder planning and negotiation processes, multisector linkages, and dynamic adaptation under uncertainty. This session will feature state-of-the-art contributions to water and multisector resource system management solutions under uncertainty.
title: Water resources policy and management – System solutions for uncertain futures

description: The ongoing and projected intensification of the water cycle under uncertain future conditions represents a significant global challenge that necessitates adaptive, robust, and inclusive adaptation strategies. Climate change is causing increased frequency and severity of extreme weather events such as floods and droughts, making it difficult to predict and manage water resources since historical data is no longer a reliable guide for future conditions. Growing urban populations demand more water and can outpace water infrastructure development, leading to shortages and inequities in water distribution, often exacerbated by political, economic, and social factors that influence water governance. The pace of technological change in water treatment, distribution, and conservation can improve the efficiency of water systems management, but it introduces uncertainty regarding their long-term viability and integration into existing human-water systems. Decision Making Under Deep Uncertainty (DMDU) represents a promising approach to help decision-makers confront such a wide range of unpredictable and variable future conditions. Unlike traditional frameworks that depend on accurate predictions and precise probabilities, DMDU accepts that the future is inherently unpredictable, especially in complex systems like human-water systems, and emphasizes adaptive planning that evolves with new information on water supply, demand, and ecosystem health. This session aims to gather scientists to discuss and exchange knowledge of existing and emerging approaches for supporting the design and implementation of adaptive and robust water management strategies under deep uncertainty. We welcome contributions focused on recent methodological advances, including uncertainty and sensitivity analysis, scenario generation techniques, robust optimization, and experiences related to real-world applications.
title: Decision Making Under Deep Uncertainty for Planning Water Systems Adaptation to Global Change

description: The field of socio-hydrology and hydro-social research emerged as an attempt to better understand the dynamic interactions and feedbacks within diverse coupled human-water systems and its implications for the assessment and management of water resources and associated risks. An integrated perspective offers novel entry points for a more fertile engagement between hydrological and social sciences across different scales ranging from the plot level to entire watersheds, encompassing both surface water and groundwater. Its interdisciplinary nature involves (and integrates) various methodological approaches, epistemologies, and disciplines. We welcome contributions from researchers from social and natural sciences who are keen to look beyond their research perspective and who like to discuss their research findings in a broader context of coupled human-water systems. Papers should 1) contribute to the understanding of complex human-water interactions and their management, 2) discuss the benefits and shortcomings of different inter- and disciplinary perspectives based on empirical, conceptual or model-based research; and 3) shed light on the added value of socio-hydrological modelling and hydro-social analysis for water resources management, risk management and adaptation design. We specifically welcome contributions which reflect how the hydro-social and socio-hydrological research approach supports the new IAHS decade HELPING Science for Solutions aim. This session is co-sponsored by the IAHS under the umbrella of the ICHWF - Commission on Human-Water-Feedbacks. We are happy to have TBA as a solicited speaker.
title: Coupled human-water systems: Advances in socio-hydrological and hydro-social research

description: This session welcomes abstracts that consider how to observe, analyse and model feedbacks between social, political and economic processes and hydrological and other environmental processes. The session is organised by the International Commission on Human-Water Feedbacks (ICHWF) of the IAHS, which provides a home for interdisciplinary research on the dynamics of human-water systems, particularly involving the social sciences. Relevant topics include but are not limited to: • Observations of human impacts on, and responses to, hydrological change • Interactions of communities with local water resources • Hydrological models that include anthropogenic effects • Interdisciplinary qualitive and quantitative methods • Theoretical models to isolate, conceptualize and/or simulate feedbacks in human-water systems • Critical reflections on inter- and transdisciplinary projects (problem framings, roles, methods, exclusions, suggested interventions) • Creation of databases describing the hydrology of human-impacted systems • Data analyses and comparisons of human-water systems around the globe and especially in the global south • Human interactions with hydrological extremes, i.e. floods, droughts and water scarcity • The role of gender, age, and cultural background in the impacts of hydrological extremes, risk and risk perception, and during/after crises and emergencies
title: Human-Water Feedbacks

description: In the Anthropocene, water resources are under unprecedented stress. To address these challenges and develop actionable, sustainable solutions, we need a thorough understanding of not only the hydrological cycle but also its interactions with other complex physical systems and social dimensions. To do this effectively, we need to move beyond a “science-as-usual” approach and leverage transdisciplinary knowledge. This includes actors such as scientists, policymakers, local communities and indigenous peoples, NGOs and local associations, media, and businesses. Each of these brings a unique perspective and expertise, and we must value their contributions not simply as sources of information or data, but as knowledge holders and active contributors to problem framing, knowledge production, solution development, and decision making. Practices such as co-creation can help bring these different forms of knowledge into dialogue, make assumptions and uncertainties explicit, identify conflicts and synergies, and collectively explore alternative pathways towards, to arrive at integrated solutions for complex water management issues. This vision fits within the framework of the IAHS HELPING decade, which emphasises bottom-up approaches that recognise and empower local stakeholders and local know-how. This session welcomes studies on co-creation approaches in hydrology and water resources management. More specifically, we welcome studies including, but not limited to: experiences and case studies of participatory and co-creation approaches applied to hydrology and water resources management; co-modelling approaches and socio-hydrological studies involving participation of stakeholders; the role of digital technologies and artificial intelligence in facilitating or transforming co-design; meta-analyses, review of other experiences, and literature reviews; critical geography, political ecology, new conceptual frameworks, and other critical approaches to co-creation and stakeholders involvement in water resources decision making. Co-organised by the Working Groups on Co-Creation of Water Knowledge and Citizens and Hydrology (CANDHY) of the International Association of Hydrological Sciences: https://iahs.info/Initiatives/Scientific-Decades/helping-working-groups/co-creating-water-knowledge/ https://iahs.info/Initiatives/Working-Groups/Candhy/
title: Co-creation in Hydrology and Water Resources Management

description: Water sustains societies, economies, and ecosystem services locally and globally. Yet, competition over freshwater is intensifying worldwide, driven by rising demand and shifting availability under climate change and variability. Addressing these challenges requires integrative water management and policy approaches that balance trade-offs across social, economic, and environmental water uses. Equally, adaptive and flexible solutions are needed to allow policies to adapt to changing and uncertain climatic and socio-economic conditions, thereby strengthening the sustainability and resilience of water systems. This session provides a forum for showcasing novel and emerging research at the intersection of agricultural production, energy security, water supply, economic development, and environmental conservation. In particular, we encourage contributions that: (i) advance understanding of critical interconnections, feedbacks, and risks within water system components, (ii) introduce novel methods or tools for evaluating and monitoring trade-offs and performance in water allocation, management, and policy across sectors, (iii) evaluate technological, policy, and/or governance innovations to address the water-food-energy-environment nexus across scales (local, regional, and/or global), and (iv) advance methods to evaluate risks to water systems and identify solutions to enhance system and user resilience. We welcome real-world examples on the successful application of these methods to facilitate integrated planning and management of the water-food-energy-environment (WEFE) nexus.
title: Balancing the water, food, energy and environment nexus for sustainable and resilient water systems under global change

description: Hydropower is a mature and cost-competitive renewable energy source, which helps stabilize fluctuations between energy demand and supply. The structural and operational differences between hydropower systems and renewable energy farms may require changes in the way hydropower facilities operate to provide balancing, reserves or energy storage. Yet, non-power constraints on hydropower systems, such as water supply, flood control, conservation, recreation, navigation may affect the ability of hydropower to adjust and support the integration of renewables. Holistic approaches that may span a range of spatial and temporal scales are needed to evaluate hydropower opportunities and support a successful integration maintaining a resilient and reliable power grid. In particular, there is a need to better understand and predict spatio-temporal dynamics between climate, hydrology, and power systems. This session solicits academics and practitioners contributions that explore the use of hydropower and storage technologies to support the transition to low-carbon electricity systems. We specifically encourage interdisciplinary teams of hydrologists, meteorologists, ecologist, power system engineers, and economists to present on case studies and discuss collaboration with environmental and energy policymakers. Questions of interest include: - Prediction of water availability and storage capabilities for hydropower production - Prediction and quantification of the space-time dependences and the positive/negative feedbacks between wind/solar energies, water cycle and hydropower - Energy, land use and water supply interactions during transitions - Policy requirements or climate strategies needed to manage and mitigate risks in the transition - Energy production impacts on ecosystems such as hydropeaking effects on natural flow regimes. This session has the support of the a) Cost Action : Pan-European Network for Sustainable Hydropower (PEN@Hydropower), and b) European Energy Research Alliance (EERA), that established the joint program “Hydropower” to facilitate research, promote hydropower and enable sustainable electricity production. Further information can be found here: https://www.pen-hydropower.eu/ https://www.eera-set.eu/eera-joint-programmes-jps/list-of-jps/hydropower/
title: Innovation in Hydropower Operations, Planning and Retrofitting to Integrate Renewable Energy Sources and Optimize the Water-Energy-Ecosystem Nexus

description: Hydroclimatic extremes, ranging from prolonged droughts to intense wet spells and flooding, are intensifying worldwide. These changes pose escalating risks to agriculture, water management, and, ultimately, global food security, livelihoods, and societies. Yet, projected changes and their cascading effects are often assessed in isolation, a practice that underestimates systemic risks. A more holistic perspective, that acknowledges uncertainties, interactions, and feedbacks of both droughts and floods, is essential to identify resilient and sustainable transition pathways for complex adaptive systems such as agriculture and other land-use systems. Farmers are traditionally experts at navigating climate variability, but the increasing severity and frequency of hydroclimatic extremes demand new strategies to mitigate systemic risks. Agriculture plays a threefold role in this context: as a sector heavily affected by climate change, as a contributor to greenhouse gas emissions, and as a key source to implement solutions and adaptation strategies. This interplay both amplifies uncertainties and opens opportunities for transformative adaptation. Understanding how individual farmers, farming communities, and agricultural governance actors evaluate risks and adjust practices under dynamic and uncertain conditions is central to clarifying how decisions at different spatial and temporal scales may trigger, accelerate, or prevent broader regime shifts. This session invites contributions from across the natural and social sciences to explore the multifaceted interactions between hydroclimatic extremes and agriculture. We particularly welcome studies that: • Provide observational evidence, case studies and methodological advancements on the interplay between climate extremes, agriculture and other land use systems. • Advance theoretical and conceptual perspectives on connected, compound, and cascading risks and uncertainties. • Apply nexus approaches, integrating environmental, socio-economic, and governance dimensions. • Share participatory, co-production, or transdisciplinary approaches engaging farmers, communities, and other stakeholders, including practical tools and interventions. • Examine decision-making processes and responses at the farm, community, and governance levels, including adaptation strategies and barriers across spatial scales. • Explore agricultural adaptability, transformation pathways, and potential regime shifts under climate extremes.
title: Agriculture under Hydroclimatic Extremes: from Systemic Risks to Pathways for Transformation

description: The Water-Energy-Food-Ecosystem (WEFE) Nexus provides a systemic understanding of cross-sectoral interdependencies, trade-offs and synergies. Yet, translating it into knowledge and tools that can effectively inform policy and collective decision-making remains challenging. This session aims to explore how transdisciplinary approaches can help move WEFE Nexus research from systems analysis towards policy, decision-making and action.Consistent with the HS context, particular attention will be given to approaches that explicitly examine the relationships between water and the other Nexus dimensions. We particularly welcome approaches that are embedded within transdisciplinary processes and combine scientific and stakeholder knowledge to conceptualise complex systems, explore cross-sectoral feedback and trade-offs, and support the co-development of scenarios, solutions and transition pathways. Emphasis will be placed on real-world case studies in which these approaches have been developed, tested or applied together with stakeholders, rather than on purely theoretical frameworks. Attention will also be given to the transparency and traceability of modelling assumptions, the validation, and the treatment and communication of uncertainty. Beyond the delivery of technical outputs, we encourage contributions that examine the wider outcomes of transdisciplinary processes, including learning, strengthened systems understanding and capacities, ownership and legitimacy, and their contribution to sustained and adaptive decision-making. Contributions may address, but are not limited to: - Integrated modelling approaches for analysing WEFE systems, including System Dynamics Modelling, Agent-Based Modelling, multi-criteria methods and hybrid frameworks; - Transdisciplinary and participatory approaches to WEFE Nexus research, involving scientists and societal actors in collaborative modelling and knowledge co-production; - Integration of biophysical, socio-economic, behavioural, institutional and governance dimensions, with explicit attention to the reciprocal relationships between water and the other Nexus components; - Integration of modelling, monitoring and evaluation to support adaptive WEFE management and decision-making; - Translation of integrated and participatory assessments into policies, management strategies, adaptation measures and transition pathways; - Real-world, participatory applications and lessons learned.
title: From WEFE Nexus analysis to action: Transdisciplinary Approaches for Water Policy and Decision Support

description: Urban areas are at risk from multiple hazards, including urban flooding, droughts and water shortages, sea level rise, disease spread and issues with food security. Consequently, many urban areas are adapting their approach to hazard management and are applying Green Infrastructure (GI) and Nature-based Solutions (NbS) as part of wider integrated schemes. This session aims to provide researchers with a platform to present and discuss the application, knowledge gaps and future research directions of urban GI and how sustainable green solutions can contribute towards an integrated and sustainable urban hazard management approach. We welcome original research contributions across a series of disciplines with a hydrological, climatic, soil sciences, ecological and geomorphological focus, and encourage the submission of abstracts which demonstrate the use of GI at a wide range of scales and geographical distributions. We invite contributions focusing on (but not restricted to): · Monitored case studies which provide an evidence base for integration within a wider hazard management system; · GIS and hazard mapping analyses to determine benefits, shortcomings and best management practices of urban implementation; · Laboratory-, field- or GIS-based studies which examine the effectiveness or cost/benefit ratio of solutions in relation to their wider ecosystem potential; · Methods for enhancing, optimising and maximising system potential; · Innovative and integrated approaches or systems for issues including bioretention/stormwater management, pollution control, carbon capture and storage, slope stability, urban heat exchange and urban food supply; · Catchment-based approaches or city-scale studies demonstrating opportunities at multiple spatial scales; · Rethinking urban design and sustainable, resilient recovery following crisis onset; · Engagement and science communication to enhance community resilience.
title: Green Infrastructure and Nature-based Solutions for Sustainable Urban Hazard Management

description: Urban and urbanizing watersheds are among the most dynamic landscapes on Earth, where land use change, population growth, infrastructure development, and evolving water demands reshape hydrological processes, water quality, and catchment functioning. Understanding watershed responses across the urbanization continuum is essential for advancing hydrological science, improving prediction, and informing integrated water and land management. This session welcomes contributions on urban watersheds across a range of topics, including but not limited to: catchment functioning and responses to land use change; runoff generation, hydrological extremes, and urban drainage processes; water quantity and quality; the sources, transport, transformation, and fate of anthropogenic inputs; urban groundwater and surface water–groundwater interactions; urban water supply and source-water protection; stormwater and wastewater management, blue-green infrastructure, and other nature-based approaches for urban water management; and ecological responses and ecosystem services in urban waters. We particularly encourage contributions grounded in field studies and monitoring networks in urban settings, including long-term and high-frequency observatories, sensor networks, tracer and isotope studies, citizen science and community-based monitoring, and paired or nested catchment designs, that advance process understanding, calibrate and validate models, or inform the design of urban water management strategies. Contributions linking such field-based approaches with remote sensing, modeling, data assimilation, and data-driven and machine-learning approaches are welcome, as are studies on urban water infrastructure, governance, community engagement, socio-hydrology, and adaptive water and land management. We encourage contributions spanning a range of climatic, geographic, and socio-economic settings, as well as studies across different stages and forms of urbanization, particularly comparative studies that help identify knowledge gaps in urban watershed processes and management challenges.
title: Urban Watersheds and Water Challenges

description: Digital Water strategies - such as artificial intelligence (including the more traditional machine learning, generative, and agentic AI), digital twins, smart sensing, real-time data systems and decision-support tools - are reshaping how human-water systems are observed, interpreted, modeled, and managed. Their value, however, depends on how effectively they can support (and explain) better decision-making, improve operational planning and strategic management, and enhance resilience in the face of changing climatic and socio-economic conditions. This session focuses on both emerging Digital Water methods and the pathways through which data and models become actionable. We welcome contributions on new technological and methodological approaches, including behavioral and human-in-the-loop models that represent how individuals, stakeholders, and institutions respond to information, incentives, risks, and changing water conditions. Relevant topics include AI, data-driven and hybrid modeling, digital twins, behavioral modeling, decision-support systems, and human–model interaction, stakeholder engagement and co-production, and institutional dynamics and governance - including data governance, responsible data sharing, accountability, responsibility, and decision authority in digitally supported water governance. Further topics include equity and human values in water decisions, as well as dealing with uncertainty, explainability and interpretability, bias, and implementation barriers. Applications may span water supply and demand, drought and flood risk, water quality, infrastructure planning and operation, water allocation, conservation, and climate adaptation. The session aims to advance both innovative Digital Water approaches and understanding of how they shape behavior, decisions, governance, and resilience in human-water systems.
title: Digital Water: From Data to Decisions in Human-Water Systems

description: The management and utilization of water storage systems, including dams, reservoirs, natural lakes, and connected groundwater storage, have historically played a central role in securing water supply during dry periods and supporting domestic, industrial, agricultural, energy, and ecological needs. However, increasing water demand, climate change, and intensifying hydroclimatic extremes are placing growing pressure on both natural and human-made storage systems. Projected warming is expected to alter reservoir inflows, evaporation, storage efficiency, water quality, sediment dynamics, and ecosystem functioning, while more frequent droughts, heatwaves, wildfires, and extreme precipitation may generate compound and cascading risks. These pressures increasingly require water storage systems to be managed not in isolation, but as interconnected components of wider river basin and landscape systems. This session invites theoretical, experimental, observational, and applied studies investigating the future of natural and human-made water storage under local and global environmental change. The session aims to bring together contributions using remote sensing, in situ observations, water resources systems modeling, AI, digital twins, and decision-support approaches to improve the monitoring, prediction, adaptive operation, and long-term sustainability of freshwater storage systems. Key topics include: • Impacts of climate variability and change on the need for water storage, reservoir performance, and water availability; • Sedimentation, water quality, and ecological consequences of reservoir operation and trade-offs among water supply, hydropower, irrigation, flood protection, ecosystems, and other users; • Reservoir operations modeling and Multi-reservoir and basin-scale management under changing climatic and socio-economic conditions; • Remote sensing, AI, digital twins, forecasting, and decision-support tools for monitoring and adaptive reservoir operation; • Governance, policy, and socio-economic dimensions of sustainable water-storage management; • Case studies demonstrating innovative adaptation strategies and restoration initiatives.
title: Fate of Water Reservoirs in a Changing Environment

description: Climate change and unsustainable water management practices are driving the world beyond water scarcity. Many areas in arid and semi-arid regions such as the Middle East, Central Asia, and Southern Africa are moving into an era of “water bankruptcy”. Shared aquifers and river systems are under growing pressure from reduced rainfall, accelerated glacier melt, and upstream interventions, intensifying competition for already limited resources. Moreover, many inland terminal lakes, such as the Aral Sea, Lake Chad and Lake Urmia, are drying up, further exacerbating the environmental and socio-economic impacts of the water crisis. In addition, gaps in data availability and technical capacity hinder effective water governance, making transboundary cooperation even more critical for regional stability and sustainability. To address these challenges, a holistic approach is required - one that integrates the Water-Energy-Food-Ecosystem (WEFE) Nexus to foster benefit-sharing between riparian states. By recognising the interdependencies among water resources, energy production, and food security in relation to environmental needs, WEFE Nexus studies offer valuable strategies for optimising resource allocation, reducing competition, and encouraging cooperative solutions across borders. Furthermore, ongoing digitalisation, AI and real-time monitoring, and advances in data-driven decision-making, including Digital Twin technologies, offer opportunities to bridge data gaps and improve water management. As water demand grows across urban, industrial, and environmental sectors, innovative solutions are needed to enhance efficiency, minimize losses, and build climate resilience. Alongside technological solutions, human capacity building plays a central role in addressing these complex challenges.
title: From Water Sharing to Water Scarcity: Managing Depleted Aquifers, Dried Lakes, and Shrinking Glaciers in Transboundary Water Systems

description: Ancient and traditional hydraulic systems record and store valuable information about the long-term interactions between humans, water, and climate. Underground aqueducts and qanats, reservoirs, terraces and irrigation systems demonstrate ancient societies’ deep understanding of hydrology, hydraulics, and waterscapes; moreover, they unveil their advanced sustainable water management practices and their ability to adapt to changes in climate and environmental conditions, and to the complexities of hydrosocial dynamics. Their preservation offers unique opportunity to examine how human-water interactions have evolved over millennia, how ancestral water knowledge has been transferred (or lost) across generations, and how this knowledge can be preserved and used to inform contemporary water pressures, and sustainable goals. This session invites interdisciplinary approaches to multi-temporal hydraulic systems beyond an archaeological perspective. We welcome contributions that view of these systems holistically, as living systems, environmental and climate archives, and the repositories of ancestral water knowledge and hydrosocial dynamics. Contributions may address, but are not limited to: -Design, construction, operation, maintenance, adaptation, and continued use; -Geospatial and other emergent technologies to document, map, reconstruct, and monitor hydraulic landscapes; -Social dynamics surrounding water infrastructure, including ancient, traditional, and local knowledge and their intergenerational transfer or loss; -Contemporary pressures, including groundwater depletion, water pollution, agriculture, land-use change and climate change; -Lessons from ancient hydraulic practices for water security, climate adaptation, community resilience, and sustainable water management; and -Integration of archaeological, hydrological, hydrogeology, geospatial approaches with ancient, traditional, and local knowledge to understand socio-hydrology and coupled human–water systems and inform public policies. The session brings together the fields of anthropology, archaeology, hydrology, hydrogeology, environmental sciences, and emerging geospatial technologies to explore how knowledge from the past, combined with contemporary science and technology, can offer new perspectives for sustaining knowledge transfer, addressing water pressures, and in informing future water policies.
title: Ancient Water, Living Knowledge: Reconnecting Hydraulic Heritage, Communities, and Sustainable Futures

description: Gradual hydrological change, including groundwater decline, altered flow regimes, wetland loss, snow and glacier retreat and salinization, can be normalized within a generation, so that communities, institutions and scientific assessments judge present conditions against progressively altered reference states. This shifting baseline problem has two components that are rarely examined together: the physical reference condition, reconstructed from instrumental, documentary, paleohydrological and Earth observation records, and the perceived reference condition held by water users and decision makers. Human observations can match instrumental records on the direction of change, yet the generational divergence between perceived and reconstructed hydrological baselines is seldom quantified, and the choice of reference period is often treated as a technical default even where multidecadal variability makes any single window unrepresentative. This session invites contributions that link evidence of long-term hydrological change to the reference conditions perceived or used by people and institutions, including: (1) reconstruction of hydrological reference conditions from long records, and the sensitivity of trends, impact estimates and restoration targets to the choice of reference period under low-frequency hydroclimatic variability; (2) quantitative comparison of perceived or reported reference conditions with reconstructed ones, using surveys, interviews, local and Indigenous knowledge, archives or media records, and of how time since the last major event or past water and land-use decisions bias perception; (3) representation of changing reference conditions, expectations and learning in socio-hydrological and agent-based models, including memory decay rates calibrated with survey, panel or archival data. (4) evaluation of whether monitoring, visualization, climate services or participatory approaches make gradual change perceptible, slow the decay of awareness and alter decisions, including panel, longitudinal or experimental studies reporting null or adverse effects. (5) consequences of baseline choice for water allocation, adaptation and restoration, including whose reference conditions are recognized. Contributions should connect at least one physical record of change with how reference conditions are perceived, modeled or used in decisions. Studies from data-scarce regions are particularly encouraged.
title: Shifting hydrological baselines: when records and perceptions of normal water conditions diverge

description: Hydrological observations, forecasting and advanced mathematical modelling provide essential tools for integrated water resources management (IWRM). Their practical value depends on how well they address management needs, represent competing objectives and account for ecological, social and institutional conditions. This session brings together hydrological science, systems analysis and practical surface water management to explore how scientific knowledge translates into implementable decisions. Aligned with the IAHS ICWRS scope and the HELPING decade, it connects technical advances with the participation, governance and capacity needed to put them into practice. We invite methodological contributions, comparative analyses and case studies addressing: • Integration of hydrological modelling, forecasting, simulation and optimization into water allocation, reservoir operation, ecosystem restoration and climate adaptation; • Problem framing and assessment of trade-offs among technical performance, ecological needs and societal priorities; • Co-development and use of decision-support tools with managers, communities and policymakers, including local knowledge and uncertainty communication; • Institutional capacity, economic constraints and governance arrangements influencing implementation, including transboundary settings; • Evaluation of management outcomes, unintended consequences and transferable lessons from successful, delayed or unsuccessful interventions. Contributions should connect analytical methods with a concrete decision context and explain the conditions affecting their use. We particularly welcome studies examining both the technical performance of proposed solutions and their practical uptake, distinguishing anticipated benefits from demonstrated outcomes. The aim is to understand how modelling capabilities and implementation conditions together support effective, equitable and adaptive water management.
title: From hydrological knowledge to action: connecting modelling, policy and practice in integrated water resources management

description: Adapting to societal challenges, such as climate change, increasing water scarcity and hydrological extremes, while advancing towards the Sustainable Development Goals, requires dynamic transition pathways across various integrated systems (water, transport, energy, food, ecosystems, etc.). Evaluating how such transition pathways play a role for water management and policy calls for modeling approaches that account for interactions and feedbacks between human decisions and natural systems represented by MultiSector Dynamics (MSD) models and approaches. The role of individual and collective human agency is increasingly recognized as a prominent and arguably paramount determinant in shaping the behavior, trajectory, vulnerability and resilience of these systems. Yet, the representation of human decision making in MSD and other coupled human and natural systems models is often highly abstracted and simplistic. Additionally, MSD models tend to ignore or largely abstract institutional dynamics in resource systems, commonly adopting rules that implicitly presume centralized, non-adaptive management of resources and infrastructure limiting our ability to understand how heterogeneous actors and institutions respond and adapt to climatic, hydrological, and societal change, and how these responses feedback across systems. This session seeks to address these limitations, providing a forum for interdisciplinary exchange around the representation of human actors and action, emerging modeling approaches, and new insights across a wide range of MSD challenges for water management and policy. We thereby aim to contribute to a broader community spanning MultiSector Dynamics, socio-hydrology, human–water systems, water resources systems analysis, focused on advancing our understanding of the role of human agency in coupled human and natural systems facing environmental risks and the need for societal transformations. We broadly invite submissions across disciplinary and methodological modeling approaches (e.g., agent-based, economic, optimization, system dynamics, data-driven, AI/ML/generative, etc.) and domains (water, energy, transport, food, land, ecosystems, etc.). We particularly invite contributions that advance methodological approaches for representing heterogenous adaptive human actors and institutions within coupled human–natural system models, and for linking these representations and their management and policy implications across sectors and scales.
title: Understanding Interactions and Impacts Across Multiple Sectors: Advances in Water Management and Policy Research

description: The climate crisis, land use change and over consumption are altering the water cycle beyond a safe planetary boundary. The so-called conventional water, i.e. snowfall, rainfall, river runoff and easily accessible groundwater, is often insufficient to meet growing demands for water and food. Sustainably increasing water availability, allocating water in an equitable way, and adapting to a changing climate are challenges that need to be urgently addressed. A promising option is to use Non-Conventional Waters (NCW), which include ancestral and modern techniques to generate, harvest, store, treat, distribute and use water. The effectiveness of such solutions has already been proven in many parts of the world, but their potential is under-recognized, limiting their widespread adoption, mainly due to socio-economic and governance barriers. This session welcomes studies on non-conventional water resources spanning technical, socio-economic and political disciplines. More specifically, we accept contributions including, but not limited to: innovative methods to design, monitor and assess NCW; social, economic, environmental and cultural sustainability of NCW water use; good practice examples for NCW solutions implementation; global and local drivers and barriers to NCW implementation technical innovations in harvesting, storing, treating, and using NCW, and innovation valorization and transfer; Stakeholder engagement and multi-actor platforms for NCW planning and implementation Co-organized by the IAHS Working Group on “Non-Conventional Water Use for Integrated Water Resources Management” of the International Association of Hydrological Sciences: https://iahs.info/Initiatives/Scientific-Decades/helping-working-groups/non-conventional-water-ncw-use-for-integrated-water-resources-management/
title: Non-conventional water resources management for climate adaptation and resilience

description: Water security is increasingly under threat from accelerating climate change and anthropogenic pressures, with particularly severe implications for Africa and other water-stressed and climate-vulnerable regions. Climate variability, recurrent droughts and floods, urbanisation, agricultural expansion, ecosystem degradation, population growth, and competing water demands are placing increasing pressure on hydrological systems. Persistent inequalities in water access and allocation further highlight the need to move beyond understanding water challenges towards translating scientific knowledge into equitable and effective action. This session explores how water science, governance, innovation, capacity development, and multi-stakeholder cooperation can bridge the gap between knowledge and implementation that contribute to equitable and climate-resilient water security. Attention is given to connecting scientific evidence with policy frameworks, institutional capacity, local knowledge, and practical implementation, while advancing integrated and multisectoral water resources management. We invite interdisciplinary and transdisciplinary contributions addressing water security under climate and societal change, with a particular focus on Africa and broader relevance through transferable lessons. Contributions may include: climate-resilient and equitable water resources management; water governance, institutions, policy implementation and allocation; drought, floods and adaptation; multisectoral approaches to competing water demands; water–agriculture–food–ecosystem interactions; participatory approaches and indigenous and local knowledge; innovative monitoring, Earth observation, modelling and decision-support tools; economic and institutional dimensions of water security; and capacity development strengthening the science–policy–practice interface. The session seeks to identify context-sensitive and scalable pathways from water science to water security by connecting scientific knowledge with governance, institutional strengthening, policy and implementation. Through cross-disciplinary, cross-sector, and cross-scale dialogue, it aims to generate actionable insights for more equitable, cooperative, and climate-resilient water management amid global change.
title: From Water Science to Water Security: Governance, Equity and Implementation under Climate Stress

description: Urban environments are at the frontline of risk, shaped by rapid expansion, climate shocks, informality, and socio-economic pressures. This session welcomes contributions that cover the full spectrum of urban risk - from physical monitoring and modelling, to dynamic vulnerability assessments, to urban governance frameworks and resilience policy. We particularly welcome contributions that (a) address urban risk in the Global South and (b) address risk in small urban centres, where much of the projected urban growth will occur. Potential themes include: -Multi-hazard profiles of urban centres: compiling case studies and theoretical evidence for potential hazard interrelationships at the city scale -Smart sensing and digital twins: exploring the use of AI, crowd-sourced data and big data to understand urban risk dynamics -Urban expansion and adaptation: understanding how both formal and informal growth of cities interact with the urban hazardscape -Policy, governance and management aspects of urban risk and resilience -Early warning systems and anticipatory action: methods to combine local knowledge and predictive capabilities to issue effective early warnings in cities We welcome interdisciplinary approaches, including: -Case studies -Modelling -Empirical data collection and monitoring -Inclusive methods such as stakeholder engagement, citizen science and participatory approaches -Innovative methods in AI and machine learning -Frameworks and tools for measuring risk and resilience This session provides an interdisciplinary forum for researchers, policy-makers, and practitioners to share cutting-edge research and practical insights, highlighting diverse approaches to understanding and reducing urban risk.
title: Urban risk in a changing world: dynamics, disruption & resilience in cities

description: The purpose of this session is to: (1) showcase the current state-of-the-art in global and continental scale natural hazard risk science, assessment, application and uptake in decision-making; (2) foster broader exchange of knowledge, datasets, methods, models, and good practice between scientists and practitioners working on different natural hazards and across disciplines globally; and (3) collaboratively identify future research avenues. Reducing natural hazard risk is high on the global political agenda. For example, it is at the heart of the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction and the Paris Agreement. In response, the last decade has seen an explosion in the number of scientific datasets, methods, and models for assessing risk at the global and continental scale. Increasingly, these datasets, methods and models are being applied in collaboration with stakeholders during the decision-making process. Understanding how risk information is translated into decisions and actions is becoming increasingly important.
