This includes the co-production of knowledge with stakeholders, communication of uncertainty, governance of transboundary risks, and the role of risk assessments in supporting policy development, adaptation planning, and disaster risk reduction strategies We invite contributions related to all aspects of natural hazard risk assessment at the continental to global scale, with particular emphasis on how risk information is generated, communicated, and used to support decision-making across sectors, scales, and borders. Topics include: • single hazards, multi- or compound hazards; • all facets of risk, including hazard, exposure and vulnerability; • risk mitigation under current and future conditions (climate & socio-economic); • the use of risk information in decision-making, policy development, adaptation planning, and disaster risk reduction; • novel globally-applicable approaches for leveraging global datasets and models to inform local risk assessment and decision-making.
title: Global and continental scale risk assessment for natural hazards: data, methods, and practice

description: Natural hazards pose serious threats to human health, settlements and the environment. The nature of impacts can be monetizable or hard to measure through economic metrics. Impacts can occur immediately due to the effects of a physical forcing or might persist, evolve and aggravate or resolve in time. This session aims at gathering researchers interested in the scientific advances related to the multiple facets of natural hazard impacts, i.e., direct, indirect, tangible and intangible losses. The session welcomes novel approaches to address impact modelling, data analysis, uncertainty analysis, calibration/validation and theoretical frameworks across all natural hazard types, e.g., floods, droughts, heatwaves, earthquakes, wildfires, landslides, storms etc. The topics include but are not limited to: - comprehensive assessment of the current and future economic impacts of natural hazards under a changing climate, emphasizing the importance of robust cost evaluations for informed decision-making in disaster risk reduction, hazard management, risk forecasting cost-effectiveness and efficiency of risk reduction strategies, and climate change adaptation planning. - impact-based forecasting and scenario development, exploring how evolving hazard, exposure and vulnerability conditions translate into future impact expectations to support anticipatory decision-making. - cascading impacts from direct losses to systemic indirect losses, e.g., business interruption, disruptions to critical services such as energy systems, or the influence of critical infrastructure interdependencies on hazard impact. - indirect and intangible impacts of natural hazards, which are increasingly significant in today’s interconnected socio-technological world. These include loss of irreplaceable items or ecosystem services, and the impacts on physical and mental health. The session also welcomes research on socially vulnerable communities and the long-term health impacts of climatic stressors. - challenges posed by the lack of empirical data and the diversity of methodologies currently applied to assess the costs associated with different natural hazards and impacted sectors, e.g., energy, agriculture, population, buildings etc. Submissions are encouraged from those engaged in both theoretical and practical aspects of impact assessment, with a view to fostering interdisciplinary dialogue and advancing the field.
title: The costs of Natural Hazards: direct, indirect, cascading and intangible aspects

description: The increase in global surface temperatures has changed the frequency and magnitude of socio-natural hazards and extreme weather events. Climate change is reshaping hydrometeorological patterns across the globe, with increasingly pronounced effects in sensitive regions, such as the Amazon. The Amazon Basin is a region of exceptional hydrological, climatic, ecological, and societal importance. Its diverse environments, extending from the Andes to the lowland rainforest and major river systems, are exposed to multiple hazards, including floods, droughts, extreme precipitation, landslides, riverbank erosion, and wildfires. Climate variability and change, land use transformations, deforestation, and infrastructure development can modify hazard processes, exposure, and vulnerability, creating complex and evolving risks. Understanding these hazards requires moving beyond isolated events to investigate interactions across spatial and temporal scales. Extreme rainfall can trigger flooding, landslides, and sediment transport, while prolonged drought and heat can create conditions that favour vegetation fires and disrupt river navigation and water availability. Such processes may generate cascading impacts on ecosystems, infrastructure, livelihoods, and communities, including indigenous peoples and traditional riverine populations. Therefore, this session aims to bring together researchers and practitioners working on the drivers, dynamics, interactions, and consequences of socio-natural hazards throughout the Amazon Basin. We welcome interdisciplinary studies combining observations, remote sensing, modelling, and local knowledge to advance hazard understanding, monitoring, forecasting, and risk reduction. Topics include, but are not limited to: • Drivers of extreme weather events, such as heavy rainfall, prolonged drought, and heatwaves; • Hydrological hazards, including floods and flash floods, sediment dynamics, river meandering process; • Geological hazards: riverbank erosion, "terras caídas", gully erosion, landslides. • Wildfire hazards and their interactions with drought, vegetation, and land use change; • Compound and cascading hazards, and their spatial and temporal dependencies; • Hazard monitoring, early warning, forecasting, and modelling using field observations, remote sensing, and emerging analytical methods; • Exposure, vulnerability, risk assessment, and disaster risk reduction, including the integration of scientific and local knowledge.
title: Socio-natural hazards in the Amazon Basin: understanding extremes, cascading processes, and evolving risks

description: Climate and environmental hazards increasingly interact with conflict, displacement, food insecurity and other social and structural vulnerabilities, creating compound and cascading crises that challenge conventional approaches to disaster preparedness and adaptation. In these contexts, the effectiveness of adaptation and anticipatory action depends on a systemic understanding of risk: how it interacts across sectors and timescales, how to plan under uncertainty, how vulnerabilities evolve, how to protect vulnerable communities, cultural heritage and ecosystems, and how actions can be financed, implemented, and adapted to rapidly changing conditions. This session explores the different stages of anticipatory action:, from understanding the dynamic interactions between natural and societal hazards in the evolution of crises and identifying early warning signs to designing, financing, implementing, and evaluating actions in complex and compound risk settings. We welcome contributions across scales and disciplines: from single-site interventions and community-based action to global modelling, from social science to physical risk, from humanitarian responses to new insurance and financial instruments. The session's purpose is to encourage dialogue and sharing between researchers who might otherwise work separately. Contributions may address, but are not limited to: - Dynamics of risks, including spatio-temporal interactions between different hazards, conflict, food insecurity, displacement and migration - Early warning monitoring and triggers for action - Decision-making under uncertainty - Anticipatory action in fragile, conflict-affected and violence-prone regions - Impact- and trigger-based financing, and financial products for more vulnerable countries and communities - Interventions to reduce economic and non-economic Loss and Damage, and approaches to staying within 'tolerable risk' - Adaptation and action for the benefit of ecosystems and biodiversity - Reviews and critiques of existing interventions and how we think about action
title: Beyond the cost-benefit: adaptation and anticipatory action in complex risk systems

description: Risk reduction and adaptation measures remain fragmented, under-scaled, and unevenly distributed across population groups, struggling with the "implementation gap". The knowledge of citizens, communities, and practitioners most exposed to hazards is key to fill this gap, and yet it is treated as a data source or audience to be informed. We argue that closing the implementation gap requires moving citizen and stakeholder participation upstream. First, moving from data provision and validation towards the co-design of research questions, methods, and assessment frameworks. Second, towards demonstrable uptake of the results in management and policy. Participatory research shows that meaningful engagement is context-dependent, adapting to local histories, capacities, and institutional settings. At the same time, this knowledge needs to resonate with the state of the art in hazard, risk, and climate adaptation science to become actionable. Equally, the value of participation is ultimately decided in policy and planning processes, where scientific evidence competes with political priorities, funding cycles, and institutional mandates. Following successful editions at previous EGU meetings, this session invites scholars from a wide range of disciplines to contribute work on: - Co-design of research, where citizens and stakeholders shape questions, priorities, and methods from the outset, like living and real-world labs or transdisciplinary frameworks. - Integration of citizen and stakeholder knowledge into hazard and risk science: approaches that couple participatory evidence with modelling, remote sensing, impact chains, scenario analysis, or machine learning. - Evaluation and uptake: methods and case studies that assess participatory processes or outcomes, including the enablers and barriers from co-produced knowledge to policy and planning practice. We explicitly welcome contributions on understudied hazards (e.g., heat or drought events) and from the Global South and encourage submissions that critically reflect on what makes participation genuine rather than tokenistic from the standpoint of method and practice.
title: From participation to impact: co-produced disaster risk reduction between citizens, hazard science, and policy

description: Resilience to both short-term disruptions and long-term systemic changes, both anticipated and unanticipated, has become a focal point of attention in both research and policy over recent years in response to a wide range of challenges. This is equally true for the water industry as for society as a whole. With long-lived infrastructure and a traditionally conservative attitude, resilience building may be particularly challenging in the water industry. Building resilience is a multifaceted challenge, including technical, organizational, financial and governance aspects. A comprehensive approach to resilience encompasses all of these, and is therefore by definition transdisciplinary. Actionable theoretical frameworks have been proposed in recent years, as well as many initiatives with practitioners.This session seeks to bring these together and explore how a coherent and comprehensive resilience strategy that spans multiple dimensions can be developed and operationalized for drinking water, wastewater and stormwater management. As such, contributions are solicited from both a) researchers studying system resilience in a practical or conceptual context, seeking to translate their insights into practice and b) practitioners already engaged in operationalizing resilience. In particular, transdisciplinary contributions that consider multiple dimensions and/or involve multiple stakeholders are called for. However, single-dimension contributions are also welcomed as pieces of the transdisciplinary puzzle.
title: Operationalization of resilience in urban water socio-technical systems

description: Due to urbanization, population growth, climate variability, and increasing pressure on freshwater resources, water-security challenges in cities are intensifying throughout the worldwide. Wastewater generated in urban areas of most of the countries is rarely reused. For example, only few cities in developing and poor countries are reusing the wastewater. Few developed countries have well developed working models for reuse of wastewater. With technological development in wastewater treatment, urban wastewater is increasingly recognized as a valuable alternative water resource. Recycling and reuse of treated wastewater can reduce freshwater demand, minimize pollutant discharge, strengthen drought resilience, and support the transition towards circular and sustainable urban water systems. Treatment efficiency, emerging contaminants, energy and infrastructure requirements, economic feasibility, regulatory frameworks, public acceptance, potential environmental and health risks are few of the challenges which restrict a developing country to reuse wastewater. This session invites interdisciplinary contributions addressing scientific, technological, environmental, socio-economic, and governance dimensions of urban wastewater recycling and reuse. Particular emphasis is placed on innovative treatment and monitoring technologies, nature-based and decentralized solutions, resource and energy recovery, removal of emerging contaminants and antimicrobial resistance determinants, risk assessment, water-quality monitoring, fit-for-purpose reuse, and integration of wastewater reuse into urban water management. The session also welcomes studies addressing circular economy approaches, life-cycle and techno-economic assessment, climate-resilient wastewater infrastructure, policy and regulatory frameworks, public perception, and successful case studies from cities across different climatic and socio-economic settings. By bringing together researchers, practitioners, utilities, policymakers, and early-career scientists, the session aims to facilitate knowledge exchange and identify scalable pathways for transforming urban wastewater from an environmental burden into a reliable resource for sustainable and resilient water security.
title: Innovations and Challenges in Urban Wastewater Recycling and Reuse for Water Security

description: How do global changes in climate, land use and development translate into water security challenges for particular places, and how can local research and responses, as well as stakeholders' perspectives, inform wider understanding and action? This session will explore connections among global, regional, and local perspectives on water availability, water quality, water-related hazards, equitable access, and ecosystem health. We bring together hydrology, environmental science, engineering, ecology, geography and social science to examine water security across scales. We welcome conceptual, methodological and empirical contributions connecting large-scale assessments with catchment-, urban- and community-level research. Topics of interest include: - Interactions between global environmental change and local water security; - Multi-scale observation, modelling and assessment; - Connections between scientific evidence, community knowledge and water management; - Adaptation and management across scales; - Comparative studies and synthesis examining how water security challenges and responses differ across climatic, socioeconomic and institutional contexts, and what can be learned or transferred between them. We encourage contributions from diverse settings worldwide, including Africa, Asia, South America and Europe, across urban, peri-urban and rural environments. Interdisciplinary and transdisciplinary studies as well as collaborations with practitioners and communities are particularly welcome. Single-location studies are also welcome where connections across scales or wider implications are made explicit. The aim is to advance dialogue between global and local research and identify opportunities for shared learning and more effective water management.
title: Water security across scales: connecting global perspectives and local responses

description: Natural hazards, such as floods, wildfires, droughts, and storms, are becoming increasingly frequent and severe due to the synergistic effects of climate change, environmental degradation, and the intensification of human activities. The growing complexity of these events demands long-term, high-resolution, and cross-domain environmental data to support monitoring, early warning, and comprehensive risk assessment. Environmental Research Infrastructures (RIs) provide an essential foundation for such an integrated approach by enabling standardized data collection, harmonized observation protocols, and shared analytical tools. Recent advances in open science and FAIR data practices, alongside emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and digital twins, have expanded the potential of RIs to enable real-time monitoring and forecasting. However, persistent challenges remain in linking these infrastructures across domains, ensuring interoperability, and translating scientific outputs into decision-ready knowledge for diverse stakeholders, including civil protection agencies, policy-makers, and the public. This Session invites Research Topics which aims to strengthen the contribution of Environmental Research Infrastructures to understanding, forecasting, and managing natural hazards within multi-hazard frameworks. It seeks to explore how improved coordination, data integration, and innovative technologies can enhance the capacity of RIs to deliver timely and actionable intelligence. The goal is to highlight practical examples and theoretical developments that demonstrate the integration of heterogeneous environmental observations, the application of machine learning and digital twin technologies, and the coupling of scientific data with operational and policy mechanisms. In doing so, the Research Topic will support progress toward a resilient and risk-informed society through the more effective use of RI services in disaster risk reduction and climate adaptation. The scope of this Session / Research Topic encompasses cross-domain environmental monitoring and the operational use of RIs for hazard-related applications. It encourages contributions from research, technical, and policy communities to foster integration and knowledge transfer across sectors.
title: Environmental Research Infrastructures for Natural Hazards (or Environmental Hazards) Monitoring, Early Warning and Risk Assessment

description: There has been substantial progress in improving water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) access globally. However, many communities continue to face barriers in accessing WASH services, leading to adverse health and safety outcomes, negative impacts on livelihoods, and reduced social and economic development. While much of WASH equity discourse centers on low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), marginalized populations in high-income countries (HICs), including racial and ethnic minorities, people experiencing homelessness, rural communities, and Indigenous groups, still lack consistent, affordable, and safely managed WASH services despite near-universal coverage. Achieving equitable WASH access globally creates opportunities for bidirectional learning and cooperation across geographies and disciplines. This session explicitly welcomes contributions from both HIC and LMIC contexts, as well as work that compares or connects them. We also invite submissions from a wide range of disciplines, including engineering, public health, epidemiology, economics, law and policy, anthropology, sociology, geography, urban planning, and data science. We especially encourage research grounded in community-engaged and participatory methods, and collaborative frameworks that center lived experience. Through these discussions, we hope to pave the way toward an equitable WASH future for all.
title: Towards Equitable Futures for Global Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene

description: Socio-ecological systems are shaped by dynamic interactions between environmental processes and human and institutional decision-making. These interactions are central for understanding natural hazards and risks, where societal interventions aimed at managing natural systems may generate intended and unintended outcomes, which themselves shape future possibilities for action. Together, these interactions can generate complex patterns of vulnerability and risk, but also create capacities for adaptation and resilience. Understanding such dynamics requires modelling approaches capable of representing feedbacks and interactions across scales, non-linear processes, and emergent outcomes. This session invites contributions that use modelling and simulation to investigate the dynamics of risk, vulnerability, resilience, and adaptation in socio-ecological systems. We particularly welcome approaches that explicitly integrate social and environmental processes, including agent-based modelling, system dynamics, hybrid and coupled models, participatory modelling, network approaches, and other computational or simulation-based methods. The session focuses on how individual and collective decision-making, institutions, and biophysical processes interact over time and across scales. Relevant topics include, but are not limited to, natural hazards and disaster risk, land-use dynamics and competition, adaptation and recovery, environmental change, and the emergence of systemic risks and resilience trajectories. The session particularly welcomes contributions addressing mountain regions and other spatially constrained socio-ecological systems, where competing demands for land and resources, environmental change, and hazard processes interact in complex ways. However, contributions from other geographical and socio-ecological contexts are equally encouraged. We aim to bring together researchers from the geosciences, social sciences, social ecology, ecology, geography, risk research, and related fields to discuss how modelling can improve our understanding of complex socio-ecological dynamics and support the analysis of future pathways towards more resilient and sustainable socio-ecological systems.
title: Modelling Risk and Resilience in Socio-Ecological Systems: Dynamics, Feedbacks and Future Pathways

description: This session explores how creative, interactive and participatory approaches are reshaping risk communication and engagement across the geosciences, disaster risk reduction and climate adaptation. Inspired by the approach being developed within the Horizon Europe AMPLIFY , which combines creative, participatory and scientific methods to support more inclusive and trusted risk communication, the session looks beyond one-way information provision towards dialogue, experimentation, co-creation and collective learning. We invite contributions on serious games, simulations, role-play, scenario-based and counterfactual exercises, storytelling, arts-based methods, citizen science, co-design, participatory mapping and other innovative formats that support people in understanding, interpreting and acting on risk. We are particularly interested in how these approaches can engage diverse, vulnerable or underserved publics, integrate scientific and local knowledge, and strengthen preparedness, trust, risk awareness, behavioural change and collective action before, during and after disasters. The session welcomes empirical studies, methodological papers, comparative analyses, case studies, conceptual contributions and lessons learned from research and innovation projects in disaster risk reduction, anticipatory action, climate resilience and adaptation. Contributions addressing climate-related risks, multi-hazard contexts, community resilience, transferability across regions and cultures, and the scalability of participatory approaches are especially encouraged. A key focus will be on evaluation: how can the effectiveness of interactive and creative approaches be assessed, and how do they perform compared with, or in combination with, more conventional communication channels? We particularly welcome contributions proposing indicators, evaluation frameworks, mixed-method approaches, or evidence on short- and long-term impacts of creative and participatory methods on disaster preparedness and resilience.
title: From Communication to Co-Creation: Creative and Participatory Approaches for Disaster Preparedness

description: The ocean is a major sink of anthropogenic carbon and heat, and dissolved oxygen has declined across all ocean basins, with consequences for marine ecosystems and biogeochemical cycling. Oxygen, carbon, and heat are coupled through shared pathways of ventilation, circulation, and biological processes. Their regional-scale relationships, however, remain poorly constrained, because internal variability and redistribution can reinforce, mask, or decouple changes at regional scales. A multi-tracer perspective is therefore key to interpreting ongoing changes and projecting future changes in regional biogeochemistry and marine ecosystems. Here we propose a session that brings together the physical oceanography, biogeochemistry, and climate communities to examine how ocean physics and climate variability shape the coupled cycling of oxygen, carbon, and heat across paleo, present-day, and future climates, drawing on theory, observations, modeling, and data-driven approaches. We seek contributions that investigate variability, trends, and coupling among oxygen, carbon, and heat from regional to global scales. Topics can include ocean carbon uptake and storage, ocean heat uptake and redistribution, deoxygenation, and the ecological and biogeochemical consequences of these changes. Contributions using historical reconstructions and uncertainty assessments, models, model–observation synthesis, proxy records, technological developments, oceanic and atmospheric integral constraints, and data-driven approaches are particularly encouraged, as are approaches that foster cross-cutting exchanges across the physical–biogeochemical disciplines. We also welcome contributions to deepen our mechanistic understanding in driving the changes, including the roles of ventilation, circulation, mixing, air–sea exchange, and biological processes; the use of oxygen, carbon, heat, and related tracers to diagnose these processes; and the influence of climate variability, such as ENSO and Pacific decadal variability, on their regional co-variability. This session connects to ongoing international efforts, including the CLIVAR-O2CH Research Focus and the Gridded Observational Dataset Intercomparison Project (GODIP), and aims to provide a forum for advancing an integrated understanding of physical–biogeochemical coupling in a changing ocean.
title: Ocean Physical–Biogeochemical Interactions under a Changing Climate: Coupled Variability in Oxygen, Carbon, and Heat

description: Growing pressures from human activities (e.g., pollution, habitat alteration, and climate change) threaten marine ecosystems. To assess ocean environmental quality, large datasets from global observing systems and networks (e.g., GOOS, EMODnet) require observations across multiple spatial and temporal scales. These observations can be complemented by scalable and cost-effective technologies and integrated monitoring systems, particularly in coastal and highly dynamic environments, essential to improve data coverage and continuity, supporting integrated analyses of marine ecosystem processes. Citizen Science initiatives can further expand observations in space and time, while raising awareness and strengthening the connection between society and marine research. This session, whose objectives are in line with UN 2030 Agenda Goal 14 and with the UN-launched “Decade of Ocean Science for Sustainable Development”, focuses on the effects of anthropogenic pressures on marine ecosystems and on observational approaches to detect, quantify, and monitor their impacts. Special attention will be given to innovative, scalable and cost-effective technologies, integrated monitoring approaches, and methods that can be replicated across different marine environments. Multidisciplinary contributions combining in-situ observations, remote sensing, autonomous and emerging technologies, modelling, data integration, and citizen science are encouraged to support biodiversity monitoring, ecosystem restoration, environmental assessment, and the sustainable use of marine resources. Topics include the effect of natural and anthropogenic pollution; impacts of global change on marine ecosystems; assessment of cumulative anthropogenic pressures; scalable and cost-effective marine observations and innovative monitoring technologies; marine citizen science; advanced methods for data collection, integration, processing, and analysis; benthic and pelagic community dynamics; and ecosystem services evaluation.
title: Effects of anthropogenic pressures on marine ecosystems: from impacts to scalable, cost-effective observations and citizen science approaches

description: There is growing awareness that ongoing efforts to reduce CO2 emissions will be insufficient to limit global warming to below 2℃ above pre-industrial levels. To meet this target, Carbon Dioxide Removal (CDR) on the order of 10 – 20 Gt CO2/year will be required before the end of the century. While most current CDR technologies applied at scale focus on terrestrial approaches, marine CDR (mCDR) includes methods with some of the largest removal potentials. Actual mCDR field deployments remain limited in scale and operational requirements are still being explored so further research is needed before mCDR can be considered for deployment at scale. This session will focus on the various mCDR technologies, their potential for large-scale deployment and safety considerations, as well as Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) required to support them. We welcome contributions from laboratory and mesocosm experiments, small- and large-scale field trials, numerical modelling, and machine-learning approaches to data, with a particular interest in multidisciplinary submissions.
title: Marine Carbon Dioxide Removal: Progress in understanding the potential, impacts, and MRV requirements

description: Limiting global warming to within planetary boundaries requires rapid emission reductions alongside robust carbon dioxide removal (CDR) frameworks. Compared with land-based approaches, marine CDR (mCDR) approaches are at an earlier stage of development, but offer the potential for negative emissions with less competition for space/resources and great scaling potential.. Evaluating the efficiency and impacts of these marine strategies is now critical to assess whether they are environmentally safe and socially just, and to determine their viability for national carbon accounting and the voluntary carbon market. Current mCDR strategies encompass both abiotic methods (e.g., ocean alkalinity enhancement, direct ocean removal) and biotic approaches (e.g., macroalgae cultivation, iron fertilization, blue carbon ecosystem restoration). These techniques vary widely in their CDR potential, permanence of storage, and requirements for robust Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification (MRV). Additionally, their broader ecological impacts and full life-cycle assessments remain critical areas of uncertainty. This session invites abstracts addressing ocean-related CDR that can contribute to advance the understanding of mCDR potential and impacts. We welcome contributions spanning mCDR modeling and observations across scales, e.g., idealized scenarios with novel mCDR implementations, observational and experimental studies ranging from mCDR pilot sites to laboratory experiments or mesocosm experiments, as well as the impacts of terrestrial CDR (e.g. enhanced rock weathering, river alkalinity enhancement) on the marine environment. Furthermore, we encourage submissions intersecting with the broader environmental, societal, political, legal, and economic implications of scaling marine CDR.
title: Marine Carbon Dioxide Removal: Approaches, Efficiency, Monitoring, and Impacts

description: This session focuses on recent developments and research on ocean data assimilation. Data assimilation is essential for ocean forecasting, reanalysis, and climate studies. By optimally combining numerical simulations with various observations, data assimilation provides a dynamically consistent and comprehensive estimate of the present and past ocean state. This session invites abstract submissions on developments of data assimilation for the physical ocean together with coupled components such as sea ice, marine ecosystems, land-sea interface and atmosphere for ensuring consistency with other parts of the Earth system. The session also focuses on impact of the assimilation and deployment of novel space-borne and in-situ observations such as autonomous platforms, wide-swath satellite tracks, and deep in-situ observations and biogeochemistry profilers. Beyond state estimation, this session also welcomes contributions in parameter estimation, uncertainty quantification, and hybrid machine learning and data assimilation methods focused on the ocean.
title: Data assimilation in the ocean and coupled components

description: Coastal oceans are dynamic interfaces between land and sea, playing a critical role in global biogeochemical cycles with a high impact on socio-economic activities and social developments. The dynamic and physical processes as well as the human activities that take place in coastal areas make them natural laboratories to improve our knowledge about several biogeochemical interactions. In addition, these regions are affected by both natural and anthropogenic factors such as coastal acidification, organic matter, nutrients, and pollution, among others. All these factors have impacts on the natural cycles and the magnitude of these impacts should be studied and understood in order to propose solutions to the decision makers that could help to know, understand, take decisions, and protect or regulate the coastal environments. This session aims to bring together researchers from diverse fields to discuss the latest findings on the biogeochemical processes occurring in coastal oceans, improve our knowledge, identify impacts, and propose solutions in terms of coastal management and blue economy. We welcome research studies that focus on both natural and anthropogenic processes that are affecting the biogeochemical cycles in coastal waters, trace metal chemistry, CO2 system, ocean acidification, ocean alkalinization, nutrient cycle, organic matter, CO2 sequestration, blue carbon, etc.
title: Chemical Processes in Coastal Oceans: Natural and Anthropogenic impacts on the biogeochemical processes

description: The ocean absorbs about a quarter of anthropogenic CO2 emissions each year, which slows climate change but changes ocean chemistry, lowering seawater pH. Ocean-atmosphere CO2 exchange and its consequences are governed by a set of reversible chemical reactions and parameters collectively known as the marine carbonate system. This session welcomes submissions that focus on observing, understanding and modelling the changing marine carbonate system and its role in the global carbon cycle. This includes studies on anthropogenic CO2 uptake and its chemical consequences, the physical and biological carbon pumps, biominerals and the alkalinity cycle, air-sea CO2 fluxes, internal consistency of the carbonate system variables, organic alkalinity, physical chemistry, measurement techniques and data compilations. Studies may be global or regional in scope and they may cover a range of different timescales. Results may be derived from a variety of sources including in situ observations, laboratory experiments, remote sensing, machine learning, and model output.
title: Marine carbonate system and carbon cycle: past, present and future

description: Marine extreme events, including storm surges, marine heatwaves and cold spells, harmful algal and jellyfish blooms, acidification and deoxygenation extremes, ocean responses to severe storms and cyclones, and temporally or spatially compounding events, have major impacts on marine ecosystems, coastal communities and global economies. Under climate change, their frequency, intensity, duration and co-occurrence are changing, yet many of these events remain poorly understood, simulated and predicted. Their dynamics span a broad range of spatial and temporal scales and often involve complex interactions and feedback within the ocean and across the atmosphere-ocean interface. Understanding these multi-scale processes, including interactions among physical, biogeochemical and biological extremes, their cascading effects, and ecosystem impacts, is crucial to improve their detection, attribution and predictability. This session encourages contributions addressing the dynamics of marine, coastal and coupled atmosphere-ocean extremes, including event attribution and future projections. We welcome novel observations and detection strategies, numerical and coupled modelling, statistical and machine-learning approaches for understanding and forecasting extremes, as well as studies of compound and cascading events. Ecosystem and socio-economic impact assessments linked to marine extremes and relevant to risk reduction, mitigation and adaptation are also encouraged.
title: Ocean extremes: multi-scale dynamics through observations, models and machine learning techniques

description: Coastal seas lie at the interface between the open ocean, land and society, yet observing, modelling and forecasting across these scales remains challenging. In a changing climate, improving coastal monitoring capabilities and developing innovative coastal products is vital to protect and manage coastal areas. Novel coastal observations (including satellite,land-based remote sensing and in situ data), advanced hydrological and coastal models, land-ocean data integration, coupling modelling and data assimilation all serve to improve coastal monitoring, and forecasting. Novel numerical model approaches and Artificial Intelligence (AI), including hybrid physics-AI methods, are further enabling pan-European transferable approaches. This session focuses on advanced, seamless ocean observing and forecasting, from global/regional systems to high-resolution coastal systems, through new and improved observations, models, methods, and co-produced (with national or regional authorities) coastal products and services. We particularly welcome contributions that bridge European and regional ocean products with coastal systems and demonstrate interoperable workflows, uncertainty quantification, integration with operational services, and uptake by end users. These advances aim to provide the marine knowledge needed for coastal applications addressing environmental and social challenges and those enhanced by climate change, such as: pollution and eutrophication hazard/risk mapping, coastal erosion and flooding, resource management, harmful algal blooms, and combating ecosystem degradation and restoration, supporting Marine Protected Areas, and addressing natural hazards and extreme events.
title: Advancing Seamless Open-to-Coastal Ocean Observing and Forecasting for Coastal Applications

description: Ocean dynamics span a broad range of spatial and temporal scales, with interacting processes governing the transport, stirring, mixing and exchange of water masses, heat, salt, carbon, nutrients and other tracers. Understanding how these processes interact across scales, from the surface through the water column and across air–sea–ice boundaries, remains a major challenge, particularly under climate variability, climate change and extreme events. This session welcomes studies addressing circulation, sea-level variability, currents, waves, fronts, eddies, filaments, and mesoscale and submesoscale dynamics. Topics may include transport pathways and connectivity, stirring and mixing, vertical and subsurface dynamics, air–sea–ice interactions, and links with biogeochemistry and marine ecosystems. We encourage contributions using satellite and other remote-sensing observations, in situ measurements, numerical and Lagrangian modelling, theoretical approaches, and emerging data-driven methods.
title: Ocean Dynamics, Transport, Mixing and Exchange

description: This open PICO session welcomes presentations on a broad range of ocean processes and oceanographic techniques, including interdisciplinary studies that span several themes and may therefore not fit within a single specialised session. The session covers all marine disciplines, including interactions of the ocean with the atmosphere and/or cryosphere, and welcomes both global studies and regional work with broader relevance across the open ocean and shelf seas. Contributions on ocean processes may include topics such as turbulent mixing, phytoplankton bloom characterisation, and air–sea interactions. We also welcome advances enabled by new instruments and techniques, novel applications of established technologies, and the integration of complementary observational and modelling approaches. These may include gliders, autonomous vehicles, novel sensors, multi-platform observations, robotics, numerical model development and parameterisations, novel instrumentation, or new ways of combining established and emerging approaches.
title: Open session on global ocean processes and oceanographic techniques

description: Ocean stratification describes the layering of seawater, with lighter (warmer, fresher) water overlying denser (cooler, saltier) water. It plays a fundamental role in regulating the vertical exchange of heat, carbon, oxygen, and nutrients in the ocean, with important consequences for marine ecosystems, biogeochemical cycles, and climate. No single metric is appropriate for diagnosing ocean stratification across all applications. Different metrics may be better suited to different scientific question, spatial and temporal scales, and available datasets. As estimates of stratification change can be sensitive to the metric used, careful consideration of metric choice and comparability is essential. While ocean stratification is widely observed to have increased globally over recent decades, and is projected to continue increasing in the future, important questions remain regarding the spatial and temporal heterogeneity of these changes, their underlying controls, and their consequences. Improved quantification, continued development and evaluation of ocean models, and attribution of observed and simulated changes to key mechanisms are needed at both global and regional scales. Changes in ocean stratification can affect ocean deoxygenation, primary production and marine biomass, the carbon cycle, ocean circulation and overturning, ocean heat uptake, tropical cyclones, marine heatwaves, and ultimately human societies. Understanding these links is particularly important for assessing how changes in the ocean may feed back on the climate system. This session welcomes contributions from observers and modellers addressing ocean stratification over a wide range of spatial and temporal scales, including its measurement, variability, drivers, trends, modelling, and impacts. Interdisciplinary subject are particularly encouraged.
title: Ocean stratification: variability, controls, and impacts

description: The Copernicus Marine Service provides regular and systematic reference information on the physical (including sea ice and wind waves) and biogeochemical states of the global ocean and European regional seas. In the coming years, Copernicus Marine will implement next-generation ocean monitoring and forecasting systems and prepare new services for the coastal ocean, marine biology, and regional climate projections. It will also leverage digital capabilities in synergy with EDITO, the European Digital Twin of the Ocean (DTO). EDITO will connect and enable interoperability between a wide range of ocean and coastal numerical tools on a common digital platform, supporting global-to-coastal configurations and the co-development of simulations and what-if scenarios for enhanced on-demand forecasting and ocean climate projections. The session will address key scientific challenges for the coming years, including: (1) integrating Copernicus Sentinel expansion missions into the observation and modelling systems; (2) developing ocean observation design and impact assessment methods to support a harmonized, fit-for-purpose ocean observing system, in line with the ambitions of the European OceanEye; (3) improving the representation of interactions between ocean, waves, sea ice, biogeochemistry, high-trophic levels, land, and the atmosphere in modelling and data assimilation; (4) quantifying and propagating uncertainties across Copernicus Marine components; (5) further leveraging AI capacities for physical, biogeochemical and ecosystem variables, including direct observation prediction, hybrid AI-numerical modelling, quality control, field reconstruction, data assimilation, calibration, super-resolution, and subgrid-scale parametrisation; (6) developing user-oriented on-demand services and what-if scenarios that fully exploit DTO capabilities, including integration of associated datasets (e.g. socio-economic data); (7) strengthening the ocean science-policy interface through policy-relevant information to support marine hazard preparedness, conservation, early warning, climate adaptation, and evidence-based ocean governance. Presentations are invited from teams involved in Copernicus Marine, the European DTO, in situ and satellite observing systems, downstream applications, and relevant R&D projects (e.g. Horizon Europe, ESA, etc.). Contributions from the international OceanPredict community and relevant UN Decade programmes and projects are strongly encouraged.
title: Scientific challenges for the Copernicus Marine Service and the European Digital Twin of the Ocean

description: Plastic pollution is a widely recognized global problem with significant environmental and ecological risks which have been a long-standing focus of research, particularly in marine and estuarine environments. Despite extensive studies in recent years, gaps in consistent data and holistic knowledge persist. These gaps are particularly apparent regarding sources contributions, quantities, transformation and transport processes, and the distribution of plastic and litter across environmental matrices and ecosystem compartments from local to global scale. Addressing these knowledge gaps is critical to accurately assess potential risks, inform policy, and develop effective mitigation strategies. In this session, we will explore the current state of knowledge and ongoing research on litter and macro-, micro-, and nanoplastics in estuarine and marine systems. The session will cover a wide range of topics, including: • Recent findings on plastic distribution and accumulation in estuaries, shorelines, nearshore and open waters, and nearshore and deep seafloor environments. • Source-to-sink investigations, considering quantities and distribution across environmental matrices (water, sediment and biota) and compartments (coastline, surface water, water column and seabed), • Transport, accumulation and dispersal processes influenced by ocean currents, tides, density gradients, waves and gyres. • The role of extreme weather events, such as storms and floods, in redistributing plastic debris. • Impacts on biota, community structure and habitats, from estuaries and coastlines to open waters, including seabed. • Modelling approaches to estimate marine plastic accumulation and their impacts at local, regional and global scales, and to assess the effectiveness of prevention and mitigation measures. • Legislative and regulatory efforts, including international monitoring programs and measures aimed at reducing marine plastic pollution.
title: Advancements in Marine and Estuarine Plastic Pollution Research

description: The expansion of offshore wind farms is altering shelf-sea hydrodynamics, stratification, biogeochemistry, and coastal communities. The methods and findings remain fragmented. This session seeks contributions employing qualitative and quantitative methods to investigate these impacts, connecting them to carbon cycling, energy systems, and transboundary marine spatial planning implications.
title: Interdisciplinary Insights into Offshore Wind Farms Impacts

description: This session, organized by the UN Decade Program CoastPredict, aims to directly contribute to the UN Decade Challenge 6: Enhancing community resilience to ocean hazards. The focus is on addressing critical gaps in scientific knowledge, particularly in key areas such as coastal risk assessment, warning and mitigation strategies. Key topics include: (i) the collection and generation of observational and modeling datasets essential for risk assessment, including downscaled climate projections for coastal regions, all within a robust data-sharing frameworks; (ii) the promotion of interdisciplinary and international research and innovation to comprehensively address these challenges, with a particular emphasis on approaches like Digital Twin technology; (iii) the enhanced People Centred Early Warning Systems for Ocean-related Hazards through Machine learning and Predictive Modelling and the development of indicator and tools for climate adaptation in the coastal area, and (iv) the development of standards for risk communication at both national and international levels. The session will also explore multi-hazard early warning systems for events such as tsunamis, storm surges, marine heatwaves, and coastal biogeochemical hazards, including pollution and other extreme coastal events such as erratic extratropical cyclones. Contributions on machine learning applications, compound event analysis, and disaster risk reduction strategies are strongly encouraged, as are science-based management practices for enhancing coastal resilience. By leveraging innovative tools like digital twins, this session highlights how predictive modeling can significantly improve risk assessment, climate change adaptation and response strategies. Its relevance extends to policymakers, scientists, and coastal communities, fostering collaboration to strengthen coastal resilience.
title: Multi-hazard Early Warning Systems and coastal climate downscaling: Pilot Site experience and science advancement under CoastPredict and the GlobalCoast Initiative

description: Organised jointly by the UN Decade Programme CoastPredict, through its GlobalCoast initiative, and the European Digital Twin Ocean (EDITO), this session addresses how digital infrastructures such as EDITO and GlobalCoast’s prototype, ProtoCoast, can support coastal resilience services. Advancing coastal predictive science is increasingly urgent, particularly in vulnerable regions. Yet effective predictive services depend on the capacity to federate coastal data, tools, applications and HPC resources for modelling. GlobalCoast is developing an integrated, cloud-based digital platform for the global coastal ocean. ProtoCoast, its first operational prototype, is initially operating for the Mediterranean and other regions, with interoperability with infrastructures such as EDITO. EDITO is establishing the EU’s operational Digital Twin Ocean infrastructure and ecosystem, providing an interoperable environment where digital twin applications, data services, observations, modelling capabilities, AI tools and scenario-based services can be developed and delivered, with the ambition to be operational by 2030. This session will examine the scientific and technical challenges of making such systems interoperable, accessible and sustainable, and how they can be connected to strengthen coastal predictive capabilities and support resilience services. We invite contributions on federated cloud architectures for coastal science; coastal digital twins and coupled modelling; FAIR data and semantic interoperability with Copernicus Marine, EMODnet, GOOS and national systems; and cloud-based use of satellite and in situ observations, including AI, for coastal resilience services. We also welcome contributions on AI infrastructure for operational coastal prediction, including curated training datasets, model hosting and versioning, ocean foundation models, computing, benchmarking and reproducibility. Across all themes, we welcome contributions on user engagement and uptake: how public authorities reach these services; which interfaces, training and capacity-building make them usable where they are most needed; and which governance and funding models can sustain them beyond project funding. Contributions on federation between GlobalCoast, EDITO and other regional and national platforms are also encouraged, together with reflections on what the community must sustain beyond 2030 to secure the Ocean Decade’s digital legacy.
title: Coastal digital twins, Observations, and AI-ready cloud infrastructures to support coastal resilience

description: Global coastal zones are of high ecological and societal values. As the dynamic interface between land, sea, and air, they are heavily impacted by a combination of climate-driven environmental change and human interventions. Approaches to sustainably manage the coastal zone increasingly seek to provide co-benefits of risk mitigation, climate regulation, preserving biodiversity, and supporting coastal community resilience. These require scientific evidence and discourse that integrate across disciplines. This session invites multi- and inter-disciplinary contributions focusing on coastal processes, their dynamic interactions, and their role in exchanges across coastal interfaces (e.g. land-sea, air-sea, river-sea, …) under a changing climate and changing human activities. We welcome observational, modelling and theoretical studies reporting on processes linked to coastal hydrodynamics, coastal biogeochemistry, coastal ecology, or coastal sediment dynamics and geomorphology. Studies may span the wide range of spatial and temporal scales characteristic of existing and projected change in coastal seascapes and landscapes from the inner shelf shoreward to reefs, seagrass meadows, beaches and dunes, estuaries, intertidal flats, mangrove forests, saltmarshes and coastal wetlands. We encourage the submission of holistic Earth system studies that explore the role of the coastal zone in coastal sea dynamics including exchanges across coastal interfaces under the impact of climate change and human activities. We also encourage studies that focus on impacts of coastal management or coastal adaptation approaches on coastal processes and dynamics, spanning engineered, hybrid, and nature-based options related to dynamic anthropogenic activities such as coastal protection, tourism, shipping, fisheries and aquaculture, and the expansion of renewable energies and other coastal infrastructure.
title: Coastal dynamics and processes under changing climate and changing human activities.

description: The growing demands on marine space for energy security and renewable infrastructure, such as offshore wind farms, are complicated by the challenges of climate change-induced hazards and the need for environmentally sustainable development. Addressing these challenges requires a holistic and interdisciplinary approach that integrates ocean and marine sciences, marine and geotechnical engineering, geomorphology, natural hazards, and environmental science. Such an approach is essential for improving our understanding of the interactions between climate change, seabed processes, infrastructure performance, and ecosystem health across the entire life cycle of offshore assets. This session invites contributions that advance our collective capacity to plan, design and manage offshore infrastructure that is both climate-resilient and environmentally sustainable. Key themes include, but are not limited to: • Marine geomorphology and seabed processes: characterization of seabed morphology, sediment dynamics, erosion and deposition, and their evolution in offshore environments. • Offshore geohazards identification: mapping and assessing geohazard potential, towards a holistic geological understanding of submarine mass movement initiation and evolution, particularly landslides. • Geohazards and infrastructure modelling, monitoring and characterization: application of state-of-the-art data science, hydroacoustic, geophysical and in-situ monitoring approaches, and development of novel physical/numerical modelling to predict initiation, development and runout of sediments and performance of offshore infrastructure. • Climate-resilient design: novel approaches and case studies coupling engineering optimisation with ecological and geomorphological considerations for building and retrofitting critical offshore infrastructure to withstand climate-induced hazards. We particularly encourage contributions showcasing cross-disciplinary research, including those developed within intersectoral and international consortia. By bringing together diverse perspectives, this session aims to foster a new vision for a sustainable and resilient future for the coexistence of offshore infrastructures and the marine environment.
title: Towards climate-resilient and environmentally sustainable offshore infrastructure

description: The Southern Ocean is vital to our understanding of the climate system. It is a key region for vertical and lateral exchanges of heat, freshwater, carbon, oxygen, and nutrients, with significant past and potential future global climate implications. The role of the Southern Ocean and the Antarctic Circumpolar Current in driving heat and biogeochemical exchanges as well as their response to changing atmospheric forcing and increased Antarctic melting remains uncertain. Indeed, the sparsity of observations of this system and its inherent sensitivity to small-scale physical processes, not fully represented in current Earth System Models, result in large climate projection uncertainties and considerable discrepancies between observations and models. To address these knowledge gaps, ongoing and upcoming efforts, such as Antarctica InSync, SYNCHRONY, ICED, IPY-5, exploit increasingly advanced observational platforms as well as theoretical, numerical and machine learning techniques. These efforts are providing deeper insight into the three-dimensional patterns of Southern Ocean dynamics and their changes on sub-annual, multi-decadal and millennial timescales, as well as their potential future modifications under a changing climate. In this session, we welcome contributions concerning the role of the Southern Ocean in past, present, and future climates. These include (but are not limited to) small-scale physics and mixing, water mass transformation, gyre-scale processes, nutrient and carbon cycling, ventilation, ocean productivity, climate-carbon feedbacks, and ocean-ice-atmosphere interactions. We also welcome contributions exploring the two-way interactions between the Southern Ocean and lower latitudes, including how changes in Southern Ocean circulation, heat and carbon transport affect lower latitudes and vice versa.
title: The Southern Ocean in a changing climate: physical, biogeochemical, and ecosystem processes

description: Natural variability in the North Atlantic spans interannual to centennial time scales and remains large enough to obscure emerging trends in observational records. Changes in the ocean circulation are nonetheless anticipated under continued warming, with consequences for the atmosphere and cryosphere, for regional sea level, and for the uptake and storage of heat and carbon. Understanding this circulation, and separating its natural variability from forced change, rests on sustained observing arrays such as OSNAP and RAPID, on satellite records, and on models spanning a wide range of complexity. We invite contributions on: - variability, dynamics and drivers of the Atlantic meridional overturning and gyre circulations - water-mass transformation and the transport and storage of heat, freshwater and carbon - ocean–atmosphere–cryosphere coupling, overflows, and exchanges between the open ocean and the marginal and shelf seas - observed variability and its interpretation using theory, models, reanalyses and proxy records - response to anthropogenic forcing, including detection and attribution of forced change - predictability of North Atlantic circulation across time scales - implications for regional climate and society, from extremes such as heatwaves, storms and floods to their consequences for infrastructure, health and livelihoods The session brings together the observational, modelling and theoretical communities, and welcomes those working on impacts, to advance understanding of the North Atlantic from the processes governing its circulation and variability to the consequences of their change.
title: North Atlantic: Natural Variability, Global Change and Impacts

description: The oceans are changing rapidly in response to climate change. In this period of rapid change, long-term trends are now emerging across ocean variables, while natural variability operates across a wide range of spatial and temporal scales, placing long-term observations at fixed locations in a unique position to be compared with models and reanalyses to investigate this variability and assess how well they represent changes in the ocean across timescales. In this session, we invite contributions that bring together long-term ocean time series and numerical models and/or reanalyses and satellite data to examine the representation of ocean variability, from daily and seasonal cycles to subseasonal and interannual variability, and longer-term changes and trends. We encourage studies that go beyond model–observation validation and use the comparison to identify processes and timescales that are not adequately represented and investigate the physical causes of observed differences. Such approaches can improve the representation of ocean variability and the processes driving it in models and reanalyses and contribute to better estimates of long-term trends and their uncertainties, improved understanding of ocean–climate interactions, and enhanced skill in seasonal-to-decadal predictions. Contributions are welcome at global, basin-wide and regional scales, and across ocean compartments, from the air–sea interface to the deep ocean and seafloor. Studies addressing ocean circulation and transports, biogeochemical or biological variables are encouraged. Contributions using CMIP models, ocean reanalyses, high-resolution regional models, process models, or other modelling and statistical approaches are all welcome. We particularly welcome contributions demonstrating the scientific value of sustained, high-frequency and long-term observations for improving models and reanalyses and advancing our understanding of a changing ocean.
title: The Changing Ocean – Long Time-Series Observations and Models Across Timescales

description: Energy conservation is a fundamental physical principle, yet it is generally not achieved in state-of-the-art models of geophysical flows owing to, for instance, the governing equations and their discretization, the coupling between model components, or the parameterization of unresolved processes. It is thus non-trivial to close the energy budget, which becomes even more challenging due to the multitude of oceanic processes that undergo nonlinear interactions and drive energy transfers across a range of scales: from eddies to internal waves to small-scale turbulence. This session is devoted to understanding these multi-scale interactions and associated energy transfers in the ocean, which are ultimately crucial for developing energetically consistent models, confidently predict climatic changes, and quantify associated uncertainties, and thus improve our understanding of the climate system. We invite contributions on oceanic energy pathways and their consistent representation in numerical models from theoretical, modeling, and observational perspectives. These include, but are not limited to, the processes involving mesoscale eddies, internal gravity waves, instabilities, turbulence, small-scale mixing, and ocean-atmosphere coupling. Contributions on energy transfer processes and their quantification from in-situ measurements, (semi-)analytical approaches, and numerical models, as well as their parameterizations and spurious energy transfers associated with numerical discretizations, are also welcome along with interdisciplinary contributions such as novel applications in data science that diagnose, quantify, and minimize energetic inconsistencies and related uncertainties. We particularly encourage early career researchers to participate in this session.
title: Eddies, waves and instabilities: observing, modelling, and parameterizing oceanic energy transfers

description: ENSO and the Tropical Pacific, together with their interactions with other tropical basins, are a dominant source of interannual climate variability in the tropics and across the globe. Improving our understanding and modelling of ENSO dynamics, predictability, and impacts, as well as anticipating how these may change in the future, is therefore important for society. This session welcomes contributions addressing all aspects of ENSO, the Tropical Pacific, and tropical basin interactions, including dynamics; multi-scale interactions; decadal and paleo variability; theoretical approaches; ENSO diversity; global teleconnections; impacts on climate, society, and ecosystems; seasonal forecasting; climate change over recent decades, including changes in tropical ocean mean states; climate change projections; and interactions between ENSO and other tropical oceans. We also welcome studies of extreme ENSO events and their associated climate, societal, and ecosystem impacts, including emerging events such as the anticipated 2026 El Niño. Studies aimed at evaluating and improving model simulations of ENSO, tropical ocean mean states, and tropical basin interactions are particularly encouraged, with special attention to the roles of mesoscale variability and ocean–atmosphere coupling.
title: aida

description: The oceans are changing rapidly in response to the changing climate, as evidenced by record-breaking sea surface temperatures in several different regions around the world, altered ocean currents, and shifts in the marine carbon ecosystem. Additional transformations are expected in a warmer future climate. Identifying the mechanisms of oceanic climate change and variability are crucial to developing realistic ocean projections. Projections simulated using the recent Climate Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP) phase 6, provide meaningful insights on the ocean circulation responses under various climate change scenarios. These models are essential to quantify the impacts of oceanic warming and to develop successful adaptation strategies. This session will bring together researchers focused on shaping our understanding of future ocean circulation. First insights from CMIP7 simulations are very much encouraged! We encourage submissions from studies covering global, basin wide, regional, and coastal oceanic changes. Topics covering altering ocean circulation and transports, variability and trends, tipping points and extremes, as well as temperature, salinity and biogeochemistry are welcomed. This session is not limited to CMIP analysis and submissions using other modelling datasets and statistical projections are very much encouraged.
title: The Future Ocean - CMIP and Beyond

description: The ocean surface layer mediates the transfer of energy, momentum, heat, matter, and trace gases between the ocean, atmosphere, and sea ice, and thus plays a central role in the dynamics of the climate system. This session will focus on the ocean surface layer globally, from the coasts – including the marginal sea ice zone – to the pelagic ocean, and its interactions with the overlaying low atmosphere. Of special interest will be contributions describing the impact of ocean surface-layer processes on air-sea fluxes and atmosphere-ocean feedback. These include the parameterization of air-sea interactions, the impact of tropical cyclones, and the role of extreme events. We also welcome studies about the understanding of ocean surface-interior interactions, particle and tracer dispersion, ice-ocean interactions, (sub-)mesoscale and internal-wave dynamics, as well as boundary-layer turbulence and surface-wave effects. Finally, we also encourage studies focusing on the coupling of physical, biological, and biogeochemical processes. Our session welcomes observational (from in-situ to remote sensing), theoretical, and numerical investigations focusing on the ocean surface layer and its interactions with the atmosphere and sea ice, regardless of the temporal and spatial scales considered.
title: The ocean surface layer: multi-scale dynamics and atmosphere-ocean interactions

description: The South Atlantic Ocean is a key component of the global climate system, connecting the tropical Atlantic with the Southern Ocean and linking the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Ocean basins. Its circulation mediates regional redistributions and inter-basin exchanges of heat and freshwater, as well as of carbon, oxygen, nutrients, and other tracers. These transports are shaped by interacting processes across a wide range of spatial and temporal scales, including air-sea interactions, small-scale turbulence and mixing, mesoscale dynamics, boundary currents, and basin-scale overturning circulation. Moreover, the South Atlantic features intricate regional ocean circulation patterns, such as the Agulhas leakage, Benguela Upwelling System and the Brazil-Malvinas confluence zone. Together, these processes influence regional to global climate, extreme events, biogeochemical cycles, marine productivity, and ecosystem variability. Yet, understanding the natural seasonal to interannual variability of these processes and how they evolve under long-term climate change remains challenging, as observations are often still too sparse and model simulations can show contrasting behavior. We invite contributions that advance our knowledge of South Atlantic ocean processes across spatial and temporal scales, based on observations, modelling, theory, and paleo-proxy approaches. Interdisciplinary process studies linking physical oceanography, biogeochemistry, and marine ecosystems are particularly encouraged. We aim to foster exchange across disciplines, methods, regions, and career stages, strengthen collaborations within the South Atlantic scientific community, and promote discussions on future inclusive South Atlantic observing and modelling strategies. We seek to identify knowledge gaps and future research priorities.
title: South Atlantic Ocean Processes Across Scales: Regional Dynamics, Inter-Basin Exchanges and Regional and Global Impacts

description: The interaction between the ocean and the cryosphere in the Southern Ocean has become a major focus in climate research. Antarctic climate change has captured public attention, which has spawned a number of research questions, such as: What to expect in a new Antarctic sea ice regime? Where and when will ocean-driven melting of ice shelves yield a tipping point in the Antarctic climate? Which processes drive the redistribution of heat around Antarctica and onto the shelf? How is Antarctic Bottom Water production affected by changing ice-ocean interactions? What role do ice-related processes play in nutrient upwelling on the continental shelf and in triggering carbon export to deep waters? We look out for progress in observing and understanding the interaction — and changes thereof — between ice shelf, sea-ice, ocean and atmosphere in a rapidly warming climate. Recent advances in observational technology, data coverage, and modelling provide scientists with a better understanding of the mechanisms involving ice-ocean interactions in the far South. Processes on the Antarctic continental shelf have been identified as missing links between the cryosphere, the global atmosphere and the deep open ocean that need to be captured in large-scale and global model simulations. This session calls for studies on physical and biogeochemical oceanography linked to ice shelves and sea ice. This includes work on all scales, from local to basin-scale to circumpolar; as well as paleo, present-day and future applications. As the community gears up for a circumpolar, year-round internationally coordinated campaign: Antarctica InSync, we would like to highlight the importance of seasonality and lack of winter data as an overarching challenge. Studies based on in-situ observations and remote sensing, and employing regional to global models as well as AI tools are welcome. We particularly invite cross-disciplinary topics involving glaciology, sea ice physics and biological oceanography.
title: Under cover: The Southern Ocean’s connection to sea ice and ice shelves

description: Modes of tropical climate variability such as the El Niño-Southern Oscillation, Indian Ocean Dipole, tropical Atlantic variability, Madden Julian Oscillation, monsoons, and interactions among tropical basins, influence hydroclimate, extremes, ecosystems, and societies far beyond the tropics. Despite sustained development, climate models continue to exhibit biases in tropical mean states, precipitation, convection, air-sea coupling, circulation, variability, and teleconnections. These errors distort predictability and contribute to uncertainty in projections of climate modes and their impacts. This session will connect three parts of the modelling challenge: identifying the origins and consequences of persistent biases; evaluating improvements in resolution, parameterizations, coupling, initialization, and data-driven or hybrid methods; and determining how better present-day simulations can yield more credible predictions and future projections. We welcome work using observations and reanalyses, hierarchy-of-model approaches, coupled model intercomparisons, large ensembles, initialized predictions, perturbed-physics experiments, emergent constraints, machine learning, and novel diagnostics. Contributions may address tropical atmosphere-ocean-land interactions across weather, subseasonal, seasonal, interannual, decadal, and climate-change timescales. Studies that link process understanding to model development, compare generations of models, quantify uncertainty, or assess the global and regional impacts of tropical simulation errors are especially encouraged. By bringing together model developers, observational researchers, and prediction and projection communities, the session aims to identify advances, unresolved barriers, and practical priorities for the next generation of climate simulations.
title: Simulating Tropical Climate Variability: Model Biases, Advances, and Future Projections

description: We invite presentations on ocean surface waves, and wind-generated waves in particular, their dynamics, modelling and applications. This is a large topic of the physical oceanography in its own right, but it is also becoming clear that many large-scale geophysical processes are essentially coupled with the surface waves, and those include climate, weather, tropical cyclones, Marginal Ice Zone and other phenomena in the atmosphere and many issues of the upper-ocean mixing below the interface. This is a rapidly developing area of research and geophysical applications, and contributions on wave-coupled effects in the lower atmosphere and upper ocean are strongly encouraged.
title: Surface Waves and Wave-Coupled Effects in Lower Atmosphere and Upper Ocean

description: Contributions are invited on recent advances in our understanding of circulation and fluid dynamical processes in coastal and shelf seas. We welcome observational, modelling, theoretical and interdisciplinary studies spanning a wide range of temporal and spatial scales, from the shelf break to the coastal zone. The session aims to bring together studies addressing the diverse and dynamic processes that shape coastal and shelf environments, including shelf circulation, canyon flows, exchange flows in semi-enclosed seas, mesoscale and submesoscale eddies and dynamics, river plumes and estuaries, as well as flow interactions with biogeochemistry, sediment dynamics and nearshore physics. Contributions addressing the effects of climate change, extreme events, and anthropogenic activities—including offshore wind farms and other marine renewable-energy developments—on coastal seas and estuaries are also welcome. Early-career scientists are especially encouraged to submit their work to this session.
title: Open session on coastal and shelf seas

description: Coastal zones are rapidly changing environments exposed to interacting processes and hazards across a wide range of spatial and temporal scales. Understanding and anticipating these changes requires continuous observations that capture both long-term trends and rapid responses to extreme events. Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) provides unique advantages for coastal monitoring through its all-weather, day-and-night imaging capability and sensitivity to surface roughness. Combined with multisource Earth observation, in situ measurements, numerical and data-driven modelling and artificial intelligence (AI), SAR offers new opportunities for integrated coastal monitoring, forecasting and dynamic virtual platforms for simulation and interactive scenario testing (digital twins). This session welcomes contributions presenting new methods and innovative applications of SAR and advanced SAR techniques to support coastal monitoring, understanding, forecasting, adaptation and management. We invite studies addressing applications including multiscale coastal geomorphology, coastal hydro-morphodynamics and coastal–ocean interactions, coastal hazards and their drivers (e.g. flooding, erosion, subsidence and extreme events), coastal vegetation and ecosystems, and land-cover and land-use change. Contributions combining SAR with complementary data sources, AI/ML and numerical modelling across different coastal typologies and scales are particularly encouraged, from the reconstruction of historical changes to forecasting, near-real-time applications, as well as the development and continuous updating of coastal digital twins. The session aims to bring together the SAR and broader Earth observation, coastal and ocean science and management communities to exchange new methodologies and applications. It will explore how SAR-derived information can contribute to the continuum from coastal observation and monitoring to forecasting and digital twins, supporting coastal adaptation pathways, planning and management.
