Attendees will gain an overview of emerging methods, applications and opportunities in this fast-developing frontier, while connecting with researchers and practitioners across the coastal, Earth observation, modelling and management communities. The session will provide an opportunity to hear updates on work progressing across Europe, understand how these efforts are being integrated, and identify potential synergies, knowledge gaps and avenues for future collaboration.
title: From satellite to the coast: SAR-enabled coastal monitoring, forecasting and digital twins

description: Our understanding of the Indian Ocean’s physical, biogeochemical, and ecological characteristics and their variability across a range of spatiotemporal scales has advanced in recent years. However, there remain significant gaps in our knowledge in observing, modeling, and predicting the Indian Ocean’s changing environmental conditions and its role in regional and global climate. This session invites Indian Ocean contributions based on observations, modelling, theory, and palaeo proxy evidence across a range of timescales from synoptic, interannual, decadal to centennial and beyond. Topics of interest include past, current, and projected changes in Indian Ocean physical and biogeochemical properties and their impacts on ecological processes, diversity in Indian Ocean modes of variability, interactions and exchanges between the Indian Ocean and other ocean basins via both oceanic and atmospheric pathways, as well as impacts on regional hydroclimate and the adjacent Asia-Australia-Africa monsoon systems. Submissions are sought on assessing and predicting weather and climate extremes of societal relevance in the Indian Ocean and surrounding regions. We especially welcome submissions addressing compound extreme events that span across the ocean, atmosphere, land, and/or biogeochemical and ecological realms. Furthermore, studies evaluating climate risks, vulnerability, resilience, adaptation and mitigation strategies in coastal and watershed regions affected, for example, by a warming climate, tropical cyclones, and extremes in sea level are encouraged. We also welcome contributions that address research on the Indian Ocean, using advanced techniques such as artificial intelligence/machine learning, and new technological advances in observing systems.
title: Understanding the Indian Ocean’s past, present and future

description: As the densest water mass in the abyssal ocean, Antarctic Bottom Water (AABW) occupies more than one-third of the global ocean volume and constitutes the lower limb of the global meridional overturning circulation. The production and properties of AABW are largely determined by Dense Shelf Water (DSW) that is formed by intense sea ice formation and brine rejection in coastal polynyas around Antarctica. As the precursor water mass, DSW cascades down the continental slope after crossing the shelf break, entrains ambient deep water, and ultimately transforms into AABW. Beyond driving abyssal circulation, these dense water masses also play a major role in the transport and long-term storage of heat, carbon, oxygen, nutrients, and other biogeochemical tracers in the abyss, and further modulate the productivity of marine ecosystems and biogeochemical cycles. Exploring the dynamics and variability of DSW and AABW is essential to improve our understanding of the global heat distribution, carbon budgets, and long-term climate variability. Observational evidence has revealed a widespread contraction in AABW volume across global abyssal waters. At the same time, changes in DSW and AABW properties are not spatially uniform around Antarctica, highlighting substantial uncertainty in their future evolution. This session aims to advance a comprehensive and process-based understanding of AABW, bridging gaps between DSW and AABW transport, formation, transformation, and variability mechanisms, and corresponding impacts on climate variability and change and biogeochemical cycles. To encourage broad participation, we welcome contributions based on in-situ observations, remote sensing, and numerical simulations covering the full pathway from DSW formation and export to AABW transformation and spreading, with an emphasis on Ross Sea-originated DSW and AABW.
title: From Dense Shelf Water to Antarctic Bottom Water: Formation, Transport, Transformation, Variability, and Climate Impacts

description: The Mediterranean, Marmara, and Black Seas - collectively referred to here as the Southern European Seas, are experiencing rapid climate-driven transformations. Recent trends reveal accelerating sea surface warming, intense marine heatwaves, intermediate and deep-water salinization, sea-level rise, and expanding deoxygenation. Given their semi-enclosed nature, strong interbasin connectivity, densely populated coasts, and vulnerability to climate change, understanding the physical and biogeochemical drivers behind these trends is critical. Recent years have seen significant progress in deciphering basin-scale circulation, strait exchange dynamics, wave dynamics and extremes, sea-level variability, and land-coast-ocean interactions - spanning high-frequency meteo-oceanographic extremes to long-term climate projections. Crucial to this progress are sustained and innovative observing systems (especially in regions where in-situ observations remain sparse or have recently declined, as is the case in the Black Sea and the Eastern Mediterranean), citizen science integration, high-resolution numerical modelling and reanalyses including data assimilation, validation and intercomparison frameworks, and advanced data-driven or AI/ML approaches complementing operational ocean and wave forecasting systems. This session welcomes multidisciplinary contributions on physical and biogeochemical processes across the Mediterranean, Marmara, and Black Seas. We invite submissions addressing: Novel Monitoring Strategies: Basin-scale to coastal observing systems, autonomous platforms, remote sensing, innovative measurement approaches, and citizen science, addressing in-situ observational gaps and long-term observing capacity. Process Understanding: Short-to long-term variability, basin circulation and interbasin connectivity, strait dynamics, land-sea interfaces, wave dynamics and extremes, biogeochemical dynamics and deoxygenation, and extreme event impacts. Modeling & AI Advancements: Numerical models, data-driven ML//AI frameworks and approaches, including methods for data-sparce regions (such as the Black Sea and Eastern Mediterranean), validation frameworks and data assimilation. Operational Oceanography & Climate services: Forecasting systems, downstream applications, digital twins, coastal and marine hazards, climate indicators and tools to support climate adaptation and coastal resilience.
title: Advances in Understanding the Dynamics of the Southern European Seas (Mediterranean, Marmara and Black Seas)

description: Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are prolonged and extreme warm ocean conditions, both surface and subsurface, with potential to cause substantial ecological and socio-economic damage. Understanding the physical mechanisms that generate MHWs is important to improving our capacity to predict them. Meanwhile, gaining a better understanding of MHW impacts on ecosystems, and their interactions with other parts of the climate system, is significant for promoting sustainable development in the face of climate change. We welcome abstract submissions across all aspects of MHW research and particularly encourage studies of the following themes. Drivers and methods: novel physical analyses, definitions which challenge the now-traditional statistical framework, observational and modelling requirements for reliable monitoring, AI/ML-based detection and prediction for surface and subsurface MHWs. Impacts and mitigation: Socio-economic damage to marine activities and industries including but not limited to tourism, fisheries, aquaculture; discussions with stakeholders. Timescales of predictability: sub-seasonal to seasonal forecasting, long term projections, attribution, precursors, and sources of uncertainty. Compound events: ecosystem and biogeochemical implications (e.g. on nutrient/oxygen availability/harmful algal blooms/ocean acidification and trophic web), compound extremes with atmospheric circulation/extreme weather events (e.g. tropical cyclones/monsoon circulation). This session welcomes studies across all spatial and temporal scales; studies on compound extremes and subsurface events are particularly welcome.
title: Marine Heatwaves: drivers, impacts, and compound extremes

description: To study the pathways and fate of marine contaminants, such as anthropogenic hydrocarbons, marine litter (including plastics), heavy metals, HNSs, POPs, radionuclides, PFAS, pharmaceuticals, and other pollutants, researchers widely use oceanographic monitoring, modeling, and laboratory experiments. This session explores in situ and remote monitoring approaches, including satellite observations, aerial and marine drones, laboratory studies, computational tools, and digital applications (web- and mobile-based) to understand the distribution and impact of marine pollutants at various scales. It also welcomes emerging citizen science initiatives that help track pollution sources and validate remote observations, as well as transdisciplinary studies highlighting broader impacts on ecosystem services and related socioeconomic aspects affecting communities. Solicited topics include new and varied monitoring protocols, toxicity testing, ensemble and multi-model simulations, machine learning, and AI-based approaches. Marine pollution and its effects on ecosystems continue to pose serious challenges for the sustainable management of coastal and open-ocean areas. Thus, studies linking marine pollution to broader ecosystem stressors, such as climate change and environmental degradation, are especially welcome. The growing human impact on the Arctic Ocean, driven by melting polar ice, underscores the need to understand the fate of marine pollutants in ice-covered waters. This session aims to answer key questions: What do we know about marine pollution sources? Which factors influence the dispersion of pollutants in the aquatic environment? What happens to contaminants in the water column, sediments, and at the sea surface? How do marine pollutants interact with biota? The impact of other environmental stressors, such as artificial light, noise, and thermal pollution, on marine ecosystem resilience is also an important topic for discussion.
title: Monitoring, Modeling, and Risk Mapping of Marine Pollution and Its Environmental and Socioeconomic Impacts

description: The Arctic region has undergone rapid and often abrupt changes over the past decades. Sea ice has become thinner, more mobile, and more prone to sudden breakup. Extreme temperature events have also become routine, with 2023 recording the warmest Arctic summer so far. The Arctic is warming nearly four times faster than the global average, driving ice sheet melt, sea ice retreat in the Kara and Laptev Seas, permafrost thaw, glacier loss, and wildfire activity. Consequently, the exposed ocean is increasingly prone to eddies, extreme events, and low-frequency climate oscillations and more susceptible to abrupt transitions in water mass structure and atmospheric circulation. Together with rising freshwater volumes, increased coastal runoff from Siberia and Greenland, and stronger exchange with the Atlantic and Pacific, these shifts are drastically reshaping the region's already fragile ecosystems. Projections point to a seasonally ice-free Arctic Ocean by mid-century. This raises pressing questions: What might the future Arctic Ocean look like? How do Arctic changes interact with, and respond to, conditions at lower latitudes? What mechanisms drive the ongoing loss of sea ice, and how might they evolve in an increasingly ice-free system? Where should observational, remote sensing, and modeling efforts focus next? This session invites contributions spanning the recent past, present, and future of the Arctic and subarctic oceans. We welcome studies of ocean-atmosphere-sea ice interactions; ocean eddies, extremes, and climate oscillations; the processes and feedbacks driving trends, transitions, and abrupt shifts in the Arctic system; small-scale dynamics, internal waves, and mixing; the sources and downstream impacts of freshwater change, including subarctic deep convection; and the broader coupling between the Arctic and global ocean circulation. Cross-disciplinary submissions are especially encouraged, particularly those connecting physical, cryospheric, biogeochemical, and ecological processes, as well as their links to terrestrial systems. We welcome discussions on the future of Arctic Ocean observation, remote sensing, and modeling strategies (including the upcoming CMIP7 cycle) and on ways to validate and improve models against observations. Submissions drawing on recent field programs such as MOSAiC, the Nansen Legacy Project, and the Synoptic Arctic Survey are welcome, as are contributions from those planning the upcoming International Polar Year 2032-33.
title: Changes in the Arctic Ocean, sea ice and subarctic seas systems: Observations, Models and Perspectives

description: The observation of ocean velocities is of key importance for understanding the ocean and managing human activities at sea. Yet, these observations face challenges due to sampling issues and the absence of direct satellite measurements. Currently, High-Frequency Radars (HFR) stand as the sole operational tools capable of delivering extensive surface current observations. HFR can offer high-resolution velocity data, typically ranging from 1 to 5 km, for coastal areas extending up to 100 or 200 km, contingent on the frequency used. Over recent years, HFR networks have strengthened and emerged as a crucial source for measuring ocean velocities. This expansion has been paralleled by advancements in analysis techniques and an increase in HFR applications. Additionally, upcoming satellite missions like ESA's Harmony missions are anticipated to enhance the scope of coastal HFR measurements. This session aims to foster interdisciplinary dialogue among scientists innovating HFR methods, oceanographers utilizing HFR data in their studies, and researchers exploring new satellite-based concepts for measuring surface velocities. We invite contributions covering all facets of HFR development and application in oceanographic research. Topics for discussion include, but are not limited to, the application of HFR data to oceanographic challenges, novel methods for HFR data analysis, and leveraging synergies with existing missions (such as the Sentinel constellation, SWOT, etc.) or future missions like Harmony.
title: High-Frequency Radar observations of ocean surface velocities: advances, applications and synergies with present and future satellite missions

description: Organic molecules preserved in sediments and other environmental archives record the organisms, environment, and process-specific dynamics from which they originated. Interpreting their signals, however, requires disentangling biological, physical, and chemical overprints from the original signal. Lipid biomarkers from diverse source organisms spanning archaea, bacteria, algae and higher plants to animals, together with their stable isotopic composition, remain one of the most powerful tools for this work. Analyses often integrate various compound classes such as n-alkanes, fatty acids, alkenones, sterols, hopanoids, HBIs (Highly Branched Isoprenoids), HGs (Heterocyst Glycolipids), GDGTs (Glycerol Dialkyl Glycerol Tetraethers), and intact polar lipids, applied across settings ranging from modern process studies to deep-time reconstructions. This session draws together biomarker-based research across terrestrial, lacustrine, marine and anthropogenically influenced environments. We encourage submissions of studies using new biomarker tools, proxy development, compound-specific isotope analyses (e.g., δ¹³C, δ²H, δ18O, Δ¹⁴C), lipid biosynthesis and phylogeny of source organisms, and transport and diagenetic processes. We also invite studies applying biomarker and isotopic evidence to reconstruct environmental variables such as temperature, hydroclimate, vegetation change, human impact, and biogeochemical cycling across modern and past environments. We particularly encourage contributions from early-career scientists.
title: Lipid biomarkers across the tree of life: novel molecular and isotopic tools for environmental and biogeochemical studies

description: Life on Earth depends on a thin and dynamic layer at the interface of atmosphere, vegetation, soil, and water. Within this complex system, remote sensing (RS) provides unique insights by capturing signals generated through the interaction of incoming, reflected, and emitted electromagnetic (EM) radiation with these surfaces. Vegetation, soil, and water play a critical role as mediators between terrestrial ecosystems and the atmosphere, and their properties can be observed through optical, thermal, and microwave remote sensing, including fluorescence signals across the EM spectrum. This session invites contributions that advance our understanding of the biosphere through strategies, methods, and applications of remote sensing. We welcome studies on: • Integrating RS data across spectral regions, angular configurations, and fluorescence signals • Combining RS with in-situ measurements for modelling carbon, water and nutrients cycles • Applications in climate change mitigation and adaptation, food production and security, sustainable development, land and nature conservation and protection, biodiversity, epidemiology, and public health (e.g., allergenic pollen-related impacts) • Air pollution from both natural and anthropogenic sources (e.g., fires emissions, GHG emissions form land-sector, VOCs) • Data assimilation of RS and in-situ observations in bio-geophysical, land surface models and atmospheric models • Innovative RS signal extraction and processing techniques We encourage submissions showcasing novel approaches, interdisciplinary applications, and case studies that highlight the growing potential of remote sensing for addressing urgent environmental and societal challenges.
title: Remote Sensing Applications for the Biosphere

description: Quantifying biodiversity and assessing its role in preserving ecosystem functions is essential for mitigating biodiversity loss and sustaining ecosystem services. However, large-scale quantification of plant diversity requires cost-effective and comparable methodologies to enable global and frequent mapping of plant diversity. New methods, such as remote sensing, genomics, or artificial intelligence might enable such global monitoring. This information could be combined with independent measurements or model-based estimates of ecosystem functions to characterize the role of plant diversity in maintaining ecosystem functions and services. Despite the potential of this approach, numerous conceptual gaps and methodological challenges still need to be overcome. On one side, the new technological alternatives to quantify plant diversity face conceptual and methodological gaps with traditional field ecology. These gaps should be filled, or the limitations of each technology well understood, so that the information provided is adequately used. On the other hand, the analysis of biodiversity-ecosystem functions must account for numerous additional factors to avoid spurious relationships and, therefore, a misunderstood role of how diversity supports ecosystem services. This session calls for recent studies showing advances in this field. We welcome both specialized and multidisciplinary contributions that advance the estimation of plant diversity and the use of these estimates to assess its role in the stability, resilience, and magnitude of ecosystem functions and services. The session is also open to out-of-the-box approaches and biodiversity studies involving taxa beyond plants.
title: New methods for large-scale quantification of plant biodiversity and its interactions with ecosystem functions and services

description: Land-atmosphere coupling modulates the exchange of water, heat and carbon between the land surface and the atmosphere. Therefore, it can dampen or exacerbate climate extremes (e.g., heat waves and droughts) and affect ecosystem processes (e.g., the land carbon sink). However, there are several key aspects related to uncertainties that hinder the accurate quantification of land-atmosphere coupling. Firstly, different metrics/indices can be used to describe (aspects of) land-atmosphere coupling, introducing uncertainties between the respective estimates. Secondly, an increasing amount of data describing land-atmosphere coupling is available, together with increasingly powerful methods for analysing them. In response to this, a more thorough consideration of uncertainty stemming from data and methods is critical in interpreting the robustness of emerging patterns. Lastly, physical processes underlying land-atmosphere coupling occur on different spatiotemporal scales ranging from in-situ to the regional scale and from seconds to months, which may or may not be reflected in the data we use to study them, in turn further inducing uncertainties. Only by considering these aspects it is possible to determine accurately where available information is (not) sufficient to draw robust conclusions. Addressing the uncertainty challenge aims at a more precise identification of e.g. accurate observational constraints for process-based modelling or a more accurate determination of the role of land-atmosphere interactions for changes in (surface) weather and climate. We invite abstracts that quantify uncertainties of various origins relevant for studying land-atmosphere interactions, including but not limited to inter- and intracomparisons of observations and model output, evaluations across spatiotemporal scales, and assessments of variables capturing surface carbon or water fluxes and indices/metrics. We are especially interested in abstracts that move beyond solely quantifying the uncertainties, but motivate us to address and reconcile them and abstracts focusing on the implications of uncertainties related to land-atmosphere interactions on the evolution and location of extremes, carbon processes or the location of land-atmosphere coupling hot spots, among others.
title: Uncertainties in land-atmosphere interactions: What we (don’t) know

description: Marine sediments are an important sink of organic carbon and source of alkalinity, providing a valuable climate regulating function (“Blue Carbon”). Human activities that disturb the seabed might, however, compromise the effectiveness of the seabed in storing organic carbon through a net increase of organic carbon remineralisation, or reduction of its alkalinity-generation capacity by stimulating re-oxidation of reduced minerals. For example, intense mobile bottom fishing may lead to reductions of organic carbon and pyrite stocks, especially in muddy sediments. Other human activities that disturb marine sediment include marine construction, dredging and dumping, offshore wind infrastructure, and submarine cables and pipelines. Sediment disturbance impacts on coastal carbon cycling are largely site or region-specific and difficult to generalise due to the many mechanisms that support stock creation and responses to disturbance, often in opposing directions. In addition, the fate of the ‘lost’ organic carbon or oxidized minerals, and consequences for the marine environment and global climate are currently not well understood. The roles of benthic fauna and of the water column biological carbon pump in carbon cycling under disturbance are also unclear. Until recently, field and modelling studies have focussed on processes in or near the seabed. It is, however, becoming increasingly clear that a holistic approach is necessary to assess the impacts. Only then will it be possible to provide robust advice for marine spatial management and policy. We therefore invite abstracts that cover any aspects relating to understanding and quantifying the climate impacts of human activities disturbing the seabed that may be relevant for carbon cycling. These may be observational, experimental, predictive or frameworks to support management. Key topics of this session include, but are not limited to: - Carbon stocks, accumulation rates, reactivity, and provenance - The role of flora and fauna in mediating remineralisation, accumulation and burial of carbon, and how disturbance may alter these functions. - Disturbance impacts on water column nutrients, ecosystem processes, inorganic carbon chemistry and alkalinity dynamics - Management of carbon stocks under uncertain disturbance outcomes
title: Towards a holistic understanding of anthropogenic marine sediment disturbance impacts on the carbon cycle

description: Peatland restoration for conservation purposes has been implemented for decades now, but recently the focus has been shifting towards a reconciliation of the production of biomass with ecological goals, especially the reduction of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, while peatland management in conservation-focusses projects increasingly has to be adapted to climate change. Management measures include, but are not limited to, productive use of wet peatlands (paludiculture), improved water management in conventional agriculture and forestry, photovoltaic on wet peatlands, solutions for peat originating from infrastructure projects and innovative approaches in conservation-focused rewetting projects. We invite studies addressing all types of peatland management and their impacts on GHG exchange, ecosystem services and biodiversity. Work on all spatial scales from laboratory to global level addressing biogeochemical and biological aspects as well as experimental and modelling studies are welcome. Furthermore, we invite contributions addressing policy coherence e.g., in the context of the EU Nature Restoration Law and evaluating policy instruments for initiating and implementing new management practices on organic soils. Implementation and efficiency of management practices depends not only on hydrogeology and climate but also on other regional factors. Therefore, we hope to host contributions from different geographical regions where peatlands are important including boreal, temperate and tropical peatlands.
title: Paludiculture, peatland management and restoration

description: Organic carbon (OC) plays a fundamental role in the Earth’s climate system and biogeochemical cycles. Understanding the sources, transport, transformation, and fate of OC, as well as exchanges between dissolved and particulate phases, is critical for constraining regional and global carbon budgets, assessing carbon sequestration, and predicting ecosystem responses to natural and anthropogenic environmental change. The land–ocean continuum, which encompasses rivers and coastal waters to continental margins and the deep ocean, provides important pathways for carbon transfer, transformation, and storage across a wide range of spatial and temporal scales. During transport, biological, chemical, and physical processes, such as mineral-organic interactions and hydrodynamic transport, could profoundly alter the composition, reactivity, and age of OC, thereby influencing its preservation, redistribution, and ultimate burial. As a result, identifying carbon sources, quantifying carbon fluxes, assessing carbon burial efficiency, and constraining long-term carbon sequestration remain major challenges in understanding land-to-ocean carbon cycle research. This session aims to bring together researchers investigating OC transport and cycling across the land–ocean continuum, from terrestrial and freshwater sources to coastal and marine sinks. We welcome observational, experimental, paleoenvironmental, and modelling studies addressing carbon sources, fluxes, transport pathways, transformation processes, preservation, burial, and sequestration in both particulate and dissolved forms. Contributions spanning the water column to the sedimentary record, including water sample, suspended particulate matter, sediment-trap observations, aquatic sediments, and sediment cores, are particularly encouraged. Remote sensing, autonomous observations, and numerical modelling approaches, either as standalone tools or integrated with field and laboratory studies, are likewise encouraged. We also welcome studies exploring the impacts of human activities and climate variability on carbon cycling across both modern and past environments.
title: Organic Carbon Transport and Cycling Across the Land–Ocean Continuum

description: Marine calcifiers play a fundamental role in ocean ecosystems and the global carbon cycle by producing and exporting calcium carbonate (CaCO₃). Pelagic calcifiers, chiefly coccolithophores, foraminifers and pteropods account for a major fraction of pelagic CaCO₃ production, but benthic calcifiers such as foraminifers and coralline red algae are also important ecologically and are used as proxy archives. Understanding their future under climate change requires connecting processes operating at the level of biomineralization with organismal physiology, ecology, biogeochemical cycling and ecosystem change. This session will bring together experimental, field-based, geochemical, modelling and palaeoceanographic approaches to investigate how environmental change affects marine calcification and the fate of calcifiers. We particularly invite contributions addressing the mechanisms underlying biomineralization, including ion transport, carbonate chemistry, elemental and isotopic fractionation, and the controls on calcification and dissolution. We also welcome studies examining how physiological responses translate into changes in growth, reproduction, species distributions, community structure and ecosystem functioning and how these responses shape the vulnerability and resilience of marine calcifiers to ocean change. A central goal is to bridge traditionally separated perspectives: controlled laboratory experiments that identify the mechanisms governing calcification; observations and experiments across natural environmental gradients that reveal organismal responses in situ; and biogeochemical and Earth-system models that translate these processes into consequences for the marine carbonate cycle. We encourage contributions from research on all major pelagic and benthic calcifiers as well as comparative studies across taxa, life stages and environments. Studies using modern observations, experiments, sedimentary archives, geochemical proxies and modelling are particularly welcome. By bringing these approaches together, the session aims to advance a mechanistic understanding of how marine calcification responds to environmental change and how these responses may propagate from individual organisms to ecosystems and the global carbon cycle.
title: How biomineralization and ecology shape the future of marine calcifiers

description: Tiny changes in tree stem radius, often only a few micrometres, contain a wealth of information about tree growth dynamics, water status and responses to environmental stress at hourly, daily or seasonal timescales. Dendrometers provide this data, in some cases with near-real time online access. A network of dendrometers over larger regions allows monitoring of biological dynamics of forests across ecosystems and species ranges, identifying trends, disentangling stressors, and more. To bring together dendrometer users, create synergies, and foster collaboration, we are in the process of establishing a global dendrometer network (https://globaldendro.org/), accompanied by a metadatabase with easy-to-access information about region, species coverage, number and type of dendrometers, and more. In this session, we invite contributions to share ideas, results and discuss implications from all areas of dendrometer-related research, including but not limited to - Forest productivity - Dendrometers and carbon sequestration - Dendrometers and water regulation - Comparison of dendrometer types - Dendrometers to build drought stress indicators - Dendrometers and remote sensing proxies - Methodological developments for dendrometer data analysis
title: From microscopic movements to global insights - a spotlight on dendrometer research

description: Climate change is increasing the frequency, extent, and severity of forest disturbances, including drought, heatwaves, fires, windthrow, pathogens, insect outbreaks, and their compound effects. These disturbances can cause rapid carbon losses through reduced productivity, increased mortality, and reshape forest structure and composition. At the same time, forests face diversifying management pressures: growing wood demand is driving more intensive harvesting, while climate and biodiversity goals are expanding restoration and conservation efforts. Therefore, climate-driven disturbances and management interventions increasingly co-occur and interact, making it critical to understand how forests will reconcile or trade off carbon sequestration, wood provision, and biodiversity conservation. This session focuses on detecting and attributing forest disturbances, quantifying their ecological and carbon consequences, and evaluating management responses across spatial and temporal scales. We invite studies that combine remote sensing, forest inventories, eddy-covariance observations, atmospheric inversions, experiments, machine learning, and process-based models to monitor disturbance occurrence and severity; distinguish natural disturbances from anthropogenic interventions; quantify impacts on productivity, biomass, mortality, regeneration, and carbon fluxes; and track post-disturbance changes in forest structure, composition, and function. We particularly welcome data-driven and AI-enabled approaches that integrate complementary observations across spatial and temporal scales, constrain model representations of mortality and recovery, and evaluate management pathways and their synergies and trade-offs across carbon sequestration, wood provision, biodiversity conservation, and forest resilience. The session will connect advances in forest disturbance monitoring, impact attribution, and management-relevant modelling to identify pathways that reconcile carbon sequestration, sustainable wood provision, biodiversity conservation, and forest resilience, providing an evidence base for forest management and policy decisions under intensifying climate and societal pressures.
title: From Forest Disturbance to Management: Carbon–Wood Synergies and Trade-offs

description: Our ability to understand biogeochemical cycles of carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus and other elements in aquatic ecosystems has evolved enormously thanks to advancements in in situ sensor and laboratory techniques and predictive models. The aim of this session is to demonstrate how this methodological advancement improves our understanding of coupled hydrological, biogeochemical and ecological processes in freshwater aquatic environments, streams, rivers, lakes, wetlands and estuaries, controlling the fate of organic matter, nutrients, sediments and other chemical substances. In particular, our session focuses on improving the characterization of the origins, delivery pathways, transformations and environmental fate of organic matter, nutrients and sediments in aquatic environments along with identification of robust numerical tools for advanced processing and modelling of biogeochemical data. As hydrological, biogeochemical, and ecological processes undergo accelerated change, this session welcomes also studies presenting approaches and tools to monitor, model, and predict water quality and sensitivity of aquatic ecosystems to global change and human disturbances.
title: Aquatic biogeochemical cycles: From measurements to understanding patterns and processes in stream networks, lakes, wetlands and estuaries

description: Despite its considerable potential for agricultural monitoring and precision agriculture, the operational adoption of remote sensing remains limited by several challenges, including the robustness of measurements under varying acquisition conditions and the transferability of models across different environments and datasets. This session aims to address the methodological challenges associated with scaling remote sensing approaches from experimental settings to reliable operational applications in agriculture. We welcome contributions focusing on methods for improving the consistency and comparability of remote sensing measurements under varying acquisition conditions, including atmospheric and weather effects, illumination and viewing geometry, and bidirectional reflectance distribution function corrections. We also encourage studies developing and evaluating robust and transferable models, including AI-based approaches, with particular emphasis on validation using independent datasets and assessment of model generalization across different sites, seasons, crops, sensors, and environmental conditions. The session is open to all remote sensing platforms, including UAS, ground-based and tractor-mounted systems, and satellites, as well as a wide range of sensors, such as RGB, multispectral, hyperspectral, and thermal. Contributions may address diverse agricultural applications, including pest and disease detection, weed mapping, nutrient and chlorophyll assessment, crop monitoring, and yield estimation. By advancing reliable and transferable remote sensing approaches, this session can contribute to evidence-based agricultural and environmental policies by enabling consistent large-scale monitoring of crop conditions, resource use, and climate-related impacts.
title: Remote sensing for precision agriculture: advancing robustness, transferability, and operational applicability

description: Agricultural production is increasingly vulnerable to climate variability, extreme weather, and growing resource limitations. To better understand these challenges and support adaptation, regional crop modeling, whether process-based, data-driven, or hybrid, has become an essential tool for assessing agricultural productivity, food and water security, and the impacts of climate variability and change. At the same time, the growing availability of satellite observations provides unprecedented opportunities to better constrain, calibrate, and validate crop model simulations, from field to continental scale. This session focuses on recent methodological and applied advances in linking regional crop models with Earth observation datasets to improve predictive accuracy and robustness. We invite contributions that address: • Advances in regional crop modeling frameworks, including process-based, data-driven (machine learning/AI, statistical), and hybrid approaches • Data assimilation techniques and model parameterization methodologies • Integration of remote sensing data into regional crop modeling systems • Pre- and in-season yield forecasting • Applications to water use, irrigation, and agro-hydrological monitoring • Applications to assess and optimize climate change adaptation strategies • Benchmarking and intercomparison of crop models with remote sensing data This session brings together researchers in crop modeling, remote sensing, climate science, and data assimilation, spanning both process-based and data-driven approaches, to advance integration across disciplines and tackle global challenges in agriculture, water, and food security. We particularly welcome contributions on coupling satellite-derived soil moisture, evapotranspiration, and vegetation data with crop and land surface models for forecasting and irrigation applications at regional to continental scale.
title: Advances in regional crop modeling and integration of remote sensing data

description: Dissolved organic matter (DOM) is a key component of biogeochemical cycles in the ocean and on land. It contains as much carbon as all living biomass on the continents and oceans combined. DOM accumulates in the ocean over several millennia and acts as a substantial carbon storage pool. On the other hand, microbes rely on dissolved molecules for carbon uptake, processing DOM on short time scales. DOM is therefore the main link between organic and inorganic carbon in marine and freshwater ecosystems. A multitude of biogenic and abiotic processes shape the so-called “DOM geometabolome” which parallels sedimentary records as an information-rich set of molecular tracers. These compounds carry the signatures of their source and subsequent journey through the environment. For our session, we invite contributions from all areas of research on DOM biogeochemistry, from empirical to modelling studies, from groundwaters and lakes across the freshwater-to-marine continuum. Molecular-level and interdisciplinary studies including modeling approaches are particularly welcome. Also, contributions that apply innovative analytical approaches, or identify novel concepts, fundamental challenges and the future directions of this fast-growing field of research are encouraged.
title: From molecules to models: Understanding the biogeochemistry of dissolved organic matter

description: This session focuses on volatile organic compounds (VOCs) at the biosphere-atmosphere interface, encompassing innovative analytical methods, laboratory and field studies, and emission modeling approaches. We invite contributions on plant and other biogenic VOC emission sources (e.g., from soil, litter, and freshwater) under environmental changes, methodological advances in sampling and analysis techniques, and modeling frameworks that bridge experimental observations with atmospheric processes.
title: Volatile Organic Compounds at the Biosphere-Atmosphere Interface: From Molecular Mechanisms to Global Models

description: After carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O) are among the most potent greenhouse gases (GHGs), exacerbating global warming. Their rapidly rising concentrations in the atmosphere require urgent action. Forest ecosystems play an important role in the exchange of GHGs with the atmosphere; however, their global role is still far from being understood. It has been shown that not only soils but also trees can emit and/or consume CH4 and N2O in forests. Trees contribute to ecosystem exchanges in various ways. They can uptake and transport soil-produced CH4 and N2O to the atmosphere; produce and consume both gases in situ in tree tissues; and modify carbon and nitrogen turnover in adjacent soils. However, the individual processes involved beyond net ecosystem GHG exchange remain unclear and seem to depend on various factors, including tree characteristics, tree species traits, forest ecosystem type, environmental variables, and seasons. Moreover, there are also other, but still rarely studied co-players in the forest GHG exchange, such as ground vegetation, cryptogamic covers, or water bodies in case of forested wetlands. Interactions between soil, plants, and the atmosphere play a crucial role in controlling the global budget of these gases. Our session will link scientists studying the CH4 and N2O cycles in forest ecosystems under different climatic, hydrological and scale conditions. This is crucial for improving our understanding of CH4 and N2O exchange in these ecosystems. We welcome contributions on production and consumption processes and mechanisms in soils and plant/tree tissues, as well as gas transport processes within the soil-tree-atmosphere continuum. We highly encourage gas flux measurements from forest soils, cryptogams, ground vegetation, water bodies (in forested wetlands), tree stems, leaves, and canopies using chamber systems or integrated ecosystem approaches (e.g., flux towers with eddy covariance, satellites, or modelling). We also encourage methodological studies investigating CH₄ and N₂O exchange in forest ecosystems. Solicited author: Dr. Josep Barba (CREAF, Spain)
title: Forest methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O) cycles

description: Agricultural systems are increasingly exposed to droughts, heatwaves, floods, and compound extremes, with impacts that can cascade across water resources, crops production, and rural livelihoods. Addressing such challenges requires better hazard monitoring or sensing technologies. A stronger link between observation, prediction, and the practical adaptation decisions is also needed that allow agricultural systems to anticipate, cope with, and recover from natural hazards. This session brings together research that connects these different steps, from monitoring and prediction to adaptation and decision-making in agriculture under hydro-climatic extremes. Although hazard monitoring and precision agriculture technologies have advanced rapidly, turning these developments into tangible improvements in resilience remains challenging. This requires closer integration of hydrology, agriculture, remote sensing, climate science, and decision-support approaches. We welcome contributions covering the full chain from observation to action, including Earth Observation and in situ monitoring of agricultural exposure and impacts; AI, machine learning, and hybrid modelling for impact prediction and early warning; agro-hydrological and land surface modelling under changing and compound climate conditions; and the use of monitoring and prediction to support adaptation, such as smart irrigation, precision water management, nature-based solutions, and climate-resilient cropping systems. We particularly encourage studies that show how advances in observation and modelling can be translated into practical decision-support and adaptation. Contributions addressing compound and cascading hazards, especially those linking monitoring and modelling with agricultural impacts and management responses, are also welcome.
title: Resilient Agricultural Systems under Hydro-Climatic Extremes: Advances in Monitoring, Prediction and Adaptation

description: The session includes studies presenting a critical analysis of the sources of uncertainty in volcanic hazard assessment and offering an integrated quantification of the multihazards associated with volcanic activity. The purpose of the session is to discuss the contributions of new methodological and technological advances and the results arising from the integration of well-established methodologies, which have permitted major advances in the assessment of volcanic hazard in specific sites and to highlight both positive and negative impact to develop educational programs on preparedness, response, and overall influence on vulnerability. We here invite contributions highlighting the i) most recent advances in volcanic hazard assessment, both on recently active volcanic systems and on volcanoes with long lasting quiescence periods and ii) exploring the influence of recent advances on educational strategies and, specifically, the role of Earth Science Museums and targeted research programmes including educational initiatives in modifying the adaptive response to, as well as the recovery of populations from volcanic disasters.
title: Bridging the Gap: Translating Advances in Hazard Science into Educational Action for Safer Volcanic Communities

description: Recent volcanic activity worldwide has provided exceptional opportunities to study magmatic systems in near-real time. These events show both the societal impact of volcanism, from threats to infrastructure and communities to the challenges of crisis response. They also offer important opportunities to investigate magma storage, transport, and eruption dynamics. This session invites contributions encompassing geochemistry, petrology, and geophysics, as well as monitoring, modeling, and crisis management, to advance our understanding of eruptive processes and their consequences. Case studies from recent eruptions in Iceland, Hawai‘i, the Canary Islands, Italy, Mexico, Indonesia, the Philippines and other active volcanic regions are particularly welcome. We welcome studies based on field observations, laboratory experiments, geochemical and petrological analyses, numerical modeling and data-driven approaches, as well as contributions that consider the operational and societal dimensions of eruptive crises. By bringing together diverse perspectives, this session aims to promote dialogue across disciplines and between scientists and hazard managers. Topics of interest include magma plumbing system architecture, eruption triggers, timescales of magmatic processes, real-time geophysical and geochemical monitoring, and hazard assessment and mitigation strategies. The session will provide a platform to synthesize lessons learned from recent eruptions, highlight methodological innovations, and promote integrated strategies for advancing volcanological research while strengthening responses to volcanic activity.
title: Magma in motion: tracking eruptions in near-real time

description: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are becoming increasingly important tools in volcano science, with applications spanning geophysical monitoring, remote sensing, numerical modelling, volcano-tectonics, igneous petrology, geochemical data analysis, and volcanic hazard assessment. These approaches offer new opportunities to automate tasks, enhance modelling strategies, analyse increasingly complex datasets, and accelerate knowledge discovery. At the same time, their integration into scientific research introduces important methodological and epistemological challenges, including understanding what AI models actually learn, assessing the physical and geological meaning of identified patterns, and ensuring transparency, reproducibility, robustness, and interpretability. Beyond their predictive capabilities, AI and ML also raise broader questions about how data-driven methods contribute to scientific understanding. In volcano science, where observations are often incomplete and direct constraints on subsurface processes are limited, identifying correlations is not necessarily equivalent to understanding the mechanisms that generate them. Integrating domain knowledge, physical constraints, and causal reasoning may therefore help develop approaches that are both effective and scientifically meaningful. These issues become especially important in high-risk contexts such as volcanic hazard assessment, risk mitigation, crisis management, and risk communication. This session welcomes contributions across volcano science, including geophysics, remote sensing, experimental and numerical modelling, volcano-tectonics, igneous petrology, geochemistry, monitoring, and hazard assessment. We particularly encourage work on data-driven discovery, physics-informed ML, automated data analysis, model interpretability and explainability, uncertainty assessment, reproducibility, and the integration of AI-derived results with geological and physical understanding. We also welcome emerging approaches such as digital twins and agentic AI, as well as epistemological perspectives on how AI may influence scientific inference, explanation, hypothesis generation, and scientific understanding. Finally, the session welcomes studies on the responsible use of AI in volcanic-hazard applications and its interaction with scientists, volcano observatories, stakeholders, and decision-makers.
title: Opportunities, risks, and perspectives of AI applications in volcano science and hazard assessment

description: Mountains are an essential component of the Earth system and are widely recognised as major sources of freshwater. Their water resources support communities and ecosystems within mountain regions and are also critical for social-ecological systems further downstream. The strong heterogeneity in hydro-meteorological conditions arising from elevation gradients, complex topography, and geological conditions makes hydrological processes highly variable across space and time. Climate change and growing human pressures are altering these processes, highlighting the need to better understand the controls on water resources and related ecosystem services. Mountains are therefore unique sentinels of global change, providing a setting for detecting, understanding, and monitoring its effects. This session brings together researchers working on mountain hydrology worldwide to share the latest findings, innovative approaches, and new perspectives. Emphasis will be placed on the role of mountain regions in the water cycle and in providing, storing, and regulating water resources, as well as on the challenges of observing and understanding hydrological change in these complex environments. We invite contributions addressing past, present, and future conditions, including changes driven by climate and land-use change, their impacts on mountain and downstream regions, and adaptation strategies to support the long-term sustainability of mountain ecosystem services. We particularly encourage contributions on technological and methodological innovations that help overcome observational challenges. Topics of interest include, but are not limited to - sources of information for assessing past and present conditions in mountain surface-water and groundwater systems; - innovative observational approaches and emerging data sources for characterising hydrological processes in mountains and their spatio-temporal variability; - modelling approaches for assessing, attributing, and projecting hydrological change; - methods to identify and disentangle drivers of hydrological change; - prediction, evolution, and impacts of hydrological extremes; - case studies on adaptation to changes in availability of water resources and associated risks; - integration of complementary sources of evidence and knowledge, including citizen science, Indigenous knowledge systems, and other approaches that improve understanding of mountain systems and support the sustainable management of water resources
title: Mountain hydrology under global change: observations, modelling and adaptation

description: Hazard situations involve multiple forms of knowledge and institutional action, including scientific assessment, scenario development, planning, risk communication and emergency management. These dimensions are often addressed separately, despite their interdependence across the different phases of risk governance. The session examines how scientific scenarios are translated into institutional decisions, how risks are communicated to exposed communities, and how knowledge and responsibilities evolve during and after emergencies. Contributions are invited to analyse the interaction between these dimensions across different hazards, institutional settings and geographical contexts, including approaches that focus on individual disciplines or phases.
title: Science, before and after: hazard, institutions and risk communication in parallel cases

description: Volcanic islands are dynamic and hazard-prone environments where the interplay of complex geological processes poses unique scientific and logistical challenges for disaster risk reduction. Assessing these hazards is inherently difficult because phenomena operate across wide spatial and temporal scales, often complemented by limited observations and high uncertainty. These challenges are further amplified by the fact that islands geography severely restricts evacuation routes, logistics, and emergency response, as well as the study and the monitoring of large offshore sectors of the volcano. Moreover, high seasonal tourist mobility, land-use pressures, and offshore observation gaps further compound socio-economic vulnerabilities and monitoring limits. In this context, we request contributions of eruptive as well as non-eruptive hazards like flank instabilities, landslides, tsunamis, earthquakes, and gas emissions that can generate complex, cascading multi-hazard scenarios with particularly high impacts. This session brings together researchers working on the assessment, monitoring, modelling, and mitigation of volcanic hazards in island settings. We welcome contributions addressing advances in hazard characterization, remote sensing, geophysical and geochemical monitoring, numerical modelling, and probabilistic hazard assessment. Particular attention will be given to approaches addressing uncertainty, variability, and multi-hazard interactions. The session explores cutting-edge methodologies in hazard modeling, innovative monitoring techniques, and interdisciplinary approaches to be translated into effective risk-reduction strategies and build resilient island communities.
title: Challenges to assess hazard and develop mitigation strategies in volcanic islands

description: Significant reductions in Arctic sea ice extent, concentration and thickness have been consistently observed over recent decades. Whilst Antarctic sea ice extent remained relatively stable until 2016-2017, the subsequent period has been characterised by a marked decline and increased interannual variability, including several years of exceptionally low sea ice extent. These recent changes have raised questions about the mechanisms driving Antarctic sea ice variability and the extent to which the post-2016 decline represents a persistent shift or enhanced variability. Climate projections suggest continued reductions in sea ice cover at both poles, with the Arctic becoming seasonally ice-free during the latter half of this century. The scientific community is investing considerable effort in consolidating our current knowledge of the physical and bio-geochemical properties of sea ice, improving our understanding of poorly understood sea ice processes, and forecasting future changes in sea ice cover, including through initiatives such as CMIP6. In this session, we invite contributions addressing all aspects of sea ice science and sea ice–climate interactions in both the Arctic and Southern Ocean, including snow and sea ice thermodynamics and dynamics, sea ice–atmosphere and sea ice–ocean interactions, sea ice biological and chemical processes, remote sensing and field studies, related laboratory studies, and modelling. Contributions addressing emerging processes, feedbacks and their implications for sea ice and the wider climate system are particularly welcome.
title: Rapid changes in sea ice: processes and implications

description: The Arctic Ocean is transitioning from a perennial to an increasingly seasonal sea-ice cover, implying an emerging new Arctic. However, major uncertainties remain regarding (1) when, where and how ice-free conditions will emerge, (2) the physical mechanisms governing the timing, pace, and regional expression of this transition, (3) whether the first ice-free summer will mark a persistent new regime, and (4) how predictable this transition is. This session explores climate predictability across different timescales, ranging from short-term forecasts to centennial projections, including sub-seasonal to multidecadal predictions. The aim is to better understand and predict the emerging Arctic sea-ice regime, including but not limited to ice-free summers. In particular, we want to explore how the sources and limits of sea-ice predictability evolve as the Arctic warms and transitions toward a new regime. This session also targets the studies of both the drivers and effects of a new Arctic sea-ice regime, such as but not limited to the analysis of sea ice - atmosphere - ocean interactions, the connection to the North Atlantic and North Pacific Oceans, the regional Arctic climate, and Arctic marine heatwaves. We welcome contributions that make use of a range of tools, including dynamical and statistical models, machine learning, causal methods, hybrid approaches, and process-based diagnostics using observations.
title: Causal understanding and predictability of the emerging Arctic sea-ice regime

description: New theoretical approaches, grounded in field observations and experimental manipulations, are increasingly providing improved understanding the response of organisms to environmental changes, for processes operating at organ level, through whole organisms to ecosystems. This provides a basis for addressing functional biodiversity within communities, the different timescales of ecosystem response to changing environments, and the feedbacks between ecosystems and their environment. Since these changes and feedbacks regulate carbon, nutrient and energy flows, this in turn provides a basis for developing new and simpler models of the biosphere and its interactions in the earth system. Addressing these complex issues requires and interdisciplinary perspective. This session will explore new approaches to understanding the two-way interactions between the biosphere and it environment across terrestrial, aquatic and marine ecosystems – encompassing observational, theory and modelling perspectives. We invite contributions that examine shifts in traits and community composition across different ecosystems. We welcome contributions that address this through experiments, observations, empirical analysis and conceptual, eco-evolutionary or process-based modelling. By examining work on soil communities, terrestrial vegetation and freshwater and marine ecosystems, the session aims to foster a cross-system perspective on ecosystem functioning.
title: Eco-evolutionary optimality approaches to understanding biosphere responses to environmental change

description: The landscape of earth science education is shifting quickly due to emerging technologies and shifting priorities, which present both challenges and opportunities in pedagogy. Satellites, genetic sequencing, long-term in situ sensors, model results and reanalyses, digitized collections and citizen science are producing massive datasets, requiring students in earth and environmental sciences to learn scientific computing skills to utilise them. However, many students in earth and environmental science degree programs report lacking the computational skills needed to work with earth observation data. At the same time, ubiquitous access to computing can help universities meet goals around educating more scientists by accelerating learning and lowering the barrier to entry with technologies such as virtual labs and cloud-based learning environments. Emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, further expand these possibilities but also raise questions about ethical use and how best to support meaningful student engagement and scientific understanding. This session invites researchers, educators, industry practitioners, and representatives from other organisations working in Earth and environmental science education to share innovative and effective approaches to developing geospatial and computational skills in Earth and environmental science education. We welcome contributions describing successful courses, programmes, learning environments, and other educational tools, as well as experiences evaluating their impact and accessibility. We are particularly interested in highlighting initiatives with a proven track record of targeting and including intersectional identities traditionally under-represented among earth, environmental and/or computer scientists. This session is being organized jointly with a short course with the same name, where there will be a hands-on opportunity to share educational tools. If you are looking to demonstrate your educational tool or module in an interactive setting, we encourage you to apply to this session, and we will contact you about the short course.
title: Computational education in the Earth and Environmental Sciences: Best Practices, Opportunities, and Challenges

description: Since 2016, this session series has provided a welcoming forum for discussing equity, diversity and inclusion (EDI) in the geosciences. At a time when EDI initiatives are facing significant challenges in many parts of the world, we invite researchers, practitioners, decision-makers and policy analysts to join us in sharing experiences, exchanging ideas and identifying actions that can help build a more inclusive, equitable and supportive geoscience community. The session will explore the factors contributing to the under-representation of different groups—including those defined by gender identity, sexual orientation, racial and cultural background, disability, religion, nationality or geography, socioeconomic status, age and career stage—and will provide an opportunity for constructive dialogue on both persistent challenges and effective solutions. We welcome contributions that present research, data, case studies, personal experiences or examples of good practice. Topics of interest include, but are not limited to: • Role models who inspire and support others through their experiences and/or their contributions to advancing equality, diversity and inclusion. • Evidence of imbalanced representation, preferably supported by data, in awards, medals, grants, leadership positions, invited talks and publications. • Perceived and structural barriers to inclusion at the individual, institutional and cultural levels. • New and innovative approaches to identifying and overcoming barriers. • Gender Equality Plans (GEPs) in European host institutions: successes, challenges and lessons learned. • Effective initiatives and best practices, including: - mentoring programmes; - professional networks; - targeted funding schemes; - institutional initiatives; and - conference and meeting practices that foster inclusion. We particularly encourage contributions that reflect on the impact of recent socio-political developments on EDI activities, as well as experiences of sustaining or advancing inclusive practices in changing institutional, national or international contexts. The session is co-organised with support from the European Research Council (ERC).
title: Promoting and supporting inclusive excellence in the geosciences

description: The quadrupole mass spectrometer, originally developed as a mass filter in the 1950s, has since evolved into an adaptable tool across research and industry. Its unique ability to monitor gaseous compounds over an exceptionally wide concentration range—from ppb to percent levels (to 100%)—sets it apart from gas-specific sensors, enabling comprehensive, real-time analysis of complex gas mixtures. Modern quadrupoles offer improved response times and detection limits, making in-situ measurements feasible even in dynamic experimental environments. In this session, we invite contributions that highlight the expanding applications of quadrupole mass spectrometry. Specifically, in the areas of: • Stable isotope analysis, • Real-time monitoring of analytes, • Respiration analysis with bio reactors, or • Innovative uses of the technology for analyzing both gaseous and aqueous components The research presented should underscore the ongoing evolution of quadrupole mass spectrometry as a key analytical technique, opening new avenues for research and industrial applications.
title: Old dog, New tricks: Advances in Quadrupole Mass Spectrometry Applications

description: Plenary geomorphology division session and ECS award lecture. This session will consist of the Geomorphology Early Career Scientist Award winner’s lecture, talks from the GM OSPP winners, and additional invited talks.
title: Frontiers in Geomorphology

description: The study on superficial grain size dynamics has been a fundamental tool in comprehending surface processes such as erosion, fluvial geomorphology, landslides, volcanic activity, coastal dynamics, and glacial areas, particularly in the context of changing climate. Traditional techniques for grain characterization are related to a high time and labour costs and have been reinventing for decades. This session aims to present various methodologies applied to grain size characterization across different geomorphological subjects.
title: Current trends and future on granulometric surface characterization.

description: Hydrogeomorphic processes emerge from interactions among fluid motion, sediment and granular materials, and evolving landforms. They span spatial and temporal scales from the entrainment and collective motion of individual grains to sediment-laden flows, reach-scale morphodynamics and landscape evolution. Although dynamic grain-scale mechanisms are increasingly resolved through high-resolution imaging, embedded sensing and particle-resolved simulations, translating this understanding into continuum representations and reliable field-scale forecasts remains a fundamental challenge in riverine geomorphology, hydrology, fluvial hydraulics and environmental fluid mechanics. This session brings together field observations, physical experiments, theory, numerical modelling and data-driven approaches that advance process measurement, mechanistic understanding, scale bridging and prediction. We particularly welcome studies developing or integrating novel instrumentation and sensing, imaging and remote sensing, particle tracking, laboratory experiments, particle-resolved and discrete-element simulations, continuum modelling, data assimilation, uncertainty quantification, and model calibration, verification and validation. Contributions may address particle entrainment and granular dynamics; grain–fluid and grain–grain interactions; stochastic sediment transport and size segregation; particle-laden, debris and granular flows; erosion, deposition and evolving boundaries; bedform development and morphodynamics; extreme or rapidly varying flows; and the representation of these processes across particle, reach and landscape scales. Applications may include rivers, hillslopes, infrastructure, environmental management, natural hazards and forecasting. Studies that connect observations to grain-scale mechanisms, upscale those mechanisms into reduced-order or continuum representations, and evaluate predictive capability across environments and scales are especially encouraged.
title: Measuring and modelling geomorphic and geophysical flow processes across scales

description: The action of a fluid moving over a mobile surface often generates bedforms which in turn influence the flow and how particles are transported. On Earth, bedforms are found in many environments: deserts, rivers, estuaries, continental shelves, deep seas, volcanic regions and glacial environments. Bedforms have also been observed in extra-terrestrial environments, such as on Mars and Venus. Understanding the links between flow, particle transport, and bedform morphodynamics and stratigraphy is of interest for a wide range of applied and fundamental research. For example, this knowledge is used to manage contemporary environments, such as rivers and coastal seas. Recently, the societal relevance of bedform research has been highlighted, as bedforms are shown to interact with offshore structures. Furthermore, bedform morphology and sedimentology can provide insights into fluid movement across modern and ancient, otherwise unknown, landscapes. This session aims to highlight many aspects of the complex interaction between flow, sediment transport, stratigraphy and bedforms in terrestrial and planetary environments. The session welcomes contributions from theoretical, field, laboratory and numerical approaches related to bedforms found in aeolian, shallow and deep waters, glacial and planetary environments. The session intends to advance our knowledge of how to decipher information contained in terrestrial and extra-terrestrial bedforms and help foster fruitful discussions on understanding bedform morphodynamics and stratigraphy.
title: Bedform morphodynamics in terrestrial and planetary environments

description: In seismically active regions, landscape evolution and Quaternary geology give rates of crustal deformation averaged over long time intervals: marine terraces and palaeoshorelines, fluvial terraces and river profiles yield uplift and fault throw rates and, through fault geometry, extension or shortening rates. Shorter intervals are covered by other records. Palaeoseismology, coastal geology and archaeoseismology span centuries to millennia and, like the geological rates, record permanent deformation on identified structures. GNSS and InSAR geodesy span years to decades and measure ongoing strain loading, part of which may never become permanent offset. This session brings these timescales together and asks whether, where and why the resulting rates are comparable. Several explanations are possible and rarely tested against one another: the long-term rate may contain a regional component the fault did not produce; the geodetic rate may include elastic strain never released as permanent offset; deformation may be distributed across structures a fault-based model does not include; or the slip rate may genuinely have changed, because clustering, fault interaction and fault growth make rates non-steady over exactly the intervals being compared. Distinguishing between these explanations, rather than documenting the discrepancy, is what the session asks for. We invite contributions that derive long-term deformation rates from landscape evolution and Quaternary geology, compare them with palaeoseismological and geodetic rates in the same region, and diagnose the reasons for agreement or disagreement. Studies from all tectonic settings are welcome, from landscape evolution modelling to seismic hazard applications. Early career scientists are strongly encouraged to submit.
title: Landscape evolution, palaeoseismology and geodesy in seismically active regions: comparing long-term and short-term deformation rates

description: Coastal wetlands, such as salt marshes, mangroves, seagrass beds, and tidal flats provide numerous ecosystem services, including coastal protection, biodiversity provision and climate change mitigation. However, coastal wetlands are under pressure from both natural and anthropogenic drivers of coastal change, and shifting climatic boundary conditions, hence are declining in area and habitat quality globally. At the same time, these environments are increasingly in the focus of restoration and nature-based solutions for coastal adaptation, where the aim is to work with, rather than against, the natural processes to build and maintain wetlands. Understanding how sedimentation, vegetation establishment, and self-organisation sustain these systems is therefore essential to designing interventions that remain functional over decadal timescales. This is the case for pristine, natural, managed, and restored systems alike. This session will bring together studies of coastal wetlands across different climates and geomorphological settings to enhance the understanding of ecosystem service provisioning, interactions between hydrodynamics, sediment, and ecology, and to identify best future management practices and effective nature-based solutions. Studies of all processes occurring within coastal wetlands are invited. This includes, but is not limited to, hydro- and morphodynamics, bio-morphodynamics, bio-geochemistry, ecological change and evolution, and impacts and management implications of climate change, sea level rise, and anthropogenic pressures. We equally invite social science and interdisciplinary contributions, including stakeholder participation and co-design in wetland restoration, governance and institutional arrangements, public perception and acceptance of coastal nature-based solutions, and the distribution of costs, benefits and ecosystem services among coastal communities. This session aims to enhance our understanding of basic processes governing coastal wetland dynamics and to propose sustainable management solutions for contemporary environmental pressures.
title: Coastal wetlands: Processes, interactions, management

description: Underwater landscapes, from shallow coastal zones to deep ocean, are shaped by a complex interplay of geologic, biologic, oceanographic and anthropogenic processes. These dynamic interactions create diverse landforms that reveal valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms driving their formation. Understanding these processes, which operate across varying spatial and temporal scales, is essential for assessing offshore geohazards and ensuring the sustainable management of marine environments. This interdisciplinary session explores the causes and consequences of processes shaping submarine landforms and seafloor evolution. Topics include erosional and depositional dynamics, marine bioconstructions, gravitational driven and current-induced sediment transport, submarine landslides, active deformation, volcanic activity, faulting and folding, and emphasis is given to subseafloor fluid migration and venting at the seafloor. Contributions may address marine or lacustrine environments across all physiographic regions, including coastal zones, marginal seas, continental shelves and slopes, oceanic plateaus, abyssal hills, mid-ocean ridges and accretionary wedges. We welcome studies that integrate diverse approaches, such as satellite-derived and hydroacoustic seabed characterizations, visual and ROV-based observations, seismic imaging and sedimentary, geochemical, and/or geological sampling. Such interdisciplinary studies provide exciting opportunities to advance quantitative geomorphology, extend it offshore, and deepen our understanding of the processes shaping submarine landscapes.
title: Submarine Geomorphology

description: Fibre-optic based techniques enable highly precise point and distributed sensing of the full ground motion wavefield including translation, rotation and strain, as well as environmental parameters such as temperature at scales and with a degree of coverage previously unattainable with conventional geophysical sensors. Considerable improvements in optical and atom interferometry enable new concepts for inertial rotation, translational displacement and acceleration sensing. Laser reflectometry and polarisation analysis on commercial fibre-optic cables allow, for the first time, spatially dense and temporally continuous sensing of the ocean’s floor, successfully detecting a variety of signals including microseisms, local and teleseismic earthquakes, volcanic events and ocean dynamics. A significant breakthrough in the use of fibre-optic sensing techniques came from the new ability to interrogate already existing telecommunication cables to high temporal and spatial precision across a wide range of environments. Applications based on this new type of data are numerous, including seismic source and wavefield characterisation with single point observations in harsh environments such as active volcanoes and the seafloor, ambient seismic noise interferometry, earthquake and tsunami early warning, and infrastructure stability monitoring. We welcome contributions on developments in instrumental and theoretical advances, applications and processing with fibre-optic point and/or distributed multi-sensing techniques, light polarisation and transmission analyses, using standard telecommunication and/or engineered fibre-optic cables.
