We seek studies on theoretical, instrumental, observation and advanced processing across all solid earth fields, including seismology, volcanology, glaciology, geodesy, geophysics, natural hazards, oceanography, urban environment, geothermal applications, laboratory studies, large-scale field tests, planetary exploration, gravitational wave detection and fundamental physics. We encourage contributions on data analysis techniques, novel applications, machine learning, data management, instrumental performance and comparison as well as new experimental, field, laboratory, and modelling studies in fibre-optic sensing studies.
title: Fibre-optic sensing in the Geosciences

description: Water shapes the Earth system in all its states: liquid in aquifers, soils, peatlands, rivers, lakes, and oceans; ice in glaciers and permafrost; and vapor in geothermal, hydrothermal, and volcanic systems. Its phase, distribution and movement influence the mechanical properties of the subsurface and are therefore imprinted on how seismic waves propagate. This makes seismology a powerful, non-invasive tool to quantify where water is stored, how it moves, and how it changes phase, across scales from pores to catchments, from the near surface to the deep crust, and from hours to decades. This session focuses on seismic approaches that image and monitor water, and translate seismic observables into hydrological, cryospheric and fluid-related information. We welcome theoretical, laboratory and field contributions using active and passive methods, including ambient noise, velocity changes, attenuation, dense nodal arrays and distributed acoustic sensing. Themes include groundwater storage and aquifer dynamics, soil moisture and the critical zone, peatland water tables and gas content, glacial hydrology and subglacial and englacial drainage, permafrost and freeze-thaw cycles, crustal fluids in geothermal reservoirs and in hydrothermal systems at volcanoes, and the role of changing hydrological conditions in preconditioning mass movements and other geohazards. We especially encourage interdisciplinary studies that integrate seismic results with hydrological models, in-situ measurements and remote sensing. Our aim is to bring together seismologists, hydrologists, cryosphere scientists and researchers studying geothermal and volcanic fluids to build a quantitative, physically grounded picture of water in the Earth system.
title: Seismological Perspectives on the Hydrosphere: Water Across Phases and Scales

description: Meteorological events and climate extremes can generate a wide range of environmental processes, from intense rainfall, floods and sediment transport to landslides, snow avalanches, glacier dynamics and coastal and ocean responses. Many of these processes generate seismic signals that can be continuously recorded by seismic networks, dense nodal arrays and emerging technologies such as Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS). Environmental seismology therefore offers a complementary observational approach to conventional meteorological, hydrological, remote-sensing and geophysical techniques. This session aims to bring together recent advances in the use of seismic observations to detect, characterize and quantify meteorological events and their environmental impacts. We welcome contributions addressing both the generation and interpretation of environmental seismic signals and their use for monitoring environmental processes. Topics of interest include, but are not limited to, seismic signatures of rainfall, storms, floods and river discharge; sediment transport and debris flows; rainfall-triggered landslides and other mass movements; snow and avalanche dynamics; glacier and permafrost responses to meteorological forcing; ocean- and atmosphere-generated seismic signals; freeze–thaw processes; and cascading responses to extreme weather events. We particularly encourage contributions demonstrating how seismic observations can provide quantitative information on environmental conditions, process rates or event evolution. The session also welcomes methodological advances, including ambient seismic noise analysis, seismic interferometry, dense seismic arrays, nodal instrumentation, Distributed Acoustic Sensing, machine learning and real-time seismic monitoring. Contributions combining seismic observations with meteorological, hydrological, remote-sensing or other environmental observations are especially encouraged. By bringing together researchers from seismology, geomorphology, hydrology, cryospheric sciences and environmental monitoring, this session aims to highlight the potential of environmental seismology as an emerging tool for observing and understanding the response of the Earth system to meteorological forcing and extreme events.
title: Seismology for Monitoring Environmental Processes

description: Computational earth science uses modelling to understand complex physical systems which cannot be directly observed. Over the last years, numerical modeling of earthquakes has provided new approaches to apprehend the physics of earthquake rupture and the seismic cycle, seismic wave propagation, fault zone evolution, and seismic hazard assessment. Recent advances in numerical algorithms and increasing computational power enable unforeseen precision and incorporation of multi-physics components in physics-based simulations of earthquake rupture and seismic wave propagation but also pose challenges in terms of fully exploiting modern supercomputing infrastructure, realistic parameterization of simulation ingredients, and the analysis of large synthetic datasets. Meanwhile, advances in laboratory experiments link earthquake source processes to rock mechanics. This session brings together modelers and data analysts interested in the physics and computational aspects of earthquake phenomena and earthquake engineering. We welcome contributions spanning all aspects of seismic hazard assessment and earthquake physics - from slow slip events, fault mechanics and rupture dynamics, to wave propagation and ground motion analysis, to the seismic cycle and interseismic deformation and links to long-term tectonics and geodynamics - as well as studies advancing the state-of-the art in the related computational and numerical aspects.
title: Physics-based earthquake modeling and engineering

description: Seismic data come in many forms, from raw waveforms to tomographic models. Throughout acquisition, processing, and inversion, uncertainties propagate and obscure our understanding of Earth's interior and subsurface. Quantifying and interpreting these uncertainties is vital for robust geological and geodynamical inferences. In seismic tomography and imaging, uncertainties are often described by resolution metrics, such as resolution matrices or resolving kernels, or by summary statistics derived from posterior samples via Bayesian methods. Recently, machine learning techniques—including variational inference, learned distributions, and likelihood-free approaches—have been introduced to quantify uncertainty, offering promising alternatives. However, fully understanding the meaning of these uncertainties, their interactions, and their influence on model interpretation remains a major challenge. Once quantified, how do these uncertainties affect downstream applications in geodynamics, mineral physics, or earthquake hazard assessment? Are tomographic inferences reliable enough to support these fields, or do uncertainties limit our conclusions? Beyond observational data, other uncertainty sources—such as model parameterisation, prior assumptions, and the choice of forward models—add complexity. How do these modelling choices influence the recovered Earth structure and its uncertainties? How can we distinguish genuine Earth features from modelling artefacts? This session invites contributions that: • Develop or apply novel methods for quantifying uncertainty in seismic imaging, • Explore how uncertainty impacts Earth structure interpretations, • Compare different uncertainty quantification approaches, • Address model validation, benchmarking amid uncertainty, • Investigate how tomographic uncertainties propagate into fields like geodynamics, mineral physics, or hazard modelling. We welcome studies covering global and regional scales, body-wave and surface-wave tomography, full-waveform inversion, ambient noise imaging, and any seismic method where uncertainty is crucial. Cross-disciplinary and innovative methodological contributions are particularly encouraged.
title: Quantifying and Interpreting Uncertainties in Seismic Tomography

description: Earthquake sequences frequently diverge from simple mainshock-aftershock models, exhibiting complex spatio-temporal patterns and moment release. This complexity is especially prevalent in volcanic regions, where earthquake swarms and pronounced foreshock activity occur across various tectonic settings, challenging established earthquake laws (e.g., Båth's law, Omori-Utsu, and Gutenberg-Richter). Proposed triggering mechanisms encompass changes in pore pressure, aseismic slip events such as creep and slow slip, stress perturbations induced by magma, and interactions between earthquakes. Recent advancements in earthquake catalog generation, utilizing machine learning, template matching, and double-difference techniques, offer unprecedented resolution for investigating complex seismic sequences, identifying triggering mechanisms, and elucidating underlying physical processes. This session aims to assemble research on earthquake swarms and complex seismic sequences from a range of natural or induced settings and spatial scales. Contributions are invited that analyze earthquake swarms and complex seismic sequences with respect to spatio-temporal evolution, frequency-magnitude distributions, scaling properties, and triggering mechanisms. Submissions employing laboratory and numerical modeling to simulate mechanical conditions leading to swarm-like and complex seismic sequences are also encouraged. The objective is to synthesize knowledge from diverse tectonic environments to advance understanding of the physical processes governing complex seismic sequences. Multidisciplinary studies integrating deformation data, geophysical imaging, geological analysis, and fluid geochemistry are particularly welcome.
title: Unraveling Complex Seismic Sequences and Earthquake Swarms

description: The oceans cover about 71% of the Earth’s surface, yet our understanding of the oceanic crust, mantle, and dynamic processes remains limited. A major reason is the difficulty of observing Earth's structure and seismicity beneath the oceans compared to land. To address this gap, a wide range of amphibian instruments are increasingly being used, from ocean-bottom seismometers (OBS) to distributed acoustic sensing (DAS), MERMAIDs, and other novel geophysical and environmental sensors. Together, these tools are transforming our ability to explore and monitor the oceans and the solid Earth beneath them. Over the past two decades, these approaches have led to fascinating discoveries, from earthquake processes and subduction dynamics to mantle plumes, mid-ocean ridges, transform faults, thermal heterogeneity, and volatile cycling. They also reveal exciting new opportunities to study oceanographic, biological, and environmental processes. Yet challenges remain: large-scale deployments are costly and logistically complex, data sharing and best practices are often limited, and many valuable data sets remain inaccessible for years, reducing the long-term impact of these community investments. This session invites contributions from the global community on the full spectrum of amphibian geophysics: from new scientific results to experiment and observable design, novel analysis methods (e.g. machine learning, data fusion, cross-disciplinary approaches) to instrument development. We particularly encourage submissions that integrate different types of amphibian instrumentation and highlight the role of ocean observations in advancing our understanding of both the oceans and the Earth’s deep interior.
title: Advancing Ocean-bottom and Amphibian Geophysics: from novel instrumentation to new scientific discoveries

description: This session is open to all contributions in seismology, including earthquake sources, recent earthquakes and sequences, Earth structure at local, regional and global scales, and new methods and observations, in particular work that does not fit a more specialised session.
title: General Contributions to Earthquakes, Earth Structure, and Seismology

description: This special session will synthesize rapid scientific insights from recent large and/or disruptive earthquake sequences, highlighting what we have learned, what remains uncertain, and which methods prove most informative. We aim to feature concise, data-driven and integrative modeling spotlights on earthquake physics, rupture dynamics, ground motions, geological field analysis, geodesy, tsunami observations, early analyses, and community data/model sharing. Emphasis is on timely results emerging up to March 2026, with flexibility to include very recent events of scientific and societal relevance. The format is a moderated panel with invited talks and time for Q&A, designed to surface cross-disciplinary takeaways and priorities for follow-up studies. No abstracts are required.
title: Rapid Analyses of Recent Important Earthquakes: Findings & Open Questions

description: Latin America is home to major hydrological systems in the world. The combination of diverse climates, biomes, and ecosystems with a rapidly growing human footprint makes Latin America a unique test bed for exploring hydrological knowledge at the interface of science, policy, and practice in water resources. This session welcomes both theoretical and case study applications that consider observation and/or modelling to study hydrological processes and the possible effects of social and environmental changes on water resources systems. We will explore advances in hydrology at regional, national and continental scales in Latin America. Aligned with the IAHS Scientific Decade HELPING (Hydrology Engaging Local People IN one Global world), we especially welcome contributions that: (1) investigate interactions of water resources across different spatial scales (2) provide holistic solutions for water security, (3) engages with hydrological knowledge co-creation. We want to offer a platform to discuss how science could improve operational hydrology, how practical problems can inform important scientific questions, and the skills and tools necessary for translating hydrological research into operation and decision-making in the management of water resources systems of Latin America.
title: Advances in Latin American Hydrology

description: The South American hydroclimate encompasses a wide range of regimes shaped by complex interactions among the Amazon, the Andes Cordillera, and large-scale atmospheric circulation and oceanic variability. This diversity presents unique opportunities to advance hydrometeorological science, while posing significant challenges for understanding, monitoring, predicting, and managing water resources in a changing climate. Advances in Earth observation, remote sensing, artificial intelligence, and numerical modeling are improving our ability to observe, model, and forecast these processes across spatiotemporal scales. This session brings together researchers and practitioners across climatology, meteorology, hydrology, hydroclimatology, water resources, environmental risks, and climate services to showcase recent research advances, experiences, challenges, and opportunities in South America. We invite contributions in four areas: (1) Process understanding: hydroclimatic processes, conceptual and physically based modeling, AI-driven approaches and hypothesis testing locally and across large scales as well as under past and future climate conditions; (2) Monitoring: in situ observations, remote sensing, and low-cost innovative monitoring systems; observational datasets at a regional scale (3) Prediction and assessment: forecasting across timescales, hydroclimatic extremes, downscaling approaches, trend analyses, climate change impact assessments, and compound and multi-hazard risks; and (4) Management and solutions: water resources management, climate services, decision-support tools, and climate adaptation strategies. By fostering regional and international collaboration, this session provides a dedicated space to exchange experiences, compare approaches across diverse hydroclimatic regimes, and advance hydrometeorological science, ultimately strengthening resilience to hydroclimatic variability and change across South America.
title: Advances in hydrometeorological sciences in South America: experiences, challenges, and opportunities

description: Weather and climate extremes, such as intense precipitation, tropical and extratropical storms, drought, heatwaves, and compound events, pose substantial risks to society, infrastructure, and ecosystems across the globe. Yet directly and explicitly modelling such extremes and their future behaviour remains challenging, owing to the high computational cost of resolving relevant processes, incomplete understanding of many driving mechanisms, and the chaotic nature of atmospheric dynamics, which further limits predictability at longer lead times. Consequently, model-based projections often carry large uncertainties, especially in how complex and non-linear interactions among atmospheric variables shape these extremes in a future warmer world. Observational constraints and statistical approaches offer a complementary pathway. Observations from ground-based networks, radars, and satellites, together with reanalysis simulations, can provide information on the characteristics and physical drivers that can be used to evaluate and constrain models. Statistical and data-driven models, when constrained by associated temperature, moisture, storm characteristics, and regional and global circulation teleconnections, can provide viable alternatives for problems that remain too computationally expensive, while incorporation of constraints in explicit physical simulations can help narrow uncertainties and reduce model biases. This session aims to bring together research on the use of observational constraints, physical theory, and statistical approaches for improved understanding, prediction and projection of past and future extremes. We welcome contributions including, but not limited to, assessing the drivers of extremes, scaling relationships based on physical theory, storyline approaches, and statistical and hybrid approaches, as well as studies critically evaluating the physical basis and robustness of the proposed constraints. Contributions spanning various types of extremes, spatial and temporal scales, and observational and modelling frameworks are encouraged.
title: Using observational constraints for better prediction of future weather and climate extremes

description: Clouds are ubiquitous and play a fundamental role in Earth’s climate by modulating incoming solar and outgoing terrestrial radiation. A challenge in understanding the impact of clouds arises from the multi-scale nature of cloud processes, which span from aerosol activation at the nanometer scale to the dynamics of cloud systems at the scale of hundreds of kilometres. Key microphysical processes, including droplet collision-coalescence, ice crystal formation, and their modulation by turbulence, occur at scales smaller than 100 m, which poses a challenge to observe or simulate them. The uncertainty is further exacerbated by turbulent interactions with the environment through entrainment, mixing of air, and radiative changes within the cloud. Hence, we need to improve our understanding on the small-scale to increase our confidence in climate projections. The superposition of small-scale processes calls for an integrated approach that combines laboratory experiments, field observations, and numerical modelling. Field observations characterise cloud processes within their natural, dynamic environment using a combination of remote sensing and in-situ measurements. Recent advances in observational platforms (e.g., uncrewed aerial systems), measurement techniques (e.g., multi-frequency cloud radar), and experimental designs have enhanced these capabilities. Controlled laboratory experiments allow for the isolation and systematic study of specific cloud processes under defined and repeatable conditions. High-resolution, process-oriented numerical modelling enables the study of fundamental interactions, can test hypotheses, and synthesises datasets. These models need constraints and validation by data from both laboratory and field campaigns. This session invites contributions that advance the understanding of small-scale cloud processes, with particular interest in the regime beyond the single particle, at scales of metres to hundreds of meters. A particular emphasis is placed on synergistic studies that combines laboratory experiments, field observations and/or numerical modelling.
title: Small-scale Cloud Processes

description: Agriculture covers nearly one-third of the Earth’s land surface and plays a vital role in sustaining global food and fodder production. Yet, it is increasingly threatened by the impacts of climate change while still contributing to biodiversity of loss, soil degradation, and environmental issues. Policy frameworks and regulations at national and EU level create incentives and commitment towards more sustainable management. However, meeting these challenges and needs requires innovative approaches that enhance agricultural resilience, efficiency, and sustainability while reducing the environmental footprint and safeguarding ecosystems. Recent advances in Earth observation, environmental research infrastructures, monitoring networks (e.g., FLUXNET), and the growing availability of in-situ measurements and open data provide unprecedented opportunities to monitor, understand, and manage agroecosystems. Coupled with advancements in data science, machine learning, and process-based modelling, these tools enable the transition from observation to actionable solutions that support climate-resilient agriculture and sustainable land management. This session welcomes contributions that explore and integrate diverse approaches—including (but not limited to): • Large-scale mapping strategies of agroecosystem processes and dynamics. • Integration of multi-modal remote sensing data (spectral, thermal, high-resolution RGB from current and future satellite constellations, UAVs, or airborne campaigns) with in-situ observations and environmental monitoring networks. • Applications of machine learning, radiative transfer modelling, and hybrid approaches. • Foundation model development and applications within agroecosystems and agriculture • Monitoring or modelling of soil–plant–water interactions and nutrient dynamics. • Assessment of biotic and abiotic stresses, including water demand and evapotranspiration. • Quantification of climate change impacts (e.g., biodiversity loss, hydrological extremes, soil degradation, ecosystem shifts) on agricultural systems and their resilience. Contributions should be presented through a lens that aims not only to advance technical understanding, but also to demonstrate how these efforts translate into practical pathways for improving agroecosystem monitoring and management—across intensively and extensively managed crop and grassland systems—towards a more sustainable and climate-resilient future.
title: Data science, earth observation and AI for sustainable agroecosystem monitoring and management

description: Land-use-based carbon dioxide removal (CDR) plays a prominent role in pathways towards net-zero and net-negative emissions. However, its realised climate benefit cannot be determined from carbon sequestration alone. CDR outcomes are shaped by land-use legacy, atmospheric CO₂, climate change, nutrient availability, ecosystem composition and disturbances. Land-based CDR can also alter surface energy and water exchanges, producing local and remote climate responses that may strengthen or offset its carbon-related benefits. This session invites studies that use Earth system models to improve understanding of these interactions. We particularly welcome research on coupled carbon–nitrogen cycling and nutrient constraints; biogeochemical and biophysical feedbacks involving albedo, evapotranspiration, surface roughness and hydrology; and remote effects mediated by moisture recycling, atmospheric circulation and climate teleconnections. Relevant CDR and land-management approaches include afforestation and reforestation (A/R), agroforestry, forest and soil management, peatland restoration, and bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS). We also encourage model development, benchmarking, intercomparison and observational evaluation, alongside assessments of uncertainty, additionality, permanence and reversal risks associated with drought, heat, fire, pests and other disturbances. Studies examining future mitigation pathways, temperature overshoot, declining atmospheric CO₂ and the long-term resilience of terrestrial carbon sinks are especially welcome.
title: Earth system modelling of land-based carbon dioxide removal (CDR): model development, biogeophysical and biogeochemical interactions, risks, and future pathways

description: Terrestrial ecosystems function varies substantially within a single day: plant water and carbon exchange, canopy temperature, and land–atmosphere coupling all shift with light, heat, and moisture over the course of hours. Yet our understanding of ecosystem function is still largely built from daily-to-monthly observations, leaving sub-daily dynamics underexplored despite their relevance to heat and drought stress, phenological transitions, and rapid disturbance. Recent advances are changing this. Eddy covariance networks continue to provide high-frequency flux records, while geostationary satellites (e.g. MSG, GOES, Himawari) now deliver sub-hourly imagery of vegetation, land surface temperature, and land–atmosphere exchange. Complementary tools, such as phenocams, proximal and UAS-based sensing, and diurnal solar-induced fluorescence, add further resolution to how ecosystems respond across the day. This session invites contributions that use these and other approaches to characterize ecosystem function at the diurnal scale. We welcome studies on diurnal cycles of carbon, water, and energy exchange; vegetation and phenological dynamics at sub-daily resolution; formation of clouds, detection of rapid ecosystem stress or disturbance; and methodological advances in data fusion, upscaling or modelling that resolve sub-daily processes. We particularly encourage contributions that bridge observation platforms and spatial scales, from tower to landscape to continent, to build a more complete picture of how ecosystems function across the day.
title: The Diurnal Frontier: Exploring ecosystem function at sub-daily timescales

description: Rapid change in contemporary ice sheets and glaciers pose a major challenge for predicting future sea-level rise, in large part because many key processes operate beyond the range of modern observations. Palaeo glaciology provides critical natural experiments for exploring these processes, yet the palaeo and modern glaciology communities often use different data, modelling approaches, and forums for knowledge exchange. This session aims to bridge that divide by bringing together researchers working on modern and palaeo glaciology to explore shared processes, transferable methods, and common uncertainties. We welcome contributions that integrate geological and geophysical observations, numerical modelling, model-data comparison, and theory across temporal scales. Particular emphasis is placed on insights into marine ice sheet instability, surface mass balance, ice-water interactions, ice stream dynamics, and solid Earth processes. By fostering dialogue across communities, this session seeks to strengthen physically grounded projections of future glacial change.
title: Bridges Between Palaeo and Modern Glaciology

description: The frequencies and intensities of extreme events such as floods, tropical cyclones, heat waves, droughts etc. are increased in many regions across the globe and now of serious concern due to their socio-economic Impact. Hence understanding of the mechanism, pattern and characteristics of such events have been the focus of many recent studies. This session invites abstracts on observational and numerical modeling studies aimed to enhance the understanding of the spatial and temporal characteristics and predictability of the extreme events. This session also welcomes the submissions on model simulations and evaluations aimed to advance the understanding of the physics and dynamics associated with the extreme events. In particular, abstracts are encouraged on regional-scale analysis of the historical extreme events and their projections which would assist the policy makers to build more resilient societies to face the extreme event related disasters.
title: Extreme Events: Observations and Modeling

description: Weather prediction and climate modelling extensively use numerical models of the Earth system. Both the atmosphere and ocean components of such models consist of a fluid dynamics solver (dynamical core) that solves a system of partial differential equations numerically. The dynamical core is coupled to physical parameterizations that represent processes that occur below the grid scale (physics). Enabled also by substantial improvements of the underlying numerical algorithms, these models can deliver accurate and efficient simulations. Researchers are constantly working to further improve the accuracy, efficiency, and scalability of the dynamical core, the physics, and their coupling. The rapid development of computing systems towards massive use of graphics processing units and extreme parallelism requires adaptation of algorithms to further increase model efficiency via strong or weak parallel scaling. Recent years have also seen a rapid increase in hybrid approaches that combine physics-based modelling with data driven techniques, adopting techniques from scientific machine learning for Earth system modelling. This session invites presentations on the development, testing, and application of novel numerical techniques for Earth system models in a broad sense. The scope includes modifications to the governing equations, horizontal and vertical discretizations, structure preserving methods, time stepping schemes (including parallel in time schemes), advection schemes, adaptive multi-scale models, physics-dynamics coupling, regional and global models, classical and stochastic physical parameterizations, as well as hybrid schemes combining numerical methods and machine learning.
title: Advances in algorithm design for Numerical Earth System Modelling

description: Rossby wave dynamics stands at the intersection of several open research questions, ranging from our basic understanding of mid-latitude variability, to the short- and medium-range predictability of high-impact weather events, and to the circulation changes expected from anthropogenic global warming. Rossby waves exist and propagate along vorticity gradients such as the one related to the tropopause-level jet stream, whose complex meandering often "breaks" creating nonlinear circulation features, such as atmospheric blocking. Recent extreme weather and climate episodes, like heavy rainfall events leading to flash floods, recurrent and concurrent summer heatwaves or unforeseen winter cold spells, highlight the need to improve our understanding of jet streams and of the associated linear and non-linear, planetary and synoptic-scale Rossby wave dynamics in the atmosphere to better constrain the impacts of Rossby waves and of atmospheric blocking on extreme weather and climate events. Abstracts are invited on a wide range of topics, with a focus on, but not limited to, the following areas: (1) Theoretical developments in the dry and moist dynamics of Rossby waves, wave breaking, atmospheric blocking, and of jet streams acting as atmospheric Rossby waveguides. This includes the role of local and remote drivers (e.g., the tropics, Arctic, or stratosphere) in affecting Rossby wave evolution. (2) Linkages between extreme weather/climate events and the jet stream, as well as the associated linear and non-linear Rossby wave evolution during such events, including Rossby wave breaking, cut-off formation and re-absorption, and atmospheric blocking. (3) Application of cutting-edge methods to study the multi-scale interaction of Rossby waves from the convective scale to the large-scale dynamics, and its representation in existing weather and climate models (e.g. hierarchical and/or high-resolution modelling, machine learning/AI-based approaches). (4) Exploring the effect of Rossby wave packets on predictability at lead times from medium range (~2 weeks) to seasonal time-scales. This includes the potential role of blocking and of teleconnections involving Rossby wave propagation. (5) Projected future changes in planetary or synoptic-scale Rossby waves, and in their connection to extreme weather and events in a changing climate.
title: Atmospheric Rossby waves and Jet Stream Dynamics, and their Impacts on Extreme Weather and Climate Events

description: Mountains cover approximately one quarter of the earth’s land surface, and a significant fraction of the world’s population lives within them, in their vicinity, and downstream of them. Orography critically affects weather and climate processes across all scales and, in connection with factors such as land-cover heterogeneity, is responsible for high spatial variability in mountain weather and climate. This session showcases research that contributes to improving our understanding of weather and climate processes in mountain and high-elevation areas around the globe, as well as their modification induced by global environmental change, including studies connected to the TEAMx research programme. We invite theoretical, modeling and observational contributions that address the influence of mountains on the atmosphere from meteorological to climate time scales, including terrain-induced flows, orographic gravity waves, orographic precipitation, land-atmosphere exchange over mountains, forecasting and predictability of mountain weather, and the interaction of mountain weather and climate with the terrestrial cryosphere. Furthermore, we invite studies that investigate climate processes and climate change in mountain areas based on monitoring and modeling activities, including in particular contributions that address the interdisciplinary objectives of the Elevation-Dependent Climate Change (EDCC) working group of the Mountain Research Initiative, as well as the application and development of high-resolution (kilometer-scale) climate models over complex mountainous terrain, such as advances in model design, challenges, and observational gaps needed for robust model evaluation and improvement.
title: Mountain Weather and Climate: Theory, Observations, and Modeling

description: Complementary middle-atmosphere sounding techniques—such as infrasound, lidar, radar, microwave spectrometry, and mesospheric airglow observations, further strengthened by satellite measurements—have become significantly more accessible over the past decade. We expect that developing multi-instrument platforms will expand the community involved in operational infrasound monitoring for near-real-time observation of high-impact natural hazards—including volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, meteoroid entries, and bright fireballs—while creating new opportunities for atmospheric remote sensing research, such as improving gravity wave parameterizations. In particular, global and regional infrasound station networks have proven highly effective in detecting and locating a wide range of natural and anthropogenic phenomena— including space debris re-entries. Recent studies have shown that multi-technology analyses provide foundations for addressing geophysical inverse problems, enabling novel probing of both global-scale and small-scale structures in the middle atmosphere for enhanced weather prediction and climate modeling. In addition to data-driven contributions, this session invites model-based papers dealing with the dynamics of the middle atmosphere across scales and altitudes, as well as its predictability. We welcome contributions on the characterization of atmospheric phenomena (gravity or planetary waves for example), using complementary observational methods across both local and global scales. Contributions addressing advances in wave propagation modeling, signal processing, and machine learning applications are also of great interest. Additional areas of focus include the development of derived data products and services for scientific and civilian use, as well as innovative instrumentation, including sensors deployed on mobile or elevated platforms such as balloons on Earth or other planets. Seismo-acoustic studies investigating the coupled Earth–ocean–atmosphere system, particularly focusing on ionospheric responses to processes originating from the ocean and solid Earth, are also encouraged.
title: Middle atmosphere dynamics: modeling and observations

description: The understanding of tropical phenomena and their representation in numerical models still raise important scientific and technical questions, particularly in the coupling between the dynamics and diabatic processes. Among these phenomena, tropical cyclones (TC) are of critical interest because of their societal impacts and because of uncertainties in how their characteristics (cyclogenesis processes, occurrence, intensity, latitudinal extension, translation speed) will change in the framework of global climate change. The monitoring of TCs, their forecasts at short to medium ranges, and the prediction of TC activity at extended range (15-30 days) and seasonal range are also of great societal interest. The aim of the session is to promote discussions between scientists focusing on the physics and dynamics of tropical phenomena. This session is thus open to contributions on all aspects of tropical meteorology between the convective and planetary scale, such as: - Tropical cyclones, - Convective organisation, - Diurnal variations, - Local circulations (i.e. island, see-breeze, etc…), - Monsoon depressions, - Equatorial waves and other synoptic waves (African easterly waves, etc…), - The Madden-Julian oscillation and intraseasonal variability,, - Large-scale circulations (i.e. ITCZ, etc…) - etc… We especially encourage contributions of observational analyses and modelling studies of tropical cyclones and other synoptic-scale tropical disturbances including the physics and dynamics of their formation, structure, and intensity, and mechanisms of variability of these disturbances on intraseasonal to interannual and climate time scales. Findings from recent field campaigns are also encouraged.
title: Tropical Meteorology and Tropical Cyclones

description: Severe convective storms (SCS) are among the most impactful weather phenomena, producing hazards such as hail, extreme precipitation, damaging winds, tornadoes, and lightning. Understanding them requires bridging scales that are usually studied separately: hydrometeor growth and updraft dynamics operate on scales of metres and minutes, storm organisation and longevity on the mesoscale, and the environments that permit severe convection are set by synoptic and large-scale circulation. The resulting hazard climatologies, and how they shift under a warming climate, emerge from the interaction of all of these. Progress on the central questions — why some storms produce severe hazards and others do not, how far ahead this is predictable, and how hazard frequency and intensity will change — depends on work that connects these scales rather than treating them in isolation. This session provides a venue for that exchange across the SCS community, from process studies to global assessments and societal impacts. This session welcomes contributions on: - dynamical and microphysical processes governing storm severity and hazard production, including updraft dynamics, storm development, organisation, evolution and intensity - pre-storm environments, convective parameters, and the large-scale drivers of severe convection - storm-scale and environmental predictability, nowcasting and forecasting, and their verification - hazard, storm, and environmental climatologies and trends, including regional climatologies and under-observed regions - changes in storm dynamics, hazard evolution, and storm frequency and intensity under climate change - societal impacts of severe convective storms, including compound and consecutive events - aerosol–cloud interactions and their influence on storm microphysics and hazard severity We welcome studies using high-resolution numerical modelling, machine learning, statistical analysis, in-situ observations and field campaigns, remote sensing, crowd-sourced data, reanalyses, and global climate models. Contributions from operational services and the private sector are explicitly welcome.
title: Severe convective storms - from storm-scale dynamics to global climatologies

description: The subtropics are global hotspots of climate change, yet climate model simulations and projections for these regions remain highly uncertain. These regions are home to a large share of the world's population, including many communities with the least historical GHG emissions that are disproportionately exposed to extreme events and climate change. As a zone of interaction between tropical and extratropical circulation regimes, the subtropics are characterised by a unique hydroclimate, with strong spatial gradients, distinct seasonal cycles, and high sensitivity to climate variability and change. Despite their importance for both society and the climate system, subtropical weather and climate processes remain comparatively understudied. This session invites contributions that advance process understanding and prediction of weather and climate with a particular focus on the subtropics. We welcome studies based on observations, theory, numerical models, and machine learning. Topics of interest include, but are not limited to: - Atmospheric processes, such as tropical–extratropical interactions, subtropical jet fluctuations, Rossby wave dynamics, transient eddies, monsoon circulations, and convergence zones, shaping surface weather, clouds, and transport of dust and air pollution. - Weather, climate, and compound extremes – droughts, heatwaves, wildfires, heavy precipitation, floods, dust storms, and windstorms – spanning their drivers, future changes, and impacts on society and ecosystems. - The water cycle – rainfall, evapotranspiration, and moisture transport – modulated by weather systems such as cyclones, cut-off lows, cold air outbreaks, mesoscale convective systems, easterly waves, atmospheric rivers, and cloud bands. - Coupled interactions between Earth system components, including land-atmosphere and ocean-atmosphere feedbacks, and the role of sea surface temperature patterns in shaping subtropical climate. - Climate variability and remote linkages with ENSO, the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO), and the Hadley circulation. - Observations and climate model simulations addressing past and future changes in regional circulation patterns and surface weather, and novel approaches for identifying model biases and for reducing uncertainties in projections.
title: Subtropical weather and climate processes in the past, present, and future

description: Weather forecasting and its application is one of the most important subject in meteorology. This session will focus on R&D on understanding the weather, forecasting techniques and its applications, both with AI and physics based. Contributions related to nowcasting, numerical weather prediction, ensemble techniques, NWP post-processing and forecast application are very welcome. Topics may include: - Nowcasting and warning methods and systems, use of observations and weather analysis - Studies on high impact weather - Data driven and physics based numerical modelling; explainable Artificial Intelligence (xAI) in weather models - Development of AI for ensemble prediction techniques and products - Weather forecasting application - Seamless prediction and application - Statistical and AI NWP Post-processing - Use of machine learning, data mining and other advanced analytical techniques - ML for weather warning
title: Weather forecasting and application: knowledge, techniques (AI and physics based)

description: This session invites contributions spanning all aspects of prediction and predictability on the subseasonal (2 weeks to 2 months) forecasting timescale, also known as subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) prediction. We welcome research that covers predictions, processes, warning capabilities and which supports applications and decision-making across sectors (including, but not limited to, the examples listed below). In light of recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) techniques for subseasonal prediction, contributions on AI/ML model developments, benchmarking frameworks and applications are very welcome. Of special interest are contributions related to the AI Weather Quest, an open international competition benchmarking AI-based subseasonal forecasts in real-time. Physical drivers and processes: - Role of the atmosphere, ocean, land, and ice processes in extended-range/S2S predictability - Modes of variability (e.g. Madden Julian Oscillation (MJO), quasi-biennial oscillation (QBO), polar vortex strength, and others) impacting the extended-range/S2S predictability - Impact of global warming on early warning systems, changes in risks Prediction systems: - Evaluation and improvement of S2S prediction systems, including advancements in model physics and comparison between dynamical and data-driven prediction models, data assimilation, ensemble forecasting, and initialization techniques - Use of AI/ML methods for S2S prediction, data-driven models, post-processing, and attribution, including innovative techniques for improving forecast accuracy Extreme events and early warnings: - Early warnings for single- and multi-hazard events - Sources of predictability for extreme events, including multi-hazards events, on the S2S timescale (including driver identification and teleconnections) - Case studies of extreme or high-impact event prediction and impacts on early warnings - Predictability and predictive skill of atmospheric or surface variables, and other variables relevant for socio-economic sectors, such as sea ice, snow cover, soil moisture, and land surface Applications and societal relevance: - Sector-specific applications, impact studies on the S2S/extended range timescale - New approaches for incorporating S2S forecast in decision-making - Examples of integration of S2S predictions into decision support systems at local, regional, or global levels and co-production of knowledge with stake-holders and decision-makers
title: Subseasonal prediction, processes and applications

description: Science is best learned by doing, but the beginning of a scientific career is rarely easy. This session invites reflections on the challenges encountered during research, ranging from forgetting a screwdriver during a field day to not being able to compile software. Sharing challenges and their solutions is critical for Early Career Scientists, as it can (1) lead to the development of better protocols for fieldwork, modeling, and data analysis, (2) reduce impostor syndrome and self-doubt, and (3) highlight the human side of science through people in the community and their lived experiences. The goal of this session is to bring together a wide variety of experiences, stories, and people. We invite submissions from any geoscientific field in two specific categories: First, any submissions that showcase a specific problem, your Eureka moment, and your solution. The goal of these submissions is to show that unforeseen problems happen to everyone, but that it is possible to overcome them. Examples may include (but are not limited to): • Designing computing codes that run with fewer computational resources • Using sensors, technologies, and data beyond their traditional applications • Developing computational workflows that integrate different approaches in novel ways (e.g., machine learning, trap cameras, and social media) • Merging methods from several disciplines into new approaches. Second, any submissions that provide an Early Career Perspective on the challenges in your field, geoscience in general, or combining life and science, and proposed solutions. Examples may include (but are not limited to): • Community initiatives that facilitate the use of fieldwork techniques and computational resources. • Grand challenges framing from a perspective that highlights equality, diversity and inclusion (EDI). • Community perspectives and synthesis to reduce barriers of entry in transdisciplinary paths focused on problem-solving. • Juggling how problem-solving was applied to a research career (e.g., having a family, migration)
title: Learning to fly: Inviting diverse Early Career Perspectives on Research Challenges

description: Knowledge co-creation can be defined as a collaborative process, focused on an iterative interaction leading to new knowledge – e.g. a new understanding of a problem. A key element of co-creation is the inclusion and integration of diverse knowledge systems, including traditional and indigenous knowledge systems. Experiences of ways to recognize, valorize and integrate traditional and indigenous knowledge in geosciences in a just and equitable way are present but they still receive little attention and are not recognized as fundamental milestones towards more inclusive, effective, and sustainable scientific practices. This section welcomes experiences of inclusion of traditional and indigenous knowledge in geosciences, including reflections on the governance and management of indigenous data. Approaches focusing on the decolonization of geosciences, recognition of the role of native scientists and avoiding parachute sciences and data extractivism are particularly encouraged. Co-organized by the Working Group on Co-Creation of Water Knowledge of the International Association of Hydrological Sciences: https://iahs.info/Initiatives/Scientific-Decades/helping-working-groups/co-creating-water-knowledge/
title: Inclusion of traditional and indigenous knowledge and governance of indigenous data in geosciences

description: Climate change is one of the defining societal challenges of the 21st century, and its impacts increasingly affect communities worldwide. By the time of EGU27, a “super El Niño” fuelled by unprecedentedly high tropical Pacific sea surface temperatures is expected to exacerbate extreme weather and rainfall patterns in many parts of the world, causing severe impacts and potentially lasting damages. Despite growing evidence, political and societal responses remain inadequate for mitigation, adaptation, and loss and damage, resulting in persistent vulnerabilities and accumulating impacts on societies and ecosystems. This shortfall in climate action has prompted citizens and organizations to pursue legal action, seeking remedies for climate-related damages and putting pressure on decision-makers to commit to and implement meaningful emission reductions. This interdisciplinary session invites contributions that advance the integration of insights from the geosciences into legal practice. We welcome new scientific methods to support legal arguments, as well as inter- and transdisciplinary approaches on the consolidation of scientific insights in climate litigation, and on the effective communication of scientific findings to legal practitioners and the broader society. Submissions may also address questions of climate change and impact attribution, responsibility, human, non-human and broader environmental rights, burden sharing of efforts, translation between science and law, and science communication, that link beyond disciplinary boundaries. Please note that all first authors of an abstract to any Programme Group (PG) within the General Assembly are allowed to also submit a second regular abstract to a Geoscience & Society (GS) session like this one.
title: Bridging the gap between climate science and legal practice: informing laws and litigation

description: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML), including Deep Learning, Computer Vision and Remote Sensing techniques, are increasingly used across the geosciences for hazard forecasting, Earth observation, environmental monitoring, climate services and other applications that may inform operational and policy decisions. Examples such as Google Flood Hub, GraphCast, ECMWF’s AIFS, post-disaster damage assessment pipelines and geospatial foundation models show the growing potential of these approaches. However, strong performance on standard benchmarks does not automatically make an AI-derived product suitable for high-stakes decisions. This session asks what AI-enabled geoscience needs to demonstrate before it can be relied upon in operational, policy or governance contexts. We welcome contributions that move beyond conventional performance metrics and address reliability, uncertainty, transparency, robustness and practical usability. Technical approaches may include Physics-Informed Neural Networks, uncertainty quantification methods such as Conformal Prediction or Bayesian Neural Networks, and Explainable AI approaches assessed against the information needs of end-users and decision-makers. Relevant contributions may examine validation against rare or out-of-distribution events, uncertainty communication, robustness across locations and time periods, data quality and bias, reproducibility, provenance and traceability, and approaches to operational readiness, including Technology Readiness Level frameworks. Contributions based on systems tested or used in practice are particularly encouraged, including early warning systems, automated hazard mapping, environmental monitoring, climate adaptation tools and Earth observation applications for disaster risk reduction. The session will also address the governance and societal implications of AI-derived scientific evidence, including standards and regulatory frameworks, human oversight, algorithmic bias, equity, public trust, stakeholder participation, accountability and the potential for AI-supported decisions to affect communities differently. The aim is to connect geoscientists developing AI methods with those working on how scientific evidence is assessed, communicated and governed. The central question is not only whether an AI model works, but whether there is sufficient transparent, robust and actionable evidence to justify its use in real decisions.
title: AI-Enabled Geoscience for Decision-Making: Reliability, Responsibility and Governance

description: Geoscientists inform decisions with environmental, social, and economic consequences, so their responsibilities extend beyond scientific analysis. Challenges such as climate change, risks, and sustainable resource management require ethical engagement with society. Geoethics examines the ethical, social, and cultural implications of geoscience, promoting responsible, just, inclusive, and transformative approaches. Through case studies and interdisciplinary discussion, this session explores how geoethics can shape responsible geoscientific practices and policies. We welcome theoretical, methodological, and practical contributions on topics including: • Ethical and social aspects of the geosciences, particularly at the interface between geoscience, society, politics, and decision-making • Responsible and sustainable management of georesources, including surface water, groundwater, soils, rocks, minerals, and energy resources • Ethical and social aspects of geoscience and environmental education and communication • Geoethics in relation to natural hazards, georisks, and disaster risk reduction • The ethical and social significance of geoheritage, geodiversity, geoconservation, geotourism, and geoparks • The role of the geosciences in achieving the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals • Ethical and social issues related to climate change • Ethical challenges associated with emerging frontiers in the geosciences, such as geoengineering and deep-sea mining • Ethical implications of data life-cycle management, big data, and the use of artificial intelligence in the geosciences • Ethical questions across geoscience disciplines, including economic geology, engineering geology, hydrogeology, palaeontology, forensic geology, medical geology, and planetary geoscience • Integrity in geoscience research and practice, publication ethics, and professional conduct • Inclusivity, diversity, harassment, discrimination, accessibility, and disability in the geosciences • The respectful and meaningful integration of Indigenous and local knowledge into the geosciences • Neocolonialism in geoscience research and practice • Geoscience diplomacy and ethical and social issues in international geoscience cooperation, including the role of geoscientific knowledge in fostering dialogue, collaboration, and peace • The philosophy of the geosciences and the history of geoscientific thought
title: Geoethics: Responsible Geosciences for Society and the Environment

description: Scientific software is fundamental to modern geoscientific research, yet its development and maintenance often receive less attention and recognition than the scientific results it enables. Time constraints, limited resources, and the pressure to deliver scientific outcomes can lead to software practices that compromise reproducibility, traceability, and long-term sustainability, ultimately limiting the reuse of methods and opportunities for scientific collaboration. This session explores how good software development practices contribute to reproducible, sustainable, and open geoscientific research. We invite contributions sharing practical experiences, methodological approaches, and lessons learned in areas such as software design, modularisation, documentation, testing, version control, portability, and data workflows. We particularly welcome contributions addressing the challenges of implementing and maintaining these practices in real-world research environments. We also encourage discussions on the opportunities and challenges of AI-assisted software development, including its implications for code quality, reproducibility, maintainability, and scientific responsibility. Hence, with this session we aim to foster an exchange on how software development can be better integrated into scientific practice and recognised as an essential component of research quality and scientific integrity.
title: Scientific software development in the Geosciences: Towards reproducible, sustainable and open research

description: Geoscience is critical to environmental decision-making. For scientific evidence to be trusted, challenged, reused, and communicated responsibly, the research behind it must be as open, transparent and reproducible as possible. While the technical building blocks for computational reproducibility are well-established, their adoption remains uneven, and sustaining reproducible workflows in daily research and operational settings remains challenging. Ultimately, open science requires more than just technical tooling; it demands a cultural shift in how scientific knowledge is created, shared, and evaluated. This session bridges technical solutions and daily research practice, exploring both practical approaches to reproducibility and the human factors that shape their adoption. We invite contributions that move beyond the basic "how-to" of reproducibility tools to explore how we can support widespread, sustainable, and equitable use across the geosciences. Topics may include: » Reproducible workflows in practice: Approaches to data governance, analysis design, documentation, automation, and long-term access to geospatial code and data. » Culture, community & vulnerability: Concerns around sharing (e.g. public scrutiny, imposter syndrome, data ownership, credit) and ways to normalize sharing non-traditional research outputs. » Incentives & evaluation: Assessing how institutional structures (i.e., funding, hiring, promotion) can better reward research robustness and reproducibility alongside scientific novelty. » Global equity & infrastructure: Digital and governance disparities, resource constraints, and the often invisible work required to make research reusable across communities and regions. » Education & capacity building: Integrating computational literacy, open-source practices, and reproducibility principles directly into geoscience education. » Systemic & institutional change: The roles of journals, publishers, funders and science communication in moving beyond checkbox compliance to foster a vibrant open science ecosystem. We welcome technical guidelines, case studies, qualitative and interdisciplinary research, institutional strategies, practitioner perspectives, communication approaches, and honest accounts of reproducibility challenges, failures, and lessons learned. Together, we aim to spark constructive dialogue on how we can collectively move toward a more transparent, collaborative, equitable, and socially impactful geoscience ecosystem.
title: Why don’t we share? Bridging the gap between technical tools and cultural barriers in open and reproducible geoscience

description: Early Warning Systems (EWS) are a cornerstone of disaster risk reduction, protecting lives and livelihoods through timely, actionable information. Their efficacy depends not only on scientific robustness but also on integration and connections across disciplines, from risk knowledge and hazard detection to communication and community and institutional response. Despite ambitious targets in the Early Warnings for All (EW4ALL) action plan and the Sendai Framework towards multi-hazard, all-vulnerability, and impact-based EWS, gaps persist between these ambitions, operational realities, and the supporting science. This session fosters dialogue on EWS implementation and methodological innovation among researchers working toward more effective, inclusive, and actionable systems. We invite contributions from all disciplines and sectors involved in EWS development and implementation, including natural hazards science, atmospheric and hydrologic research, social sciences, and disaster management practice. We welcome work on any element of the early warning value chain, from forecasting advances to tools, platforms, or systems in use or development, as well as reflections on successes and failures in closing the gap between ambition and action. We encourage submissions addressing: ■ Early warning frameworks, tools and multi-stakeholder implementation; ■ Multi-hazard advancements: efforts to extend from single-hazard to multi-hazard systems; ■ Technological innovations: advances in AI, machine learning, Earth observation, IoT and other technologies in EWS components; ■ Dissemination, communication and community engagement: strategies that integrate behavioral and psychological insights, build trust, and ensure effective warning dissemination and last-mile reach, particularly at community level; ■ Data integration and system interoperability: approaches to integrating diverse data sources and addressing challenges in cross-agency data sharing and platform integration; ■ Bridging ambition and implementation: case studies showing how scientific progress translates into operational practice; ■ System-level evaluation and learnings: reviews of efficacy of the entire early warning value chain. This session is developed in cooperation with the RiskKAN Working Groups "Warnings and Preparedness for a Riskier World" and "AI for Complex Climate Risk Mitigation”.
title: Early Warning Systems (EWS): Bridging Research to Operations for Effective Disaster Risk Reduction

description: Citizen science and community-based approaches are increasingly used in disaster risk reduction (DRR), particularly where formal monitoring networks are sparse, resources are constrained, or locally observed changes are poorly captured by conventional systems. Yet their potential extends far beyond filling observational gaps or recruiting communities as data collectors. When genuinely participatory and co-created, citizen science can influence what questions are asked, what is monitored, whose knowledge is recognised, how decisions about risk are made. This session explores citizen science as a process of knowledge co-production, rather than simply a method of data collection. We therefore invite empirical, methodological and conceptual contributions that examine citizen science and participatory approaches to natural hazards across the Global South and other data-scarce, remote or marginalized contexts. We welcome studies addressing, among others: - Community-based hazard monitoring, forecasting and early warning for hazards such as floods, landslides, droughts, earthquakes, volcanic unrest…; - Co-design and co-production of monitoring systems and risk-reduction strategies – moving beyond communities as data collectors towards participation in interpretation, decision-making and action; - Relationships between scientific, local and Indigenous knowledge, and their integration into institutional risk management frameworks; - Ethical and equity considerations – power, trust and data ownership – in co-designing citizen science with communities experiencing high hazard exposure; - Citizen-generated data – from low-cost technologies to qualitative, non-digital and place-based approaches – for filling observational gaps in data-scarce regions; - Capacity strengthening and community ownership as pathways to the long-term sustainability of participatory monitoring networks; - Comparative and transferable lessons (what can/cannot be transferred across different geographical, cultural and institutional contexts); - Examples of failure, unintended consequences, contested knowledge and lessons learned, alongside successful practice. By bringing together researchers, practitioners, and those working directly with communities, this session will create space for critical reflection on citizen science practice. Alongside presentations, we propose dedicated discussion time to identify shared challenges, evidence gaps and priorities for future research and collaboration.
title: Beyond Data Collection: Citizen Science for Disaster Risk Reduction in the Global South

description: Across geoscience, software is central to how research is conducted, shared, and reproduced. From the complex Earth-system simulations on high-performance computers to processing raw instrument data from fieldwork, software is a cornerstone of the modern open science process. Supporting this collaborative research effort involves not only researchers, but many other digital research technical professionals (RTPs), for example research software engineers (RSEs) and data stewards. As the saying goes, “Better Software, Better Research” and their unique skills enable more efficient, reproducible, openly accessible science. This session highlights how engagement between researchers and RTP/RSEs enhances science, facilitates collaboration and communication, and supports sustainable reuse of research outputs across domains. We aim to build a RTP/RSE community at EGU, recognise their contributions, and facilitate future collaboration. To achieve this we invite stories of both success and failure, with lessons learned to be shared with others. How has the engagement of RTP/RSEs on a project enhanced scientific quality or facilitated transfer of research to operation? We want to hear about cross-cutting software or workflows developed and used across the geosciences and beyond. We welcome examples of software reuse: where adopting and extending existing tools and workflows enabled new science, and where making software publicly available has had an impact across communities. How were these projects conceived, supported, and their userbase grown? Beyond the software, we also invite contributions that explore how open software intersects with open data, reproducibility studies, the application of FAIR principles or reuse in ways that would not otherwise have been possible. Finally, we invite talks on research software policy. How are projects funded, what is the role of RTP/RSEs in this process, and how does this differ between institutions? How are teams built and organised to have the greatest effect - centralised vs. embedded - and how are careers developed and recognised? What impact can RTP/RSEs have on technical policies and training within their institution, for example around environmental/green computing initiatives, the use of generative AI, or advocating for open science principles? We solicit submissions from anyone working towards open science across academia and industry sharing transferable experiences relating to any of the above.
title: Better software, better research? The role of research software engineering in enhancing open science across disciplines.

description: All science has uncertainty. Global challenges such as disaster risk, environmental degradation, and climate change illustrate that an effective dialogue between science and society requires clear communication of uncertainty. Responsible science communication conveys the challenges of managing uncertainty that is inherent in measurements, input data, and model outputs, facilitating the society to understand the contexts where uncertainty emerges and enabling active participation in discussions. Uncertainty communication can play a major role across the risk management cycle, especially during decision-making, and should be tailored to the audience and the timing of delivery. Therefore, research on quantification and communication of uncertainties deepens our understanding of how to make scientific evidence more actionable for risk reduction. This session invites presentations by individuals and teams on communicating scientific uncertainty, addressing topics such as: 1. Innovative and practical tools (e.g. from social or statistical research) for communicating uncertainty. 2. Visual, verbal and numerical approaches for communicating uncertainty. 3. Pitfalls, challenges and solutions to communicating uncertainty to different audiences (e.g. experts, policymakers, media, general public, first-responders). 4. Communicating uncertainty in risk and crisis situations (e.g., natural hazards, climate change, public health crises). Examples of research fitting into the categories above include a) new, creative ways to visualize different aspects of uncertainty, b) new frameworks to communicate the level of confidence associated with research, c) testing the effectiveness of existing tools and frameworks, such as the categories of “confidence” used in expert reports (e.g., IPCC), or d) research addressing the challenges of communicating high-uncertainty high-impact events. This session encourages you to share your work and join a community of practice to inform and advance the effective communication of uncertainty in earth and space science.
title: How to communicate scientific uncertainty

description: Virtual and augmented reality, immersive visualization environments, and related interactive techniques are rapidly transforming the way we communicate, teach, and conduct geoscientific research. These technologies allow learners, stakeholders, and researchers to experience complex processes and datasets in new and engaging ways, from exploring outcrops and landscapes virtually to interacting with model simulations in three dimensions. Their potential spans education and outreach, where they enhance accessibility and engagement for diverse audiences, as well as scientific research itself, where immersive environments can provide novel perspectives on data analysis, hypothesis testing, and collaborative work. This session invites contributions showcasing innovative uses of virtual reality, augmented reality, mixed reality, and other immersive techniques across the geosciences. We particularly welcome examples from education, outreach, citizen science, and communication, as well as case studies and technical developments that demonstrate the added value of immersive approaches for scientific discovery. The session aims to foster exchange between developers and users, between research and education, and across disciplinary boundaries to highlight best practices and future opportunities for immersive technologies in geoscience.
title: Immersive Geoscience: Virtual and Augmented Reality in Education, Outreach and Research

description: Contemporary environmental and social challenges, such as climate change, pollution, desertification, natural hazards and species extinction, demand urgent and multifaceted responses. Art, with its own methods and long trajectory of exploring the relationships between human beings and the natural world, constitutes a specific pathway of inquiry and knowledge production. It operates differently from and complementary to scientific research. Art has the ability to evoke emotion and facilitate deep connections, making it a powerful tool for cognitive learning and delivering messages that reignite a sense of beauty and responsibility. Science transforms our understanding of the world. Art transforms the ways in which we perceive, experience, and relate to it. This complementarity makes collaboration between scientists and artists especially fertile. It allows complex questions to be approached through experience, the senses, the body, and the imagination. Art also opens an experiential path toward diverse audiences of different ages, backgrounds, and cultures, with or without specialized knowledge that can enhance scientific communication without replacing it. The scientific and artistic communities share an interest and responsibility in exploring how we inhabit a planet whose systems are under increasing pressure, and in generating new forms of knowledge and dialogue around these transformations. Traditional educational and communication methods have long addressed these challenges. Art-science collaborations open up further pathways for research and dialogue, grounded in direct, embodied experience. But this collaboration is not simply about art communicating or making science accessible: when both disciplines meet on equal terms of exchange, new questions, methods, and languages can emerge that neither discipline would reach on its own. This session aims to explore these interdisciplinary conversations. By bringing STEM and the arts together as equal partners, we want to open a space to discuss how these disciplines can collaborate in the research, exploration, and communication of contemporary social, economic, political, and environmental challenges, and what new forms of knowledge can emerge from this encounter. We encourage talks on all forms of artistic expression be it visual, audio, or performative. However, we do ask that talks be restricted to artistic expressions in which the end result was produced by a human and not artificial intelligence.
title: Building Bridges: Art-Science Collaborations for a Sustainable Future

description: Hands-on exploration, conversation, observation, play, and time away from screens are central to how people learn. At the same time, digital technologies, including AI, digital storytelling tools, multimedia platforms, and accessible Earth system science data, are creating new possibilities for teaching and engagement. The challenge is not choosing one approach over the other, but understanding when each can best support meaningful learning. This session invites talks on how educators and communicators balance analogue and digital approaches across Earth system science education and engagement. What kinds of learning are strengthened by technology, and what are better supported through direct experience, construction, discussion, art, play, and time to think? How can AI and other digital tools be used responsibly where they add value while preserving opportunities for curiosity, creativity, exploration, and productive struggle? And as technology makes it easier to access and process information, how do we continue to teach students and the public how to learn, think critically, ask questions, and make meaning? We invite presentations across formal and informal education, public engagement, and lifelong learning to share approaches to balancing digital and analogue experiences, from hands-on and place-based learning to technology-light spaces, creative approaches, AI-supported teaching, and digital storytelling.
title: Hands-on meets high tech: Innovative approaches to training and engagement in Earth system science

description: As evidence of the climate and ecological crisis mounts, climate and environmental scientists increasingly face a question: how to make their results actually matter? To what extent should they incorporate elements of public and civic engagement into their day-to-day research practice? Civic engagement remains rare among scientists, unevenly supported, and often contested on the premise that it is incompatible with scientific neutrality and detrimental to scientific credibility. Yet both public and civic engagement may take many forms — public communication, policy advice, art-science collaboration, advocacy, and civil disobedience — each of these forms raises its own questions of legitimacy, credibility, and personal or professional risks. This session invites contributions that document, analyse, or reflect on the many ways scientists engage in response to the climate crisis. We particularly welcome works that try to unravel the tensions such engagement raises: between perceived need for neutrality and academic freedom, between critique and defence of science, and between individual initiatives and institutional support. We are interested both in conceptual contributions (philosophy of science, sociology of the scientific field, legal frameworks of academic freedom and civil-service duties) and in concrete experiences — individual trajectories, collective initiatives, and institutional practices — from across disciplines and countries. We want this session to contribute to the discussion on science's relation to society in face of the climate crisis. A central aim of this session is to connect the initiatives — individual and collective, grassroots and institutional — that are emerging across Europe and beyond, and to foster exchange on what responsible, effective, and sustainable academic engagement can look like. We especially welcome submissions from collectives and networks at any career stage, and welcome reflective and interdisciplinary formats alongside conventional presentations.
title: Forms of scientific engagement in the face of the climate crisis
