description: Games have the power to ignite imaginations and place you in someone else’s shoes or situation, often forcing you into making decisions from perspectives other than your own. This makes them powerful tools for communication, through use in outreach, disseminating research, in education and teaching at all levels, and as a method to train the public, practitioners, and decision-makers in order to build environmental resilience. Games can also inspire innovative and fun approaches to learning. Gamification and game-based approaches add an extra spark of engagement and interaction with a topic. Gaming technology (e.g. virtual reality) can transport and immerse people into new worlds providing fascinating and otherwise impossible experiences for learners. In this session we welcome contributions from anyone who has used games, gaming technology, and/or game-based approaches in their research, their teaching, or public engagement activities. Visit www.games4geoscience.wordpress.com to learn more about the session.
title: Games for Geoscience

description: Social media provides geoscientists with opportunities to connect with diverse audiences, share discoveries, and explain how Earth's processes shape everyday life. However, turning complex research into content that is accessible, engaging, and scientifically robust while also appealing to algorithms remains a challenge. Short formats require concise messages, and the rapidly changing landscape of platforms, along with AI-generated content and misinformation, adds further complexity. The main challenge is capturing attention without losing scientific nuance and turning that attention into meaningful understanding. This session explores how individuals, groups, or institutions can effectively communicate geosciences on social media, covering topics such as climate change, geological hazards, and the history of our planet. We welcome contributions that present practical approaches and creative experiments, such as visual storytelling, humor, short videos, multilingual and community participation, and critical reflections and assessments on what works and what does not. Additionally, we aim to discuss strategies for reaching audiences beyond existing scientific networks, building trust, and evaluating impact beyond just the algorithms.
title: Communicating geosciences on social media: strategies, successes, and lessons learned

description: Youth are very aware of climate change, natural hazards, and other global environmental challenges, and many want to do something about it. If we can reach students in their teens, an age when individuals either maintain or lose interest in STE(A)M (science, technology, engineering, arts, and mathematics), we can show how geoscience gives you tools to understand the world and be part of the solution. Additionally, we can demonstrate the value and breadth of a geoscience career. Mission Earth, an initiative supported by the EGU Special Activity Fund, aims to connect students' natural curiosity about the environment to real-world action. During the project, early-career scientists across the globe worked with local youth to share their own career path into the geosciences, as well as impart storytelling and filmmaking skills to empower the students to produce their own short videos about local environmental and geoscience issues important to them. Youth groups were also able to receive a free science show from a Germany-based science entertainer, showcasing how science and curiosity can be fun. In this session, we will discuss successes from the Mission Earth project, best practices learned running a youth filmmaking program, and the environmental issues that are currently of importance to youth. We’ll also engage session attendees in some of the hands-on activities used to teach youth the skills needed to produce their own short films.
title: Leveraging video, storytelling, and entertainment to connect youth to their local environment - EGU Special Activity Fund Project Mission Earth

description: Disasters caused by natural hazards can lead to long-lasting disruptions across economic, social and ecological systems. Climate change and systemic risks can intensify these impacts through compound, concurrent and cascading events. Floods, wildfires, heatwaves, storms and droughts result from interactions between physical, social, human and economic drivers, challenging approaches that assess hazards in isolation. Their impacts are also unevenly distributed: some households may face displacement, debt or poorer health for years, while others recover much faster. Strengthening resilience is therefore central to disaster risk reduction and recovery. Yet limited empirical evidence and the diversity of resilience definitions, measures and applications make it difficult to understand how resilience develops and for whom. This calls for frameworks and methods that capture resilience mechanisms across interconnected systems, while also examining how resilience is experienced by households, communities and different social groups. This session seeks to advance an inter- and transdisciplinary perspective on systemic resilience to multi-hazards. We welcome contributions on single, compound and cascading hazards, particularly where they improve understanding of resilience mechanisms, drivers and strategies. Topics include: • Conceptual and analytical approaches for assessing, measuring and modelling resilience, including process- and outcome-based methods. • Systemic resilience mechanisms linking hazards, infrastructure, ecosystems, institutions and outcomes for people. • Human and demographic dimensions, including differences in exposure, coping and recovery; displacement and mobility; health, wellbeing and livelihoods; social protection and informal support. • Strategies and interventions for building resilience, including early warning systems, nature-based solutions, infrastructure, digital technologies, AI and adaptive planning. • Justice and equity, including local knowledge, historical and cultural perspectives and climate-resilient development. • Drivers, constraints and enabling conditions for multi-hazard resilience. • Comparative and longitudinal studies across regions and scales. • Stakeholder engagement through citizen science, participatory methods, co-production and research-practice partnerships. We encourage local, regional and global contributions from interdisciplinary and transdisciplinary research.
title: Investigating Systemic Resilience to Multi-Hazard Risks: Mechanisms, Methods, and Interventions

description: Rapid urban growth is reshaping the relationships among water, heat, and land in arid and semi-arid cities. These cities often face chronic water scarcity, yet they can also experience short, intense rainfall and episodic flooding. Urban expansion, land-cover change, and rising demand for cooling and urban greening further alter surface energy balance, evapotranspiration, runoff, and water use. For example, irrigation-based greening may reduce summer heat but increase pressure on already limited water supplies, while rapid surface sealing can intensify runoff during short, high-intensity storms. These processes create difficult trade-offs, and adaptation measures may reduce one risk while shifting pressure to another part of the urban system. This session focuses on how coupled water–heat–land processes shape climate risk and resilience in rapidly developing arid and semi-arid cities. We welcome studies on urban growth, heat stress, water availability, hydrological extremes, land-use change, and ecosystem processes, drawing on field observations, remote sensing, modelling, and comparative case studies. We are particularly interested in adaptation strategies that address multiple interacting risks rather than single hazards, including urban greening and cooling, blue-green and nature-based infrastructure, and water-sensitive planning. We also welcome work examining trade-offs among water conservation, flood management, thermal comfort, ecological quality, and urban development. Across arid and semi-arid regions, similar interventions can produce very different outcomes because of differences in climate, water availability, urban form, and land-use context. This session therefore asks when, where, and under what conditions water–heat–land trade-offs can be reduced or resolved, rather than simply displaced.
title: Water–Heat–Land Interactions and Adaptation in Arid and Semi-Arid Cities

description: Climate change is creating increasingly dynamic and interconnected challenges for human–environment systems, while conventional approaches to climate-risk assessment often struggle to capture nonlinear interactions among hazards, infrastructure, human behaviour, institutions, and environmental change. Rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI), geospatial data science, machine learning, and digital technologies provide new opportunities to understand, predict, and enhance climate resilience. This session brings together interdisciplinary research exploring how data-driven and AI-enhanced approaches can advance the assessment, modelling, and practice of climate resilience. We particularly welcome contributions that move beyond conventional vulnerability and risk assessment toward understanding adaptive capacity, resilience dynamics, and pathways for proactive adaptation. Topics include GeoAI and spatial-temporal data analytics; AI-enhanced climate-impact and resilience modelling; integration of machine learning with agent-based and other process-based models; human mobility, behaviour, and social networks; urban digital twins and interactive visual analytics; remote sensing and Earth observation; data-driven assessment of adaptation potential; and AI-supported planning and decision-making. We encourage empirical, theoretical, methodological, and applied contributions across different hazards, spatial scales, and geographical contexts. Particular interest lies in approaches that integrate physical and social data, combine data-driven and knowledge-driven modelling, incorporate stakeholder and human dimensions, or translate AI-based insights into actionable adaptation strategies. By bringing together researchers from climate science, geography, environmental science, data science, AI, and related disciplines, the session aims to advance a human-centred and solution-oriented research agenda for climate resilience and explore how emerging technologies can support more effective, adaptive, and sustainable responses to climate change.
title: Data-driven and AI-enhanced Climate Resilience: From Assessment, Modeling to Practical Action

description: Grassland systems are foundational to global food security, occupy roughly 40% of the terrestrial surface, and play a key role in climate regulation by storing around 20% of global soil carbon (C) stocks. These systems, however, sit at the intersection between opportunity and risk. On the one hand, improved management can reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, enhance C sequestration, strengthen nutrient cycling and improve soil health. On the other hand, decades of intensification have contributed to widespread land and soil degradation, increased GHG emissions, soil C losses, and disrupted nutrient cycling, undermining ecosystem resilience. Practices such as adaptive grazing management, silvopastoral systems, and the integration of legumes or organic fertilisers could unlock substantial mitigation potential, including up to 150 Tg CO₂-eq annually in soils, while reducing dependence on synthetic N fertilisers. Yet, major knowledge gaps remain. We still have a limited understanding of the mechanisms governing GHG mitigation, soil C sequestration, nutrient cycling, and soil health across diverse systems and environmental conditions, constraining our ability to assess their potential for building resilient systems. Addressing these uncertainties is particularly important as grasslands face growing pressures from land-use conflicts, biodiversity decline, climate change, shifting protein demands, and socioeconomic transformations in rural areas. Our session invites contributions that shed light on how grassland management, restoration, and grazing practices shape climate mitigation, soil processes, and ecosystem resilience across diverse environmental conditions. We particularly welcome studies that advance our understanding of the interactions among vegetation, soils, and livestock, and their implications for climate mitigation and sustainable food systems. Contributions from all regions and diverse perspectives are encouraged to foster a more holistic understanding of these challenges. The session will include, but not be restricted to, field and modelling studies, mesocosm experiments testing hypotheses related to C and N cycling in grasslands, and literature syntheses, with the aim of advancing knowledge and informing sustainable grassland management worldwide.
title: Grassland systems: GHG emissions, carbon dynamics, nutrient cycling, and pathways to soil health and resilience

description: Human activities on land (LULCC) shape climate by altering land-atmosphere fluxes of carbon, water, energy, and momentum. An increasing focus on land-based climate mitigation and adaptation strategies to meet more stringent targets has expanded the range of land management practices considered specifically for their potential to alter terrestrial carbon cycling or mediate favorable environmental conditions. This focus has also called attention to potential tradeoffs between climate-centric aspects of LULCC and its influences on biodiversity, hydrology and other environmental factors. Advancements in modeling and measurement techniques are opening new possibilities to better describe LULCC and its effects on the Earth system at multiple temporal and spatial scales. This session welcomes all contributions aimed at furthering our understanding of LULCC in the Earth system, including those addressing LULCC effects on carbon, climate, hydrology, and/or biodiversity, and aims to present studies that can inform adoption of appropriate land-based strategies for climate mitigation, adaptation, and ecosystem restoration.
title: Land use, land management, and land cover change (LULCC) and their effects on the Earth system

description: This session brings together researchers studying small bodies, dust, and space debris, and their interactions with planetary surfaces, atmospheres, and the surrounding space environment. The goal is a better understanding of the evolution and composition of small bodies, and of how they influence surrounding environments. We especially encourage contributions that bridge traditionally separate communities, from small-body dynamics and impact processes to atmospheric dust, space debris, and in-situ observations. With BepiColombo entering its science phase at Mercury and Hera exploring the Didymos system, we welcome contributions on small bodies, dust, and their surrounding environments from across recent and upcoming space missions. We welcome early-career scientists.
title: Small Bodies – Big Impact: Asteroids, Meteorites, Dust, and Space Debris

description: The aim of this session is to bring together interdisciplinary research addressing the formation, evolution, physical properties, and exploration of Small Bodies, including comets, Kuiper Belt Objects, asteroids, rings, meteorites, and dust, through numerical modeling, laboratory investigations, and artificial intelligence techniques. We welcome contributions combining theoretical and numerical modeling, laboratory experiments, computational methods, and data-driven approaches, including artificial intelligence and, in particular, machine learning. Laboratory studies under simulated space-like conditions, including ground-based and microgravity experiments, are especially encouraged, together with new experimental techniques and their use in interpreting and validating physical and numerical models. Topics of interest include, but are not limited to: - gas-dust interactions and activity in cometary atmospheres and comae; - volcanic and cryovolcanic activity on Solar System bodies, including Enceladus and Io; - formation and early evolution of planetary bodies, including dust and pebble growth, accretion, and planetesimal formation and dynamics; - thermophysical evolution, internal structure, and surface processes of Small Bodies; - modeling of atmospheres, exospheres, comae, dust environments, and surface-exosphere interactions; - development and application of numerical and computational methods; - AI and machine-learning techniques applied to simulations, laboratory experiments, spacecraft and observational data, and small bodies characterization and exploration; - laboratory experiments and numerical simulations supporting the development, calibration, and scientific exploitation of instrumentation for planetary exploration. The session particularly encourages studies bridging different methodological approaches, linking laboratory measurements with numerical simulations, physical models with observations, and AI and data-driven techniques with traditional computational methods. We invite contributions presenting new models, numerical methods, experiments, and interdisciplinary methodologies, as well as studies comparing or validating models against experimental, observational, or spacecraft data.
title: Small Bodies: Bridging Laboratory Experiments, Numerical Modeling, and Artificial Intelligence

description: The giant planets of the outer Solar System possess complex and dynamic magnetospheric environments shaped by a combination of strong magnetic fields, rapid planetary rotation, internal plasma sources and solar wind coupling. This session aims to bring together observational, theoretical,experimental, and numerical modeling studies focusing on the magnetospheric environments of the outer planets. We invite contributions addressing physical processes across multiple spatial and temporal scales, including but not limited to: magnetic reconnection, velocity shear-driven instabilities, plasma transport, auroral processes, and magnetosphere-ionosphere-thermosphere coupling; radiation belts and energetic particle acceleration and transport; magnetosphere–planet and magnetosphere-moon interactions; moon exosphere generation processes and surface weathering. Comparative studies involving different combinations of outer planet and/or terrestrial magnetospheres are encouraged. Studies involving also asymmetrical/tilted systems (Uranus and Neptune) or exploring links to exoplanetary systems are also very welcome. We encourage submissions leveraging data from past, current, and upcoming space missions (e.g., Juno, Cassini, New Horizons, JUICE, Europa Clipper, and proposed Ice Giant concepts), alongside ground- and space-based observations (e.g., HST, JWST, VLT) and numerical simulations. We particularly encourage contributions from early-career researchers.
title: Outer planet magnetospheres: environments, dynamics and interactions

description: Jupiter’s magnetosphere is one of the most dynamic and complex systems in the solar system. Juno’s mission extension is currently awaiting NASA’s decision. If selected, continued in situ and remote exploration, supported by Hubble, Hisaki, JWST, and ground-based telescopes, will further our understanding of Jupiter’s auroras and magnetospheric environment. These findings, combined with data from past missions, are reshaping our understanding of the Jovian system. This session addresses how Juno’s discoveries advance our knowledge of auroral acceleration and wave–particle interactions, auroral phenomenology, magnetosphere–ionosphere coupling, moon–magnetosphere interaction, magnetopause structure, and plasma transport across the Jovian magnetosphere. These results provide key constraints to prepare for the next phase of Jovian exploration with ESA’s JUICE mission and NASA’s Europa Clipper. We welcome contributions highlighting Juno results, along with insights from past and future missions, to better understand Jupiter’s magnetosphere.
title: Current and Future Exploration of the Jovian Magnetosphere

description: Tides and storm surges are among the most fundamental drivers of variability in the open ocean and along coasts, linking short-term hazards to long-term Earth system change. Together, they are the principal cause of coastal flooding. Tides and surges interact with mean sea level, waves, morphodynamics, river flow, and human infrastructure, shaping sediment transport, pollutant dispersal, coastal ecosystems, and navigation. Barotropic and internal tides supply mechanical energy to ocean mixing with consequences for stratification, nutrient transport, marine biogeochemistry, and large-scale ocean circulation. Tidal processes also interact directly with cryospheric systems, e.g., modulating ice-shelf flexure and grounding-line dynamics. Both tides and storm surges evoke substantial ocean and Earth System variability on timescales ranging from minutes to centuries and are increasingly affected by sea-level rise, climate change, sea-ice loss, and local interventions such as dredging, land reclamation, and estuarine engineering. These changes have implications for flood risk, ecological processes, tidal energy resource assessments, and ocean mixing and circulation. Within geodetic observations (e.g., GNSS, altimetry, gravimetry), tidal and storm-surge signatures are pervasive and encode diagnostics of a wide range of Earth system parameters, thereby making them accessible. On geological timescales, shifts in continental configuration, ocean bathymetry, and sea level have profoundly reshaped tidal dynamics, with cascading effects on circulation, mixing, and even evolutionary processes. This session welcomes contributions that use in situ observations, remote sensing, numerical and data-driven models, and geological/paleo-reconstructions to advance understanding of tide- and/or surge-driven processes, their broader implications for coastal, ocean, and Earth system dynamics, and applications to tidal energy, navigation, and beyond. We invite submissions spanning regional to global scales, past, present, and future perspectives, and settings ranging from estuaries and rivers to the open ocean and other planetary bodies.
title: Tides and Storm Surges

description: Managed agricultural ecosystems (grassland and cropland) are an important source and/or sink for greenhouse gases (GHG) as well as for reactive trace gases. Representative measurements and modelling under typical conditions as well as for potential mitigation options are necessary as a basis for recommendations to policy makers and farmers. Due to the simultaneous influence of various environmental drivers and management activities (e.g. fertilizer application, harvest, grazing) the flux patterns are often complex and difficult to attribute to individual drivers. Moreover, management related mitigation options may often result in trade-offs between different GHG or between emission of GHG and reactive gases like NH3, NOx, or VOCs. To investigate these interactions, the session addresses experimentalists and modelers working on carbon and nitrogen cycling processes and related fluxes on plot, field, landscape, and regional scale. It is open to a wide range of studies including the development and application of new devices, methods, and model approaches as well as field observations and process studies. Particularly welcome are studies on multiple gases and on the full carbon, nitrogen or GHG budgets. We also encourage contributions about the applicability and overall potential of mitigation options.
title: Exchange of GHG and reactive gases in agricultural ecosystems

description: The purpose of this session is to: - Showcase the state of the art in agent-based and other bottom-up modelling approaches of how natural hazards affect households and firms, from direct impacts to long-run recovery. - Advance the use of such models to assess impact on multiple dimensions, distributional consequences, and policy effectiveness - Stimulate exchange of models, data, calibration strategies, and identify priorities for making these models more empirically grounded, credible and useful for decision-making. Risk assessment for natural hazards has traditionally focused on direct impacts to physical assets. But disaster losses and recovery trajectories vary widely across households and firms and depend on their characteristics such as household income and savings or firm size. Moreover, at least part of the loss is also indirect and unfolds over time, through lost income, forgone care, business interruptions, and disrupted supply chains. These consequences emerge from the decisions of many interacting, adaptive agents (e.g., households, firms) and from the feedbacks between them. Agent-based models (ABMs) can represent this heterogeneity explicitly, together with adaptive behaviour and feedback loops, making them well suited to study the distributional, direct and indirect consequences of hazards. The same applies to the policies trying to mitigate losses: they do not act on the average household or a representative firm alone, and a measure that is effective in aggregate can be regressive for some or be improved upon by targeting specific subpopulations. However, how much such models can inform real decision-making depends on how well they are grounded in data, account for uncertainty and are validated. We invite contributions that develop, calibrate, validate or apply agent-based and other bottom-up models of disaster impacts on households and/or firms. Topics include: - Representations of household and firm decision-making, adaptation and post-disaster recovery, including behavioural and economic mechanisms. - Empirical grounding using household survey, census, administrative, firm-level, remote-sensing or post-disaster damage data. - Coupling with hazard and climate models, including multi-hazard, compound and repeated events. - Methodological advances: such as sensitivity analyses, comparison with other approaches and validation. - Conceptual contributions on what these models can and cannot do for risk assessment and policy design.
title: Simulating disaster impacts and recovery: households, firms and their interactions

description: Biodiversity loss and climate change amplify one another through coupled ecological and societal processes, yet their risks are still assessed and governed largely in parallel. The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, the Paris Agreement and the Sustainable Development Goals call for integrated action, but operational frameworks capable of connecting climate hazards, ecosystem condition, biodiversity responses, human vulnerability and governance capacity remain fragmented. This session advances a resilience-based science-policy agenda for aligning biodiversity goals with climate mitigation, adaptation and disaster risk reduction. We invite conceptual, methodological and empirical contributions that: (1) identify cascading, compound and cross-scale climate-biodiversity risks, thresholds and feedbacks; (2) develop integrated indicators and assessment frameworks linking biodiversity, ecosystem services, carbon, adaptation and equity; (3) combine Earth observation, in situ monitoring, environmental DNA, ecological and climate models, artificial intelligence, scenarios and uncertainty analysis; (4) evaluate synergies, trade-offs and maladaptation in nature-based solutions, ecosystem restoration, protected areas, renewable-energy transitions and land- and sea-use planning; and (5) examine governance arrangements, finance, stakeholder networks and monitoring, reporting and review systems that connect the Convention on Biological Diversity, the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change and related policy processes. Comparative studies and place-based evidence from terrestrial, freshwater, coastal, marine and urban socio-ecological systems are especially welcome, including work with Indigenous Peoples and local communities. By bringing together geoscientists, ecologists, social scientists, practitioners and policymakers, the session will distil transferable methods and context-sensitive pathways for ecological security and just, climate-resilient development.
title: Aligning Biodiversity Goals with Climate Resilience: Risk Governance, Integrated Assessment, and Global Evidence

description: Hydrology has a long history, with many of its concepts, methods and observations developing through a combination of scientific advances, practical needs and contributions from different research communities. Looking back at this history can help us understand how ideas in hydrology have developed, changed and sometimes been forgotten. This session invites contributions on the history of hydrological concepts, methods, observations and models, as well as on the people, institutions, projects and research communities that have shaped the discipline. We are particularly interested in examples where looking at the past can improve understanding of current hydrological practice, including historical data, approaches that have been abandoned or overlooked, traditional and indigenous knowledge, and lessons from past successes and failures. We also welcome contributions on how (traditional) hydrological knowledge is passed on and how it has supported sustainable water management across different cultures over long periods. How does research become established knowledge, and how does it eventually find its way into textbooks and teaching? A considerable gap often exists between scientific research and what becomes established textbook knowledge: findings that are already well established may take many years to enter teaching, while others may be simplified or interpreted differently as they are passed on. The session aims to bring together different perspectives on the history of hydrology and to discuss how understanding the development of the discipline can contribute to both current research and the education of future hydrologists.
title: History of Hydrology: The evolution and transmission of hydrological knowledge for sustainable development

description: Climate and ocean change are deeply interconnected, both as physical processes and as societal challenges. The ocean plays a fundamental role in the climate system, while anthropogenic climate change is altering ocean environments in profound and increasingly visible ways. Addressing these changes requires more than scientific knowledge: it also depends on how that knowledge is communicated, learned, interpreted and used across diverse societal contexts. This interdisciplinary session explores the intersections of climate and ocean science, communication, education, public engagement and ethics. It invites research and practice that examine how individuals, communities, institutions and decision-makers navigate and interpret climate and ocean science, and how effective communication, learning and engagement drive informed societal responses. We welcome contributions including empirical studies, theoretical and methodological approaches, case studies and evidence-informed practices addressing a broad range of issues, including but not limited to: • climate and ocean literacy, education, pedagogical approaches and curricula; • science communication, media, visualisation and storytelling; • public engagement and communication with policymakers, stakeholders and communities; • misinformation and disinformation, trust, risk perceptions and the communication of uncertainty; • evaluation of communication and educational processes, outcomes, limitations and unintended impacts; • geoethical perspectives, including climate justice, equity, responsibility and the societal roles of scientists, educators and communicators. By bringing together researchers, educators, communicators and practitioners, this session aims to advance our understanding of how knowledge about climate and ocean change is communicated, interpreted, negotiated and used across different institutions, communities and publics.
title: Climate and ocean change: Communication, learning and engagement

description: Science is deeply intertwined with societal and geopolitical issues. Geopolitical conditions affect the choices that we make about which research to fund, whose knowledge to value, where to collaborate and who can attend academic conferences. Geoscientists cannot ignore the human and environmental consequences that stem from their work, both direct and indirect, all the way from disaster risk management to war and conflicts. This geoethical challenge, for example, is urgent in Earth observation, where many satellites operate with dual-use capabilities for both scientific and military purposes. In many cases, scientific tools have enabled massive resource exploitation under neocolonial structures. Security discussions remain crucial during conflict, but securitisation raises real questions about the ethical, social and environmental aspects of scientific practice. This session invites presentations that address questions such as: - Should and how should geoscientists conduct research and sustain cooperation in geopolitically fragile or unstable regions? - How do geopolitical tensions or decisions influence geoscience research and cooperation, and what can geoscientists do about it? - In what ways do political decisions and borders influence geoscience research priorities and Earth system studies? - What responsibilities do scientists carry when their research tools or data are used to harm or kill people or ecosystems, inadvertently and on purpose? - What roles can and should academic institutions like geoscience university departments and the EGU play in supporting at-risk scholars and facilitating academic advocacy? - How do military funding and trade shape the direction and outcomes of geoscience research? - What role, if any, should academic activism play in fostering non-militarised research and prioritising human and environmental protection? - What strategies can geoscientists adopt to address geoethical dilemmas and resist complicity in violence? We welcome insight and case studies that show how geoscientific knowledge may prevent or escalate conflict, increase transparency regarding the impacts of war (such as InSAR monitoring of building damage) or intersect with resource extraction, forced migration and regional instability and war.
title: Geoscience research and collaboration in times of geopolitical crises

description: The rapidly changing cryosphere due to climate change is creating increasingly urgent adaptation and socio-economical challenges: sea level rise, mountain and glacier collapse, land subsidence, glacial lake outbursts, and impacts on ecosystems, sustainable energy production, livelihoods and cultural heritage. Recent events in mountain regions like Nepal, Tibet, Peru and Switzerland are showing us that rapidly melting glaciers, snow and permafrost are triggering catastrophic hazards directly threatening local communities safety, vital infrastructure, livelihoods, water security, and cultural heritage. Slow-onset events like sea-level rise are affecting communities that have little to no responsibility for such impacts. Yet, fragmented communication of both scientific knowledge and the urgency to act continues to expose important bottlenecks at the interface between science, policy and society. This session invites researchers, policymakers, government agencies, practitioners and other stakeholders working across these interfaces. We welcome examples of successful and unsuccessful engagement, alongside critical reflections on persistent gaps around cryosphere-related challenges. How can researchers engage effectively with decision-makers? What kind of knowledge or scientific input do policymakers or stakeholders need, and in what form? Where does available science fall short of what decisions require? Our aim is a space for mutual exchange and learning that builds capacity, communication and collaboration across the science-policy-society interface. We invite contributions from across all realms of the cryosphere—including glaciers, ice sheets, permafrost, sea ice, snow, lake and river ice—and encourage perspectives on challenging and emerging topics. These may include communicating concepts such as climate overshoot and tipping points and their implications for populations to non-expert audiences, the role, potential risks and framing of geoengineering and other intervention proposals in cryosphere policy debates, countering misinformation and rebuilding trust in science, and addressing how cryospheric research can better support adaptation, resilience and long-term planning.
title: Cryosphere policy, science and society: experiences, lessons and gaps from working across boundaries

description: Deep geological repositories (DGRs) remain the preferred option in many national programs for the long-term management of high-level radioactive waste (HLW). Their development requires studies of complex geological systems, processes over extended time scales, and assessments of uncertainties and safety. The results must then be translated into safety arguments and regulatory decisions that are transparent, robust, and understandable to the various stakeholders and to society. In this session, we are particularly interested in how the results obtained from site characterization, geological and numerical modeling, uncertainty analysis, and long-term safety assessment are evaluated and used in site selection, safety cases, and the licensing. We seek contributions that address how different national programs and regulatory systems handle geoscientific evidence and uncertainty; how responsibilities and interactions are organized among implementing agencies, regulatory authorities, policymakers, scientists, NGOs, local communities, affected populations, and the general public; and how transparency, participation, communication, and differing perceptions of risk influence these processes. Ethical and legal aspects of decisions with very long-term / intergenerational consequences are also welcome. Comparative perspectives and lessons learned from various national disposal programs are particularly encouraged. DGRs remain the central theme of the session. However, we also welcome transferable lessons from other subsurface activities, including geological carbon storage, geothermal energy, and methane storage. By bringing these perspectives together, the session aims to better understand how geoscientific evidence can support technically sound, transparent, and societally legitimate decisions for the long-term disposal of radioactive waste.
title: From Geoscientific Evidence to Societal Decisions: Risk, Regulation and Governance for Deep Geological Repositories

description: UNESCO Global Geoparks (UGGps) are territories with significant geodiversity, used to promote geoconservation, geoeducation and geotourism. Over 250 UGGPS around the world are engaged in developing different strategies of communication, adapting it to local cultures and realities. This Session aims to bring together the presentation of best practices related to public engagement with geoscience and geoheritage within the framework of UGGPs. Looking at this diversity will contribute to improving our of Geoscience Communication and Outreach skills.
title: Geoparks as living laboratories for geoscience education and public engagement

description: Whether you thrill at the chance to tell taxi drivers and dinner-table companions about your research or want to hide every time someone asks, “What do you do?”, we offer an exciting and entertaining science communications challenge for you. Inspired by the XKCD comic that describes the Saturn V Rocket using only the thousand most common words in English (http://xkcd.com/1133/), we ask speakers to present short (~5-minute) scientific talks using this basic set of vocabulary, determined via the Up-Goer Five Text Editor: http://splasho.com/upgoer5. The talk is preferably about your own research but can also be about a general topic you are interested in. Why should you contribute to this session? The section below is written using the Up-Goer Five Text Editor: When you change the words to explain what you do, you: - Find what is at the heart of your work, - can now tell ANYONE what you study, because you can make things as simple as they can be, even if that is hard at first, - show that it matters to you that everyone can really understand what you do. In addition, this session allows you to submit a second abstract. So you can use it to reach out to a wider audience or show additional work, gain experience in presenting, and train your outreach skills in the process. For some inspiration, check out the abstracts from last year's session: https://meetingorganizer.copernicus.org/EGU26/session/57008 or some videos from AGU: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lxWrerZhfrk. Join us for an interesting and fun session and learn about your and others' research in new and beautifully simple ways!
title: Up-Goer Five Challenge: Making Big Ideas Simpler by Talking About Them in Words We Use a Lot

description: There are many ways to involve the public in geoscience beyond talks, posters and traditional outreach. Museums, research projects and science centres are increasingly experimenting with interactive exhibitions, games, virtual and augmented reality, hands-on activities and citizen science. These approaches can make processes that are difficult to see or understand more tangible, and can give people a more active role in exploring geoscience and the research behind it. In this session, we would like to bring together people who are developing or using these kinds of approaches. We welcome contributions on interactive exhibitions and installations, digital and immersive experiences, citizen science projects, games, hands-on activities and other forms of public participation in geoscience. Contributions can focus on finished projects, work in progress, or simply on what was learned during development and testing. We are also interested in the practical side: What works with different audiences? How do you involve stakeholders in developing an activity? How do you balance scientific content with an engaging experience? And how do you know whether an activity actually works? Examples that did not work as expected, or that changed substantially after testing with users, are just as valuable. The aim of the session is to exchange ideas and experiences between geoscientists, educators, science communicators, museum professionals and developers, and to learn from approaches that have already been tried in different settings. We hope it will also provide a place to find potential connections between projects working on similar forms of public engagement and citizen science.
title: Beyond the screen: Interactive public engagement and citizen science in the geosciences

description: Science communication is a valuable component of scientific research, policymaking and public engagement - involving natural, physical, and social scientists, communications professionals, and teams who communicate the processes and values of science to non-specialist audiences both within and outside of formal educational settings. The goals of science communication can include enhanced dialogue, understanding, awareness, enthusiasm, influencing sustainable behaviour change, improving decision making, and/or community building. Methods of facilitating science communication can include in-person interaction, online activities through social media, web or app-based activities, press, podcasts or radio, video, and many more. In this session, we invite practitioners and developers of science communication activities / initiatives to explore their processes and learnings on themes like: - What kind of science communication efforts are you engaging in and how have you developed, iterated and implemented them? - What are the biggest challenges or successes you’ve had in engaging non-specialist public with science and how have you evaluated these? - How can geosciences learn from other disciplines (such as social sciences) about understanding audiences, developing communication and engagement strategies, conducting evaluation or understanding the impact of activities? - What are lessons learned from long-term, impactful, or innovative science communication efforts? - What have been your experiences with communicating science with emotion, purpose, and values to better connect with your intended audience? This session invites you to share your learnings and join a community of practice to inform and advance the effective communication of earth and space science. We value contributions across the wide range of science communication activities possible, and all levels of experience - including new, pioneering, innovative and early career contributions- are encouraged to take part.
title: Science and Society: Science Communication Practice, Research, and Reflection

description: As the urgency for climate action increases, so does the need for a climate-literate global population — able to understand how the climate system works, how human actions affect it, and how climate change impacts people and ecosystems, and to combine this knowledge with evidence-based reasoning and systems thinking, with the capacity to evaluate evidence, information and perspectives, and with the agency to shape sustainable futures, individually and collectively. This is frequently summarised as fostering concern and hope. In this session we will explore how scientists can work with educators and communicators to counter mis- and disinformation, develop critical thinking, and support teachers and others to deliver high-quality climate education. This might be through social media, face-to-face or virtual events, engagement with high-level policy or strategy, or research and publications. We invite individuals and teams to share good practice, insights and reflections on science communication and education practice and research, including: • What interventions or collaborations have been tried, or are being developed, to bring scientists, educators and communicators together? • What are good measures of the impact of interventions on the climate literacy of individuals, groups or communities? • How can scientists become good educators and/or communicators, or form productive partnerships with them? • How to achieve the right balance between ‘concern’ (understanding the causes and impacts of anthropogenic climate change) and ‘hope’ and/or agency?
title: Fostering concern and hope in climate communication and education for youth and the public

description: This session explores innovative digital and non-digital approaches to hazard and risk education and communication, with particular attention to how they can connect research, policy and practice. It considers hazards and risks arising from natural and human-induced processes, and how innovative methods can strengthen understanding, support evidence-informed decision-making and translate knowledge into action. Effective education and communication are central to building resilience, yet traditional methods can struggle to engage diverse audiences, connect scientific knowledge with practice or influence policy. Digital tools—including serious games, massive open online courses (MOOCs), simulations, and immersive virtual and augmented reality—can bring hazard scenarios to life and enable learners, communities, practitioners and policymakers to explore uncertainty, cascading consequences, response options and trade-offs. Non-digital methods, including role-play, participatory mapping, scenario workshops, classroom activities and tabletop exercises, can support deliberation, mutual learning, preparedness and policy. We welcome abstracts exploring the development, application and evaluation of these innovations across contexts ranging from primary to postgraduate education, professional training, policy and implementation. Contributions addressing co-production with communities, policymakers, public authorities and practitioners are particularly encouraged, alongside work examining inclusivity, transferability and outcomes such as learning, engagement, decision-making, policy uptake and institutional change. By bringing together researchers, educators, policymakers and practitioners, the session will share best practice, showcase cutting-edge tools and methods, and critically reflect on their contribution to hazard and risk education, decision making and practice. A PICO format will combine concise presentations with poster-based interaction and lively cross-sector discussion.
title: Innovative Approaches to Hazard and Risk Education and Communication: Connecting Research, Policy and Practice

description: The session aims at collecting relevant experiences on geoheritage in its in situ and ex situ dimensions, that is, geological sites, heritage stones, and geological collections. Experiences should be about geological sites as places that have contributed significant values to society, scientific knowledge, or culture on a national or international level; heritage stones as geological materials that have been significant additions to architecture, engineering, sculpture and cultural heritage; geological collections from museums, universities, and geological survey repositories that have outstanding scientific, historical, and educational value. Aspects of interest include geoheritage conservation, legislation, management, digital inventory, and outreach, including the use of analogs for planetary and space geology. The session is organised by the International Commission on Geoheritage established by the International Union of Geological Sciences (IUGS), working in collaboration with the International Geoscience Program of UNESCO.
title: Geoheritage: conservation, legislation, management, inventory, and outreach of significant geological assets.

description: Scientific conferences are an important part of scientific infrastructure. Their design and organization influence whom we meet, which research we discover, how early-career scientists can engage with established researchers, and ultimately how knowledge is shared within our community. The EGU General Assembly has evolved over the years, introducing new presentation formats, digital tools, hybrid participation, and increasingly diverse opportunities for scientific interaction. However, the scale of the meeting creates challenges and raises questions about how the conference experience could be improved. For instance: -What lessons can be drawn from other conferences and experimental formats? -How could the overall programme structure be optimized to reduce fragmentation and overlaps? -How might navigation and orientation throughout the conference be improved? -Can participants be encouraged to engage with research beyond their immediate scientific fields and foster interdisciplinary collaboration? -How can we better support “opportunistic” participation, where attendees spontaneously join sessions, and what implications would this have for scheduling, signage, and session design? -How can different presentation formats be better balanced, and which alternative formats could foster deeper scientific discussion? -How could poster sessions be organized to better support interaction and exchange? Could alternative organization, structure, and timing be explored? -How can networking and informal exchange be supported, especially for early-career participants? -How can the conference support inclusivity and accessibility for a diverse community, including hybrid participants? -How can participant feedback be integrated into future changes? We invite contributions from across the EGU community, including quantitative analyses, surveys, experiments, comparisons with other conferences, experience reports, prototypes, and unconventional ideas. We particularly encourage contributions that go beyond identifying problems and instead propose or evaluate possible solutions. The session aims to create a space for structured discussion among participants, going beyond a traditional sequence of presentations, and to collect concrete proposals emerging from the community. We believe that our collective experience of the EGU General Assembly provides a valuable basis for exploring how future meetings can foster better scientific exchange, discovery, and collaboration.
title: Rethinking the EGU: How Can We Design a Better General Assembly?

description: Environmental research is increasingly expected and needed to produce societal impact, i.e. “an effect on, change or benefit to the economy, society, culture, public policy or services, health, the environment or quality of life, beyond academia” (Reed, 2018). However, a persistent gap remains between research outputs and societal needs, controlled by strongly disciplinary education and the research-driven supply of new knowledge and services. Thus, the realization of the research impact potential (whether, how, and for what purposes) by relevant stakeholders remains uncertain. We propose bridging this science-societal impact gap through two broad pathways. First, we need inter- and trans-disciplinary training and capacity-building in geosciences, but also among professionals; this pivotal need is further emphasized in current research funding instruments. Addressing complex environmental challenges requires diverse competencies and transferable skills. Higher education and life-long/wide learning are critical approaches in closing the gap, often referred to as universities' “third mission” (Secundo et al., 2017). Second, we need development and better adoption of stakeholder- and demand-driven research practices throughout the research process, from co-design and co-production of research projects towards output communication and implementation tailoring. This includes closer collaboration both with the public sector and with the private sector stakeholders. The demand-driven approach includes mapping of stakeholder needs and ongoing management processes, and co-creation of research outputs with stakeholders. This session welcomes empirical and conceptual contributions along the broad two societal impact strands: 1. Societally impactful education and capacity-building in geosciences 2. Societally impactful research practices We invite contributions covering all aspects of bridging the science-societal impact gap in geosciences, across the transition from case studies to theoretical and conceptual works. The session will facilitate exchange, learning, and networking around interdisciplinarity, collaboration, and impact pathways. The targeted output of our session will be one or a set of articles synthesizing the identified academic approaches and pathways to bridge the research-societal impact gap.
title: Mind the gap: from research to societal impact

description: The future of scientific publishing has become one of the defining questions facing modern science. Rising publication costs, increasing dependence on commercial publishing infrastructures, the rapid expansion of AI-assisted workflows, and growing concerns about research assessment have all prompted fundamental questions about who scientific publishing should ultimately serve. The EGU26 Great Debate on scientific publishing highlighted both the urgency of these discussions and the diversity of opinions across the geoscience community. Yet one important perspective remains comparatively underexplored: the collective responsibility of researchers themselves in shaping the publishing ecosystem. While discussions on scientific publishing often focus on publishers, business models, or policy reforms, researchers themselves remain central actors in shaping the scholarly communication ecosystem. Through their choices as authors, reviewers, editors, committee members, and society members, scientists collectively determine the future of publishing. Publishing is not an external service provided to science: it is an integral part of scientific practice. Every day, researchers make decisions as authors, reviewers, editors, hiring committee members, grant reviewers, society members, and institutional leaders. These choices influence which journals thrive, how scientific quality is assessed, what incentives early-career researchers receive, and ultimately what kind of publishing landscape future generations of researchers will inherit. This session invites contributions exploring how researchers can actively shape scholarly communication. We welcome contributions exploring four interconnected dimensions of scholarly communication: community governance, research quality and trust, incentives and assessment and emerging challenges. We particularly encourage contributions that document successes and failures of publishing initiatives, evaluate publishing policies, assess researcher incentives, or present evidence-based approaches for reforming scholarly communication. The session aims to bring together researchers from all career stages, particularly early-career researchers, journal editors, publishers, librarians, funders, scientific societies, and research institutions to discuss how publishing can better support open, rigorous, equitable, and sustainable practices in geoscience.
title: Beyond Publish or Perish: Scientific Publishing as a Community Responsibility

description: Environmental issues are not only ecological but also societal and cultural. To address them effectively, we need to understand how human societies interact with the environment. This session highlights the importance of social science in environmental research and vice versa, and invites contributions that explore how interdisciplinary collaboration can lead to innovative and sustainable solutions. We welcome scientists from all disciplines of environmental and social sciences, data analysts, methodologists, and metadata experts to share their insights, case studies, and challenges. We aim to foster meaningful discussions and exchange of ideas across academic groups, research infrastructures, the private sector, and policy makers. By integrating the expertise of social scientists with environmental research, we can develop a more comprehensive and holistic understanding of environmental problems leading to pathways for viable climate action plans and supporting policies. Let's work together to contribute to a more sustainable relationship between people and the environment. Topics may include, but are not limited to: – Climate action plans and solutions for green and sustainable cities – Cultural heritage and environmental sustainability – Environmental policy and governance – Air quality and climate indicators – Sustainable agriculture and land use – Biodiversity conservation and ecosystem services – Climate adaptation and resilience – Development of resilient communities through disaster risk reduction – Citizen and participatory science and public engagement – Best practice methodologies for specific use cases – Metadata standards for integration of data from different research domains – Project reports or infrastructure requirements related to multidisciplinary use cases
title: Merging Social Science and Environmental Studies

description: Ten years after the Paris Agreement, global climate action has bent the curve of projected warming, but a temporary overshoot of 1.5°C is now unavoidable. Even full implementation of all announced NDCs, long-term strategies and net-zero pledges falls well short of what's needed, and global emissions continue to rise. This session looks to explore how we can achieve the lowest temperature outcome feasible in 2100, as well as the timing of net-zero greenhouse gas emissions globally, in line with the requirements of the Paris Agreement and Article 4.1. We do this through three angles: where we stand, where we are headed, and how to get back on track. First, where the world stands. The latest climate science is essential to understand the actions necessary to minimize the extent and duration of overshoot. Here we welcome submissions that quantify the latest science around anthropogenic emissions and warming, or that assess changes in the Earth system with implications for overshoot such as updates to climate sensitivity or tipping point dynamics. At the same time, continued development and technological progress is potentially opening up new opportunities (and challenges) for mitigation pathways, looking across developments in electro-tech, innovative new technologies, and AI. We welcome submissions which capture these latest developments and explore how they could impact on mitigation pathways. Second, where the world is heading under current policies and targets. We welcome submissions that quantify our current emissions and energy system trajectories and assess the implications of this for global temperatures and associated impacts. Third, where we need to go: what it will take to limit the magnitude and duration of any eventual overshoot. Here we welcome submissions that cover the pace and shape of decarbonization pathways able to limit peak warming and bring temperatures back down after mid-century, through multiple interlinked levers including fossil fuel phase-out; electrification of buildings, transport and industry; methane abatement and other short-lived climate pollutants (SLCPs); and scaling up carbon dioxide removal. We are particularly interested in assessing the feasibility of different options, and aim to interrogate the actions that can most plausibly limit the magnitude and duration of overshoot. Each of these levers is examined at global, regional and sectoral resolution.
title: Rescuing 1.5°C: Where We Stand, Where We're Headed, and the Lowest Feasible Path Forward

description: The energy transition is reshaping the geography of resources, production, infrastructure and trade. Growing demand for critical raw materials is creating new centres of extraction and processing; clean-technology manufacturing is concentrating in some regions while expanding into others; and new energy and transport infrastructures are changing how technologies, materials and energy move across regions. These shifts are unfolding alongside geopolitical fragmentation, industrial policy, environmental constraints and growing concern over the resilience of global value chains. This session invites research on the changing spatial and material foundations of the energy transition. We welcome contributions that: examine critical raw materials, resource availability, extraction and processing; investigate clean-technology manufacturing, innovation, deployment and shifting centres of production; analyse renewable-energy, electricity, hydrogen, transport and other infrastructure associated with the transition; study trade, logistics, supply-chain networks and changing patterns of global interdependence; explore recycling, substitution, material efficiency and circularity; examine how geopolitics, industrial policy, finance and strategies for diversification or domestic production reshape transition pathways; and investigate how environmental burdens, economic opportunities, vulnerabilities and benefits are distributed across producing and consuming regions, workers and communities. We particularly encourage studies that connect physical and technological change across these domains: how resource endowments influence industrial development; how manufacturing and infrastructure choices create new dependencies; how trade and policy reshape the location of production; and how strategies for resilience, security and circularity alter outcomes across regions. By bringing together perspectives from geoscience, energy systems, industrial ecology, economics, geography and the social sciences, the session aims to build a more integrated understanding of how the geography of the energy transition is evolving, and what those changes imply for resilient, sustainable and equitable transition pathways.
title: Energy transitions in a fragmented world: Resources, technologies, infrastructure and value chains

description: Artificial intelligence (AI) is currently transforming data analysis and modelling of the Earth system. While statistical and data-driven models have been used for a long time, recent advances now allow for encoding non-linear, spatio-temporal relationships robustly without sacrificing interpretability. This has the potential to accelerate climate science by providing new physics-based modelling approaches; improving our understanding of the underlying processes; reducing and better quantifying climate signals, variability, and uncertainty; and even making predictions directly from observations across different spatio-temporal scales. We encourage participants to discuss the limitations of AI methods (including their often substantial training-data requirements, susceptibility to data leakage, poor generalisation, and physical inconsistencies) to help ensure that these methods are applied where they are fit for purpose and add value. This session aims to provide a venue to present the latest progress in the use of AI applied to all aspects of climate science and we welcome abstracts focussed on, but not limited to: - Causal discovery and inference: causal impact assessment, interventions, counterfactual analysis - Learning processes, equations, and feature representations across models and observations - Hybrid physics-AI and differentiable models, climate model emulators, data-model integration - AI-based detection and attribution approaches, including for extreme events - Probabilistic modelling and uncertainty quantification - AI-based climate downscaling, including super-resolution and bias-correction - Climate model analysis in the AI era, including benchmarking and stress-testing - Explainable AI applications to climate data science and climate modelling - Distributional robustness and transfer learning, including out-of-distribution generalisation tasks - AI reasoning and agent-based workflows for analysing climate data, developing, improving, testing, and porting scientific code, and climate information
title: AI for Climate Science

description: This session highlights emerging technologies and strategies for measuring and monitoring bedload sediment transport in river systems. It welcomes contributions on particle tracking (RFID tracers, ‘smart’ pebbles, etc.), acoustic and seismic sensing, distributed monitoring networks, data integration techniques, and real-time observations, with a particular emphasis on improving process understanding and supporting river management applications.
title: Innovations in bedload sediment transport monitoring

description: Active mountain belts are among the most dynamic components of the Earth system, where tectonic deformation, climate variability, weathering and sediment transport interact to shape landscapes over timescales ranging from individual, episodic extreme event to millions of years. Understanding how mountain landscapes respond to these interacting forcings is fundamental for reconstructing their evolution and anticipating their response to future environmental and climatic change. Recent advances in remote sensing, geochronology, climate models, landscape evolution numerical methods and machine learning tools, provide new opportunities to quantify surface processes across multiple spatial and temporal scales. While modern observations enable investigation of ongoing erosion, sediment transport and landscape adjustment to extreme events, Quaternary sedimentary archives such as fluvial terraces, paleoflood records and river-dammed lakes provide important windows into past environmental conditions. Integrating these records with process-based and data-driven models of landscape changes offers a pathway towards revealing dynamics over geological time and predicting how active mountain landscapes may evolve under changing climate scenarios. This session invites novel contributions that investigate the evolution, functioning and future trajectories of landscape in active mountain belts. Studies depicting and/or quantifying mass movements, sediment routing, landscape evolution process under different climatic conditions and future scenario are encouraged.
title: Surface processes in active mountain belts: past dynamics to future trajectories.

description: Ever since, channel control structures and soil conservation techniques have been fundamental to managing catchment dynamics and regulating water resources and forest and agricultural activities. Yet despite their established role, important scientific gaps persist around how these interventions influence sediment dynamics and the natural processes they are meant to control. Further work is needed on: i) how to plan effectiveness and suitable interventions; ii) interaction between sediment connectivity and interventions; iii) quantification of the effectiveness of actions as a function of their desired purposes; iv) suitable criteria for designing restoration projects. Remote sensing techniques (RS) can support the lack of long-term monitoring studies to assess the evolution of catchment morphology and analyse past and current phenomena by exploiting multi-temporal surveys at different scales and open-source big data. This session offers a platform for collaboration and discussion among soil scientists, hydrologists, geomorphologists, foresters, and stakeholders, facilitating a dialogue on critical issues about planning, design, and management of channel control structures and soil conservation techniques at the catchment scale. Research about the following topics is welcome: i) novel guidelines and protocols for intervention planning; ii) RS-based methods for tracking sediment dynamics over multi-temporal or real-time monitoring; iii) standardized frameworks for assessing how interventions reshape sediment connectivity in catchments; iv) forward-looking challenges, such as bioengineering solutions and the use of living vegetation within check dam design. The session especially welcomes contributions from early-career researchers presenting original and methodologically advanced work.
title: From sediment dynamics to watershed management: the role of control works and conservation practices

description: Rapid advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) are transforming scientific research. Although geoscience foundation models are still emerging, it is already clear that their development depends on access to large volumes of data. At the same time, the reliability and trustworthiness of AI systems depend on understanding the quality, provenance, timeliness, and governance of the data they are built on. As the saying goes: garbage in, garbage out. Over the past two decades, the Open Science principle of “as open as possible, as closed as necessary” has encouraged greater transparency and accessibility across the scientific process. However, the rise of AI raises new questions about how to apply this principle in an era of large-scale data aggregation and automated knowledge extraction. Who benefits from AI systems built on openly shared scientific data? Are our data, metadata, and repositories AI-ready? Can existing research infrastructures support the demands that AI agents may place on them? How can provenance, attribution, licensing, and data-governance principles (particularly Indigenous) be preserved when scientific outputs become inputs for AI models? This session invites researchers, data stewards, repository operators, infrastructure providers, and AI practitioners to discuss the opportunities and challenges that AI presents for Open Science. Contributions are encouraged on AI readiness, data quality and provenance, repository sustainability, attribution and reward mechanisms, governance frameworks, and emerging tensions between the goals of scientific openness and the development of AI systems. Together, we will explore how the scientific community can uphold the values of Open Science while adapting to a rapidly evolving AI landscape.
title: Open Science in the Age of AI: Opportunities and Barriers

description: In-situ observations are essential for understanding and monitoring the Earth system and supporting decision-making. At the same time, the in-situ data landscape is evolving, with new technologies and methods emerging, including low-cost sensors, Internet of Things (IoT), citizen science or drones. However, integrating these heterogeneous observations remains challenging due to differences in data sources, formats, quality and standards, making them difficult to discover, access and use, while relevant data gaps remain. This session aims to focus on innovative in-situ observation approaches and their integration with existing observing networks and research infrastructures. Contributions on topics as data quality, interoperability, FAIR practices and metadata management, automated processing and aggregation, as well as approaches for defining user observational requirements and identifying the variables to be measured, are particularly encouraged. Examples of integrating in-situ observations with remote sensing satellite data, modelling and other geospatial information are also of particular interest. By bringing together researchers and data users, observing networks, data managers, and open science enthusiasts, the session will highlight how emerging observing methods and open data sharing practices can address data gaps, strengthen existing data infrastructures, and contribute to more sustainable and fit-for-purpose in-situ Earth observation system.
title: Best practices and emerging approaches for in-situ Earth observation data sharing and management in open science

description: Geological mapping and modelling are fundamental pillars of the geosciences, providing the basis for understanding Earth and planetary systems. This session brings together contributions that span the full spectrum of geological mapping and modelling, including fieldwork, methodologies, tools, and case-studies. The session covers the range from traditional field-based methods to cutting-edge approaches, including AI, applied in the most extreme and inaccessible environments on Earth and beyond. We invite scientists working on: • Geological field mapping and cross-boundary harmonization • Mapping of extreme environments such as marine areas, polar regions, deserts, volcanic terrains, high-mountain ranges, and planetary surfaces • 3D geological modelling in any geological context • Development of geomodelling methodologies and tools • Application of AI methods to geological mapping and modelling • Development of geological information systems • Remote sensing, geophysical techniques, drilling, sampling, and specialized tools for inaccessible terrains for geological mapping and modelling The session aims to be highly transdisciplinary, bridging geology, geophysics, geochemistry, mineralogy, hydrogeology, engineering geology, and planetary sciences. By integrating approaches across diverse contexts, from accessible outcrops to remote and hostile terrains, participants will explore common challenges in data acquisition, interpretation, 3D modelling, visualization, and knowledge synthesis. Outcomes are expected to benefit a wide range of applications and research, including geothermal energy exploration, offshore wind energy, geological risk assessment, groundwater protection, coastal protection, habitat mapping, environmental impact assessment, marine protected area development, mineral and resource exploration, and planetary missions. Ultimately, this session seeks to foster dialogue between communities tackling mapping and modelling challenges in both familiar and extreme environments, to advance scientific understanding and practical applications across the geosciences.
title: Geological Mapping and Modelling: From Traditional approaches to Extreme Frontiers

description: Urban sustainability is shaped by complex and dynamic interactions between environmental processes and human activities. These coupled human–environment interactions influence urban climate, land-use change, ecosystem services, carbon emissions, resource consumption, mobility, environmental exposure, inequality, and resilience. Recent advances in Earth observation, geospatial big data, in-situ and crowdsourced sensing, cloud computing, machine learning, and artificial intelligence provide unprecedented opportunities to observe, model and predict these interactions across spatial and temporal scales. This session invites contributions that use new observations, integrated datasets, data-driven analytics, and AI-based approaches to advance the understanding of urban human–environment systems. We particularly welcome studies addressing multi-source urban data integration, machine learning and GeoAI, urban climate and heat, land-use change, urban ecosystems, carbon emissions, mobility, environmental exposure, inequality, vulnerability, resilience, open datasets, benchmarks, uncertainty assessment, explainable AI, and reproducible workflows. The session aims to foster interdisciplinary exchange among remote sensing, geospatial science, urban studies, environmental science, climate science, and data science communities. We encourage contributions from local to global scales, especially those demonstrating how new data and analytics can reveal interactions between people and urban environments and support more sustainable and resilient urban futures.
title: Data-Driven Understanding of Urban Human–Environment Interactions: Earth Observation, GeoAI and Urban Sustainability

description: Multi-modal machine learning models for atmospheric and Earth system dynamics that are trained on many different datasets and predict a range of outputs, such as the WeatherGenerator, ESFM, or WeatherNext, are emerging as the next frontier in machine learning-based Earth system modeling. These models pose unique challenges, such as how to combine many input datasets at different resolutions in space and time, how different datasets should be scheduled at different training stages, or what data should be used as target during pre-training and what can be decoded afterwards. They also open research questions such as how model parameter count should depend on the number and resolution of input datasets or how to quantify the expected benefit of adding an additional dataset. This session collects contributions both on the development of multi-modal machine learning models as well as their use in applications, from short- and medium-range forecasting to scientific investigations that probe the model itself. Submissions can address either methodological questions, evaluations (e.g. conservation of physics), technical aspects (training on HPC systems) or focus on applications.
title: Multi-modal Machine Learning Models for Earth System Modeling

description: The increasing complexity and resource intensity of state-of-the-art Earth System Science (ESS), from Earth System Model simulations to large-scale data processing and analysis, require advanced approaches to orchestrate, automate, document and reproduce scientific processes.
