Scientific workflows provide a fundamental means to manage this complexity and to enable scalable and reproducible research across increasingly complex computational and data infrastructures. Researchers in ESS are faced with heterogeneous computing architectures, federated research infrastructures, distributed and increasingly large datasets and restrictive data-movement policies. Workflows thus have to operate across systems while making efficient use of available computational and data resources. Portability, interoperability and provenance therefore become essential characteristics of scientific workflows rather than optional additions. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) introduce an additional dimension. AI can support the composition, optimization and execution of scientific workflows. Emerging agentic approaches may increasingly enable workflows to adapt autonomously to data, computational environments and scientific tasks. Such capabilities also raise new questions: How can scientific intent, assumptions, dependencies and execution environments be represented in AI generated workflows? How can AI-assisted and agentic workflows remain transparent, verifiable and reproducible? How can their decisions and adaptations be captured through appropriate provenance and metadata? This session explores advances in scientific workflow concepts, technologies and applications for ESS, ranging from established workflow management approaches to emerging AI-assisted and agentic systems. We particularly welcome contributions addressing workflow orchestration and portability, scalable HPC and data-intensive workflows, distributed, federated and hybrid infrastructures, data locality and efficient resource utilisation, workflow FAIRnes, and AI-assisted generation, adaptation, optimization and execution of scientific workflows. We encourage contributions presenting methods, tools, lessons learned and concrete use cases from ESS, including European and international research infrastructures and initiatives. Contributions demonstrating both mature solutions and emerging approaches that explore emerging capabilities of scientific workflow technologies are particularly welcome.
title: Scientific Workflows for Scalable, Reproducible and AI-Enabled Earth System Science

description: Making data Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable (FAIR) is now widely recognised as essential to advance open and reproducible research. Increasingly, this requires not only shared principles but also concrete digital implementations that enable interoperability across systems, disciplines, and infrastructures. However, it is very difficult to translate these principles into practical data management guidelines or operational digital solutions across disciplines. The goal of the session is to explore how best data management practices are developed, implemented, and adopted across disciplines, including through interoperable digital objects, persistent identifiers, and emerging data space concepts. As part of this session, we invite submissions that: 1) Share good or bad experiences developing, implementing, and adopting data practices that align with both FAIR principles and the evolving needs of specific research communities. 2) Propose strategies for engaging researchers in adopting and refining best practices, with a focus on community-driven approaches to technical standards and infrastructures. 3) Explore the role of cultural change in enabling adoption of sustainable data practices. 4) Highlight efforts that harmonise data formats and workflows across disciplines while respecting domain-specific requirements, for example through interoperable data architectures or research data spaces. 5) Present technical or conceptual approaches that support the transition from data silos to interoperable, FAIR-aligned data ecosystems. This session is aligned with the objectives of the Research Data Alliance (RDA) Earth, Space, and Environmental Sciences (ESES) Data Community of Practice and aims to foster cross-disciplinary dialogue, particularly among researchers in hydrology, seismology, and ocean sciences. However, we welcome contributions from all disciplines, especially where they provide insights or novel approaches to community engagement. By learning from diverse experiences, this session seeks to advance collective understanding of how to build and sustain data practices that are both FAIR and fit for purpose, from community processes to concrete, interoperable digital implementations.
title: From Principles to Practice: Community-Driven Approaches to FAIR, Open Data and Interoperable FAIR Digital Objects in Earth and Environmental Sciences

description: Spatio-temporal datasets are constantly growing in size, due to increases in extent and resolution. Because of this, existing software to read, write, and store data, and translate the data may not be able to perform the work in a timely manner anymore. This limits the potential of numerical simulation models and machine learning models, for example. In this session we bring together researchers working on novel software for processing large spatio-temporal datasets. By presenting their work to their colleagues we aim to further strengthen the field of high-performance computation in the geosciences. We invite everybody recognizing the problem and working on ways to solve it to submit an abstract to this session. Topics of interest for this sessions are, for example, related to: - High-performance computing, parallel computing, distributed computing, cloud computing, asynchronous computing, accelerated computing, green computing - Algorithms, libraries, frameworks - Parallel I/O, data models, data formats, data compression, data cubes, HDF5, NetCDF, Zarr, COG - Containerization, Docker, Kubernetes, Singularity, Apptainer - Physically based modelling, physics informed machine learning, surrogate modelling - Model coupling, model workflow management - Large scale hydrology, remote sensing, climate modelling - Lessons learned from case-studies We recommend authors to highlight the generic aspects of their work that may be especially of interest to their colleagues.
title: High-performance computation in the geoscience

description: The FAIR principles are key to reusing Earth system data for analytics and AI. A primary challenge for reuse is judging a dataset's fitness for purpose, which depends on its representational, relational, contextual, and error characteristics, aspects not necessarily captured by traditional curation and documentation. As machine learning and AI become central to Earth system modeling and prediction, unintentional misuse becomes a critical hazard: data unfit for training models or their components can lead to downstream societal harm. The session covers observations, simulations, reanalyses, and synthetic data. Training, fine-tuning, evaluation, data assimilation, downscaling, bias correction, and attribution each impose distinct data requirements, and provenance of these processes helps trace how data characteristics and uncertainties propagate to results. A key question is how to tell users and automated processes whether a dataset supports the intended use. Topics include: - Metadata standards and documentation of intended and unsupported uses and dataset limitations - Assessment methods combining metadata-derived indicators, content checks, lineage, validation, and domain expertise, and the limits of each - Purpose-specific assessment of resolution, coverage, representativeness (extremes, transferability across regions, periods, and observing systems), physical consistency, and uncertainty - Time, financial, and energy costs of assessing and improving fitness, how they are distributed, and the consequences of unsuitable reuse Some reuse challenges can be addressed through curation or supplementary information; others require alternative data or narrower scientific claims. Contributors are encouraged to state the intended use, present assessment evidence, and describe resulting decisions and their effects on conclusions. Comparative studies, negative results, and post-mortems with transferable lessons are particularly welcome, including assessments that find a dataset unsuitable. Contributions may address single assessment steps or complete data-to-discovery workflows. The session convenes data producers, repositories, research infrastructures, AI practitioners, and domain scientists to identify shared assessment practices that avoid redundant effort and to clarify when scientific judgment is essential. Its focus is how data properties and assessment evidence support or constrain scientific claims.
title: From FAIR to Fit for Purpose: Assessing Earth System Data for AI-Enabled Science

description: Geospatial foundation models (GeoFMs) are enabling increasingly large-scale applications across Earth observation and the geosciences. Leveraging advances in representation learning, GeoAI, and the growing volume of satellite observations available for pre-training, recent models transfer knowledge across regions, sensors, spatial and temporal scales, and downstream tasks. Since the previous EGU session on remote sensing geospatial foundation models (ESSI1.11), research in model development and applications has expanded, with models increasingly evaluated across diverse regions and Earth science disciplines. This session focuses on large-scale, satellite-based foundation models built from image-based Earth observation modalities, including multispectral, optical, synthetic aperture radar (SAR), hyperspectral, and related remote sensing data. We distinguish this scope from foundation models primarily developed for climate and weather data, numerical weather prediction, or atmospheric modelling. Our focus is on models that learn generalizable representations from large-scale Earth observation imagery and their applications to mapping, monitoring, and understanding Earth’s surface. We aim to investigate challenges shaping the scientific and practical impact of these models, including transferability across regions and datasets, real-world downstream performance, scaling with data and computational resources, and the uncertainty, interpretability, and reliability of foundation-model predictions. We invite contributions covering, but not limited to: * New geospatial foundation models * Novel pre-training and representation-learning strategies * Large-scale datasets and benchmarks * Multimodal and multisensor learning * Model evaluation and transferability * Geospatial embeddings as data * Applications of GeoFMs to Earth observation and Earth science Relevant applications include: * Natural and anthropogenic disaster mapping and monitoring * Crop and agricultural monitoring * Natural ecosystem monitoring * Forest and biodiversity monitoring * Built environment mapping and monitoring * Environmental monitoring and Earth system science The session brings together researchers developing GeoFMs and applying them to scientific and societal challenges, with the aim of identifying emerging opportunities, methodological gaps, and future directions for large-scale Earth observation foundation models.
title: Geospatial Foundation Models for Earth Observation and Earth Sciences: From Foundations to Applications

description: Cloud computing now underlies most industrial and academic work, making it well-suited for processing big data close to its source. Combined with HPC, cloud infrastructure, enhanced by GPUs, containerization, and microservices, they increasingly supports AI/ML workloads once limited to HPC environments. Quantum computing is also emerging as a complementary tool, with hybrid quantum-classical methods showing promise for optimisation, simulation, and machine learning in Earth system science. Session Focus This session focuses on use cases involving the entire computing spectrum, from Cloud to HPC and to emerging Quantum computing, to o assess current progress and identify steps for wider adoption of these resources in Earth Observation and Earth Modeling. Contributions are welcomed across the following areas: • Big Data Infrastructures and Platforms: Case studies, techniques, models, and algorithms for data processing on the cloud and HPC. • Cloud Federations, Interoperability, and Sustainability: Scalability and interoperability across domains, multi-provenance data management, security, privacy, and green/sustainable computing practices. • Cloud-Native and HPC AI/ML Frameworks: Tools and frameworks for processing data using AI and ML on the cloud and/or HPC, including operational deployment and data lake/warehouse management. • Convergence of Cloud Computing and HPC: Workload unification and hybrid architectures for Earth Observation (EO) data processing across cloud and HPC environments. • Quantum Computing Algorithms for Earth Science: Quantum and quantum-inspired algorithms for optimisation, simulation, and data analysis in EO and Earth system modeling. • Hybrid Quantum-Classical and Quantum-HPC Architectures: Integration of quantum processing units (QPUs) with classical HPC and cloud infrastructures, including workflow orchestration and resource scheduling. • Quantum Machine Learning: Quantum-enhanced ML techniques for remote sensing, climate, and geospatial data processing. • Benchmarking, Access, and Readiness for Quantum Resources: Evaluating quantum hardware/simulators, cloud-based quantum access models, and assessing technology readiness for operational Earth science applications. We encourage researchers, practitioners, and industry experts to share their insights, case studies, and innovative solutions that promote the integration of cloud computing, HPC, and quantum computing in Earth Observation and Earth Modeling.
title: Enabling Seamless Workflows Across Cloud, HPC, and Quantum Computing for Earth Observation and Modeling

description: Africa’s biodiversity and ecosystems are central to the continent's green transition, yet effective conservation strategies rely heavily on the availability of accurate, accessible, and interoperable environmental data. While emerging initiatives, such as the Africa Regional Centers of Excellence Programme (ArcX), are establishing critical reference points for biodiversity data, significant technical and systemic challenges remain in harmonizing fragmented datasets across borders. This session addresses the intersection of open science, spatial data harmonization, and cloud-based environmental computing applied to African landscapes. We aim to showcase innovative technological solutions and collaborative frameworks that bridge the gap between data scarcity and actionable ecological insights. We welcome contributions from researchers, data scientists, and practitioners focusing on, but not limited to: • The development, deployment, and scaling of open-source architectures and Spatial Data Infrastructures (SDIs) tailored to African contexts. • Novel Earth Observation (EO) applications and machine learning workflows for feature extraction and biodiversity monitoring in data-scarce regions. • Strategies, standards, and case studies for cross-regional data harmonization (e.g., integrating data across Central, Western, and Eastern Africa). • Successful capacity-building frameworks, FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data practices, and cross-border partnerships that enable open environmental data sharing. By bringing together geospatial informatics and spatial ecology, this session aims to foster interdisciplinary dialogue on building robust data ecosystems that empower sustainable ecosystem management across Africa.
title: Open Science and Interoperable Geospatial Data for African Ecosystems

description: The Earth’s Critical Zone (CZ) is the “heterogeneous, near surface environment in which complex interactions involving rock, soil, water, air, and living organisms regulate the natural habitat and determine the availability of life-sustaining resources”. Understanding this heterogeneity requires integrating highly diverse datasets across space, time, formats, and domains. However, dealing with the extreme data fragmentation in environmental Earth sciences remains a major challenge. This session highlights the implementation of FAIR geospatial methodologies to accelerate data assimilation, predictive modelling, and the generation of actionable Earth Intelligence regarding Critical Zone behaviour. We welcome contributions showing technical workflows, digital infrastructures, and methodologies designed to break down domain silos. These should address the seamless integration of in-situ monitoring networks with multi-sensor remote sensing (RS) data products, focusing on: • Format harmonization strategies bridging disparate spatial-temporal models and interdisciplinary data sources. • The application of standard APIs (e.g., OGC standards, openEO) for scalable data access. • Modern, distributed metadata catalogues enhancing data discoverability. • Semantic harmonization efforts, including domain ontologies and controlled vocabularies to eliminate ambiguity across disciplines (e.g., Essential Variables (EVs) across the hydrosphere, biosphere, atmosphere, and geosphere). • The use of geospatial data pipelines for Analysis Ready Data (ARD) and AI-ready data to streamline machine learning workflows. • Advanced AI modelling (e.g., physics-informed neural networks, deep learning) to extract scalable CZ Earth Intelligence. • The alignment of CZ science with large-scale initiatives, such as Digital Twins (DestinE) and the Common European Data Spaces (e.g., Green Deal Data Space). This session aims to foster an interoperable, open-science ecosystem that transforms fragmented observations into scalable Earth Intelligence and actionable insights for modelling and managing our living planet.
title: FAIR-compliant Geospatial Methodologies to advance the understanding of the Critical Zone

description: Artificial intelligence is rapidly transforming the Earth and environmental sciences, yet the effectiveness and reliability of AI depend fundamentally on the quality, interoperability, semantics, provenance, and machine-actionability of the underlying data. While FAIR principles have substantially advanced scientific data stewardship, emerging GeoAI, foundation models, multimodal AI, and agentic systems require research data infrastructures that move beyond data accessibility toward AI readiness. This session brings together the geoscience, data science, research infrastructure, and semantic-web communities to explore how FAIR and interoperable data ecosystems can support trustworthy AI-enabled scientific discovery. We particularly welcome work addressing semantic interoperability, FAIR Digital Objects, knowledge graphs, machine-actionable metadata, controlled vocabularies and ontologies, provenance, AI-ready data standards, and emerging frameworks such as CDIF, Croissant, Semantic Croissant, and GeoCroissant. We invite methodological developments, infrastructures, standards, demonstrators, and applications involving Earth observation, climate and environmental data, geospatial information, urban digital twins, sensor networks, social and human-generated data, and other heterogeneous scientific resources. The session aims to connect data stewardship and interoperability communities with researchers developing the next generation of AI-enabled Earth and environmental science, and to identify practical pathways toward open, interoperable, trustworthy, and AI-ready scientific ecosystems.
title: AI-Ready Geoscience: FAIR Data, Semantic Interoperability and Intelligent Research Infrastructures

description: Two consecutive EGU sessions have demonstrated how the convergence of time-series aerial and satellite remote sensing, geospatial technologies, and artificial intelligence is transforming our ability to detect, monitor, and understand environmental change. Applications have ranged from local studies of agricultural systems and natural resources to large-scale analyses leveraging foundation-model embeddings derived from tens of millions of Earth observation scenes. As these capabilities mature, the next challenge is operational: translating scientific advances into decision-ready products and services that support action by hazard managers, conservation organizations, agricultural and water authorities, resource managers, and communities. This third session in the Connected Earth series invites contributions that apply time-series Earth observation, geospatial technologies, and machine learning and AI to address environmental challenges across scales, from local sites to global systems. We welcome contributions using optical, SAR, and other remotely sensed data acquired from aerial and satellite platforms, as well as integrated geospatial workflows that connect Earth observation insights to real-world decisions. Topics of interest include, but are not limited to: • Operational and near-real-time monitoring systems based on cloud-native Earth observation platforms and GIS-integrated workflows. • Multi-decadal environmental monitoring and approaches for maintaining consistency across evolving sensor generations. • AI and machine learning methods, including foundation-model embeddings, for environmental analysis, classification, prediction, and change detection. • Open, reproducible, and interoperable geospatial workflows that improve transparency and collaboration. • Applications supporting hazard monitoring, natural resource management, agriculture, water resources, conservation, cryosphere research, climate adaptation, and environmental resilience. The session welcomes both methodological and applied contributions from academia, government, industry, and community-based organizations. By bringing together advances in Earth observation, AI, and geospatial technologies, Connected Earth III aims to highlight pathways that move beyond proof-of-concept research toward scalable, operational solutions that support informed environmental decision-making.
title: Connected Earth III: Time-Series Remote Sensing, AI, and Geospatial Technologies for Global Decision-Making

description: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs), Natural Language Processing (NLP), multimodal AI, and AI agents are rapidly changing geosciences research. These technologies offer new opportunities for knowledge discovery, data analysis, evidence synthesis, and real-time monitoring. At the same time, the rapid growth of digital archives, from scientific literature and news articles to social media and historical documents or photographs, offers opportunities to explore new data sources in geosciences research. This session examines how geoscientists are using LLMs, NLP, AI agents and text-as-data approaches across hydrology, climate, natural hazards, and the broader earth system sciences research fields. We invite contributions that develop or apply such methods to extract, organize, and interpret information from unstructured data sources; address methodological challenges such as uncertainty, bias, and validation; or integrate text and image mining approaches into geoscientific workflows. We particularly welcome submissions on topics including, but not limited to: - Text and image-based analysis of geoscientific data, e.g. assessment of natural hazard impacts and real-time disaster monitoring. - Chatbots and AI agents in geosciences - Evidence synthesis and literature mapping - Public sentiment and perception analysis - Policy tracking and narrative analysis - Social media analyses - Enhancement of metadata and data descriptions - AI agents for automated or semi-automated geoscientific workflows - Integration of LLMs with remote sensing or image data - Methodological challenges in using LLMs and NLP-based analyses, including bias, reproducibility, and interpretability By sharing case studies, technical developments, and lessons learned, we aim to promote the effective use of these tools while also highlighting the challenges that newcomers may encounter, including issues with data coverage, quality control, and reproducibility concerns. By sharing best practices, this session aims to inspire collaboration and innovation in harnessing LLMs, NLP, and text-as-data in geosciences.
title: Natural Language Processing and Large Language Models in Geosciences, Natural Hazards and Hydrology

description: Effective analysis of modern geospatial big data requires more than the application of existing ML tools; it requires the development of new strategies that account for the characteristics of spatial and temporal data and processes. This session highlights advances in the methodological foundations of geospatial AI, focusing on the proposal and development of new methods, tools, and strategies to improve prediction, interpretation, and uncertainty assessment. This session discusses challenges and advances in spatial and spatio-temporal machine learning methods and the software and infrastructures to support them. Application-based studies are also welcome, particularly those that demonstrate the practical utility of new tools or methodological approaches. By focusing on the development of methods, this session aims to bridge the gap between theoretical AI advances and practical geoscientific challenges.
title: Methodological Innovations in Spatial and Spatio-Temporal Machine Learning and AI

description: Currently geological collections, including the institutions and professionals curating them, face growing operational and financial threats. Several University Earth Science Departments and scientific Institution face merging with other disciplines or closure and their historical collections are at risk of destruction. Museums and other institutions are struggling with financial resources and space. Yet, in an era dominated by modelling and big data, the strategic, scientific, and educational value of geo-collections is frequently unrecognized. While there is the need to preserve important and, in some cases, unique collections of specimens, historical photographs, field documents, geological maps and scientific instruments, there is an urgent need to discuss how to collect for the future and what it is the best way to use both existing and future collections. This session provides a platform to showcase the scientific, educational, and societal value of physical and digital sample repositories. We invite contributions demonstrating how collections drive the advance of geological research. In this context, “collections” encompasses repositories managed by museums, universities, volcano observatories etc. We welcome submissions exploring case studies using physical or digital sample repositories for research, innovative methodologies for enhancing FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) data principles and Open Science, interdisciplinary applications of geo-collections, best practices for physical preservation, archiving and conservation, funding strategies, community engagement and lessons learned. We aim to bring together curators and researchers to foster international collaboration, advocate for institutional support, and promote the active use of geo-scientific collections.
title: The Role of Geo-Collections for advancing Research in Earth Sciences

description: Data sovereignty has several scales. We can refer to the sovereignty of individual data producers. We can also refer to sovereignty in a community that works together in a data space. We can scale the issue to sovereignty of some territories that they are investing in a digital economy and they do not want benefits to leak to other territories. Among the different interpretations, there is also the sovereignty of scientists that want to secure their reputation by ensuring acknowledgment and recognition. Scientifics data sovereignty faces three main challenges: (1) the scientific community is globalised, and while scientists may suspect some issues surrounding lack of sovereignty, it is often perceived as a constraint on their autonomy and freedom to choose the most efficient tools and workflows; (2) there is no specific European directive for data sovereignty. Instead, a collection of policies was approved in different moments in time lacking a consistent framework; and (3) scientists are not familiar with the tools and technologies used to implement data sovereignty at different restriction levels. While several efforts have been recently focusing on restricted data (e.g. EU Data Spaces), this session focuses on the open science spirit of “as open as possible, as closed as necessary” under Horizon Europe and other funding programs, but reinterprets it from the perspective of data sovereignty. This session will focus on why data sovereignty is important for Europeans, how scientists are currently addressing this issue and how we can ensure data sovereignty in Europe. Some possible topics to address in the session are acceptability of data to specific communities, governance of the data and interoperability of data and technologies. Papers participating in the session will collaborate to propose changes in practices in the scientific community; balancing open science and data sovereignty to maximize impact on society. We are interested in understanding how you perceive the outcomes of restricting global open science with sovereignty safeguards. In particular we would like hear your thoughts and fears on why sovereignty is necessary and the barriers it can create for operating European Research Infrastructures.
title: Technologies for data sovereignty on open science and the impact on European society

description: Digital Twins of the Earth system are emerging as an approach for combining Earth observations, modelling, high-performance computing, data-driven methods and interactive simulation to better represent environmental processes and their interactions across spatial and temporal scales. Initiatives such as Destination Earth (DestinE), together with national, European, and international Digital Twin developments, provide new opportunities to explore how these capabilities can contribute to understanding and reducing disaster risk. This session invites contributions examining how Earth-system and environmental Digital Twins, and the data, models and technologies underpinning them, can contribute to disaster risk reduction (DRR). The focus extends from improving the representation and understanding of hazards and their interactions to assess exposure, vulnerability and impacts, exploring risk scenarios, and supporting preparedness, early warning and risk-reduction decisions. We welcome contributions addressing single, compound, cascading and multi-hazard risks, including floods, droughts, heatwaves, wildfires, storms, landslides and other geophysical, climate- and weather-related hazards. Relevant topics include the integration of Earth observations and environmental data; coupling of Earth-system, hazard and impact models; high-resolution and multi-scale simulations; representation of exposure and vulnerability; scenario and what-if analysis; impact-based forecasting and early warning; and the translation of complex simulations into risk-relevant information. The session also welcomes research on the role of artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) in Digital Twin workflows, including data integration, emulation and surrogate modelling, pattern and anomaly detection, hazard and impact modelling, and the extraction of risk-relevant information from large simulations and datasets. Contributions addressing uncertainty, validation, interpretability, interoperability and computational challenges are particularly encouraged. We invite both methodological developments and case studies that critically assess the added value and limitations of Digital Twins for DRR, including their potential use by civil protection authorities, public administrations, infrastructure operators and other risk-management communities. Contributions from Destination Earth and other European and international Digital Twin initiatives are welcome.
title: Digital Twins of the Earth System for Disaster Risk Reduction: From Risk Understanding to Decision Support

description: Environmental science, scientists and developers increasingly use or build Artificial Intelligence in tools, Digital Twins and models, but are concerned about trust, transparency and digital sovereignty when supporting Open Science practices. AI-ready research assets and VRE's are crucial enablers. Fair Digital Objects (FDO)'s become the technical backbone that makes AI trustworthy enough to use. Agentic search is the clearest case for this: an agent querying across catalogues can only return trustworthy results if the underlying objects carry typed metadata, provenance and clear licensing. Research Infrastructures, providing the standards for FDO's and trustworthy data are at the center of these developments and have a responsibility to do a risk and value assessment before any AI tool is adopted, model cards, transparency, and shared European compute rather than dependence on commercial cloud providers. Virtual Research Environments (VRE) and workflow builders provided by Research Infrastructures need to take these requirements into account and provide solutions that are machine actionable while at the same time are trustworthy for any AI application. We envision Virtual Research Environments (VREs) that are not only machine-actionable but also deeply trustworthy, designed to integrate AI assistance while upholding FAIR principles, digital sovereignty, and Open Science standards. These VREs should empower scientists to safely explore AI-driven opportunities -whether in data sharing, integration, or analysis- with full confidence in the tools, data, and workflows provided. By embedding provenance, interoperability, and ethical AI practices, we can ensure that VREs become catalysts for collaborative, reproducible, and impactful environmental research. This session aims to bring together practitioners, developers and stakeholders to discuss the technical challenges and share practices with the aim to contribute to the emerging ENVRI & Data Terra/EOSC nodes. abstracts can focus on (but are not limited to): - Describing concepts, principles, visions and challenges underlying the use and implementation of AI-readyness in environmental research and data management - Demonstrating tools and applications, research assets that take these requirements into account and at the same time revolutionise the possibilities of data sharing, integration and analysis - Presenting challenges, lessons learned and achievements in AI enhanced environmental and earth science
title: Machine and AI actionable FAIR Digital Objects enabled VRE's, for Environmental and Earth Science

description: Recent advances in large language models have enabled agentic systems that autonomously plan, reason, and act on problems in Earth Observation (EO) and the geosciences. By interacting with data catalogues, models, processing services, and computational environments, these systems move beyond generating answers to constructing and executing multi-step scientific workflows. This shift raises fundamental questions about how such systems can be designed to be not only capable, but also grounded, verifiable, reproducible, and trustworthy. This session invites contributions on the design, integration, evaluation, and responsible deployment of agentic AI across EO and the geosciences. We welcome work on how agents reason over long-horizon tasks, interact reliably with heterogeneous data and computational infrastructure, and maintain coherent state, context, and provenance across multiple steps. Topics include agent architectures and orchestration, multi-agent systems, memory and self-evolving mechanisms, as well as protocols and shared conventions that enable agents to discover, communicate with, and use scientific tools and services. A central focus is the evaluation and verification of agentic scientific reasoning: not only final answers, but also the trajectories through which agents reach them, including tool selection, planning, code execution, intermediate results, and provenance. Contributions addressing uncertainty, hallucination, and failure modes are particularly encouraged, as are approaches that promote physical consistency through domain knowledge, foundation models, retrieval, world models, and physics-aware constraints. Work on human oversight, intervention, and verification is also relevant, particularly for autonomous systems deployed in operational or high-consequence settings. More broadly, the session aims to advance agentic AI as a paradigm for computational Earth Observation and the geosciences. By bringing together AI researchers, geoscientists, and providers of scientific data and computational infrastructure, we seek to characterize the capabilities and limitations of agentic systems, develop principled methods for evaluating and improving them, and establish what is required for autonomous scientific workflows to operate reliably and reproducibly.
title: Towards trustworthy Agentic AI for Earth Observation and the geosciences

description: Every day, research vessels collect continuous data underway, improving our understanding of the state of the ocean. Most importantly, they reveal how the marine environment is changing. These underway data streams together with stationary data are fundamental to global ocean observations. They support applications of societal significance that influence our everyday life, most prominently weather forecasts. However, workflows and digital infrastructures remain mostly standalone solutions scattered across institutions and countries. Unifying the work is essential, however there is often a lack of attention for addressing the issue in detail. Often the focus spreads across broader topics (sessions) where its unique challenges and solutions often remain unseen. Standardization of data workflows can help to optimize data output of research cruises around the world. The German Marine Research Alliance (DAM) brought together a consortium of data experts from several German research institutions, universities and federal agencies. Since 2019, DAM has been developing an integrated framework to enhance the acquisition, transportation, processing and publication of data and metadata from German research vessels, particularly from permanently installed systems, to enable subsequent reuse. The extension and connection of research data infrastructures and existing modular workflows is used by a team of data stewards to combine sensor streams, automated quality‑control routines aiming for standardized data products and open data services. Early results show clear gains in consistency, reproducibility and accessibility leading to higher visibility and accelerated usage of acquired data from German research vessels. This session brings these stories together. By gathering other national and international initiatives in one place, this session aims to build a shared space for a global community. Since similar efforts are emerging in Europe and worldwide this session shall support meaningful exchange and future global collaboration. We welcome submissions that share the overall vision of disseminating data globally. We invite contributions that advance shipboard data workflows, real‑time and delayed‑mode automation, interoperable observing infrastructures and FAIR data practices. We welcome innovative quality‑control methods, scalable data pipelines, and end‑to‑end sensor‑to‑archive solutions that strengthen transparency and cross‑platform compatibility.
title: Advancing FAIR compliant data management workflows of marine research platforms: Scalable stories from acquisition towards data dissemination

description: The rapid growth of missions, observatories, and monitoring systems across the heliosphere and Solar System, together with surface-based and airborne facilities, has created an unprecedented volume and diversity of data. Making sense of these observations requires methods that can efficiently process large datasets while extracting meaningful physical insight. Machine learning has become an important tool in this effort, complementing established physics-based approaches by offering new ways to identify patterns, develop predictive models, and work with complex or incomplete measurements. In recent years, increasing attention has been given to hybrid approaches that combine machine learning with physical models. These methods are now being applied across planetary science and heliophysics, from forecasting solar eruptions and solar wind conditions to automating the analysis of planetary surfaces and improving on-board data processing. They demonstrate how data-driven methods can benefit from physical knowledge, while physics-based models can in turn be enhanced through modern data analysis techniques. This session aims to provide an inclusive and interdisciplinary forum for researchers applying machine learning in planetary science and heliophysics, as well as for those developing methods at the interface between data-driven and physics-based approaches. We particularly encourage contributions that demonstrate the wide range of possible applications, foster exchange across disciplines, and showcase the transition of new methods from research to operations.
title: Machine Learning in Planetary Sciences and Heliophysics

description: The Solar Orbiter mission, an international cooperation between ESA and NASA, is currently orbiting the Sun with an orbital inclination of 17° (24° from December 2026 onwards) at heliocentric distances between 0.95 to 0.29 au, providing a new perspective of the Sun’s polar regions. As the mission continues towards its max. inclination of ~33° in June 2029, it is an exciting time to study dynamics within the solar atmosphere and the inner-heliosphere from this unique perspective. The overall goal of Solar Orbiter is to understand how the Sun creates and controls its atmosphere and the heliosphere. The mission provides unprecedented imaging of the Sun’s photosphere, chromosphere, and corona, enabling studies of the origin and evolution of the Sun’s atmosphere, the solar wind, flares, solar eruptions, and energetic particle events. The combination of high-resolution imaging and simultaneous in-situ measurements from Solar Orbiter’s inner-heliospheric vantage point offers a unique opportunity to link solar sources directly to their heliospheric impacts. This session invites contributions that address the Solar Orbiter science objectives, exploit multi-mission data sets, and studies involving the dynamic solar atmosphere to the inner-heliosphere. We also welcome Solar Orbiter-related contributions in the fields of theory and numerical simulations that contribute to a better understanding of the solar origins of heliospheric variability and space weather.
title: Solar Orbiter: From the Dynamic Solar Atmosphere to Heliospheric Variability

description: Cosmic rays provide an important probe of particle acceleration and transport processes throughout the heliosphere. They include solar energetic particles (SEPs), accelerated during solar eruptive events, and galactic cosmic rays (GCRs), which originate outside the heliosphere and are modulated by heliospheric conditions. Their variability reflects the complex interplay between energetic particles and solar and heliospheric activity across a wide range of spatial and temporal scales. This session will focus on the acceleration, transport, modulation, and variability of cosmic rays in the heliosphere, including, but not limited to, SEPs, Forbush decreases, anisotropic cosmic ray enhancements (ACREs), and longer-term variations in GCR fluxes. We invite contributions addressing observations, modelling, data analysis, and the phenomenology of cosmic rays in the heliosphere, as well as their connections to solar and heliospheric dynamics. We particularly encourage contributions that employ or combine multi-spacecraft and ground-based observations, numerical and theoretical models, novel data-analysis techniques, and forecasting approaches, as well as studies that connect measurements across different spatial and temporal scales and regions of the heliosphere.
title: Cosmic Rays in the Heliosphere

description: The subsurface is increasingly recognized as a finite, shared and strategic space in which multiple, often competing uses must coexist over long time horizons. Energy storage and production, carbon dioxide removal, groundwater supply, underground infrastructure, and the storage or disposal of waste all rely on carefully a managed subsurface resource. How these uses interact has become a critical question for sustainable development. This challenge is particularly acute in urban regions, where pressures from climate change, growing energy demand, environmental pollution, and social transformation converge. Densely populated cities are hotspots of resource consumption and vulnerability, but also key sites of innovation where resilient, low-carbon and just futures can be actively co-designed. At the same time, urban growth increasingly depends on subsurface resources located beyond city boundaries that support cities through the provision of energy and water, as well as through the removal of waste. Understanding urban resilience and transformation therefore requires an integrated view of surface and subsurface systems across urban and extra-urban spaces, and across spatial and temporal scales. Yet, the role of surface and subsurface geo-processes within broader socio-technical and socio-ecological dynamics remains underexplored. Addressing this gap is essential for ensuring that subsurface resources are used in ways that are environmentally sustainable, socially just and mindful of future needs. We invite contributions addressing these aspects and research gaps supportive of ways that are environmentally sustainable, socially just and mindful of future needs and aim to increase the connectivity between the partially isolated science domains.
title: Multi-uses of the subsurface and meeting environmental pressures in urban areas - challenges and opportunities on the way to a sustainable future

description: The heliosphere is permeated by several species of suprathermal and energetic particles (protons, electrons, heavy ions), exhibiting a diverse range of energy spectra and originating at different heliospheric and interstellar locations. Such energetic particles are of paramount importance to address many unconstrained aspects of energy conversion in astrophysical systems, as well as being impactful to society as they can pose a hazard to both human activities and technological systems in space. Suprathermal particles, in particular, are a key population that bridges the low-energy (1 keV in the heliosphere) plasma and high-energy (> 1 MeV) population, often treated independently. The dynamics of suprathermal and energetic particles in the heliosphere encompass various processes, from the acceleration of solar wind electrons/ions to solar energetic particle events related to solar eruptive phenomena. Despite decades of research, several aspects of suprathermal and energetic particle production remain unknown, with the main candidate production mechanisms being magnetic reconnection, collisionless shocks and several categories of wave-particle interactions. How suprathermal and energetic particles are transported through the heliosphere is also object of active debate, and largely unconstrained. Recent missions, such as Solar Orbiter and Parker Solar Probe, have delivered excellent observations from the inner heliosphere, both remotely and in situ. When combined with data from missions like ACE, SOHO, Wind, and STEREO at 1 AU, these observations across varying radial distances offer an unprecedented opportunity to characterize the sources and transport mechanisms of suprathermal and energetic particles in the heliosphere. This session invites contributions that explore space-borne and ground-based observations, as well as theoretical and modelling approaches, to deepen our understanding of the acceleration and transport of suprathermal and energetic particles in the heliosphere. We encourage submissions that provide new insights, propose innovative methodologies, or synthesize data across multiple missions to address these critical scientific challenges.
title: Acceleration and Transport of Suprathermal and Energetic Particles in the Heliosphere

description: This session traditionally provides a forum for the discussion of all aspects of solar and heliospheric physics. Popular topics have included solar cycle dependencies of the Sun, solar wind and heliosphere, Coronal Mass Ejection research, studies of energetic particles throughout the heliosphere, and the outer boundaries of the heliosphere. We encourage contributions related to all ongoing and planned space missions, to ground-based experiments and to theoretical research. Papers presenting ideas for future space missions and experiments are very welcome in this session. The session will consist of both oral and poster presentations.
title: Open Session on the Sun and Heliosphere

description: Coronal mass ejections (CMEs) can be listed amongst the most extreme manifestations of the Sun’s dynamic activity and are prominent drivers of space weather disturbances at Earth as well as other solar system bodies. Over the past few decades, remarkable advances through remote-sensing and in-situ measurements combined with analytical and MHD modeling have been made, but many fundamental questions remain regarding CME formation and eruption mechanisms, early coronal evolution, 3D interplanetary configuration, and interactions with the structured solar wind and other transients. As Solar Cycle 25 progresses beyond its maximum phase and towards the minimum, it is time to reassess our current understanding and identify promising directions for advancing CME observations, analysis, modeling, and forecasting capabilities. This session encourages contributions that advance CME science across a wide range of approaches, taking advantage of the wealth of currently available observational data and models. We welcome presentations employing remote-sensing and/or in-situ observations, multi-spacecraft studies, modeling efforts focusing on CME eruption and/or propagation, and mission concepts that can significantly advance fundamental research while addressing remaining observational and knowledge gaps. Particular emphasis will be given to contributions employing novel theories, measurements, and techniques.
title: Observing and modelling coronal mass ejections from the Sun to the heliosphere

description: The solar corona is the birthplace of the magnetic activity that drives the heliosphere, from flares, coronal mass ejections, and jets to waves, turbulence, and radio emissions. These processes govern coronal heating, solar wind acceleration, and the acceleration and transport of energetic particles, ultimately shaping the space weather environment throughout the heliosphere. Yet understanding their underlying physical mechanisms remains one of the fundamental challenges in heliophysics. Over the past decade, observations from Parker Solar Probe, Solar Orbiter, PROBA-3, PUNCH, Aditya-L1, DKIST, BBSO, and complementary space- and ground-based observations have transformed our view of the near-Sun environment. Combined with advances in theory and numerical modeling, these observations have revealed the interplay of magnetic reconnection, waves, turbulence, shocks, and fine-scale plasma structuring, substantially narrowing the range of viable physical mechanisms. This session will assess how far these advances have brought us toward resolving the long-standing problems of coronal heating, solar wind acceleration, and energetic particle acceleration and transport, while identifying the key observational, theoretical, and modeling challenges that remain. We particularly welcome contributions addressing: • Which physical processes now appear to dominate coronal heating, and what evidence is still needed to distinguish among competing mechanisms? • How have recent observations reshaped our understanding of solar wind acceleration, and what key questions remain? • What progress has been made in understanding the acceleration and transport of energetic particles, and what is required to achieve predictive capability? • How can coordinated observations and advanced modeling bridge scales from the solar atmosphere to the heliosphere? We welcome contributions spanning observations, theory, and modeling, particularly those leveraging recent results from Parker Solar Probe, Solar Orbiter, PROBA-3, PUNCH, Aditya-L1, DKIST, and coordinated multi-mission investigations.
title: Coronal Heating, Solar Wind Acceleration, and Energetic Particle Acceleration and Transport: Progress Toward Closure

description: The heliosphere represents a cornerstone astrophysical laboratory where fundamental plasma processes can be investigated in situ. Understanding the origins of heliospheric variability, the mechanisms responsible for particle acceleration and particle transport, and the coupling between the solar wind and the local interstellar medium remains central to both heliophysics and astrophysics. With its recent deployment to the Earth-Sun L1 point, NASA’s Interstellar Mapping and Acceleration Probe (IMAP) has begun delivering a new generation of observations aimed at understanding energetic particle acceleration, heliospheric structure, and the interaction between the heliosphere and the local interstellar medium. IMAP’s suite of a interstellar neutral atom detectors, for the first time, bridges the neutral atom intensity spectrum over nearly five orders of magnitude in energy, enabling unprecedented analysis of the heliospheric interaction with the local interstellar medium. Through its dedicated dust instrumentation, IMAP offers new insight into the composition, origin, and transport of interplanetary and interstellar dust grains. When combined with other spacecraft at L1, IMAP’s in situ measurements provide unique opportunities for coordinated studies of the mesoscale structure of the ambient solar wind, shocks, energetic particle events, and solar transients. This session welcomes contributions spanning heliophysics and astrophysics, including theory, numerical modelling, and analyses of observations from current and past missions. Topics of interest include particle acceleration and particle transport from 1 au to the heliopause, the sampling and characterization of interstellar material, heliospheric boundary dynamics, and the coupling between the Sun, heliosphere, and local interstellar medium. We particularly encourage presentations featuring the first scientific results from IMAP, synergistic investigations leveraging the L1 constellation and broader heliophysics fleet, and new insights into the structure and evolution of the heliosphere across multiple spatial and temporal scales.
title: The First Year of NASA’s Interstellar Mapping and Acceleration Probe: Connecting the Inner and Outer Heliosphere through Unified Observations

description: Space and astrophysical plasmas are typically in a turbulent state, exhibiting strong fluctuations of various quantities over a broad range of scales. These fluctuations are non-linearly coupled, and this coupling leads to the transfer of energy (and other quantities, such as cross helicity and magnetic helicity) from large to small scales and to dissipation. Turbulent processes are relevant for the heating of the solar wind and the corona, and the acceleration of energetic particles. In these environments, many aspects of turbulence are not well understood, in particular, the injection and onset of the cascade, the cascade itself, the dissipation mechanisms, as well as the role of coherent structures and waves. Specific phenomena such as magnetic reconnection, shock waves, solar wind expansion, plasma instabilities, wave activity and their relationship with the turbulent cascade and kinetic dissipation processes are under debate. The session will explore these open questions through observational, theoretical, numerical, and laboratory studies, aiming to advance our understanding of these processes. For observational studies, we welcome contributions utilizing data from a wide range of relevant space missions, including single-spacecraft WIND, STEREO, Van Allen Probes, and DSCOVR, with particular emphasis on recent findings from Solar Orbiter and Parker Solar Probe, and multi-spacecraft Cluster, MMS, THEMIS. We also particularly welcome studies preparing for the science and analysis of the upcoming HelioSwarm and Plasma Observatory missions.
title: Turbulence in Space Plasmas: Structures, Waves, and Dissipation

description: Radio waves are ubiquitous in the heliosphere. Sources range from thermal emission due to the quiet Sun, radio bursts emitted by accelerated electrons from transient solar eruptions, planetary magnetospheres, and spacecraft and extra-solar sources whose signals propagate through the heliosphere. Together, these radio emissions provide powerful diagnostics of the Sun and the heliospheric environment. This session is devoted to the fundamental processes underlying radio-wave generation and propagation, and the broad range of heliospheric diagnostics enabled by radio emissions from GHz to kHz, whether of solar or extra-solar origin. We welcome contributions on a range of radio-focused topics, including gyrosynchrotron emission from the solar atmosphere, excitation of Langmuir waves and the resulting radio-wave production, as well as radio-wave generation in laboratory plasmas. We also encourage contributions that exploit radio observations to diagnose solar and heliospheric conditions, including investigations of density turbulence, magnetic fields, particle acceleration regions, and radio-wave propagation effects. Contributions related to space-weather applications, studies that combine observations and simulations, advances in radio instrumentation, and multi-wavelength, multi-instrument, multi-vantage point investigations are particularly welcome.
title: Radio waves in the heliosphere

description: Collisionless shocks are ubiquitous in the universe, occurring in diverse astrophysical environments, from planets to galaxy clusters. Significant efforts have been made to understand their rich dynamics and their effects on the surrounding environment, including particle thermalization and acceleration, turbulence generation, and the evolution of various transient phenomena. Heliospheric shocks offer the unique advantage of being directly accessible by in situ measurements. Missions, such as Solar Orbiter, STEREO, and Parker Solar Probe, have deepened our knowledge of interplanetary shocks and the associated regions, while MMS, Cluster, THEMIS, Cassini, Maven, and others have similarly enhanced our knowledge of planetary bow shocks. High-performance computing has also played a critical role in filling key knowledge gaps, enabling global and local simulations to provide insights into the nature of collisionless shocks. Despite these efforts, many questions remain open. In particular, we still do not fully understand the mechanisms associated with certain aspects of particle heating and acceleration, wave generation, wave-particle interaction, and energy redistribution at shocks. The interplay of collisionless shocks and pre-existing plasma turbulence also remains poorly understood. Additionally, details about the formation and impact of transient structures, such as hot flow anomalies, foreshock bubbles, cavitons, spontaneous hot flow anomalies, magnetosheath jets, etc., are still unknown. We thus welcome observational, numerical, and theoretical works that explore plasma processes at collisionless shocks and surrounding regions.
title: Collisionless shocks and associated transient phenomena at Earth and beyond

description: Understanding how the solar wind is formed, accelerated, and transported through the heliosphere remains central to advancing both heliophysics and space weather forecasting. Measurements from recent missions such as Parker Solar Probe, Solar Orbiter, Proba-3, PUNCH and BepiColombo have been opening up new paths to unexplored regions of near-Sun space and provided unprecedented perspectives on solar wind variability. Looking ahead, upcoming observatories like ESA’s Vigil will further expand our capability to connect coronal drivers with in-situ measurements across the heliosphere, and to better predict their space weather impacts. This session invites contributions that make use of theoretical advances, innovative modelling approaches, and multi-platform observations to probe the solar wind and to determine its properties from its source regions to its interactions with planetary environments. Topics of interest include the origins of the fast and slow solar wind, mechanisms of heating and acceleration, evolution of large-scale structures, fine-scale dynamics, and the role of magnetic connectivity. We particularly welcome studies that integrate data and models to bridge scales and regions, as well as perspectives that outline future priorities for solar wind research.
title: Understanding the origins and evolution of the solar wind across the heliosphere with modeling and observations

description: In 2017 the international multi-agency Next Generation Solar Physics Mission (NGSPM) Science Objectives Team published its final report, setting out the highest-priority science questions for solar physics in the coming decade and the measurements and instrumentation needed to answer them: - How is the hot, dynamic outer solar atmosphere formed and sustained? - What drives large-scale solar eruptions, and how can we predict them? - What mechanisms govern the solar cycle and irradiance variability? JAXA's multi-agency SOLAR-C and NASA’s Multi-slit Solar Explorer (MUSE) will soon launch to address these recommendations. SOLAR-C combines the EUV High-throughput Spectroscopic Telescope (EUVST), which will observe the solar atmosphere with unprecedented plasma diagnostic capability, with the Solar Spectral Irradiance Monitor (SoSpIM), which provides complementary full-Sun EUV spectral irradiance measurements. MUSE is a multi-slit spectrograph that will provide imaging spectroscopy of the corona at multiple wavelengths, up to 100 times faster than current instruments. The collective power of SOLAR-C and MUSE will transform our ability to probe the multi-scale physics of the corona, from small-scale energy release to its large-scale impacts. Europe is central to delivering SOLAR-C. France is fabricating the EUV grating, Germany is contributing to calibration, testing and components, Italy is providing the slit, and Switzerland is building SoSpIM. The European Space Agency is providing the short-wavelength camera (which is being built in the UK). This session invites observers, modellers and theoreticians to present current work and discuss future directions across solar physics to promote strong European science return from these missions. It also welcomes work highlighting the strong European contribution to SOLAR-C.
title: The next generation of solar physics with SOLAR-C and MUSE

description: Energetic solar eruptions encompass a range of interconnected phenomena, including fast coronal mass ejections (CMEs), strong X-ray flares, large solar energetic particle (SEP) events, and the coronal waves and shocks associated with them. Understanding how these phenomena are related, how energy is partitioned between them, and how they contribute to the acceleration and release of energetic particles remains an open question in solar and heliospheric physics. The respective roles of flares, CMEs and CME-driven shocks in particle acceleration and release, as well as the role of magnetic connectivity, are still being investigated. The propagation of CMEs, shocks and magnetic structures through the heliosphere can also affect galactic cosmic rays (GCRs), producing Forbush decreases (FDs) that provide information on the evolution and large-scale structure of interplanetary disturbances. The expanding fleet of heliospheric spacecraft, together with remote-sensing and ground-based observations, allows these processes to be studied over a wide range of heliocentric distances. Observations from Solar Orbiter, Parker Solar Probe, STEREO-A, BepiColombo and near-Earth spacecraft can be combined with observations of the solar corona, radio measurements and ground-based cosmic-ray data. This makes it possible to study the evolution of solar eruptions, their magnetic connections, particle acceleration and transport, and the modulation of GCRs from the Sun to interplanetary space. Projects such as SPEARHEAD and SOLER have contributed to this effort through coordinated datasets, catalogues, analysis tools and modelling approaches for energetic solar eruptions and energetic particles. This session invites observational, theoretical and modelling studies of energetic solar eruptions and their interrelations, from the solar corona to interplanetary space. Contributions on flares, CMEs, coronal waves and shocks, SEP acceleration and release, magnetic connectivity and particle transport are welcome, as are studies of Forbush decreases and the modulation of GCRs by CMEs, ICMEs and magnetic structures. We also welcome presentations on new data products, analysis methods and tools for studying energetic solar eruptions and their heliospheric consequences.
title: Energetic solar eruptions and particle transport: from solar acceleration to heliospheric modulation

description: The solar wind is a highly structured and continuously evolving plasma environment spanning a broad range of spatial and temporal scales. Large-scale features originating at the Sun evolve during heliospheric propagation, interact with the ambient plasma and with one another, and coexist with smaller-scale magneto-plasma formations generated locally. Together they create a complex hierarchy extending from streams, transients, shocks, and interaction regions to flux ropes, current sheets, discontinuities, turbulent fluctuations, waves, and kinetic-scale phenomena. This session addresses the cross-scale evolution of this hierarchy and its role in energy transfer and dissipation throughout the heliosphere. We welcome studies of Interplanetary Coronal Mass Ejections (ICMEs) and ICME sheaths, interplanetary shocks, stream and corotating interaction regions (SIRs/CIRs), magnetic flux ropes, current sheets of different origins and scales (including the heliospheric current sheet), discontinuities, and other coherent magneto-plasma structure. Particular emphasis will be placed on how these environments generate, enhance, or modify turbulence, magnetic reconnection, plasma instabilities, and particle acceleration, and on how the resulting processes influence subsequent plasma evolution. This session is organized within the activities of the SCOSTEP Working Group under the same title.
title: Cross-scale processes and magneto-plasma structures in the dynamic solar wind

description: The total solar eclipses of 12 August 2026 and 2 August 2027 offer exceptional opportunities for heliophysics and planetary science. This session invites contributions presenting results from the 2026 eclipse, including coordinated ground-based and space-borne observations, modelling, and public outreach and engagement. In particular, results from a multi-site observing campaign coordinated by EGU, COSPAR and LUNEX will be presented. The session will also address preparations for the 2 August 2027 eclipse, whose path of totality crosses southern Spain, North Africa and the Middle East, with a maximum duration of totality of more than six minutes. We welcome contributions on instrumentation, space-based observations, modelling and predictions, as well as citizen science and public engagement.
title: From Total Solar Eclipse 2026 ground and space observations , modelling, citizen engagement and preparation for 2 August 2027

description: The "Theory and Simulation of Solar System Plasmas" session is a forum for presenting recent results related to theoretical and numerical investigation of heliospheric plasmas. Our regions of interest are the Sun and its corona, the solar wind and planetary magnetospheres. Processes of interest are magnetic reconnection, turbulence, shock waves, plasma instabilities, plasma heating and particle acceleration. We welcome particularly studies integrating numerical modeling, theoretical investigations and in-situ measurements/ remote observations from current and future space missions (MMS, Parker Solar Probe, Solar Orbiter, Bepi Colombo, ASO-S, Aditya-L1, SMILE, HelioSwarm, SPO, Plasma Observatory...). This year we intend to focus in particular on demonstrating how spacecraft observations, numerical models and theory can be integrated for deeper understanding of the heliospheric environment. Example of this integration are data-driven simulations, validation of theory and simulations against observations, the several ways methods rooted in Machine Learning to the system can be applied to the heliospheric system, data assimilation.
title: Theory and Simulation of Solar System Plasmas

description: This open session traditionally invites presentations on all aspects of the Earth’s magnetospheric physics, including the magnetosphere and its boundary layers, magnetosheath, bow shock and foreshock as well as solar wind-magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling. We welcome contributions on various aspects of magnetospheric observations, remote sensing of the magnetosphere’s processes, modelling and theoretical research. Presentations related to current and planned space missions, as well as value-added data services, are also encouraged. Additionally, we welcome comparative studies of processes in the magnetospheres of Earth and other planets. This session is particularly suitable for any contribution which does not fit more naturally into one of the specialised sessions and for contributions of wide scientific interest.
title: Open Session on the Magnetosphere

description: This open session investigates the complex interplay within the Sun–Earth system, focusing on the dynamic processes that drive space weather and climate. Topics include the progression from solar phenomena, including flares, coronal mass ejections, and the solar wind, to their subsequent interactions with Earth’s magnetosphere, ionosphere, and thermosphere. The session also assesses the cascading risks to critical infrastructure, specifically satellite operations, navigation and communication networks, power grids, and aviation. By bridging observational data, theoretical modeling, and operational insights, this session highlights the necessity of understanding both acute space weather events and the long-term implications of solar variability for our increasingly technological society.
title: Open Session on Space Weather and Space Climate

description: The joint European Space Agency/Chinese Academy of Sciences (ESA/CAS) Solar Wind Magnetosphere Ionosphere Link Explorer (SMILE) mission was successfully launched from Kourou, French Guiana, on 19 May 2026. SMILE is a novel mission, directly imaging the Sun-Earth interaction. In particular, SMILE images the magnetosheath/magnetopause and cusp regions using a novel soft X-ray instrument, complemented by a UV instrument that is imaging the Northern auroral oval for more than 40 hours continuously. In addition, the solar wind and magnetospheric plasma in the vicinity of the spacecraft is simultaneously measured by a magnetometer and an ion instrument. After reaching its science orbit of 1.7 x 19 RE (geocentric distance) inclined at 70 deg and completing commissioning activities, the nominal mission began in September 2026. In this session, the first results from the mission will be presented along with information for the community on how to access the SMILE data systems. We encourage presentations on complementary measurements from other missions and ground-based facilities and modelling results in support of the SMILE mission goals.
title: The SMILE mission: first results

description: The lower thermosphere-ionosphere (LTI) system is the transition region between Earth’s atmosphere and space. It is characterized by large changes in the dynamics, energetics, composition, and ionization of the atmosphere. In this region, the atmosphere transitions from a well-mixed to a diffusively separated state, and the atmosphere becomes increasingly ionized. Meanwhile, the electrodynamic wind dynamo couples different regions across latitudes and altitudes. The spatial-temporal morphology of the LTI is influenced by forcing from the lower atmosphere and solar and geomagnetic activity. Their interplay leads to complex regional and global variability on timescales from hours to months, creating a challenge for understanding the LTI behavior. Although a basic understanding of the connection between the lower and upper atmosphere via waves and global circulation changes has been achieved, we still have a limited understanding of the LTI structure itself, e.g., spatial-temporal structure and variability of neutral and plasma density, composition, temperature, and wind, as well as the processes determining them, and their relative importance. This limited understanding is partly due to the fact that we lack continuous and high-resolution observations in the LTI region. Consequently, LTI processes were often investigated indirectly with data taken remotely from ground or at Low-Earth-Orbit (LEO) altitudes (> 300 km). However, Very LEO (VLEO) altitudes (< 300 km) are increasingly becoming important for modern space-based infrastructure, and therefore there is a growing need to better understand the variability of the VLEO environment and the processes controlling the region, including but not limited to neutral and plasma composition, wind, and temperature, and electrodynamics. This session invites presentations that define the critical environmental knowledge needs at VLEO altitudes. We equally solicit studies that quantify LTI structure, variability, and driving processes using numerical, statistical and machine learning models and current observations, including uncertainty quantification, as well as new observing techniques or proposed mission concepts.
title: Bridging the Lower Thermosphere-Ionosphere Gap: Structure, Variability, and Coupling Processes

description: Magnetic reconnection is a key process in space, astrophysical, and laboratory plasmas that explosively converts magnetic energy into kinetic energy of charged particles. Thanks to recent spacecraft missions (e.g., MMS, Cluster, THEMIS, Parker Solar Probe, etc.) and the development of numerical simulations, many new findings have been achieved in the last several years. Also, many important issues remain: the triggering mechanisms, quantitative aspects of the energy conversions, identification of the electron diffusion/dissipation region, coupling across multiple scales, and so on. This session invites presentations on all of the aspects associated with magnetic reconnection from the spacecraft measurements, theoretical analysis, numerical simulations, and laboratory experiments.
title: Magnetic reconnection and associated multi-scale coupling in the collisionless environments

description: Scientific software development dates back 80 years, however, software sharing is still a relatively new discipline, and many approaches and guidelines are still evolving. Research software is an essential component of modern geoscience, supporting data analysis, modelling, visualization, machine learning, and computational workflows. Like scientific data, software plays a critical role in enabling research outcomes, yet the effort involved in developing, adapting, maintaining, and applying software is often under-recognized. In this session, we welcome contributions that demonstrate how software has enabled scientific discovery, streamlined research workflows, accelerated analysis, facilitated collaboration, or helped address geoscientific challenges. We particularly encourage real-world applications, case studies, lessons learned, and practical experiences from across the geosciences, including geophysics and seismology, environmental sciences, geochemistry, geomorphology, hydrogeology, and planetary sciences. Contributions may present software developed, adapted, or integrated to support scientific workflows, as well as best practices related to usability, reproducibility, FAIR and Open Science, interoperability, documentation, sustainability, and software reuse. Live demonstrations, videos, and interactive examples are particularly encouraged (supplementary materials can be hosted on the EGU27 platform for access after the conference). Join us to share examples, experiences, and best practices that demonstrate the value of software as a research asset and help advance geoscience through more effective, accessible, and reusable scientific workflows.
title: Advancing Geoscience Research Through Robust and User-Friendly Software: Case Studies, Applications, and Best Practices

description: Large-scale deployments such as USArray and Hi-Net have driven the rise of dense seismic arrays, supported by advances in autonomous nodes and Distributed Fiber Optic Sensing (DFOS). Combined with array processing and seismic interferometry, these technologies deliver unprecedented spatial resolution for imaging, seismicity studies, and monitoring of geological processes across scales. This growth brings challenges. Instrument management suffers from a lack of standards for nodal and DFOS acquisitions, along with calibration, synchronization, and maintenance issues across large sensor counts. Field operations for installation, maintenance, and recovery, often in remote or difficult environments, need smart solutions that preserve data quality and continuity while easing the logistical burden. The data volumes generated call for efficient handling, storage, processing, and analysis (cloud computing, machine learning, and others), alongside user-friendly tools and standardized protocols for metadata tracking and archiving. We plan to split the session in two: a technical part where engineers and network operators present their latest work, and a scientific part where researchers show their latest results. We therefore invite contributions on the operational, logistical, technical, and data management challenges of dense seismic arrays. We particularly welcome instrument comparisons, practical tools for deployment strategies (such as QField or alternatives), instrument access (including how to reach the European nodal pools and the DFOS interrogators available for collaboration), data management, and metadata standardization (e.g. through ORFEUS, EPOS, or European research infrastructure projects). We also encourage submissions on innovative scientific and methodological developments, applications, and cutting-edge results, including imaging, array analysis, and seismicity monitoring from dense networks and DFOS deployments (or other distributed fiber-optic sensing methods) at all scales, from local to regional and global.
