Finally, we welcome work on the management and exploitation of multi-instrument and multi-physics arrays enabling joint interpretation, analysis, and inversion.
title: Advancing dense seismic arrays management and science

description: Seismological data infrastructures underpin both earthquake monitoring and scientific discovery. Anchored in national and regional observatories managing permanent and temporary seismic networks, these infrastructures have traditionally focused on the detection and characterization of seismicity, while also delivering timely, authoritative, and reliable information to civil protection agencies and the broader public. At the same time, they generate vast volumes of high-quality data that support a broad spectrum of research and operational applications. As user needs evolve, seismological infrastructures must adapt to accommodate increasingly diverse, multidisciplinary, and data-intensive workflows. Beyond traditional waveform and earthquake products, they are now expected to manage and deliver emerging data streams, support advanced computational environments, and facilitate interoperability across scientific domains. This session invites contributions addressing: (a) the acquisition, management, preservation, and dissemination of seismic and earthquake-related data and products from local to global scales; (b) the integration of emerging technologies and data types, including Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS), smart cables, and other novel geophysical observations; (c) innovative approaches, including artificial intelligence and machine learning, for earthquake monitoring, characterization, rapid-response applications and quality assurance; (d) the generation and delivery of advanced seismological and multidisciplinary products and services; and (e) the incorporation of observational data into computational workflows, digital twins, and next-generation Earth system applications. Promoted by ORFEUS and EarthScope, the session aims to foster interoperability, data discoverability and reuse through standardization within the FDSN, cross-disciplinary collaboration, and the adoption of Open Science principles to maximize the scientific and societal value of seismological observations.
title: Seismic Networks and Seismological Datacenters

description: Tectonic faults exhibit a spectrum of failure modes ranging from aseismic creep, to slow slip and devastating earthquakes. In recent years there has been a significant increase in the detection of slow earthquakes: slow-slip events, low- and very low-frequency earthquakes, tremor episodes. However, debates remain open about their mechanisms, scaling properties, and interplay with fast (ordinary) earthquakes. Leveraging cutting-edge technologies in the laboratory, advanced observational methods and sophisticated modeling, this session aims to bring together the diversity of works associated with several aspects listed below, to broaden our understanding of slow earthquakes and encourage discussions: Underlying Mechanisms: What mechanism(s) limits slip speed? We encourage studies about micro-mechanics, frictional behaviors, rupture dynamics, fluids and temperature and pressure conditions initiating and driving slow slip events. Scaling Relationships: Decoding the scaling of slow earthquakes across time, space, and energy dimensions, offering insights into their core dynamics. Technological Innovations: New tools and methods that extend our ability to detect and analyse slow earthquakes, including dense arrays, distributed acoustic sensing, seafloor geodesy and borehole observatories, InSAR and GNSS time series, and machine-learning approaches. Interplay between Slow and Fast Earthquakes: Analysis of the seismic cycle, mutual impacts and potential warning signs exhibited by different seismic phenomena. We encourage contributions that span from laboratory experiments to volcanic and tectonic research; from geological and geophysical observations, including but not limited to seismic and geodetic, to imaging and modeling including Artificial Intelligence based techniques.
title: A comprehensive understanding of slow earthquakes

description: The discovery of slow slip events along active faults has transformed our understanding of fault mechanics, yet the physical mechanisms that keep slow slip “slow” remain poorly understood. Intriguing seismological observations show that this aseismic release is often accompanied by seismic moment release (e.g., low-frequency earthquakes, tectonic tremor, regular earthquakes, repeating earthquakes, earthquake swarms). However, the spatial and temporal relationship between these seismic and aseismic components is far from straightforward, and challenges our understanding of how and when slow slip transitions into fast rupture, as well as the underlying multi-scale heterogeneities underpinning its seismic manifestation. This session aims to explore how and why aseismic slip becomes seismic, to improve our understanding of the dynamics of tectonic moment release in slow-slip-prone areas, from shallow to deep plate interfaces as well as continental intraplate regions. We welcome contributions building towards a multidisciplinary understanding of the spatiotemporal variability of slow slip and its interactions with (a)seismic events, employing geodetic and seismic data, geological records, laboratory experiments, and numerical modeling, as well as emerging technologies such as machine learning and distributed acoustic sensing (DAS).
title: Why do we hear silent slip? Connecting aseismic slip and its seismic manifestation across scales

description: Earthquakes are among the most impactful natural phenomena, responsible for significant human and economic losses. To mitigate their effects, it is important to characterise seismic hazard across different regions and understand the factors that control it. Reliable earthquake hazard assessment requires a comprehensive understanding of seismic source processes, propagation paths, and local geological and geotechnical conditions. In particular, site effects associated with these conditions can significantly modify the amplitude, frequency content, and duration of seismic shaking, making their characterisation essential for seismic microzonation, local hazard assessment, and the development of reliable ground-motion models. This session aims to bring together recent methodological and observational advances in earthquake hazard assessment, site effect characterisation, and seismic microzonation, including approaches based on earthquake recordings, ambient vibrations, and numerical modelling. Studies on the following topics, including but not limited to, are welcome: ● Seismic hazard analysis ● Seismic source characterisation ● Characterisation of seismicity in seismic hazard analysis ● Ground-motion prediction analysis ● Site effect and microzonation ● Earthquake-induced effects (e.g. liquefaction and landslide) ● 1D, 2D, and/or 3D numerical site effect modeling ● Soil-structure interaction and analysis ● New approaches in seismic hazard characterisation ● Machine learning for seismic hazard, site effect, and microzonation
title: Assessment of Earthquake-Related Hazards, Site Effects, and Microzonation

description: The estimation of ground motion for future earthquakes is one of the main tasks of seismology. Among the processes affecting ground motion, local site conditions play a significant role. Earthquake site effects encompass several phenomena, such as amplified ground shaking due to local geological and topographical features, liquefaction events, ground failures, cavity collapses, and earthquake-triggered landslides. The estimation of these effects is a necessary step for seismic hazard assessment and seismic risk mitigation as well as to build effective strategies for urban planning, historical heritage preservation, and emergency management. This session aims to gather multidisciplinary contributions bridging the fields of seismology, geology, geotechnics, and engineering. We focus on the following topics: - Site characterization and seismic microzonation; - Empirical and physics-based assessments of stratigraphic and topographic amplification effects; - Quantitative evaluation of linear and non-linear seismic site response in 1D, 2D, and 3D configurations, including High-Performance Computing (HPC) simulations; - Earthquake-induced ground effects, such as landslides, liquefaction and cavity collapse, under changing environmental conditions and climate-induced variations; - Soil-structure interaction, urban seismology and characterization of building response to seismic events; - Proposals for integration and/or revision of building codes and seismic regulations; - Analysis of historical and cultural heritage sites. The session also aims to collect results based on different geophysical techniques (e.g., earthquake data, ambient noise analysis, HVSR, array measurements, active surface wave prospecting, ERT, GPR, seismic refraction tomography, etc.) and their integration. Contributions regarding innovative methodologies - such as Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) systems, dense nodal arrays as well as the application of Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence for automated data processing and large-scale site effect mapping - are highly welcome.
title: Advances in Estimation and Understanding of Earthquake Site Effects

description: Geophysical data are increasingly available with ever improving quality, which allow new observations of seismicity and slow deformation transients. In parallel, ever-improving computation capacity allows new theoretical and numerical advances in the study of the dynamics of complex fault systems. These recent advances show that crustal deformation proceeds in diverse spatio-temporal patterns of seismic and aseismic slip —e.g. aperiodicity, clustering, synchronization— which cannot be fully accounted for in canonical statistical descriptions of seismicity or models of strain accumulation and release on simple faults. Nonetheless, it is essential to fundamentally characterize and understand the complexity of slip activity in natural fault systems to enhance our capacity to assess earthquake hazard and predictability. Thus, new theoretical and observational tools must be developed to better characterize these complex phenomena and further understand the physical processes at play. In this session, we welcome observational, theoretical, numerical and experimental studies addressing some aspects of the complexity in seismicity and in faulting, from the event to the cycle scale, including but not limited to: characterizing emergent properties of seismicity (clustering, intermittency etc), exploring the physics of fault-fault interactions and stress transfer, seismic-aseismic feedbacks, the role of geometrical and material complexity in shaping fault slip patterns, the interaction of fault systems with complex external forcings.
title: Collective Behaviors in Seismology: Models and Observations for Complexity in Seismicity, Crustal Mechanics, and Faulting

description: Interferometric techniques turn seismic networks into observatories continuously monitoring the Earth’s dynamic processes, including time-varying structures, volcanic and hydrologic activity, and ocean-solid Earth interactions. The application of these techniques has expanded to signals beyond ocean microseismic noise, capturing seismic energy from other natural and anthropogenic sources. Great strides have been made in obtaining high-resolution images of seismic velocity and other elastic/rock physics properties, identifying and quantifying the sources of various ambient noise wave types, and interpreting variations in seismic properties. However, challenges persist, such as using signals from suboptimally situated sources like urban noise or ambient noise body waves from localised storms, interpreting the seismic ambient field’s polarisation, and analysing ambient noise amplitudes for elastic effects and anelastic attenuation. Additionally, the spatial localisation of seismic property changes and the implementation of spatial wavefield gradient measurements using advanced sensors, such as fibre optic or rotational sensors, present ongoing challenges. This session invites discussions on recent advances in ambient noise seismology and seismic interferometry, including both theoretical and numerical developments, as well as novel applications and observational studies. We welcome studies on topics including, but not limited to, ambient seismic sources and their spatiotemporal dynamics, ocean wave quantification through ambient noise, urban seismic noise, interferometric imaging, monitoring subsurface properties, and assessing subsurface deformation under both internal (e.g., earthquakes, volcanic activity, slow movements, etc.) and external forces (e.g., tidal effects, environmental effects, anthropogenic effects, etc.). Additional topics of interest include spatial sensitivity studies for imaging and monitoring under diverse source conditions, quantification of site effects, amplification and attenuation, AI-based signal processing, and interdisciplinary applications of seismic interferometry.
title: Ambient Seismic Noise and Seismic Interferometry

description: Geophysical imaging techniques are widely used to characterize and monitor structures and processes in the shallow subsurface. Active methods include seismic, electrical resistivity, induced polarization, electromagnetic, and ground-penetrating radar, whereas passive approaches draw on ambient noise and electrical self-potential measurements. Advances in experimental design, instrumentation, acquisition, processing, numerical modelling, open hardware and software, and inversion continue to push the limits of spatial and temporal resolution. Nonetheless, the interpretation of geophysical images often remains ambiguous. Challenges addressed in this session include optimal acquisition strategies, automated processing and associated error quantification, spatial and temporal regularization of model parameters, integration of non-geophysical data and geological/process realism into imaging workflows, joint inversion, as well as quantitative interpretation through suitable petrophysical relations, and uncertainty quantification throughout the workflow. We invite submissions spanning the full spectrum of near-surface geophysical imaging, from methodological innovation to diverse applications at different scales. Contributions on combining complementary methods, machine learning, and process monitoring are particularly encouraged.
title: Geophysical imaging of near-surface structures and processes

description: Seismic hazard assessment is resting on earthquake rupture forecasts (ERFs), constraining where earthquakes will occur, how large they will be, and how often. Building a reliable ERF requires knowing how faults behave over many seismic cycles. Instrumental catalogs, however, span only decades to about a century, far shorter than the recurrence intervals of most damaging earthquakes. Improving ERFs therefore means extending the earthquake record to achieve longer and more complete catalogs. Physics-based earthquake cycle simulations have this capability. Using fault geometry, slip rates and frictional properties as input, they generate synthetic catalogs spanning thousands to millions of years to establish comprehensive rupture forecasts, capturing the behavior that short observational records cannot, such as multi-fault ruptures, clustering, and variability in recurrence times and magnitudes. Their results are, however, only as credible as their input constraints -observational data from active tectonics are therefore essential to calibrate and test the simulations, including paleoseismic records, fault slip rates, geodetic strain, fault geometry and maturity, and historical seismicity. In the spirit of the Fault2SHA community, this session brings together modelers, field geologists, geodesists and hazard practitioners. We invite contributions on: the development and application of physics-based earthquake cycle simulations; the observational data that inform and constrain them, including paleoseismology, tectonic geomorphology and geodesy; approaches to validating simulated catalogs and quantifying their uncertainties; and the integration of physics-based results into ERFs and probabilistic seismic hazard assessment.
title: From faults to forecasts: earthquake cycle simulations for seismic hazard assessment (Fault2SHA)

description: The Einstein Telescope (ET), Europe’s planned next-generation underground gravitational-wave observatory, faces unprecedented geoscientific challenges as its sensitivity extends to a few hertz, making detector performance dependent on its geological and environmental setting. At these frequencies, seismic, geophysical, atmospheric, and anthropogenic processes become important noise sources. The subsurface can therefore no longer be regarded simply as the host of the observatory: it becomes an integral part of the experiment. Earthquakes, ambient seismic wavefields, surface deformation, groundwater dynamics, atmospheric processes, and other environmental phenomena continuously redistribute mass and perturb the local gravitational field, generating so-called Newtonian noise. These gravitational perturbations can directly affect the sensitivity of gravitational-wave detectors and, unlike mechanical vibrations, cannot be removed using conventional seismic isolation. Understanding, predicting, and ultimately mitigating Newtonian noise requires a detailed characterisation of the geological structure and seismic and geophysical processes around a detector site. This session aims to bring together geologists, geophysicists, seismologists, hydrogeologists, geotechnical engineers, geodesists, gravimetrists, atmospheric scientists, and gravitational-wave physicists to characterise and model the Earth system across scales relevant to ET, from regional geological structures to processes near the underground observatory. We invite contributions on geophysical imaging, rock and soil properties, hydrogeology, gravimetry, seismicity, ambient seismic noise, surface deformation, and seismic-wavefield characterisation. We particularly welcome developments based on seismic networks and arrays, ambient-noise interferometry, distributed acoustic sensing, borehole observations, microgravity, GNSS and InSAR, electromagnetic and atmospheric monitoring, numerical modelling, uncertainty quantification, and multi-sensor integration. Of particular interest are studies of how earthquakes, ambient seismic wavefields, and subsurface and site conditions influence gravitational perturbations. Bringing these perspectives together will advance our understanding of how the Earth system shapes detector performance, while ET’s extensive observational infrastructure will open new opportunities to study the Earth.
title: Einstein Telescope and the Geosciences: from subsurface characterisation to gravitational wave detection

description: The CTBT's International Monitoring System (IMS) combines a global network of seismic, hydroacoustic, and infrasound sensors with the air sampling of radionuclides to detect nuclear explosions worldwide. The data recorded by the IMS stations undergo a multi-step automatic and interactive processing and analysis procedure at the International Data Centre (IDC) to detect, locate, and characterize natural and human-made events underground, underwater, or in the atmosphere. Atmospheric transport modelling is used to relate radionuclide detections to their possible source regions. Data fusion approaches can further combine radionuclide observations with waveform information to improve event characterization. On-site inspection (OSI) technologies apply comparable seismo-acoustic methods at a smaller scale, together with geophysical techniques such as ground-penetrating radar and geomagnetic surveying, as well as radionuclide and environmental sampling methods, to identify evidence of a nuclear explosion. This session invites studies on methods and applications for event detection, location, and characterization using seismic, hydroacoustic, infrasound, and radionuclide technologies. Contributions are invited to advance seismic and acoustic velocity models, acoustic wave propagation, atmospheric transport modelling for source localization of radionuclides, and data fusion techniques that integrate data from different verification technologies. Studies on nuclear-test-ban monitoring that rely on IMS or OSI instrumentation, data, or methods are just as welcome, whether they address the monitoring of present-day or historical explosions or consider hypothetical scenarios such as the National Data Centre Preparedness Exercises (NPE). Contributions addressing the civil and scientific applications of IMS data are equally encouraged. Civil applications include disaster risk reduction through early warning and hazard assessment for earthquakes, tsunamis, volcanic activity, and other natural hazards. Earth science applications encompass the characterization of natural and anthropogenic sources, as well as studies of climate change, ocean processes, solid Earth structure, and atmospheric circulation. Finally, contributions on the application of machine learning and other data-driven approaches to event detection, location, discrimination, and monitoring are particularly welcome. Submissions from early career scientists and from National Data Centres are warmly encouraged.
title: Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT) monitoring technologies and their civil and scientific applications

description: Subduction zones host the largest earthquakes on Earth and display the full spectrum of fault slip behaviors, from tremor and slow slip events to megathrust ruptures. Yet the instrumental record covers only a small fraction of their seismic cycles. How transient deformation (slow slip, afterslip, viscoelastic relaxation) contributes to the accumulation and release of strain on the megathrust remains poorly understood. This session invites contributions that combine disciplines and datasets to provide new perspectives on the subduction seismic cycle, from days to to geological timeframes. Relevant approaches include onshore and offshore geodesy, seismology, geological and paleoseismic records, drilling and exhumed-fault studies, laboratory experiments, and numerical modeling. We particularly welcome studies that examine how transient processes modulate interseismic coupling and shape seismic and tsunami hazard. We also welcome work on how along-strike and down-dip variations in fault zone structure, frictional properties, fluid pressure and stress control where megathrust earthquakes nucleate, propagate and arrest. Comparative studies across subduction margins, and work on both the shallow (near-trench) and deep (transition zone) portions of the interface, are encouraged.
title: Understanding the subduction zone seismic cycle and the role of transient deformation: a multidisciplinary approach

description: Driven by intrinsic absorption and scattering, seismic attenuation strongly affects wavefield propagation. Quantifying this energy loss provides critical insights into subsurface fluids, fractures, composition, and structural heterogeneity. Understanding attenuation mechanisms also supports robust source characterization and accurate ground-motion modeling, with important implications for seismic hazard and risk assessment. Over the past few decades, theoretical, numerical, and observational breakthroughs have reshaped attenuation research. Modern high-resolution 3D simulations can now capture complex wavefield interactions through heterogeneous structures, from the deep Earth to shallow soils and built environments. At local scales, resolving attenuation is vital for understanding site effects, ground-motion variability, and site–city interactions, where geology and infrastructure jointly alter shaking. Furthermore, novel inversion frameworks and seismic interferometry offer refined approaches to distinguish scattering from intrinsic absorption, while dense seismic deployments and emerging sensing tools provide rich datasets capable of resolving attenuation with unprecedented spatial and temporal detail. This session aims to bring together researchers working across different scales and approaches to present recent advances in seismic attenuation research. We welcome theoretical, numerical, observational, and applied contributions that deepen our understanding of scattering and intrinsic absorption, explore the role of attenuation in wave propagation and energy transport, and constrain Earth's internal structure and material properties. Contributions addressing numerical simulations in heterogeneous and attenuating media, attenuation-based imaging and tomography, and the redistribution of seismic energy by geological heterogeneities, including faults, fractures, and material property variations, are particularly encouraged. We also invite studies exploring the implications of attenuation for source characterization, ground-motion modeling, and seismic hazard assessment, with particular interest in near-surface attenuation, site effects, spatial variability, and wave propagation in urban environments. Applications to geothermal and volcanic systems, where attenuation provides insights into energy conversion and absorption, are equally welcome, alongside studies investigating the internal structure and dynamics of other planetary bodies.
title: Seismic Scattering and Attenuation: Advances and Applications

description: Topography results from the interaction of processes operating across a wide range of spatial and temporal scales. Tectonic and volcanic activity, climate, surface processes, and transient events such as earthquakes and landslides all leave fingerprints on modern landscapes, making it challenging to disentangle their relative contributions. A major goal in Earth sciences is therefore to quantify the processes, rates, and timing of topographic change and to understand how landscapes respond to tectonic, climatic, and surface-process forcing across different scales. Recent advances in geophysical observations, remote sensing, geochronology, and modelling provide new opportunities to quantify landscape dynamics. InSAR, GNSS, high-resolution topography, and other geophysical and remote-sensing techniques allow us to characterize tectonic and volcanic deformation, transient events, and associated surface responses. We invite contributions using field observations, geophysical and remote-sensing datasets, quantitative geomorphology, geochronology, and analogue, numerical, or mathematical modelling to investigate tectonic, volcanic, surface, and topographic processes across different spatial and temporal scales. Contributions addressing active deformation and natural hazards, as well as long-term landscape and topographic evolution, are all welcome.
title: Topographic evolution across spatial and temporal scales: observations, geochronology and modelling

description: This session will focus on investigations about the physics of earthquakes – fast and slow. On the one hand contributions deal with imaging and numerical simulations of earthquake physics. On the other hand we solicit studies towards a comprehensive understanding of slow earthquakes. We invite abstracts on works to image rupture kinematics and simulate earthquake dynamics using numerical methods to improve understanding of the physics of earthquakes. In particular, these are works that aim to develop a deeper understanding of earthquake source physics by linking novel laboratory experiments to earthquake dynamics, and studies on earthquake scaling properties. For instance assessing the roles fluids and heterogeneities play in influencing, directing, or obstructing the behavior of earthquakes and how they impact rupture mechanics. Other works show progress in imaging earthquake sources using seismic data and surface deformation measurements (e.g. GNSS and InSAR) to estimate rupture properties on faults and fault systems. We look for technological innovations, showcasing cutting-edge tools and methodologies that boost our proficiency in detecting, analyzing, and understanding earthquakes in general. We want to highlight strengths and limitations of each data set and method in the context of the source-inversion problem, accounting for uncertainties and robustness of the source models and imaging or simulation methods. Contributions are welcome that make use of modern computing paradigms and infrastructure to tackle large-scale forward simulation of earthquake process, but also inverse modeling to retrieve the rupture process with proper uncertainty quantification. We also welcome seismic studies using data from natural faults, lab results and numerical approaches to understand earthquake physics.
title: Source physics of earthquakes and insights into slow-to-fast earthquakes

description: The physical and structural properties of the crust and deeper lithosphere are often explored independently through a range of geophysical modelling and inversion methods, from tomographic to potential field techniques, among others. Recent developments in joint processing and modelling have highlighted the value of combining complementary, multi-disciplinary datasets for a more comprehensive understanding of Earth's structure. This session invites studies imaging the Earth at multiple spatial scales — from near-surface to lithospheric depths — using joint modelling and inversion of complementary geophysical datasets (e.g. passive seismology, gravimetry, magnetics, geochemistry, active seismics). Applications may include constraining the physical state of the medium, identifying seismogenic zones, mapping natural resources, and seismic hazard assessment, among others. Submissions are not restricted to the approaches listed above, and we welcome novel integrated methods as well. Given recent natural hazard events - including the Türkiye–Syria and Venezuela earthquake doublets, the eruption of Mt. Etna, and the destructive landslide in the Nepal Himalaya - we particularly encourage (but do not limit) submissions focused on these and similar regions. We strongly welcome submissions from Early Career Scientists.
title: Joint modelling and inversion of multi-disciplinary geophysical datasets: crust and lithosphere

description: Volcanoes are among Earth's most dynamic and complex geological systems, posing significant risks to lives, infrastructure, and ecosystems worldwide. Unraveling their internal architecture, magmatic evolution, and past eruptive behavior, including the frequencies and volumes of recurrent eruptions, remains a vital prerequisite for effective hazard mitigation. While petrological models and surface exposures historically laid the groundwork for volcanic research, modern subsurface geophysical methods now allow us to image these systems in the subsurface in unprecedented detail. Seismic techniques have become indispensable for mapping volcanic structures and dynamic processes across diverse spatial and temporal resolution scales. Advanced seismic inversion approaches illuminate deep crustal mush zones, trans-crustal magmatic networks, and shallow melt accumulation zones. Concurrently, high-resolution controlled-source reflection imaging reveals the internal stratigraphy of volcanic constructs, intrusive complexes, submarine and subaerial eruptive deposits, and flank collapse structures. Furthermore, emerging methodologies such as Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) offer transformative, high-density spatial observations of volcanic activity and subsurface structures. Integrating these multi-scale seismic perspectives provides key constraints on structural stability, eruptive frequencies, and mass-wasting hazards. This session brings together research utilizing active- and/or passive-source seismic methods across land, coastal, and marine environments to study modern or ancient volcanic settings. We especially welcome multi-disciplinary studies that integrate seismic datasets with scientific drilling, seabed/surface sampling, or complementary geophysical and geological constraints to advance our understanding of volcanic plumbing, edifice evolution, and associated hazards.
title: Seismic Imaging of Volcanic Systems

description: Advances in seismological machine learning applications have resulted in new ways to image the Earth on multiple scales, across diverse settings, from risk mitigation in engineering, to studying heterogeneous and dynamic volcanic environments. Examples include seismic phase picking (transfer learning), fault detection (U-nets) and sparse data tomography (artificial neural networks). Of interest for this session are machine learning tools with potential to harness the scattered seismic wavefield, for future physical world insights, at progressively finer imaging scales. For example, neural operators solve the wave equation several orders of magnitude faster than conventional forward solvers and can rapidly invert seismic waveforms for domain velocity structure. Fourier Neural Operators (FNOs) are used for retrieval of multi-frequency seismic waveforms generated in highly scattering 3D settings. U-shaped neural operators have been embedded in ambient full waveform inversion workflows, successfully inverting real datasets for crustal-scale seismic velocities. Research continues into using FNOs to directly invert facies-representative, statistically-informed synthetic seismic data for velocity structure, however ‘simulation-to-real’ applications remain to be achieved. Our ability to advance applications towards improved ‘sim-to-real’ performance depends on three key research challenges: i) producing training sets with sufficient statistical distribution to fully capture physical environment scattering properties ii) considering effects from environmental noise, near-surface effects and topography on physical world seismic waveforms iii) overcoming prohibitive computational costs in 3D applications. These barriers to progress are common to all inference-based seismic approaches. We invite submissions engaging with inferential seismic imaging and/or that address some of the key themes above, across all scales local to global. We wish to bring together seismic imaging researchers working in different contexts (e.g. industrial risk, geohazards, volcano seismology, urban seismology, regional/global-scale tomography, imaging using distributed dynamic strain sensing (DSS/DAS)). We hope that common further research challenges can be identified during the session. Submissions addressing the forward/inverse problem are welcome. Machine learning architectures need not necessarily be neural operator-based. We are interested in submissions using other methodologies.
title: Advances in Machine Learning Applications For Inferential Seismic Imaging

description: In the past, the main challenge of obtaining a seismic velocity model was the scarcity of data, especially if the objective was high resolution imaging. Nowadays, with the availability of DAS, seismic nodes, borehole seismometers, classic permanent broadband stations or active seismic surveys, there is a variety of datasets that can be utilized to obtain subsurface images. Often, for geothermal or volcanic monitoring or imaging, multiple different receiver systems are deployed in the same area, collecting data on the same seismic events. However, most are typically treated as independent datasets, which are processed using a variety of methods, resulting in multiple velocity models optimized for each respective dataset. Within this session, we want to explore how different datasets can be merged to retrieve velocity models from all the available data, from broadband to very narrowband. Such models allow a better understanding of the subsurface and its potential resources and can in turn be used as robust starting models for further research in respective areas of interest. We encourage submissions on a) case studies ranging from the efforts of building community velocity models to very local scale integrations of different datasets for very specific purposes such as the improvement of resolution and illumination, and b) highlighting the challenges of combining such datasets, including but not limited to the complexities of different resolutions, sampling frequencies or acquisition timelines.
title: Achieving the all-in-one velocity model: How to combine different seismic datasets into a single model

description: Hydrological science is increasingly dependent on computational tools for modelling, prediction, uncertainty quantification and decision-making. At the same time, a growing community of researchers is developing open-source software, models, packages, graphical user interfaces and computational workflows that can make hydrological methods more accessible, transparent and reproducible. However, these tools are often developed independently and remain scattered across different programming languages, platforms and research communities. This session aims to bring together researchers and developers of open-source tools for hydrology, providing a platform to move beyond conventional research outputs and showcase the software, models and workflows they have built for the hydrological community. Contributions are welcome across a broad range of approaches, including statistical and stochastic modelling, numerical and process-based models, hydrological extremes, machine learning and artificial intelligence, hybrid modelling, uncertainty quantification, data assimilation, forecasting and decision-support systems. We particularly encourage contributions that introduce new open-source packages, software libraries, graphical user interfaces, modelling frameworks, APIs, workflows, benchmark datasets or computational platforms. Presentations may address the scientific problem the tool solves, its methodological framework, implementation, validation, interoperability and practical applications, encouraging collaboration, reuse, benchmarking and further development of open-source hydrological software.
title: Building the Open Hydrology Community: Open-Source Tools, Models and Reproducible Workflows

description: The rapid growth in the availability and diversity of hydro-meteorological data is transforming our ability to monitor, understand, model, and predict hydrological extremes. Global and continental datasets, including reanalysis, satellite and gridded products, provide unprecedented spatial and temporal coverage, while national, regional and local networks often offer higher-resolution observations of catchment-scale processes. This diversity creates new opportunities but also raises key questions: Which data are best suited to different purposes, how should they be integrated, and how does data choice affect hydrological analyses and modelling outcomes? This PICO session brings together researchers working with different types and scales of hydro-meteorological data to explore how data choice, quality, spatial and temporal resolution, uncertainty and availability influence hydrological modelling and the assessment of extremes. Rather than focusing primarily on the development of individual precipitation, evapotranspiration or other hydro-meteorological products, or on hazard and risk processes themselves, the session focuses on how the choice, quality and scale of data shape the analysis, modelling and interpretation of hydro-meteorological extremes. We particularly encourage studies comparing global products with national, regional, catchment-scale or local datasets and observational networks. Contributions may address precipitation, temperature, evapotranspiration, soil moisture, snow, streamflow, groundwater and remote-sensing products, with applications to rainfall-runoff modelling, droughts, floods, compound events, trend and frequency analysis, forecasting and water-resources assessment. The session also welcomes studies on data quality and gaps, aggregation, bias correction, downscaling, data fusion, ensemble and multi-model approaches, uncertainty propagation and reproducible workflows. Machine learning, artificial intelligence, cloud computing and multi-source data integration are encouraged where they improve the reliability, transferability or operational value of hydrological analyses. A key objective is to move beyond identifying which dataset performs best towards understanding why different data sources, resolutions and processing choices lead to different hydrological interpretations, model responses and decisions.
title: Hydro-meteorological Data for Extremes: Bridging Global Products and Local Observations

description: In this Hydroinformatics session, we explore innovative and state-of-the-art computational and data-driven methods that transform modern Earth observations, climate data, and IoT streams into actionable water management solutions. We focus on novel modeling frameworks, machine learning, and optimization techniques that advance our ability to simulate, forecast, and manage water resource systems. This session offers a forum for showcasing and debating the integration of emerging techniques and technologies across water-related applications, from novel algorithms to real-world deployment. Topics addressed in the session include: • Methods for analysing Big Data and complex datasets (remote sensing, IoT, Earth system and climate models): representation learning, time series analysis, clustering, information theory • Predictive and exploratory models drawing on statistics, computational intelligence, machine learning, and data science • Multi-model and hybrid approaches blending process-based (mechanistic) and data-driven (machine learning) models, including data assimilation and methods for quantifying and propagating model uncertainty • Optimisation methods based on heuristic search (genetic and evolutionary algorithms, randomised and adaptive search) applied to hydrology and water resources systems • Scalable and efficient computational methods and software tools for hydrological modelling and analysis, including model reduction, graph- and network-based approaches, and High-Performance Computing (HPC) • Decision-support systems for water management, with particular interest in those including digital twins and integrated tools for monitoring, forecasting and control, also focusing on how agentic AI can enhance their interactivity and capabilities Applications span the full breadth of hydrology and water resources — rainfall-runoff modelling, hydrometeorological forecasting, groundwater level modelling, sedimentation modelling, analysis of meteorological and hydrologic datasets, coupling of numerical weather prediction with hydrologic models, model calibration and uncertainty, optimisation of water resources, and smart water management.
title: Computational and data-driven methods for hydrology and water management: from methods to applications

description: Deep Learning has seen accelerated adoption across Hydrology and the broader Earth Sciences. This session highlights the continued integration of Deep Learning and its many variants into traditional and emerging hydrology-related workflows. We welcome abstracts related to novel theory development, new methodologies, or practical applications of Deep Learning in hydrological modeling and process understanding. This might include, but is not limited to, the following: (1) Development of novel deep learning models or modeling workflows. (2) Probing, exploring and improving our understanding of the (internal) states/representations of deep learning models to improve models and/or gain system insights. (3) Understanding the reliability of deep learning, e.g., under non-stationarity and climate change. (4) Modeling human behavior and impacts on the hydrological cycle. (5) Deep Learning approaches for extreme event analysis, detection, and mitigation. (6) Natural Language Processing in support of models and/or modeling workflows. (7) Applications of Large Language Models, Large Multimodal Models and Agentic frameworks in the context of hydrology. (8) Deep Learning-based uncertainty estimation methods. (9) Advances towards foundational models in the context of hydrology and Earth Sciences more generally. (10) Exploration of different training strategies, such as self-supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and reinforcement learning. (11) Transfer learning and generalization of deep learning models across hydrological, climatic and geographical settings.
title: Deep Learning in Hydrology

description: Data imperfection is a persistent and multi-faceted challenge in hydrology and more broadly in geosciences. Researchers and practitioners regularly work with datasets that are incomplete, imprecise, erroneous, heterogeneous, or redundant—whether originating from in-situ measurements, remote sensing, modelling outputs, or participatory sources. While traditional statistical methods have long been used to address these limitations, the growing complexity and diversity of hydrological and environmental data have created new demands—and opportunities—for innovation. Advances in artificial intelligence, data fusion, knowledge representation, and reasoning under uncertainty now allow for more robust integration and interpretation of heterogeneous information. This session aims to gather contributions that explore how we can move from imperfect, fragmented data toward coherent and actionable hydrological and environmental knowledge. We welcome abstracts on: - Applications and case studies in hydrology or other domains, addressing missing data imputation, model inversion, uncertainty propagation, or multi-source integration—using time series, spatial data, imagery, videos, etc. - Methodological developments in data fusion, completion, uncertainty quantification, and AI-based knowledge extraction from heterogeneous data. - Cross-disciplinary approaches that connect geosciences, and specifically hydrological sciences, with AI, data mining, and knowledge systems, including citizen science, crowd-sourced data, or opportunistic sensing. - Experimental contributions in hydrology and geosciences addressing the challenges originating from imperfect data through AI, such as novel models and algorithms, explainable methods, and comparative studies on domain-specific datasets. We particularly encourage contributions that highlight novel practices or conceptual frameworks for dealing with imperfect and multi-source data in complex environmental systems. Indeed, this session is the home of imperfection - missing, imprecise, erroneous, duplicated and contradictory data, and how to work with them - while the development and evaluation of dataset products belongs to the precipitation and evapotranspiration datasets session, and the data questions specific to extremes belong to the two extremes sessions.
title: Managing and Processing Heterogeneous and Imperfect Data: current practices and challenges in Hydrology and Geosciences

description: In recent years, the field of geo-statistics has seen significant advancements. These methods are fundamental in understanding spatially and temporally variable hydrological and environmental processes, which are vital for risk assessment, input for other models, and management of extreme events like floods and droughts. This session aims to provide a comprehensive platform for researchers to present and discuss innovative applications and methodologies of geostatistics and spatio-temporal analysis in hydrology and related fields. The focus will be on traditional approaches and the assessment of uncertainties, whereas Machine Learning approaches have their specific and other dedicated sessions. We invite contributions that address the following topics (but not limited to): 1. Spatio-temporal Analysis of Hydrological and Environmental Anomalies: - Methods for detecting and analyzing large-scale anomalies in hydrological and environmental data. - Techniques to manage and predict extreme events based on spatio-temporal patterns. 2. Innovative Geostatistical Applications: - Advances in spatial and spatio-temporal modeling. - Applications in spatial reasoning and data mining. - Reduced computational complexity methods suitable for large-scale problems. 3. Geostatistical Methods for Hydrological Extremes: - Techniques for analyzing the dynamics of natural events, such as floods, droughts, and morphological changes. - Utilization of copulas and other statistical tools to identify spatio-temporal relationships. 4. Optimization and Generalization of Spatial Models: - Approaches to optimize monitoring networks and spatial models. - Techniques for predicting regions with limited or unobserved data e.g., using physical-based model simulations or using secondary variables. 5. Uncertainty Assessment in Geostatistics: - Methods for characterizing and managing uncertainties in spatial data. - Applications of Bayesian Geostatistical Analysis and Generalized Extreme Value Distributions. 6. Spatial and Spatio-temporal Covariance Analysis: - Exploring links between hydrological variables and extremes through covariance analysis. - Applications of Gaussian and non-Gaussian models in spatial analysis and prediction.
title: Advanced Stochastic and Geostatistic Methods for Simulation of Hydrological and Environmental Sciences

description: Hydroclimatic extremes such as droughts, floods, heatwaves and compound events emerge from complex interactions between atmospheric, hydrological and human processes across multiple spatial and temporal scales. The growing availability of Earth observation, in-situ and low-cost monitoring, citizen science observations, reanalysis and modelled data, together with advances in data-driven methods, provides new opportunities to detect, characterize and understand these events and their evolution. This session invites contributions that use data-driven, computational and hybrid approaches to advance the understanding of hydroclimatic extremes. We particularly welcome studies that integrate multiple data sources, investigate spatial and temporal patterns, identify drivers and dependencies, improve prediction, or connect hazard dynamics with impacts and risk. Relevant approaches include, but are not limited to, machine learning and artificial intelligence, remote sensing and Earth observation, data fusion, spatiotemporal analysis, event detection and tracking, statistical and causal methods, process-informed machine learning, hybrid modelling, and the integration of observations with hydrological and climate models. We welcome applications addressing droughts, floods, heatwaves, low flows, compound and cascading events, and transitions between extremes, from catchment to regional and global scales. Contributions addressing uncertainty, interpretability, and transferability are particularly welcome, as are studies focusing on the Global South and other data-scarce regions, where limited observations create distinct challenges for characterizing and predicting extremes. The session aims to bring together researchers working across hydrology, climate science, Earth observation, data science and risk assessment to discuss how emerging data and methods can improve our understanding of hydroclimatic extremes and their impacts.
title: Data-driven understanding of hydroclimatic extremes: from observations to processes, prediction and risk

description: Hydrological time series provide essential information for identifying trends and variability in surface and subsurface water systems, understanding their response to extreme events such as floods and droughts, and improving predictive capabilities for sustainable water-resource management. Recent developments in statistical modelling and machine learning offer new opportunities to extract information from increasingly large and complex hydrological datasets and to improve forecasting across a range of temporal and spatial scales. This session welcomes contributions on the analysis, forecasting, and interpretation of hydrological and hydroclimatic time series using statistical, machine learning, and hybrid approaches. Methods may include, but are not limited to regression, SARIMAX, LSTM, transformers, foundation models, knowledge-guided AI, and related approaches. We particularly encourage studies that evaluate model performance, interpretability, transferability, and robustness under changing or extreme conditions. Applications may address streamflow, flooding, groundwater, soil moisture, surface runoff, water quality, and other hydroclimatic and environmental variables.
title: Statistical and Machine Learning Approaches for Hydrological Time Series: Recent Developments and Applications

description: Reliable precipitation (P) and evapotranspiration (ET) datasets are essential for understanding, modeling, and predicting hydrological processes. Recently, the number of products has expanded rapidly, including products based on observations, remote sensing, reanalysis, land surface models, machine learning, and hybrid approaches. These products allowed for new opportunities, while also raising challenges related to evaluation, uncertainty characterization, and fitness for purpose. Addressing these challenges requires methods that assess hydrological consistency, transferability across regions, and requirements for diverse applications. This session brings together advances in the development, evaluation, integration, and application of P and ET datasets across scales, climates, and hydrological contexts. We invite contributions in the following: 1 Evaluation and benchmarking of P and ET datasets How can we systematically evaluate the growing number of datasets across hydroclimates and spatial scales? Which statistical and hydrological metrics are most appropriate for assessing quality and suitability? How can we quantify and propagate uncertainty and biases in water-related analyses? Can community datasets and evaluation frameworks enhance comparability and reproducibility? 2 Approaches for dataset development and integration How can hydroinformatics, including artificial intelligence, uncertainty quantification, data fusion, and data assimilation, improve datasets? How can cloud computing, high-performance computing, and open-source workflows facilitate evaluations? What role can FAIR principles accelerate the development and adoption of new datasets? 3 Applications in hydrological modeling and assessments How does uncertainty in datasets impact model calibration, evaluation, and prediction? Which datasets are most appropriate for various applications, including flood forecasting or drought monitoring? How can multiple datasets be combined to improve hydrological consistency and reduce uncertainty in changing environmental conditions? 4 Emerging datasets and future directions How can next-generation satellite missions, reanalysis products, and hybrid datasets improve P and ET estimation and evaluation? What methods are required to evaluate increasingly high-resolution and multi-source datasets? How can we establish standards, benchmark protocols, and collaborative platforms to support transparent evaluation and fitness for purpose assessment?
title: Precipitation and Evapotranspiration Datasets for Hydrological Studies: Development, Evaluation, and Applications

description: Advances in differentiable modelling and artificial intelligence are creating new opportunities to improve how hydrologic processes are represented, diagnosed, and learned from data. This session welcomes contributions spanning process-based, data-driven, physics-informed, and hybrid hydrologic modelling. Topics include differentiable model structures, large-sample learning and regionalisation, sensitivity analysis, uncertainty quantification, diagnosis of model misspecification, and methods for discovering or refining process representations. We particularly encourage studies that use artificial intelligence to identify missing or inadequate processes, develop interpretable model components, quantify predictive and structural uncertainty, or improve transfer across locations, time periods, and hydrologic regimes. Contributions on numerical methods, analytic and automatic differentiation, trustworthy evaluation, and applications across spatial and temporal scales are also welcome. By bringing together hydrologists, hydroinformaticians, and machine-learning researchers, the session aims to advance models that are computationally efficient, scientifically interpretable, and better able to characterise uncertainty and structural limitations.
title: Differentiable and AI-Assisted Hydrologic Modeling: Process Representation, Uncertainty, and Model Discovery

description: In recent decades, dry-hot compound extremes, characterized by concurrent droughts and heatwaves, have significantly changed in their intensity, spatial modes, and temporal evolution. These emerging changes may reflect that the climatic boundary conditions causing dry-hot compound extremes could cross critical thresholds, with potential cascading effects that are fundamentally shifting the pattern of dry-hot compound extremes toward a new regime. This poses novel and often unanticipated extreme disasters, severely challenging the adaptability of local ecosystems and human health. This session aims to advance our understanding of dry-hot compound extremes by integrating observational analyses, climate modeling, and artificial intelligence frameworks. Key focuses include: 1) Novel theories and methodologies for terrestrial heatwave understanding—elucidating mechanisms from the perspective of land-atmosphere-ocean coupling; 2) Drivers and mechanisms—elucidating dynamic (e.g., shifts of atmospheric circulation, and transitions of ocean circulation state) and thermodynamic (e.g., direct warming effect of greenhouse gases) processes changing compound events; 3) Long-term changes—quantifying historical trends, current intensification, future trajectories and abrupt changes under emission scenarios; 4) Climate effects—assessing cascading impacts on vegetation, ecosystem carbon cycling, and its modulation on aerosol formation.
title: Dry-hot compound extremes in a warming world: critical thresholds, emerging regimes, and tipping cascading risks

description: Kelvin-Helmholtz Instability (KHI) is a fundamental plasma process driven by velocity shears, being ubiquitous in both fluids and plasmas. It has been observed in the magnetospheres of planets with (e.g. Earth, Mercury, Jupiter, Saturn) and without a magnetic field (e.g. Mars, Venus), as well as in the solar corona and solar wind at the boundary of coronal mass ejections. Contrary to neutral fluids, which are always unstable to KHI, in a magnetized environment, the magnetic field plays a crucial role acting as a stabilizer. As a driver of large-scale vortices along the boundary, KHI contributes to mass and momentum transport, enabling plasma mixing that would otherwise be limited in a highly magnetized environment. Moreover, as the instability grows, vortices become increasingly steepened and rolled-up. The nonlinear interaction of modes produces an energy cascade from the large-scale vortices to kinetic scales, where dissipation mechanisms such as wave-particle interactions and reconnection heat the plasma. The nonlinear evolution of KHI-generated vortices can trigger secondary processes or waves, such as Rayleigh-Taylor instability, lower hybrid waves, and generate thin current sheets where magnetic reconnection can occur, as well as develop a turbulent environment.
title: Kelvin-Helmholtz Instability dynamics in the solar system

description: The importance of ionospheric research is increasing alongside the development of modern terrestrial and space-based technologies, given that the ionosphere reflects and modifies the radio waves used for communication and navigation. Understanding coupling processes is crucial to understanding ionospheric dynamics and variability. The ionosphere is influenced by various solar and magnetospheric processes from above. The strongest of these are well-developed magnetic storms. These are both ICME- and CIR/HSS-related. However, many other drivers remain poorly understood. Conversely, the ionosphere is primarily forced from below by atmospheric waves, such as planetary, tidal, and acoustic-gravity waves. This symposium invites observational, simulation and modelling studies addressing ionospheric dynamics, with a particular focus on magnetospheric and lower atmospheric forcing and the associated feedback on ionospheric variability. We particularly welcome new results focusing on the latitudinal, seasonal and hemispherical effects of magnetic storms and substorms on the ionosphere. Regarding atmospheric forcing, contributions focusing on atmospheric waves, wave-wave interactions, wave-mean flow interactions, atmospheric electricity and electrodynamic coupling processes are sought. Contributions examining ionospheric effects caused by other phenomena, such as the solar terminator, solar eclipses, seismic activity, or human-made explosions, are also welcome. This session invites contributions on the use of AI as a tool for searching for, processing and analysing ionospheric measurements, as well as for validating and refining ionospheric models. Therefore, knowledge of how to use AI as a tool in ionosphere research is highly desirable.
title: Open Session on the Ionosphere and Thermosphere

description: This session discusses plasma processes at and around the Moon, from kinetic scales such as plasma-surface interactions and mini-magnetospheres to the global-scale Earth-Moon magnetospheric system. We invite contributions on space plasma processes occurring at and around the Moon, including the lunar wake, mini-magnetospheres, plasma-surface interactions, surface charging, plasma-exosphere-dust-regolith coupling, energetic particle environment, and space weather at the Moon. Studies using the Moon as an observing platform for terrestrial magnetospheric and heliospheric processes, as well as for space weather monitoring, are equally welcome. Comparative studies of plasma processes at the Moon and at Earth, Mercury, Mars, Venus, asteroids, Phobos, Deimos, and outer planetary moons are also encouraged. We welcome contributions based on data analysis, theoretical studies, numerical simulations, new methodology, laboratory experiments, space instrumentation, future mission concepts, and combinations thereof.
title: The Moon as a Heliophysics Laboratory: Space Weather, Plasma-Surface interactions, and Interdisciplinary Magnetospheric Physics

description: The Sun-Earth system changes on timescales from decades to millennia. Solar activity has declined from the twentieth-century Grand Maximum, geomagnetic activity has followed with its own lag and response, and the coupled magnetosphere-ionosphere-thermosphere system responds to these drivers while also undergoing anthropogenic change from increasing greenhouse gases and ozone recovery. Disentangling these trends and their interactions is essential for understanding the long-term behaviour of the heliosphere and for interpreting historical, proxy, and instrumental records. This session brings together the communities studying long-term change across all sub-systems of Sun-to-planet interactions. We invite contributions on: secular variability of solar activity, irradiance and magnetic field, including proxy reconstructions and the solar-stellar connection; the long-term evolution of the solar wind, heliospheric magnetic field, and cosmic-ray modulation; centennial trends in geomagnetic activity and solar-terrestrial coupling; trends in the ionosphere, thermosphere and mesosphere and their separation into solar, geomagnetic, and anthropogenic components; and the multi-cycle response of planetary upper atmospheres and ionospheres, notably at Mars and Venus, as revealed by long-lived orbiter missions. Observational, proxy-based, and modelling studies are welcome, as are contributions on data homogeneity and trend-detection methodology. Contributions from international working groups and programmes addressing long-term trends in solar-terrestrial relations (e.g. SCOSTEP, IAU, ISSI) are particularly welcome.
title: Long-term trends and variability in the Sun-planet system: solar, heliospheric, magnetospheric and upper-atmospheric changes

description: The high-latitude ionosphere is a highly dynamic environment shaped by solar and magnetospheric forcing, atmospheric dynamics, and plasma transport across a wide range of spatial and temporal scales. Understanding these processes requires coordinated observations and modelling, supported by complementary techniques including incoherent scatter radars, GNSS networks, magnetometers, optical instruments, satellites, and other remote-sensing systems. This session brings together observational and modelling studies that use multiple techniques to investigate high-latitude ionospheric variability, plasma structuring and transport, auroral processes, and atmosphere-ionosphere-magnetosphere coupling. We particularly encourage contributions addressing multi-instrument observations, observation-model comparisons, cross-validation, data integration, and challenges associated with observing and modelling processes across different spatial and temporal scales. The session will also provide a forum to discuss the coordination of high-latitude observations, development of integrated observational and modelling approaches, and opportunities for collaborative campaigns and shared strategies in preparation for the 5th International Polar Year (2032-2033).
title: Observations and Modelling of the High-Latitude Ionosphere

description: This session presents an integrated approach based on infrasound records from the I17CI station to reconstruct the atmospheric dynamics and thermal structure of the atmospheric column over Côte d’Ivoire and the wider West African region. The session will cover the full methodological chain, including spectro-temporal signal processing, inversion of propagation parameters, and joint assimilation with MERRA-2 reanalysis data. It will also highlight operational applications such as seismic and explosion detection, early monitoring of convective storms, detection of volcanic eruptions, and identification of industrial incidents. Finally, the session will discuss the technical implementation using MATLAB tools, validation through case studies, and the benefits for forecasting, civil security, and national capacity building.
title: Infrasound in West Africa: Atmospheric Dynamics and Operational Monitoring Using the I17CI Station

description: Solar wind and the interplanetary magnetic field (IMF) power and drive the dynamics in the geospace and planetary magnetospheres and ionospheres in the solar system. Characteristics of the processes involved in the solar wind-magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling are essential to be studied to better understand how mass, momentum and energy are transferred between these regions. The consequences of the coupling are also vital to be investigated to fully understand all phenomena that are controlled by the solar wind conditions, such as the magnetosphere configuration, plasma convection, electric currents, ULF waves and ring current/radiation belt dynamics. This session welcomes presentations on recent advances in the solar wind-magnetosphere and/or ionosphere coupling within Earth and planetary space environments. Also, presentations connecting various ionospheric and auroral phenomena with their magnetospheric counterparts/solar wind drivers and exploring coupling mechanisms are invited. Studies discussing space-based and/or ground-based observations as well as theoretical and/or modelling perspectives are highly encouraged.
title: Solar Wind Coupling to Magnetospheres and Ionospheres, and Phenomenological Consequences

description: The Earth's middle atmosphere, mesosphere, and lower thermosphere (MLT) region provide a great platform for studying ionospheric dynamics, disturbances, eddy mixing, atmospheric drag effects, and space debris tracking. The thermal structure of these regions is influenced by numerous energy sources such as solar radiation, chemical, and dynamical processes, as well as forces from both above (e.g., solar and magnetospheric inputs) and below (e.g., gravity waves and atmospheric tides). Solar atmospheric tides, related to global-scale variations of temperature, density, pressure, and wind waves, are responsible for coupling the lower and upper layers of the atmosphere and significantly impact their vertical profiles in the upper atmosphere. With evidence of climate change impacts on the middle and upper atmosphere, monitoring and understanding trends through observational data is critical. There has been a contraction of the stratosphere and a decrease in the density of the upper atmosphere, which could impact the accumulation of space debris. This session invites presentations on scientific work related to various experimental/observational techniques, numerical and empirical modeling, and theoretical analyses on the dynamics, chemistry, and coupling processes in the altitude range of ~ 20 km to 180 km of the middle atmosphere and MLT regions, including long-term climatic changes.
title: Dynamics, Chemistry, and Coupling in the Middle Atmosphere and MLT Regions

description: Internal gravity waves (IGWs) still pose major questions in atmospheric and ocean sciences and stellar physics. Fundamental issues include IGW radiation from various sources, reflection at boundaries, propagation through and interaction with larger-scale flows, wave-induced mean flow, wave-wave interactions, wave breaking and its implications for mixing, and parameterizing these processes in models that do not explicitly resolve IGWs. The observational record, both globally and for local small-scale processes, is not yet sufficient to yield appropriate constraints. The session aims to bring together experts from all fields of geophysical fluid dynamics working on related problems. Presentations on theoretical, modeling, experimental, and observational work on all aspects of IGWs are welcome, including those on major collaborative projects that seek to accurately resolve or parameterize IGWs in numerical models. Participation from early-career researchers is encouraged.
title: Internal Gravity Waves

description: Mid-latitude cyclones and storms are key drivers of weather variability, extremes, and associated socio-economic impacts across densely populated regions of the globe. Understanding their observed and projected trends is crucial for improving climate diagnostics, risk assessments, and adaptation strategies in a warming climate. This topic therefore addresses both fundamental scientific challenges and urgent societal needs by linking physical processes, climate change signals, and potential impacts. This session encourages contributions covering mid-latitude storm systems, including but not limited to the following topics: • Fundamental dynamics of cyclones - in all different stages of their life cycle - and their mesoscale features (e.g., fronts, jets, precipitation structures, dry intrusions, and diabatic processes) • Representation of mid-latitude storms in AI-based weather and climate models • Diagnostics of observed and projected trends in cyclone frequency, intensity, and storm tracks; including potential insights from contributions from measurement campaigns • Predictability and forecasting on synoptic to sub-seasonal time scales • Innovative methods, including AI/ML approaches, for cyclone detection, classification, or impact assessment • Storm-related impacts, vulnerabilities, and risk-transfer mechanisms under a changing climate By bringing together communities working on dynamics, diagnostics, impacts, field campaigns, and new methodologies, this session aims to provide a comprehensive platform for advancing our understanding of mid-latitude cyclones and their role in the past, present, and future climate system.
title: Mid-latitude Cyclones and Storms: Dynamics, Diagnostics of Observed and Future Trends, and Related Impacts

description: The atmospheric water cycle is a key component of the climate system, and links across many scientific disciplines. Processes interact with dynamics at different scales throughout the atmospheric life cycle of water vapour from evaporation to precipitation. This session sets the focus on understanding the interaction between processes, their dynamics and characteristics of the water cycle, covering the entire atmospheric life cycle from evaporation, atmospheric moisture transport, to cloud microphysics and precipitation processes as observed from in-situ and remote sensing instrumentation, recorded by paleo-/climate archives, and as simulated by models for past, present and future climates. We invite studies * focusing on the understanding and impacts of features of the atmospheric water cycle related to weather systems, with a special focus on the role of Atmospheric Rivers, Cold-Air Outbreaks, Warm Conveyor Belts, Tropical Moisture Exports, and the global Monsoon systems; * investigating the large-scale drivers behind the past, ongoing and future variability and trends within the atmospheric water cycle, from field campaigns (CAESAR, NAWDIC, (AC)3, ISLAS, AWACA etc.), long-term observations, reanalysis data, regional to global model simulations, or (isotopic) data assimilation; * reconstructing past hydroclimates based on paleo-proxy records from archives such as ice cores, lake sediments, tree-rings or speleothems; * applying methods such as tagged water tracers and Lagrangian moisture source diagnostics to identify source-sink relationships and to evaluate model simulations of the water cycle; * using the isotopic fingerprint of atmospheric processes and weather systems to obtain new mechanistic insights into changes in the water cycle through isotope-enabled models and observations; * describing the global and regional state of the atmospheric water cycle (e.g. monsoon systems) with characteristics such as the recycling ratio, life time of water vapour, and moisture transport properties. We particularly encourage contributions linking across neighbouring disciplines, such as atmospheric science, climate, paleoclimate, glaciology, and hydrology.
title: The atmospheric water cycle: processes, dynamics, isotopic tracers, and characteristics

description: This session welcomes contributions on atmospheric convection, including dry, shallow, or deep convection. A particular session focus is the organization of convection, such as mesoscale convective systems, convectively-coupled waves, idealized studies of self-aggregation, or research on the importance of organization for climate sensitivity. Additionally, submissions that address other aspects of convection like the convective lifecycle and structures including cold pools, interactions of convection with other physical processes or the representation of convection in numerical weather prediction and climate models are strongly encouraged. The research can use any tool, from idealized theoretical models, large-eddy simulations, convection-permitting simulations, to coarser-resolution simulations using parameterised convection, machine learning techniques, or observations and field campaigns.
title: Atmospheric convection

description: The uncertain response of clouds to global warming is a major contributor to uncertainty in climate sensitivity. Cloud feedback uncertainty is related to a limited understanding of the coupling between clouds, convection and the large-scale circulation across various spatial and temporal scales. Today's wealth of advanced remote-sensing observations and high-resolution modelling data provides comprehensive and complementary information that enables detailed process and lifecycle-based analyses. This session focuses on (1) efforts to advance our understanding of the cloud-circulation coupling and its role in climate change, and (2) Lagrangian studies related to clouds and water vapour. We invite contributions from dedicated field campaigns, from ground-based and satellite remote sensing or in situ measurements, as well as modelling and theoretical studies. We particularly welcome the results from various ongoing model inter-comparison projects, like EUREC4A-MIP, CP-MIP and Lagrangian LES MIP. We also invite abstracts focusing on the role of mesoscale convective organisation, aerosol-cloud interactions, feature tracking, and Lagrangian cloud modelling.
title: Advancing understanding of the circulation-coupling and Lagrangian evolution of clouds

description: Interactions between organised deep convection and large-scale scale circulations are increasingly recognised to play a crucial role in shaping atmospheric dynamics. Convective organisation itself depends on smaller-scale interactions involving individual convective plumes and cloud microphysical processes. A cascade of interactions across scales thereby underpins mesoscale convective systems and other meteorological phenomena that drive extreme hydroclimatic events. Understanding these interactions is important for assessing changes in hazardous convective weather and its impacts in a warming climate. Challenging the conventional assumption of strict scale separation, these interactions may also be key to understanding persistent discrepancies between observed and simulated regional climate change. Global kilometre-scale atmospheric models and multidecadal observations over large domains are opening new opportunities to gain insights into the role of mesoscale convection in shaping circulation patterns for the first time. This session aims to brings together recent advances in understanding how atmospheric convective scale-interactions feedback on larger-scale circulations, and influence local and downstream climate extremes and their changes under warming. The session is intended to translate advances in modelling and observations into improved physical understanding of atmospheric dynamics. We invite contributions focusing on mesoscale convective system dynamics and cloud microphysics, upscale effects of convection, and large-scale controls on convective organisation. Relevant contributions include advances in high-resolution modelling, forecasts and climate projections of these interactions, and insights from novel observations. We also invite contributions on the processes driving the formation and evolution of organised deep convection, and how these factors shape spatio-temporal patterns of deep convective intensity, precipitation, and on-the-ground hazards. This includes, but is not limited to, contributions on land-convection interactions in connection with mesoscale and severe storms. Examples include effects of complex topography, soil moisture feedbacks, and land use or land-use change, such as urbanisation, deforestation, or irrigation. We welcome diverse perspectives towards advancing physical understanding of convective processes, and quantifying their interactions across scales.
title: Mesoscale deep convection and scale-interactions: from cloud processes to extremes, upscale growth, and large-scale circulation feedbacks
