description: Atmospheric rivers (ARs) are narrow and transient channels of intense water vapor transport in the lower troposphere. They account for 90% of poleward moisture transport and drive high-impact weather and hydrological extremes all around the globe. Future projections suggest that landfalling ARs will become even more hazardous as they further intensify in a warmer climate. Given the fundamental role of ARs in the global water cycle, relevant research is rapidly expanding across different disciplines. With new data sources and novel methodological approaches, the multidisciplinary AR community has been breaking ground and posing fundamental questions for the understanding of AR processes and impacts. By bringing together experts from diverse disciplines, this session aims to provide a comprehensive platform for discussing the latest advances in AR science. We invite all contributions that aim at a better understanding of AR uncertainties, processes, and impacts across past, present, and future climates at regional to global scales. Relevant topics of the session include, but are not limited to: • Observation, identification, and monitoring of ARs • Physical, dynamical, & microphysical aspects of ARs • Aerosol & biochemical aspects of ARs • ARs and the surface energy budget • Environmental and socioeconomic impacts of AR-induced weather extremes • ARs as a component of compound events • AR dynamics and impacts in understudied regions • Role of ARs in the changing Cryosphere • Forecasting of ARs • ARs in past, present, and future climates
title: Atmospheric rivers: Understanding their processes and impacts across past, present, and future climates

description: Cold clouds (mixed-phase and ice) play an important role in the Earth’s radiation budget because of their high temporal and spatial coverage and their interaction with long wave and short wave radiation. Yet, the variability and complexity of their macro- and microphysical properties, the consequence of intricate ice particle nucleation and growth processes, make their study extremely challenging. As a result, large uncertainties still exist in our understanding of cold cloud processes, their radiative effects, and their interaction with their environment (in particular, aerosols). This session aims to advance our comprehension of cold clouds by bringing observation- and modelling-based research together. A diversity of research topics shall be covered, highlighting recent advances in cloud observation techniques, modelling, and subsequent process studies: (1) Airborne, space borne, ground- or laboratory-based measurements and their derived products (retrievals), which are useful to constrain cloud properties like extent, emissivity, or crystal size distributions, to clarify formation mechanisms, and to provide climatology. (2) Process-based, regional, and global model simulations that employ observations for better representation of cloud microphysical properties and radiative forcing under both current and future climate. The synthesis of these approaches can uniquely answer questions regarding dynamical influence on cloud formation, life cycle, coverage, microphysical and radiative properties, crystal shapes, sizes, and variability of ice particles in mixed-phase as well as ice clouds. Joint observation-modelling contributions are therefore particularly encouraged.
title: Mixed-phase and ice cloud observations and modelling

description: The session is addressed to experimentalists and modellers working on air-land interactions from local to regional scales. The programme is open to a wide range of new studies in micrometeorology and related atmospheric and remote sensing disciplines. It is also open to studies investigating how turbulent transport and surface-layer processes upscale from the atmospheric boundary layer to mesoscale dynamics and ultimately to large-scale circulation in weather and climate systems. The topics include the development of new devices, measurement techniques, experimental design, data analysis methods, as well as novel findings on surface layer theory and parametrization, including local and non-local processes. The theoretical parts encompass soil-vegetation-atmosphere transport, internal boundary-layer theories and flux footprint analyses. Of special interest are synergistic studies employing experimental data, parametrisations and models. This includes energy and trace gas fluxes (inert and reactive) as well as water, carbon dioxide and other GHG fluxes. Specific focus is given to outstanding problems in land surface boundary layer descriptions such as complex terrain, effects of horizontal heterogeneity on sub-meso-scale transport processes, energy balance closure, stable stratification and night time fluxes, dynamic interactions with atmosphere, plants (in canopy and above canopy) and soils.
title: Air-Land Interactions (General Session)

description: Polar clouds play a fundamental role in high latitude climate but are challenging to model due to uncertainties in representing fundamental cloud processes, such as microphysical processes that determine phase partitioning between ice and radiatively important cloud liquid water, which drives the turbulence that maintains the system. New observations of polar clouds can address questions about the role of surface fluxes, coupling with atmospheric radiation, potential secondary ice production, sources of aerosols, impacts on sea ice and the surface energy budget, and triggers for transitions, among other processes. Recent field campaigns provide new insights, new hypotheses, but also new questions, about the mechanisms and feedback that cause the formation and persistence of polar clouds. This session welcomes papers on scientific results from recent campaigns such as ARCSIX, CAESAR, (AC)³, MOSAiC, among other Arctic expeditions and campaigns. Clouds of interest include mixed-phase clouds, ice clouds, cold-air outbreaks, and clouds over different surface conditions. In addition, we welcome papers on new technologies and strategies for observing polar clouds.
title: Insights into polar clouds from recent field campaigns: Advances in understanding and new challenges to inform future campaigns

description: The stratospheric circulation exerts an important influence on tropospheric weather and climate. Key phenomena—including the stratospheric polar vortex, the Brewer–Dobson circulation, and the Quasi-Biennial Oscillation—modulate atmospheric wave propagation, drive downward dynamical influences on the troposphere, and control the transport and mixing of climatically important chemical constituents. Understanding, observing, and accurately simulating stratospheric dynamics are therefore essential for improving predictions of weather and climate variability and change. This session will examine the causes and consequences of variations in stratospheric circulation, including natural and anthropogenic drivers, chemical transport and mixing processes, stratosphere–troposphere coupling, and implications for weather and climate prediction. We welcome abstracts that address these topics from observational, modeling, or theoretical perspectives and across a wide range of spatial and temporal scales.
title: Stratospheric Dynamics and Connections to Surface Weather and Climate

description: Precipitation, both liquid and solid, is central to the global water/energy cycle through its coupling of clouds, water vapor, atmospheric motion, ocean circulation, and land surface processes. While precipitation is the primary source of freshwater, it also has tremendous socio-economic impacts associated with extreme weather events such as hurricanes, floods, droughts, and landslides. Knowledge of precipitation characteristics from local to global scales is essential for understanding how the Earth system operates under changing climatic conditions and for improved societal applications that range from numerical weather prediction to freshwater resource management. This session will host papers on all aspects of precipitation, especially contributions in the following four research areas: 1. Precipitation measurements (amount, duration, intensity etc) by ground-based in-situ sensors (e.g., rain gauges, disdrometers); estimation of accuracy of measurements, comparison of instrumentation. 2. Precipitation climatologies at regional to global scales; areal distribution of measured precipitation; classification of precipitation patterns; spatial and temporal characteristics of precipitation; methodologies adopted and their uncertainties; comparative studies. 3. Remote sensing of precipitation (spaceborne, airborne, ground-based, underwater, or shipborne sensors) and retrieval techniques; methodologies to estimate areal precipitation (interpolation, downscaling, combination of measurements and/or estimates of precipitation); methodologies used for the estimation (e.g., QPE), validation, and assessment of error and uncertainty of precipitation as estimated by remote sensors. 4. Contributions to current and future missions, such as the international Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) mission, Atmospheric Observing System (AOS), EUMETSAT Polar System-Second Generation (EPS-SG), Time-Resolved Observations of Precipitation structure and storm Intensity with a Constellation of Smallsats (TROPICS), Arctic Weather Satellite (AWS), Earth Clouds, Aerosol and Radiation Explorer (EarthCARE), tomorrow.io constellation and the Advanced Microwave Scanning Radiometer-3 (AMSR-3).
title: Precipitation: Measurement, Climatology, Remote Sensing, and Modelling

description: Storm and convective-scale weather data analysis and prediction still present significant challenges for the atmospheric sciences. Making progress requires synergy of advances in high spatial and temporal resolution observations, storm and convective-scale data assimilation methodology, machine learning and ensemble modeling. This session intent is to provide a platform for exchange on the state-of-the-art developments, ongoing progress and ideas for future directions in all aspects of this multifaceted challenge This session invites contributions from developments in • Storm and convective-scale data assimilation techniques • Multi-scale data assimilation techniques • Use of machine learning in convective-scale data assimilation • Applications of machine learning to forecasting on convective scales • Convective-scale model and observation uncertainty representation • Ensemble design and uncertainty quantification at storm and convective scales using machine learning • Convective-scale modeling and parameter estimation • Assimilation of ground and space-based radar data • Assimilation of geostationary satellite observations • All-sky satellite data assimilation at storm and convective scales • Observation operators for remote sensing • Assessment of the impact of convective-scale data assimilation on weather prediction • Observations at convective scales: new observing technologies and strategies
title: Developments in Convective-Scale Data Assimilation, Machine Learning and Observations

description: This session welcomes papers on applying physical principles and artificial intelligence, or their fusion, to develop, evaluate, and improve numerical weather prediction models. Papers on using physics, machine learning techniques and observations to address research and applications questions in the following topics are highly encouraged: 1) Forecasting and simulating high-impact weather events - research on using advanced artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques to improve numerical weather model prediction of severe weather events (such as winter storms, tropical storms, and severe mesoscale convective storms); 2) Development and improvement of model numerics - basic research on advanced numerical techniques for weather and climate models (such as cloud-resolving global models and high-resolution regional models specialized for extreme weather events on sub-synoptic scales); 3) Development and improvement of model physics - progress in research on advanced model physics parameterization schemes (such as stochastic physics, air-wave-ocean coupling physics, turbulent diffusion and interaction with the surface, sub-grid condensation and convection, grid-resolved cloud and precipitation, land-surface parameterization, and radiation); 4) Verification of model physics and forecast products against theories and observations; 5) Data assimilation systems - progress in the development of data assimilation systems for operational applications (such as reanalysis and climate services), research on advanced methods for data assimilation on various scales (such as treatment of model and observation errors in data assimilation, and observational network design and experiments); 6) Ensemble forecasts and predictability - strategies in ensemble construction, model resolution and forecast range-related issues, and applications to data assimilation; 7) Advances and challenges in applying data from various conventional and avant-garde observation platforms to evaluate and improve high-resolution simulations and forecasting.
title: Numerical Weather Prediction as Applications of Physics and Artificial Intelligence

description: Midlatitude dynamics emerge from the interaction of different scales, ranging from planetary-scale atmospheric jets and synoptic storms to mesoscale circulations associated with fronts and convection. While we have well-established theories for the development of fronts, extratropical cyclones, climatological jet streams, and convection, our understanding on the feedback and dynamical linkages between these spatio-temporal scales is still incomplete. Another prominent challenge is related to diabatic processes that are regularly not well represented in weather and climate models and for which we often lack a theoretical foundation. These processes, including surface fluxes, latent heating, and radiative processes, provide key dynamical linkages across scales. Recent efforts attributing climatological signals to synoptic-scale features have revealed nuanced dynamical insights in the functioning of the general circulation as well as the role of sub-synoptic scale structures, such as fronts, warm conveyor belts, and atmospheric rivers, on the evolution of synoptic storms and large-scale waves. Relatedly, there has been significant progress on linking limits in predictability to up- and down-scale error propagation, ranging from convective to planetary scales. However, our fundamental understanding of the dynamic and diabatic interactions between these scales remains rather limited. We therefore invite contributions that aim to address our understanding of the role of dynamic and diabatic interactions across scales including, but not limited to, the following topics: • Dynamic and diabatic processes connecting scales from convection, clouds, and fronts to cyclones, storm tracks, and large-scale waves • Coupling between the ocean and land surface and the atmosphere across scales • Predictability and forecasting across scales, including representation in AI-based weather and climate models • Innovative methods (for example linking Eulerian, feature-based, and Lagrangian methods) to diagnose cross-scale interactions
title: Dynamic and diabatic processes linking across scales in the midlatitudes – from convection and fronts to cyclones and storm tracks

description: This session is intended to provide an interdisciplinary forum to bring together researchers working in the areas of atmospheric and snow/ice physics, atmospheric chemistry, air quality, biogeochemistry, oceanography, meteorology and climate in the polar regions. The emphasis is on the role of polar boundary layer processes that drive exchange fluxes of heat, momentum and mass between the Earth's surface (snowpack, sea-ice, surface ocean and land) and the atmosphere as well as the local to large-scale influences on these exchanges. An adequate understanding and quantification of these processes is necessary to improve modelling and prediction of future changes in the polar regions and their teleconnections with mid-latitude weather and climate. These changing processes include meridional transport of heat, moisture, chemical trace species, and aerosols; regional emission and vertical mixing of climate active trace gases and aerosol, such as cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) and ice nucleating particles (INP), their precursors, and their radiative effects; and air-sea(ice) fluxes of CO2 and CH4. It is expected that observations from recent field campaigns, data from existing networks, and modelling efforts, will help diagnose long-range and local moisture, trace gas, aerosol and greenhouse gas sources as well as the coupling between local and large-scale dynamics and their impacts on climate, health and ecosystems. Reporting on progress as well as critical knowledge gaps will contribute to upcoming research programmes Antarctica InSync and the 5th International Polar Year. We encourage submissions such as (but not limited to): (1) External controls on the boundary layer such as clouds, radiation and long-range transport processes (2) Results from field programs and routine observatories, insights from laboratory studies, and advances in modeling and reanalysis, (3) Use of data from pan-Arctic and Antarctic observing networks, (4) Surface processes involving snow, sea-ice, surface ocean, land/atmosphere chemical exchanges, natural aerosol sources and gas air-sea flux (5) Studies on atmospheric chemistry and air pollution during polar winter (6) The role of boundary layers in polar climate change and implications of climate change for physical and chemical surface exchange processes, especially in the context of changes in sea ice coverage and age, wetter snow packs, and increased glacial discharge.
title: Surface Exchange Processes in the Polar Boundary Layer: Physics, Chemistry, and Aerosols

description: Surface exchange fluxes of mass over the global oceans have significant impacts on atmospheric composition, biogeochemistry and climate at regional to global scales. Atmospheric boundary layer processes mediate these fluxes. This session is intended to provide an interdisciplinary forum to bring together researchers working in the areas of meteorology, atmospheric chemistry, air quality, biogeochemistry, stable isotope research, oceanography, and climate over the global oceans, focusing on new research in a range of relevant topics. These include: air-sea fluxes of radiatively active trace gases (CO2, CH4, N2O, CO), regional emissions and transport of climate-relevant aerosols and their precursors (e.g., dimethyl sulfide [DMS], marine organic compounds, and halogenated species), atmospheric deposition of nutrients (e.g., nitrogen, phosphorus, and iron) and associated impacts on ocean biological systems, and biogeochemistry-climate feedback loops in the ocean-atmosphere system. Studies on characterization of these fluxes, their underlying control processes and how they may change in response to climate change in different scales are welcome. The session has long-standing links to the Surface Ocean ̶ Lower Atmosphere Study (SOLAS) and GESAMP Working Group 38 on atmospheric input of chemicals to the ocean. We welcome submissions from all remit areas of these programs, and from a range of analysis approaches: field measurements, remote sensing, laboratory studies, and atmospheric and oceanic numerical models. This year we particularly welcome contributions on the following specialist themes: The impacts of extreme events on air-sea gas exchange of climate-relevant compounds in marine systems. Studies addressing physical drivers such as marine heatwaves, storms and tropical cyclones, flooding events circulation anomalies, or changes in sea ice; biogeochemical drivers, like hypoxic or anoxic conditions and acidification pulses; biological drivers, like harmful algal blooms; or compound events. The role of anthropogenic activities in the production and air-sea exchange of gases, aerosols, pollutants in coastal regions (e.g. direct ship traffic emissions, indirect emissions caused by ship wakes, effects of wind parks, effluents from waste water treatment plants, and mariculture activities). Studies on these special topics may address impacts in all oceanic domains; e.g., open ocean, shelf waters, and shallow coastal ecosystems.
title: Air-Sea Biogeochemical Fluxes: Impacts on Atmospheric Composition, Biogeochemistry and Climate

description: Driven by atmospheric turbulence, and integrating surface processes to free atmospheric conditions, the Atmospheric Boundary Layer (ABL) plays a key role not only in weather and climate, but also in air quality and wind/solar energy. It is in this context that this session invites theoretical, numerical and observational studies ranging from fundamental aspects of atmospheric turbulence, to parameterizations of the boundary layer, and to renewable energy or air pollution applications. Below we propose a list of the topics included: - Observational methods in the Atmospheric Boundary Layer - Simulation and modelling of ABL: from turbulence to boundary layer schemes - Stable Boundary Layers, gravity waves and intermittency - Evening and morning transitions of the ABL - Convective processes in the ABL - Boundary Layer Clouds and turbulence-fog interactions - Micro-Mesoscale interactions - Micrometeorology in complex terrain - Agricultural and Forest processes in the ABL - Diffusion and transport of constituents in the ABL - Turbulence and Air Quality applications - Turbulence and Wind Energy applications - Urban boundary layers
title: Atmospheric Boundary Layer: From Basic Turbulence Studies to Integrated Applications

description: Air pollution remains a pressing global issue, prompting nations worldwide to implement various mitigation strategies, often targeting specific pollutants such as particulate matter. While these strategies are crafted with the best intentions, they sometimes yield unintended effects, including changes in atmospheric chemical composition that lead to phenomena such as increases in ozone or unforeseen climate impacts. This session aims to shed light on the unintended consequences of air pollution mitigation strategies, focusing on the changes in chemical composition induced by these strategies. We invite contributions that delve into the observational data, modeling approaches, and projections of future changes to better understand the full spectrum of effects of pollution control measures. By fostering a discussion grounded in rigorous scientific analysis, we hope to pave the way for more holistic and effective strategies in the future, balancing the urgent need to reduce pollution with a deep understanding of potential unintended effects. We welcome submissions that employ a range of research methods, including - but not limited to - observational studies and modeling to forecast future changes, encouraging a multidisciplinary approach to a complex issue.
title: Atmospheric composition responses to anthropogenic emission changes

description: The aim of this general session is to bring together the scientific community within air pollution modelling. The focus is ongoing research, new results and current problems related to the field of modelling the atmospheric transport and transformation of air pollutants and precursors on global, regional and local scales. All presentations covering the research area of air pollution modelling are welcome, including recent model developments, applications and evaluations, physical and chemical parameterisations, process understanding, model testing, evaluation and uncertainty estimates, emissions, numerical methods, model systems and integration, forecasting, event-studies, scenarios, ensembles, assessment, machine learning, etc.
title: Air Pollution Modelling

description: One of the most intriguing and challenging frontiers in climate science is small-scale air-sea interactions and their potential impact on large-scale circulations. Recent advances in numerical modelling and observational capacity, particularly increased horizontal resolution, have revealed rich small-scale features spanning the ocean submesoscale through the mesoscale (O[1-100 km]) in both the ocean surface and marine atmospheric boundary layer. Submesoscale (permitting) ocean-atmosphere coupled simulations have shown that these small-scale features interact across the fluid interface, thereby modifying exchanges between the ocean and the atmosphere. These exchanges – air-sea fluxes of heat, moisture and momentum – are essential for large-scale circulations, modes of variability in the coupled climate, extreme events, cloudiness, rainfall, and winds, as well as ocean waves, upper-ocean mixing and stratification, and sea surface temperature. This session welcomes submissions that examine air-sea interactions at ocean submesoscale-to-mesoscales, including high-resolution air-sea flux variability, influences of surface heterogeneity and coupled boundary layer dynamics, as well as their impacts on large-scale weather statistics, overturning circulations, and climate. All observational, modelling, and theoretical approaches are welcome. We particularly encourage submissions that use km-scale coupled modelling outputs (including those generated at regional-to-global scale hackathon events) and new observational data from space or field campaigns; present novel theoretical understanding; and those that apply integrated observation-modelling-theory or multi-scale modelling approaches.
title: Submesoscale-to-Mesoscale Air-Sea Interactions and Their Role in Weather and Climate

description: This session focuses on the application of spectroscopic remote sensing techniques for measuring atmospheric trace gases and related properties. We welcome studies on any method that exploits absorption along open atmospheric light paths using natural or artificial light sources. This encompasses the full range of DOAS applications (e.g. MAX-DOAS, zenith-sky, direct-sun, long-path DOAS), hyperspectral imaging techniques, direct-sun and open-path Fourier-transform spectroscopy (FTS), and related or emerging techniques. Collectively, contributions to this session help to bridge the spatial and temporal scales between in-situ point measurements and satellite remote sensing, including: – Greenhouse gas and air quality monitoring, – Gas transport and quantification of emission fluxes, – Retrieval of spatial distribution of trace gases and aerosols. Moreover, the aim of this session is to gain insights into algorithm developments, instrument improvements, and practical field application, including instrument synergies, satellite validation, and cross-platform comparison.
title: Spectroscopic Remote Sensing of Atmospheric Composition

description: Organic compounds play a key role in biosphere-atmosphere exchange, anthropogenic emissions, and the reactive chemistry responsible for ozone and particulate matter production. Coming from diverse sources and constituting thousands of individual compounds, with varying oxidation mechanisms, the organic composition of the troposphere is complex. With their wide range of lifetimes and volatilities, these species partition between gas and particle phases and make up a substantial fraction of fine particulate matter. Organics are also a major source of atmospheric reactivity, with implications for the oxidative capacity of the atmosphere. Some individual organic compounds are of interest due to their toxicity or use as specific source tracers. Because of organics’ role in secondary pollutant formation and reactivity, this chemistry is highly relevant to air quality from urban to remote regions. Finally, while global budgets of organic species are central to understanding tropospheric oxidative chemistry and aerosol budgets, they remain poorly constrained. This session invites contributions about tropospheric organics on local, regional and global scales, from theoretical studies, laboratory experiments, field measurements, modeling studies, satellite studies, and including measurement technique development. The emphasis of this session is on gas-phase organics, including aerosol precursors and semi-volatile species.
title: Atmospheric organics: Sources, chemistry, and fate

description: Space weather and space climate encompass the dynamic interactions between the Sun and Earth, occurring across timescales from minutes to decades. These interactions involve processes occurring at the Sun, in the heliosphere, magnetosphere, ionosphere, thermosphere, and lower atmosphere. Key drivers include coronal mass ejections (CMEs), interplanetary shocks, and solar energetic particle (SEP) events. Predicting extreme space weather events and developing mitigation strategies is essential because space assets and critical infrastructures, such as satellite systems, communication and navigation networks, power grids, and aviation operations, are highly sensitive to the space environment. Conducting post-event analyses is crucial for improving and maintaining numerical models that can predict extreme space weather events and prevent the failure of critical infrastructures. This session focuses on the current state of space weather products and explores new ideas and developments that can improve our understanding of space weather and space climate and their impact on critical infrastructure. We invite contributions on topics including, but not limited to: forecasting and nowcasting tools and services; satellite observations and data assimilation techniques; numerical model development, validation, and verification; machine learning applications in space weather prediction; generation and refinement of solar, geomagnetic, and ionospheric indices. We particularly welcome interdisciplinary and collaborative approaches that bridge research and operational communities. Contributions that address the drivers and the real-world impacts of space weather on systems such as aviation, pipelines, power distribution, human spaceflight, and auroral tourism are strongly encouraged.
title: Nowcasting, forecasting, operational monitoring, and post-event analysis of space weather and space climate in the Sun-Earth system

description: Collisionless space plasmas present a unique physical environment where charged particles interact not through direct collisions but through electromagnetic waves, making wave-particle interactions a cornerstone of space plasma physics. These interactions shape the spectral properties of plasma waves, regulate particle energisation and loss across a wide range of energies, and drive the evolution of particle distribution functions far from thermal equilibrium. Alongside these processes, a rich variety of kinetic phenomena add further complexity, including current sheet dynamics, nonlinear wave structures such as phase space holes and solitary waves, wave-mode conversion, and non-resonant wave-particle interaction. Together, these processes operate across electron and ion scales, connecting microscale plasma physics to the macroscale evolution of space plasma systems, and challenging traditional frameworks such as quasilinear diffusion theory. A growing fleet of spacecraft, including historical missions like Van Allen Probes, Cluster, Cassini and ongoing missions like MMS, Arase, THEMIS, MAVEN, Juno, Parker Solar Probe, Solar Orbiter, along with CubeSat platforms like ELFIN, FY, CIRBE, REAL, LLITED provide multi-point, high-resolution observations that reveal both common physical mechanisms and intriguing differences across the solar wind, radiation belts, and planetary magnetospheres. These datasets, combined with increasingly sophisticated simulation and modelling tools, are opening new avenues for advancing our understanding of kinetic plasma processes across diverse space environments. This session welcomes contributions from theorists, observationalists, and modellers working across all aspects of wave-particle interactions and kinetic physics in collisionless space plasmas.
title: Wave-Particle Interactions and Plasma Kinetic in Heliosphere and Planetary Magnetospheres

description: Earth's inner magnetosphere contains diverse charged-particle populations, including the Van Allen radiation belts, ring current, and plasmasphere, spanning energies from eV to several MeV. These populations are dynamically coupled through various processes that produce feedback across different plasma regimes. Ring current particles can generate waves, including EMIC and chorus waves, which in turn influence radiation belt dynamics through wave-particle interactions. Ring current electrons can be accelerated to relativistic energies and contribute to the radiation belts, while the plasmaspheric environment can regulate wave generation, propagation, and particle scattering. Coupling also extends beyond the inner magnetosphere. Precipitation of ring current and radiation belt particles modifies the ionosphere and upper atmosphere, while ionospheric outflows can influence magnetospheric plasma populations and dynamics. Understanding such interactions is essential both for advancing fundamental knowledge of magnetospheric dynamics and for improving space weather specification and forecasting. Beyond Earth, the magnetospheres of the outer planets are driven by different combinations of internal and external processes, yet they exhibit many analogous forms of plasma transport, acceleration, loss, and coupling. Comparative studies therefore provide valuable opportunities to identify common physical mechanisms as well as processes unique to individual planetary environments. We invite theoretical, modelling, and observational studies addressing the dynamics and coupling of Earth's and other planetary inner magnetospheres. Relevant topics include interactions among radiation belt, ring current, and plasmaspheric populations; wave particle interactions; magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling; particle precipitation and ionospheric outflow; responses to solar wind disturbances; and comparative magnetospheric physics. Contributions using numerical simulations, satellite and ground-based observations, data assimilation approaches, and new mission concepts are welcome. We particularly encourage studies using observations from missions and facilities such as MMS, THEMIS, Van Allen Probes, Arase (ERG), Cluster, CubeSats, Juno, SuperDARN, magnetometers, optical imagers, incoherent-scatter radars, and ground-based VLF measurements.
title: Inner-Magnetosphere Interactions and Coupling

description: Understanding plasma energisation and energy transport is a grand challenge of space plasma physics. Due to its proximity, the Earth’s Magnetospheric System provides an excellent natural laboratory for the investigation of these phenomena. Fundamental processes such as collisionless shocks, magnetic reconnection, turbulence, wave-particle interactions, plasma jet braking, and their combination initiate and govern particle energisation and energy transport. These processes occur in key magnetospheric regions including the foreshock, the bow shock, the magnetosheath, the magnetopause, the magnetotail current sheet, and the transition region. ESA/Cluster and NASA/MMS four-point constellations, as well as the large-scale multipoint mission NASA/THEMIS, have greatly improved our understanding of these plasma processes at individual scales compared to earlier single-point measurements. However, these missions have also revealed that such processes inherently operate across multiple scales, ranging from large fluid scales to smaller kinetic scales, demonstrating the need for multi-scale in situ observations. In particular, simultaneous measurements at fluid and kinetic scales are required to resolve how energy is transferred between scales and ultimately converted into particle energisation and transported throughout the plasma system. Building on previous single-scale missions, the Plasma Observatory (PO) mission represents the next generation of space plasma physics investigations. PO is a seven-spacecraft multi-scale mission, tailored to study plasma energisation and energy transport in the Earth’s Magnetospheric System simultaneously at both fluid and ion scales. Plasma Observatory has been recommended by the ESA science advisory committees for selection as the M7 mission in the ESA Science Programme. This session invites submissions on multi-scale and cross-scale coupling, including simulations, multi-point techniques, instrumentation, and theory. Submissions addressing connections between in situ measurements, remote sensing, and ground-based observations are also strongly encouraged.
title: Unveiling plasma energization and energy transport in Geospace via multiscale observations

description: The session focuses on the variability of the tropospheric and stratospheric chemical composition on the timescales from diurnal to decadal. It discusses the processes driving this variability and attribution of changes to specific processes. Special emphasis is put on the value of high-quality long-term measurement data sets, including in the context of science-policy applications, and observations sustainability. Supporting model simulations on different scales that utilize observational data will also be discussed. Contributions related to emerging constituents, new data sources and approached to atmospheric composition measurements (e.g. low cost sensor, emerging measurement techniques), measurement campaign that addresses specific processes and long-term projections of the atmospheric chemical composition are also welcome in the session. Researchers are invited to present novel scientific results from mid- and long-term observational time series from various programmes and networks such as the Global Atmosphere Watch (GAW) Programme, European Monitoring, and Evaluation Programme (EMEP), Network for the Detection of Atmospheric Composition Change (NDACC), Southern Hemisphere Additional Ozonesondes (SHADOZ), Advanced Global Atmospheric Gases Experiment (AGAGE), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), regular airborne (e.g. CARIBIC, IAGOS, CONTRAIL) and other campaigns as well as satellite data and model simulations. Data relevant to tropospheric and stratospheric composition, in particular, related to climate change, ozone depletion, ecosystems and health impacts, and air quality as well as firn data on past atmospheric composition are welcome. We welcome contributions from multi-year modeling studies and inter-comparison exercises that address past and future tropospheric or stratospheric composition changes, carried out in the framework of international projects and initiatives.
title: Atmospheric composition variability and trends

description: The urgency, complexity, and economic implications of greenhouse gas (GHG) emission reductions demand strategic investments in science-based information for planning, implementing, and tracking the impact of emission reduction policies and actions. An increasing number of applications succeed by combining activity-based emissions data with atmospheric GHG measurements and analyses – this hybrid approach can yield additional insights and practical information on GHG emissions and removals at different scales. Inspired by this potential, the Integrated Global Greenhouse Gas Information System (IG3IS) of the World Meteorological Organization works to identify and document good practice guidelines for creation and utilisation of decision-relevant information, while promoting scientific advances in methodologies and facilitating two-way linkages between practitioners and stakeholders. This session continues to showcase how scientific data and analyses can be created, characterized and transformed into actionable information services for a wide range of user-communities. This session seeks contributions from researchers, inventory compilers, government decision and policy makers, non-government and private sector service providers that produce or utilize science-based methods for detecting, quantifying, tracking GHG emissions using a combination of observations, activity-based emissions data and modelling and analysis tools. We especially welcome presentations of work guided by IG3IS good practice research guidelines at urban and national scale and for specific economic sectors. The scope of the session spans measurements of all GHGs and from all tiers of observation.
title: Science-based, measurement-based greenhouse gas emission monitoring to inform climate change mitigation across decision-making scales and sectors

description: Anthropogenic and natural aerosols play key roles in driving climate change over a range of spatial and temporal scales, both close to emission sources and also remotely through teleconnections. Aerosols can directly interact with radiation by scattering and absorption and indirectly through modulating cloud properties, and thereby modify the surface and atmospheric energy balance, cloud dynamics and precipitation patterns, and the atmospheric and oceanic circulation. Changes in regional aerosol emissions accelerate greenhouse gas-driven climate changes in some regions, counteract them in others, and may interact with natural variability to further stress human and ecological systems. However, our understanding of these impacts still lags those due to greenhouse gases. The poor aerosol integration in many climate risk and impact studies currently leads to potentially dangerous omissions in projections of near-term climate change impacts. This session addresses: the strong and spatially complex trends in temperature, hydroclimate, air quality, and extreme events driven by aerosol changes over the historical era, and those expected in the near future; the interplay between aerosol-driven changes and those induced by other forcing factors; and their extensions to climate risk and impact studies. We encourage contributions based on model and observation-based approaches to investigate the effects of aerosols on regional decadal climate variability and extremes, tropical-extratropical interactions and teleconnections, and the interactions with modes of variability such as the NAO, ENSO, AMV, and PDO. This year we especially welcome studies focusing on the climate effects of African air pollution, notably how absorbing aerosols influence Sub-Saharan precipitation, and any analyses using the RAMIP dataset. We also welcome focused studies on aerosol influences on monsoon systems, midlatitude and Arctic responses, extreme temperature and precipitation, atmospheric and oceanic circulation changes, tropical cyclones, and daily variability, using for example CMIP6 and CMIP7 projections, large ensemble simulations, or specifically designed experiments. We also encourage studies focusing on climate risk and concrete regional impacts on nature and society resulting from changes in anthropogenic and natural aerosol emissions.
title: Anthropogenic and natural aerosols in regional climate change: From physical hazards to climate risk and impacts on nature and society

description: Aircraft condensation trails (contrails) are currently estimated to contribute a similar effective radiative forcing as all CO2 emitted from the aviation sector thus far. They also constitute the ultimate short-lived forcer, with lifetimes estimated in hours and local radiative forcings on the order of several watts per meter squared. This has made them the subject of an ongoing explosion in interest from the scientific, aviation, and regulatory communities, including fierce debate regarding potential measurement and regulation of contrail formation alongside aircraft CO2 emissions. Although there have been several recent in-situ measurement campaigns and significant recent advances in the detection of contrails using remote sensing data, understanding their overall climate effects - as well as the development of effective strategies to mitigate said impacts - requires accurate models of contrail formation and evolution. This is a substantial challenge, given that contrails form at the scale of an aircraft engine exhaust but can spread to be tens or hundreds of kilometers wide. Furthermore there remains relatively little observational data to directly constrain contrails due to the difficulty of directly sampling contrail ice and the high degree of temporal and spatial variability in cruise altitude conditions. With these concerns in mind, this session complements ongoing efforts in contrail observation by aiming to bring together the growing community of contrail modellers who are seeking to advance our ability to represent and understand the full lifetime of a contrail and its long term impacts. This includes those who are working on: high-fidelity modelling of contrail formation in the exhaust plume; LES or RANS models of the exhaust plume and contrail; 0-, 1-, 2-, or 3-D models of long-term contrail behaviour; models of regional- and global-scale contrail evolution and climate responses, including potential cloud feedbacks; and studies using new datasets to evaluate the performance of existing contrail models. Particular attention will be given to research using open-source models and data.
title: Advances in modelling contrails and aircraft-cirrus interactions

description: Artificial intelligence and machine learning are opening new opportunities across atmospheric science, enabling information to be extracted from increasingly complex observations, improving the representation and understanding of atmospheric processes, and providing new approaches to weather and climate modelling and prediction. At the same time, the growing use of AI raises fundamental scientific questions about how data-driven approaches can be integrated with physical knowledge, numerical models, and observations while maintaining physical consistency, interpretability, robustness, and generalizability. This session aims to bring together researchers developing and applying AI and machine-learning approaches across the atmospheric sciences. We welcome contributions spanning scales from clouds, aerosols, precipitation, radiation, and boundary-layer processes to regional and global weather and climate. Topics may include, but are not limited to, AI-assisted analysis and retrievals from atmospheric observations; process discovery and understanding; data-driven and hybrid parameterizations; emulation of computationally expensive model components; differentiable and hybrid physics–AI modelling; foundation models and other data-driven approaches for weather and climate prediction; AI-enhanced data assimilation; and methods for improving physical consistency, interpretability, uncertainty quantification, and robustness. By connecting methodological developments with atmospheric applications, the session seeks to foster exchange between the AI, observational, process-modelling, weather, and climate communities. We particularly encourage studies that go beyond predictive skill alone to investigate how AI can advance physical understanding, improve atmospheric models, and contribute to more reliable prediction across spatial and temporal scales.
title: Artificial Intelligence for Atmospheric Science: From Physical Process Understanding to Weather and Climate Prediction

description: Clouds and aerosols play a key role in climate and weather-related processes over a wide range of spatial and temporal scales. An initial forcing due to changes in the aerosol concentration and composition may also be enhanced or dampened by feedback processes such as modified cloud dynamics, surface exchange or atmospheric circulation patterns. This session aims to link research activities in observations and modelling of radiative, dynamical and microphysical processes of clouds, aerosols, and their interactions. Studies addressing several aspects of the aerosol-cloud-radiation-precipitation system are encouraged. Contributions related to the EU projects CERTAINTY (Cloud-aERosol inTeractions & their impActs IN The earth sYstem) and CleanCloud (Clouds and climate transitioning to post-fossil aerosol regime) are also invited. Topics covered in this session include, but are not limited to: - Cloud and aerosol macro- and microphysical properties, precipitation formation mechanisms and their role in the energy budget - New constraints on aerosol, clouds or precipitation from EarthCARE and PACE - Impacts of changes in aerosol composition and sources on clouds, radiation and precipitation - Observational constraints on aerosol-cloud interactions - Use of observational simulators to constrain aerosols, clouds and their radiative effects in models - Explorations of cloud seeding or artificial cloud brightening techniques - Experimental cloud and aerosol studies - High-resolution modelling, including large-eddy simulation and cloud-resolving models - Parameterization of cloud and aerosol microphysics/dynamics/radiation processes
title: Clouds, Aerosols, Radiation and Precipitation

description: Methane is an important greenhouse gas that has contributed to ∼25% of the increase in radiative forcing experienced to date. Despite methane’s short atmospheric lifetime (~10 years), the global average methane mole fraction has increased three times faster than carbon dioxide since 1750. Rapid and severe reductions in methane emissions are required to lower peak warming, reduce the likelihood of overshooting warming limits and reduce reliance on net negative carbon dioxide emissions. In order to track mitigation efforts and ensure emission quantification required in legislation can be met, we must be able to accurately attribute and quantify emissions and are actively doing so through activities such as the UNEP International Methane Emissions Observatory (IMEO). This session will highlight measurement studies at all scales and from ground-based to satellites, that focus on quantification and source attribution of methane emissions from human activities. We especially encourage submissions from both IMEO and non-IMEO funded work that focus on the following topics: (1) new technologies / methods to provide accurate and repeatable emissions measurements, (2) demonstration of affordable and reliable quantification methods for mitigation tracking, (3) attribution of emissions to specific sources and, (4) methods for upscaling measurements into inventories and creating policy relevant datasets.
title: Quantification and attribution of anthropogenic methane sources through measurement: Where to focus for mitigation?

description: Organic aerosols (OA) are a significant fraction of atmospheric particulate matter (PM) in different environments from urban landscapes to pristine regions, and from the boundary layer to the upper troposphere. Due to their complex chemical composition, OA remains one of the least understood parts of PM, with effects on Earth's climate and human health that are still inadequately characterized. Ongoing efforts enhance our understanding of the origin and (trans)formation processes of OA. This encompasses studying natural sources and assessing how anthropogenic emissions change the chemical composition and physical properties of organic aerosols. This session welcomes submissions on ambient observations, chamber and modelling studies of OA, which contribute to a deeper understanding of their origins (such as secondary OA formation or biomass burning), analysis of the molecular composition (e.g. targeted analysis of organic pollutants), investigation of physico-chemical properties, exploration of atmospheric transformation reactions (for example aging or brown carbon formation), and examination of gas-to-particle partitioning of organic molecules.
title: Sources, Formation, and Properties of Organic Aerosols

description: Reactive halogen species can have an important influence on the chemistry of the troposphere. For instance, chlorine atoms react faster with most hydrocarbons than OH does and inorganic bromine and iodine can catalytically destroy tropospheric ozone and oxidise mercury. These reactions have been shown to be important in in environments as different as the polar troposphere during the springtime ozone depletion events, the boundary layer over salt lakes, and volcanic plumes. There is strong evidence that halogens play a spatially even wider role in the marine boundary layer and free troposphere for ozone destruction, changes in the ratios of OH/HO2 and NO/NO2, destruction of methane, in the oxidation of mercury and in the formation of secondary aerosol. There are indications that both, oceanic sources as well as the chemistry of halogens and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and oxygenated VOCs (OVOCs) in the tropics are linked with potential implications not only for the photochemistry but also the formation of secondary organic aerosol (SOA). More recently, marine emissions of active halogens have been linked to potential impacts on oxidants loading in coastal cities. Finally, bromine and iodine are also being proposed as proxies of past sea ice variability. We invite contributions in the following areas dealing with tropospheric halogens on local, regional, and global scales: - Model studies: Investigations of the chemical mechanisms leading to release, transformation and removal of reactive halogen species in the troposphere. Studies of consequences of the presence of reactive halogen species in the troposphere. - Laboratory studies: Determination of gas- and aqueous-phase rate constants, study of complex reaction systems involving halogens, Henry's law and uptake coefficients, UV/VIS spectra, and other properties of reactive halogen species. - Field experiments and satellite studies: Measurements of inorganic (X, XO, HOX, XONO2, ..., X = Cl, Br, I) and organic (CH3Br, CHBr3, CH3I, RX, ...) reactive halogen species and their fluxes in the troposphere with in situ and remote sensing techniques. - Measurements and model studies of the abundance of (reactive) halogen species in volcanic plumes and transformation processes and mechanisms. - All aspects of tropical tropospheric halogens and links to (O)VOCs: their chemistry, sources and sinks, and their impact on local, regional, and global scales.
title: Halogens in the troposhere

description: Aerosol particles are key components of the Earth system, with important roles in atmospheric chemistry, climate and radiative balance, air quality, human health, and other areas of societal concern. Understanding their formation, evolution, properties, and impacts requires contributions from multiple disciplines, including laboratory experiments, field observations, remote sensing, theory, and numerical modelling. This session welcomes contributions across the full breadth of aerosol chemistry and physics, and submissions do not need to address the focus topic described below. Alongside this broad scope, this year we particularly welcome studies highlighting emerging technologies for aerosol research, spanning both physical and digital approaches. These may include advances in aerosol sensing and measurement, instrumentation and ionisation techniques, new experimental platforms, high-resolution and computationally efficient modelling, cloud computing, digital twins, and AI. Such technologies are creating new opportunities across scales, from individual particles and molecular processes to regional and global aerosol systems, and from fundamental process understanding to prediction and impact assessment. We welcome submissions across a broad range of aerosol topics, including but not limited to: - Fundamental aerosol chemistry and physics, including particle formation, composition, mixing state, phase state, morphology, and physicochemical properties - Primary and secondary aerosol formation and evolution, including new particle formation, gas-to-particle conversion, photochemistry, aqueous and heterogeneous chemistry, and aerosol ageing - Aerosol observations from laboratory experiments, field campaigns, long-term monitoring, and remote sensing - Aerosol interactions with radiation, clouds, climate, air quality, ecosystems, and human health - Development and application of aerosol measurement, sensing, instrumentation, ionisation, and experimental technologies - Development of process-based, data-driven, and hybrid process–machine-learning aerosol models - Advances in numerical methods, model resolution, computational efficiency, and multiscale aerosol modelling - Applications of AI and emerging digital approaches, including machine learning, generative AI, foundation models, cloud computing, and digital twins - Open science approaches, including benchmark datasets, reproducible workflows, model and data sharing, and evaluation standards
title: Aerosol Chemistry and Physics

description: This session explores the diverse and dynamic field of visualization and interaction within the geosciences, with particular emphasis on 3D approaches. It aims to bridge gaps between different scales and forms of geoscientific data, explore their applications, and highlight the importance of visual and interactive methods for scientific interpretation and communication. We welcome contributions spanning a broad spectrum of geoscientific research and practice. Topics may include the visualization and interactive exploration of data across scales, from microscopic mineral structures to geological formations, subsurface systems, numerical simulations, and planetary-scale models. We also invite applications from fields such as environmental monitoring, resource exploration, natural hazard assessment, geodynamics, and planetary science. The session welcomes advances in visualization tools, software, hardware, and workflows, including interactive and web-based environments, virtual and augmented reality, and approaches for handling large or time-dependent datasets. This may include tools that allow users to navigate, query, manipulate, or compare geoscientific data and models. Particular attention will be given to methods that enhance the perception, exploration, and understanding of geodata through meaningful interaction. We invite researchers, professionals, and students developing new visualization and interaction methods, creating compelling geological models, or applying these approaches in novel ways to share their insights and experiences. Although 3D visualization forms a central theme, contributions presenting other innovative approaches to geoscientific visualization and interaction are equally welcome. By fostering a multidisciplinary dialogue, we hope to stimulate innovation and drive the geosciences forward into new dimensions.
title: Exploring new dimensions in geoscientific visualization and interaction

description: This session aims to provide a platform to highlight and discuss the diverse experiences of women in the geosciences, as well as the challenges and opportunities they encounter throughout their careers. We welcome contributions that share personal perspectives, institutional practices, leadership roles in projects and research addressing gender equity in geoscience. Topics may include, but are not limited to: career progression, work–life balance, mentoring and role models, fieldwork experiences, inclusivity in research teams, and structural or cultural barriers within academia, industry, and policy. We particularly encourage submissions that offer solutions, best practices, or new initiatives fostering a more inclusive geoscience community. By bringing together these contributions, the session seeks to promote dialogue, raise awareness, and inspire actionable steps toward greater gender equity and diversity in the field.
title: Women in Geoscience: Experiences and Challenges

description: Disasters caused by natural hazards can have long-lasting impacts on economic, social, and ecological systems. These challenges are increasingly complex in a world facing multiple, interconnected, and recurring hazards. Decisions made during disaster response and recovery can redirect resources and attention away from long-term risk reduction, while recovery itself can provide opportunities to reduce future risk and strengthen resilience. Recovery processes can also create opportunities for transformative change, enabling a shift towards more sustainable, low-carbon, and equitable development pathways. Understanding how recovery and resilience develop over time, and how they can be effectively supported, is therefore important. Yet definitions, assessment approaches, and applications vary widely across disciplines and contexts, making it difficult to compare and understand recovery and resilience across systems, scales, and time, and to identify effective actions and investments to support long-term resilience. This session focuses on disaster recovery and longer-term resilience building, and how these processes can be better understood, assessed, and supported in science and practice. We welcome research on individual hazards as well as multi-hazard, compound, and consecutive events, and studies addressing recovery and resilience across spatial and temporal scales. The session brings together methodological advances, empirical evidence, and practical experiences to improve our ability to adapt to and recover from disasters while advancing long-term sustainability goals. We encourage contributions on topics including: - empirical analyses of disaster recovery and resilience, and their dynamics over time; - methods, indicators, and frameworks for assessing recovery and resilience; - links between recovery, disaster risk reduction, climate adaptation, and resilience building; - resilience and recovery in multi-hazard, compound, or consecutive disaster contexts; - adaptation synergies and trade-offs in resilience-building and risk-reduction actions, including implications for long- term sustainability; - decision-making and prioritisation of resilience-building investments and actions; - practical applications, case studies, and lessons from science–practice collaboration. - build back better and transformative recovery: opportunities and barriers to align recovery and resilience building with sustainable development goals.
title: From recovery to resilience – Analysis, applications, and experiences from science and practice

description: Molecular hydrogen (H₂) is gaining global attention as a key component of the transition to sustainable energy systems, with the potential to significantly reduce greenhouse gas emissions and air pollutants. However, the biogeochemical cycle of H₂ and its impacts on atmospheric chemistry and climate present critical knowledge gaps. While hydrogen itself is not a greenhouse gas, its chemical oxidation can influence methane, ozone, and stratospheric water vapor, with potential effects on the Earth’s radiative balance. This session aims at advancing our understanding of the hydrogen budget and the implications of increased hydrogen use. Topics of interest include: - Quantifying hydrogen emissions from direct sources, including leakages, venting, and incomplete combustion, as well as oxidation by volatile organic compounds. - Investigating the removal of hydrogen by soil bacteria and by reaction with OH in the atmosphere. - Assessing the indirect climate effects of hydrogen emissions on methane, ozone, stratospheric water vapor and aerosols/clouds. - Utilizing observations and modeling to refine estimates of hydrogen sources and sinks across various spatial and temporal scales. - Exploring scenarios of future hydrogen economies, including their potential to reduce fossil fuel emissions and the associated environmental and climatic co-benefits. We welcome studies that employ experimental, observational, and theoretical approaches to hydrogen biogeochemistry and atmospheric processes, contributing to a more comprehensive understanding of H₂ in the context of the global energy transition.
title: Climate impacts of a growing hydrogen economy

description: This session brings together advances in artificial intelligence, Earth observation, and atmospheric modelling to improve air quality monitoring and emission inversion. We welcome studies on the synergistic uses of satellite-based monitoring and deep learning—ranging from data-driven surrogates and emulators to hybrid physical-AI integration within chemistry transport models, alongside synthetic data approaches. While advances for well-monitored regions are of interest, we particularly encourage applications in resource-constrained, data-scarce, and under-monitored environments where traditional infrastructure is lacking
title: Leveraging AI and EO for Air Quality Monitoring and Emission Inversion

description: Clouds remain a leading source of uncertainty in climate projections. This PICO session brings together research on how clouds are represented in global climate and Earth system models, and on how choices in model formulation, parameterisation, and process representation influence simulated clouds, climate feedbacks, and projection uncertainty. We welcome contributions on new cloud parameterisations and model developments, evaluations of simulated clouds against observations, and experiments that perturb cloud processes to quantify their climatic impacts, including studies of cloud-based climate intervention. We also welcome studies using large-eddy simulations, kilometre-scale models, and Lagrangian approaches that provide process-level constraints for the development and evaluation of cloud representations in global models.
title: Clouds in Climate Models: Development, Evaluation, and Implications

description: Rocket launches and re-entries of reusable and discarded objects inject familiar and exotic anthropogenic gases and aerosols to all layers of the atmosphere. The space sector is the only anthropogenic source that releases these gases and aerosols directly to the middle and upper layers of the atmosphere. Once emitted to these layers, pollutants may persist for years or decades, leaving a long legacy of atmospheric pollution. These pollutants are increasingly ubiquitous due to recent exponential space sector growth, yet there are no regulatory controls to mitigate harm. Quantification of the complex risks to the atmosphere is hindered by many uncertainties and data gaps, such as the chemical composition of exhaust from novel propellants, the locations and trajectories of ablative re-entry, the radiative properties of pollutants, the material composition of objects ablating on re-entry, and the physical and chemical evolution of chemicals released during re-entry. Lack of openly-available modelling tools is compounded by a scarcity of real-world experiments and ambient observations, and expected massive growth of space launches and, consequently, re-entries. This session invites submissions across all geophysical and related disciplines in and beyond academia to share planned, ongoing, or recently completed research that provides new knowledge in this area, explores new open-source modelling techniques, or exposes methodological gaps that need to be resolved to inform sustainability initiatives and global regulation. We are also interested in innovative and interdisciplinary approaches adopted by researchers in other domains that could be applied to advance understanding of environmental harm from the space sector. These include related topics such as geoengineering, space weather, space engineering, upper atmosphere circulation and chemistry, meteoritics, stratospheric aerosols and space debris management.
title: Atmospheric impacts of spacecraft launches and re-entries: knowns, unknowns, and research priorities

description: Contrail cirrus are among the largest non-CO₂ climate impacts of aviation and have become a major focus of research and mitigation efforts. Recent advances in laboratory experiments, flight campaigns, remote sensing techniques, and operational demonstrations have substantially improved our understanding of contrail formation and evolution. At the same time, increasing interest in alternative aviation fuels, new engine technologies, and operational contrail avoidance has highlighted the need for observational evidence to quantify the effectiveness of mitigation strategies, support future implementation and monitoring, and assess their economic costs. With these developments in mind, this session aims to bring together the growing community working on observations and investigation and evaluation of contrail mitigation strategies. The session complements ongoing efforts in contrail modelling by focusing on experimental and observational studies across a range of spatial scales. Contributions may include laboratory, ground-based, and in-flight measurements of aerosols, contrails, and atmospheric background conditions. Ground-based cameras, active and passive remote sensing, including ground and airborne lidar, and satellite observations of contrails and cirrus are also of interest. Experimental studies of contrail mitigation using alternative aviation fuels, including SAF, and new engine technologies such as hydrogen combustion are particularly encouraged. Air traffic management, weather and climate model evaluations, and observational validation of operational contrail management and avoidance strategies are also relevant topics. The session also covers research assessing the environmental, economic, and life-cycle implications of contrail mitigation. Contributions combining observations with model evaluation or validation are also welcome.
title: Contrail Observations and Mitigation

description: Non-exhaust emissions (tyre-wear particles, TWP; brake-wear particles, BWP; road dust) are a major urban pollution source as exhaust declines. These heterogeneous particles contain metals, minerals, carbonaceous material, polymers, organics and micro-/nanoplastics; their behavior cannot be understood from emission composition alone. During transport, deposition and resuspension, they undergo multi-stressor ageing (precipitation, drying, UV, temperature, freeze–thaw, oxidation, interactions with salts, organic matter and particles). Ageing alters morphology, size, surface chemistry, mineralogy, magnetic properties, aggregation, mobility and reactivity, modifying signatures and environmental fate. TWP and BWP are chemically and mineralogically complex. Constituents transform, dissolve, oxidise, fragment, aggregate and interact with natural minerals, affecting transport, resuspension, deposition and transfer between compartments. The session focuses on post-emission evolution of non-exhaust particles, coupling composition, ageing, mineral transformations and mobility. We welcome studies addressing: • quantification of non-exhaust particles in the atmosphere; • source apportionment via multivariate statistics and modelling, including signature changes; • shifting traffic source signatures; • health impacts and risk assessment of fresh vs aged particles, including bioavailability; • generation and composition of BWP, TWP and road dust; • inorganic constituents of BWP/TWP; • environmental ageing under UV, oxidation, humidity, temperature, wetting–drying and freeze–thaw; • changes in size, morphology, surface chemistry, aggregation and stability; • mineral transformations, dissolution, oxidation and secondary mineral formation; • mineral, elemental and magnetic signatures as tracers and their relevance through time; • environmental magnetism identifying Fe-bearing components; • interactions and heteroaggregation of TWP/BWP with minerals, metals, organics and micro-/nanoplastics; • resuspension, transport and deposition of fresh/aged particles; • transfer to soils, runoff, surface waters and sediments; • changes in particle reactivity, mobility, persistence and bioavailability; • lab experiments, field observations and modelling linking transformation with fate; • advanced analytical approaches combining mineralogical, magnetic, spectroscopic, microscopic, thermal and geochemical methods.
title: From Emission to Environmental Fate: Ageing and Transformation of Non-Exhaust Traffic Particles

description: African–European research and capacity-development partnerships play an important role in addressing the interconnected challenges of climate change, water security, land degradation, food security, and sustainable development. Over recent years, increasing attention has been given not only to strengthening scientific capacity, but also to ensuring that collaborative research translates into practical solutions and long-term societal impact. Building on previous discussions on capacity development and African–European research cooperation, this session focuses on the next step: how partnerships can evolve from individual projects and training activities towards sustained research capacity, institutional strengthening, locally led innovation, and implementation. We invite contributions examining innovative and equitable approaches to African–European collaboration across climate change impact and adaptation, water and land management, environmental sustainability, and related fields. Particular attention will be given to co-creation of knowledge, long-term institutional partnerships, early-career researcher development, research mobility, South–South and African–European networks, science–policy–practice interfaces, and mechanisms for translating research into locally relevant solutions. The session welcomes both successful examples and critical reflections on challenges such as unequal partnerships, short-term funding cycles, continuity beyond individual projects, and the measurement of capacity-development and societal impacts. Contributions from researchers, practitioners, policymakers, funders, and capacity-development programmes are encouraged.
title: From Capacity Development to Lasting Impact: Advancing African–European Partnerships for Climate Resilience

description: Plant traits extend Earth observations to the level of individual organisms, providing a critical link between biodiversity, ecosystem functioning, and biogeochemical modeling under rapid global change. However, bridging the temporal and spatial mismatches between plant trait data and biogeochemical cycles remains a major challenge. This session addresses the role of plant traits, biodiversity, acclimation, and adaptation in regulating the biogeochemical cycles of water, carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and sulfur across scales. We welcome conceptual, observational, experimental, and modeling studies from local to global levels, including in situ and remote sensing approaches.
title: Plant traits, adaptation, and biogeochemical cycles – from measurements to models

description: Our capacity to estimate regional and global budgets of greenhouse gases (GHG, including CO2, CH4 and N2O) from aquatic ecosystems has significantly improved during the past decade, thanks to the substantial increase in field measurements. However, global estimates of these fluxes remain highly uncertain. Moreover, compared with terrestrial ecosystems, the field of aquatic GHG research is still young and the mechanisms behind the spatiotemporal patterns and variability of GHG concentrations and fluxes in aquatic ecosystems are not sufficiently understood, constraining model development. Therefore, to improve our estimates and understanding of regional and global GHG budgets from aquatic ecosystems, this session welcomes contributions on e.g.: 1) Field observations of GHG dynamics and fluxes in aquatic ecosystems, both freshwater and marine systems. 2) Experiments investigating physicochemical or biological processes or factors relevance to GHG production, consumption, transport, emission, or uptake. 3) Model development or simulation efforts to estimate GHG dynamics and fluxes across different spatial and temporal scales along the aquatic continuum. Contributions providing additional perspectives of relevance for aquatic GHG cycling and fluxes are also of interest.
title: Greenhouse gas dynamics and fluxes in aquatic ecosystems

description: Reactive nitrogen (N) is essential for agricultural productivity, yet its inefficient use contributes to emissions, N losses, and environmental impacts. Improving our understanding of reactive N turnover and fate is crucial for reducing uncertainties in N budgets and supporting sustainable nutrient management. While the factors controlling N turnover are relatively well established under laboratory conditions, quantifying N transformations under field and landscape conditions remains a major challenge. High spatial and temporal variability, methodological limitations, and complex interactions among biological, chemical, and physical processes create substantial uncertainties in N turnover pathways and environmental controls. Limited availability of in situ datasets hampers evaluation of mineralization, nitrification, and denitrification in process-based models, reducing confidence in predictions across scales. Addressing these challenges requires integrating experiments, field measurements, monitoring, and modelling across scales. Improved process understanding and quantification of N transformations are essential for predicting reactive N losses, assessing greenhouse gas emissions, and evaluating mitigation options. This session welcomes contributions advancing understanding of reactive N turnover and fate in agricultural systems, focusing on linking measurements, monitoring, and modelling approaches across temporal and spatial scales. Topics of interest include: • Experimental studies investigating nitrogen transformation processes, turnover rates, and reactive N loss pathways under laboratory, field, or landscape conditions; • Advances in field measurements and monitoring approaches for quantifying reactive N pools, fluxes, and turnover; • Novel approaches to constrain N turnover, including 15N tracer techniques, isotopic methods, controlled incubation experiments, and other innovative methodologies; • Process-based, data-driven, and hybrid modelling approaches for simulating N cycling and reactive N fate across scales; • Studies evaluating management and mitigation strategies aimed at reducing reactive N losses and greenhouse gas emissions; • Integration of measurements, monitoring, and modelling for improving N budgets, model evaluation, and uncertainty reduction; • Linking N transformation processes with soil microbial communities, environmental drivers, and agricultural management practices.
title: Reactive nitrogen turnover and fate in agricultural systems: measurements, monitoring and modelling across scales

description: Remote sensing is an essential tool for observing, quantifying, and monitoring forest ecosystems across vast spatial and temporal scales. Advances in sensor technology, data availability, and computational methods enable detailed observations from terrestrial, mobile, UAV, airborne, and space-borne platforms. Optical, multispectral, and hyperspectral imagery, alongside SAR, LiDAR, photogrammetry, and Structure-from-Motion (SfM), provide complementary data on forest composition, structure, function, and dynamics across natural, managed, and urban environments. The availability of multi-source observations creates unprecedented opportunities but also raises significant scientific challenges. Because forest information is scale-dependent, no single sensor can capture all ecological characteristics.
