Integrating observations across spatial, temporal, and spectral scales is therefore essential for developing robust, transferable, and scalable approaches. Furthermore, in-situ measurements remain crucial for the calibration, validation, uncertainty assessment, and physical interpretation of remote sensing products. Remote sensing supports qualitative and quantitative assessments, from mapping forest cover, species, and vegetation characteristics to estimating tree height, DBH, biomass, timber volume, canopy structure, and density. In urban environments, these tools support tree inventories and green infrastructure assessment. At larger scales, remote sensing enables the detection of critical disturbances like fire, drought, and insect outbreaks, supporting sustainable management, carbon monitoring, and ecological modeling. This session invites research on integrating heterogeneous remote sensing and in-situ observations. We welcome contributions on multi-sensor/multi-platform data fusion, field observations, and methods for transferring information across scales. Submissions may address terrestrial laser scanning, mobile mapping, UAV, airborne, and satellite observations, as well as GeoAI and AI-based approaches (machine learning, deep learning, foundation models, transfer learning, and domain adaptation). We emphasize methodological developments and operational applications, with interest in uncertainty, validation, scalability, transferability, generalization, interpretability, and reproducibility.
title: Remote Sensing for forest applications

description: Agricultural production is increasingly exposed to hydroclimatic extremes, including drought, extreme heat, heavy precipitation, flooding, frost, and water scarcity. Yet detecting a hydroclimatic extreme alone does not establish when and where crops will experience damaging stress, how severe that stress will become, or whether it will lead to substantial yield losses or crop failure. The growing availability of Earth-observation, meteorological, reanalysis, and seasonal forecast data, together with advances in crop and hydrological modelling, statistics, and artificial intelligence, provides new opportunities to complement retrospective monitoring with crop-impact prediction and early warning. Realising this potential requires robust quantification of predictive uncertainty, rigorous evaluation of model performance during extreme events, and assessment of how well prediction systems generalise across years, crop types, environments, and regions. Cross-regional comparisons can therefore help identify key controls on crop vulnerability and resilience while improving the transferability and interpretation of crop-risk prediction systems. Another important challenge is predicting whether, and to what extent, crops can recover following hydroclimatic stress and how this recovery affects final yield. We invite contributions addressing, but not limited to: - crop responses to individual, sequential, and compound hydroclimatic extremes, including drought, extreme heat, frost, heavy precipitation, flooding, and water scarcity; - early and in-season prediction of crop stress, yield anomalies, yield loss, and crop-failure risk; - Earth-observation indicators for detecting and anticipating crop stress, including vegetation condition, evapotranspiration, soil moisture, and canopy temperature; - advances in data-driven, process-based, physics-informed, and hybrid prediction frameworks that draw on statistical modelling, AI, and crop, hydrological, and land-surface models; - probabilistic prediction, uncertainty quantification, forecast calibration, and reliability; - crop recovery following hydroclimatic stress and differentiation between recoverable and yield-damaging stress; - identification of intervention windows and decision-relevant thresholds for agricultural early warning. The session aims to advance robust and transferable approaches for predicting crop stress and yield risk and translating these predictions into actionable agricultural early warning.
title: Predicting Crop Stress and Yield Risk under Hydroclimatic Extremes

description: Non-vascular photoautotrophs, including bryophytes, lichens, algae, and cyanobacteria, are widely distributed in all terrestrial habitats around the globe. They occur growing on and within rocks, epiphytically on plants, and growing on soil they often form so-called biological soil crusts. Despite their often small stature, these organisms (together with the microbiomes and cyanosphere they host) play a significant role in key ecological processes such as water, carbon, and nitrogen cycling, as well as the regulation of atmospheric and belowground processes. Yet, these critical organisms remain underrepresented in ecological research. Because non-vascular photoautotrophs are highly responsive to changes in environmental conditions, understanding and quantifying their functional roles is becoming increasingly important under rapid global change. Encouragingly, a growing body of data, such as functional traits, microbiome information, and greenhouse gas quantifications, is now emerging for non-vascular vegetation across diverse ecosystems, which has opened new avenues for linking to ecosystem functions in the context of climate change. However, significant challenges remain. These include limited quantitative understanding of how non-vascular photoautotrophs mediate interactions between the atmosphere, vegetation, soil, and associated microbial communities; mismatches in temporal and spatial scales of available observations and ecosystem-level processes; and difficulties in scaling physiological and community-level processes from local measurements to regional and global ecosystem functions. To address these challenges, this session aims to bring together cutting-edge research that examines non-vascular photoautotrophs as crucial drivers of ecosystem functioning and to raise awareness of their inclusion in ecosystem function research frameworks within the field of ecology. We welcome all studies investigating the roles of bryophytes, lichens, cyanobacteria, algae, and their associated microorganisms, both individually and as communities in ecosystem processes, with particular interest in water, carbon, nitrogen, and other biogeochemical cycles. Contributions may make use of conceptual, observational (in-situ or remote sensing), experimental, and modelling approaches, and may cover a range of scales from organismal ecophysiology to community, ecosystem, regional, and global dynamics.
title: Non-vascular photoautotrophs as drivers of biogeochemical cycles under global change

description: Cold regions, including Arctic, boreal and alpine regions, are warming at a much faster rate than the global average, putting cold regions and their ecosystems under increasing pressure. These environments harbour well-adapted yet fragile ecosystems, including permafrost peatlands and Arctic tundra, which have acted as natural carbon sinks for millennia. This may change as warming induces snow cover loss, rain-on-snow events, increased wildfire frequency and intensity, widespread permafrost thaw and thermokarst formation, and other landscape disturbances that transform the biogeochemistry, hydrology, ecology, and morphology of the cold regions. Ultimately, these phenomena can trigger local and large-scale climate feedbacks through shifts in the exchange of carbon, water and energy to the atmosphere. The goal of this session is to facilitate an interdisciplinary discussion on the dynamics of cold region ecosystems under a rapidly changing climate. We aim to bring together varied perspectives from researchers working on biogeochemistry, including greenhouse gas flux measurements, microbiology and plant-soil processes. We welcome studies focusing on observational, experimental, remote sensing and modelling approaches to understand plant and microbial functioning, biogeochemical cycling, ecosystem disturbances, permafrost carbon loss, export to aquatic systems, and associated impacts. Because most prior research on cold region ecosystems has focused on the growing season, we particularly welcome contributions from the non-growing season. We further encourage contributions that aim at a quantification of permafrost feedback strengths, at the regional to global scale, and those that improve our understanding of mechanisms at the process-level.
title: Cold regions in a changing climate: ecosystem dynamics and feedback mechanisms across seasons

description: Fire is a fundamental Earth system process and a major driver of terrestrial ecosystem change, with cascading effects on the atmosphere, biosphere, cryosphere, biogeochemical cycles, and human societies. Changes in climate, vegetation, land use, and human activity are in turn altering fire regimes, creating complex feedbacks across spatial and temporal scales. Understanding these coupled interactions is therefore essential for assessing the role of fire in a rapidly changing Earth system, particularly as the frequency, intensity, and impacts of extreme fire events increase in many regions. This session brings together interdisciplinary research investigating fire–Earth system interactions across the past, present, and future. We welcome studies using observations, remote sensing, proxy records, field and laboratory measurements, statistical and process-based models, artificial intelligence, and data–model fusion approaches, spanning local to global scales. We particularly encourage contributions addressing interactions between fire and: (1) weather, climate, atmospheric composition, chemistry, and circulation; (2) vegetation dynamics, ecosystem structure and function, terrestrial and ocean biogeochemical cycles; (3) cryospheric processes and components, including permafrost and sea ice; and (4) human health, land management, conservation, livelihoods, and other societal dimensions. We also welcome studies of (5) past, present, and projected changes in fire regimes, with particular emphasis on extreme and compound fire events; (6) fire datasets, products, and models, including validation, uncertainty, bias assessment, and correction; and (7) analytical and predictive tools that support fire monitoring, situational awareness, early warning, and decision-making. By bringing together perspectives from across the Earth and environmental sciences, the session aims to advance an integrated understanding of fire as both a response to and a driver of Earth system change, and to identify emerging challenges and opportunities for predicting and managing fire in a changing world.
title: Fire in the Earth System: Coupled Interactions Across Climate, Ecosystems and Society

description: Extreme fire events have become increasingly frequent all over the world, as seen in recent fire seasons in Turkey, Southern Europe, Brazil, Chile, California, South Korea, and Canada. These extreme fire events have disproportionate impacts on society and all components of the Earth system, yet much remains to be understood about their characteristics, drivers, links to climate change, methods for quantifying their impacts, and effective mitigation and prevention strategies. A key area of research is how extreme fires are represented in fire models. Their stochastic behaviour, uncertainties in observations, and the difficulty of capturing local processes within global frameworks make simulating extremes and their impacts a persistent challenge for coupled models. Emerging big data and machine learning approaches show promise in capturing such events but remain limited in their ability to represent feedback to vegetation, soils, and the broader Earth system. This session also invites case studies of regional extreme wildfire events, their impacts, and experiences with prevention and mitigation strategies from around the world. We welcome contributions from a wide range of disciplines, including global, regional, and landscape-scale modelling; statistical and process-based modelling; observational and field studies; and social science research on all time scales. Our goal is to foster knowledge exchange across disciplines and between scientists, decision-makers, and practitioners, to advance our collective ability to understand, model, and respond to the challenges posed by present and future extreme wildfires.
title: Extreme Fires and their Impacts

description: Water is continuously redistributed laterally across terrestrial landscapes and scales, from hillslopes and catchments to regional and continental river networks, through surface and subsurface pathways that connect groundwater, riparian zones, wetlands, floodplains, and rivers. These lateral hydrological connections redistribute water, energy, carbon, and nutrients across space, linking terrestrial and aquatic processes and influencing where carbon and nutrients are taken up, stored, mobilized, transformed, transported, or released. This session focuses on biogeochemical responses to lateral water redistribution and how they change across spatial and temporal scales. We welcome contributions on how laterally redistributed water alters ecosystem productivity, respiration, methane cycling, and soil carbon and nutrient dynamics; how hydrological flow paths mobilize, transport, and transform carbon and nutrients; and how these effects interact, accumulate, or change across connected landscape positions and scales. We also welcome studies examining how these relationships vary with hydroclimate and landscape structure, and how they respond to environmental change. Contributions may span hillslope, catchment, river-network, regional, continental, and global scales. We welcome field observations, experiments, remote sensing, synthesis studies, and modeling approaches, including process-based, data-driven, and hybrid models. The session aims to connect perspectives from terrestrial biogeochemistry, ecohydrology, critical zone and groundwater hydrology, and watershed science to better understand how the biogeochemical consequences of lateral water redistribution emerge and change across scales.
title: Lateral water redistribution and biogeochemical cycling from landscape to global scales

description: Direct anthropogenic perturbations of the P cycle, coupled with other human-induced stresses, is one of the biggest threats to global Earth functioning today. Widespread application of P fertilizers has changed the P cycle from relatively closed to a much more “leaky” cycle, with increased P losses to aquatic ecosystems, influencing their trophic state. Meanwhile, forest ecosystems may be losing their ability to recycle P efficiently, due to excessive N input, extensive biomass removal, and climatic stress. Throughout geological history, P availability has regulated biological productivity with impacts on the global carbon cycle. Climate change and its mitigation affect and will further alter global P cycles. This interdisciplinary session invites contributions to the study of P from all disciplines, and aims to foster collaborations between researchers working on different aspects of the P cycle. We target a balanced session giving equal weight across the continuum of environments in the P cycle, from agriculture, forests, soils and groundwater, through lakes, rivers and estuaries, to oceans, marine sediments and geological P deposits. We welcome both empirical studies furthering process-level understanding of P cycling and modeling studies leveraging that knowledge to larger spatial scales.
title: Recent advances in phosphorus cycling: from micro to global scale

description: Climate extremes, including heatwaves, droughts, heavy rains, floods, storms, wildfires and compound events, are becoming more frequent and intense under ongoing climate change. These events can exert strong, nonlinear and persistent effects on greenhouse gas fluxes (CO₂, CH₄ and N₂O) variabilities, altering carbon and nitrogen cycling from short-lived emission pulses to ecosystem changes lasting years or decades. However, the mechanisms controlling these responses across spatial and temporal scales remain poorly understood, creating substantial uncertainty in predictions of biosphere–atmosphere feedbacks. This session invites observational, experimental and modelling studies examining greenhouse gas dynamics during and following climate extremes across terrestrial, freshwater, coastal and marine ecosystems, including tundra, forests, wetlands, grasslands, croplands, rivers, lakes and oceans. We welcome contributions using in situ measurements, eddy covariance, chamber observations, isotopic techniques, experimental manipulations, process-based and Earth system models, satellite or airborne remote sensing, artificial intelligence, machine learning and causal-inference methods. Studies integrating multiple approaches are particularly encouraged, especially those seeking to identify underlying mechanisms, quantify resistance, resilience and legacy effects, or upscale responses from organisms and ecosystems to regional and global scales. By bringing together diverse disciplines and methods, this session aims to identify common and contrasting greenhouse gas responses to climate extremes, showcase methodological advances and define critical knowledge gaps. Ultimately, we seek to foster cross-disciplinary collaboration and improve predictions of greenhouse gas exchange under an increasingly extreme climate.
title: Cross-scale responses of greenhouse gas fluxes variabilities to climate extremes

description: The Paris Agreement aims to limit global warming to well below 2°C. Meeting this goal requires robust estimates of past, present and future sources and sinks of the major greenhouse gases (CO2, CH4 and N2O). Translating the temperature target into allowable emissions depends on how land and ocean sinks respond to future change. For this, accurate present-day fluxes at national to global scales are needed to track progress towards Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) and to detect emerging changes early, such as a weakening of natural sinks. Observations of past and present fluxes, in turn, constrain projections of their future evolution. Yet all of these remain limited by large uncertainties in observing and modelling GHG fluxes from regional to global scales. Quantifying the transient response to emissions and the magnitude of remaining GHG budgets requires a substantial improvement in our ability to estimate the budgets and trends of major greenhouse gases across all spatio-temporal scales. This session aims to bring together studies to help understand and quantify past, present, and future global and regional GHG budgets in the atmosphere, the ocean, and on land, as well as processes controlling their trends and variability. We welcome contributions using a variety of approaches, such as (national) emissions inventories, field and remotely sensed observations, terrestrial and ocean biogeochemical modeling, Earth system modeling, and inverse modeling. We encourage contributions integrating different datasets and approaches at multiple spatial (regional to global) and temporal scales (diurnal, seasonal, interannual variability and long-term trends) that provide new insights on processes influencing GHG budgets and trends in the past, present and future.
title: Budgets, trends, and drivers of major Greenhouse Gases in the atmosphere, on land, and in the ocean from regional to global scales

description: A transformation towards sustainable agriculture is essential to secure food for both current and future generations while restoring natural resources. Agricultural productivity today faces multiple challenges, including climate change, water scarcity, limited access to essential inputs, socio-economic disparities, and rising global demand for agricultural products. Additionally, agriculture must play a pivotal role in mitigating climate change, reducing environmental pollution, and preserving biodiversity. Addressing these complex demands necessitates a comprehensive evaluation of alternative land management practices across local to global scales, with a focus on assessing entire agricultural production systems rather than isolated products. This session will address the modeling of agricultural systems in the context of global change, focusing on challenges related to climate change adaptation and mitigation, sustainable intensification, and the environmental impacts of agricultural production. We invite contributions on methodological approaches, data innovations, assessments of climate impacts and adaptation strategies, environmental consequences, greenhouse gas mitigation, and economic evaluations.
title: Modeling agricultural systems under global change

description: Extremes in temperature, vapor pressure deficit, and soil moisture severely endanger critical functions and services provided by terrestrial ecosystems. Both increasingly extreme long-term trends in environmental conditions and extreme events such as heatwaves, droughts, floods, and unseasonal freezes directly impact key physiological processes such as carbon uptake, transpiration, growth, and mortality. Abundances or scarcities of water, atmospheric dryness, heat, and cold can operate separately or in tandem to reduce terrestrial gross and net primary productivity and elevate risks of plant mortality. However, due to the complexity of these interactions and the lack of continuous time series, it is difficult to quantify the magnitude and timing of stress-related impacts on ecosystem function. As climate change accelerates the occurrence and severity of climatic extremes with consequences for terrestrial ecosystems, we must harmonize our efforts to characterize plant and ecosystem functions and develop frameworks for monitoring and prediction. In this session, we broadly explore the roles of temperature extremes, evaporative demand, and soil moisture in carbon, water, and energy relations, along with plant mortality across various spatial and temporal scales. We encourage submissions dealing with novel approaches for measuring and modeling plant and soil water status, responses to extreme conditions, and their impacts on ecosystem function. We invite contributions on these topics at scales ranging from individual plant tissues to entire ecosystems, applying experimental, observational, or modeling approaches and dealing with diverse disciplines such as plant physiology, community ecology, ecosystem ecology, land management, and biogeochemistry.
title: Impacts of climatic extremes on plants and ecosystems across scales

description: Savannas are open woody-herbaceous systems where low woody plant density permits substantial herbaceous productivity. Savanna ecosystems cover around 20 % of Earth’s land surface, supporting the livelihood of hundreds of millions of people, harboring unique biodiversity, and regulating regional to global carbon, water, and energy fluxes. Despite shared structural features, their geographical distribution spans multiple continents adding a wide range of climates, soils, biotas, and diverse management regimes - with fire and herbivory further regulating tree-grass coexistence. Both semi-arid and tropical savannas generally exhibit pronounced wet-dry seasonality and high intra- and interannual climate variability. Rapid changes such as rising temperatures, extreme droughts and heat events, shifting precipitation patterns, altered fire regimes, and land-use intensification are reshaping savanna structure and functions. These pressures can drive nonlinear dynamics, including woody encroachment, aridification of forests, biome boundary shifts, and changes in ecosystem services, raising urgent questions about resilience and tipping points. This session brings together observational, experimental, and modeling studies that advance our understanding of savanna function, land-atmosphere feedbacks and biome resilience in a changing world. Topics include, but are not limited to: · carbon, water, nutrient, and energy cycles and their variability across different scales · disturbance regime shifts and interactions with vegetation structure and function, seed banks and soils · detection and prediction of changes in tree-grass balance, woody encroachment and critical transitions · integration of process-based and statistical models to represent savanna dynamics and feedback mechanisms · biodiversity, ecosystem services, and social-ecological resilience, including integration of Indigenous and local knowledge in land management
title: Savanna function and resilience in a changing world

description: We have an urgent need to understand and predict terrestrial ecosystem responses to global change and disturbances, and how these responses shape these interconnected carbon, water, and nutrient cycles. However, ecosystem responses to global change span both above- and below-ground and are investigated through diverse approaches, from observations and experiments to modelling. Tackling these together is critical for enhancing the predictive capacity for our shared planetary future. This session focuses on two complementary connections: links between above- and belowground ecosystem processes, and links between experiments, observations, and models. We welcome studies addressing either or both, including research on carbon, water and nutrient processes, plant traits and physiological responses, ecosystem interactions, and scaling from individuals to ecosystems. Contributions are welcome across a range of scales and approaches, from greenhouse and mesocosm experiments to large-scale field manipulations, remote sensing, and machine learning and process-based modelling. We particularly encourage contributions presenting novel methods, ideas and hypotheses, including those from early-career researchers, and aim to create a space where such ideas can be discussed openly.
title: Above- and Belowground Ecosystem Processes from Observations and Modelling

description: Studying the impact of environmental change on soil C cycling has a long and established history. Soils are heterogeneous, requiring a multidisciplinary approach integrating biogeochemistry, physics, microbial diversity, and other drivers. Although we can increasingly integrate multiple processes into soil C cycling models, challenges remain in determining the appropriate level of complexity or abstraction, calibrating parameters, and selecting ecologically relevant variables. Meanwhile, growing data from (long-term) experiments can support model design, calibration, and validation, alongside advances in hybrid modelling and machine learning. However, integrating climatic and biotic interactions into biogeochemical process models for heterogeneous soils remains limited by methodological challenges. Long-term datasets are scarce, especially those designed to test model structures, parameterisation strategies, and process representations. Modelling studies may also fail to incorporate the latest experimental insights because model development and evaluation is time consuming or required data are unavailable. Conversely, experiments are not always designed with modelling applications in mind, limiting their use for model testing and generalisation across sites and scales. This session brings together experimental and modelling scientists to discuss advances and challenges in soil C cycling. We particularly welcome contributions demonstrating successful integration of experimental and modelling approaches, identifying critical knowledge gaps, and exploring pathways toward more robust predictions of soil carbon dynamics under global change. We invite contributions linked to: • Soil C and nutrient cycling and microbial diversity experiments, especially those designed to support model development and/or containing long time series. • (Hybrid) modelling at various spatial scales, including data-model integration, mechanistic process representations, parameterisation and calibration, model evaluation, uncertainty analysis, and machine learning. • Studies linking climatic and biological drivers of soil C cycling. • Research integrating experiments and modelling, including data assimilation, model validation, long-term datasets, and identification of key processes controlling soil C dynamics under environmental change. • Studies addressing transferability and scaling of soil C processes from laboratory and field experiments to ecosystem, landscape, and global scales
title: Bridging gaps between data and models: integrating process understanding through soil experiments and modelling techniques

description: The global nitrogen cycle is a fundamental component of the Earth system, influencing terrestrial and marine ecosystem productivity, atmospheric chemistry and climate dynamics. Anthropogenic perturbations have profoundly altered this cycle, leading to environmental challenges such as greenhouse gas emissions, air pollution, and eutrophication. Despite decades of research, significant uncertainties remain in quantifying the key fluxes and transformations of nitrogen across the terrestrial, aquatic, and atmospheric domains. Addressing these challenges requires an Earth system perspective that integrates diverse insights into a coherent global framework and ensures robust representation of nitrogen–carbon–climate interactions in Earth System Models (ESMs). This session invites contributions that advance understanding of the global nitrogen cycle, its regional and global budget closure, its interactions with carbon, water and climate, including studies that: • Quantify nitrogen fluxes (N₂O, NH₃, NOx, N₂, BNF, lateral N) across atmosphere, vegetation, soil, and aquatic/marine systems. • Reconcile regional and global nitrogen budgets using observations, inversions, process-based models, and data-driven approaches. • Evaluate uncertainties, benchmarking strategies, and emergent constraints for nitrogen–carbon and nitrogen–climate interactions in ESMs and Integrated Assessment Models. • Assess nitrogen’s role in regulating air and freshwater pollution, land carbon sinks, climate feedbacks, and mitigation pathways. • Provide synthesis-level insights relevant to global assessments (e.g., IPCC). By emphasizing budget closure, cross-domain integration, and benchmarking frameworks, this session provides a platform for advancing global nitrogen cycle research and strengthening its connections to Earth system modeling and sustainability challenges.
title: Global Nitrogen Cycle in the Earth System: Benchmarks, Budgets, Coupled Cycles and Feedbacks

description: Anthropogenic disturbance of the global nitrogen (N) cycle has more than doubled the amount of reactive N circulating in the terrestrial biosphere alone. Exchange of reactive/non-reactive nitrogen gases between land and atmosphere are strongly affecting Earth’s atmospheric composition, air quality, global warming, climate change and human health. This session seeks to improve our understanding of a) how intensification of reactive N use, land management and climate change affects the pools and fluxes of nitrogen in terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems, b) and how reactive N enrichment of land and water will affect the future carbon sink of natural ecosystems as well as atmospheric exchanges of reactive (NO, N2O, NH3, HONO, NO2 and non-reactive N (N2) gases with implications for global warming, climate change and air quality. We welcome contributions covering a wide range of experimental and modelling studies, which covers microbes-mediated and physico-chemical transformations and transport of nitrogen across the land-water-air continuum in natural ecosystems from local to regional and global scales. Furthermore, the interactions of nitrogen with other elemental cycles (e.g. phosphorus, carbon) and the impacts of these interactive feedbacks for soil health, biodiversity and water and air quality will be explored in this session. Latest developments in methodological innovations and observational and experimental approaches for unravelling the complexities of nitrogen transformations and transport will also be of interest.
title: Nitrogen Cycling in the Anthropocene: Microbiological Processes, Land-atmosphere- Interactions and Global Change Feedbacks

description: Methane emissions are produced by a variety of natural and anthropogenic sources across different ecosystems, spatial scales and time periods. Quantifying these emissions and removals, and understanding their variability is challenging as the production, oxidation, transport and emission of methane are influenced by a variety of interactions between biological, physical and human disturbance processes. There is also a significant lack of observations in key regions that have been estimated to be major sources, such as tropical forests and heterogeneous Arctic landscapes. Thus, there remains substantial mismatch between bottom-up and top-down estimates, particularly for natural sources such as wetlands, peatlands, inland waters, permafrost and other ecosystems, as well as uncertainties in methane atmospheric oxidation and consumption by bacteria in the soil. This session aims to promote interdisciplinary collaboration and improve our understanding of methane sources and sinks, their variability, and associated uncertainties across spatial and temporal scales. We encourage studies applying a variety of complementary observational, experimental and modelling approaches, from ecosystem measurements, such as chamber and eddy-covariance techniques, and remote sensing, to inventories, process-based models and Earth system models, as well as atmospheric observations and inversions. We particularly welcome studies that explore upscaling of measurements from ecosystem and landscape scales to integration within regional and global methane budgets, as well as studies that identify and reduce uncertainties in methane source estimates. We welcome contributions addressing all sources of methane with a particular focus on improving the quantification and understanding of the processes involved in natural methane emissions, as well as their representation in models and global budgets.
title: Methane emissions and removals across scales: from ecosystem and local processes to regional and global budgets

description: We welcome contributions that use stable isotopes of light elements (C, H, O, N, S) and novel tracers (e.g., COS) to advance our understanding of biogeochemical and atmospheric processes. We invite studies based on field and laboratory experiments, analytical and instrumental developments, theoretical approaches, and modelling. We particularly welcome contributions addressing: Isotopologues of carbon dioxide (CO₂), water (H₂O), methane (CH₄), carbon monoxide (CO), oxygen (O₂), carbonyl sulfide (COS), and nitrous oxide (N₂O) Novel tracers and biological analogues Polyisotopologues, including clumped isotopes Non-mass-dependent isotopic fractionation and related isotope anomalies Intramolecular stable isotope distributions and isotopomer abundances Quantification and interpretation of isotope effects Analytical, methodological, instrumental, and modelling developments Isotope-based flux measurements
title: Stable isotopes and novel tracers in atmospheric and biogeosciences

description: This session is open to all contributions in biogeochemistry and ecology where stable isotope techniques are used as analytical tools, with foci both on stable isotopes of light elements (C, H, O, N, S, …) and new systems (clumped and metal isotopes). We welcome studies from both terrestrial and marine, aquatic and sedimentary environments as well as methodological, experimental and theoretical studies that introduce new approaches or techniques (including natural abundance work, labeling studies, modeling). Results from the successful EGU session that took place earlier have been published in several special issues of Organic Geochemistry and Isotopes in Environmental & Health Studies.
title: Application of Stable Isotopes in Biogeosciences

description: The gross photosynthetic CO2 uptake is the largest component of the global carbon cycle. It is a crucial variable for monitoring and understanding global biogeochemical cycles along with fundamental ecosystem services. Nowadays, routine measurements of the net biosphere-atmosphere CO2 exchange are conducted at the ecosystem scale in a large variety of ecosystem types worldwide. Gross photosynthetic and ecosystem respiratory fluxes are typically inferred from the net CO2 exchange and used for benchmarking of terrestrial biosphere models, or as backbones for upscaling exercises. One major source of uncertainty in predictions of ecosystem-atmosphere feedbacks under climate change is the response of photosynthesis and respiration to changes in environmental conditions. Furthermore, transpiration estimates are highly uncertain at ecosystem to global scales, with estimates ranging from 20 % to 90 % of total evapotranspiration. The most important bottleneck in narrowing down transpiration estimates is the fact that direct measurements of transpiration are uncertain and techniques like eddy covariance measure only the total evapotranspiration. During the last decade, technological developments in field spectroscopy have enabled alternative approaches for constraining ecosystem-scale photosynthesis, respiration and transpiration. These include remote and proximal sensing of sun-induced fluorescence, as well as isotope flux measurements and quantum cascade laser-based trace gas measurements, including carbonyl sulfide as a proxy for GPP. Additionally, a variety of other approaches have been developed to directly assess the gross fluxes of CO2 and transpiration by using both process based and empirical models, as well as machine learning techniques. In this session, we aim at reviewing recent progress made with novel approaches of constraining ecosystem gross primary productivity, respiration and transpiration. We will discuss their weaknesses and future steps required to reduce the uncertainty of present-day estimates. To this end, we invite contributions that use emerging constraints to improve the ability to quantify respiration and photosynthesis processes, transpiration and water use efficiency, from leaf to ecosystem and global scales.
title: Emerging constraints of photosynthesis, respiration and transpiration at ecosystem to global scales

description: Direct flux measurements of heat, water, greenhouse gasses (GHGs) and pollutants between the earth’s surface and its atmosphere unlock fair and equitable climate solutions across natural and built environments. Innovations and markets based on such an approach help resolve global climate and air quality challenges and fairly reward small and big stakeholders. This session, organized collaboratively by research and industry, welcomes ideas and examples of how to utilize direct flux measurements for tangible societal benefits, such as carbon removal, agriculture and forestry, reduction of anthropogenic emissions, environmental impact management, and more. For instance, these measurements can be applied to irrigation scheduling, soil and plant treatments, GHG reduction and sequestration, global warming potential, urban heat management, satellite and model products, industry emissions, severe weather impacts, air quality management, and can be used as a diagnostic tool for meeting net-zero targets by different organizations, regulatory, and government agencies. Join us to discuss together developing a global paradigm for maximum-integrity, low-latency and economically sound earth stewardship, anchored in direct flux measurements.
title: Flux Measurements for Immediate Societal Benefits.

description: European peatlands are a major emitter of greenhouse gasses, particularly carbon dioxide and methane, contributing to climate warming. Monitoring these emissions is essential to understand their contribution to emission budgets and to design effective mitigation strategies. Greenhouse gas emissions from peatlands are currently accounted for by countries through mandatory national greenhouse gas inventory reporting. However as emission reduction targets become more ambitious and the targeted reduction deadlines approach, the need for reliable and robust monitoring systems is increasing. In addition, the growing number of peatland restoration projects and carbon crediting schemes also require reliable, transparent and spatially explicit monitoring systems. Peatland greenhouse gas emissions are highly variable in both time and space and measurement techniques come with considerable uncertainty, challenging the applicability of current approaches. Furthermore substantial differences exists between countries in monitoring methods and reporting approaches, hampering international comparisons and the harmonisation of emission estimates. This sessions aims to bring together researchers who contribute directly or indirectly to peatland greenhouse gas monitoring to exchange ideas and share best practices from across Europe and beyond. We invite contributions focusing on the development and application of methods and tools for peatland greenhouse gas monitoring. Both contributions discussing current practices and those presenting novel approaches are welcome. Relevant topics include, but are not limited to, process-based modelling, greenhouse gas measurement networks, monitoring methodologies, mapping products and approaches, monitoring requirements, and supporting research that advances peatland greenhouse gas assessment. This session is supported by the European Peatland Greenhouse Gas Monitoring Group.
title: Methods and tools for peatland greenhouse gas emission monitoring

description: Global change and anthropogenic influences pose complex, multi-layered challenges to terrestrial ecosystems. Consequently, essential ecosystem functions and services are threatened, with negative impacts on key areas such as food production in agroecosystems. To analyze these dynamics, multidimensional environmental experiments are becoming essential. Within this context, ecotrons enable the controlled manipulation and observation of ecosystem components and processes, while weighing lysimeters deliver highly precise, high-resolution measurements of soil water balance dynamics. Enhanced by state-of-the-art control and monitoring systems – such as temperature regulation (heating/cooling), elevated CO2 regimes, non-destructive root monitoring, and stable isotope technologies to trace water, gas, and nutrient fluxes – these platforms allow the simulation and investigation of complex, realistic (future) scenarios. In combination, ecotrons and lysimeters close a gap in the Soil-Plant-Atmosphere Continuum (SPAC), enabling a holistic, integrated system view. We invite contributions that utilize these experimental platforms or similar techniques to address fundamental and applied questions in the fields of ecosystem research, soil science, hydrology, biogeochemistry, plant ecology, agricultural sciences, and climate impact research. We welcome contributions on the following topics (including but not limited to): (1) Processes in the SPAC: analyzing water, nutrient, and gas fluxes, including non-rainfall water inputs (e.g., dew, fog, soil water vapor adsorption). (2) Ecosystem functioning and multi-stress analyses: assessing and comparing ecosystem functions under controlled conditions (e.g., by decoupling individual environmental drivers and analyzing combined stressors). (3) Scaling, representativeness, and validation: approaches for upscaling to the landscape scale, comparisons with other in-situ instruments, representativeness and uncertainty assessments, and validation studies (e.g., via remote sensing). (4) Modeling ecosystem processes: application and advancement of hydrological and ecosystem models directly utilizing high-resolution in-situ data from ecotrons and lysimeters. (5) Methodological and technological developments: innovations in ecotron and lysimeter technology, including approaches and algorithms for data processing.
title: Ecosystem research using ecotrons and lysimeters as a central platform for experiments on multidimensional environmental change

description: Blue carbon ecosystems, including mostly salt marshes, mangroves, seagrasses, tidal forests and mudflats, rank among the most carbon-dense ecosystems on Earth. They provide nature-based solutions essential to mitigate residual anthropogenic carbon emissions, while also delivering co-benefits such as biodiversity support or coastal protection. However, their resilience and capacity to sustain these functions are increasingly threatened by climate change and human pressures. To safeguard their role, it is essential to better understand their carbon cycle—particularly the feedback loops between soil and plants, the exchanges of carbon among the atmosphere, soil, and water, but also how human activities, vegetation, and carbon processes interact. This session seeks to bring together scientists from multiple disciplines, including biogeochemists, ecologists, geographers, geologists, social scientists, biologists, alongside environmental managers. By bridging perspectives across the natural and social sciences, the session aims to showcase pioneering research that i) advances understanding processes related to biomass and carbon in blue carbon ecosystems under current and future environmental conditions; and ii) spotlights effective management, conservation, and restoration practices to sustain or enhance carbon sequestration and broader ecosystem services, coupling the ecological functioning with social needs. Through this integration, the session will contribute to the goals of the United Nations Decade for Ocean Sciences, with co-convenorship from the Decade Programme for Blue Carbon in the Global Ocean.
title: Beyond Blue Carbon

description: A robust representation of terrestrial carbon, nitrogen, and water cycles requires a fundamental understanding of biosphere-atmosphere interactions, particularly in the context of a rapidly changing climate. However, a significant challenge arises from the mismatch that occurs when carbon, water, or nitrogen fluxes are measured or modelled at different spatio-temporal scales. Multiple processes determine how mass and energy exchanges scale from the leaf, to the whole plant, to the ecosystem, and eventually to the globe. Despite the evolution of Earth system models to incorporate increasingly complex processes across these scales, uncertainties persist due to these mismatches. The unprecedented rate of climate change, along with the increasing frequency and intensity of extreme events, further complicates our ability to robustly formulate mechanistic underpinnings of biogeochemical processes across scales. The increasing volume of data at multiple scales—from leaf-level measurements (e.g., gas exchange), tree-level measurements (e.g., sap flow and dendroecology), ecosystem-level measurements (e.g., eddy covariance towers, UAVs, aircraft), to Earth observation from space—presents new opportunities to address these challenges. This session invites studies that improve our overall understanding of biosphere-atmosphere interactions by addressing the mismatches across different temporal and spatial scales and integrating these insights into modeling strategies. We particularly encourage contributions that explore the effects of climate extremes (e.g., drought, heatwaves, excess rainfall, winter warming) on carbon, nitrogen, and water fluxes. In addition to empirical multi-scale observations, we welcome research that delves into data-driven diagnostics and constraints for model evaluation, data-driven parameterisations in mechanistic models, and the development of data-driven/hybrid modelling strategies (i.e., seamless fusion of data-driven approaches and mechanistic models) for an integrated understanding of carbon, nitrogen, and water fluxes across scales.
title: Novel methods for bridging understanding of carbon, nitrogen, and water fluxes from leaf to continental scales

description: Urban forests and green infrastructure are increasingly recognized as key components of climate-resilient and low-carbon cities. Through carbon sequestration and storage, regulation of surface energy and water exchanges, shading and evapotranspiration, urban vegetation can contribute simultaneously to climate change mitigation and adaptation, while also providing important benefits for human health and well-being. However, the magnitude and persistence of these benefits depend on complex interactions among vegetation structure and functioning, climate, urban morphology, land-use dynamics and management practices. This session aims to advance understanding of the role of urban forests and vegetation in regulating carbon dynamics and urban microclimate, bringing together observational, modelling and remote-sensing perspectives across spatial and temporal scales. We welcome contributions addressing carbon uptake, storage and greenhouse-gas balances of urban vegetation; vegetation–atmosphere exchanges; evapotranspiration and cooling processes; urban heat-island mitigation; tree responses to heat, drought and other climatic extremes; and interactions between carbon sequestration, water use and cooling benefits. The session also welcomes studies exploring how urban expansion, land-use change, vegetation configuration and management influence the long-term mitigation and adaptation potential of urban forests, as well as approaches integrating Earth Observation, in-situ monitoring, process-based modelling, machine learning and digital twins to assess present and future urban vegetation dynamics. By connecting carbon-cycle science, urban climatology, ecophysiology, Earth Observation and in-situ observations, and urban planning, the session seeks to improve our capacity to quantify the multiple climate, environmental and societal benefits of urban forests and to identify strategies for designing and managing greener, healthier, more resilient and climate-neutral cities.
title: Urban Trees for Climate Change Mitigation and Adaptation: Carbon Dynamics and Microclimate Cooling

description: Accurately representing land-atmosphere interactions remains one of the key challenges in Earth system science. Process-based models, including land surface components of Earth System Models and dynamic global vegetation models, encode our understanding of these interactions and underpin projections of current and future climate. They also provide essential insight into carbon and water dynamics within ecosystems and help us extract richer information from our ever-growing observations. Yet advances in machine learning and artificial intelligence show that significant performance gains remain within reach. Harnessing these tools for modelling and understanding land-atmosphere interactions is of great potential to keep process-based models fit for purpose and at the cutting edge, supporting more robust climate projections. Robust benchmarking frameworks and rigorous comparisons are essential to evaluate, track and quality-control their applications. This session invites contributions exploring how machine learning, artificial intelligence, and benchmarking can help address these challenges and accelerate model development. We welcome a broad range of perspectives, including: new AI-driven approaches to closing knowledge gaps; advances in benchmarking and model evaluation; physics-informed machine learning frameworks for operational use, process discovery and understanding; the growing role of emulators in model development and application; and the development of novel observational products and datasets. By bringing together researchers across disciplines, the session aims to highlight emerging opportunities for building more robust, reliable, and insightful land-surface models.
title: Leveraging machine learning and benchmarking frameworks for better understanding and modelling of land-atmosphere interactions

description: Biophysical parameters have been traditionally measured at the point or plot level on the ground. Remote sensing provides a way to map biophysical parameters at up to the global scale and over decades, with machine learning methods or radiative transfer modeling. This session calls for studies producing various biophysical parameters maps, such as plant traits, phenology, plant species, land cover types, and soil properties etc., using remote sensing observations and discussion on current shortcomings of the gridded datasets.
title: Remote sensing of biophysical parameters and dataset production

description: This session aims to unite scientists employing stable isotope analyses of light elements (e.g., carbon, oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen) to address ecophysiological questions concerning climate change and other abiotic and biotic stressors. We invite researchers studying a variety of compounds (e.g., lipids, cellulose, lignin, non-structural carbohydrates, water) from both aquatic/marine (e.g., fish, micro and macroalgae) and terrestrial (e.g., mosses, grasses, crops, trees) ecosystems. Contributions that explore any spatiotemporal scale and use archival materials (e.g., herbarium samples, peat, sediments, loess, tree rings) are particularly welcome. Researchers utilizing a range of analytical techniques (e.g. IRMS, NMR, Orbitrap and spectroscopy-based methods), as well as different isotope techniques (e.g. natural abundance work, labelling studies, modeling) are encouraged to present their methodological advancements. By showcasing cutting-edge research and methodological innovations, we aim to highlight the crucial role of stable isotope analysis in ecophysiological studies and foster interdisciplinary collaboration. We look forward to your contributions to this exciting and dynamic session.
title: From molecules to ecosystems: stable isotope approaches to ecophysiology

description: The body of remotely sensed observations is growing, while Earth system models move to km-scales. Together, these tendencies require land surface models to integrate heterogeneous observations, address incomplete process knowledge, and overcome computational constraints. Machine learning (ML) offers tools for addressing these challenges, and has demonstrated a strong ability to learn complex non-linear relationships from data when high-quality data is available. However, many land surface applications do not meet this condition and must instead rely on sparse, irregular, or imbalanced observations or represent processes that are only partially observable. Hybrid and AI-enabled models combine the flexibility of ML with physics-based knowledge to produce predictions that are both data-informed and physically constrained. The spectrum of physics-ML integration ranges from a physical model core that is extended by ML for parameterization, data assimilation, emulation, or bias correction, to an ML model core that is constrained through physical pretraining, regularization, causal pathways, or explicit equations. When and how physics-ML fusion is useful is highly use-case specific, and its potential for operationalisation is an open question. This session brings together researchers from ecosystem and land surface modeling, boundary layer meteorology, hydrology, Earth observation, and Earth system data science across this spectrum. We welcome contributions including but not limited to: hybrid process-ML models and learned process representations; emulators, surrogate models, and reduced-order land model representations; discovery of governing scientific equations from data; differentiable and end-to-end trainable modelling frameworks; AI-based models hard- or soft-constrained by physical principles or causal structure; model-data integration, data assimilation, and uncertainty quantification. We also encourage work on neural operators, foundation models, digital twins, and other AI-enabled approaches to land, ecosystem, and hydrological dynamics - especially studies that systematically compare modelling strategies, assess generalization and physical consistency, or identify conditions when physics-ML integration succeeds or fails.
title: Hybrid and AI-enabled modeling of terrestrial systems

description: Understanding the dynamics of the terrestrial carbon cycle is essential for developing strategies to reduce atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations and mitigate global warming. Although this topic is extensively studied, key uncertainties remain—particularly regarding the temporal dynamics of the carbon cycle and how long carbon persists in terrestrial ecosystems after assimilation. Addressing these gaps is critical for a deeper understanding of carbon cycle processes. The temporal dimension of the carbon cycle emerges from how carbon moves through ecosystems. Carbon enters via photosynthesis and is initially allocated to fast-cycling pools, where much of it is rapidly returned to the atmosphere. Only a fraction is gradually transferred to slow-cycling soil pools, where it can persist for years to centuries. The efficiency of this transfer depends on plant allocation strategies, microbial processing, soil properties, and climate. This session explores how carbon isotopic tracers improve our understanding of carbon accumulation, transfer, and retention over time. Stable carbon isotopes (δ¹³C) trace recent carbon assimilation and allocation (from hours to days), while radiocarbon (∆¹⁴C) provides insights into carbon age and persistence over years to centuries. We welcome contributions that use natural and induced carbon tracers—both stable and radioactive isotopes—across in situ and laboratory experiments, as well as modeling approaches. Studies investigating carbon allocation, transfer among pools, and retention in different terrestrial pools are encouraged, including those aiming to understand the variables driving the temporal dynamics of these processes. All types of terrestrial ecosystems and spatial scales are welcome. By bringing together recent advances in the use of carbon isotopes, this session aims to enhance understanding of the temporal dynamics of carbon in terrestrial ecosystems and identify key knowledge gaps under ongoing environmental change.
title: Temporal dynamics of carbon in terrestrial ecosystems through carbon Isotopes

description: Mycorrhizal fungi are central to the functioning of terrestrial ecosystems, playing a critical role in ecological processes such as nutrient cycling and carbon storage. Mycorrhizal fungi enhance nutrient uptake by plants, primary productivity, decomposition, and they contribute to organic matter accumulation. This session aims to bring together research investigating the diverse roles and functions of mycorrhizal fungi in forest, grassland, wetland, and other “natural” ecosystems, with a focus on ectomycorrhizal, arbuscular, and ericoid mycorrhizal associations. We will explore how mycorrhizal fungi drive ecosystem functioning in its broadest sense, and how these processes respond to environmental changes, from climate change to management. We welcome contributions from research conducted across all biomes and scales, ranging from the global to petri dish environment, encompassing observational, experimental, and modeling approaches. By fostering discussion and sharing cutting-edge research, this session aims to deepen our understanding of mycorrhizal fungi as mediators of ecosystem function, clarify their ecological importance, and highlight the need for continued exploration in this rapidly evolving field.
title: Mycorrhizal fungi in natural ecosystems

description: Environmental change is altering the soil–plant continuum, with consequences for ecosystem functioning, crop productivity, biogeochemical cycles, and land management. Drought, salinity, temperature extremes, nutrient imbalances, and soil degradation affect element mobility and bioavailability, root uptake, carbon assimilation, and plant performance. Understanding these interconnected responses requires approaches that link below- and above-ground processes across spatial and temporal scales. This session will explore how isotope and trace-element geochemistry can be integrated with plant phenotyping to investigate the soil–rhizosphere–plant–atmosphere system under changing environmental conditions. We welcome contributions from natural and managed ecosystems, including forests, grasslands, croplands, orchards, vineyards, and marginal lands. We particularly encourage studies integrating stable isotopes (e.g. δ¹³C, δ¹⁵N, δ²H, δ¹⁸O, and δ³⁴S), trace-element and isotope geochemistry, and plant phenotyping methods such as spectral and thermal imaging, chlorophyll fluorescence, and root-stem-leaf hydraulic system structural-functional characterization. These complementary approaches can help trace water and nutrient pathways, assess element bioavailability and soil-to-plant transfer, and identify physiological responses across species, cultivars, and genotypes. Contributions may range from controlled experiments to field and landscape-scale studies, including methodological advances and the integration of experimental data with modelling or remote sensing. By connecting geochemistry, soil biogeochemistry, plant ecophysiology, hydrology, phenotyping, and crop science, the session aims to translate fundamental knowledge of the soil–plant continuum into applications for ecosystem and crop resilience, climate-smart agriculture, and sustainable land management.
title: Tracing water, elements, and plant function across the soil–plant–atmosphere continuum: integrating isotope geochemistry, phenotyping, and transport modelling

description: Tropical peatlands store around 105 Gt carbon (C), although their total extent remains uncertain due to inadequate data. In a natural condition, tropical peatlands are long-term C stores and support livelihoods, but anthropogenic disturbances are increasing in extent. These transformations result in high C loss, reduced C storage, increased greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, loss of hydrological integrity, peat subsidence, increased risk of fire, and negative social impacts. For agricultural peatlands, changes in nutrient storage and cycling necessitate fertilizer use, with enhanced emissions of N2O. Under a warming climate, these impacts are likely to intensify and reduce the benefits to rural communities. This session welcomes contributions on all aspects of tropical peatland science, including peatland mapping and monitoring; the impact of climate on past, present and future tropical peatland formation, accumulation and C dynamics; peatland ecology and hydrology; GHG and nutrient flux dynamics; management strategies for GHG emissions mitigation and the maintenance or restoration of C sequestration and storage; and valuing ancestral knowledge of peatlands. Field based, experimental and modelling studies of intact and modified systems from all tropical regions are welcomed.
title: Tropical Peatlands: Past, Present, Uncertain Future

description: Although climate change is a natural process, it is significantly stimulated by anthropogenic activities. The acceleration of climate change is directly connected with ecological stability, soil degradation, and hydrological extremes, which are considered as the main consequences of climate change. As climate change intensifies, extreme and unexpected weather events are becoming more frequent. The aim of this session is to highlight a broad range of research methods and results related to climate change. This interdisciplinary session should reflect, discuss, and share scientific knowledge on a local and regional scale with the aim to increase innovative knowledge on climate change and its impacts, ecosystem response and new techniques to prevent and reduce the negative consequences. This session encourages contributions from several fields related to: - climate change impacts (biodiversity loss, rising temperatures, hydrological extremes, soil degradation, ecosystem response to climate change); - droughts and floods; precipitation deficiency or extreme precipitation with solutions aimed at reducing the negative impacts; - ecological stability and climate change; changes of ecological stability, deforestation, human interactions with the environment and evaluation of restoration success; - green cities to increase the ecological stability of the urban landscape; - techniques and methods to prevent and reduce the negative impacts of climate change (such as soil degradation, carbon sequestration, changes in natural, agricultural, and forest ecosystems, reduction of overall ecological stability and character of the landscape); In addition, attention will be given to the sustainability of management practices, the importance of appropriate land use management as the main tool for preventing degradation processes, the distribution and vitality of ecosystems, and improving the condition of forest ecosystems in order to increase the overall character of the landscape.
title: Complex case studies for ecosystem responses to global change, climate and hydrological extremes

description: Tropical forests are biomes of global significance due to their exceptional biodiversity, carbon storage capacity, and key role in the hydrological cycle. In recent decades, ecosystems across South America, Central America, Central Africa, and Southeast Asia have experienced increasing pressures from human activities, climate change, and intensified natural variability, including a growing frequency of extreme events such as droughts, heatwaves, and storms compounded by ENSO and increased fire occurrency. These drivers have altered the cycling of nutrients, carbon, water, and energy, while also affecting human livelihoods. Yet the ecological consequences of extremes are rarely limited to single, isolated events: repeated disturbances can compound over time, shifting forests from resilient recovery trajectories toward cumulative, and potentially irreversible, stress. In this session, we aim to place a particular emphasis on how tropical forest ecosystems respond to both individual extreme events and their cumulative effects of multiple stressors over time. We invite contributions that examine the consequences of single versus repeated disturbances across multiple dimensions, including above- and belowground biomass, forest-atmosphere interactions, carbon budgets, biodiversity, and social livelihoods. We welcome studies using diverse approaches, ranging from experimental and field-based investigations to remote sensing and modeling. Our goal is to foster a holistic understanding of how the transition from single events to cumulative stress shapes both the current and future states of tropical vegetation and the communities that depend on it.
title: Tropical forests in transition under repeated extremes: from single events to cumulative stress

description: Ecosystem models remain limited by how they represent key ecological and biogeochemical processes and their responses to climate variability, extremes, and long-term environmental change. Persistent challenges include representing vegetation demography and trait diversity, acclimation and adaptation, stress responses and disturbances, carbon allocation, and coupled carbon–nutrient–water cycles. Uncertainties and biases in these process representations limit our ability to predict ecosystem dynamics and further climate feedbacks. Meanwhile, rapidly expanding Earth observations, data-synthesis efforts, and advances in artificial intelligence (AI) are creating new opportunities for ecosystem process development, including identifying missing process connections, emulating computationally demanding components, and complementing certain processes. This session brings together scientists working on process-based, data-driven, and hybrid approaches to advance process understanding in land ecosystem modelling. Contributions may address model development, benchmarking and evaluation, uncertainty reduction, or the integration of ecological knowledge and observations into models. We invite abstracts addressing one or more of the following themes: 1. Advances in representing ecosystem responses to climate variability, extremes, disturbances, or long-term environmental change; 2. Improved representation of vegetation demography and dynamics, species interactions, functional diversity, acclimation, adaptation, and carbon allocation; 3. Advances in modelling biogeochemical processes and interactions, including coupled carbon, nutrient, and water cycles across ecosystems and scales; 4. Applications of AI and machine learning to ecosystem modelling, including process emulation or replacement, parameter estimation, and discovery of missing or poorly represented processes; 5. Emergent constraints, causal inference, and other observation-based approaches for reducing uncertainty in ecosystem responses and land–climate feedbacks; Session format The session will include oral and poster presentations. As conveners from five universities, we aim to create a forum to discuss transferable model developments, evaluate emerging datasets and relationships, and share knowledge across modelling frameworks. We plan to host a session dinner to facilitate discussion and networking further, and we will announce more details later.
title: Advancing land ecosystem models through process understanding, observations, and artificial intelligence

description: Oxidation of peat organic carbon is a critical determinant of greenhouse gas emissions from peatland ecosystems. This session aims to bridge the gap between biogeochemical processes at the pore scale and their environmental impacts at the ecosystem scale. At the heart of peat carbon oxidation are microorganisms that act on molecular carbon substrates, driving biogeochemical reactions at a microscale. These microbial processes are fundamental, yet they operate on a scale that poses challenges for direct observation and measurement, and modeling. Our current methodologies provide valuable data on carbon turnover and peatland dynamics. However, there remains a significant challenge in inferring processes at the microscale and extrapolating or linking these drivers to the ecosystem scale. This linking is needed to be able to make estimations and future predictions of carbon emissions from peatlands and the consequences of a changing climate. This scientific session will focus aims to integrate across the multiple scales of peat carbon oxidation. We will explore: 1. Microscale Processes: Understanding the role of biogeochemistry and microorganisms in peat decomposition and the processes that determine peat carbon oxidation potentials and rates 2. Intermediate-Scale Measurements: Applying techniques and methodologies to measure carbon turnover and emissions, the insights they provide in underlying processes, and techniques for upscaling 3. Challenges in Upscaling: Addressing the links between small-scale processes and ecosystem-scale emissions. This includes modeling approaches and integrative methods to connect scales. Our goal is to foster a dialogue that integrates these different scales of study, ultimately enhancing our ability to predict and manage the effects of peat carbon oxidation on the global carbon cycle. By integration across scales, we aim to advance our understanding of peatland functioning and to develop more accurate models reflecting the true complexity of peatland ecosystems. Join us in this session to contribute to a comprehensive understanding of peat oxidation and its far-reaching implications.
title: Oxidation of Peat Carbon: From Process Understanding to Emissions Estimates

description: Climate extremes are reshaping forest disturbance regimes worldwide. Hotter droughts, heatwaves and compound events are increasingly associated with growth decline, canopy dieback and pulses of tree mortality, reducing the carbon sink potential of forests, threatening biodiversity and impairing ecosystem services. Yet a central challenge remains unresolved: when does climate stress cross the threshold from reversible impairment to irreversible decline and death? This session focuses on the early-warning signals, mechanisms and projections of tree mortality focusing on these irreversible shifts or transitions. We invite studies that connect hydraulic dysfunction, carbon and nutrient dynamics, wood formation, phenology and biotic stressors with growth, canopy condition and mortality data. We particularly welcome contributions that address: • critical thresholds, drought legacies, compound extremes and early-warning signals preceding canopy dieback and tree death; • hydraulic and carbon-related proxies and mechanisms of tree decline and mortality; • resilience and recovery failure, including carryover effects or legacies across seasons and years; • integration of tree rings, dendrometers, ecophysiological measurements, forest inventories, flux observations and remote sensing for monitoring forest health from trees to biomes; • detection, mapping and forecasting of forest decline and mortality using Earth observation, machine learning, data-driven approaches and process-based models; • vulnerability of large, old and senescent trees and old-growth forests, and the role of forest structure, composition and functional diversity in modulating climate risk; • interactions among drought, heatwaves, fire, insects, pathogens and other natural or anthropogenic disturbances; • harmonization of monitoring approaches and development of global datasets and networks for detecting changes in forest vitality and mortality; • translation of vulnerability science into adaptive forest management, restoration strategies and decision-support tools. By bringing together field ecologists, experimentalists, ecophysiologists, dendroecologists, forest and remote-sensing scientists, modelers and managers, the session will identify why some trees, stands and forests persist while others decline, which indicators provide robust and transferable warnings, and how those insights can support climate-resilient forest management.
title: Crossing vulnerability thresholds: early-warning signals, mechanisms, and forecasts of tree mortality

description: Soils sustain complex patterns of life and act as biogeochemical reactors that produce and consume large quantity of gases, including greenhouse gases, biogenic volatile organic compounds, nitrous acid etc. Interactions with primary producer activity add further complexity to the ongoing gas exchange between soils, ecosystems and the atmosphere. Measurements of gas exchange are not only relevant for deriving emission factors for GHG accounting, for example for agricultural systems, which are central for climate mitigation actions. Such measurements are also important for understanding the underlying processes and their drivers. New technologies including automated chamber systems are developing fast and produce large, high-frequency datasets consisting of thousands of flux measurements of greenhouse gas (GHG) fluxes, carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), and nitrous oxide (N2O), in terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems. They enable new insights into key biogeochemical cycles and their temporal and spatial regulation. However, the increased amount of data also creates a need for new methodologies for raw data processing, data curation, and data analysis to harness the complexity in these data sets. We are looking for abstracts on innovative analyses of the drivers of the gases production/consumption and transport in the ecosystems including field and laboratory studies utilising automated systems for measuring surface-atmosphere GHG exchange, novel processing and analytical approaches and modelling studies based on automated chamber data.
title: Approaches to measuring, processing and understanding the exchange of gases in soils and ecosystems

description: Carbon allocation is central to plant functioning and ecosystem carbon cycling. Recently assimilated carbon can be partitioned among a range of above- and belowground sinks including growth, respiration, storage, reproduction, symbiotic interactions and rhizodeposition, including root exudation. Environmental conditions can alter these allocation patterns, with consequences for the fate and persistence of carbon above- and belowground. Despite the importance of carbon allocation, we still lack a comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms controlling the fate of newly fixed carbon, how allocation patterns vary across species and ecosystems, and how they respond to environmental drivers. This session aims to address key questions such as: 1. What drives carbon allocation above- and below-ground? 2. How is recently assimilated carbon partitioned among sinks (e.g. growth, metabolism, storage, reproduction, symbioses and rhizodeposition)? 3. How do allocation patterns respond to global changes, involving a.o. warming, drought, elevated CO₂, or alterations in nutrient availability? 4. What trade-offs exist between aboveground and root growth, storage and exudation? 5. How does belowground carbon allocation support nutrient acquisition, water relations, stress tolerance and plant-microbe interactions? 6. How can carbon allocation, including root exudation, be quantified, traced and represented across spatial and temporal scales? We invite observational, experimental, methodological and modelling studies that investigate plant carbon allocation from organ to ecosystem scales. We particularly welcome studies that explore carbon allocation dynamics, including trade-offs among growth, storage, defence and reproduction, as well as root functioning, symbiotic carbon transfer and rhizodeposition in a changing environment. By bringing together research on plant physiology, root ecology, carbon tracing, rhizosphere processes and ecosystem modelling, this session seeks to advance an integrated understanding of how plants allocate carbon above- and below-ground, how these allocation strategies respond to global changes, and how they ultimately affect plant performance, ecosystem functioning and terrestrial carbon cycling.
title: Carbon allocation above- and belowground: environmental drivers, plant responses and ecosystem consequences

description: Environmental data from large measurement campaigns and automated measurement networks are increasingly available and provide relevant information of the Earth System. However, such data are usually only available as point observations and only represent a small part of the Earth´s surface. Upscaling strategies are hence needed to provide continuous and comprehensive information as a baseline to gain insights on large-scale spatio-temporal dynamics. In the upscaling, machine learning algorithms that can account for complex and nonlinear relationships are increasingly used to link remote sensing datasets to reference measurements. The resulting models are then applied to provide spatially explicit predictions of the target variable, often even on a global scale. Due to easy access to user-friendly software, model training and spatial prediction using machine learning algorithms is nowadays straightforward at first sight.
