However, considerable challenges remain: dealing with reference data that are not independent and identically distributed, accounting for spatial heterogeneity when scaling reference measurements to the grid cell scale, appropriately evaluating the resulting maps and quantifying their uncertainties, generating robust maps that do not suffer from extrapolation artifacts as well as the strategies for model interpretation and understanding. This session invites contributions on the methodology and application of large-scale mapping strategies in different disciplines, including vegetation characteristics such as foliar or canopy traits and photosynthesis, soil characteristics such as soil organic carbon, or atmospheric parameters such as pollutant concentration. Methodological contributions can focus on individual aspects of the upscaling approach, such as the design of measurement campaigns or networks to increase representativeness, novel algorithms or validation strategies, feature attribution/explainability as well as uncertainty assessment.
title: Large-scale mapping of environmental variables by combining ground observations, remote sensing, and machine learning

description: Robust, policy-relevant assessments of the terrestrial carbon cycle depend on reconciling top-down (atmospheric inversion) and bottom-up (process model, inventory) estimates - which continue to show persistent regional disagreement in the magnitude (and sometimes in the sign) of land carbon fluxes. Closing this gap requires better integration of Earth Observation (EO), in-situ measurements, and process-based models through data assimilation, alongside improved representation of the disturbances (fire, land management, drought) that drive much of today's uncertainty in regional carbon fluxes. We welcome contributions on: EO-based characterisation of ecosystem and canopy structure, disturbance, and carbon dynamics; the use of EO and in-situ data to constrain, evaluate, or improve process-based land surface and dynamic vegetation models; data assimilation and model-data fusion techniques merging observations into carbon cycle and Earth system models; disturbance representation in models; and regional-to-global carbon budget assessments reconciling top-down and bottom-up approaches, including near-real-time systems and applications relevant to national greenhouse gas inventories. This session is co-organised by members of the NextGenCarbon and CONCERTO Horizon Europe projects and the ESA THRAC3E project, aligned with the carbon flagship of the EC-ESA Earth System Science Initiative.
title: Reconciling Earth Observation and Process-Based Modelling to Constrain the Terrestrial Carbon Cycle

description: Human societies have transformed terrestrial landscapes well before and throughout the Holocene through fire, cultivation, deforestation, and, more recently, large-scale industrial land-use, intensive agriculture, and forestry. Datasets that capture this trajectory of land use change represent essential boundary conditions for global climate and carbon cycle models. However, such datasets are difficult to create at high enough spatial and temporal scales, especially as we go further back in time. These legacy impacts of land use transitions is the reason why land use emissions continue to have the highest uncertainty in the global carbon budget at approximately 60%. Over the recent decades, historical land use change datasets have evolved from coarse representation of a limited number of land use classes to complex frameworks that capture multiple land use transitions and land management practices. The integration of recent high-resolution earth observation data, LiDAR, historical archives with archeological and paleo-ecological evidence, historical maps, and dynamic vegetation modeling into long-term reconstruction workflows are enabling researchers to constrain historical LULCC at higher accuracies. This session invites researchers working across the interface of paleo-environmental science, remote sensing, and Earth system modeling to showcase recent advances in historical and contemporary land-use reconstructions. The themes include, but are not limited to 1) long-term historical LULCC reconstructions using historical, archeological or paleo-environmental data, 2) earth observation driven approaches to quantify post-industrial LULCC, 3) harmonizing high resolution observations with millennial scale global land use forcing datasets. We encourage interdisciplinary submissions from remote sensing scientists, ecological modelers, historical geographers, and paleoecologists to have discussions on building the next generation of LULCC datasets.
title: Advances in historical land-use and land-cover change (LULCC) reconstructions for global carbon and climate modeling

description: Plant hydraulics regulate water transport, photosynthesis and transpiration, thus controlling vegetation productivity, carbon uptake, and vulnerability to droughts and extreme heat. Key hydraulic traits such as conductivity and capacitance are fundamental to ecosystem resilience but remain challenging to monitor and model across scales. Vegetation water content (VWC) provides a critical integrative measure of hydraulic status and dynamics, offering actionable indicators for ecosystem monitoring, agricultural and forestry management, and early warning of stress. Nevertheless, hydraulic variables and VWC remain difficult to observe consistently across spatial and temporal scales: signals vary from leaf to landscape, and are confounded by soil moisture, vegetation structure, biomass and temperature, and exhibit strong diurnal/seasonal dynamics that challenge cross-sensor harmonization and validation. This session welcomes methodological advances, applications, and validations. We emphasize developments in passive and active microwave (radiometry, radar) retrievals, GNSS-based approaches (transmissometry, reflectometry), and optical/thermal methods, alongside in situ measurements (e.g., leaf/stem water potential, dielectric probes, dendrometry) and model-data integration. We invite contributions that: (i) improve retrieval algorithms, including cross-frequency synergies; (ii) fuse microwave/optical/LiDAR with in situ data to bridge scales; (iii) quantify uncertainties and disentangle confounding factors; (iv) integrate observations into ecohydrological and land-surface models via data assimilation, and advance model representation of plant hydraulics, improve the coupling between the water and carbon cycles, and make use of emerging observations; and (v) use hydraulic observations and products, including VWC and related metrics, to resilience and disturbance/recovery assessment, drought monitoring and early warning, phenology, and agricultural/forestry management. Case studies, global syntheses, and contributions providing open datasets, intercomparisons and community benchmarks are encouraged. The session aims to foster discussion between attendees from various scientific communities and academic backgrounds approaching plant hydraulics from different perspectives.
title: Observing Plant Hydraulics Across Scales and Perspectives: Methods and Use Cases

description: With climate change, many terrestrial ecosystems are experiencing more frequent and intense (hot) droughts. Plant responses to drought reflect the combined effects of soil water limitation and vapour pressure deficit, often compounded by heat. Understanding changes in transpiration, photosynthesis, and recovery after drought requires quantifying water transport and water stress along the soil–plant–atmosphere continuum. Advances in in-situ measurements and remote sensing provide unprecedented information on plant responses to drought and their drivers. Continuous measurements of plant and soil water status, sap flow, dendrometry, and ecosystem fluxes from eddy-covariance can now be combined with satellite observations of evapotranspiration, canopy temperature, solar-induced fluorescence, soil moisture, vegetation water content and optical depth, linking plant- and ecosystem-level processes. This wealth of data presents a unique opportunity for mechanistic modellers to improve simulations of water transport across the soil–plant–atmosphere continuum. Models increasingly account for plant hydraulics, plant water storage, detailed root water uptake, and access to subsurface water. Data assimilation, inverse modelling and hybrid or physics-informed machine learning can integrate these new observations to improve our understanding of the processes that control plant responses. Despite these new opportunities, transferring knowledge across disciplines and scales remains a major challenge. Further work is needed to determine how hydraulic limitations in the rhizosphere and root zone affect stomatal regulation and canopy fluxes, and which hydraulic traits explain responses from individual plants to communities. Other challenges include bridging the gap between field and satellite observations and adequately representing heterogeneity, acclimation, drought legacy effects and recovery in models, together with the combined effects of soil water limitation and atmospheric drought. This session aims to connect the fields of ecophysiology, ecohydrology, soil science, climate science, remote sensing and modelling. We encourage interdisciplinary contributions based on field experiments, monitoring networks, Earth observation, model development, model-data integration and data assimilation across natural and managed ecosystems. We particularly welcome studies that connect measurements, processes or scales, and contributions led by students and early career researchers.
title: Missing links in drought research: connecting plant-water interactions across scales

description: Tree mortality has been a focus of ecological research in the recent past, supported by a wide range of approaches such as permanent plot inventories, remote sensing, and dynamic vegetation models. These approaches have substantially improved our understanding of where and when trees die off, and of how mortality varies across environmental gradients. Although our understanding of the processes leading to tree mortality has increased significantly in recent years, we are still far from having a complete picture that would enable us to predict patterns in natural forest ecosystems, particularly across spatial and temporal scales. The International Tree Mortality Network (ITMN) aims to bridge these complementary data sources to gain new insights in the processes leading to tree mortality, ranging from empirical observations to process-based approaches. This session invites contributions investigating tree mortality resulting from both biotic and abiotic pathways, including extreme climate events such as the 2026 European drought. Contributions focusing specifically on identifying the ultimate processes and mechanisms leading to tree mortality are particularly welcome: * Bridging observations across spatial and temporal scales to identify pathways leading from environmental stress to tree mortality. * Linking mortality patterns to underlying physiological and ecological mechanisms, including hydraulic failure, pests and pathogens, growth reductions, and their interactions. * Using long-term observations (tree rings, plot inventories, satellite time series, …) to identify pre-mortality trajectories and legacy effects. * Improving the representation of tree mortality mechanisms in vegetation models.
title: Understanding the processes leading to tree mortality

description: Plant-soil interactions shape how ecosystems respond to climate change, yet many of the underlying processes remain difficult to observe across scales and are challenging to represent in models. This session brings experimentalists and modellers together to examine how evidence from the plant-soil continuum can improve predictions of carbon, water and nutrient cycling from plots to whole ecosystems. We welcome studies from forests, grasslands, wetlands and permafrost systems that combine experiments, observations and modelling, or use one approach to challenge and guide the other. Contributions may address shared mechanisms across ecosystems, the translation of measured processes into model structure and parameters, and the design of experiments that can distinguish between competing model assumptions. By connecting these perspectives, the session aims to identify key knowledge gaps and practical ways to improve predictions of ecosystem responses to climate change.
title: Plant-soil interactions under climate change: linking experiments and models from roots to ecosystems

description: Although peatlands cover only about 3% of the Earth's surface, they store roughly one third of the global soil organic carbon. They also play a key role in water regulation, flood attenuation, and the conservation of rare and threatened species. Centuries of drainage, peat extraction, agricultural conversion, deforestation, grazing and burning (a trend that is now being compounded by climate change) have degraded a large proportion of these ecosystems, turning long-term carbon sinks into active carbon sources. Reversing this trend has therefore become an explicit policy objective. The EU Nature Restoration Regulation sets out binding targets for restoring and rewetting drained organic soils. Meanwhile, the European Green Deal, the EU Biodiversity Strategy for 2030, the LULUCF (Land Use, Land Use Change, and Forestry) Regulation, national greenhouse gas inventories and voluntary carbon codes all stipulate that the extent, condition and change of peatlands must be consistently and repeatedly documented over large areas. However, meeting these requirements remains a scientific challenge. Peatland boundaries are often poorly mapped or misclassified in land cover databases. Ecohydrological condition is difficult to observe directly. Furthermore, degradation and recovery evolve over years to decades, and field networks are sparse in the remote regions where peatlands are most extensive. The aim of this session is to bring together the full range of approaches used to observe, quantify and interpret peatland extent, condition and dynamics, and to connect them to ecosystem functioning, carbon accounting and management. Contributions are welcome on the following topics, but not limited to: mapping and inventories of peat soils, including updating and validating existing databases; optical, multispectral, hyperspectral and thermal Earth Observation (EO); LiDAR, UAV and airborne surveys; airborne and radiometric; SAR backscatter, coherence, polarimetry and InSAR surface motion; multi-source data fusion and time-series analysis; in-situ monitoring of water tables, peat properties and greenhouse gas fluxes; ecohydrological modelling; and the assessment of rewetting and restoration effectiveness. Studies dealing with all peatland types and climatic settings, from boreal and permafrost peatlands to temperate blanket bogs, mountain mires, coastal and tropical peatlands, and at all scales, from single sites to continental products, are equally welcome.
title: Observing peatlands in a changing climate: remote sensing, field monitoring and modelling in support of restoration policy

description: Peatlands store large amounts of carbon and water, regulate greenhouse-gas emissions and hydrological processes, and provide unique habitat for biodiversity while buffering landscapes against environmental change. Understanding their vulnerability and resilience is therefore critical for predicting climate feedbacks and guiding effective protection and restoration. This session welcomes observational, experimental, and modelling studies from all peatland. We invite contributions that investigate peatlands’ response to natural and anthropogenic stressors, and the impacts these disturbances create on ecosystem structure, biogeochemical processes including hydrological regimes, carbon dynamics and exchanges of greenhouse gases. Relevant topics include peat formation and decomposition; vegetation change; temperature and climatic induced changes; fire; land use, drainage, resource extraction; and ecosystem restoration. Studies highlighting field or laboratory experiments along environmental gradients, long-term observations, remote sensing, data synthesis, and theoretical or process-based modelling will be adequate for this session. Contributions that integrate observations and models, connect processes across spatial and temporal scales, compare peatland types or regions, or evaluate restoration outcomes are especially welcome.
title: The Future of Peatlands – Sinks or Sources of Atmospheric Carbon?

description: Agriculture is at the center of the climate and biodiversity crises as it is both a major contributor to GHG emissions and a driver of species loss, freshwater depletion and eutrophication while also being highly exposed to rising temperatures, water scarcity and extreme events. Nature-based solutions (NbS) in agricultural landscapes are increasingly considered multifunctional practices and transformative measures that can support climate change adaptation and mitigation, restore soil health and water regulation, and support biodiversity. Yet implementation remains uneven: trade-offs with food production and carbon stocks can emerge where agriculture expands into semi-natural land, practices must be tailored to local biophysical and socio-cultural contexts and scaled from field to landscape, and uptake depends on the knowledge networks and processes that connect farmers, science and policy. EU policies set binding targets for restoring degraded ecosystems and promote NbS as a means to reconcile food production with climate and biodiversity objectives, making scientific evidence on their effectiveness a research and policy priority. At the same time, critical perspectives caution against technocratic framings of NbS that overlook governance, equity and the role of indigenous and local knowledge systems in delivering transformative outcomes. This session invites contributions that advance the process-based understanding, field- and landscape-scale implementation, and monitoring of NbS in agricultural landscapes for climate change adaptation and mitigation. We welcome studies on GHG, soil carbon and nutrient cycling, and water regulation under NbS practices such as agroforestry, conservation and regenerative agriculture, crop and landscape diversification, hedgerows, buffer strips, restored wetlands and silvopastoral systems. Particular attention will be made to studies on empirical data from active land transformations, farm conversions, and nature restoration initiatives. We also welcome experimental and modelling approaches quantifying synergies and trade-offs between production, climate and conservation objectives, as well as monitoring through long-term experiments, inventories, sensor networks, Earth observation, and participatory approaches assessing the persistence and scalability of NbS outcomes. Moreover, contributions addressing the socio-economic, governance and knowledge-transfer dimensions that shape adoption practices will be considered.
title: From experiments to implementation: monitoring nature-based solutions in climate-resilient agricultural landscapes

description: Terrestrial ecosystems are responding to rapid environmental change, but merely observing an ecosystem response does not necessarily reveal the processes responsible for it. Similar changes in carbon uptake, nutrient cycling, plant growth or soil processes can arise from different, interacting mechanisms. With the increasingly detailed information provided by ecosystem monitoring and measurement, a central challenge for ecosystem science arises: how can we use experiments and observations to distinguish different mechanisms, test their consequences, and improve our ability to predict ecosystem change? This session focuses on approaches that move from documenting ecosystem responses towards identifying and testing the mechanisms that generate them. We welcome studies that combine experiments, observations, data synthesis and modelling to investigate alternative process hypotheses, discriminate between mechanisms, identify missing processes, or constrain model parameters and structure. Studies may consider responses to elevated CO₂, climate change, altered nutrient availability or combinations of environmental changes, with focus on the mechanisms underlying ecosystem responses rather than on individual global-change drivers.
title: Disentangling mechanisms of terrestrial ecosystem responses to global change

description: Climate change and biodiversity loss are increasingly recognised as interdependent processes rather than parallel crises. Shifts in climate reshape species composition, phenology and community structure; biodiversity in turn modulates carbon, water and energy exchange, ecosystem stability and the capacity of ecosystems to buffer climate extremes. Despite this coupling, the two domains are still largely investigated with separate observational systems, model families and scientific communities. Closing that gap is a prerequisite for credible projections of ecosystem functioning and for the ecosystem services that societies depend on. This session invites contributions that explicitly address the climate–biodiversity nexus and its consequences for ecosystem functioning and service delivery. We welcome work across terrestrial, freshwater and coastal ecosystems, from the plot to the continental scale, and across natural, agricultural, forest and urban systems. Topics of interest include, but are not limited to: • Joint effects of climate variability, extremes and biodiversity change on productivity, carbon and water fluxes, and ecosystem stability and resilience; • Integrated monitoring of climate and biodiversity — flux towers, ecological and biodiversity networks, eDNA, acoustic and camera-based sensing, satellite and airborne remote sensing, and the fusion of these streams; • Process-based, trait-based and coupled climate–ecosystem models that represent biodiversity explicitly; • Artificial intelligence and machine learning for detecting biodiversity and functional change, upscaling in-situ observations, emulating and constraining models, and handling sparse or heterogeneous ecological data; • Quantification, mapping and valuation of ecosystem services under combined climate and biodiversity pressures; • Evidence supporting nature-based solutions, restoration and adaptation planning, including uncertainty communication and use in policy and climate services. We particularly encourage submissions that cross disciplinary boundaries — combining ecology, climate science, remote sensing and data science — and contributions from early career scientists.
title: The Climate–Biodiversity Nexus: monitoring, modelling and AI for ecosystem functioning and services

description: The terrestrial vegetation carbon balance is controlled not just by photosynthesis, but by respiration, carbon allocation, turnover (comprising litterfall, background mortality and disturbances) and wider vegetation dynamics. Recently observed changes in vegetation structure and functioning are the result of these processes and their interactions with atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration, nutrient availability, climate, and human activities. Their quantification and assessment has proven extremely challenging because of a lack of observations at the spatio-temporal scales needed for evaluating trends and projecting them into the future. This limited observational base gives rise to high uncertainty regarding the future terrestrial carbon sink. Many questions need answer to determine if this negative feedback to climate change will be sustained under future environmental changes, or whether increases in autotrophic respiration or carbon turnover might counteract it, for example through accelerated tree mortality or more frequent and more severe disturbance events (e.g. drought, fire, insect outbreaks). Shifts in the dynamics of plant mortality, establishment, and growth are expected to significantly influence forest composition. Uncertainties and/or data gaps in large-scale empirical products of vegetation dynamics, carbon fluxes and stocks may be overcome by extensive collections of field data and new satellite retrievals of forest biomass and other vegetation properties. Such novel datasets may be used to evaluate, develop and parametrize global vegetation models and hence to constrain present and future simulations of vegetation dynamics. Where no observations exist, exploratory modelling can investigate realistic responses and identify priorities for field and experimental campaigns. We welcome contributions that make use of observational approaches, vegetation models, or model-data integration techniques to advance understanding of the effects of environmental change on vegetation dynamics, tree mortality as well as carbon stocks and fluxes at local, regional or global scales and/or over long periods.
title: Present and future global vegetation dynamics and carbon stocks from observations and models

description: Peatlands play a significant role in regulating Earth’s climate system, storing around 30% of global soil organic carbon. Emissions from drained and degraded peatlands contribute around 4% of global anthropogenic greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and are a substantial share of the national GHG budget of some countries. Peatland degradation can also cause subsidence, altered hydrology and increased flood risk, reduced water quality, biodiversity loss and increased fire risk, while intact peatlands support hydrological regulation, nutrient cycling, habitats and cultural values. Because these processes operate at landscape scale but are subject to policy at national scale, land-use inventories and GHG accounting depend on spatially explicit information over large areas. Recent policy, such as the EU Nature Restoration Regulation, aims to rewet and restore drained peatlands to reduce emissions, sequester CO₂ and improve ecosystem services - often in landscapes with competing land-use interests. Implementation of rewetting and restoration at scale requires not only robust policy but accurate inventories, monitoring, and models that provide information on peatland status and the effectiveness and trade-offs of different measures. National monitoring efforts can vary in completeness and depth and are often based on historical categories and data. Harmonisation is increasingly required to enable benchmarking and compatibility with international reporting standards. This session invites contributions on peatland systems globally that address 1) GHG accounting, especially higher-tier methods, emission factors and activity data, 2) monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) schemes, 3) mapping of peatland extent, depth, subsidence, water table and condition, 4) national and international standards for carbon markets, and 5) economic and social aspects of peatland rewetting for restoration or paludiculture. We welcome studies on methodological development, field measurements, remote sensing, modelling and interdisciplinary studies, including site-level research where it informs assessment at larger scales.
title: Peatland mapping, monitoring and greenhouse gas accounting from regional to global scales

description: Climate hazards are already causing disasters with huge environmental, humanitarian, and economic impacts across the globe. As climate change continues to worsen and weather extremes become more frequent and intense, the consequences of these disasters will continue to escalate and our ability to anticipate and recover from them will be limited, including irreversible impacts for physical and social systems. Science has made significant progress in projecting climate and related natural hazard risks and developed useful approaches for risk management and adaptation. However, the policy response to climate risks and the implementation of such approaches have often been limited and fragmented across the continent. Whilst some policies and approaches have been taken to anticipate and minimise the harm of such hazards, action remains insufficient, and often reactive rather than preventive. This session will connect what we know about climate hazards and risks, what we are currently doing to prepare for them or manage them, and what can be done to ensure adapted and comprehensive policies can be implemented. A panel of experts including scientists, policymakers and practitioners will outline Europe’s current adaptation approaches as well as other methods that are currently working well. They will then discuss the limitations of existing approaches, policies, and tools and some of the challenges that exist exist in various sectors and spatial scales. Among the themes to be tackled, this GeoPanel will discuss the challenge of preparing for and managing cascading and compounding risks, building cohesive, EU-wide legislation and tools, and address climate impacts such as chronic, slow-onset hazards. Lastly, the panel will explore concrete solutions currently in development, including the Integrated Resilience Framework, tools such as the European Climate Viewer, and examples of how effective climate hazards management have been implemented on a local level by policymakers, practitioners, and industry leaders.
title: From legislation to implementation: How tools for hazard and risk reduction work in practice

description: Granular materials are ubiquitous in the Earth system: gouge in fault cores; fragmented volcanic rock, tephra and crystal mush; and soils, sediments and debris on hillslopes and in river channels. Although these settings span orders of magnitude in pressure, strain rate and scale, their mechanical behaviour is governed by shared grain-scale processes: shear localisation, force chains, dilatancy and compaction, grain breakage, cohesion, and coupling with pore-fluid pressure. They let granular media switch abruptly between solid-like and fluid-like states, controlling how failure starts, evolves and stops. In the solid Earth, granular mechanics sets the frictional strength and slip stability of fault gouge, and thus the nucleation, arrest and healing of earthquakes and slow slip, and fault reactivation by natural or induced pore-pressure changes. In volcanic systems, it shapes crystal-rich magma rheology, frictional sliding along conduit plugs and lava domes, flank and dome collapse, and pyroclastic density currents. At the surface, the same physics governs soil shear strength and its sensitivity to moisture and suction, landslide initiation and creep, rock avalanche runout, slope failures evolving into debris flows and lahars, and sediment transport and erosion. Rainfall, seismic shaking, snowmelt and freeze-thaw act through the same grain-fluid couplings that operate at depth. We invite laboratory experiments (shear, flume, centrifuge and shake-table tests, grain-scale imaging), field observations and remote sensing, numerical modelling (discrete element, coupled fluid-particle and continuum) and theory (rate-and-state friction, critical state, μ(I) and non-local rheologies). We especially welcome work crossing the solid Earth and surface divide: controls of grain size, shape, comminution and cohesion on friction and dilatancy; hydro-mechanical and thermal coupling (dilatancy hardening, thermal pressurisation, liquefaction); transitions from creep to catastrophic failure; triggering by pore pressure, cyclic loading and seismic waves; and precursors of failure. Interface topics such as earthquake-triggered landslides and coseismic liquefaction are a natural focus. By bringing together fault mechanics, volcanology, geomorphology, soil mechanics and natural hazards, the session aims to identify common mechanisms and transferable models, and to discuss how grain-scale insights upscale to natural systems and hazard assessment.
title: Granular materials across the earth system: from solid earth to earth surface processes.

description: This session provides the opportunity for contributions that fall within the broad spectrum of Rock Physics, but are not directly appropriate to any of the other proposed sessions. We solicit contributions on theory and simulations, instrumentation, laboratory experiments and field measurements, data analysis and interpretation, as well as inversion and modelling techniques.
title: Open session in Rock Physics

description: The session focuses on the characterization and modeling of the mechanical behaviour of weak/soft and heterogeneous rocks and rock masses, i.e., rocks that, due to their intrinsic properties and/or to the effect of differential weathering or deformative processes, have mechanical strength and deformability that are particularly unfavorable or strongly heterogeneous. They include, among others, fault rocks, turbidites, flysches, complex geological units (e.g., Block-In-Matrix – BIM rocks and soils), salts and sulphates. They represent a challenge in several geoengineering contexts, due to their low strength, high heterogeneity, high proneness to drastic weathering or fracturing processes, and to the fact that they can develop time-dependent and water-interaction-dependent deformations (e.g., creep, swelling, squeezing). These peculiarities pose risks to the safety and longevity of geo-engineering projects, with specific problems in the case of underground infrastructures excavated for civil, mining or energetic purposes, and to the stability of natural slopes and seacliffs. The session aims to collect contributions that integrate geological observations, investigation surveys, laboratory data and modeling of soft and heterogeneous rocks and rock masses to offer a fruitful discussion about the behaviour of these materials.
title: Soft rocks and heterogeneous rocks: challenges in the field and laboratory characterization and numerical modelling

description: This session covers all methods and case histories related to measuring, processing and modeling potential field anomalies for geological, environmental and resources purposes. It will concern gravity and magnetic data from satellite missions to airborne and detailed ground-based arrays. Contributions presenting the theoretical, mathematical and computational progress of data modelling techniques as well as new case studies of geophysical and geological interest are welcome. This session will also encourage presentations on compilation methods of heterogenous data sets, multiscale and multidisciplinary approaches for natural resources exploration and geological gas storage purposes, and other environmental applications. Potential field applications in exploration and geological interpretation of magnetic anomalies, jointly with other geodata, are warmly welcome.
title: Advances in gravity and magnetic field studies and natural resources exploration

description: This session provides the opportunity for contributions that fall within the broad spectrum of Geomagnetism and Electromagnetism, but are not directly appropriate to any of the other proposed sessions. We solicit contributions on theory and simulations, instrumentation, laboratory experiments and field measurements, data analysis and interpretation, as well as inversion and modelling techniques. This session also welcomes studies of extreme geophysical events from space and ground and attempts to integrate, model, and interpret the effects detected in separate geolayers.
title: Open Session in Geomagnetism and Electromagnetism

description: Quantum Diamond Microscopy (QDM) is emerging as a powerful tool in palaeomagnetism and rock magnetism. Much of the excitement surrounding the technique stems from its ability to resolve individual magnetic anomalies at the microscale, allowing the direction and intensity of magnetic remanence to be investigated at the level of individual magnetic carriers. Combined with chemical, mineralogical, and imaging techniques, QDM provides a level of spatial control that is difficult to achieve using conventional bulk palaeomagnetic methods. Yet QDM is not simply a palaeomagnetic tool. It is a broadly applicable geoscientific microscope for investigating processes recorded by magnetic minerals. Rocks form, deform, and undergo alteration through a wide range of geological processes, and their remanence carriers can preserve spatially resolved signatures of these events. In volcanic rocks, for example, magnetic inclusions within feldspar phenocrysts may define fabrics that record magma flow and emplacement. In sedimentary or altered rocks, fluid circulation may trigger the crystallisation of new magnetic minerals, allowing remanence directions within microveins or reaction zones to be compared directly with those of the surrounding matrix. At still smaller scales, QDM can be used to investigate magnetic particles biosynthesised by microorganisms, providing insight into (e.g.) how magnetosome arrangements and magnetic interactions contribute to magnetotaxis. As QDM becomes increasingly accessible across geosciences, a key challenge is identifying the scientific questions for which this technique can provide unique insights, and developing an understanding of its methodological challenges, limitations, and best practices as the community gains experience with QDM. This session aims to bring together not only palaeomagnetists, but geoscientists from a broad range of disciplines who use or would like to use QDM to address spatially localised scientific questions. By showcasing applications across geological, geochemical, biological, and planetary materials, we seek to demonstrate how microscale magnetic imaging can reveal processes that are obscured in bulk measurements and to inspire new ways of using QDM to tackle geoscientific problems.
title: Tackling Diverse Microscale Problems in the Geosciences with Quantum Diamond Microscopy

description: This session invites contributions of electromagnetic (EM) geophysics, from near-surface investigations to the deep Earth imaging. We welcome contributions covering various EM research: advances in instrumentation and data acquisition (e.g., magnetotelluric, controlled-source EM, time-domain and frequency-domain systems); mathematical and numerical developments in data processing, forward modelling, and 1D/2D/3D inversion, including machine-learning approaches; and applications drawing on ground, marine, airborne, and even satellite EM measurements. Target problems include global EM induction studies constraining mantle conductivity and composition; imaging of regional tectonic, magmatic, and volcanic systems to understand fluid pathways, melt distribution, and crustal deformation; exploration for hydrocarbons, geothermal resources, and critical minerals; and characterisation of near-surface structure relevant to environmental issues, urban infrastructure, geomagnetically induced currents (GIC), and hydrological systems such as groundwater and permafrost. We particularly encourage multidisciplinary contributions that integrate EM results with rock physics, seismic, gravity, magnetic, geochemical, and geological datasets to build a complete picture of subsurface structures, and case studies that demonstrate how combining methods resolves model ambiguities that EM data alone cannot.
title: Electromagnetic Induction in Geophysics: Data, Models, Inversions and Interpretations

description: Satellite data and geomagnetic observatories give us a detailed picture of the modern geomagnetic field and the Sun–Earth system. To look further back, we can turn to geological archives, offshore cores, stratigraphic sequences, cosmogenic radionuclide records (e.g., ¹⁰Be), and geo/paleomagnetic reconstructions. Together, these records allow us to investigate how the Earth’s magnetic field, environmental conditions, and solar activity have changed over centuries, millennia, and longer geological timescales, and to explore the links between them. This long-term perspective is essential for understanding the modern Earth–Sun system, in which the geomagnetic field connects processes ranging from the Earth’s deep interior to the atmosphere and near-Earth space. It also often requires combining magnetic information with other proxies, models, and observations across different timescales. This combination can bring additional benefits, for example, helping to tackle the dating uncertainties that many paleo-sciences face. This session welcomes studies linking geomagnetism, paleomagnetism, rock and environmental magnetism with solar variability (irradiance), cosmogenic radionuclides, paleoclimate proxies, space climate and other fields. We particularly encourage contributions that combine different geophysical and geological records, proxies, methods or timescales, including links with paleoclimate records, modelling, and modern ground-based and satellite observations. The session aims to bring these communities together and explore the links between geomagnetic, solar and Earth-system variability across different timescales.
title: Magnetic records and geomagnetic variability as a bridge between geological archives and the modern Sun–Earth system

description: Low-Earth orbit (LEO) satellites provide unique opportunities to characterize the Earth's magnetic field, ionospheric currents and plasma parameters, and thermospheric density and winds across a wide spectrum of time and spatial scales, and for a large range of solar and geomagnetic activities. At the forefront of this advance are the three ESA Earth Explorer Swarm satellites, which have been providing high-accuracy measurements of the Earth's magnetic field, electric field, plasma parameters, precise-orbit determination, and accelerometer observations since their launch in November 2013. They have proven very valuable for studying the near-Earth magnetic field and the coupled ionospheric-thermospheric environment, and enabled the development and implementation of advanced models and operational space weather services. The scientific potential of the polar-orbiting Swarm satellites is today augmented by newly available data, especially those collected by the low-inclination Macau Science Satellite 1 and CSES satellites. In addition, the ESA Scout NanoMagSat constellation, consisting of one near-polar and two 60° inclination satellites, is scheduled to launch near the end of 2027, with full operation planned for 2028. It will acquire high-accuracy magnetic vector and scalar data, electron density, and electron temperature data, navigation data, and collect ionospheric radio-occultation profiles. All these data are also complemented by increasingly available platform-magnetometer data, such as from the CryoSat-2, GRACE, GRACE-FO, GOCE, and E-POP satellites. The new abundance of satellite data provides unprecedented space-time data coverage at LEO satellite altitudes, opening the way for new scientific opportunities.
title: LEO satellites for Exploring the near-Earth Magnetic Field and the Ionosphere-Thermosphere Environment

description: This open session provides the opportunity for contributions that fall within the broad topic of Palaeomagnetism but do not fit into any of the other proposed sessions. The session invites new studies from all areas of palaeomagnetism, rock and bio and environmental magnetism, which have an impact on climatic, stratigraphic, tectonic or environmental applications. This also includes new theoretical models or measurement techniques.
title: Open session in Palaeomagnetism, Rock Magnetism and Environmental Magnetism

description: Palaeomagnetic observations underpin reconstructions of plate motions, investigations of geomagnetic-field evolution and reversals, and studies of the timing and environmental setting of geological processes. Their interpretation, however, relies on the extent to which natural remanent magnetisation (NRM) faithfully records both the ambient field and the geological history of a material. Establishing that fidelity, and identifying the circumstances in which it is degraded, remains a central challenge in palaeomagnetism, rock and environmental magnetism, planetary science, as well as magnetic-materials research. This session will explore the acquisition, stability, alteration, and measurement of magnetic remanence in natural and synthetic materials. It hopes to bring together those who examine how processes operating at the scale of magnetic domains and individual grains with those looking at larger mineral-scale behaviour and, ultimately, to the bulk signals measured in palaeomagnetic samples and used in geological interpretation. While micromagnetic theory and modelling offer powerful ways to bridge these scales, the session will take a deliberately broad approach, bringing together theoretical and numerical studies with laboratory experiments, magnetic imaging, observational work, and geological applications. Contributions are invited that test the assumptions underlying palaeomagnetic interpretation; identify sources of bias, overprinting, and uncertainty; and develop methods to recognise, quantify, and, where possible, correct unreliable magnetic records.
title: Understanding the reliability of paleomagnetic recorders: models, theories and observations

description: Recent methodological and instrumental advances in paleomagnetic and magnetic fabric techniques are continuously increasing their already high potential in solving research questions in various Earth science disciplines. Integrated paleomagnetic and magnetic fabric studies, together with structural geology and petrology, are very efficient tools in increasing our knowledge about sedimentological, tectonic or volcanic processes, both on regional and global scale. This session is intended to give an opportunity to present innovative theoretical or methodological paleomagnetic and magnetic fabric works and their direct applications in different geological settings. Especially welcome are contributions combining paleomagnetic and magnetic fabric data retrieved by several means of fabric analysis (magnetic and non-magnetic), or showing novel approaches in data evaluation. We also solicit contributions from both experimental and theoretical aspects of paleomagnetic reconstructions, remagnetisation processes and acquisition of petrofabrics.
title: Directional paleomagnetism and magnetic fabric: Recent advances and applications

description: Earthquakes are inherently non-linear and multi-scale phenomena, with dynamics that are strongly dependent on the geometry and the physical properties of faults and their surrounding media. To investigate their complex behavior (fault stability, rupture nucleation and propagation, seismic cycle complexity), fault systems are often scaled down in laboratory experiments to explore their underlying physics under controlled conditions. However, extrapolating laboratory-scale observations to natural fault systems remains a significant challenge. Numerical simulations help bridge this gap by linking processes across scales and improving our understanding of fault mechanics. Together, laboratory experiments, numerical simulations, and geophysical observations provide complementary approaches that are essential to understanding fault mechanics across scales. In this session, we aim to bring together multidisciplinary contributions that address key aspects of earthquake mechanics, combining laboratory, geophysical, and numerical observations, including: (i) thermo-hydro-mechanical processes governing fault behavior throughout the seismic cycle; (ii) the fault slip spectrum, from aseismic slip to dynamic earthquake rupture; (iii) bridging spatial and temporal scales of fault deformation mechanisms. We particularly encourage contributions with novel observations and innovative methodologies for studying earthquake faulting. Contributions from early-career scientists are highly welcome.
title: Fault deformation across scales: from laboratory to geophysical observations via numerical simulations

description: Unconventional reservoirs, including organic-rich shales, tight sandstones, and low-permeability carbonates, present major challenges for petrophysical characterization and formation evaluation because of their strong heterogeneity, anisotropy, complex pore systems, and rock–fluid interactions. Addressing these challenges requires linking pore-scale physical processes and laboratory measurements with borehole observations and reservoir-scale interpretation. This session focuses on advances in the petrophysical characterization and formation evaluation of unconventional reservoirs across multiple spatial scales. We welcome contributions on advanced wireline and logging-while-drilling methods; pore structure, fluid occurrence, and transport properties investigated through imaging, digital rock physics, NMR, and laboratory measurements; rock-physics relationships, forward modeling, and joint or multiphysics inversion; integration of core, logging, seismic, and production data; and geomechanical and fracture characterization for reservoir evaluation and development. The session also welcomes data-driven and physics-informed approaches for reservoir-property estimation, sweet-spot identification, and uncertainty quantification, particularly studies emphasizing interpretability, generalization, and reliability. We especially encourage contributions that connect fundamental physical understanding with practical formation-evaluation challenges, integrate observations across pore, core, borehole, and reservoir scales, and critically assess the limitations and transferability of emerging characterization methods.
title: Petrophysical Characterization and Formation Evaluation of Unconventional Reservoirs: From Pore-Scale Insights to Reservoir-Scale Interpretation

description: The development of petrophysical models, which link geophysical measurements such as electrical conductivity or seismic velocity to subsurface parameters fluid content , hydraulic properties, pore and fracture networks characteristics, is critical for characterizing subsurface properties and informing hydrogeological, geological reservoir and biogeochemical studies. As geophysical techniques evolve, particularly with the rise of distributed monitoring systems, their application extends beyond static measurements. Increasingly, they are used to study dynamic processes such as fluid flow, solute transport, and biogeochemical reactions. These developments highlight the necessity of refining petrophysical relationships through multidisciplinary approaches that combine theoretical, laboratory, and field-scale studies. Each geophysical method has its own resolution and depth constraints, while complex relationships between physical properties and interfacial, geometrical, and biogeochemical characteristics further complicate the scaling of laboratory experiments to field applications, making it vital to establish accurate, adaptable petrophysical models. This session invites contributions from diverse research communities to explore new petrophysical models, numerical simulations, laboratory experiments, and field case studies. We aim to foster interdisciplinary discussions on advancing petrophysical relationships and improving our understanding of complex subsurface processes across a wide range of natural and engineering settings, including low-carbon energy technologies and subsurface storage solutions. We encourage submissions focused on studies that combine insights from geomechanics, geochemistry, petrophysics, and material science. Additionally, we welcome submissions on the development of cutting-edge experimental apparatus, novel sensor technologies, and innovative methods for simulating in situ conditions.
title: Advances in Petrophysics and Rock Physics: Integrating Models, Experiments, and Field Geophysics Across Scales

description: Rock mass deformation and failure at different stress levels (from the brittle regime to the brittle-ductile transition) are controlled by damage processes occurring on different spatial scales, from grain (µm) to geological formation (km) scale. These lead to a progressive increase of micro- and meso-crack intensity in the rock matrix and to the growth of inherited macro-fractures at rock mass scale. Coalescence of these fractures forms large-scale structures such as brittle fault zones, rockslide shear zones, and excavation damage zones (EDZ) in open pit mining and underground construction. Diffuse or localized rock damage have a primary influence on rock properties (strength, elastic moduli, hydraulic and electric properties) and on their evolution across multiple temporal scales spanning from geological time to highly dynamic phenomena as earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, slopes and man-made rock structures. In subcritical stress conditions, damage accumulation results in brittle creep processes key to the long-term evolution of geophysical, geomorphological and geo-engineering systems. Damage and progressive failure processes must be considered to understand the time-dependent hydro-mechanical behaviour of fault damage zones and principal slip zones, and their interplay (e.g. earthquakes vs aseismic creep), volcanic systems and slopes (e.g. slow rock slope deformation vs catastrophic rock slides), as well as the response of rock masses to stress perturbations induced by artificial excavations (tunnels, mines) and loading. At the same time, damage processes control the brittle behaviour of the upper crust and are strongly influenced by intrinsic rock properties (strength, fabric, porosity, anisotropy), geological structures and their inherited damage, as well as by the evolving pressure-temperature with increasing depth and by fluid pressure, transport properties and chemistry. In this session we will bring together researchers from different communities interested in a better understanding of rock deformation and failure processes and consequence, as well as other related rock mechanics topics. We welcome innovative and novel contributions on experimental studies (both in the laboratory and in situ), continuum / micromechanical analytical and numerical modelling, and applications to fault zones, reservoirs, slope instability and landscape evolution, and engineering applications.
title: Multiscale rock damage and progressive failure in geomechanics, geophysics and geo-engineering

description: Earth observation provides repeated and consistent measurements across most of the planet, including regions where field observations and monitoring infrastructure are limited. AI makes it possible to process these data systematically and to develop global workflows that study different regions through a consistent analytical framework and at comparable levels of detail. This combination can widen access to evidence on climate change and reduce some of the geographical, economic and technical barriers that still shape climate research. Global coverage, however, does not automatically guarantee global knowledge. Models developed in data-rich regions may perform differently under other environmental or socioeconomic conditions. Their evaluation is often constrained by sparse reference data, uneven monitoring capacity and limited local validation. Geographical bias, uncertainty and transferability therefore need to be assessed explicitly rather than assumed. This session focuses on the use of AI and Earth observation to make climate change research more accessible, systematic and geographically inclusive. It welcomes studies of climate impacts, risks, vulnerability and adaptation, including their links with natural hazards, public health, ecosystems, population, infrastructure, early warning and disaster response. Relevant contributions may address scalable and reproducible workflows, validation in data-scarce settings, uncertainty assessment and generalisation across regions. Studies combining satellite observations with field measurements or local knowledge are particularly relevant, as are open data, accessible tools and methods that can be adapted to different contexts. The aim is to understand how global Earth observations can make robust and actionable climate knowledge available across different communities and contexts, including those where conventional monitoring and research capacity remain limited.
title: AI for Global Good: Democratising Climate Research with Earth Observation

description: Remarkable advances in recent years demonstrate that geodesy today is driven by a broad spectrum of interactions, including theory, science, engineering, technology, observations, and practice-oriented services. Geodetic science accumulates significant results in studies towards classical geodetic problems and problems that have only recently emerged or gained new interest - in many cases due to synergistic activities in geodesy and tremendous advances in instrumentation and computational tools. In-depth studies have progressed in parallel with investigations that led to a broadening of the traditional core of geodesy. Within this concept, we seek contributions concerning problems of reference frames, gravity fields, geodynamics, or positioning, but also studies surpassing the frontiers of these topics. We invite presentations discussing analytical and numerical methods in solving boundary-value or inverse problems, geoid determination, advances in spatial/temporal modelling, estimation theory, or the use of high-performance facilities. Demonstrations of mathematical and physical research directly motivated by geodetic practice and ties to other disciplines are welcome. In parallel with theory-oriented results, examinations of novel data-processing methods in various branches of geodetic science and practice are also acceptable. The scope of the session is conceived with a degree of freedom, even though it intends to provide a forum for all theoretical and methodological investigations and results.
title: Recent Developments in Geodetic Theory

description: Global Navigation Satellite System Reflectometry (GNSS-R) has come of age. Two decades after the first spaceborne demonstrations, and almost a decade into the CYGNSS mission, GNSS-R has moved to a established source of Earth observation, with a growing constellation of missions delivering frequent and all-weather observations of ocean winds and sea state, soil moisture, freeze/thaw, inundation and wetlands, snow and sea ice, and vegetation. The recent launch of HydroGNSS, ESA's first Scout mission and the first GNSS-R mission dedicated to the terrestrial water cycle, marks the start of a new phase in which GNSS-R can address Earth system science questions at the scale, quality, and continuity required for operational monitoring and modeling. Until now, GNSS-R contributions at EGU have been distributed across sessions. This session, the first at EGU dedicated to GNSS-R, brings this community together in one place and shifts the emphasis from the technique to its use. Its focus is on how GNSS-R observations, alone and in combination with other satellite and ground-based data, advance understanding of the hydrosphere, cryosphere, atmosphere, biosphere, and ocean, and how they are integrated into Earth system models to constrain water, energy, and carbon exchanges and to improve weather, hydrological, and climate prediction. We welcome, but do not limit, contributions on: • First results, validation, and early science from HydroGNSS • Monitoring of soil moisture, floods and wetlands, snow, sea ice, freeze-thaw, permafrost, and vegetation with GNSS-R • Ocean surface winds, sea state, and extreme events such as tropical cyclones observed with GNSS-R • Assimilation of GNSS-R products into land surface, hydrological, ocean, weather, and climate models • AI-based data fusion, gap filling, and emulation of forward models, as well as integration of GNSS-R into AI-based weather and Earth system models • Use of GNSS-R for model evaluation, parameter calibration, and process understanding • Synergy of GNSS-R with passive microwave, SAR, altimetry, optical, and in-situ observations • Long-term records, product intercomparison, and machine learning approaches bridging observations and models • Airborne GNSS-R supporting Earth system applications • Perspectives on future GNSS-R missions and the role of GNSS-R in the multi-mission Earth observing system
title: GNSS Reflectometry for Earth System Science: HydroGNSS Era

description: The redistribution of geophysical fluids across the Earth’s surface and near surface driven by water cycle dynamics and its extremes can cause measurable load-induced deformation. In the last decades, increasingly accurate and available space geodetic measurement techniques (among others GNSS, InSAR, satellite gravimetry and altimetry) have enriched our understanding of this response. Accurate observations of crustal deformation together with geophysical models can be applied to quantify the hydrological loads, and through that, they provide new insight into the related hydrological processes. With changing climate also cryospheric mass changes get increasingly important to consider, but usually hydrological models do not explicitly address them. There is still a lack of a unified global mass transport model. This session aims to attract research that further advances our ability to accurately quantify hydrological mass loads across different temporal and spatial scales, and involving different hydrological compartments (e.g., groundwater, surface water, snow, ice). We invite studies focusing on innovative measurement and modeling approaches and reconciling observations from different geodetic measurement techniques used to study hydrological loading as well as the disentangling of cryospheric and hydrologic signals. Research that assesses the strengths and limitations of each approach and that proposes strategies for a seamless and accurate integration, particularly of cryospheric processes, is highly encouraged. Additionally, we seek studies that conduct intercomparisons of different hydrological model data (land surface, hydrological models) and geodetic measurement techniques to understand their relative strengths, weaknesses, and accuracies.
title: Hydrological and Cryospheric Loading: Measuring and Modelling

description: The rapid growth of SAR constellations, continental-scale ground-motion services, cloud computing, and artificial intelligence is transforming radar remote sensing from specialist analysis toward scalable and operational monitoring. Beyond interferometric phase and displacement time series, SAR amplitude observations can support rapid change detection and contextual interpretation of surface processes. A key challenge is no longer only how to generate interferograms or deformation maps, but how to convert large volumes of radar observations into reliable, interpretable, predictive, and actionable information. Important barriers include automated quality control, large-scale processing, complex spatio-temporal interpretation, model transferability, uncertainty quantification, forecasting, and integration with operational decisions. This session focuses on the transition from scalable SAR and InSAR processing to predictive and actionable ground-motion intelligence. We welcome contributions on AI and machine learning for SAR amplitude and InSAR processing; scalable, cloud-native, high-performance, and near-real-time workflows; automated detection, classification, attribution, and change-point analysis of radar image stacks and deformation time series; physics-informed, explainable, and uncertainty-aware learning; deformation forecasting, anomaly detection, early warning, and alert generation; and integration with GNSS, optical, geological, meteorological, infrastructure, and in-situ data. Applications may include subsidence, landslides, infrastructure, mining, groundwater or hydrocarbon extraction, volcanic and seismic deformation, and other natural or human-induced ground-motion processes. We also encourage studies on validation, benchmarking, reproducibility, transferability, failure modes, and operational implementation. Particular emphasis is placed on contributions that critically assess when AI adds measurable value, quantify uncertainty and limitations, and demonstrate how SAR- and InSAR-derived information can support transparent, timely, and defensible decisions for hazard assessment, infrastructure management, early warning, and risk-informed decision-making.
title: AI-enabled SAR and InSAR for scalable ground-motion monitoring, forecasting, and decision support

description: This session showcases novel applications of artificial intelligence and machine learning in geodesy. In recent years, the exponential growth of geodetic data from various observation techniques has created challenges and opportunities. Innovative approaches are required to efficiently handle and harness the vast amount of geodetic data available for scientific purposes, for example, when dealing with “big data” from Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) and Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR). Likewise, numerical weather models and other environmental models important for geodesy come with ever-growing resolutions and dimensions. Artificial intelligence and machine learning have shown great potential not only in this context but also when applied to more limited datasets to solve complex non-linear problems in geodesy. We invite contributions related to applying methods from artificial intelligence and machine learning (including shallow, deep, and generative learning architectures, as well as geospatial foundation models) to geodetic problems and datasets. We welcome investigations related to (but not limited to): more efficient and automated processing of geodetic data, pattern and anomaly detection in geodetic time series, images, or higher-dimensional datasets, implicit neural representations for continuous spatial field modeling, improved predictions of geodetic parameters, such as Earth orientation, atmospheric, or hydrological parameters into the future, combination and extraction of information from multiple inhomogeneous datasets (multi-temporal, multi-sensor, multi-modal fusion), feature selection and sensitivity, downscaling geodetic data, and improvements of large-scale simulations. We strongly encourage contributions that address crucial aspects of uncertainty quantification and integration of physical relationships into data-driven frameworks (physics-informed machine learning). Moreover, reproducibility, interpretability, and explainability of machine learning outcomes are fundamental to ensuring the scientific rigor of novel AI-based solutions. By combining the power of artificial intelligence with geodetic science, we aim to open new horizons in our understanding of Earth's dynamic geophysical processes. Join us in this session to explore how the fusion of physics and machine learning promises advantages in generalization, consistency, and extrapolation, ultimately advancing the frontiers of geodesy.
title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning for Geodesy

description: In recent years, we have observed steady progress in signals, services, and satellite deployment of Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS). Consequently, modernizing and developing GNSS constellations have moved us towards an era of multi-constellation and multi-frequency GNSS signal availability. Also, the deployment of LEO constellations brings opportunities for LEO-augmented PNT services and applications, which, however, require revisiting existing processing algorithms and developing novel ones when fusing LEO and GNSS. Meanwhile, technological development has provided high-grade GNSS user receivers capable of collecting high-rate, low-noise, and multipath-impact measurements. Also, recent extraordinary progress in low-cost GNSS chipsets, smartphones, and sensor fusion must be acknowledged. Such advancements boost GNSS research and catalyze an expansion of satellite navigation to novel areas of science and industry. On one side, the developments stimulate a broad range of new GNSS applications. On the other hand, they pose new challenges for data processing. Hence, algorithmic advancements are needed to address the opportunities and challenges in enhancing the accuracy, availability, interoperability, and integrity of high-precision GNSS applications. This session is a forum for discussing advances in high-precision GNSS algorithms and their applications in geosciences, including geodesy, geodynamics, seismology, tsunamis, the ionosphere, and the troposphere. We encourage but do not limit submissions related to: - GNSS processing algorithms, - Multi-GNSS benefits for Geosciences, - Multi-constellation GNSS processing and product standards, - High-rate GNSS, - Low-cost receiver and smartphone GNSS observations for precise positioning, navigation, and geoscience applications, - LEO observations modeling and processing algorithms, - Precise Point Positioning (PPP, PPP-RTK) and Real Time Kinematic (RTK), - GNSS and other sensors (accelerometers, INS, etc.) fusion, - GNSS products for high-precision applications (orbits, clocks, uncalibrated phase delays, inter-system and inter-frequency biases, etc.), - Troposphere and ionosphere modeling and sounding with GNSS, - CORS services for Geosciences (GBAS, Network-RTK, etc.), - Precise Positioning of EOS platforms, - GNSS for natural hazards prevention, - Monitoring crustal deformation and the seismic cycle of active faults, - GNSS and early-warning systems, - GNSS reflectometry.
title: High-precision GNSS: methods, open problems, and geoscience applications

description: Global Terrestrial Reference Frames (TRF) are fundamental for monitoring the Earth's rotation in space, and to many Earth science applications that need absolute positioning and precise orbit determination of near-Earth satellites. Accurate and stable TRFs are especially needed for the quantification of global change phenomena such as sea level rise, current ice melting, tectonic, and seismic deformations. This session generally welcomes contributions on the computation, the evaluation and the use of TRFs. The computation of TRFs relies on space geodetic observations acquired by ground networks of stations. Nowadays, measurement biases and imperfect background models in space geodetic data analysis are the main factors limiting the accuracy of TRFs. This session therefore welcomes contributions that develop strategies to overcome systematics in space geodetic observing systems such as range biases in SLR observations, gravitational deformation of VLBI antennas, GNSS antenna phase patterns, etc. The understanding of the discrepancies between the terrestrial scale observed by the different space geodetic techniques, and the improvement of geocentre motion determination are of particular interest. Another key ingredient to the construction of TRFs are geometric ties between instruments of the different space geodetic techniques, be they co-located on ground (“local ties”) or onboard satellite missions (“space ties”). Contributions are therefore strongly encouraged on the determination of new local ties at co-location sites, on new methods for local tie determination, as well as on the handling and impact of space ties in TRF determination, with the perspective of exploiting ESA’s dedicated GENESIS mission. Papers that explore new TRF construction strategies, e.g., combination of the different techniques at the observation level, or any type of development that could improve future TRF solutions, are also highly welcome. Besides reviewing improvements in TRF determination, another objective of this session is to bring together contributions from individual technique services, space geodetic data analysts, ITRS combination centers and TRF users to discuss the TRF solutions produced by different groups, with a special focus on their comparison and evaluation. Papers on the exploitation of different TRF solutions for various geodetic and geophysical applications are therefore also solicited.
title: Terrestrial Reference Frames: determination, evaluation and applications

description: Advances of recent decades made high accuracy gravimetry widely available as a reliable tool to not only realize the terrestrial gravity reference with absolute gravimeters, but also to monitor gravity changes with high precision continuously over years by deploying superconducting gravimeters or with new survey concepts using quantum gravimeters. Mass change processes such as loading effects of atmosphere and ocean, volcanic activities, land uplift and glacial isostatic adjustment or water storage changes at different temporal scales can now be detected. Technological leaps made quantum and MEMs based gravity sensors available, enabling new measurement scenarios including mobile measurements and observations of gravity gradients. Ultra stable optical clocks allow to directly determine gravity potential differences based on Einstein's theory of general relativity. Thereby, different functionals of the Earth gravity field are now accessible by measurements, opening new fields of applications with great future potential. The session is dedicated to all aspects of high accuracy terrestrial gravity field determinations and its applications, reaching from monitoring of sub-daily variations to long-term processes in the different fields of geosciences. Contributions that document the stability and traceability of applied gravimeters and the progress of the International Terrestrial Gravity Reference Frame of IAG are as welcome as reports about the state of the art of novel techniques, improvement of established measurement solutions and advances in instrumental developments. We also strongly invite studies on field applications, e.g. volcanoloy, geothermal energy, hydrology as well as tidal, atmospheric and non-tidal loading effects. This session is organized jointly with the IAG (International Association of Geodesy) Subcommission 2.1, IAG project "Novel Sensors and Quantum Technology for Geodesy (QuGe)" and the Horizon Europe projects EQUIP-G (Grant ID 101215427) and ERIgMEA (Project Nr: 25IEM07).
title: High accuracy terrestrial monitoring of the time varying gravity field

description: In the some parts of the world, the request of precise regional geoid determination has been still ongoing. Thus, scholars need to share their own experiences about geoid modelling in their study areas. This session will collect all scholars which are interested in precise geoid determination in countries.
title: Regional Geoid Determination

description: In this session we search for contributions of general interest for the geodesy community which fall outside the scope of the other sessions. Contributions can cover theoretical aspects to practical or experimental nature.
title: Open Session in Geodesy

description: The increasing availability of affordable hardware for global navigation satellite systems (GNSS) and open-source software for GNSS data processing is shaping geoscience research in novel ways. By using these technologies, researchers can now perform highly accurate positioning and data analysis at a fraction of the cost of geodetic quality hardware and software. Given that positioning, reflectometry, radio occultation, space weather monitoring, and atmospheric sounding with GNSS have become operational techniques, and new experiments are being conducted with low-cost GNSS hardware and open source GNSS processing software, it augurs well for the geosciences at large to exploit these developments for furthering our understanding of the Earth system. In this session we solicit abstracts on use, development and novel geoscience applications of low-cost GNSS hardware and open source GNSS software. In addition, we welcome other contributions highlighting the opportunities and challenges in using low-cost GNSS hardware and open source GNSS software.
title: Applications of low-cost GNSS hardware and open source GNSS software in geosciences

description: The growth and decay of large ice sheets on the Earth's surface during the past, present and future leads to glacial isostatic adjustment (GIA) triggered by the redistribution of surface ice and ocean masses, and the flow of mantle rocks. It changes solid Earth's geometric shape, sea levels, the Earth's gravity field, rotational motion, lithospheric bending, and the state of stress inside the Earth. This process is primarily driven by ice-sheet dynamics and Earth's structure, while it crucially feedbacks other Earth systems like the cryosphere and hydrosphere. GIA controls relative sea-level change through vertical land motion and gravitational–rotational effects, making it fundamental for ocean sciences, hydrological sciences, and climate investigations. Furthermore, differential uplift and tilting due to GIA reshapes landscapes and drainage networks, while emergent land and basin connections drive ecosystem succession and carbon burial. Moreover, GIA-related stress redistribution influences a region’s seismicity and its seismic hazard, which must be considered in nuclear waste storage safety assessments. Similarly, such stress changes can alter volcanic activity even thousands of kilometres away from the glaciated area. GIA effects are present in a wealth of standardized observational data, such as GNSS measurements, tide gauges, relative sea levels, and terrestrial and satellite gravimetry. These data help refine GIA models, which enhance our understanding of ice-sheet history, sea-level changes, Earth's rheology and near-surface processes. The GIA theory can also be applied to study other planets and moons. We welcome contributions studying GIA's effects across various scales, including geodetic measurements, complex GIA modelling, the Earth's response to current ice-mass changes, and overview on emerging GIA data collections. We also invite abstracts on Earth structure and rheology, ice history and on GIA's impact on nuclear waste sites, volcanism, groundwater, permafrost, and carbon resources. We especially appreciate new model developments, model intercomparisons and model benchmarks in local, high spatial and temporal resolution for GIA assessments, results of fully coupled ice dynamics-GIA models, studies of broader environmental relevance, and improved GIA corrections for other geoscientific fields.
title: Glacial isostatic adjustment - omnipresent and shaping Earth’s future

description: Gravity and magnetic data are fundamental tools to investigate lithospheric structures over a wide range of spatial scales. The expansion of innovative acquisition systems (airborne, helicopter and UAV) and satellite surveys has considerably increased the volume, resolution and diversity of potential field datasets. These developments raise important challenges related to data acquisition, processing, harmonization, levelling and integration of heterogeneous datasets into coherent regional grids. The integration of gravity and magnetic data with complementary geological and geophysical information (e.g. petrology, geochemistry, structural geology, seismic, electromagnetic) provide powerful constraints on the architecture and tectonic evolution of the lithosphere in various tectonic settings.
