We invite contributions combining gravity and/or magnetic data with complementary geological and geophysical constraints through joint inversion, forward and inverse modelling, machine learning or other innovative approaches. Contributions spanning scales from local to lithospheric, addressing methodological developments, data processing, uncertainty assessment, and applications across a broad range of tectonic settings are particularly welcome.
title: Integrating gravity and magnetic data for lithospheric structure characterization

description: Geodesy contributes to atmospheric science by providing some of the essential climate variables of the Global Climate Observing System. Water vapor is currently under-sampled in meteorological and climate observing systems. Thus, obtaining more high-quality humidity observations is essential for weather forecasting and climate monitoring. The production, exploitation, and evaluation of operational GNSS Meteorology for weather forecasting is well established in Europe thanks to a long-lasting cooperation between the geodetic community and the meteorological services. Improving the skill of numerical weather prediction (NWP) models, e.g., to forecast extreme precipitation, requires GNSS products with higher spatio-temporal resolution and shorter turnaround. Homogeneously reprocessed GNSS data (e.g., IGS repro3) have high potential for monitoring water vapor climatic trends and variability. Advances in SLR atmospheric delay modelling are using NWP data and 3D ray-tracing to improve tropospheric corrections. With shorter orbit repeat periods, SAR measurements are a source of information to improve NWP models. Additionally, emerging LEO-PNT missions offer capabilities for atmospheric and environmental monitoring due to their dense geometry, rapid revisit times and new signals that will be defined. Their integration with GNSS and other geodetic techniques could open new possibilities for real-time correction models. Reflected signals of GNSS and future LEO-PNT provide additional opportunities for remote sensing of the Earth system. GNSS-R contributes to environmental monitoring with estimates of soil moisture, snow depth, ocean wind speed, sea ice concentration and can be used to retrieve near-surface water vapor. We welcome, but do not limit, contributions on: -Estimates of the neutral atmosphere using ground- and space-based geodetic data -Retrieval and comparison of tropospheric parameters from multi-GNSS, VLBI, DORIS and multi-sensor observations -Nowcasting, forecasting, and climate research using RT and repro tropospheric products, employing NWP and machine learning -Assimilation of GNSS tropospheric products in NWP and in climate reanalysis -Production of SAR tropospheric parameters and assimilation in NWP -Homogenization of long-term GNSS, VLBI tropospheric products -Detection and characterization of sea level, snow depth, and sea ice changes, using GNSS-R -Monitoring of soil moisture and ground-atmosphere boundary interactions using GNSS data
title: Atmospheric and Environmental Monitoring with Space-Geodetic Techniques

description: This session invites contributions on the observation, processing, modelling, integration, and application of the Earth’s gravity field at regional to global scales. Topics include the acquisition, evaluation, processing, and combination of terrestrial, airborne, shipborne, and satellite gravity observations; forward and inverse gravity modelling, including approaches incorporating laterally varying density structures; the development, evaluation, combination, and application of regional and global gravity field models; and gravity field modeling for physical height determination and vertical datum definition. Contributions integrating gravity with complementary geodetic, geophysical, seismic and oceanographic observations for the investigation and interpretation of crustal and lithospheric structure, retrieval of Mean Dynamic Topography, studies related to monitoring sea level as well as the contribution of recent, novel, altimetry missions like SWOT to the determination of the Earth’s marine gravity field are particularly welcome. We further invite contributions on emerging methods and technologies for gravity data processing, filtering, modelling, combination, and interpretation, including artificial intelligence and machine learning, as well as approaches that integrate heterogeneous and multi-sensor observations for geophysical and oceanographic applications.
title: Earth’s Gravity Field: Advances in Observations, Filtering, Modelling, Integration and Applications

description: 25 years ago, with the launch of the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE, 2002-2017) mission, a new era of satellite gravimetry began, enabling a wide variety of studies related to climate research as well as other geophysical or geodetic applications. Currently, the GRACE Follow-on (GRACE-FO, launched in 2018) mission continues this successful US-German partnership, providing this invaluable data record to monitor global gravity variations from space. Yet another US-German mission, GRACE Continuity (GRACE-C, planned launch end of 2028), is already in its implementation phase and will ensure that the GRACE data record becomes even longer. At the same time, ESA's Next Generation Gravity Mission (NGGM) is approved and planned for a launch in 2033. With its low altitude (~400 km) and controlled inclined (70 degrees) orbit, NGGM offers higher spatial and temporal resolution compared to the presently available near-polar orbit missions, in particular when combined with GRACE-C. This planned concept consisting of two satellite pairs is referred as MAss Change and Geosciences International Constellation (MAGIC). Apart from the above-mentioned GRACE-like missions, observations of other satellite missions can be used to compute high-resolution static gravity field models (GOCE mission) and to bridge gaps in the GRACE/-FO time series or to enhance gravity field models and scientific results derived thereof (e.g., Swarm, satellite laser ranging). The important role of satellite gravimetry in monitoring the Earth from space has led to various ongoing initiatives preparing for future gravity missions (beyond NGGM/MAGIC), including simulation studies, the definition of user and mission requirements and the investigation of potential measurement equipment and orbit scenarios. This session solicits contributions about: (1) Results from satellite gravimetry missions as well as from non-dedicated satellite missions in terms of - data analyses to retrieve time-variable and static global gravity field models, - combination synergies, and - Earth science applications. (2) The status and study results for future gravity field missions.
title: Satellite Gravimetry: Data Analysis, Applications and Future Mission Concepts

description: This session invites innovative Earth system and climate studies employing geodetic observations and methods. Modern geodetic observing systems have been instrumental in studying a wide range of changes in the Earth’s solid and fluid layers at various spatiotemporal scales. These changes are related to surface processes such as glacial isostatic adjustment, the terrestrial water cycle, ocean dynamics, and ice-mass balance, which are primarily due to changes in the climate. To understand the Earth system response to natural climate variability and anthropogenic climate change, different time spans of observations need to be cross-compared and combined with several other datasets and model outputs. Geodetic observables are also often compared with geophysical models, which helps in explaining observations, evaluating simulations, and finally merging measurements and numerical models via data assimilation. We look forward to contributions that: 1. Utilize geodetic data from diverse geodetic satellites, including altimetry, gravimetry (CHAMP, GRACE, GOCE, and GRACE-FO, SWOT), navigation satellite systems (GNSS and DORIS) or remote sensing techniques that are based on both passive (i.e., optical and hyperspectral) and active (i.e., SAR, Sentinel, NISAR) instruments. 2. Cover a wide variety of applications of geodetic measurements and their combination to observe and model Earth system signals in hydrological, ocean, atmospheric, climate, and cryospheric sciences. 3. Show a new approach or method for separating and interpreting the variety of geophysical signals in our Earth system and combining various observations to improve spatio-temporal resolution of Earth observation products. 4. Work on simulations of future satellite missions (such as MAGIC and NGMM) that may advance climate sciences. 5. Work towards any of the goals of the Inter-Commission Committee on "Geodesy for Climate Research" (ICCC) of the International Association of Geodesy (IAG). We are committed to promoting gender balance and ECS in our session. With the author consent, highlights from this session will be shared on social media with a dedicated hashtag during the conference in order to increase the impact of the session.
title: Geodesy for climate research

description: Accurate modeling and prediction of Earth rotation is important for numerous applications in geodesy, astronomy, navigation, and geophysics. In recent years, geodetic observation systems have made significant progress in monitoring the temporal variability of the Earth's rotation, which is largely related to dynamic processes in the planet's fluid components. The increase in observation accuracy must go along with the improvement of theories and models. Estimates of variability over a wide range of time scales have been noted as well. We welcome contributions that highlight new determinations and analyses of Earth Orientation Parameters (EOP), including combinations of different geodetic and astrometric observational techniques for deriving UT1/length-of-day variations and polar motion. We welcome discussions of EOP solutions in conjunction with a consistent determination of terrestrial and celestial frames. We are interested in the latest achievements in EOP forecasting, especially reports exploring the potential of innovative techniques, such as machine learning, in improving forecast accuracy. We invite contributions on the dynamical links between Earth rotation, geophysical fluids, and other geodetic quantities, such as the Earth gravity field or surface deformation, and of explanations for the physical excitations of Earth rotation. Besides tidal influences from outside the Earth, the principal causes for variable EOP appear to be related to angular momentum exchange from motions and mass redistribution of the fluid portions of the planet, including the atmosphere, oceans, hydrological reservoirs, and the fluid core. We welcome contributions about the relationship between EOP variability and the variability in fluids due to climate effects or global change. Forecasts of these impacts are important especially for the operational determination of EOP, and the effort to improve predictions is an important topic, and projections of EOP variability into the future. We are interested in the progress in the theory of Earth rotation. We seek contributions that are consistent internally with the accurate observations at the mm-level, to meet the requirements of the Global Geodetic Observing System and respond to IAG 2019 Res. 5 and IAU 2021 Res. B2, as well as those derived from the research of current IAU/IAG/IERS working groups on these topics. We also welcome contributions on the variability and excitation of the rotation of other planetary bodies.
title: Earth Rotation: Theory, temporal variability, physical interpretation, observing system determinations, and prediction

description: The Global Geodetic Observing System (GGOS) of the International Association of Geodesy (IAG) collaborates with IAG components and other entities to provide precise, consistent and long-term observations of the Earth's shape, rotation and gravity field, and to maintain global reference frames. In line with the essential variables that are already operational in the climate and ocean domains, GGOS has introduced the Essential Geodetic Variables (EGVs) framework. This framework identifies and characterizes the geodetic observations and products that are fundamental to monitoring and understanding changes in the Earth system. It also supports a wide range of scientific and societal applications on Earth and in space. Advancing the implementation of the EGVs requires their systematic identification and classification, together with assessments of their availability, quality and performance against user. It also requires sustainable observing infrastructure, reliable data and product supply chains, adequate human resources, and effective access to geodetic data and products in accordance with FAIR principles. This session welcomes contributions across the full EGV value chain, ranging from the definition and nature of EGV and their user requirements to observing techniques and infrastructure, data processing and product generation, assessments of availability, quality and performance, sustainable supply chains and human resources, and FAIR access to essential geodetic data and products.
title: GGOS and Essential Geodetic Variables for Earth System Monitoring

description: Following the launch of the first artificial satellite in 1957, geodesists refined knowledge of Earth’s flattening and used orbital drag observations from Sputnik to estimate upper atmosphere density. Since then, Precise Orbit Determination (POD)—where the satellite itself acts as a sensor through its orbital perturbations—has progressed to absolute orbit solutions at the centimeter (or sub centimeter) level to demanding long term stability on the order of 0.1 mm yr⁻¹ over decadal timescales, a prerequisite for quantitative climate change studies. Today four Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) constellations are operational, and numerous Earth Observation missions rely on POD (e.g., satellite altimetry, gravimetry, InSAR, and Satellite Laser Ranging to passive spheres). Together they provide an unprecedented data set that can push orbit determination to its limits and enable new geophysical applications across the atmosphere (density and water vapor content), the ocean (sea level rise), land (large scale fluid mass redistribution and present day deformation), and the deep Earth (rheology at decadal scales). This session aims to make the emerging challenges of orbit determination and modeling accessible to a broader community and to quantify how dynamics errors affect the many applications that depend on POD as their primary source of observations. Contributions are solicited (but not limited) to the following areas: 1. Precise orbit determination and absolute validation approaches. 2. Advances in modeling solar/terrestrial/thermal radiation pressure, atmospheric density and their interaction with space vehicles. 3. Updates on large-scale time-variable changes in the Earth’s gravity field (e.g., motion of the Earth’s center of mass relative to the crust). 4. Observational constraints on essential variables defining the status of climate change. 5. Improvements in observable modeling for all tracking systems (SLR, DORIS, GNSS) and assess their impact on POD. 6. Integration of refined clock modeling methods/space clocks into POD. 7. Studies for the co location of geodetic techniques in space (e.g., GENESIS) to strengthen the stability of future terrestrial reference frames.
title: Precise Orbit Determination : Sensing Changes on the Earth System

description: GNSS stations represent one of the major observation infrastructures for geoscientific research. Depending on where one needs measurements, the station design needs to weigh up several factors including signal to noise, power consumption, data telemetry, and expense of installation. Recent years have seen the increase in deployments of lower cost hardware, in particular multi-frequency receiver modules and cheaper antennas which have lowered the financial stakes for more risky, experimental installations. Some teams have deployed large numbers of such lower-cost stations while others have successfully continued working with higher tier geodetic-grade hardware. In this session, we welcome contributions from researchers involved with GNSS station deployment, design, and maintenance. In particular, topics of interest for this session include the evaluation of data quality, innovative case study uses of these data, and we welcome insights from the community on collaborative ways forward for sustainable GNSS station densification.
title: Latest developments in GNSS station design

description: The frequency and intensity of extreme floods are increasing worldwide, with direct consequences such as loss of life and property. Cutting-edge monitoring and simulation technologies are instrumental in guiding flood risk management. A variety of physical and conceptual hydrological and hydrodynamic models, as well as data-driven approaches (such as artificial intelligence, including machine learning), are available to inform flood risk assessment and management, including prevention, preparedness and recovery. These techniques provide the scientific community with a platform to explore the drivers of flood risk and develop effective flood risk reduction strategies. However, they also come with associated uncertainties. This session aims to bring together experts, researchers, and practitioners to present and discuss recent developments in the field of flood risk mapping, assessment and management. Topics such as 1D, 2D and 3D modelling for flood risk assessment, emergency action planning and the analysis of dam and levees breaching, as well as the design of structural, non-structural and nature-based measures, are welcome. Research on the associated uncertainties, sensitivity analysis, and flood impact modelling is also relevant to the session.
title: Advances in Flood Risk Modelling: Forecasting, Monitoring, Assessment, Mitigation and Recovery

description: Hail is one of the most damaging weather hazards worldwide, with far-reaching impacts on infrastructure, agriculture, ecosystems, and society. Despite recent advances, significant challenges remain in understanding, observing, predicting, and projecting hail across weather and climate timescales. This session welcomes contributions on all aspects of hail research, from fundamental process understanding to societal applications. Topics include, but are not limited to, observational studies using both historic and/or novel datasets, storm-scale and microphysical processes, extreme and compound events, numerical and statistical modelling, forecasting and nowcasting, machine learning and AI, climate variability and change, as well as risk assessment and insurance-related applications. Within these areas, studies may lean towards either process- or impact-oriented perspectives. We also encourage contributions where hail is an important aspect of the broader research scope. This can be severe convective storm research, such as studies of supercells or mesoscale convective systems, but also natural hazard risk frameworks that include hail. Studies linking atmospheric science with hazard and risk assessment, impact modelling, insurance applications, impact-based forecasting and warning, resilience, and adaptation are especially encouraged. This session aims to foster interdisciplinary exchange and strengthen links between atmospheric science, climate research, natural hazards, and the insurance and risk communities to advance our understanding of hailstorms across weather, climate, and society. We thus look forward to receiving interdisciplinary contributions connecting academia, operational weather services, industry, government, and decision makers.
title: Hailstorms and their impacts across weather, climate, risk and society

description: Heat extremes are one of the deadliest meteorological events and they are increasing in intensity and frequency due to climate change. Their impacts on society will increase dramatically in the future, with some studies suggesting that human habitability limits could be crossed locally. This session invites new research that addresses the challenges posed by extreme heat and its impacts. We encourage submissions from a broad range of disciplines including weather and climate sciences, climate impact studies, global and occupational health and epidemiology.Studies focusing on the Global South as well as submissions focusing on recent heatwaves and their systemic impacts, extreme heat episodes associated with the 2026-2027 El Niño event and projected unprecedented events, are particularly welcome. Suitable contributions may: (i) assess the definitions and indicators typically used to describe extreme heat (stress) and its impacts, (ii) quantify the drivers and underlying processes of extreme heat in observations and/or models; (iii) quantify historical climate trends and projections (iv) examine the challenges of monitoring and predicting extreme heat on all temporal scales; (v) assess impacts on human and occupational health and mortality; (vi) focus on societal response and adaptation to extreme heat in a warming climate, including heat-health early warning systems and anticipatory action, adaptation and management solutions; (vii) introduce transdisciplinary research frameworks for assessing impacts on human health, economic productivity, and the environment.
title: Extreme heat: characterization, drivers, prediction, impacts and adaptation

description: With climate change and an accelerating hydrological cycle, dry/hot hydrological extremes are no longer represented by classic, slow-evolving droughts. Over the past decade, heatwaves, dry spells and flash droughts have emerged as threats producing major impacts across multiple sectors. Furthermore, their rapid development hinders our ability to forecast and mitigate. Beyond their rapid development, their timing, intensity, preceding conditions, and locally significant vulnerabilities can worsen their impacts, including high plant mortality and crop losses, depletion of freshwater resources, wildfires, degraded air quality and ecosystem health, and even fatalities. Due to the rapid intensification, rapid response is vital, which demands improving monitoring strategies beyond the existing standards developed for slow-evolving droughts. Challenging to identify, difficult to compare across different climates and ecosystems, and driven by a complex combination of various physical processes, rapidly emerging dry/hot-extreme events are not yet well understood nor clearly defined. Consequently, there are few practical solutions for risk management and stakeholders. This session invites novel contributions on statistical, physically based, remote sensing-based, and qualitative methods for improving our physical understanding, monitoring, modelling, predicting, and assessment of environmental, social, and economic impacts of rapidly emerging dry/hot-extremes. Contributions that discuss and propose definitions for different types of rapidly emerging dry/hot-extremes, and investigate their changes, trends, and impacts are also invited. Contributions that investigate the atmospheric drivers and land-atmosphere feedback loops are highly encouraged. We encourage submissions from atmospheric sciences, hydrometeorology, hydrology, social sciences, and inter- and trans-disciplinary studies. Case studies, large-sample studies, statistical and time series analyses and machine-learning applications, socio-hydrology approaches, and citizen science experiences are welcome. Note that submissions that do not relate specifically to flash droughts, dry spells or other rapidly emerging droughts will be transferred into more relevant sessions. Submissions from early career researchers and diverse backgrounds are especially encouraged.
title: Flash Droughts, Heatwaves and Dry Spells: Drivers, Monitoring and Impacts of Rapidly Emerging Extremes

description: Rapid transitions between droughts and floods are an emerging frontier in compound hydrometeorological extremes under climate change. These dry-wet whiplash events can trigger cascading impacts on agriculture, ecosystems, water resources, energy, and critical infrastructure that exceed those of isolated drought or flood events. Warming-induced changes in precipitation variability, atmospheric circulation, moisture transport, land–atmosphere feedbacks, and human water management are reshaping their frequency, intensity, seasonality, and predictability, yet key mechanisms and risk implications remain poorly constrained. This session invites cutting-edge abstracts on the identification, physical mechanisms, predictability, attribution, risk assessment, and governance of rapid drought–flood or flood–drought transitions across spatial and temporal scales. We welcome contributions on event definitions and indicators; flash drought-flash flood linkages; atmospheric rivers, monsoon variability, and moisture transport; land–atmosphere–human feedbacks; climate variability and anthropogenic forcing; nonstationarity, regime shifts, and tipping points; and cascading socio-economic and ecological impacts. We particularly encourage studies using advanced approaches, including remote sensing, high-resolution Earth system modeling, and machine learning, with a specific emphasis on hybrid physics-AI approaches. Contributions that bridge process understanding with operational applications are also invited, such as subseasonal-to-seasonal prediction, impact-oriented extreme event forecasting, dynamic multi-hazard risk mapping, multi-hazard early warning, adaptive water management, and disaster risk reduction. By linking physical science, data science, and decision-making, this session aims to advance actionable knowledge and strengthen societal resilience to increasingly complex hydroclimatic extremes. We welcome diverse regional perspectives, as well as interdisciplinary collaborations that bridge natural science, engineering, social science and management practices.
title: Drought-Flood Whiplash in a Changing Climate: Mechanisms, Predictability, Cascading Risks, and Resilience

description: Lightning is a powerful manifestation of atmospheric electrical breakdown, which results from micro- and macro-scale charge separation processes within thunderstorms. Lightning is associated with deep convective storms, severe weather, hail, torrential rains, and flash floods. It is also responsible for numerous wildfires, burned areas, and atmospheric fire emissions. Furthermore, lightning impacts Earth atmosphere from the troposphere to the mesosphere and serves as a strong indicator of regional and global convective processes linked to climate change. It produces nitrogen oxides, which are precursors to ozone production. Finally, thunderstorms and lightning are essential parts of the Global Electrical Circuit (GEC) and control the fair-weather electric field. They are also associated with energetic radiation up to tens of MeV, spanning from sub-millisecond Terrestrial Gamma-ray Flashes (TGFs) to tens of seconds of gamma-ray glows. This session seeks contributions from research in atmospheric electricity with emphasis on: Atmospheric electricity in fair weather and the global electrical circuit Effects of dust and volcanic ash on atmospheric electricity Thunderstorm electrification, dynamics and microphysics Lightning initiation, propagation, and attachment Middle-atmospheric Transient Luminous Events Energetic radiation from thunderstorms and lightning In natura and laboratory experimental investigations of lightning discharge physics processes Remote sensing of lightning and related phenomena by space-based sensors Thunderstorms, flash floods, tropical storms and severe weather Lightning-ignited wildfires and ecological effects of lightning Connections between lightning, climate and atmospheric chemistry Modelling of thunderstorms and lightning Nowcasting and forecasting of thunderstorms using machine learning and AI Regional and global lightning detection networks Lightning Safety and its societal effects Planetary lightning in the solar system and beyond
title: Atmospheric Electricity, Thunderstorms, Lightning and their Effects

description: Droughts affect ecosystems, economies, and societies in diverse and often interconnected ways. Understanding drought risk requires not only characterizing drought hazards and water scarcity, but also examining who and what is exposed, how vulnerability shapes impacts, and how societies respond and adapt. These dimensions interact across sectors and scales, with drought impacts evolving over time and being influenced by water use, management and other human activities, as well as by changing conditions such as land use and climate change. This session will have Kerstin Stahl (Albert-Ludwigs-Universität Freiburg) as a solicited speaker and it brings together interdisciplinary research across the different dimensions of drought risk, from drought impact monitoring and hydrological responses to impact assessments, exposure analysis, vulnerability studies and adaptation and risk management strategies. We welcome contributions focusing on individual dimensions as well as research exploring their interactions, feedbacks, and dynamics. Topics of interest include, but are not limited to: - Dynamics, feedbacks, and socio-natural interactions of drought risks - Drought (impact) monitoring, indicators, forecasting, and early warning - Human responses and adaptive behaviour to drought and water scarcity - Exposure and vulnerability assessments, including their dynamics - Interactions between impacts across sectors (agriculture, forestry, energy production, livelihoods, among others) and scales - Drought early action, preparedness, and adaptation - Water management and allocation under drought conditions - Water governance and decision-making - Novel conceptual, data, modeling, and AI-based approaches for understanding drought risk We welcome contributions from hydrology, geography, climate science, socio-hydrology, disaster risk research, water management, environmental governance, behavioral economics, and humanities.
title: Drought in the Anthropocene: understanding risk, impacts, vulnerability and adaptation

description: With global climate change affecting the frequency and severity of extreme meteorological and hydrological events, it is particularly necessary to develop models and methodologies for a better understanding and forecasting of present-day weather induced hazards. Future changes in the event characteristics as well as changes in vulnerability and exposure are among the further factors for determining risks for infrastructure and society, and for the development of suitable adaptation measures. This session considers extreme events that lead to disastrous hazards induced by severe weather and climate change. These can, e.g., be tropical or extratropical rain- and wind-storms, hail, tornadoes or lightning events, but also floods, long-lasting periods of drought, periods of extremely high or of extremely low temperatures, etc. Papers are sought which contribute to the understanding of their occurrence (conditions and meteorological development), to the augmentation of risks and impacts due to specific sequences of extremes, for example droughts, heavy rainfall and floods, to assessment of their risk (economic losses, infrastructural damages, human fatalities, pollution), and their future changes, to studies of recent extreme events, to the ability of models to reproduce them and methods to forecast them or produce early warnings (in line with the “Early Warnings for All” initiative, launched in March 2023 by the United Nations and the World Meteorological Organization), to proactive planning focusing on damage prevention and damage reduction. In order to understand fundamental processes, papers are also encouraged that look at complex extreme events produced by combinations or sequences of factors that are not extreme by themselves. The session serves as a forum for the interdisciplinary exchange of research approaches and results, involving meteorology, hydrology, environmental effects, hazard management and applications like insurance issues.
title: Extreme meteorological and hydrological events induced by severe weather and climate change

description: Debris flows are among the most dangerous natural hazards that threaten people and infrastructure in both mountainous and volcanic areas. The study of the initiation and dynamics of debris flows, along with the characterization of the associated erosion/deposition processes, is of paramount importance for hazard assessment, land-use planning, design of mitigation measures and early-warning systems. In addition, climate change and economic development challenge risk management, and further research is needed to understand the consequences. A growing number of scientists with diverse backgrounds are studying debris flows. The difficulties in measuring parameters related to their initiation and propagation have progressively prompted research into a wide variety of laboratory experiments and monitoring studies. However, there is a need to improve the quality of instrumental observations that would provide knowledge for more accurate modelling and hazard maps. Nowadays, the combination of distributed sensor networks and remote sensing techniques represents a unique opportunity to gather direct observations of debris flows to better constrain their physical properties. At the same time, computer-aided simulations of physical processes, hazard assessment, and mitigation design are undergoing a revolution due to the widespread adoption of AI and data-driven numerical models. Not only do these developments mark an exciting era for advancing our understanding of complex natural hazards, but they also require researchers from diverse disciplines to collaborate in order to unlock their full potential. Scientists working in the field of debris flows are invited to present their recent advancements. In addition, contributions from practitioners and decision makers are also welcome. Topics of the session include field studies and documentation, mechanics of debris-flow initiation and propagation, laboratory experiments, modelling, monitoring, impacts of climate change on debris-flow activity, hazard and risk assessment and mapping, early warning, and alarm systems.
title: Debris flows: advances in mechanics, monitoring, modelling and risk management

description: Landslides can trigger catastrophic consequences, leading to loss of life and assets. In specific regions, landslides claim more lives than any other natural catastrophe. Anticipating these events proves to be a monumental challenge, encompassing scientific curiosity and vital societal implications, as it provides a means to safeguard lives and property. This session revolves around methodologies and state-of-the-art approaches in landslide prediction, encompassing aspects like location, timing, magnitude, and the impact of single and multiple slope failures. It spans a range of landslide variations, from abrupt rockfalls to rapid debris flows, and slow-moving slides to sudden rock avalanches. The focus extends from local to global scales. Contributions are encouraged in the following areas: Exploring the theoretical facets of predicting natural hazards, with a specific emphasis on landslide prognosis. These submissions may delve into conceptual, mathematical, physical, statistical, numerical, and computational intricacies. Presenting applied research, supported by real-world instances, that assesses the feasibility of predicting individual or multiple landslides and their defining characteristics, with specific reference to early warning systems and methods based on monitoring data and time series of physical quantities related to slope stability at different scales. Evaluating the precision of landslide forecasts, comparing the effectiveness of diverse predictive models, demonstrating the integration of landslide predictions into operational systems, and probing the potential of emerging technologies. Should the session yield fruitful results, noteworthy submissions may be consolidated into a special issue of an international journal.
title: Forecasting of landslides in space and time

description: Landslides rarely occur as isolated events, nor can they be fully understood through a single methodological lens. As climate change and human activities alter environmental forcing, assessing landslide hazards requires capturing complex physical processes across diverse spatio-temporal scales, from micro-scale geomechanics to slope stability and catchment-wide hazard chains. At the same time, rapid advancements in data-driven methods, remote sensing, and machine learning / AI offer novel tools for spatial and temporal prediction, albeit often at the cost of physical explainability. This session aims to bridge the gap between process-based physical understanding and data-driven prediction in landslide and (multi-)hazard assessments. We seek contributions that showcase how coupling empirical data, physics-informed statistical frameworks, and geomechanical models can yield robust, transparent hazard forecasting. We welcome submissions addressing, but not limited to, the following topics: - Bridging geomechanics-based slope stability with broad-scale susceptibility and hazard assessments. - Integrating machine learning with physical process understanding, including explainable AI tools and physics-informed data-driven methods. - Assessing process chains and cascading hazard interactions, covering landslide lifecycles with integrated methodologies, especially under non-stationary climate and environmental forcing. - Mapping uncertainty propagation and information loss when scaling models from slope to catchment levels.
title: Integrating data-driven and physically-based approaches in landslide hazard modelling

description: Landslides and geo-hydrological hazards affect every region of the world each year, and their impacts are being reshaped by climate change, urban expansion and land-use pressure. The rising toll of damaging events has pushed authorities, practitioners and scientists towards monitoring strategies that are reliable, operational and, where possible, low-cost. A well-designed monitoring system for landslides and ground deformation is today fundamental for both long- and short-term risk reduction. The temporal evolution of a slope can be captured in many ways: conventional and novel in situ instrumentation (inclinometers, sensors arrays, distributed fibre-optic sensing, low-cost IoT networks), ground-based platforms (GB-InSAR, terrestrial laser scanner, robotic total stations), UAV surveys, and satellite data (both optical and radar), including the opportunities opened by recent and forthcoming SAR missions and constellations (Sentinel-1C/D, SAOCOM, LuTan-1, NISAR). All these approaches share one purpose: measuring displacement through time in order to anticipate future behaviour or, at least, to reconstruct the recent past. Real-time, near-real-time and deferred-time strategies can each be effective, depending on the process under study, the instrument selected and the level of risk considered acceptable. The session is aligned with the aims of the International Consortium on Landslides, namely: i) promote landslide research for the benefit of society; ii) integrate geosciences and technology within cultural and social contexts in order to evaluate landslide risk; and iii) combine and coordinate international expertise. We welcome contributions on: i) innovative in situ, ground-based, airborne and satellite monitoring applications; ii) multi-temporal, multi-sensor and multi-platform case studies supporting risk management; iii)integration and synergistic use of different techniques, including cross-validation between sensors; iv) displacement-based early warning, velocity thresholds and failure forecasting; v) new tools and processing chains, from big-data management to AI and machine-learning approaches; vi) lessons learned from operational monitoring systems, including their limitations and failures. Case studies from data-scarce regions and low-cost, transferable solutions are particularly encouraged.
title: Landslide monitoring: recent technologies and new perspectives

description: Landslides and slope instability phenomena – affecting diverse materials with a variety of mechanisms (e.g., earthslides, rockfalls, debris flows) – are recognised to be driven by weather patterns largely differing in terms of variables (rainfall, temperature, snow melting) and significant time span (from a few minutes up to several months). However, local modifications induced by human intervention, such as socio-economic-induced land use/cover changes, reduced soil management due to land abandonment, or the implementation and maintenance of Nature-Based Solutions, are recognised to play a key role in defining landslide hazard and risk. In turn, these local human-induced factors can be strongly influenced by weather dynamics and climate change. For instance, hydrological and thermal regimes regulate vegetation suitability, then land cover and, in turn, landslide hazard and risk. A clear and robust evaluation of how ongoing and expected global warming and the resulting climate change can affect these factors and, hence, landslide risk represents a clear key need for practitioners, communities, and decision-makers. This session aims to provide a discussion forum for studies concerning the analysis of the role of climate-related variables and slope-atmosphere interaction on landslide triggering, propagation, hazard, and risk, and/or on the effectiveness of protection measures across different geographic contexts and scales. Test cases and investigations (by exploiting monitoring and modelling approaches) to evaluate ongoing and future landslide activity are welcome. Furthermore, investigations focused on data-driven approaches (Machine Learning, AI), through which the variations induced by climate and environmental changes on triggering, dynamics, and hazard are analysed, are greatly welcome.
title: Investigating the impact of climate and environmental changes on landslides

description: Landslides and slope instabilities are major hazards worldwide, yet the fundamental mechanisms governing their initiation, evolution, and failure dynamics remain active areas of research. These processes are controlled by complex, heterogeneous subsurface properties and dynamic processes operating across broad temporal (seconds to decades) and spatial scales (grain size to entire slopes). Improving the characterization and forecasting of slope instabilities requires innovative frameworks that explicitly account for these multidimensional variabilities. This session invites contributions presenting novel methodologies, emerging trends, and case studies in the characterization, monitoring, forecasting, and early warning of slope failures. We particularly encourage submissions that demonstrate the integration of geophysical, geotechnical, geological, and remote sensing datasets to build robust landslide models capable of characterizing subsurface structure, identifying controlling processes, and tracking temporal evolution. Specific topics of interest include: Multi-method frameworks combining geophysical, geotechnical, and remote sensing techniques. Applications of machine learning and AI to landslide hazard assessment, forecasting, data integration, and pattern recognition. Time-lapse geophysical monitoring of subsurface deformation, hydrological processes, and other changes. Joint or constrained inversion of geophysical and geomechanical parameters using geological data and geophysical imaging. Integrated monitoring and early warning frameworks combining in situ, subsurface, and remote observations. Recognizing the inherently interdisciplinary nature of slope stability research, we welcome contributions that bridge disciplinary boundaries and advance integrated approaches to understanding, monitoring, and anticipating slope failure addressing a broad spectrum of instability types, including natural landslides, engineered slopes, and climate-induced failures.
title: Integrating Geophysical, Geotechnical, and Remote Sensing for landslide monitoring and early warning systems.

description: Over the last decade there has been increasing recognition that patterns of landsliding vary across temporal and spatial scales challenging previous assumptions regarding the invariance of processes. Short-term temporal effects such as landslide preconditioning following large earthquakes, deforestation or wildfire, and long-term temporal effects related to river incision, drainage caption and hillslope readjustments show that a few years of data may not fully capture longer timescales. At the same time, recent work on path-dependency and correlated landsliding highlights knowledge gaps in the understanding of how the spatial and temporal context shapes landslide patterns, with past damage shaping failure processes. These interrelated processes have profound implication for landslide susceptibility, risk mitigation and understanding the broader role of landslides in landscape evolution. This session invites contributions that explore these interrelated themes through field survey, laboratory analysis, remote sensing, data analysis, and diverse modelling approaches to understand the mechanisms and processes from small to large temporal and spatial scales.
title: Space-time variation in landsliding across short and long timescales – from antecedent conditions to landscape memory

description: Rockfalls, rockslides and rock avalanches as well as other alpine mass movements are among the primary drivers of landscape evolution in steep terrain and they are some of the most hazardous and least anticipated processes. This session aims to bring together state-of-the-art methods for identifying, predicting, assessing, quantifying, and protecting against rock slope hazards and alpine mass movements. We seek innovative contributions from investigators dealing with all stages of rock slope and alpine hazards such as rock-ice avalanches, glacier-related hazards, debris flows or hazard cascades originating from the periglacial environment. Innovative contributions dealing with alpine mass movement predisposition, triggering, transport, and deposition are welcome, including (1) insights from field observations and/or laboratory experiments; (2) applications of statistical methods and/or artificial intelligence to identify and map mass movements; (3) in-situ or remote-sensing based monitoring approaches; (4) mass movement modeling for the analysis and interpretation of the governing physical processes – from conceptual frameworks to theoretical and/or advanced numerical approaches; (5) the development of strategies applicable for hazard assessment, mitigation and protection; (6) the impact of weather and climate on alpine mass movements, climate change attribution strategies, as well as the role of science at the interface with society; as well as (7) preparedness and risk reduction, and studies that integrate social, structural, or natural protection measures.
title: Rockfalls, rockslides, rock avalanches and other alpine mass movements

description: Debris flows and snow avalanches are among the most catastrophic hazards in mountainous settings. Surface erosion, slope failure or dam breaching are among the initiation mechanisms of debris flow, which can be magnified during the subsequent flowing process, with disastrous consequences for urbanized settings. Understanding whether an initial rainfall forcing evolves into a hazardous debris flow requires a modelling framework capable of representing the different stages of the process and their interactions. To this end, analytical approaches and numerical modelling provide fundamental insights into the interplay of mechanical equilibrium, soil saturation and flow propagation. These components can be combined into predictive applications for the design of early warning systems. We invite contributions addressing the modelling of debris flows at different levels of complexity and scales, from watershed to the interaction with hydraulic works, including rainfall-induced slope failure and surface erosion, transformation of landslides into debris flows, flow initiation and acceleration, entrainment of bed material, flow-topography interactions, rheological behaviour and deposition. Similar modelling challenges arise in snow avalanches, where the thermal forcing often causes the transition from snowpack instability to rapid flow development involving strongly nonlinear interactions between snow properties, terrain and flow dynamics. Contributions combining different modelling approaches or coupling different physical processes are particularly encouraged, as are studies investigating how information generated at one stage of the process can be transferred to the next. The session aims to foster discussion on how process-based numerical modelling can move from the simulation of individual phenomena towards integrated predictive frameworks, contributing to bridge the gap between fundamental process understanding and operational applications for hazard mitigation and early warning.
title: Process-based numerical modelling of debris flows and snow avalanches: from triggering to deposition, hazard assessment and early warning applications

description: Landslide research benefits from a multidisciplinary approach that integrates observations of slope morphology, surface conditions, and their evolution over time. The growing availability of different sensor types and long-term datasets, along with recent advances in remote sensing techniques and data-driven methods, offers great opportunities to investigate landslides. This session brings together recent developments in landslide identification and characterization and particularly welcomes contributions including: • Automatic and semi-automatic landslide detection and classification, including machine- and deep-learning approaches; • Regional-scale landslide inventories, landslide susceptibility assessment, monitoring and early-warning applications; • Integration of heterogeneous datasets from different techniques (optical, SAR, InSAR time series, DEM-derived, and geophysical information) for landslide identification and characterization; • Application of geomorphological mapping, repeated topographic observations, long-term monitoring, and multi-temporal DEMs (e.g., bistatic SAR/TanDEM-X); We welcome contributions addressing large landslides across different triggering mechanisms, scales, and environmental settings, from local case studies to regional-scale applications.
title: From landslide detection to monitoring: integrating multi-sensor and multi-temporal observations

description: Landslide Inventory Maps (LIMs) are the simplest tool to report the spatial distribution of landslides in a territory. They can be prepared using different techniques and base data (e.g. remote sensing images), each bringing intrinsic limitations and potential sources of mapping errors, hence affecting the overall accuracy and reliability. LIMs are a precious source of information for any subsequent analyses in landslide research (e.g., land management and planning, model training and validation, susceptibility, hazard, and risk assessment, among others). A common operational assumption carried out when using such data is to consider them as “correct”, which results in transferring/propagating the mapping error(s) to the subsequent products. Recent research works have defined the quality of LIMs as the result of three factors: geographic accuracy, thematic accuracy, and completeness/statistical representativeness. Geographic accuracy refers to the location, size, and shape of each landslide reported in the LIM. Thematic accuracy refers to the consistency of attributes assigned to each landslide in the LIM (e.g. classification, degree of activity, age/date of occurrence, among others). Completeness refers to the ratio of landslides reported in the LIM and the “ground truth”. Since the ground truth is hardly available, more recently the concept of statistical representativeness has been preferred, i.e. assuring that the statistical distribution of landslides reported in the LIMs is a statistically representative sample of the actual distribution of landslides in an area. Each of these aspects is currently under-explored in terms of evaluation/quantification/metrics, propagation, and handling/management in derivative maps. Within this general framework, this session welcomes contributions specially focused on (but not necessarily limited to) the following topics: • Definition of metrics (numeric, heuristic, morphometric, etc.) for the evaluation of mapping accuracy, errors, and uncertainty; • Statistical modelling of mapping errors; • LIMs quality assessment methods; • Impact of error propagation in maps obtained from LIMs, including training of machine learning and/or AI-based detection algorithms, susceptibility models, hazard and risk assessment; • Defining links between LIMs quality and use limitations. In contributions, all methods for the preparation of landslide inventories are welcome, from manual to semi- and fully automated.
title: Evaluating and Handling the Quality of Landslide Inventory Maps

description: Mountain environments are highly sensitive to dynamic hydroclimatic forcing. Intense precipitation, rain-on-snow events, snowmelt and prolonged wet periods interact with topographic, geological, cryospheric, and ecological controls to govern the initiation of rapid alpine mass movements, including rockfalls, rock avalanches, shallow landslides, debris flows, and snow avalanches. Environmental changes such as rising temperatures, retreating glaciers, degrading permafrost, and shifting snow or precipitation regimes can fundamentally alter the thermal and hydrological dynamics of mountain slopes and subsequently the frequency, magnitude, timing, and spatial distribution of mass movements. While the complex and nonlinear mechanisms of rapid alpine mass movements have traditionally been analyzed at the local slope scale, understanding and predicting them across regional, national, and transnational scales remains a major scientific frontier. Growing archives of Earth observation and environmental monitoring data, combined with continuous advances in modeling approaches and tools, propel the shift. These developments now enable the delineation of hazardous zones and the explicit inclusion of elements at risk across vast regions, facilitating a transition toward large-area, impact-based assessments. At the same time, the adoption of sophisticated sampling techniques is increasingly vital to address and mitigate data biases inherently present in large and heterogeneous hazard inventories. We welcome contributions that leverage emerging data sources and technologies on a large scale, integrating physics-based simulations, empirical-statistical modeling, and machine learning to capture these complexities, improve spatio-temporal susceptibility mapping, hazard mapping, and regional early warning systems, and further integrate potential consequences, risks, and impacts. Contributions from across disciplines and areas of disaster risk management are highly encouraged. Particular interest lies in studies that bridge the gap between localized, process-based physical understanding and large-area predictive modelling, as well as research that translates scientific outputs into actionable strategies for climate adaptation and resilient mountain communities. We explicitly welcome submissions that address the limitations and bottlenecks of these approaches, enabling the scientific community to learn from shared challenges and avoid common pitfalls.
title: Modelling Rapid Alpine Mass Movements across Mountain Regions: Drivers, Hazards, and Risk

description: Large landslides in rock, debris, and ice in glacial masses, represent enormous risks. These complex systems are difficult to describe, investigate, monitor, and model. Hence a reliable model of these phenomena requires acquisition and analysis of all available data to support successive steps up to the management of early warning systems. Large instabilities affect all materials (rock, weak rocks, debris, ice), from low to high altitudes, evolving as slow or fast complex landslides. This and the complex dependency on forcing factors result in different types and degrees of hazard and risk. Some aspects of these instabilities are still understudied and debated, because of difficult characterization and few cases thoroughly studied. Regional and temporal distribution, relationships with controlling and triggering factors are poorly understood resulting in poor predictions of behavior and evolution under present and future climates. How will it change their state of activity under future climatic changes? How this will impact on existing structures and infrastructures? How can we improve our predictions? Relationships among geological and hydrological boundary conditions and displacements are associated with the evolution in space and time of thermo-hydro-mechanical controls as well as the properties of the unstable mass. Even for well-studied and active phenomena warning thresholds are mostly qualitative, based on semi-empirical approaches. Hence a multidisciplinary approach and robust monitoring data are needed. Many modeling approaches can be applied to evaluate instability and failure, considering triggerings, and failure propagation, leading to rapid mass movements. Nevertheless, these approaches are still phenomenological and have difficulty explaining the observed behavior. The impacts of such instabilities on structures represent a relevant risk and an opportunity in terms of investigations and quantitative measurements of the effects on tunnels, dams, and roads. The design of these structures and knowledge of their expected performance are fundamental. We invite to present case studies, share views and data, discuss monitoring and modeling approaches and tools, to introduce new approaches for threshold definition, including advanced numerical modeling, machine learning for streamline and offline data analyses, development of monitoring tools, and dating or investigation techniques.
title: Large landslides monitoring, modeling and early warning

description: Landslide early warning systems (LEWS) are cost effective non-structural mitigation measures for landslide risk reduction. For this reason, the design, application and management of LEWS are gaining consensus not only in the scientific literature but also among public administrations and private companies. LEWS can be applied at different spatial scales of analysis, reliable implementations and prototypal LEWS have been proposed and applied from slope to regional scales. The structure of LEWS can be schematized as an interrelation of the following main components: monitoring, modelling, forecasting, warning, response. However, tools, instruments, methods employed can vary considerably with the scale of analysis, as well as the characteristics and the aim of the warnings/alerts issued. For instance, at local scale instrumental devices are mostly used to monitor deformations and hydrogeological variables with the aim of setting thresholds for evacuation or interruption of services. At regional scale hydro-meteorological thresholds are widely used to prepare a timely response of civil protection and first responders. Concerning modelling techniques, analyses on local slopes generally allow for the use of numerical models, while statistical, probabilistic and physical-based models are widely used for large areas. This session focuses on LEWS at all scales and stages of maturity, from prototype to active and dismissed ones. Test cases describing operational application of consolidated approaches are welcome, as well as works dealing with promising recent innovations, even if still at an experimental stage. Contributions addressing the following topics will be considered positively: - real-time monitoring systems (IoT) - prediction tools for warning purposes - in-situ monitoring instruments and/or remote sensing devices - analysis of hydro-meteorological drivers to enhance forecasting - warning models for issuing warning - operational applications and performance analyses - machine learning techniques applied for early warning purposes
title: Landslide Early Warning Systems for Emergency Preparedness and Societal security

description: This session focuses on the hydrological and eco-hydrological processes that control landslide predisposing and triggering conditions, focusing on surface and subsurface water dynamics from local slopes to regional catchments. As rainfall regimes shift under climate change, understanding and quantifying these hydrological processes is critical for reliable landslide forecasting and early warning. We welcome research on slope (eco-)hydrological processes and their upscaling to catchments, including evaporation, pore-water pressure buildup, preferential flow, and soil-bedrock interactions, as well as eco-hydrological mechanisms such as root-regulated drainage, suction dynamics, transpiration, and canopy interception. Disentangling these coupled water dynamics is essential for moving beyond the limitations of traditional empirical rainfall thresholds. We invite contributions from field monitoring, novel measurement techniques, and physics-based, numerical, and data-driven modeling that advance our understanding of how these processes affect landslide occurrence.
title: Recent advancements in landslide eco-hydrology

description: Coastal cliff collapse across Europe poses an escalating threat to human lives and critical infrastructure due to accelerated erosion driven by climate change and sea-level rise. Coastal cliff response is governed by complex interactions between geological, geomorphological, oceanographic and climatic processes. Environmental forcings such as temperature fluctuations, moisture variations, rainfall, sea-level changes and wave impacts can progressively alter stress conditions within coastal cliffs. These processes can promote cumulative damage, progressive degradation and cliff retreat. Understanding how these drivers influence the degradation, deformation and progressive failure of coastal rock masses is becoming increasingly important for reliable hazard assessment and long-term risk mitigation in highly vulnerable coastal environments. This session, promoted under the auspices of the AIGA’s (Italian Association of Engineering and Environmental Geology) Working Group on Rocky Coasts, brings together researchers investigating coastal landslides, rockfalls and cliff instability through monitoring, remote sensing, field and laboratory investigations, numerical modelling and data-driven approaches. While focused on coastal environments, the session also welcomes contributions investigating the response of similar slopes to environmental and climatic forcings in analogous settings, where progressive damage accumulation and climate-driven degradation processes play a key role. We encourage submissions addressing multi-scale monitoring strategies, satellite and ground-based remote sensing, geophysical investigations, laboratory and in-situ testing, and the characterization of material properties controlling cliff response to environmental forcing. Contributions integrating monitoring observations with numerical models (e.g. FEM, DEM, FDEM, CFD and coupled thermo-hydro-mechanical approaches) are particularly encouraged. The session also seeks studies exploring future evolution scenarios through climate projections, digital twins, and applications of machine learning and artificial intelligence. Special emphasis will be given to predictive frameworks combining monitoring data, environmental forcing and climate scenarios to support hazard assessment and coastal adaptation.
title: Coastal Cliffs in a Changing Climate: From Advanced Monitoring Strategies to Predictive Modelling of Future Scenarios

description: Exposure, i.e. the situation of people, infrastructure, housing, production capacities, and other tangible human assets located in hazard-prone areas, is one of the main components for risk assessment. While exposure at the country scale is often well-defined, fine-grained exposure datasets are key to making risk assessments more detailed and reliable, both in terms of spatial and temporal resolutions, and in identifying which people and assets are most at risk. Models, input, and output datasets range from geospatial representations of population or built-up area to complex datasets describing people’s characteristics (e.g., gender, age, education) and detailed asset information (e.g., building material, number of floors, road types). Models cover a wide range of scales and resolutions, with local implementations closely grounded in field observations and providing high-resolution detail, while others cover continents or even have a global reach. Other approaches are designed around specific sectors or economic activities, such as agriculture, tourism, or embodied carbon accounting. Various data sources range from census data, cadastral surveys, and grassroots activities, including OpenStreetMap-based exposure models, to big data generated through remote sensing and AI-driven methods, often developed by larger organisations (e.g., WorldPop, Open Buildings by Google, or Overture Maps). Recent efforts increasingly move beyond static representations of exposure to capture its dynamics, including the modelling of Shared Socioeconomic Pathways and human displacement. This broad and growing landscape of exposure science is reflected in the wide variety of stakeholders, ranging from the insurance industry to local and national governments, research organizations, the tourism sector, and NGOs. In this session, we will welcome submissions addressing (1) geospatial methods and tools for the creation of exposure models, such as Volunteered Geographic Information (VGI) or Earth Observation (EO) and AI models; (2) assessment of the quality or completeness of the data sources of exposure models, such as remote sensing, crowd-sourced, or official registry datasets; (3) exposure models for single hazards, for multi-hazard or hazard-independent contexts; (4) comparison, validation, and analysis of exposure models; (5) Cat model, insurance, government, and financial exposure models and datasets; and (6) innovative applications of exposure models.
title: Exposure modeling for natural hazards – creation, analysis and application

description: Natural hazards and extreme events pose major challenges for monitoring and risk management across space and time, particularly due to interconnected exposure, vulnerability, and cascading impacts. During rapidly evolving crises, timely and reliable information on hazard evolution, exposure, damage, and impacts is essential. Before disasters occur, up-to-date information on exposure, vulnerability, critical infrastructure, and the built environment is equally important for preparedness, mitigation, and establishing reliable baseline conditions. Advances in Earth observation (EO), UAVs, ground sensors, IoT networks, and geospatial infrastructures are enabling near-real-time monitoring from local to global scales. In parallel, artificial intelligence (AI) and GeoAI are transforming the analysis of large and heterogeneous geospatial datasets, supporting hazard detection and forecasting, susceptibility and risk assessment, damage mapping, and decision support. They also provide new opportunities for continuously updating exposure and vulnerability information. Despite this progress, challenges remain in moving from experimental models to reliable operational systems, including model generalization, data scarcity and imbalance, multi-sensor fusion, uncertainty, explainability, scalability, reproducibility, and trustworthy AI. Interoperability with disaster-management standards and operational workflows is also essential for effective uptake by civil protection and emergency-management authorities. This session welcomes methodological, experimental, and operational studies combining remote sensing, geospatial information, and AI for floods, wildfires, landslides, earthquakes, volcanic hazards, droughts, coastal hazards, extreme weather, land deformation, subsidence, and multi-hazard or cascading events. Topics include rapid hazard mapping and forecasting; susceptibility, exposure, vulnerability, and risk assessment; damage analysis; explainable, trustworthy, and physics-informed AI; satellite-UAV-ground data fusion; transfer learning and foundation models; decision-support systems; and integration of EO/AI products into disaster-management practice.We particularly encourage studies that bridge research and operations, demonstrate transferability across regions or hazard types, provide open datasets or reproducible workflows, and connect scientific information products with established disaster-management practices.
title: Earth Observation and Trustworthy GeoAI for Hazard Prediction, Risk Assessment and Disaster Monitoring

description: Remote sensing and Earth Observations (EO) are used increasingly in the different phases of the risk management and in development cooperation, due to the challenges posed by contemporary issues such as climate change, and increasingly complex social interactions. The advent of new, more powerful sensors and more finely tuned detection algorithms provides the opportunity to assess and quantify natural hazards, their consequences, and vulnerable regions, more comprehensively than ever before. Several agencies have now inserted permanently into their program the applications of EO data to risk management. In fact, EO revealed fundamentals for hazard, vulnerability, and risk mapping from small to large regions around the globe, during the pre/post-hazards, the occurrence of disasters, the emergency response and recovery phases. In this framework, the Committee on Earth Observation Satellites (CEOS) has been working for several years on disaster management related to natural hazards (e.g., volcanic, seismic, landslide and flooding ones), including pilots, demonstrators, recovery observatory concepts, Geohazard Supersites, and Natural Laboratory (GSNL) initiatives and multi-hazard management projects. Many case studies can be taken into account for natural hazards processes such as landslides, floods, seismic and tectonic studies, infrastructure damages and so on. The session is dedicated to multidisciplinary contributions focused on the demonstration of the benefit of the use of EO for natural hazards and risk management. The contributions might focus on: - Addressed value of EO data in hazard/risk forecasting models; - Innovative applications of EO data for rapid hazard, vulnerability and risk mapping, the post-disaster recovery phase, and in support of disaster risk reduction strategies; - Development of tools for assessment and validation of hazard/risk models. The use of different types of remote sensing data (e.g. thermal, visual, radar, laser, and/or the fusion of these) or platforms (e.g. space-borne, airborne, UAS, drone, etc.) is highly recommended, with an evaluation of their respective pros and cons focusing also on future opportunities (e.g. new sensors, new algorithms). Early-stage researchers are strongly encouraged to present their research. Moreover, contributions from international cooperation, such as CEOS and GEO initiatives, are welcome.
title: Application of remote sensing and Earth-observation data in natural hazard and risk studies

description: Compound extremes and cascading hazards represent complex manifestations of coupled Earth-system processes in which multiple drivers interact simultaneously or sequentially across spatial and temporal scales. Heatwaves may develop in association with drought and atmospheric stagnation; precipitation extremes may trigger floods and landslides; drought and heat can precondition landscapes for wildfire; and cyclones can generate interacting wind, rainfall, flood and storm-surge hazards. Such events may involve nonlinear amplification, feedbacks, thresholds and transitions that are difficult to identify through conventional single-hazard analyses. Earth observation provides a unique observational basis for investigating these processes through thermal infrared, optical, microwave/SAR and atmospheric observations of land-surface temperature, soil moisture, evapotranspiration, vegetation stress, precipitation, surface water, fire activity, aerosols and atmospheric composition. We particularly welcome studies that integrate multisource and multiscale Earth-observation datasets with in situ observations, reanalysis, numerical models and high-resolution simulations. The session also invites contributions demonstrating how artificial intelligence and machine learning, including deep learning, spatiotemporal learning, explainable AI, hybrid physics–ML approaches and data-driven process discovery, can improve the detection, characterisation and prediction of compound extremes and hazard cascades while addressing uncertainty and generalisation. Topics of interest include, but are not limited to, heat–drought, heat–humidity, heat–air-pollution, drought–wildfire, precipitation–flood, flood–landslide, cyclone–flood and other compound or sequential hazards. Contributions addressing land–atmosphere coupling, surface-energy and water-balance feedbacks, nonlinear dependence, threshold behaviour, regime transitions, hazard propagation, precursor identification, attribution, predictability and early warning are particularly encouraged. The session aims to advance understanding of how compound extremes emerge, intensify, transition and cascade, and how Earth observation and AI/ML can reveal the underlying physical mechanisms across scales.
title: Earth Observation of Compound Extremes and Cascading Hazards: Land–Atmosphere Coupling, Nonlinear Dynamics and Transitions

description: European Ground Motion Service (EGMS) has significantly improved the ability to monitor and analyse geohazards using InSAR (satellite interferometry) data since its products became available for downloading in mid-2022. These interferometric products are provided by the Copernicus Land Monitoring Service (CLMS) under the responsibility of the European Environment Agency (EEA). EGMS overcomes the long-standing challenge of complex SAR (Synthetic Aperture Radar) images processing, making ground displacement monitoring accessible to a wider range of users. EGMS provides millimetre-accurate measurements, which are available for downloading via the EGMS platform. EGMS delivers full-resolution velocity and displacement time series for both ascending and descending satellite orbits (Level 2a), aligned with the GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite System) reference network within a common reference frame (Level 2b), and computed displacement vectors in the vertical and E-W directions (Level 3), with a spatial resolution of 100 x 100 m. In this session, we welcome contributions that use EGMS data to monitor and investigate different kinds of geohazards. Topics of interest include subsidence, slow-moving landslides, sinkholes, groundwater and hydrocarbon exploitation, Underground Gas Storage (UGS) activities, mining impacts, volcanic activity, environmental analysis and many more. We also welcome studies transforming EGMS data into analysis ready products for several topics, e.g, coastal studies or climate change estimations. We also encourage studies that explore the impact of these geohazards on critical infrastructure and buildings, or that integrate EGMS data with other methods to improve geohazard assessment. We aim to highlight the versatility and value of EGMS data in understanding and mitigating the risks associated with natural and man-made induced geohazards. Contributions demonstrating innovative applications, cross-disciplinary approaches and case studies with practical implications are particularly welcome.
title: EGMS data for natural and man-made induced geohazards

description: SAR remote sensing is an invaluable tool for monitoring and responding to natural and human-induced hazards. Especially with the unprecedented spatio-temporal resolution and the rapid increase of SAR data collections from various SAR missions (such as ERS, Envisat, ALOS, Radarsat, Sentinel-1a/b/c/d and NiSAR), we can exploit hazard-related signals from the SAR phase and amplitude imagery, characterize the associated spatio-temporal ground deformations and land alterations, and decipher the operating mechanism of the geosystems in geodetic timescales. Yet, optimally extracting surface displacements and disturbance from SAR imagery, synergizing cross-disciplinary big data, aggregating useful information by multimodal remote sensing fusion along with machine learning methods, and bridging the linking knowledge between observations and mechanisms of different hazardous events remain challenging. Therefore, in this session, we welcome contributions that focus on (1) new algorithms, including machine and deep learning approaches and multi-modal/platform integration, to retrieve critical products from SAR remote sensing big data in an accurate, automated, and efficient framework; (2) SAR applications for natural and human-induced hazards including such as flooding, landslides, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, glacial movement, permafrost destroying, mining, oil/gas production, fluid injection/extraction, peatland damage, urban subsidence, sinkholes, oil spill, and land degradation; (3) multimodal remote sensing fusion to enhance information extraction related to hazards, agriculture, forestry, land management, and environmental monitoring; and (4) mathematical and physical modeling of the SAR products such as estimating displacement velocities and time series for a better understanding on the surface and subsurface processes.
title: SAR remote sensing for natural and human-induced hazard applications

description: This session highlights recent advances in Earth observation, from high-resolution imaging to AI-driven analytics and near-real-time monitoring, and examines how these capabilities can move beyond research into disaster risk governance. It explores pathways for translating EO-derived insights into early warning, risk-informed planning, policy decisions, and institutional practice, emphasizing collaboration among scientists, practitioners, and decision-makers to build resilient, evidence-based disaster management systems. It would also cover aviation resilience to highlight the impacts of natural hazards on airports, air transport infrastructure and operations, including early warning, risk-informed planning and operational resilience.
title: Harnessing GeoAI & Earth Observation for Disaster Risk Governance to achieve SDGs

description: Wildfires modify the physical, hydrological and mechanical properties of soils and rocks, influencing slope stability, sediment availability and catchment response.
