Loss of vegetation cover and root reinforcement, changes in soil water repellency and cohesion, and thermal damage to near-surface rock masses can initiate or condition geohydrological processes during and after fire. Understanding how these changes propagate across hillslopes and catchments, and evolve from the immediate aftermath to subsequent years, remains essential for assessing post-fire hazards and landscape evolution. This session focuses on the links between fire-induced material alterations, process initiation and sediment transfer in burned landscapes. Relevant processes include rock spalling and rockfalls, dry ravel, shallow landslides, accelerated erosion, debris and mud flows, and sediment-laden floods. Particular attention is given to the controls exerted by burn severity, geological and geotechnical conditions, rainfall and sediment connectivity, and to their implications for cascading hazards. Contributions addressing individual processes and their interactions are equally welcome. We invite new field evidence, laboratory characterization, inventories and monitoring studies using in-situ and remote sensing methods. Modelling advances may address post-fire slope instability, initiation thresholds, runout, sediment mobilisation and hillslope–catchment connectivity. We particularly encourage studies that relate measured changes in soil and rock properties to observed geomorphic responses, constrain spatial and temporal variability, and evaluate model performance and uncertainty. Comparative and multitemporal analyses can help establish the transferability of methods across geological settings, fire regimes and stages of post-fire recovery. The session also welcomes rapid post-fire assessments, susceptibility and hazard mapping, exposure and risk analysis, early-warning approaches, and evaluations of mitigation and management strategies. Case studies from the Mediterranean region, California, Australia, higher-latitude environments and other fire-affected regions are invited, especially those providing practical lessons and transferable examples for future wildfire scenarios. By integrating process characterisation, inventories, monitoring and modelling, the session aims to advance the understanding and mitigation of post-fire geohydrological hazards.
title: Wildfire-induced Geohydrological Hazards and Landscape Evolution: Processes, Modelling and Risk Management

description: The destructive wildfire season of 2026 once again demonstrated that wildfire risk is intensifying and expanding across Europe and beyond. Severe fires affected traditional wildfire-prone regions, while significant events also occurred in areas with more limited experience of large fires, including the United Kingdom and western France. These developments highlight the need to understand wildfire risk as the outcome of interacting climatic, environmental, social, economic and institutional processes – and to strengthen resilience across landscapes, communities, infrastructure and the built environment. This session welcomes research and practical initiatives addressing all dimensions of wildfire risk, vulnerability and resilience. Contributions may focus on risk assessment, exposure modelling, vulnerability indicators and functions, damage and loss assessment, the vulnerability and resilience of buildings and critical infrastructure, land and fuel management and nature-based solutions. We particularly encourage social and interdisciplinary studies addressing risk perception, preparedness, risk communication and public awareness, public participation and community-based risk reduction, stakeholder engagement, institutional capacity, governance, policy, responsibility and the social impacts of wildfire. Contributions may examine wildfires as an established hazard or as an emerging risk in regions with limited experience and preparedness. Studies can cover the entire risk management cycle from prevention activities to recovery and lessons learned. By bringing together perspectives from the natural sciences, social sciences, engineering and practice, the session aims to promote exchange across disciplines and regions and support more integrated, equitable and effective approaches to wildfire risk reduction and resilience.
title: Wildfire exposure, vulnerability, resilience and disaster risk reduction

description: Wildfires pose a significant and growing threat to both human populations and the environment. Climate change exacerbates this risk by increasing their frequency, duration, and severity. Rising temperatures, prolonged droughts, and shifting weather patterns create increasingly favourable conditions for fire ignition and spread, expanding the range of vulnerable areas and making wildfires a complex global challenge. The increasing availability of high-resolution, georeferenced data calls for advanced approaches to analyse and model wildfire dynamics. Remote sensing, geospatial analysis, artificial intelligence, and data-driven and numerical modelling offer new opportunities to transform large and heterogeneous datasets into actionable information for wildfire prediction, risk assessment, and management. This session aims to bring together experts from geosciences, climatology, forestry, and territorial planning to improve our understanding of fire-related dynamics and explore innovative strategies for mitigation and resilience. By fostering interdisciplinary collaboration, we seek to advance wildfire prediction, prevention, and post-fire recovery, contributing to more effective responses to the growing threat posed by wildfires in a changing climate. We welcome contributions on topics such as: • Remote sensing, geospatial and computational methods for recognizing, modelling, and predicting wildfire spatio-temporal patterns. • Pre- and post-fire assessments, including fire mapping, severity evaluation, and risk management. • AI, machine learning, and data-driven approaches for wildfire analysis and prediction. • Long-term analyses of wildfire trends in relation to climate and land-use changes. • Fire spread modelling and fire-weather relationships. • Post-fire vegetation recovery and phenology. Join us in advancing wildfire research and developing innovative strategies to better understand and mitigate its impacts.
title: Spatial and Temporal Dynamics of Wildfires: Models, Data, and Reality

description: As wildfires intensify under changing climatic and socio-ecological conditions, Earth Observation (EO) has become indispensable for monitoring, modelling, and understanding wildfire dynamics across spatial and temporal scales. Advances in remote sensing have enabled the development of wildfire-related models. However, the reliability and transferability of such models depend fundamentally on the quality and accessibility of the datasets upon which they are trained. Over the past decades, rapidly expanding wildfire-related datasets have emerged from airborne and spaceborne observations. These datasets span diverse sensor modalities, spatial resolutions, temporal coverages, and geographic domains. Nevertheless, many remain highly application-specific and regionally constrained. Such fragmentation hinders cross-comparison, interoperability, benchmarking, and reproducibility, ultimately limiting the broader scientific and operational uptake of both datasets and downstream modelling approaches. This session focuses on the challenges associated with the development, maintenance, validation, and reuse of remote sensing-derived wildfire datasets. We welcome contributions drawing upon airborne and spaceborne observations, including data acquired from polar-orbiting and geostationary platforms, and encompassing optical, thermal infrared, hyperspectral, SAR, and LiDAR sensors. Contributions addressing multi-sensor and multi-platform integration are particularly encouraged. Topics of interest include, but are not limited to: • Methodologies for the generation of wildfire-related datasets (data acquisition, annotation, semantic segmentation). • Scalable data dissemination frameworks (FAIR-compliant data management, STAC-based catalogues, geospatial data cubes). • Scientific reproducibility • Dataset validation This session seeks to advance best practices in the development, validation, stewardship, and dissemination of wildfire remote sensing datasets, while promoting interoperability, transparency, reproducibility, and long-term reusability. Contributions presenting openly accessible resources are especially encouraged. Early career scientists are particularly welcome to contribute.
title: Remote Sensing-Derived Datasets for Wildfires: From Data Acquisition and Fusion to Dataset Curation, Validation, Maintenance, and Reuse

description: From the uranium, thorium and potassium in rocks and soils to the cosmic rays reaching the ground, natural radioactivity shapes the environment we live in. Radon, a gas produced by the decay of uranium, is the main contributor to public radiation exposure and a major indoor health hazard. On top of this natural background, artificial radionuclides released by nuclear activities, accidents and legacy contamination leave a long-lasting footprint on environmental health. Radioactivity surveys are needed to characterize environmental radiation, assess exposure and guide remediation. They drive the development of new detectors, portable instruments and analytical methods. Radionuclides are also used as tracers of groundwater flow, surface water–groundwater interactions, geological processes and ecosystem dynamics at different scales. Monitoring is becoming more autonomous and data-driven, with AI-based data analysis, robotic platforms for mapping complex sites and UAVs carrying sensors for fast, large-scale and 3D surveys. The session covers all aspects of environmental radioactivity, including geological surveys, mineral exploration, atmospheric and groundwater contamination, radiological hazards in building materials, and radon hazard and risk assessment. We particularly welcome studies using natural and fallout radionuclides as environmental tracers, work on ecosystem dynamics and impacts on public health, and contributions on Naturally Occurring Radioactive Materials (NORM). Studies presenting methodological advances in measurement, modelling and mapping approaches and novel instrumentation for radioactivity monitoring are also encouraged.
title: Environmental Radioactivity: Sensing, Tracing, Protecting

description: Reconstructing the spatial and temporal evolution of the Earth’s magnetic field relies on high-quality paleomagnetic and archaeomagnetic records, robust chronological constraints, and increasingly sophisticated modelling approaches. Integrating these different components is essential for advancing our understanding of geomagnetic field behaviour over timescales ranging from decades and centuries to millions of years. This session aims to bring together researchers working across the different stages of geomagnetic field reconstruction, from the acquisition and interpretation of directional and absolute paleointensity data to their integration into regional and global geomagnetic field models. We welcome contributions presenting new paleomagnetic records from all kinds of archives, including archaeological materials, volcanic rocks, and sediments, as well as studies addressing directional and paleointensity methods, data reliability and selection criteria, chronological uncertainties, and the development and improvement of paleomagnetic databases. The session also welcomes contributions on magnetostratigraphy and geomagnetic field variations recorded in sedimentary and volcanic sequences, including studies that refine chronological frameworks and provide new constraints on the long-term evolution and polarity behaviour of the geomagnetic field. Particular attention will be given to approaches that bridge observations and modelling, including regional and global geomagnetic field reconstructions, data assimilation and statistical approaches, the treatment and propagation of uncertainties, and comparisons between different datasets and models. By bringing together paleomagnetists and geomagnetic field modellers, the session seeks to foster dialogue and collaboration across these communities and to explore how new data, improved chronologies, and advances in modelling strategies can jointly contribute to more robust reconstructions of the Earth’s magnetic field through time.
title: From Paleomagnetic Records to Geomagnetic Field Models: Bridging Data, Models, and Field Reconstructions

description: The last decades have been characterized by increasing climatic extremes and a foreshadowing of what is to come in a rapidly warming world. The disturbance of climatic extremes, such as droughts, floods, heatwaves and fires, to soil biogeochemistry and plant resilience has major consequences for the cycling of carbon and nutrients. Yet, the magnitude and direction of these responses differ strongly among soil types, climatic regions, and ecosystem settings. The session aims to identify both common mechanisms and soil-specific responses to climatic extremes, and to better understand how short-term perturbations by such climatic extremes translate into long-term changes of soil systems. The session will bring together experimental, observational, and modelling studies that investigate specific fundamental biogeochemical mechanisms as well as soil development and soil functioning at larger scales. We welcome contributions that give a perspective on biogeochemical changes in plant-soil systems from all climate zones and both natural and managed soil systems. Topics may include carbon and nutrient transformations, microbial and mineral controls on organic matter persistence, plant and rhizosphere shifts, nutrient mobilization and limitation, redox-driven processes, greenhouse-gas fluxes, and the legacy effects of climatic extremes and its effects on soil functioning.
title: Climatic extremes driving soil biogeochemistry and carbon cycling

description: Drought is a major driver of changes in soil-water availability and vegetation functioning, with impacts that vary across spatial and temporal scales. This session welcomes contributions investigating soil moisture dynamics and vegetation responses to drought across spatial and temporal scales. We invite studies using in-situ soil moisture sensors, field observations, proximal sensing, UAV and satellite observations, and environmental modeling to characterize soil-water availability and its links to vegetation functioning under water-limited conditions. Contributions addressing drought impacts on soil systems, soil moisture-vegetation interactions, multi-scale monitoring, and the integration of field measurements with Earth observation data are particularly encouraged.
title: Detection and forecasting soil moisture dynamics and vegetation responses to drought

description: Soils are central to terrestrial ecosystem functioning, supporting food production, biodiversity, water regulation, nutrient cycling, and climate resilience. They are also crucial for the health of connected freshwater and saline ecosystems. However, soils face multiple, compounding threats. These include increasing exposure to established and emerging contaminants, such as microplastics, alongside severe degradation from erosion, soil sealing, nutrient depletion, salinisation, biodiversity loss and climate-driven disturbances. Addressing these challenges requires moving beyond linear approaches to soil management towards soil circularity. This concept focuses on restoring and reintegrating soil resources, nutrients, organic matter and biological functions into productive and natural systems. This session addresses how frontiers in soil science and environmental technologies can support both the restoration of degraded soils and the prevention of further degradation. We specifically welcome research connecting soil processes with ecosystem interactions, circular resource use, and long-term resilience. A key focus is understanding how restoration and circular soil-management practices simultaneously impact multiple soil functions with different results and consequences for soil ecosystem services. Contributions are encouraged on the co-benefits of nature-based solutions and regenerative approaches that enhance soil organic carbon (SOC) storage, nutrient availability, soil structure, biodiversity, water quality, crop productivity and ecosystem restoration. Furthermore, we welcome studies utilizing advanced monitoring, sensing, and predictive modelling to identify early signs of soil degradation and support preventive management. Emerging tools, such as proximal and remote sensing, spectroscopy, soil biodiversity indicators, machine learning, digital soil mapping, process-based modelling and integrated monitoring platforms are vital for shifting soil management from reactive remediation to proactive, adaptive intervention. Dr. Saia research is funded by SHARInG-MeD (GA n 2211, PRIMA) Dr. Marazuela research is funded by PACTOSAL (PID2024-160795OA-I00) Dr. Lizaga research is funded by UPSTREAM (PID2024-162386OA-I00)
title: Soil Circularity: Regenerating Agroecosystems and Restoring Natural Land

description: Geotechnical and geo-environmental engineering are shifting toward sustainable, bio-driven solutions. Whether soil is transformed by living organisms, engineered by bio-inspired solutions, or built with earthen material, these approaches share a common thread: harnessing biological processes, bio-inspiration, and natural earthen materials for sustainable ground engineering and construction. This session is built around two linked questions: how do biological and biomimetic agents interact with soil and earthen materials across scales, and how can we harness them from pore-scale processes to field- and structure-scale applications? [OdSJ(E1.1]We connect communities that rarely meet: researchers developing bio-inspired subsurface locomotion and self-burrowing robotics; those quantifying root and organism mechanics in soil; and those advancing bio-mediated and bio-based geo- and construction materials. We welcome experimental, imaging-based, field, numerical, and sustainability assessment contributions, and strongly encourage Early Career Scientists. Topics of interest include, but are not limited to: - Bio-inspired subsurface locomotion & robotics: earthworm-, root-, and seed-inspired self-burrowing probes; peristaltic penetration and tip-extension burrowing in granular media; soft robotics and autonomous sensors for site characterisation; mechanics of the probe–soil interface. - Root & organism biomechanics for geo-engineering: root growth forces, tip penetration, and directional growth; anchorage, root-induced soil deformation, bioturbation; root-based and bio-engineered slope stabilisation. - Bio-mediated soil improvement: microbially and enzyme induced calcite precipitation (MICP, EICP), biopolymers, and bio-grouting for stabilisation, liquefaction mitigation, erosion /dust control; durability and pore-scale imaging (e.g. X-ray CT). - Bio-stabilised earthen construction materials: raw-earth and stabilised-earth materials, biopolymer- and bio-cement-stabilised earth, and natural fibres, with their hygrothermal, durability, and life-cycle performance. - Sustainability assessment: life cycle assessment (LCA), life cycle costs analysis (LCCA) and social LCA (S-LCA) of bio-treated soils and “low-carbon” geomaterials. We especially encourage novel experimental setups, multi-scale imaging, field deployments, numerical modelling, and cross-disciplinary work linking soil mechanics, biology, robotics, materials, and sustainability assessment.
title: Bio-Mediated, Bio-Inspired, and Bio-Based Solutions for Sustainable Geotechnics and Construction

description: The present context of accelerated changes in both climate and land use imposes an unprecedent pressure on a number of vulnerable ecosystems including wetlands, forests and rangelands, in which vegetation closely interacts and coevolves with soils and landforms. Complex interactions between climate, soils and biotic factors are involved in the development of landform-soil-vegetation feedbacks and play an important role in making ecosystems resilient to disturbances. In addition, large shifts in the distribution of vegetation and soils are associated with losses of ecosystem services (including carbon capture), frequently involving thresholds of ecosystem stability and nonlinear responses to both human and climatic pressures. This session will focus on ecogeomorphological and ecohydrological aspects of landscapes (including their connectivity), conservation of soil resources, and the restoration of ecosystem services and functions. We welcome theoretical, modelling, and empirical studies addressing the distribution of vegetation and coevolving soils and landforms, and particularly, contributions with a wide appreciation of the soil erosion-vegetation relationships that rule the formation of landscape-level spatial organization. We also welcome studies describing the implications of these spatial patterns of soils and vegetation for the resilience and stability of ecosystems under the pressure of climate change and/or human disturbances.
title: Coevolution and interactions of soils, landforms and vegetation: patterns, feedbacks and landscape stability thresholds

description: Soils play a crucial role in the functioning of terrestrial ecosystems, providing key ecosystem services such as carbon storage, water retention, nutrient cycling, biodiversity preservation, and protection against soil degradation processes (e.g., erosion, compaction, or fertility loss). There is broad consensus that the implementation of management practices focused on soil conservation and restoration can help to improve soil functioning and resilience. The basis for building these resilience practices, lies halting the loss of soil carbon. For instance, agricultural practices such as no-till farming, cover crops, crop rotation and the use of compost. However, the dynamics of carbon change are a slow process in the medium and long term, which creates uncertainty in the short term. Furthermore, change sometimes begins with a negative response from the soil or with recommendations that have been proven in site-specific pedoclimatic contexts but cannot be scaled up to other contexts. This raises the following question: how can science help to build confidence and reduce uncertainty whilst we await the anticipated changes in the medium and long term? We strongly encourage submissions that include the evaluation of proven practices in operational contexts, ideas for communicating and sharing scientific knowledge, as well as access to useful data, user-friendly knowledge, tools and models to support decision-making, the valuation of ecosystem services, or resilient business models. Acknowledgments: Project PID2023-146177OB-C22, funded by MICIU/AEI/10.13039/501100011033 and by the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF), European Union.
title: Soil resilience: from knowledge to real case implementation

description: Soils are dynamic interfaces connecting the atmosphere, vegetation, surface water, and groundwater, and their physical and chemical properties strongly regulate water movement, contaminant transport, environmental processes, and ecosystem functioning. This session brings together experimental, modelling, remote sensing, and field-based approaches to investigate how soil-environment interactions across spatial and temporal scales affect ecosystems. We welcome contributions addressing, but not limited to, soil hydraulic characterisation, soil structure and heterogeneity, soil amendment and treatment, and dynamic interactions between soil, water, and ecosystems. Studies integrating hydrological and environmental modelling, remote sensing, and GIS are particularly encouraged. The session aims to foster interdisciplinary understanding of how changes in soil properties and functioning influence water movement, environmental transport, and ecosystem processes.
title: Soil Hydraulic Functioning and Environmental Interactions Across Scales

description: Biocrusts represent highly diverse communities formed by intimate associations between photoautotrophic organisms (i.e., cyanobacteria, algae, lichens, and bryophytes) and heterotrophic microorganisms inhabiting the uppermost millimeters of soil, where they form a thin, cohesive living layer. Although often overlooked, biocrusts cover nearly 12% of soils worldwide and play a pivotal role in regulating ecological processes that underpin ecosystem functioning and the provision of ecosystem services. Increasingly recognized as ecosystem engineers, biocrusts regulate the physical, chemical, and biological properties and processes of soils. Yet, their contribution to key ecosystem and Earth-system processes remains poorly quantified, and we still lack an integrated understanding of how processes operating at microbial and organismal scales scale up to influence ecosystem functioning and global change. In this session, we invite contributions addressing the biodiversity, functioning, and ecological roles of biocrusts across spatial, temporal, and organizational scales, from microbial processes and organismal interactions to ecosystem and global processes. We welcome studies investigating biocrust effects on biogeochemical, carbon, nutrient, and water cycles; energy and surface–atmosphere exchanges; soil development, mineral weathering, erosion and dust emissions; geomorphological processes; biodiversity and species interactions; vegetation dynamics; and ecosystem stability, degradation, and restoration. We particularly encourage contributions exploring the responses, resilience, thresholds, and feedbacks of biocrusts under climate and other global changes, as well as their consequences for ecosystem functioning and large-scale environmental dynamics. Studies combining field and laboratory observations with experimental approaches, remote sensing, modelling, and other approaches to upscale biocrust processes across spatial and temporal scales are also encouraged.
title: Biocrust impacts on Earth system processes: Bridging microbial processes, ecosystem functioning and global change

description: This session will explore the practical implementation of the United Nations Framework Classification for Resources (UNFC) focusing on applications to mineral deposits and related topics, such as those extracted from brines in geothermal fields. The session sets particular emphasis on its application in Europe in the context of the EU Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA). It calls for contributions reflecting on Strategic Projects, National Exploration Programmes, monitoring of critical raw materials projects and extractive waste as the CRMA establishes UNFC as key classification framework for various aspects of critical raw materials management. Progress, practical experiences and emerging challenges related to the implementation of UNFC across European countries will be discussed. Particular attention shall be given to how UNFC can support consistent and comparable information on primary and secondary raw materials, facilitate monitoring and reporting, and contribute to informed decision-making on critical raw materials. Previous European implementation work has already addressed applications ranging from extraction and processing to recycling and substitution projects. The session will also provide a forum for discussing practical issues encountered during implementation, including the interpretation and application of UNFC categories, alignment with existing national classification and reporting systems, data availability and quality, capacity building, and the development of appropriate guidance. Through examples, lessons learned and discussion among policymakers, geological surveys, resource experts, industry and international organisations, the session aims to identify best practices and highlights areas where further harmonisation, methodological development and international cooperation are required. We would very much welcome the sharing of experiences and ideas on how the framework can support a common approach to the classification and management of resources across different legal systems.
title: Implementation of the United Nations Framework Classification for Resources (UNFC): European and Global Perspectives

description: Earth system models are essential for understanding and projecting future climate change. However, these models operate at spatial resolutions of tens to hundreds of km, whereas many of the observations and the processes they aim to represent, occur at much finer spatial scales. Bridging this gap is a fundamental challenge for Earth system science. For biosphere processes large-scale models simulate variables such as leaf area index, vegetation productivity, and carbon uptake on grid cells covering thousands of km². In contrast, observations of phenological events at individual plants, eddy-covariance flux measurements towers, or high-resolution remote sensing describe behaviour at much finer scales. The understanding of these processes, derived from experiments and theory, operates at individual or plot scales. Aggregation of nonlinear responses make the response to mean conditions differ from the mean of individual responses, while spatial averaging across heterogeneous processes smooths their contrasting sensitivities. Addressing these scale mismatches requires advances across multiple fronts: sub-grid parameterizations in mechanistic models, observational networks designed to capture spatial heterogeneity, and methods to link fine-scale processes to emergent large-scale behaviour. Machine learning is being combined with mechanistic Earth system models, offering possibilities and risks. Models trained on plot-level data may predict grid-cell averages without accounting for sub-grid variability, sampling biases, or nonlinear aggregation. Approaches that represent multiple scales, incorporate spatial structure, or learn mappings between individual-level processes and emergent large-scale variables show promise for improving how biosphere processes are represented. The session aims to foster knowledge exchange between mechanistic modelers, machine learning practitioners, observational scientists, and experimentalist to develop more reliable, scale-consistent approaches for representing and evaluating biosphere processes in Earth system models. Hence, the session invites contributions on topics including, but not limited to, the following: • Trait-based upscaling beyond PFTs • Sub-grid scale modelling, nonlinear spatial aggregation and emergent behaviour • Upscaling in situ observations to grid scale • Phenology across spatial scales • Hybrid ML-physics modelling • ML solutions to sampling bias • Learning emergent grid-scale variables
title: From leaves to climate grid cells: bridging scales for biosphere processes in Earth system models and machine learning

description: The use of imaging spectroscopy for monitoring Earth surface processes has progressed rapidly in recent years, driven by the growing availability of spaceborne data from missions such as DESIS, PRISMA, EnMAP and EMIT. These missions have enabled advances in retrieval methods, applications and multi-temporal observations. Regional-to-continental products and emerging global thematic products demonstrate the transition from experimental acquisitions towards systematic Earth observation. This provides critical building blocks for the next generation of missions, including the Copernicus Hyperspectral Imaging Mission for the Environment (CHIME), which will establish an operational European capability with systematic global coverage of land and coastal areas every 11 days. Preparing for CHIME requires robust retrieval algorithms, scalable processing, well-characterised uncertainties, calibration and validation strategies, reference datasets, and methods exploiting spatial and temporal observations in combination with other Copernicus and international missions. This session focuses on preparing for future global and operational imaging spectroscopy missions through novel methods, products and applications transferable and scalable from current missions to future observing systems. We welcome regional-to-global contributions addressing agriculture, vegetation and forestry, biodiversity and ecosystems, soils, minerals and raw materials, coastal and inland waters, environmental degradation and hazards, and the cryosphere. Contributions using current spaceborne imaging spectroscopy as precursors for CHIME and other future missions like NASA EAGLE VSWIR are encouraged, including multi-mission harmonisation, time-series analysis, large-scale processing, retrieval robustness and transferability, uncertainty, and synergies with Sentinel and other Earth observation data. Large-scale field campaigns, calibration and validation activities, spectral reference databases and regional in-situ initiatives supporting operational use of imaging spectroscopy data are equally relevant. The session also welcomes contributions on ongoing international coordination to strengthen interoperability and synergies among current and future missions. By bringing together mission teams, algorithm developers, application scientists and users, it aims to advance sustained, interoperable and operational global imaging spectroscopy in support of Earth System Science and applications.
title: Progressing towards global-scale high-resolution imaging spectroscopy from space: preparing for CHIME and future global missions

description: The transition to renewable energy depends on reliable resource assessment and sustainable planning across diverse geographical and environmental settings. Geospatial data, advanced modelling and artificial intelligence offer valuable tools to integrate different data sources, assess resource potential, address uncertainty and support informed decision-making. Combining geological, geophysical, meteorological, hydrogeological and environmental data with satellite imagery, terrain models and operational records can improve both resource assessment and spatial planning. This session welcomes contributions on geospatial data, GIS, remote sensing and modelling for geothermal, solar, wind and hydropower. Topics include resource mapping, multi-source data integration, spatial suitability analysis, environmental and numerical modelling, data interoperability, uncertainty assessment and the use of AI and machine learning for spatial prediction and automated interpretation. We also welcome contributions on the use of geospatial information in municipal and regional planning, site selection, land-use assessment and energy infrastructure development. Particular interest lies in approaches that connect spatial data and physical models with practical planning and decision-making, including monitoring, forecasting and operational optimization. Open datasets, reproducible workflows and open-source tools are encouraged, as are studies assessing model performance and transferability across regions and renewable energy technologies. The session aims to bring together geoscientists, geospatial specialists, planners, engineers and energy researchers to advance the use of geospatial data and digital technologies for renewable energy assessment, planning and sustainable development.
title: Geospatial Data and Digital Technologies for Renewable Energy

description: As climate change accelerates, the transition to renewable energy systems, such as geothermal energy, underground hydrogen storage, and carbon capture and storage (CCS), are essential. These technologies rely on the exploitation of subsurface porous or fractured reservoirs whose hydraulic and mechanical behavior is fundamentally governed by geological heterogeneities comprising the natural variability in lithology, stratigraphic architecture, and structural fabric. This variability spans different spatial scales, from pore-scale contrasts in grain size and selective cementation, up to basin-scale facies distributions and fault networks, and exerts a strong control on fluid flow, mechanical response, and long-term storage or production performance. However, capturing this heterogeneity and connecting observations across spatial scales remains a major challenge, often limited by data resolution, sampling bias, and the difficulty of upscaling local measurements to reservoir- or basin-scale models. This session brings together the different disciplines working on geological heterogeneity, with a focus on studies supporting the energy transition and sustainable subsurface use. Fundamental and methodological contributions, as well as applied case studies are welcome! Topics of interest include, but are not limited to: • Outcrop, core, and well-based characterization of geological heterogeneity in reservoir rocks • Fault and fracture network architecture, damage zones, and structural controls on flow • Depositional and stratigraphic controls on facies heterogeneity • Diagenetic processes involving reservoirs • Pore- to core-scale heterogeneity and its upscaling • 3D geological, structural, stratigraphic and diagenetic modelling • Single- and multiphase fluid-flow and reservoir modelling • Representative elementary volumes (REVs) and multi-scale upscaling • Applications to geothermal energy, CCS, and hydrogen storage • Uncertainty quantification linking characterization to model predictions
title: Dealing with geological heterogeneity: Characterizing, modelling, and upscaling rock properties for the energy transition

description: As climate change and international supply-chain disruptions have exposed the chronic vulnerabilities of our global systems, there is an urgent need to develop new strategies that can strengthen resilience and reduce dependence on fragile supply chains. This session provides a platform for new ideas, multidisciplinary approaches, and alternative strategies for building a more resilient future by using the subsurface to store energy carriers and other critical products. The subsurface offers significant potential for providing large-scale, long-duration storage that can help buffer fluctuations in supply and demand and strengthen the security of critical resources. We invite submissions encompassing a wide range of interdisciplinary approaches, including feasibility studies, techno-economic analyses, energy-system modelling, life-cycle assessments, real-world case studies, and field projects. All innovative ideas are welcome, and here we provide only suggestions of potential topics: • As climate change accelerates, new approaches and methods to reduce greenhouse gas emissions that make use of the subsurface are urgently needed. We invite contributions exploring sustainable energy storage solutions, including hydrogen storage—either as pure hydrogen or as chemical hydrogen carriers (e.g., methanol and liquid organic hydrogen carriers)—as well as heat storage, compressed-air energy storage, and other innovative approaches. • Current and future supply-chain disruptions may also require the stockpiling of critical products, for which the subsurface could provide a safe and efficient storage solution. We invite contributions addressing the storage of critical products, such as ammonia for fertiliser production or helium for future industries, with a focus on storage operations, life-cycle assessment, and other approaches to evaluating their technical, economic, and environmental feasibility. • Strategic energy reserves (SERs), such as the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve, have played a vital role in enhancing the resilience of our societies. But how will these carbon-based, large-scale and ultra-long-term energy storage systems evolve in the future? As electricity use continues to increase and efforts to decarbonise the energy system accelerate, what might future strategic energy reserves look like? What energy carriers should they store, and how will their design and operation need to change to meet the demands of a low-carbon energy system?
title: Innovative Subsurface Solutions for a Resilient Future

description: The rapid expansion of offshore wind energy (OWE) is transforming coastal and marine ecosystems. Offshore wind farms modify atmospheric boundary layer dynamics, generate large wind wakes, alter air-sea exchanges, and influence ocean circulation and mixing processes. These physical disruptions affect marine ecosystems through cascading impacts on stratification, nutrient availability, primary productivity, biodiversity, and biogeochemical cycling. In seasonally ice-covered regions, offshore wind infrastructure may also interact with sea ice processes and winter navigation. As developments scale up and move into deeper and higher-latitude waters, managing their footprint requires integrated approaches spanning atmospheric sciences, oceanography, sea ice physics, ecology, biogeochemistry and engineering. Sustainable OWE deployment relies on effective use of marine space that balances ecological constraints with shifting socioeconomic and climate realities. Digital Twin Ocean (DTO) solutions serve as a critical bridge in this landscape. By integrating multi-source data, high-fidelity ocean-atmosphere models, and machine learning, DTOs enable real-time tracking, prediction of cumulative impacts, understanding feedback mechanisms across Earth system components, and virtual stress-testing of turbine and farm placement to optimize OWE efficiency while minimizing ecological degradation. Ideally, DTOs inform Marine Spatial Planning (MSP) and enable sustainable use of marine space. This session invites studies investigating OWE impacts on atmospheric, oceanic, and sea ice processes, marine ecosystems, and their interactions using simulations, data-driven methods, in-situ observations, and remote sensing. Contributions on innovative cumulative impact assessment, DTO integration, multi-disciplinary modelling and decision-support tools are particularly welcome.
title: Assessing the environmental impacts of offshore wind farms through simulations, observations, and remote-sensing

description: Climate change is reshaping the fate, mobility, persistence, and toxicity of contaminants across environmental systems. Shifts in temperature, precipitation, flooding, drought, wildfires, sea-level rise, and permafrost thaw are altering transport pathways, remobilising sequestered pollutants, and creating new exposure routes. These processes affect both legacy contaminants and contaminants of emerging concern (CECs), including PFAS, microplastics, pharmaceuticals, pesticides, and antibiotic resistance genes, complicating monitoring and risk assessment. Climate change is also transforming indoor environments, where people spend most of their time. Heatwaves and wildfire smoke are raising energy demand and accelerating building retrofits. Changes to building envelopes, insulation, airtightness, and cooling and ventilation systems affect airflow, moisture transport, pollutant infiltration, and thermal comfort. Understanding how outdoor climate, building energy balance, ventilation, indoor air quality, and occupant exposure interact is essential for designing healthy, climate-resilient buildings. Topics include: 1. Sensing, monitoring, and early-warning tools for climate-driven contaminants outdoors and indoors. 2. Modelling contaminant fate, transport, and exposure across air, water, soil, and indoor environments under future climates. 3. Building energy balance, urban heat, and climate-responsive performance. 4. Indoor air quality, including infiltration, ventilation effectiveness, moisture dynamics, and outdoor–indoor source interactions. 5. Thermal comfort under climate change and the role of cooling, design, and ventilation in occupant health. 6. Retrofitting and decarbonization impacts on ventilation, indoor pollutants, and thermal resilience. 7. Remobilization of legacy contaminants by floods, wildfires, drought, sea-level rise, and permafrost thaw. 8. CECs under climate-driven environmental change. 9. Cross-compartment transfer linking air, water, soil, and indoor environments. 10. Nature-based and engineered remediation, exposure mitigation, and climate-resilient policy and governance. We invite environmental, atmospheric, soil, and building scientists, hydrologists, exposure and public health researchers, toxicologists, and policy experts to advance integrated solutions for contaminant exposure in a changing climate.
title: Emerging and Climate Change‑Derived Contaminants Across Air, Water, and Soil: Advances in Monitoring, Modelling, and Management

description: Deep geological repositories (DGR) for radioactive waste place unique demands on geological site characterization. In particular, robust, yet efficient characterization strategies are needed to reduce geological uncertainties and assess the suitability of potential host rocks and their surrounding geological environment that act as natural barriers with respect to the long-term containment of radionuclides. This includes, among other aspects, the evaluation of geological structure, hydrogeological and hydrogeochemical conditions, potential transport pathways for radionuclides, geomechanical properties, and the continuity of low-permeable storage formations. While underground research laboratories (URL) have significantly advanced our knowledge about storage formations for nuclear waste disposal and the coupled processes governing their long-term evolution, an important challenge remains the transfer into a practical site characterization programme. This session invites contributions on integrated approaches to DGR site characterization, from laboratory to regional scales. We welcome studies addressing the design and optimization of characterization programmes, including deep drilling, geological and structural investigations, hydrogeological and hydrogeochemical testing, borehole logging, geophysical imaging, laboratory analyses, monitoring concepts, and numerical modelling. Particular emphasis is placed on multidisciplinary workflows that combine complementary datasets to efficiently evaluate key repository relevant characteristics, reduce uncertainties, and support evidence-based site assessment. Contributions from underground research laboratories, national site investigation programmes, and international collaborative projects are particularly encouraged, especially those demonstrating how fundamental research, methodological developments, and integrated characterization strategies can be translated into practical site characterization for deep geological repositories.
title: Deep geological repositories for nuclear waste – assessment and advances in site characterization

description: Geoscientific knowledge is crucial to assess safety requirements for radioactive waste disposal strategies. Safety requirements include i) isolation of the nuclear waste from humans and the biosphere, ii) containment of radionuclides by retention and retardation, iii) limitation of water inflow to the geo-engineered facility and iv) long-term geological stability of the site. The session covers all waste disposal designs, from surface and near-surface facilities to deep geological repositories, as well as borehole disposal. Key topics included in this session are: • Role of geosciences in site characterisation and selection process • Disposal design optimisation, including sustainable resource usage • Geoscientific evidence supporting performance and safety assessment • Long-term evolution studies of interactions among hydro-, geo- and biosphere, and their impact on the disposal system • Impact of climate change on waste disposal facilities • Innovative technologies for site characterisation and monitoring, including digital tools and artificial intelligence (AI) • Radionuclide migration assessment • Features and evolution of natural and engineered barrier systems, including induced effects • Bio-geo-chemical processes, both natural and repository-induced Contributions on the above topics can include all aspects covering lab-scale experiments, large-scale investigations in underground research facilities, information from site characterisation campaigns, studies of natural analogues, data management, review studies, and development and application of digital tools.
title: Radioactive waste repositories - Geosciences for long-term safety and disposal design optimisation

description: Large geological storage of energy (e.g., hydrogen, heat), carbon dioxide, and wastes in porous media and engineered caverns is crucial for enabling the shift toward a sustainable, resilient, and low-carbon future. Achieving safe, efficient, and cost-effective operations at scale depends on the storage capacity and injectivity of the reservoir and the sealing performance and integrity of the confining units, faults, and wells, which are governed by a range of thermal, hydraulic, mechanical, chemical, and microbial processes. Thus, secure subsurface storage, together with public acceptance in essential technologies, demands geological expertise, continuous and effective monitoring, and careful assessment of potential risks. This session offers a platform for interdisciplinary scientific exchange between different branches of storage expertise and aims to address challenges concerning the storage of fluids in geological reservoirs from core- to field-scale. We welcome analytical studies, computational simulations, laboratory experiments, data-driven analyses, developing monitoring techniques, and field-scale investigations to advance fundamental understanding and assessments of coupled physical and chemical processes involved in subsurface storage. We also encourage contributions that investigate specific challenges associated with the scaleup of geological storage technologies. Case studies and operational projects integrating different elements of the storage chain, as well as field projects focusing on geological energy/carbon storage, are particularly welcome. By comparing results across storage applications, geological settings, scales, and deployment levels, the session aims to identify transferable methodologies, common performance drivers, and scalable solutions for the safe and effective use of the subsurface as a multifunctional storage resource.
title: Secure subsurface storage for future energy systems

description: A variety of geophysical and geological observational techniques are now mature enough to provide valuable insights into the influence that mantle convection has on Earth surface and its core. Current challenges include the need to reconcile different spatial resolutions between models and observations, uneven data coverage and the determination of appropriate sampling and simulation scales. This session will provide a holistic view of the influence of mantle convection on core dynamics and surface expressions from geodetic to geological time scales using multi-disciplinary methods, including (but not limited to): geodetic, geophysical, geological, long-term evolution of the geomagnetic field, Earth's core dynamics magnetism and the seismic imaging of mantle convective processes, as well as numerical modeling. Our session will provide rich opportunities for presenters and attendees from a range of disciplines, demographics, and stages of their scientific career to engage in this exciting and multidisciplinary problem in Earth science.
title: Influence of mantle convection from surface to core

description: About 90% of Earth’s volcanism is associated with convergent or divergent plate boundaries and can thus be explained by plate tectonics. However, understanding the origin of anomalous volcanism within continental and oceanic plate interiors (i.e. intraplate volcanism), as well as unusual on-boundary volcanism such as Iceland, is less straightforward. Such volcanism is commonly attributed to mantle plumes but in recent years alternative models have been proposed such as rifted oceanic magmatic plateaus, sublithospheric drainage, and intraplate extension. At the same time, continental crust has been detected in the roots of many oceanic LIPs. Modern improvements in instrumentation, techniques and data availability have also greatly expanded our understanding of Earth dynamics and structure. Understanding what drives anomalous magmatism is critical to understanding the evolution of Earth’s mantle, surface dynamics, volcanism, and chemistry through time including the climate, initiation of plate tectonics, and life. It is also key to understanding lithospheric deformation in the presence of magmatism, past and present volcanic catastrophes, and the environmental impacts of magmatism through time such as the coupling between LIP eruptions and mass extinctions. This knowledge is also crucial to the understanding of magmatism on other planetary bodies in the solar system and beyond. This session brings together cross-disciplinary work on intraplate and unusual on-boundary magmatism to encourage communication between researchers with diverse ideas, observations, approaches, and backgrounds. We welcome contributions applying any methods including but not limited to, geochemistry, geophysics, volcanology, numerical and analogue modelling, field observations and remote sensing. Studies focusing on LIP magmatism, wide magmatic rift systems, or magmatism associated with continental material offshore or in oceanic LIPs are particularly encouraged. Innovative studies across all spatio-temporal scales and thought-provoking ideas that challenge conventions are particularly welcomed.
title: Structure, origin, and evolution of anomalous volcanic provinces: new perspectives

description: This session will provide overview of results from interpretation and modelling of the geodynamic processes in the lithosphere-asthenosphere system and the interaction between crust and lithospheric mantle, including the formation of discontinuities in the crust and mantle. We aim at establishing links between seismological observations and process-oriented modelling studies to better understand the relation between present-day fabrics of the lithosphere and contemporary deformation and ongoing dynamics within the asthenospheric mantle. Methodologically, the contributions will include studies based on application of geochemical, petrological, tectonic and geophysical (seismic, thermal, gravity, electro-magnetic) methods with emphasis on integrated interpretations. Contributions on development of methodology are welcome. We invite, in particular multidisciplinary, contributions which focus on the structure, deformation and evolution of the continental crust and upper mantle and on the nature of mantle discontinuities. The latter include, but are not limited to, the mid-lithosphere discontinuity (MLD), the lithosphere-asthenosphere boundary (LAB), and the mantle transition zone, as imaged by various seismological techniques and interpreted with interdisciplinary approaches. Papers with focus on the structure of the crust and the nature of the Moho are also welcome.
title: Structure, deformation and dynamics of continental crust, lithosphere and upper mantle

description: Plate reconstructions provide a fundamental framework for understanding the evolution of Earth's surface and its connection to mantle dynamics through geological time. At the same time, geological, geochemical, and paleomagnetic records, geophysical observations, including seismic tomography, together with geodynamic constraints, provide opportunities to test and refine plate histories. Bridging these perspectives therefore provides a unique opportunity to jointly decipher the evolution of Earth's surface and deep interior. This session aims to bring together researchers working across plate reconstructions, tectonics, and mantle dynamics, highlighting studies that link plate kinematic histories to mantle convection and deep structure. We invite contributions on: global and regional plate reconstructions; geological, geophysical, geochemical, paleomagnetic, and geodynamic constraints on refining plate histories; incorporation of plate reconstructions into mantle convection models (both forward and inverse); data assimilation and adjoint-based approaches for constraining plate and mantle evolution; numerical models that self-consistently generate plate-like behavior; methods for identifying, tracking, and characterizing plates and plate boundaries; and approaches for evaluating reconstructions and geodynamic models against observations of the present-day and past Earth. Interdisciplinary contributions bridging kinematics, observational geology/geophysics, and computational geodynamics are especially encouraged.
title: Plate reconstructions and mantle dynamics: Reconstructing, modeling and deciphering plate tectonics

description: We invite contributions on all aspects of Meteorology and Climate for Renewable Energy (RE): • Energy: wind, solar, hydro, tidal, wave, geothermal etc • Spatial: microscale, mesoscale, synoptic and global • Temporal: seconds, minutes, diurnal, seasonal, interannual, decadal and climatological • Approach: measurement, modeling The success of wind power has pushed turbines and research need into increasingly complex environments — mountainous terrain, forested areas, high in boundary layer and offshore. For solar power, new installation sites such as floating PV both rivers, water reservoirs for artificial snow, and “alpine PV farms” are gaining more attention. We need accurate measurements and short-term forecasts of cloud fields and aerosol effects. For weather-dependent renewables, the challenge of integrating shares into the power grid requires advances in understanding forecast uncertainty and spatio-temporal variability. Furthermore, meteorological conditions define how much power can be sent through the power grid and could help prevent curtailment or negative energy pricing. Specifically, we invite contributions including but not limited to: • Measurement techniques and analysis for e.g., wind, solar, hydro, and marine resources. • Wind conditions (resource, extremes, turbulence) on all scales in complex environments (mountains, forests, coastal, offshore, urban). • Wake effect models and measurements • Forecast performance and uncertainty of RE at different time horizons • Forecasts and detection of extreme and adverse weather events (wind ramps, droughts, heatwaves, storms, compound and consecutive) • Detection and forecasting of dynamic line rating suitable conditions • RE resource and atlas development (wind, solar, hydro, wave, thermal) • Hydro-meteorological analyses of inflow variability, snowpack, precipitation extremes, and their implications for hydropower • Tidal and wave resource assessment and predictability • Impacts of renewable power plants or their large-scale integration on local, regional, and global scales • Tools for strategic planning of RE in urban areas and smart energy systems. • Climate Change Impact studies for renewables and weather-driven energy demand • Interannual to decadal variability of renewable resources • Typical Meteorological Years and probability of exceedance metrics • AI and Machine Learning for weather and climate forecasting and applications to RE
title: Energy Meteorology

description: This session addresses spatial and temporal modelling of renewable and climate neutral energy systems, both in a prospective as well as in a retrospective manner. Therefore, contributions which model the characteristics of future systems are equally welcome as contributions assessing the characteristics of their past performance. Session contributions may range from assessments of climate data based simulations of renewable generation, over assessments of land use implications of renewables, to economic assessments linked to spatial and temporal variability of renewables and full energy system model studies applied to understand climate neutral energy systems. Studies may for instance: Show the spatial and temporal variability of renewable energy sources, including resource droughts and complementarity between technologies and locations. Assess the resilience of energy systems to weather and climate extreme events, with a focus on infrastructure and resource adequacy, and analyze economic incentives to ensure reliable energy systems under current regulatory, market and tariff conditions. Derive scenarios for the spatial allocation of renewable energies based on climatic, technical, economic, or social criteria. Assess past spatial deployment patterns of renewables. Assess past impacts on land cover and land-use, including impacts on biodiversity and other environmental indicators Explore and quantify impacts of wind and solar power deployment on the social and natural environment in a spatially explicit way, including economic valuations of such impacts Derive integrated scenarios of climate neutral energy systems (Including systems from the local scale, e.g. in form of local Energy Communities, to the national or continental scale). Explore the flow of energy and carbon between energy-, and land- systems in climate neutrality scenarios The objective of the session is to provide an insight into recent advances in the field of renewable energy system modeling. The session welcomes research dedicated to climatic and technical issues, assessments of environmental impacts, economic analysis of markets, policies and regulations, and forecasting applications , concerning renewable energy systems.
title: Spatial and temporal modelling of renewable and climate neutral energy systems

description: The global transition towards “Net zero” requires rapid decarbonisation across multiple sectors, with the electricity system playing a key role. On the supply side, renewable energy resources exhibit variability across multiple timescales, from minutes to seasons to interannual. Climate change is expected to alter not only the mean patterns of renewable resources but also their variability and the possibility of disruptive, compound, and cascading extreme events. On the demand side, extreme weather events and climate change will affect both overall consumption and peak load. Unmanaged demand growth can raise mitigation costs, intensify pressure on renewable resources, create supply reliability and affordability challenges. Considerable uncertainty remains in projecting long-term spatio-temporal changes in renewable sources, demand and low probability extremes that can disrupt the energy system. There is an urgent need for deeper dialogue between climate science, climate risk, and energy systems research communities. This session invites contributions on pathways to accelerate energy transitions under climate change; approaches to just and equitable transitions; insights from climate modelling for demand or supply challenges; approaches for balancing supply with demand and flexibility across timescales; innovative concepts to address uncertainty in energy-climate interactions; implications of climate risks for the energy transition. We encourage model-based, empirical, and conceptual studies, including: *Impacts of climate change and variability, including extremes, on energy systems, and associated uncertainties *Effects of renewable resource variability on energy systems, and technical approaches, including storage and interconnection, to balance supply and demand *Climate-related drivers of energy demand, and the role of demand reduction and management in low-carbon transitions *Influences of extreme events and spatio-temporal complementarities on both demand and supply within energy systems *Integrated assessments combining supply and demand side approaches to low-carbon transitions *Spatio-temporal data needs from climate modelling to advance understanding of renewable supply and demand under climate change *Implications of climate change and extreme events for energy system reliability and security of supply, including outage risk and electricity price impacts *Risk-modelling frameworks for quantifying climate-related risks to the energy system
title: Bridging the gap: climate science, risk models and renewable energy research

description: Geothermal energy emerges as a critical component of the urban energy transition, offering constant base-load energy supply, minimal land requirement, and integration into multicomponent energy networks. This session explores the scientific, engineering, and strategic foundations necessary to unlock the potential of geothermal energy in urban settings. We invite contributions across the spectrum of geothermal technologies: hydrothermal, petrothermal, closed-loop, enhanced geothermal systems (EGS), and aquifer or borehole thermal energy storage (ATES/BTES). Reliable forecasting and sustainable geothermal utilization require solid understanding of the subsurface structure and physical properties. Integrated exploration strategies–seismic, geological, and geophysical investigations–combined with consistent monitoring during operation are vital for optimal reservoir management and for minimizing environmental impacts. The session further addresses the complex interaction between reservoir heterogeneity, imposed perturbations by operation, and impact on governing physical processes. These coupled mechanisms may cause stress redistribution or rock deformation and–in faulted/fractured reservoirs or EGS projects–enhance the seismic risk. Understanding the coupled thermal-hydraulic-mechanical-chemical (THMC) response of geothermal systems is thus crucial for predictive analyses, sustainable operation, and risk mitigation. Contributions on predicting and mitigating induced seismicity, including risk management approaches such as traffic light systems, are especially encouraged. We welcome diverse methodological approaches: analytical studies, laboratory and field experiments, multiphysics numerical modeling, and data-driven or machine learning approaches resolving the relevant physical mechanisms across spatial and temporal scales. Case studies and operating geothermal projects highlighting engineering challenges (e.g. wellbore stability, scaling), successful methodologies and engineering solutions, or novel geothermal concepts are especially valuable. Beyond engineering innovation, the session addresses the broader context of geothermal deployment in urban environments. We invite contributions on management strategies of the geothermal resource and integration into urban energy planning. By showcasing innovative research and practical applications, this session highlights the multifaceted potential of geothermal energy in advancing the urban energy transition.
title: Geothermal Systems in the Urban Energy Transition: Scientific, Engineering, and Integration Perspectives

description: Fractures exert first-order control on the hydraulic, mechanical, thermal, and chemical behaviour of many subsurface geoenergy systems. Discrete fracture network DFN models provide a powerful framework for representing fracture geometry, connectivity, transmissivity, and uncertainty across scales, from outcrops and boreholes to reservoir-scale simulations. However, robust DFN characterization and engineering remain challenging because fracture systems are heterogeneous, scale-dependent, and often only partially observable. This session invites contributions on advances in the characterization, modelling, validation, and engineering of fractured reservoirs for geoenergy applications. Relevant applications include geothermal energy, enhanced geothermal systems EGS, underground thermal energy storage, geological storage of CO2 and hydrogen, nuclear waste isolation, and other subsurface energy technologies where fractures influence performance and risk. We welcome studies integrating field observations, borehole and core data, structural geology, geophysics, hydraulic testing, tracer tests, microseismicity, remote sensing, laboratory experiments, and numerical modelling. Particular interest lies in methods that quantify fracture network geometry, topology, flow properties, and uncertainty; couple DFN models with thermal-hydraulic-mechanical-chemical THMC-processes; and support decision-making for reservoir stimulation, monitoring, and safe long-term operation. By bringing together researchers and practitioners from structural geology, hydrogeology, geomechanics, geophysics, reservoir engineering, and computational modelling, this session aims to foster interdisciplinary discussion on how DFN approaches can improve the design, operation, and risk assessment of future geoenergy systems. Particular interest lies in methods that quantify fracture network geometry, topology, flow properties, and uncertainty; coupled DFN models with thermal-hydraulic-mechanical-chemical THMC-processes; and support decision-making for reservoir stimulation, monitoring, and safe long-term operation.
title: Discrete fracture network characterization and engineering for geoenergy applications

description: Thermal Energy Storage (TES) is a key component for efficient energy supply and for achieving a low-carbon energy balance. TES allows flexible storage volumes and periods, and it represents a cross-sector technology that couples heat, cooling energy, and electricity. This session is dedicated to Underground Thermal Energy Storage (UTES) technologies, their performance and engineering, as well as new insights into related heat transport processes in the subsurface. In particular, the focus is on Aquifer Thermal Energy Storage (ATES), Borehole Thermal Energy Storage (BTES), Mine Thermal Energy Storage (MTES) and related ground-based variants such as pit storage, cavern storage and artificial water-gravel storage basins. The aim of this session is to overcome obstacles concerning the technical design and sustainable operation of TES by improving our understanding of UTES-related thermal, hydraulic and other environmental effects. In a broader context, we invite contributions that show how to enhance the societal perceptions and engagement in UTES deployment and how to integrate UTES technologies in wider energy systems. Both in research and in practice, accurate characterization of subsurface flow and heat transport based on observations of induced or natural variations of the thermal regime is essential. Thus, we also welcome contributions that reveal new insight and advances in experimental design, report novel field observations, as well as demonstrate new sequential or coupled modelling concepts. Seasonal and long-term changes in thermal and mechanical conditions in aquifers and heat transfer across aquifer boundaries are focus points. This includes the role of groundwater and geothermal energy in the context of UTES for predicting the long-term performance of storage and production of thermal energy (heating and cooling), as well as integration into urban planning and policy making. We also invite hydrogeological studies that examine heat as a natural or anthropogenic tracer with the aim of enhancing thermal response testing or improving our understanding of relevant transport processes in the underground.
title: Underground Thermal Energy Storage: application, impact and processes

description: Geological CO2 utilization and storage in geothermal systems offer a promising pathway for simultaneously achieving carbon management and low-carbon energy production. By utilizing CO2 as a working fluid or promoting its interaction with geological formations, geothermal systems have the potential to integrate CO2 storage, mineralization, and renewable energy recovery. However, significant scientific and engineering challenges remain in understanding and controlling the complex interactions among CO2, rock, formation water, and geothermal fluids across different spatial and temporal scales. This session brings together research on the geological CO2 utilization and storage in geothermal systems, covering fundamental mechanisms, laboratory experiments, molecular- and pore-scale modelling, reservoir-scale simulations, and field-scale implementation. Contributions will address topics including CO2-rock-fluid interactions, CO2 dissolution and mineralization, geochemical and geomechanical processes, CO2 circulation and heat extraction, reservoir characterization and modelling, and monitoring and risk assessment. Particular emphasis will be placed on innovative technologies and integrated strategies that bridge fundamental research and field applications. By connecting insights across scales, this session aims to advance the scientific understanding and engineering development of CO2-geothermal systems, supporting large-scale geological CO2 utilization and storage and the transition toward a low-carbon energy future.
title: Geological CO2 Utilization and Storage in Geothermal Systems

description: The successful implementation of safe deep geological disposal of nuclear waste and other long-lived waste is one of the important environmental challenges in several countries worldwide. Site investigation and selection are primarily geoscientific tasks that require collaboration of different disciplines, like geophysics, hydrogeology, geochemistry, mineralogy, geomechanics, material science, and geological as well as THMC modelling. The development of DGRs also involves the integration of technical designs, evolving regulatory frameworks, and social acceptance considerations. Barrier integrity is a crucial aspect for the assessment of nuclear waste disposal. Numerical simulations, in conjunction with experimental studies are an integral part of safety and environmental-impact assessment. Reliable comparative analyses of potential technological options require coupled THMC models capturing the particularities of each rock type and associated repository concept. Structural as well as process complexity are met by data scarcity and variability, necessitating the treatment of uncertainties and variability. The session provides a platform for the exchange on the following topics: - THMC characterization of materials in natural or engineered barriers in lab- or field-scale experiments - Hydro-mechanical behaviour of materials with extreme hydraulic properties (e.g. low permeability, high suction) and ranging from ductile viscopolastic salt rocks to quasibrittle fractured rock masses - Hydraulic and chemical behaviour of geologic and geotechnical barriers - Computational methods, models and uncertainty quantification for barrier integrity assessment in multi-barrier systems - Geotechnical aspects of repository construction, operation, and post-closure, e.g. monitoring methods, excavation and support, retrieval/recovery, etc. - Minimally invasive characterization of geology and underground installations using geophysical and geohydrological methods Contributions can include lab-scale experimentation, underground research laboratories, observation of natural analogues, physics- and data-driven modelling and code development. Furthermore, the session invites contributions addressing regulatory challenges, public outreach programs, lessons learned from national and international DGR projects, the need for transparent communication to ensure public confidence, and the relevance of geoscientific fundamentals in ensuring the safety of nuclear waste disposal.
title: Deep Geological Repositories: Characterization of Barrier Materials, Integrity Assessment, and Regulatory Insights

description: The geological storage of carbon dioxide may be needed at vast scales, rates of gigatonnes per year and accumulations of hundreds of gigatonnes sequestered, to mitigate emissions overshoot and limit global warming to less than 1.5oC over the course of the century. While subsurface storage is demonstrated at individual projects injecting at rates of millions of tonnes per year, there remain major uncertainties over how much storage is realistically available and how quickly it can be deployed at regional and global scales. The regional and global potential for subsurface CO2 storage has been assessed in government and academic studies for decades. More recently there has been an emphasis on incorporating these resources into standard classification schemes, identifying dynamic geophysical and techno-economic limits, and assessing the dynamic potential for storage at regional and global scales. The results of these analyses vary widely, with estimates of the exploitable resource base ranging from hundreds to tens of thousands of gigatonnes. This range in turn has implications for climate change mitigation pathways: depending on the availability and scalability of geological storage, it could either place no practical limits on the deployment of carbon capture, carbon dioxide removal, and storage technologies, or become a significant constraint. In addition, differences in regional data availability and experience raise concerns about fairness in assigning regional storage potential and the distribution of global climate mitigation burdens. In this session we invite presentations discussing the potential scale, constraints, uncertainties, and modelling techniques of gigatonne scale geological CO2 sequestration. Specifically, we invite work encompassing: Quantification of geophysical, techno-economic, and sociopolitical constraints on CO₂ disposal; Assessments of uncertainty around the rates and scale of deployment; Analyses of policy-relevant implications of the potential and limits to the use of CO2 storage; Modelling approaches, including integrated assessment models (IAMs), for analysing these problems.
title: The potential and limits of climate relevant scales of geological CO2 storage

description: This session focuses on the geological storage and multifunctional utilization of the deep subsurface, with particular emphasis on the safe, efficient, and sustainable use of geological formations. Topics include CO₂ and other gas storage, underground energy storage, geothermal energy, subsurface waste disposal, resource recovery, and integrated use of depleted oil and gas reservoirs, saline aquifers, salt caverns, and other geological structures. We welcome studies addressing fluid–rock interactions, multiphase flow and reactive transport, geomechanical responses, coupled thermal–hydrological–mechanical–chemical processes, storage capacity and injectivity, containment integrity, induced seismicity, leakage risks, and long-term environmental impacts. Contributions on site characterization, monitoring and verification, numerical simulation, digital twins, laboratory and field experiments, and risk-based assessment are particularly encouraged. The session also seeks interdisciplinary studies exploring the transition from single-purpose geological storage toward multifunctional and integrated subsurface systems, including synergies among carbon storage, energy storage, geothermal utilization, waste management, and resource recovery. Field demonstrations, emerging technologies, and frameworks supporting large-scale and sustainable deployment are especially welcome.
title: Deep Subsurface Geological Storage and Multifunctional Utilization
