description: The increasing deployment of ground-source heating and cooling systems relies on understanding, characterising and predicting the thermal and hydraulic behaviour of the subsurface across scales, from laboratory and experimental studies to field applications. Closed- and open-loop systems depend on interactions between heat transport, groundwater flow, geological heterogeneity, and the thermal and hydraulic properties of the subsurface. Understanding these processes is essential for system design, operation, optimisation, long-term performance and sustainability. This session focuses on ground-source heating and cooling through numerical modelling, field observations, monitoring, experiments and case studies. We welcome contributions on: • Numerical methods for coupled thermal, hydraulic, mechanical and chemical processes, including finite-difference, finite-volume, finite-element and mixed-dimensional approaches for complex subsurface systems; • Model calibration, parameter estimation, sensitivity, uncertainty and approaches for improving confidence in subsurface thermal models; • Exploratory and experimental testing, including thermal response tests and approaches for characterising subsurface properties; • Monitoring and field observations, including thermal, hydraulic and geophysical monitoring; • Integration of numerical modelling with monitoring, experimental data and field observations for system characterisation, prediction and performance assessment; • Field-scale case studies of open- and closed-loop systems, including borehole heat exchangers, aquifers and mines; • The influence of geological heterogeneity, fractures, faults, groundwater flow and other subsurface processes on system performance; • System design, optimisation and long-term operation, including interactions between subsurface systems and surface infrastructure such as heat pumps and district heating and cooling networks; • Innovative approaches to harnessing the subsurface for sustainable heating and cooling across diverse geological, climatic and operational settings. The session brings together modelling, experimental, monitoring and applied approaches to subsurface heating and cooling. By connecting numerical and experimental methods, it will foster exchange on how to better characterise, design, monitor and operate ground-source systems, while identifying opportunities and challenges for their wider deployment.
title: Understanding the subsurface for sustainable ground source heating and cooling systems: from numerical modelling to field applications

description: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) plays a critical role in regulating Earth’s climate. Therefore, a potential future weakening or even collapse of the AMOC could have major climatic and societal impacts. While some of these changes and impacts have been investigated, their wide-ranging nature has led to scattered knowledge with limited intercomparisons between different lines of evidence. In this session, we bridge multiple disciplines and bring together the latest knowledge on AMOC changes and their impacts. We welcome all contributions that investigate changes in the AMOC and their Earth System impacts. These can include direct physical impacts, such as atmospheric, oceanic, or cryospheric; biogeochemical as well as marine and terrestrial ecosystem responses; and socioeconomic impacts, such as health, agricultural, and economic repercussions. Contributions can cover any timescale, from paleoclimate and the recent past to future projections, from seasonal and decadal changes to long-term (centennial to millennial), both past and future. In addition, the AMOC can be studied in a range of settings, from internal variability to forced trends or abrupt/tipping behaviour, affecting both mean and extreme variables. We call for contributions employing a broad range of tools, from Earth System, regional, and simple models to reanalyses and observations/proxies, as well as socioeconomic and impact-related models. Finally, as the Atlantic subpolar gyre (SPG) is an ocean system whose strength, stability, and impact on the climate are strongly connected to the AMOC, we also welcome contributions discussing the impacts of SPG changes on the Earth System.
divisions: Impacts of Climate and Weather in an Inter- and Transdisciplinary context
title: AMOC changes and impacts on physical, biogeochemical, and societal systems

description: Human health risks in a changing climate: observed impacts, adaptation and future risks Climate change is increasingly affecting population health through heat, cold, floods, droughts, wildfires, storms and rapidly changing, or compound, hazards. These events contribute not only to premature mortality but also to cardiorespiratory and infectious diseases, injuries, adverse mental health outcomes and disruption of healthcare and other essential services. An estimated 489,000 heat-related deaths occur globally each year, and more than 181,000 heat-related deaths were recorded across Europe during the summers of 2022–2024. Occupational heat exposure also affects more than 2.4 billion workers globally and is associated with nearly 23 million injuries each year. These impacts are unevenly distributed. Socioeconomic position, age, sex and gender, ethnicity, pre-existing health conditions, occupation and place intersect to shape exposure, susceptibility and adaptive capacity. Marginalised populations, including older adults, children, people with chronic conditions, outdoor and manual workers, and communities living in low-income or geographically exposed areas, often bear a disproportionate burden. An intersectional and climate-justice perspective is therefore essential for understanding health risks and developing effective and equitable responses. This session, organised in collaboration with the Swedish Centre for Impacts of Climate Extremes (CLIMES), invites contributions examining the diverse and unequal effects of climate variability, climate change and extreme events on human health. We particularly welcome studies that: 1. quantify observed impacts and future health risks from single, compound and cascading climate hazards; 2. investigate the attribution of health impacts to anthropogenic climate change; 3. identify intersecting socioeconomic, demographic, occupational and spatial vulnerabilities; 4. develop or evaluate health early-warning systems, impact-based forecasting and other climate services; 5. assess the effectiveness, equity and potential unintended consequences of adaptation interventions; and 6. integrate climate, environmental, health and social data to strengthen public health preparedness, resilient health systems and equitable adaptation. 7. storylines methods and their capacity to inform decision makers. We welcome contributions using epidemiological, modelling, qualitative, participatory and interdisciplinary approaches.
divisions: Impacts of Climate and Weather in an Inter- and Transdisciplinary context
title: Human health risks in a changing climate: observed impacts, adaptation and future risks

description: Climate hazards consistently expose and often intensify socioeconomic inequalities. Vulnerability to extreme events is not evenly distributed within or across societies; rather, it is shaped by existing social, economic, and political conditions. As such, inequality, defined as the uneven distribution of resources, opportunities, and power has been recognised by the United Nations and other global policy frameworks as a central factor influencing progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). This session invites interdisciplinary contributions, bringing together geoscientists, social scientists, economists, and policy experts to examine the complex and often compounding interactions between social inequalities and climate hazards such as floods, heatwaves, droughts, storms, landslides, and wildfires across different scales, including within countries, between countries, and across continents. Topics of interest include (but are not limited to): -Case studies illustrating how environmental and social inequalities intersect. -Types of inequality: social, gender-based, infrastructural, recovery time, education, income source, wealth distribution, climate justice, food security -Impacts of climate hazards: displacement, fatalities, psychological and physical health, developmental setbacks. -Long-term recovery challenges: absence of recovery, prolonged recovery periods, slower developmental trajectories. -Historical and political-ecological perspectives on disasters and their long-term societal impacts. -Innovations in data, metrics, or methods (e.g., AI, remote sensing, socio-environmental modelling) for assessing inequality and disaster risk across spatial and temporal scales.
divisions: Impacts of Climate and Weather in an Inter- and Transdisciplinary context
title: Climate hazards and socioeconomic inequality across scales

description: Agricultural production depends on climatic conditions such as precipitation and temperature, as well as their interactions with each other and with non-climatic factors. Disentangling these effects and understanding which climatic conditions affect agriculture, how strongly, and how future production could change under global warming is crucial for safeguarding future food production, supporting timely climate adaptation through management practices, and improving impact models and assessments. We invite submissions across a broad spectrum of approaches for assessment of climate change impacts on agriculture. Submissions may include, but are not limited to, the following themes: 1- Assessment of climatic conditions, including extremes (droughts, heatwaves) and averages, and their effect on agricultural production, variability and anomalies. 2- Assessment of adaptation practices, including but not limited to crop diversification, irrigation, and fertilization in crop production. 3- Projections of future agricultural production using multi-model climate simulations as well as single-model initial conditions and assessment of time of emergence. 4- Spatial and temporal variability and the role of teleconnections in climate risks to agriculture. 5- Supply chains, financial losses, and the role of insurance in alleviating financial losses in the agriculture sector. 6- Methodological advancements and intercomparison of process-based, statistical, and AI-based models for agricultural production and climate impact assessments.
divisions: Impacts of Climate and Weather in an Inter- and Transdisciplinary context
title: Climate impacts on agriculture: from climatic drivers and constraints on productivity to adaptation options and future risks

description: Climate change and environmental degradation constitute a growing threat to the stability of societal and economical systems. The observed and anticipated increase in the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events under future emission scenarios, combined with the projected long-term shifts in climate patterns are already leading to significant economic damages on a local to global scale with repercussions in insurance and finance sectors. To mitigate systemic risks from extreme weather events an improved model representation of extreme weather and climate hazards at impact relevant scales and a better understanding of their often compounding ways they cause impacts is urgently needed. In recognition of this challenge climate risk assessments for the financial and insurance sectors have experienced amplified attention in both the academic and private spheres. This session aims at providing a platform for actors from academia and the private sector to exchange information on strategies for assessing climate risk, and is organised under three main pillars: -Physical Climate Risks: Trends, Processes and Modelling -Identifying and Managing Climate Risks -Quantifying Damages and Impacts from Climate Risks We encourage submissions on a wide range of topics including innovative climate risk modeling and model evaluation, damage functions, integrated assessment modelling, bias adjustment and downscaling methods, climate emulators, climate hazard indicators and their projections for specific sectors (e.g. food, energy, insurance, real estate, supply chains), impact data collection and categorization.
divisions: Impacts of Climate and Weather in an Inter- and Transdisciplinary context
title: Advances in physical climate risk assessment for the financial and insurance sectors

description: Extreme heat is a leading weather-related threat to human health, with risk projected to intensify as the climate warms. Robust and transferable estimates of heat-related health risk require an understanding of how socioeconomic and demographic contexts influence who is most vulnerable in addition to the role confounding environmental stressors such as humidity and air pollution play in exacerbating dangerous conditions. This session brings together environmental epidemiologists, data scientists, climate scientists, and human physiologists to advance methods for predicting and forecasting heat-related morbidity and mortality, and to better understand the factors that might modify risk beyond temperature. We seek machine-learning, statistical, physiological or hybrid approaches that provide new insights into heat-related health risks and/or translate these insights into improved predictive frameworks. Emphasis is placed on novel methodologies improving the validation and transferability of models across regions, climates, and populations. We are particularly interested in approaches that address limited or heterogeneous health data to enable prediction in data-sparse settings, where populations highly vulnerable to extreme heat may be poorly represented. These include physiologically based approaches that derive limits of human heat tolerance from thermoregulation rather than from local health records, and that resolve risk across distinct population cohorts. We also welcome contributions improving predictions under anthropogenic warming, extending model transferability into different climates. Advances in our understanding of compound risks, prediction methods and model transferability can support more effective and equitable Heat-Health Warning Systems.
divisions: Impacts of Climate and Weather in an Inter- and Transdisciplinary context
title: Lethal Heat: Compound Risks and Transferable Approaches to Heat-Health Modelling

description: This session aims to showcase recent research progress and augment existing knowledge in polar meteorology and climate, and the atmosphere-land ice-sea ice coupling in both Hemispheres. It will provide a setting to foster discussion and help identify gaps, tools, and studies needed to address these open questions. It is also an opportunity to convey newly acquired knowledge to the community. We invite contributions on all observational and numerical modelling aspects of Arctic and Antarctic meteorology and climatology that address atmospheric interactions with the cryosphere. This may include but is not limited to studies on past, present and future of: - Atmospheric processes that influence sea ice (snow on sea ice, sea ice melt, polynya formation and sea ice production and transport) and associated feedbacks, - Surface energy balance above the snow/ice surface. - The variability of the polar large-scale atmospheric circulation (such as polar jets, the circumpolar trough and storm tracks) and impact on the cryosphere (sea ice and land ice), - Atmosphere-cryosphere interactions triggered by synoptic and meso-scale weather phenomena such as cold air outbreaks, katabatic winds, extratropical cyclones, polar cyclones, atmospheric rivers, Foehn winds, and heatwaves, - Role of clouds in polar climate and impact on the land ice and sea ice through interactions with radiation, - High-latitude dust and pollution, deposition on snow and ice, and related impacts. - Teleconnections and climate indices and their role in land ice/sea ice variability. Presentations including new observational (ground- and satellite-based) and modelling methodologies specific to polar regions are encouraged. Contributions related to results from recent field campaigns in Greenland, the Arctic, and in the Southern Ocean/Antarctica are most welcome.
divisions: Impacts of Climate and Weather in an Inter- and Transdisciplinary context
title: Polar Meteorology and Climate and their Links to the Rapidly Changing Cryosphere

description: Disturbances, such as extreme weather events, play a key role in shaping ecosystems. Under climate change, extreme weather hazards undergo changes in frequency, intensity and seasonality. While ecosystem-based adaptation and nature-based solutions are gaining traction, it is crucial to investigate the diverse interactions between extreme weather risk, ecosystems, and their services. This session seeks to highlight research on the nexus of weather and climate related extreme events and ecosystems. We encourage submissions on: 1) investigations into the key attributes and patterns of extreme weather events which affect ecosystem composition, structure and functioning, 2) studies on how ecosystems respond to and recover from extreme weather events across past, present, and future climates, 3) Implications of extreme weather impacts on ecosystems for biodiversity and ecosystem service provision. We welcome a diverse array of contributions, including theoretical analyses, modelling approaches, field studies, experimental designs, and remote sensing analysis. Key topics include: - Identification of extreme weather risk hotspots, and subsequent ecosystem responses (terrestrial, coastal, or marine) in past, present and future climates - Role of extreme weather in shaping ecosystem composition, biodiversity, structure and functioning, and its impact on ecosystems service provisions across temporal and spatial scales Interactions of natural hazard, anthropogenic and biogenic disturbances with ecosystems (including compounding events) - Ecosystem vulnerability, resilience and recovery dynamics under weather extremes, including regime shifts / tipping points in ecosystems Impact and efficacy of nature-based solutions under extreme conditions, risk of maladaptation or disservices
divisions: Impacts of Climate and Weather in an Inter- and Transdisciplinary context
title: Weather and climate extremes impacts on ecosystems: Disturbance regimes, vulnerability, and resilience

description: The Mediterranean and other water-stressed regions are increasingly recognized as advanced laboratories of planetary limits, where climate change, land-system change, and biodiversity loss interact to jeopardize the interconnected Water-Energy-Food-Ecosystem-Health (WEFEH) nexus. The concept of a Safe Operating Space (SOS) for freshwaters, rooted in the planetary boundaries framework, offers a compelling lens for defining thresholds of availability, quality, and ecosystem stability beyond which irreversible damage may occur. Yet translating these thresholds into regionally adapted, policy-relevant, and operational tools remains a major scientific and governance challenge, compounded by the complexity of interlinkages among the different SOS components. This session invites contributions that bridge the gap between global planetary boundaries and their local operationalization, from scientific frameworks and safe operating spaces at the global/regional scale, to digital tools, decision support systems, and living labs at the basin and field scale. We welcome studies on Nexus approaches (WEFE-H, Source-to-Sea) that move water governance from reactive to predictive management, leveraging digitalization, data science, and Earth observation. Contributions addressing the social and equity dimensions of these transitions, access, gender, and climate justice, alongside technical and modelling approaches, are strongly encouraged. The session aims to bring together climate scientists, hydrologists, nexus and planetary-boundaries researchers, and practitioners to advance a shared operational agenda for water security under climate change, with a focus on the Mediterranean and other vulnerable regions worldwide.
divisions: Impacts of Climate and Weather in an Inter- and Transdisciplinary context
title: From Planetary Boundaries to the Basin Scale: Operational Nexus Approaches for Water Security under Climate Change

description: Extreme events such as tropical cyclones, heatwaves, and earthquakes threaten populations worldwide. Climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of many natural hazards, which can interact with community exposure, inequalities, and vulnerabilities to cause substantial harm. These harms include forced migration, health and wellbeing effects, and other societal impacts. A growing literature at the intersection of the natural and social sciences examines the impacts of extreme events on populations, as well as people’s behavioral, attitudinal, and emotional responses. Understanding the diverse societal impacts of natural hazards requires approaches that connect knowledge across disciplines, scales, and sectors. Yet, the challenges of doing so remain underexplored. Challenges include methodological choices, scales of analysis (e.g., regional, national), and means of translating scientific outputs into actionable information for policy and practice. This session provides a platform for contributions that bridge disciplines and sectors to better understand societal impacts of, and responses to, extreme events and related compound hazards. We invite contributions including, but not limited to, studies of: - Challenges for interdisciplinary and cross-sectoral collaborations - Migration, displacement, and immobility due to extreme events - Health and wellbeing effects of climate change and extreme events - Food production and security in relation to extreme weather - The interplay between climate change, environment, and conflict - Environmental attitudes and behaviors influenced by extreme events
title: Bridging natural and social sciences to study societal responses to extreme events

description: As a result of a warming Arctic, there is an increased frequency and intensity of extreme weather events such as marine and terrestrial heatwaves, rain-on-snow events, and intense windstorms. Such extreme weather events can trigger cascading, multidisciplinary impacts across the Arctic system. This session bridges the gap between physical mechanisms and on-the-ground realities by investigating the physical drivers of extreme events within oceanic, atmospheric, and cryospheric systems, alongside their wide spectrum of impacts. These impacts range from rapid physical shifts, such as enhanced meltwater runoff, sudden sea-ice loss, and snowpack depletion, to societal and ecological disruptions, including infrastructure damage, traffic disruptions, and threats to reindeer herding and Indigenous livelihoods. We welcome submissions based on modeling, observations, or interdisciplinary frameworks, such as those incorporating local and Indigenous knowledge systems, that investigate extreme weather phenomena, their physical drivers, and their direct and cascading impacts on the Arctic environment, ecosystems, and local communities.
divisions: Impacts of Climate and Weather in an Inter- and Transdisciplinary context
title: Drivers and Impacts of Extreme Weather Events in the Arctic

description: This session investigates the interaction between human-made interventions in nature and social systems, and how reliance on technology is intertwined with current and future climate hazards. While technology is meant to make the environment liveable, it can also obscure exposure to climate hazards and as such increase vulnerability. We aim to discuss risks and impacts in domains such as health, ecosystems, the built environment, financial and economic systems, as well as possible risk management and resilience practices. Reliance on technologies to create amenable conditions and expand the human climate niche may amplify risk because these technologies can fail. In addition, the increasing engineeredness of our environment creates a general sense of control and security, which reduces awareness of and preparedness for unexpected events and circumstances. We invite contributions that explore the effects of socio-technological interactions under changing climate hazards on risk perception, risk, and impacts. Topics of interest include but are not limited to: natural hazards; compounding and systemic risks; adaptation technologies; the Anthropocene. Methods of interest include, but are not limited to: modelling; case studies; event, impact, and damage attribution; climate and adaptation storylines; interviews and participatory research; and policy analysis. Presentations from all subject areas – physical sciences, geography, social sciences, and the humanities – are welcome.
divisions: Impacts of Climate and Weather in an Inter- and Transdisciplinary context
title: Adaptation failures on a hotter planet - Socio-technological interactions as mediators of physical climate risks.

description: The Mediterranean is a climate change hotspot where warming and changes in the hydrological cycle are reshaping high-impact weather and climate extremes. Heatwaves, droughts, extreme precipitation and floods, wildfires, marine extremes, and compound and cascading events interact with exposure and vulnerability, generating complex environmental and societal risks. Addressing these challenges requires connecting advances in observations, physical processes, modelling, prediction and climate projections with impact and risk assessment. Understanding exposure, vulnerability and adaptive capacity is equally essential for translating climate knowledge into effective early warning, decision-support and adaptation. This session brings together physical and social sciences, technological developments and stakeholder perspectives to advance integrated understanding of Mediterranean extremes, their impacts and pathways to resilience. We welcome contributions on: • Physical processes, observations, modelling, attribution, prediction and projections of Mediterranean weather and climate extremes. • Single, compound and cascading hazards and their interactions across spatial and temporal scales. • Impacts, exposure, vulnerability and risk across health, water, agriculture, energy, ecosystems, infrastructure and urban areas. • Methods integrating physical, environmental, social and economic dimensions of climate risk. • Climate services, impact-based forecasting, early-warning systems and decision-support tools, including Earth observation, AI and digital twins. • Adaptation and risk-reduction strategies, including nature-based solutions, and evidence of their effectiveness, limitations and trade-offs. • Co-production of knowledge, stakeholder and citizen engagement, communication and capacity building. We particularly encourage contributions bridging disciplines, sectors and Mediterranean regions, including approaches addressing inequalities in data, vulnerability and adaptive capacity. Supported by the FutureMed COST Action (CA22162), this session welcomes contributions from within and beyond the network. It aims to strengthen transdisciplinary collaboration and connect climate science with societal needs, adaptation and resilience.
divisions: Impacts of Climate and Weather in an Inter- and Transdisciplinary context
title: Mediterranean climate extremes: bridging processes, impacts, risks and pathways to resilience

description: Addressing today's environmental and climate-related challenges requires strong collaboration among researchers, public authorities, private companies, and local communities. This session will explore how the integration of field observations, scientific research, technological innovation, and stakeholder engagement can support more effective environmental protection and sustainable territorial development. Contributions are invited on multidisciplinary approaches that combine monitoring systems, Earth observation, environmental data, digital technologies, and decision-support tools with practical applications in risk management, climate change adaptation, ecosystem conservation, and sustainable land-use planning. Particular attention will be given to successful partnerships between academia, industry, public institutions, and civil society that facilitate knowledge transfer and the implementation of innovative solutions. The session aims to foster dialogue across disciplines and sectors, promoting the exchange of experiences, methodologies, and best practices to strengthen the resilience, sustainability, and long-term management of natural and human environments.
title: Integrating Field Data, Research, Enterprises, and Stakeholders for Environmental Protection and Sustainable Territorial Development

description: Cities are intricate multi-scale systems, composed of diverse sub-components such as population, energy, transport, and climate. These components interact on various time scales, from hourly to seasonal to annual and beyond. Effective urban models and digital twins, crucial for urban planning and policy-making, must account for these complex interactions as they govern the growth and functioning of cities, often giving rise to emergent large-scale phenomena. However, our ability to quantitatively describe city behaviour remains limited due to the myriad of processes, scales, and feedbacks involved. This session invites studies focused on modelling and monitoring the dynamics of multiple sectors and city-biosphere interactions. Topics of interest include, but are not limited to: - Demography - Urban transport networks - Energy consumption - Anthropogenic emissions and pollution - Urban climate - Urban hydrology - Urban ecology Our aim is to elucidate the complex dynamics within urban environments and explore how urban form and function can be optimised to enhance the liveability and well-being of their citizens.
title: Urban geosciences: modelling and monitoring complex cities

description: Recent years have seen an increasing number of armed conflicts worldwide, both within and between states. Beyond their devastating humanitarian consequences, armed conflicts and associated military activities can have profound and long-lasting environmental impacts. These impacts include, but are not limited to, land-use and land-cover change, ecosystem degradation, biodiversity loss, soil and water contamination, disruptions to food production systems, increased climate vulnerability, and greenhouse gas emissions, with consequences that may extend from local to global scales. This session welcomes empirical studies investigating the environmental dimensions of armed conflict across spatial and temporal scales. This means global as well as place-based analyses are suitable. We encourage contributions that employ a range of methods and data sources, including remote sensing, geospatial analysis, machine learning, artificial intelligence, field observations, environmental monitoring, and integrated modelling approaches. We particularly welcome conflict-engaged research, in which armed conflict is treated not merely as contextual background but as an explicit analytical component. We seek studies that directly examine the relationships between conflict dynamics, military activities (also outside of direct war contexts), and observed environmental changes, advancing our understanding of the mechanisms, impacts, and consequences of armed conflict on the environment. Contributions addressing environmental monitoring, attribution, post-conflict recovery, environmental governance, or implications for sustainability and climate policy are particularly encouraged.
title: The environmental dimensions of armed conflict: social-ecological impacts in crisis-affected landscapes

description: Nature-related decisions in finance, policy and official statistics increasingly require credible, scalable and spatially explicit evidence. Yet translating Earth observation and in situ measurements into fit-for-purpose indicators remains difficult. This session connects remote sensing, ecology, environmental sciences, accounting, finance and decision-makers to examine indicator validity, uncertainty, spatial and temporal scale, methodological transparency, data provenance, and fitness for use. We invite integrated contributions linking remote sensing or ecological methods to at least one concrete accounting, disclosure or market application. Topics include, but are not limited to, mapping and assessing ecosystem condition and services, biodiversity intactness, land use intensity, anthropogenic pressures, and water-related environmental indicators; combining Earth observation with field data and models; addressing baselines, uncertainty, scale and change; and ensuring data traceability, reproducibility, validation and auditability. Applications may include national environmental-economic accounts, including ecosystem accounts implemented under SEEA Ecosystem Accounting; TNFD-aligned reporting by companies and financial institutions; and monitoring, reporting and verification for biodiversity and nature-based carbon credits. The session will bring together Earth observation, environmental and ecological scientist, nature accountants, policymakers, standards and assurance specialists, and financial practitioners to compare what indicator producers can robustly deliver with what users need for real decisions. We particularly welcome co-designed and operational case studies, including critical assessments of where indicators fail or are misapplied, rather than only new maps or algorithms.
title: From Earth observation to decision-grade nature information: biophysical indicators for nature finance and ecosystem accounting

description: In the past few decades, observational seismology has advanced rapidly, driven by expanding computational capabilities and the growing availability of data from dense networks. Emerging approaches such as Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) and Large-N nodal arrays offer exciting opportunities to go beyond conventional catalog building for subsurface characterization, while also presenting new challenges. The integration of large datasets, advanced monitoring tools, and innovative processing techniques can lead to new discoveries. Machine learning-based methods, for example, can detect more earthquakes than conventional techniques, illuminating smaller events and previously hidden seismic patterns. Likewise, fully data-driven and waveform-based methods are enhancing the resolution of crustal imaging. However, automated approaches, which are necessary for handling big seismic datasets, can introduce errors or biases if uncertainties are not carefully assessed. Uncertainty quantification therefore remains a central challenge and is essential for ensuring robust and reliable scientific outcomes. This session invites contributions presenting new approaches to the analysis of large seismic datasets, whether in offline playback or (near-)real-time applications, across a wide range of tectonic settings and spatial scales. We particularly welcome methods that integrate uncertainty analysis. Submissions may focus on classical aspects of seismicity analysis, such as event detection, location, magnitude estimation, and source characterization, as well as novel instrumental or theoretical developments. We encourage contributions spanning diverse applications, including operational seismic workflows, enhanced geothermal systems (EGS), carbon capture and storage (CCS) monitoring, and studies ranging from the laboratory to regional scales.
title: Advances in Seismic Data Analysis: From Acquisition and Processing to Uncertainty Assessment

description: As environmental governance undergoes a digital transformation, there is a decisive shift from static reporting toward dynamic ecosystems that facilitate real-time assessment and causal attribution. However, translating scientific insight into political action remains challenging, requiring raw data to be transformed into robust, legally defensible evidence. Recent advances in data science are expanding this capacity and offering more precise tools for impact assessment, explicit quantification of uncertainty and advances in explainability. At the same time, significant hurdles remain: The "black-box" nature of certain predictive models, the difficulty of communicating scientific uncertainty to non-experts, as well as the complexities of causal attribution in open systems must be addressed to ensure these methods are fit for purpose and lead to resilient governance. This evolution enables a transition from reactive to proactive governance, providing the empirical rigor necessary to design and refine environmental interventions, such as water quality regulations and low-emission zones across spatio-temporal scales. The session aims to provide a venue to present the latest progress in bridging the gap between environmental data science and policy implementation. We welcome abstracts focused on, but not limited to: - Cross-sectoral case studies: Implementation of evidence-based governance in air quality, biodiversity, water management, or climate adaptation. - Uncertainty quantification: Probabilistic modelling and frameworks for communicating scientific uncertainty to decision-makers. - Interpretability and Explainability: Methods to ensure that data-driven models are transparent and legible for administrative and legal use. - Causal inference: Causal impact assessment of policy interventions, counterfactual analysis, and the use of quasi-experimental methods. - Evidence-based monitoring: Designing data collection networks and sensors specifically to support policy evaluation and KPIs. - Adaptive governance: The use of real-time data streams for iterative policy adjustment and "course-correction" (feedback loops). - Decision-support systems: The development of tools and metrics that translate scientific observations into actionable policy options. - Institutional frameworks: Strategies for integrating data science workflows into government agency structures and legislative processes.
title: Evidence-Based Environmental Governance: From Data Science to Actionable Policy

description: Causal inference provides a powerful framework for unraveling cause-effect relationships, disentangling complex processes within Earth system sciences and quantifying causal effects by combining domain knowledge, machine learning (ML) models, and data from observations and climate model simulations. Learning causal relationships from Earth system data across different timescales is crucial for understanding its complex emergent dynamics and validating climate models, which we count on to simulate future changes. A better understanding of the Earth system helps us design more effective mitigation and adaptation strategies to address open risks with environmental and societal relevance. This session welcomes contributions that highlight innovative approaches, methodologies, and case studies employing causality across Earth sciences. The overall aim is to foster interdisciplinary discussions, encourage collaborations, and promote the development of robust analysis frameworks. We would like to initiate discussions on experiences, challenges, and future development of causal methodologies in Earth system sciences. The topics of interest for this session include, but are not limited to: • Causal discovery and inference: algorithms and methods for uncovering causal networks among Earth system processes (e.g., weather, climate, clouds and aerosols, teleconnections, chemical-dynamical interactions); • Causal effect estimation: statistical techniques to estimate causal effects of anthropogenic or natural forcings in the Earth system; • Case studies investigating causal pathways and mechanisms driving natural and anthropogenic perturbations such as climate change, land-ocean interactions, teleconnections, extreme events, volcanic eruptions, wildfires, etc.; • Causal modelling, network analysis, and causal model evaluation: development and application of causal models, network analysis, and graphical models to capture the intricate interconnections and feedbacks within dynamical systems; • Integration of causal discovery with deep learning (DL) as a promising avenue for improving climate simulations; • Merging of explainable and causal Artificial Intelligence (AI): discovering governing equations, parameterizations, and relationships based on climate data; • Challenges and limitations: difficulties associated with the application of causal inference, such as data preprocessing, violations of assumptions, or uncertainty quantification.
title: Causal Inference for Earth System Sciences: Methods, Challenges, and Applications

description: European seas and coastal areas are facing and are projected to face growing pressures from climate change, sea-level rise, storm surges, extreme waves, coastal flooding and erosion, marine heatwaves, changing sea-ice conditions and ecosystem degradation. Addressing these challenges requires integrated approaches that combine observations with ocean, climate, wave, biogeochemical and ecosystem models, high-resolution coastal simulations, artificial intelligence, and social and economic information. This inter- and transdisciplinary session will explore how Ocean Digital Twins can bring these different sources of knowledge on future seasonal, decadal, and centennial ocean hazards together and turn model results into practical climate and ocean services. We invite contributions on advanced modeling; seasonal-to-decadal predictions and climate projections; model coupling and uncertainty; high-performance computing; AI-based/emulator-based predictions[AM1.1][AM1.2]; early warning; and interactive applications linked to European infrastructures such as EDITO and Destination Earth. Applications may include future coastal flooding and erosion, compound hazards, coastal cities and ports, offshore wind and other marine renewable-energy systems, fisheries and aquaculture, marine ecosystems, biodiversity, sea ice and safe navigation. We also welcome research on adaptation pathways, nature-based solutions, vulnerability and resilience assessment, and environmental, social and economic trade-offs. The session aims to bring together oceanographers, climate scientists, coastal engineers, ecologists, computer and data scientists, social scientists, practitioners and decision-makers. Participatory research involving public authorities, civil-protection agencies, port and energy operators, fisheries and aquaculture stakeholders, NGOs and coastal communities is also welcome. The session is jointly organized by four Horizon Europe projects—MOIRAI, SEACLIM, EU-INTERCHANGE and RIVIERADE—which address complementary aspects of ocean and climate modelling, coastal risks, the land–river–ocean continuum, as well as, digital tools and services for climate adaptation.
title: Ocean Digital Twins for Coastal Resilience and a Sustainable Blue Economy in Future Climates

description: Over the last two decades, OpenStreetMap (OSM) has evolved into a global, community-generated source of spatio-temporal geodata. Volunteers continuously document infrastructure, land use, transportation networks, environmental features and other spatial entities that are often not covered in comparable detail or at the same temporal resolution by national mapping agencies. This global grassroots mapping effort creates a continuously evolving record of changes in geographical space, reflecting processes such as urban growth, agricultural transformation, natural hazards and disasters, and the spatial impacts of global environmental change. OSM data are increasingly combined with governmental topographic data, research datasets and remote sensing observations to support research and generate new insights across the geosciences. However, the long-term preservation and scientific reuse of this evolving data commons raises important challenges. These include the preservation of spatio-temporal versions, FAIR access, persistent scientific citation, provenance documentation, reproducibility and cartographic reuse. This session invites contributions addressing the use, preservation and scientific exploitation of OpenStreetMap as a spatio-temporal data commons. We particularly welcome use cases, methodological approaches and lessons learned from different branches of the geosciences, as well as contributions discussing challenges and opportunities for long-term preservation, provenance, FAIR principles, citation, reproducibility and integration with other geospatial data sources.
title: From Open Map to Research Data Infrastructure: Preserving and Using Historical OpenStreetMap Data

description: Downscaling aims to process and refine global climate model output to provide information at spatial and temporal scales suitable for impact studies. In response to the current challenges posed by climate change and variability, downscaling techniques continue to play an important role in the development of new services and products. While the refinement of downscaling techniques proceeds at an unprecedented pace, users of climate information are facing the novel challenge of how to select amongst the choice of available datasets or how to assess their credibility with respect to a particular application. In this context, model evaluation and verification is growing in relevance and advances in the field will likely require close collaboration between various disciplines. Recent developments, including the integration of AI and machine learning applications, the emergence of kilometre-scale simulations, and the widespread availability of open-source downscaling products, add new dimensions to this challenge. These advances raise important questions about the ‘added value’ of downscaling, especially in light of the cascade of uncertainty and the need for robust evaluation frameworks. In our session, we aim to bring together scientists from the various geoscientific disciplines interrelated through downscaling: atmospheric modeling, climate change impact modeling, machine learning and verification research. We also invite philosophers of climate science to stimulate our discussion about the novel challenges that arise from evaluating complex models and modelling chains in the face of the increasingly heterogeneous needs of the growing user communities. Contributions to this session may address, but are not limited to: - newly available downscaling products, - applications relying on downscaled data and impact assessments, - downscaling method development and machine learning, - bias correction and statistical postprocessing, - challenges in the data management of kilometer-scale simulations, - verification, uncertainty quantification and the added value of downscaling, - downscaling approaches in light of computational epistemology.
title: Downscaling: methods, applications and added value

description: Monitoring carbon and greenhouse gas exchange between atmosphere, land, ocean and human systems underpins the Global Stocktake, national inventories, carbon markets and carbon dioxide removal (CDR). Yet bottom-up (inventories, process-based and data-driven models), top-down (atmospheric inversions) and bookkeeping (land-use change) estimates remain uncertain and often disagree, while the credibility of measurement, reporting and verification (MRV) rests on independent methods agreeing. Machine learning (ML) offers new ways to enhance, complement, emulate, integrate or even replace established observational, modelling and analytical workflows. This session invites contributions using ML to advance carbon cycle monitoring and understanding across all compartments (atmosphere, vegetation, soils, permafrost, wetlands, inland waters, coastal and open ocean, anthropogenic sources) and all relevant trace gases, including CO2, CH4, N2O, CO, COS and isotopes. We welcome the full breadth of ML: foundation models, transformers, GNNs, CNNs, generative models (diffusion, flow matching), hybrid and differentiable modelling, Bayesian ML, symbolic regression, interpretable, robust and trustworthy ML, and tabular methods such as gradient-boosted trees. We particularly encourage work bridging science, policy and industry. Topics include, but are not limited to: - ML-enhanced bottom-up estimates: upscaling, mapping stocks and fluxes, inventories - ML for top-down inversions: transport emulators, data assimilation, retrievals, point-source detection - ML for bookkeeping and land-use change emissions - Emulators and foundation models for process-based and Earth system models - Hybrid modelling, and generative models for gap-filling, downscaling and ensemble generation - Fusion of remote sensing with in-situ data (eddy covariance, flask networks, ocean pCO2) - ML for carbon cycle process understanding and discovery: drivers, feedbacks and emergent constraints, with explainability, causality and uncertainty quantification - Reconciling lines of evidence across methods, compartments and gases - Monitoring for policy and industry: MRV, national inventories, carbon markets, CDR verification - ML-based decision support and policy pathways (reinforcement learning, integrated assessment models) - Benchmarks, datasets & open tools
title: Monitoring the Carbon Cycle with Machine Learning: Opportunities for Science, Policy and Industry

description: Deep learning is causing a major paradigm shift in weather forecasting from physical modelling to data-driven or hybrid approaches. While the first ML-systems are now used in operational medium-range weather forecasting, the adaptation of deep learning techniques to the subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S), decadal and multidecadal range is still lagging behind. New approaches are needed for S2S since atmospheric initial conditions are no longer the main driver of predictability. Similarly, deep-learning approaches are emerging for the decadal and multidecadal timescales, when climate forcing becomes a dominant influence on the atmosphere. The scarcity of simulation data and the lack of ground truth pose serious challenges at these time ranges. For this session, we solicit abstracts that present current ideas and results at the intersection of deep learning, S2S-forecasting and climate emulation and simulation. In particular, we welcome contributions from the following areas. - Generative modelling for time-scales beyond medium-range - Calibration and uncertainty estimation for data-driven long-term forecasting - Coupled generative models of earth system components - Predictability limits and failure modes in data-driven long-term forecasting - Out-of distribution emulation and forecasting - Benchmarking and validation of long-term forecasts with data-driven models - Identification of drivers of increased predictability and forecast skill for data-driven models (XAI)
title: Deep Learning for Subseasonal to Climate Time Scales: Methods, Drivers and Predictability Limits

description: This session explores how assured, trustworthy use of AI for geospatial data can support decision-making and implementation strategies. The use of AI-enabled geospatial tools is increasing, spanning site suitability, climate resilience, risk management and investment decisions. Across all of these applications, questions of data provenance, model assurance, confidence levels and uncertainty analysis of the AI systems themselves become critical to responsible deployment. We invite contributions on: methods for validating geospatial AI models and the datasets used; approaches to closing evidence gaps in data-poor areas; and frameworks to measure confidence and uncertainty in AI-derived geospatial outputs. We particularly welcome interdisciplinary contributions, including case studies that demonstrate how responsible GeoAI approaches can support fair access and devolution.
title: Responsible GeoAI: Generating trustworthy methods and tools

description: The rapid development of pretrained models, including large language and foundation models, opens up many new applications in geosciences. Fine tuning or deploying existing models directly to geoscience problems gives us all the benefits of very large models, trained with vast data sets, whilst reducing the compute cost and required specialist data sets, compared to older deep learning techniques. The potential cost and energy saving, and scientific power of these models can revolutionise AI in geosciences. In this session, we look forward to seeing state-of-the-art fine tuning techniques specialized for geoscience; novel deployment of pretrained models of any sort; and lessons learnt from trial and error. We would love to see applications across the geosciences, from geophysics to education, remote sensing to hands on field applications.
title: Standing on the shoulders of robotic giants: using pretrained AI models in the geosciences

description: A robotic platform maps outdoor nitrogen dioxide, moves indoors and concludes that an anomaly warrants returning tomorrow. A drone communicates with a ground robot in a dense forest, profiling structure under and above the canopy. An edge device runs simulates multiple scenarios through pre-trained emulators of a regional system. Every component of both exists. The system that ties them together could be next. Environmental science is being transformed by automated platforms, new low power sensing, digital twins, foundation models and agentic AI. Almost all of it is designed to improve how we measure and simulate the environment, or how we assist a human analyst. A challenging problem is the decision layer: how a system forms a meaningful hypothesis about the environment in front of it, whether real or digital, re-plans what and where to sample or simulate as evidence accumulates, quantifies its own uncertainty well enough to act on it, and knows when to proceed, escalate to a human, or defer. Without all combined, autonomy in the geosciences remains a sophisticated remote control. But when is enough, and who decides? In this session we welcome all contributions on systems that plan, execute or adapt in the geosciences. This can include: - bespoke and LLM-powered agents with tool use over instruments and models - software that makes such systems buildable: orchestration frameworks, control interfaces, benchmarks, testbeds and digital twins for training and evaluation - instrument, sensor and platform development for autonomous operation, with its power, communications and field-hardening constraints - adaptive, information-driven sampling and autonomous re-tasking of observing networks machine-generated hypotheses and how they are validated - closed-loop experimentation controlling instrumentation and iterating on results - real-time uncertainty quantification and provenance - accounts of real deployments, including failures - oversight, escalation protocols, evidential standards and levels-of-autonomy frameworks, including what regulators require before acting on autonomously generated evidence. Work at any level of maturity is welcome, from deployed systems to position papers, and from all career stages.
title: From autonomous sensing to autonomous science: agentic systems that decide what to measure or simulate next

description: In geoscientific applications, we observe a steady increase in the amount of data and in model complexity. This development is partly driven by technological advances that provide access to higher-resolution data, greater computational capabilities, and increasingly complex coupled numerical models. However, these advances also yield major challenges, since the resulting data amount and the number of model evaluations required are becoming infeasible with traditional evaluation methods. Therefore, many applications take advantage of scientific machine learning (SciML) approaches to overcome these challenges. However, the rapid development of new methods within this field highlights one fundamental challenge: existing benchmarks typically do not adequately represent the complexity, diversity, and requirements of real-case geoscientific applications. Many commonly used benchmarks rely on relatively simple datasets, assume idealized problem setting and are defined for narrow tasks only. This makes it difficult to assess advances in SciML for their transferability and performance for a broader range of geoscientific applications. To bridge this gap, this session welcomes contributions presenting complex, realistic benchmarks that enable the validation of scientific machine learning approaches for both numerical modelling and scientific data analysis. We particularly encourage benchmarks that capture current challenges such as: large and heterogeneous datasets, high-dimensional features in terms of the spatial-temporal relationships and the parameter space, multi-scale and complex coupled physical processes, limited or noisy observations, and the need for computationally efficient, resource-aware benchmark designs that enable model training and evaluation under limited computational budgets. We encourage submission from different geoscientific disciplines as benchmark requirements can differ significantly across the domains. At the same time, we welcome contributions from the application side that illustrate limitations of existing benchmarks and discuss which characteristics need to be preserved and represented by SciML methods to be beneficial in the given application context. The session aims to bring together researchers developing SciML methods, benchmarks, and domain-specific applications. By connecting these perspectives, we seek to identify current gaps in benchmarking practices.
title: Benchmarks for Scientific Machine Learning in the context of Geoscientific Applications

description: Extreme weather and climate events can disrupt many aspects of human societies, including physical and mental health, livelihoods, food and water service, infrastructure, and human mobility. Yet these impacts are still often assessed one hazard at a time, even though severe consequences frequently arise from interacting hazards. Compound events may involve concurrent, sequential, spatially connected, or preconditioned hazards, and their impacts can be nonlinear, cascading, and greater than the sum of impacts associated with individual hazards. This session focuses on the impacts of compound weather and climate events on human societies. We welcome research on diverse types of compound events, including, but not limited to, heat and drought; drought followed by wildfire; extreme heat combined with wildfire; tropical cyclones accompanied or followed by extreme rainfall, flooding, and storm surge; and rapid transitions between opposing climate extremes. Contributions may examine mortality and morbidity, mental health, migration and displacement, food and water insecurity, livelihood losses and financial security, health-system burdens, infrastructure failure, conflict, and structural inequality. We particularly encourage work addressing unequal exposure, vulnerability, adaptive capacity, resilience, and recovery. This session welcomes empirical, modelling, qualitative, participatory, and mixed-methods studies at any spatial scale. Relevant topics include definitions and metrics; detection and attribution; historical trends and future projections; evidence linking compound events to human outcomes; causal inference and uncertainty assessment; integration of climate data with administrative records, surveys, remote sensing, and community knowledge; and applications to early warning, anticipatory action, adaptation, preparedness, risk communication, and equitable risk reduction. By bringing together climate and Earth-system science, epidemiology, public health, geography, economics, sociology, demography, engineering, disaster-risk research, and public policy and practice, the session aims to advance knowledge of how compound events are anticipated, measured, experienced, and managed.
divisions: Impacts of Climate and Weather in an Inter- and Transdisciplinary context
title: Compound weather and climate events: Cascading impacts on human societies

description: Scientific assessments play a critical role in translating rapidly evolving climate research into actionable knowledge for decision-makers. From the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) to national, regional, sectoral, and local assessment efforts, assessments provide structured syntheses of evidence that help governments, communities, businesses, and civil society evaluate climate risks, identify response options, and make informed decisions under uncertainty. Assessments increasingly serve as a bridge between scientific understanding and practical action, supporting planning processes ranging from national adaptation strategies to community resilience and infrastructure investments. At the same time, data systems have become foundational to assessment practice. The growing availability of observations, model outputs, socioeconomic datasets, and decision-support tools creates new opportunities for assessment, while also raising challenges related to transparency, traceability, accessibility, stewardship, and long-term usability. International data support activities underscore the importance of robust data infrastructure in enabling credible and policy-relevant assessments. This session invites contributions on the development, application, and future of climate assessment activities across all scales. We welcome presentations from national and international assessment programs, regional and local assessment initiatives, Indigenous and community-led assessment efforts, and organizations that employ assessments to support planning and decision-making. Contributions addressing assessment methodologies, uncertainty communication, stakeholder engagement, knowledge synthesis, data stewardship, data rescue, emerging data products, and assessment-informed policy or practice are especially encouraged. The session will also highlight emerging initiatives, including efforts by scientific societies such as the American Geophysical Union’s Science Assessment Initiative, that seek to strengthen the global assessment ecosystem and accelerate the delivery of decision-relevant climate knowledge.
divisions: Impacts of Climate and Weather in an Inter- and Transdisciplinary context
title: Science Assessment and Climate Data for Decision-Making: Connecting Knowledge, Risk, and Action Across Scales

description: High-impact climate and weather events typically result from the interaction of multiple climate and weather drivers, as well as vulnerability and exposure, across various spatial and temporal scales. Such compound events often cause more severe socio-economic impacts than single-hazard events, rendering traditional univariate extreme event analyses and risk assessment techniques insufficient. It is, therefore, crucial to develop new methodologies that account for the possible interaction of multiple physical and societal drivers when analyzing high-impact events under present and future conditions. This session aims to address several challenges and topics. These include: (1) identifying the compounding drivers, including physical drivers (e.g., modes of variability) and/or drivers of vulnerability and exposure, of the most impactful events; (2) Developing methods to better shape the definition and classification of compound events, i.e. legitimate the ‘cut-offs’ in the considered number of hazard types or variables to ultimately disentangle enough information for decision-making; (3) Understanding whether and how often novel compound events, including record-shattering events, will emerge in the future; (4) Explicitly addressing and communicating uncertainties in present-day and future assessments (e.g., via climate storylines/scenarios); (5) Disentangling the contribution of climate change in recently observed events and future projections (attribution); (6) Employing novel Single Model Initial-condition Large Ensemble simulations, which provide hundreds to thousands of years of plausible weather, to better study compound events. (7) Developing novel statistical methods (e.g., machine learning, artificial intelligence, and climate model emulators) for studying compound events; (8) Assessing the weather forecast skill for compound events at different temporal scales; (9) Evaluating the performance of novel statistical methods, climate and impact models, in representing compound events and developing novel methods for constraining/reducing uncertainties (e.g., multivariate bias correction and observational constraints); and (10) engaging with stakeholders to ensure the relevance of the aforementioned analyses. We invite presentations on all aspects of compound events, including but not limited to the topics and research challenges described above.
divisions: Impacts of Climate and Weather in an Inter- and Transdisciplinary context
title: Compound weather and climate events

description: The impacts of weather and climate extremes depend on interactions between physical hazards, exposure, and vulnerability. Beyond intensity, the duration, timing, spatial extent, and co-occurrence of extremes can strongly influence their consequences. Understanding these relationships is essential for assessing how climate change alters risks to societies and ecosystems. This interdisciplinary session connects research on the physical drivers of weather and climate extremes with assessments of their societal and environmental impacts. We particularly welcome studies that investigate how the mechanisms and characteristics of extremes shape their consequences, and how these relationships change under different climatic and socioeconomic conditions. Contributions are invited on: - Physical drivers and impact pathways: Atmospheric dynamics, ocean–atmosphere interactions, land–atmosphere coupling, and thermodynamic processes shaping extremes and their consequences. Topics include the roles of persistence, spatial extent, antecedent conditions, and compound or sequential hazards in determining impacts. - Attribution of extremes and their consequences: Assessments of how anthropogenic climate change and natural variability influence extremes and associated impacts, including approaches that distinguish climatic influences from changes in exposure and vulnerability. - Prediction and assessment of climate risks: Integration of observations, climate simulations, statistical approaches, and impact models to understand and anticipate risks under present and future conditions. Contributions may address cross-sector and cascading impacts, impact-based forecasting, and the implications of improved physical understanding for preparedness and adaptation. We welcome observational, modelling, theoretical, and empirical studies addressing heatwaves, droughts, heavy precipitation, floods, fire weather, and compound extremes. Contributions may examine individual links between physical drivers, hazards, and impacts; interdisciplinary studies connecting these elements are particularly encouraged. The session aims to strengthen dialogue between extreme-event science and impact research, advancing understanding of how physical climate processes translate into societal and environmental risks.
divisions: Impacts of Climate and Weather in an Inter- and Transdisciplinary context
title: Causes and consequences of weather and climate extremes: From physical drivers to systemic risks

description: Mangrove ecosystems provide a series of services, such as coastal protection, carbon sequestration, and biodiversity support. Despite the growing popularity of restoration initiatives, many of them continue to show low long-term survival rates. The main cause for this is the disregard for hydrological and sedimentological constraints as well as poor monitoring protocols. This session aims to connect researchers, practitioners, policy-makers, and others to combine ecological research, engineering principles, and coastal management experience. The empirical evidence, guidelines, and practical insights have the potential to subsidize the improvement of mangrove restoration strategies. We invite submissions addressing, but not only, the following themes: 1) case studies and lessons learned; 2) hydrology and geomorphology; 3) restoration methodologies; 4) monitoring and blue carbon accounting; and 5) socio-ecological dynamics.
title: Mangrove Restoration in Practice: Case Studies and Implementation Guidelines

description: Nature-based coastal solutions (NBCS), such as saltmarsh and mangrove restoration, living shorelines, beach and dune rehabilitation, and reef structures (artificial and natural), are increasingly promoted as sustainable responses to the complex challenges of coastal zone management. These approaches aim to harness natural processes to stabilise coastlines, reduce flood and erosion risk, enhance biodiversity, and provide co-benefits, including carbon storage and improved water quality. While the physical and ecological advantages of NBCS are supported by growing evidence, significant uncertainties remain about their long-term effectiveness, particularly under changing climate and socioeconomic conditions. These knowledge gaps are especially critical for informing policy and investment decisions in coastal infrastructure and adaptation strategies. We invite contributions that integrate coastal geoscience, engineering, and broader system-level thinking to evaluate the long-term performance, risks, and trade-offs of NBCS across diverse environmental and governance contexts. We encourage submissions that include, but are not limited to: (a) case studies on NBCS implementation across varied coastal geomorphologies and hydroclimatic regimes, with evidence of long-term outcomes or monitoring data; (b) modelling studies that assess NBCS performance under future climate and sea-level rise scenarios; (c) innovations in field methods, remote sensing, and data integration for evaluating NBCS impacts on geomorphic and ecological processes; (d) systems-based approaches (e.g., coupled human-natural models, scenario planning) that address feedbacks between NBCS, coastal dynamics, and socioeconomic systems; (e) studies that focus on advancing the engineering design of NBCS and may include recommendations for types and values of design parameters and criteria; (f) perspectives on the institutional, regulatory, and financial frameworks influencing the deployment and long-term maintenance of NBCS. We particularly welcome interdisciplinary studies that combine geoscientific analysis with insights from ecology, engineering, planning, and policy, and encourage dialogue on how transdisciplinary approaches can help guide the design, implementation, and long-term governance of effective NBCS.
title: Nature-based coastal solutions: integrating geoscience, engineering, and societal perspectives on successes, failures, and future uncertainties

description: The interconnections between climate, environment, and human health are becoming increasingly apparent, as climate change poses growing threats to public welfare worldwide. Rising temperatures, more frequent and intense extreme weather events (e.g., heatwaves, floods, droughts), and environmental stressors such as air pollution, degraded ecosystems, or shifting land use patterns have direct and indirect impacts on population health. Climate-related changes also affect the distribution of vector- and waterborne diseases, contribute to the severity of wildfires, and influence mental and physical health outcomes. Addressing these multifaceted challenges requires close collaboration between disciplines, bringing together climate scientists, epidemiologists, environmental and public health researchers, as well as social scientists. This session provides a platform for presenting recent advances in understanding and quantifying environment- and climate-related health risks through the integration of diverse data sources, including remote sensing, environmental monitoring, climatological measurements, health records, and socio-demographic information. We welcome contributions that explore methods to assess climate-sensitive exposures (e.g., heat, air pollution, allergens), model health impacts across different temporal and spatial scales, develop risk maps, and evaluate adaptation or mitigation strategies. Approaches using machine learning, statistical modelling, scenario analysis, and other innovative tools are encouraged. Both empirical studies and methodological advances, whether focused on local, regional, or global scales, are invited. The session aims to foster cross-sectoral exchange and support the development of data-driven strategies for climate-resilient and equitable public health.
title: Climate, Extremes, and Health: Risks and Impacts on Population Health

description: Decision-makers are increasingly required to consider extreme weather events as part of evaluating, disclosing, and responding to complex climate risks. Interdisciplinary approaches are required to properly understand these complex risks and to inform the best responses, including mitigation and adaptation approaches. In this session we examine how interdisciplinary teams across academic, industry, and government sectors are working to understand extreme weather events and their changes in a warming climate. Event types can include but are not limited to temperature, precipitation, wind, and compound extremes, and their impacts on people, the built environment, or the natural world. A specific focus will be on collaborative efforts to find and solve shared challenges across disciplines. Topics of interest include - physical climate science required for decision making - early warning systems and their use in real-world scenarios - risk management in the financial and insurance sectors - impact-based understanding of extreme weather events - assessment of varying hazard, exposure, and/or vulnerability - storyline approaches to risk understanding.
title: Interdisciplinary approaches to addressing complex climate risks related to extreme weather events

description: Climate risk and adaptation assessments generally estimate aggregate damages, avoided impacts, or cost-effectiveness. Yet aggregate metrics mask who is exposed, who can adapt, who benefits from adaptation investments, and who bears residual, transferred, or cascading risk. This session asks how conclusions about climate risk and adaptation change when distributional outcomes, adaptive capacity and adaptation limits become explicit components of assessment and decision-making. We invite quantitative, data-driven and mixed-method contributions representing inequality throughout the assessment chain, from hazard, exposure and vulnerability to impacts, adaptation appraisal and decision-making. Of particular interest are studies moving beyond generic exposure and vulnerability to capture differentiated and dynamic adaptive capacity linked to income, wealth, access to services and infrastructure, housing tenure, mobility, informality and demography. A central focus is the operationalisation of equity and justice as measurable outcomes. This includes inequality in baseline climate risk (e.g. via revised exposure and vulnerability functions), the distribution of adaptation costs and benefits, inequalities created or exacerbated by adaptation itself, and limits to adaptation. We welcome work that stratifies impacts and avoided losses across population groups, embeds equity metrics in cost-benefit and multi-criteria assessment, examines non-monetised losses, or tests whether conventional welfare and efficiency metrics underrepresent particular populations. Contributions on adaptation-induced inequalities, including displacement, green gentrification, unequal infrastructure protection, and the exclusion of underreported populations, are especially welcome. The session spans hazards, sectors and scales, including urban systems, critical infrastructure, health, accessibility, macroeconomic impacts, and loss and damage. We particularly encourage assessments of direct, indirect and cascading risks, asking who inherits risk when adaptation protects particular places, infrastructures or groups while shifting impacts elsewhere. We also welcome methodological work on data challenges in distributional risk assessment, including high-resolution socioeconomic data, Earth observation, mobility and geospatial data, citizen science, and alternative sources complementing conventional statistics.
title: Inequality and justice in climate risk and adaptation: bridging impact analysis and socio-economic assessment

description: Nature-based Solutions (NbS) are “actions to protect, conserve, restore, sustainably use and manage natural or modified ecosystems, that address socio-economic and environmental challenges, while simultaneously providing human well-being, resilience and biodiversity benefits”. Within the framework of a global ecosystem approach, NbS must encompass ecological, societal, political, economic and cultural issues at all levels, from the individual to the collective, from local to national, from the public or private sphere. As underlined by the IPCC and IPBES, climate change and biodiversity loss are deeply interconnected and must be addressed jointly. This session therefore focuses on how NbS can serve as adaptation strategies to climate change, while simultaneously preserving or restoring biodiversity. Considering various ecosystems (marine and coastal, urban, cropland, mountainous, forest, rivers…), NbS as climate change adaptation solutions includes the adaptation to: sea level rise (flooding and erosion), changes of the water regime (floods, droughts, water quality and availability), rise in temperatures (heat waves, forest fires, drought, energy consumption), plant stress and increase of pests (variation of yields, forest dieback), to minimize their associated social and economic negative impacts. Therefore, this session aims to promote discussion integrating multiple disciplines related to ecosystem restoration, preservation and management, to put forward the complexity that is often hidden by simplifying hypotheses and approaches (sector-based silo approach, homogeneity of environments...). Specific topics of interest are the followings: - Complexity: nature of ecosystems and risk of oversimplification, interconnection between NbS and complementary areas, consideration of uncertainties - Scales: spatial scales with the integration of NbS in their environment, and temporal scales considering sustainability over time, variability of bio-physical processes and climate change effects - Ecosystem services: bio-geophysical processes, spatial shift between the location of NbS and the beneficiaries one, modification under climate change (tipping point), co-benefits or negative effects - Assessment and indicators: measurement and modelling protocols, capacity to measure the complexity, resilience and stability of NbS - Co-development with stakeholders, engaging civil society, and integrating NbS into education, aligned with IAHS HELPING Decade objectives.
title: Nature-based Solutions for climate change adaptation
