description: Several subsystems of the Earth have been suggested to possibly react abruptly at critical levels of anthropogenic forcing. Examples of such potential Tipping Elements include the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, the polar ice sheets, tropical and boreal forests, as well as the tropical monsoon systems. Interactions between the different Tipping Elements may either have stabilizing or destabilizing effects on the other subsystems, potentially leading to cascades of abrupt transitions. The critical forcing levels at which abrupt transitions occur have recently been associated with Tipping Points. It is paramount to determine the critical forcing levels (and the associated uncertainties) beyond which the systems in question will abruptly change their state, with potentially devastating climatic, ecological, and societal impacts. For this purpose, we need to substantially enhance our understanding of the dynamics of the Tipping Elements and their interactions, on the basis of paleoclimatic evidence, present-day observations, and models spanning the entire hierarchy of complexity. Moreover, to be able to mitigate - or prepare for - potential future transitions, early warning signals have to be identified and monitored in both observations and models. This multidisciplinary session invites contributions that address Tipping Points in the Earth system from the different perspectives of all relevant disciplines, including - the mathematical theory of tipping points - methods to anticipate critical transitions from data - tipping points in climate models across the hierarchy, including comprehensive Earth system models - climatic, ecological and socioeconomic impacts of tipping events - decision theory in the presence of uncertain tipping point estimates and uncertain impacts
title: Tipping Transitions in the Earth System

description: Earth System Sciences (ESS) datasets are continuing to increase in terms of resolution and size. They are crucial to support critical activities such as climate change policymaking and weather forecasting. The storage and shareability of these datasets have become a pressing concern within the scientific community. State-of-the-art applications and ongoing and upcoming community initiatives, such as digital twins and the CMIP7, produce outputs so large that even the most advanced data centres and infrastructures struggle not only to store them but also to ensure their usability and processability, including by downstream machine learning applications. Similarly, the Copernicus program’s archive of satellite observations will grow exponentially in the coming years. With future investment in hardware likely to remain constrained, data volumes are increasingly restricting scientific progress. An essential and viable way forward is to explore data compression that balances efficiency with the needs of diverse stakeholders. Nevertheless, many researchers remain cautious about lossy compression, concerned that critical information or features may be lost for specific downstream use cases. Identifying these requirements and ensuring they are preserved during compression are essential steps toward building trust so that compression can become widely adopted across the community. This session will present and discuss recent advances in and concerns about data compression for ESS datasets, focusing on: 1) Advances in and reviews of methods, including classical, learning-based, and hybrid approaches, with attention to computational efficiency of compression and decompression 2) Inter-disciplinary case studies of using compressed data in scientific workflows, both with encouraging and cautionary conclusions 3) Methods and framework to evaluate datasets and data infrastructure 4) Understanding the domain- and use-case-specific requirements for safe and performant compression, and developing methods that provide these guarantees for lossy compression 5) Exploration of novel workflows enabled by machine learning that reduce pressure on disk space, e.g. through compressing input data into lower-dimensional latent spaces This session aims to address the concerns shared by the community during EGU 2026, and will conclude with a debate about how data producers, compression researchers, and domain scientists can co-steer the future development of compression for ESS.
title: Data compression for Earth System Sciences datasets

description: Making scientific data accessible, discoverable, explorable, and understandable is central to good scientific practice. At the same time, increasing spatial and temporal resolutions of models, observations, and remote sensing products are driving rapidly growing data volumes and complexity. Earth system science data are also increasingly used beyond research, for decision support, knowledge transfer, and applications involving stakeholders and other end users. These developments create challenges across the entire data and information chain, from infrastructures and metadata to interoperable services, analysis and visualization tools, and user-oriented applications. AI and agent-based workflows add a new dimension: data and services must be not only accessible and understandable to humans, but also discoverable, interpretable, and usable by AI applications and autonomous agents. This requires research infrastructures that are machine-actionable, interoperable, robust, and trustworthy, while significant gaps and barriers towards genuinely AI-ready infrastructures remain. This session brings together scientists, research software engineers, data infrastructure experts, AI researchers, and practitioners working on platforms and tools that make Earth system science data accessible, discoverable, interoperable, explorable, trustworthy, and actionable. We welcome contributions on: Open-source platforms for data discovery, exploration, analysis, and visualization AI-ready research data infrastructures and platforms Machine-actionable metadata, semantic descriptions, APIs, and standardized interfaces Robust and trustworthy services addressing provenance, quality, reliability, and reproducibility Gaps, barriers, and show-stoppers towards AI-ready infrastructures, and approaches to overcome them Decision-support systems and co-designed solutions for scientific and non-scientific users Integration and discovery across distributed and decentralized infrastructures AI-assisted data discovery, exploration, visualization, and access We particularly encourage contributions based on community-driven standards, interoperable interfaces, open-source technologies, and FAIR principles, including approaches that address remaining challenges towards robust, trustworthy, and AI-ready Earth system science infrastructures.
title: From FAIR Data to AI-Ready Earth System Science Platforms: Discovery, Exploration and Visualization

description: AI is fundamentally changing the way we do science. However, making proper use of AI in Earth System Sciences (ESS) fundamentally relies on the ability to access and integrate heterogeneous observational, experimental and simulation data across the atmosphere, land surfaces, ocean, solid Earth, biodiversity and human-environment systems. Research infrastructures have made major progress in aggregating, harmonizing, curating and providing access to these resources through FAIR data and interoperable services. The next challenge is to make this distributed knowledge ecosystem not only human-accessible, but also machine-actionable and AI-ready. The rapid emergence of foundation models, generative AI and agentic systems is opening new opportunities to discover, integrate and analyse Earth System data, substantially improve physical modeling, automatize workflows and reach a new level of scientific knowledge discovery across disciplinary and organizational boundaries. Initiatives such as GenAI4Earth, EOSC-ARENA and Earth-AID illustrate this transition towards trustworthy and interoperable AI and generative AI tools embedded within the EOSC ecosystem. This evolution raises a fundamental question: how can research infrastructures evolve from providers of FAIR data and digital services into an integrated ecosystem supporting AI-assisted and AI-driven scientific discovery? The session will explore how research infrastructures, computing infrastructures and AI communities can work together to build this ecosystem. Contributions are invited that: · demonstrate synergies between research infrastructures enabling cross-domain Earth System Science; · present AI-ready data, generative AI services supporting scientific discovery; · showcase integrated workflows combining data, models, and AI services across infrastructures; · address interoperability, provenance, reproducibility, explainability, trustworthiness and European technological sovereignty; · showcase approaches on how to build standards in ethics, scientific integrity or sustainability into AI services for ESS. The session aims to bring together research infrastructures, AI developers and data communities with Earth system scientists and technology providers to discuss concrete pathways towards a federated European ecosystem in which FAIR data, AI models and computational services can be seamlessly combined to accelerate reproducible and trustworthy Earth System Science.
title: From FAIR data to AI-ready Earth System Science: Connecting Research Infrastructures and Generative AI services through EOSC

description: Digital research infrastructures have changed how scientific data are managed, shared and reused. However, increasingly data-intensive, interdisciplinary and AI-enabled science demands fresh thinking. What if we could reimagine research data infrastructure beyond today’s technologies, institutional structures and established ways of working? Inspired by the legacy of Dr Michael Diepenbroek, a pioneer in research data infrastructure and open science, this session invites bold, unconventional, and even seemingly crazy ideas that could transform the future of research data infrastructure. Beyond his pioneering work with PANGAEA (https://www.pangaea.de/), Michael inspired collaboration, connected disciplines and helped shape the global research data community. This session aims to carry forward that spirit of curiosity, collaboration and thinking beyond boundaries. We welcome provocative, forward-looking contributions covering four themes: (1) Technology and Innovation: Exploring disruptive technologies, novel architectures and bold approaches including AI to building interconnected and future-ready data infrastructures. (2) Data Practices and Standards: Rethinking data management, sharing, preservation and reuse beyond established FAIR, CARE, TRUST and open science practices. (3) People and Capabilities: Reimagining skills, roles, cross-disciplinary collaboration and human–AI partnerships. (4) Governance and Sustainability: Exploring transformative approaches to data ownership, trust, stewardship, institutional collaboration and funding models in response to shifting geopolitical, economic and societal landscapes. (5) Resilience and Endurance: Envisioning innovative architectures, technologies and strategies to ensure research data infrastructures remain secure, interoperable, adaptable and operational over the long term. We also encourage blue-sky ideas that may seem unrealistic today but could underpin tomorrow’s scientific advances. Ideas need not be fully developed or technically proven. Originality, ambition and the potential to challenge conventional thinking are especially welcome.
title: Beyond the Possible: Bold Ideas for the Future Resilience of Research Data Infrastructure in Earth Sciences - Celebrating the Visionary Legacy of Dr Michael Diepenbroek (PANGAEA)

description: Water underpins every aspect of life, from healthy ecosystems to economic prosperity and human well-being. Climate change intensifies risks such as droughts, floods, and water quality degradation; a reality starkly evident across Europe in recent years. In this context, ensuring water resilience becomes an urgent priority. One year after the adoption of the EU Water Resilience Strategy (2025), significant efforts are needed across European regions to align governance, financing, and systemic innovation for protecting water resources and fostering a water-smart economy. Nature-based Solutions (NbS) are central to achieving these ambitions. By restoring ecosystems and their biodiversity, enhancing natural water retention, and reinforcing connectivity between terrestrial and aquatic systems, NbS offer transformative pathways to strengthen socio-economic-ecological resilience. However, moving from strategic ambition to practical and large-scale deployment has revealed complex real-world challenges. From regulatory and institutional bottlenecks to financial hurdles, social resistance, technical performance gaps, and a widespread lack of specialised technical expertise, empirical know-how, and operational capacity among solution providers, the path to mainstreaming NbS is rarely linear. This session aims to critically examine the reality of NbS projects one year into the EU Water Resilience Strategy framework. We invite contributions from both recently initiated projects and longer-standing NbS experiences that offer valuable evidence and lessons for the Strategy. Submissions should showcase both aspects of NbS implementation: success stories on one hand, but also the concrete barriers, unexpected outcomes, failures, and trade-offs encountered along the implementation process and the strategies used to overcome them. Submissions may present real-world case studies demonstrating how institutional, social, or technical hurdles were successfully navigated through adaptive management and problem-solving. Finally, submissions showcasing long-term monitoring, measurable impacts, potential for scalability, and NbS co-benefits for water availability, disaster risk reduction, and ecosystem management are highly encouraged, ensuring that the discussion bridges scientific evidence with real-world impact to enhance water resilience.
title: Mainstreaming Nature-based Solutions for the EU Water Resilience Strategy: evidence, lessons and achievements.

description: The hazard isn't the event; the hazard is the sequence. Disaster risk is usually assessed event by event, yet many of the most damaging outcomes arise when hazards follow one another. Earthquakes alter drainage, slopes and sediment supply before the next flood or monsoon; floods weaken structures before the next earthquake; wildfires change how catchments respond to rainfall. Two examples show how one event changes the conditions under which the next unfolds. The 2015 Gorkha earthquake in Nepal was followed by increased landsliding in the monsoons that came after it. The 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquakes in Türkiye were followed by flooding in the Asi (Orontes) catchment in 2026. Understanding such sequences means connecting physical processes to the people, buildings and institutions that experience them. This session invites inter- and transdisciplinary contributions on sequential and cascading hazards and their consequences. Topics include field evidence and reconnaissance of hazard sequences; modelling of how earlier events change hazard, exposure and vulnerability, including damage accumulation; health, housing and indoor-environment outcomes in multi-hazard settings; governance, accountability and responsibility for multi-hazard risk; and methods for transferring lessons across hazards, regions and institutional contexts. We welcome geoscientists, engineers, public health researchers, social scientists and practitioners, and particularly encourage early-career researchers and colleagues from affected regions. The session complements multi-hazard assessment sessions in NH by bringing physical and societal perspectives on hazard sequences into one conversation.
title: The hazard is the sequence: path dependency and cascading risk in multi-hazard settings

description: River deltas and coastal plains are highly vital environments, offering a wide range of ecosystem services that make them hotspots of biodiversity and human settlement, and key for economic production and food security. Human activities such as river damming, resource extraction and land-use land cover change have significantly altered coastal-deltaic morphodynamics, interact with and accelerate biophysical impacts from climate change. Consequently, these low-elevation environments face increased risks of land subsidence, erosion, relative sea-level rise, flooding and salinity intrusion, all of which impact the functioning of coastal social-ecological systems. These accelerating pressures are promoting key advances in understanding the driving processes, the threats generated and the ways humans are addressing these through management. Developments have come from earth observations using remote sensing, and from modelling, increasingly supported by artificial intelligence, in addition to conceptual advances in critically analyzing the human-coastal wetland relationship from both geoscience and management perspectives, preferably interlinked. Critical research gaps persist, however, regarding all aspects of processes and geomorphic responses to these threats, and these limit our capacity to predict and manage coastal lowland and delta change. A more integrated, multi- and interdisciplinary understanding of the interacting processes and impacts is needed to manage river deltas and coastal plains in a sustainable and inclusive manner. This requires taking a system’s perspective, connecting insights from coastal geomorphology and geology, hydrology and hydrogeology, natural hazards and disaster risk science, as well as human geography and social sciences. This session provides an interdisciplinary platform that welcomes contributions that advance an integrated understanding of the emerging changes, pressures and the interconnected processes and hazards they generate; assess the implications for coping capacity and resilience; explore developments in earth observation and modelling efforts to address them; point out persisting knowledge gaps and identify opportunities for effective management and sustainable development of these coastal lowlands.
title: Sinking, shrinking and saltier river deltas and coastal plains: interacting processes, hazards, impacts, knowledge gaps, and opportunities for adaptation

description: Climate change poses a significant threat to sustainability. It disproportionately affects different social groups, intensifying interconnected risks across socio-ecological systems and challenging conventional approaches to disaster risk reduction and adaptation. These challenges are particularly pronounced in climate-sensitive ecosystems, such as arid and semi-arid regions, where land degradation, water scarcity, biodiversity loss, and socio-economic vulnerability intersect. Nature-based and community-led strategies offer effective, context-specific solutions that reduce climate risks, restore ecosystems, enhance biodiversity and ecosystem services, and support local livelihoods, enabling sustainable and equitable adaptation even in highly constrained environments such as drylands. This session invites contributions that explore how nature-based and community-led approaches support disaster risk reduction, ecosystem restoration, and climate change adaptation across diverse ecological and socio-economic contexts, with a particular focus on research that: - Assesses the effectiveness of these strategies in reducing risk and enhancing climate resilience - Examines socio-ecological trade-offs and synergies by integrating ecological and social science perspectives within systems-based approaches - Evaluates long-term resilience and restoration outcomes across varied ecological and socio-economic contexts, including arid and semi-arid landscapes - Engages with Indigenous and local knowledge systems, emphasizing culturally grounded and community-driven solutions - Investigates governance challenges, structural barriers, and enabling conditions, and explores inclusive frameworks that support equity, participation, and sustainability - Investigates synergies and trade-offs between nature-based approaches and conventional measures - Examines the effectiveness, resilience, and scalability of specific nature-based solution typologies (e.g., water harvesting, vegetation restoration, agroforestry) - Examines innovative monitoring and assessment tools (e.g., citizen science, remote sensing, hydrological modelling, eDNA, AI) to evaluate, optimize, and scale nature-based and community-led strategies This session is supported by the RISK-KAN Working Group on “Nature-Based and Community-Led Climate Risk Strategies.” Contributions from diverse regions are welcome, with a particular emphasis on early-career researchers and practitioners from underrepresented areas.
title: Nature-based and community-led strategies for disaster risk reduction, ecosystem restoration (land, water and biodiversity), and climate change adaptation in socio-ecological systems

description: Cities worldwide are increasingly exposed to compound extreme weather and climate events—hazard combinations that occur concurrently, in close sequence, or across connected regions, such as heatwave–drought co-occurrence, storm surge coinciding with pluvial flooding, or extreme heat following tropical cyclones. Because their drivers interact and their impacts cascade through critical infrastructure, ecosystems, and vulnerable populations, compound events often inflict damages far exceeding the sum of individual hazards, challenging conventional single-hazard approaches to urban risk management. This session aims to bring together researchers across climate science, hydrology, urban studies, engineering, and disaster risk reduction to advance the understanding, prediction, and governance of compound extremes in urban environments. We welcome contributions addressing, but not limited to: 1. Physical drivers and dynamics of compound events (concurrent, sequential, and spatially compounding) in a changing climate; 2. Detection, attribution, and projection of compound extremes using observations, reanalyses, climate model ensembles, and event storylines; 3. Novel analytical and modeling approaches, including statistical dependence modeling, machine learning, and AI-based methods; 4. Impacts of compound events on urban systems, including infrastructure networks, public health, energy and water security, and cascading or compounding risks; 5. Assessment and enhancement of urban resilience, including risk assessment frameworks, early warning systems, adaptation planning, nature-based solutions, and governance strategies; 6. Case studies from diverse urban contexts—including the Global South—and co-production approaches engaging stakeholders and practitioners. We particularly encourage interdisciplinary submissions, contributions from early-career scientists, and studies that bridge the gap between hazard science and actionable resilience planning for cities.
title: Compound Extreme Weather and Climate Events and Urban Resilience: From Hazard Interactions to Adaptive Solutions

description: Measuring progress in climate adaptation is essential to track resilience-building, guide investments, and inform policy. Yet, adaptation measurement remains fragmented and contested: while some frameworks focus on process indicators (e.g., planning, governance, capacity), others emphasize outputs (e.g., implemented measures), or outcomes and impacts (e.g., reduced vulnerability, enhanced resilience). Each approach has strengths and limitations, and their combination is critical to capturing the complexity of adaptation and informing adaptation action. This session invites contributions that advance understanding and practice in measuring and evaluating progress in climate adaptation across scales, hazards and sectors. We welcome research that develops or applies frameworks, methods, and tools for adaptation monitoring, evaluation, and learning (MEL), as well as critical reflections on their usability, comparability, and policy relevance. Topics of interest include (but are not limited to): - Development and application of process, output, outcome, and impact indicators for adaptation, with a focus on outcomes and impacts. - Approaches to integrating multiple indicator types for holistic assessment. - Use of novel data sources and methods (Earth observation, citizen science, AI, participatory surveys) for MEL. - Cross-scale measurement: from local initiatives to national reporting and global stocktake. - Addressing uncertainty, attribution, and time horizons in adaptation measurement within the MEL process. - Considerations of equity, justice, and governance in defining and applying adaptation metrics. - Case studies showcasing practical experiences of tracking adaptation progress across geographies and contexts. By bringing together conceptual, methodological, and applied perspectives, this session seeks to identify pathways towards robust, inclusive, and actionable adaptation metrics that can guide decision-making and enhance accountability under the EU Mission on Adaptation, the Paris Agreement, and other global frameworks.
title: Measuring climate adaptation: from processes and outputs to outcomes and impacts

description: The year 2026 has been marked by a sequence of destructive landslides and earthquake-triggered ground failures across different geodynamic and climatic settings, offering the opportunity to compare hazard mechanisms, early-warning performance, and civil protection responses on a global scale. In January (16th and 25th), a destructive landslide hits the South of Italy, compromising roads, building stability, and essential services, and prompting evacuation of 1,500 people. Elsewhere, large earthquakes triggered severe secondary hazards: a Mw 7.8 quake offshore Mindanao, Philippines (8 June); a seismic doublet (Mw 7.2/7.5) in northern Venezuela (24 June) causing slope failures on steep coastal terrain; a Mw ~7.4 quake in Chocó, Colombia (10 August); and a Mw 7.7 quake off Flores, Indonesia (15 August), which blocked the Trans-Flores Highway. On 26 August, a glacier collapse in the Langtang range triggered a debris avalanche and flash flood along the Nepal–China border, destroying infrastructure and leaving over a thousand people missing. This session aims to bring together scientists, practitioners, and civil protection agencies to discuss detection, characterization, monitoring, and response strategies applicable across these diverse contexts. We invite contributions addressing, but not limited to: • Remote sensing analysis (InSAR, optical/radar imagery, LiDAR, UAV) for detection, mapping, and rapid damage assessment); • Monitoring systems and early warning, including geotechnical instrumentation and seismic detection of slope failures; • Geomorphological characterization, including susceptibility mapping and controls on landslide reactivation; • Civil protection and emergency response, including red-zone delimitation, evacuation planning, and cross-border coordination; • Comparative and multi-hazard perspectives, linking seismically-induced, gravitationally-induced, and cryosphere-related slope failures, and exploring cascading hazard chains. The session welcomes case studies, methodological advances, and policy-oriented contributions that can inform more effective cascading risks reduction strategies worldwide.
title: Compound and Cascading Landslide and Earthquake-Triggered Ground-Failure Events: Rapid Response, Monitoring, and Environmental Vulnerability in 2026

description: The implementation of many policies on the environment, climate, public health, and other societal challeges often involves the analysis of different scenarios for interventions or possible events. Advances in simulation methods – physical and data-driven – as well as simulation tools offer significant potential for making investigations more realistic, more accessible, or more tractable. At the same time, high-performance computing infrastructures like the EuroHPC systems allow scaling such analyses to global scales at sufficiently high resolutions. This is, for example, a key driver underpinning the European Destination Earth (DestinE) initiative, that aims to create a “digital twin” of the Earth System supporting exactly those kinds of applications in a variety of sectors. This session explores how developments of novel applications that exploit [CV1.1]information from large-scale Earth System Models can be exploited to develop practical applications supporting policy implementation at regional and local level. Contributions are invited in the domains of climate adaptation, disaster risk management, or environmental policies, that present practical applications of interactive simulations in climate and sustainability planning. A key emphasis will be on demonstrating and quantifying the added value of tailored and/or interactive simulations for policy implementation.
title: Supporting policy implementation through interactions with Earth System models

description: Over the past few decades, landslide research has expanded considerably, producing a wealth of scientific insights. Our understanding of slope failure processes has advanced significantly, yet it remains unclear how effectively engineering geologists and geotechnical engineers focused on slope stabilization and landslide risk reduction are translating this knowledge into practice. This session aims to bring together researchers and practitioners from diverse backgrounds to: 1. Foster collaboration and networking across disciplinary boundaries 2. Encourage the exchange of theoretical insights and practical approaches to landslide investigation and mitigation 3. Promote more efficient use of limited resources for landslide risk reduction We particularly welcome contributions on topics such as: • Expanding the affordable use of innovative technologies for landslide detection and mapping (e.g., optical and radar satellite remote sensing) • Advances in subsurface characterization using customized geophysical methods (e.g., electrical resistivity, seismic tomography) • Integration of remote sensing and ground-based data for improved landslide monitoring • Engineering geological models as integrative tools for site-specific landslide risk mitigation • Data availability, quality issues, and handling geological uncertainty in slope stability modeling • Approaches to slope stability analysis, from empirical methods to advanced numerical models • Impacts of climate variability on landslide occurrence and engineered slope performance • Low-cost, reconnaissance-level hazard assessments in data-scarce and disaster-affected regions • Case histories of slope stabilization and landslide mitigation, including both successful and unsuccessful interventions • Knowledge transfer between scientists and engineers, and effective communication of landslide risk to civil protection authorities, policymakers, media, and the general public Session sponsored by the International Association of Engineering Geology and the Environment (IAEG – https://iaeg.info)
title: Advances in Landslide Investigation and Mitigation: Bridging Research and Engineering Geology Practice

description: Global initiatives such as REDD+, afforestation, reforestation, and restoration place forests at the centre of climate action. Yet these measures are highly context dependent and can create synergies and trade-offs across carbon sequestration, water availability, biodiversity, ecosystem functions, and human well-being. Afforestation can enhance carbon sequestration, reduce erosion, regulate soil moisture, and support atmospheric moisture recycling, while in some contexts reducing streamflow, altering surface albedo, or changing groundwater recharge. Forest change can also affect evapotranspiration, precipitation recycling, and downwind water availability, highlighting the importance of green water processes and governance across spatial scales, administrative boundaries, and sectors. The long-term effectiveness of forest-based climate action also depends on the capacity of forests as social–ecological systems to cope with, adapt to, and transform in response to disturbances and changing conditions. Compound and cascading disturbances, including drought, wildfire, heat, pests, and land-use pressures, can interact with institutional constraints and competing societal demands to undermine resilience. This session aims to advance understanding of how forests can contribute to climate mitigation and adaptation while maintaining or strengthening social–ecological resilience under changing hydroclimatic and societal conditions. We welcome interdisciplinary studies, modelling approaches, case studies, governance analyses, and decision-support tools addressing trade-offs, compound and cascading risks, and green water governance, including: · Social–ecological resilience, including adaptation, learning, participation, and cross-sectoral and cross-scale governance of the forest-water nexus · Forest–water–climate interactions, including soil moisture, evapotranspiration, moisture recycling, and blue–green water linkages · Co-benefits and trade-offs of forest-based mitigation for carbon sequestration, water availability, biodiversity, ecosystem functions, and society · Forest disturbances, compound and cascading impacts, institutional capacity, and adaptation · New indicators, scenarios, and decision-support approaches for resilient forest management . Forest–green and blue water governance, including monitoring, transboundary dependencies, cross-scale coordination, and cross-sectoral decision-making.
title: Pathways to Resilient and Multi-Functional Forests: Climate, Water, Biodiversity and Social-Ecological Benefits and Trade-Offs

description: Because they are highly interdependent, most infrastructure systems are vulnerable to disasters such as severe floods. An amazing amount of data has been made available to better anticipate the impact of severe floods and become more sustainable and resilient. Yet, integrating these data sources and modeling the impact of floods remains a challenge. Here, we develop a transferable, fact-calibrated, weakly supervised, physically constrained probabilistic modeling framework. During a flood, we estimate facility-level flood risk by integrating XGBoost and depth–damage functions. Furthermore, we leverage Granger tests, distributed-lag models, and spatiotemporal Durbin specifications to examine cross-system predictive temporal dependencies and finite-horizon lag patterns. We have three main findings. First, flood-induced damage exhibits a threshold-driven structure: damage across all infrastructure types is activated within a narrow depth band (~0.20–0.26m), suggesting universal hydraulic tipping points for sustainable infrastructure management. Second, at the predictive temporal-dependence level, cascading effects are not as extensive as their physical connections suggest. Rather than spreading everywhere, these effects are highly selective, focusing on a limited set of bridging nodes, which provides a roadmap for cost-effective resilience interventions in urban contexts. Third, resilience is shaped by the network’s propagation structure, with systematic differences in response latency and finite-horizon risk-signal persistence across infrastructure types.
title: Probabilistic resilience mapping to flooding of urban multi-infrastructure systems

description: Mountain regions are changing rapidly as climate warming, cryosphere loss, hydrological and ecosystem change, and socio-economic transformations interact. Looking toward 2050 provides a shared near-term horizon for asking how mountain social-ecological systems may evolve, which risks and opportunities may emerge, and how knowledge about possible futures can inform decisions today. The session addresses key and emerging themes in mountain research while remaining open to contributions from across the wider mountain research community. A cross-cutting focus is on interactions between environmental and socio-economic change in mountain regions, including their implications for hazards, vulnerability, exposure and risk. We welcome conceptual and empirical research using observations, monitoring networks, remote sensing, models, scenarios, storylines and comparative studies to understand current trajectories and explore possible mountain futures. Contributions may address physical, ecological and societal dimensions of mountain change, from climate, cryosphere, water, ecosystems and hazards to land use, economies and governance, including mountain-lowland linkages. We particularly encourage work that connects long-term observations with future scenarios and decision-making, investigates interactions and feedbacks between biophysical and human systems, or co-produces knowledge with communities, practitioners and decision-makers. Contributions that advance integrated approaches to monitoring, risk and adaptation, governance and the translation of knowledge into action are particularly welcome. By bringing these strands together, the session aims to clarify what different mountain futures could mean by 2050 and how choices made today may shape risks, resilience and sustainable development. This session is endorsed and supported by the Mountain Research Initiative and the Institute for Interdisciplinary Mountain Research of the Austrian Academy of Sciences.
title: Towards 2050: Understanding Change and Exploring Mountain Futures

description: Earth and marine observation technologies and methods are increasingly relevant for monitoring security-related domains, including critical infrastructure and supply chains. Resilient and sustainable societies need trust. Independent observations can provide objective information that supports situational awareness, societal resilience and informed decision-making. Monitoring critical infrastructure and supply chains can provide decision makers and security practitioners with actionable information. Forensic investigations of specific and critical events, such as the Nord Stream pipeline incidents demonstrate how independent observations from multiple sensor technologies can help reconstruct events, assess their consequences and provide an objective scientific basis for their interpretation. Comprehensive and objective Earth observation data can also be an effective tool for indpendent monitoring of ongoing conflicts and other security-relevant events, providing invaluable information about potential violations of international law. This multidisciplinary session brings together research on the use of Earth and marine observations for security, resource and critical infrastructure resilience. We invitecontributions from all relevant technologies like satellite monitoring from optical or radar systems, distributed acoustic sensing (DAS), hydroacoustics, seismology and infrasound. Contributions may address: - novel method developments that strengthen resilience for urban areas, resources or critical infrastructure - forensic studies of critical events - Independent monitoring of conflicts and security-relevant events, including applications supporting transparency, verification, trust-building and peacekeeping. - practical intersection with policy makers and Security Practitioners, i.e. how the Earth and Marine observations are disseminated to stakeholders through dedicated information sharing pipelines
title: Earth and Marine Monitoring for Security, Resource and Infrastructure Resilience

description: This session presents key findings from the IPCC Special Report on Climate Change and Cities and invites research on the physical science basis of urban climate change and its implications for policy. Topics include two-way interactions between cities and weather and climate, urban emissions of greenhouse gases and air pollutants, urban climate hazards and risks, and the observations, models and climate services that underpin urban climate information and decision-making. Additional topics include urban adaptation and mitigation solutions, their effectiveness, challenges and prospects. Solicited talks by report authors will highlight key findings from the assessment, followed by contributed presentations addressing its core physical science topics. We invite contributions on: interactions between cities and the climate system across scales, including urban modification of temperature, precipitation, wind and boundary layer processes; urban climate hazards and risks, including heat, flooding, water scarcity, storms and compound and cascading events under historical and future climates; the knowledge base for urban climate information, namely through observations, urban climate projections, high-resolution and city-scale modelling and climate services that support urban climate information; and how urban climate science can support decision-making across multiple levels of governance. We also welcome contributions on urban adaptation and mitigation solutions, including assessments of their effectiveness, barriers and enabling conditions, and their implications for policy. We particularly welcome contributions from under-represented regions and works with a focus on rapidly developing and small and medium sized cities.
title: IPCC Special Report on Climate Change and Cities: the underpinning science

description: Socio-environmental systems are increasingly exposed to interacting environmental, climatic and societal pressures, while capacities to anticipate, respond to and transform in the face of these pressures remain highly uneven across territories. Rethinking resilience therefore requires moving beyond isolated assessments of hazards and vulnerability towards approaches that consider the interconnected dimensions of exposure, vulnerability and resilience, and their implications for action and transformation. This session brings together research from the Belmont Forum Resilience Collaborative Research Action (CRA), "Vulnerability and Resilience Management for Socio-Environmental Systems in Exposed Territories". The seven Resilience projects engage with diverse hazards, territories and socio-environmental contexts, including floods and droughts, wildfires, coastal hazards, climate-related risks, ecosystem degradation and changing conditions of habitability. Across these contexts, they combine natural and social sciences with participatory and transdisciplinary approaches to explore how resilience is understood, assessed and strengthened. The session will focus on cross-cutting questions emerging across this research portfolio: How are vulnerability, exposure and resilience conceptualised and assessed across different contexts? How can social, environmental and institutional dimensions be better integrated? How do local knowledge, lived experience and scientific knowledge contribute to understanding and managing risk? Under what conditions can resilience approaches support equitable adaptation and transformative pathways? Building on the inherently interdisciplinary and transdisciplinary character of the Belmont Forum, the session will foster dialogue across disciplines, territories and knowledge communities. We particularly welcome contributions that connect environmental and social sciences, integrate different knowledge systems, engage with societal partners, and address vulnerability, exposure, resilience, governance, decision-making, adaptation and transformation. Co-organised with the leading funding agencies ANR (France) and NSTC (Chinese Taipei), we welcome contributions beyond the Belmont Forum Resilience CRA that engage with the session's cross-cutting themes.
title: Rethinking resilience in exposed territories: from vulnerability and risk to transformative pathways

description: Nature-based Solutions (NbS) are embedded in climate-adaptation, disaster-risk-reduction, biodiversity, and water-management agendas. As climate change intensifies floods, droughts, heat, and water scarcity, NbS can strengthen water security and social, ecological, and economic resilience. Moving from promising interventions to transformative change requires credible evidence at decision-relevant scales: where, when, and for whom NbS work; how performance changes under compound hazards and future climates; how benefits and burdens are distributed; and which governance, finance, and stewardship arrangements sustain outcomes beyond pilots. This session examines how NbS can move from isolated interventions towards interconnected portfolios and system-wide pathways for climate-resilient landscapes. We welcome inter- and transdisciplinary contributions that: • quantify performance, uncertainty, thresholds, failure modes, and long-term change using monitoring, experiments, modeling, or Earth observation; • improve spatial targeting, design, and adaptive management through integrated models, AI, digital twins, multi-criteria assessment, or other decision-support approaches; • evaluate NbS portfolios and hybrid green-grey systems under floods, droughts, heat, water scarcity, erosion, and compound or cascading risks, including lifecycle cost-effectiveness across NbS, grey, and hybrid options (investment, maintenance, and replacement costs); • assess co-benefits and trade-offs for water security, biodiversity, carbon, health, livelihoods, and infrastructure, including distributional equity and maladaptation; • investigate multi-level and cross-sector co-creation, Indigenous and local knowledge, governance, standards, finance, procurement, maintenance, and institutional capacity for implementation and upscaling; and • share comparative, transferability, or implementation evidence from urban, rural, riverine, coastal, and infrastructure landscapes, including underrepresented regions and negative or inconclusive findings. We particularly encourage studies integrating at least two dimensions and connecting researchers with practitioners, communities, public authorities, finance actors, infrastructure owners, and decision-makers. Linking Earth-system knowledge with social, economic, and political perspectives, the session aims to advance pathways from individual NbS projects to effective, accountable, and durable system-wide climate and water resilience.
title: Nature-based solutions for climate-resilient landscapes: from evidence to effective implementation

description: Mathematical models offer an imperfect and uncertain guide to future real-world climate impacts. These models (climate models, climate impact and hazard models, and catastrophe models) and their uncertainties influence how risks are understood, anticipated and managed, and therefore also play a direct role in shaping the human experience of climate risk. When informing real world decisions about climate mitigation and adaptation, the uncertainty of projections should be clearly communicated. However, open questions remain about the construction and use of these uncertainties. This includes explorations of how to navigate modelling approaches, the socio-scientific process of informing expectations of real-world outcomes and normative questions of how our uncertain expectations should inform decision making, now and in the future. This session invites contributions from individuals and teams focused on exploring model uncertainty and decision making relating to future climate impacts, addressing topics such as: 1. Going beyond in-model uncertainty quantification (through e.g., ensemble methods, sensitivity analysis, Bayesian inference, expert judgement, scenario analysis, combining multiple lines of evidence, etc.) 2. Informing expectations of future climate impacts in the real world (e.g., escaping from model land, communicating uncertainty, social perspectives on uncertainty, storylines, etc.) 3. Informing decisions in the context of uncertainty (eg DMDU approaches, examples of co-production, ethical and responsible modelling research, integration of diverse knowledge and decision systems) In particular, we welcome contributions which consider how modelling approaches situate themselves within a broader social context when informing decisions.
title: Uncertain times: Drawing decision-relevant conclusions from modelled climate risks

description: Climate policymaking and risk assessment sit at the confluence of deeply uncertain physical, social, and economic systems. Substantial uncertainty is introduced, propagated, and transformed at every stage of the climate-impact-decision chain: from projections and emulators, through sector-specific impact models, including hydrological, agricultural, and flood-loss models, to integrated assessment, energy-system, economic, financial, and insurance risk models. Yet these outputs increasingly inform decisions with long-term consequences. Understanding how uncertainty is introduced, propagated, transformed, and communicated across this chain is therefore critical for assessing the robustness of the information on which decisions are based. This session invites contributions that advance the understanding and quantification of uncertainty across climate impacts, risk assessment, and decision-making. We welcome a range of approaches, including Monte Carlo methods, emulators, robust decision-making, sensitivity analysis, and Bayesian methods, as well as work on structural model uncertainty and inter-model comparison. We are particularly interested in studies examining how uncertainty within individual models is propagated and transformed across successive stages of an analysis, and how it can be communicated to policymakers, financial institutions, and the public in ways that support sound decision-making. We particularly encourage submissions that bridge disciplinary boundaries among physical climate science, impact modeling, economics, decision theory, and science communication, as well as case studies examining how uncertainty is handled in real-world climate policymaking and in financial or insurance risk assessment. The session focuses primarily on analyses at regional to global scales. Sub-national case studies are also welcome when they provide insights into uncertainty relevant to broader-scale risk assessment or decision-making.
title: Quantifying, Modeling and Communicating Uncertainty in Climate-Informed Decision-Making

description: Scientific drilling, both marine and continental, provides a unique window into Earth’s interior, surface processes, paleoclimates, natural hazards and the distribution of subsurface microbial life. Past and current scientific drilling programs of the International Ocean Discovery Program (IODP), the International Ocean Drilling Programme (IODP3) and the International Continental Scientific Drilling Program (ICDP) continue to drive major advances in interdisciplinary fields of socio-economic importance, including climate and ecosystem evolution, palaeoceanography, the deep biosphere, sustainable georesources, crustal and tectonic processes, as well as geodynamics and geohazards. This session invites contributions that present or review recent scientific results from deep Earth sampling and monitoring through drilling projects. Furthermore, we welcome submissions outlining visions for future drilling projects, as well as new research emerging from scientific drilling legacy data.
title: Achievements and perspectives in scientific ocean and continental drilling

description: Plastics entering natural environments immediately begin to interact with their surroundings. Rather than remaining chemically and physically inert, their surfaces are continuously transformed through physical abrasion, UV radiation, hydrolysis, oxidation, biofilm formation, adsorption of natural organic matter, eco-corona formation, and the leaching of chemical additives. These processes fundamentally modify the pristine physicochemical properties of plastics, shifting their surface chemistry, roughness, density, and buoyancy, which in turn reshapes their biological interactions and ecological impacts. Understanding these dynamic transformations is essential because they govern how plastics interact with minerals, organic matter, microorganisms and contaminants, ultimately influencing their transport, fragmentation, persistence and ecological impacts across environmental compartments. Despite rapid progress in recent years, many of these interface processes remain poorly constrained, particularly under environmentally realistic conditions and across long temporal scales. This session aims to bring together researchers investigating the processes that shape the plastic-environment interface across terrestrial, freshwater, marine and atmospheric environments. We welcome conceptual, laboratory, field and modelling studies that improve our understanding of how environmental exposure alters plastic properties and how these changes affect the behaviour, transport, and fate of plastics in natural systems. We particularly encourage contributions addressing: - Physical weathering, fragmentation, abrasion, and surface roughening of plastics - UV weathering, hydrolysis, oxidation and other chemical transformation processes - Biofilm development, eco-corona formation and microbial colonisation - Interactions between plastics and minerals, sediments, natural organic matter and contaminants - Leaching, environmental release, and toxicity of chemical additives and degradation products - Changes in plastic properties controlling transport, fragmentation, aggregation and environmental fate - Laboratory, field and modelling studies investigating environmentally realistic plastic alterations. - Analytical approaches for characterising surface alteration and plastic-environment interactions - Transport at the interface of different environmental compartments
title: The plastic-environment interface: surface alteration and its consequences for environmental behaviour, transport, and impacts

description: Urban areas are increasingly vulnerable to severe weather events, including localized intense precipitation, extreme heat, and urban windstorms. Developing effective Early Warning Systems (EWS) that are fit for purpose requires bridging high-resolution physical science, cutting-edge AI methodologies, and actionable co-produced risk communications and policies. This requires understanding both physical forecast performance and how warnings are operationalized to drive effective anticipatory action, particularly in vulnerable urban environments. This session, organized as part of the WMO Urban-PREDICT initiative, explores recent advances in high-resolution urban weather forecasting, multi-hazard prediction, and the interdisciplinary co-design of early warnings. We welcome contributions covering: • High-Resolution Physical Modelling: Sub-kilometer and hectometric-scale Numerical Weather Prediction for urban environments and their application to early warning. • AI & Machine Learning Applications: Standalone AI or physics-informed AI prediction systems, fast emulators, data-driven downscaling, and novel observational datasets (e.g., radar, crowdsourced sensors, urban IoT), including pathways for operational deployment and data accessibility. • Impact & Hazard Modelling: Translating meteorological variables into actionable hazard metrics for urban infrastructure, energy systems, and public health, considering the consequences for community response. • Interdisciplinary Co-Production: Frameworks and case studies linking physical hazard forecasts to societal response, policy, and community-level EWS resilience. This session will feature contributions from ongoing research under the Urban-PREDICT framework, including international intercomparison initiatives (e.g., RUMI high-resolution modelling over Hong Kong, HEAT-X AI heat downscaling) and local case study approaches to early warning and data availability (e.g., Hong Kong, Lusaka, and Montevideo). We encourage submissions across physical meteorology, machine learning, and social sciences.
divisions: Impacts of Climate and Weather in an Inter- and Transdisciplinary context
title: Interdisciplinary Advances in Urban Weather Hazard Prediction and Warning Systems

description: Geological materials exhibit complex mechanical behaviour across a wide range of spatial and temporal scales. When polycrystalline aggregates such as glacier ice, mantle rocks, or crustal shear zones deform, their large-scale dynamics are fundamentally influenced by evolving microstructures. Processes such as crystallographic preferred orientation (CPO) development, grain-size evolution, dynamic recrystallisation, damage accumulation, phase mixing, and strain localization can strongly modify rheology, anisotropy, and deformation patterns. Despite studying very different materials, researchers in geodynamics, tectonics, rock mechanics, and cryosphere science increasingly face the same challenge: understanding how evolving microstructure influences bulk rheology and deformation across scales, and how these effects can be represented in constitutive laws and numerical models. This session aims to bring together researchers investigating these questions across disciplines and materials. We welcome contributions addressing the links between microstructure, rheology, and deformation, including but not limited to: Deformation and flow across scales Evolution of microstructure, CPO, and the anisotropy of physical properties Rheology and constitutive laws Strain localization, weakening and damage Experimental, numerical, and observational constraints Contributions from researchers at all career stages are welcome, and we especially encourage submissions led by early career scientists. We particularly encourage contributions that bridge scales, combine multiple approaches, or foster exchange between traditionally separate research communities. We hope this session will provide a forum where ideas, methods, and modelling approaches can be exchanged across communities that do not often interact, despite facing remarkably similar questions about deformation and rheology.
title: Polycrystalline Materials in Motion: Linking Microstructure, Rheology and Large-Scale Flow

description: In March 2024, the proposal to formalize the Anthropocene as a new geological epoch was rejected (IUGS 2024). This decision constitutes a turning point in debates on the Anthropocene that have been ongoing for more than two decades. Initially proposed by Paul J. Crutzen in 2000, the Anthropocene was conceived as a new geological epoch dominated by human activities, marking the end of the Holocene (Crutzen and Stoermer 2000; Crutzen 2002). Since then, it has generated numerous debates across the natural and social sciences and beyond (Benner et al. 2021; Bohle et al. 2025), including opportunities to reconsider relations between humans and nature inherited from modernity (Latour 2017). The Holocene therefore remains the geological epoch in which we officially live (IUGS 2024). Yet the transformations that gave rise to the Anthropocene debate have not disappeared. Anthropogenic global change continues, including climate change and transformations associated with the Great Acceleration (Steffen et al. 2015; Head et al. 2022). We thus continue to live geologically in the Holocene while researchers across Earth system sciences, social sciences, and the humanities investigate the Anthropocene (Thomas, Williams, and Zalasiewicz 2020; Rockström et al. 2026). Recent debates following the 2024 decision further demonstrate that the scientific discussion remains open (Waters et al. 2026; Zhou and Bertini 2026; Zalasiewicz et al. 2026; Merritts and Walter 2026). This situation invites us to ask: What should we now do with the Anthropocene? What is the relevance of the Holocene in a time of anthropogenic global change? What kinds of interdisciplinary research can emerge from these debates? Rather than reopening the institutional vote itself, this session provides an open space to examine geological evidence and arguments surrounding the proposed Anthropocene–Holocene boundary, their implications within and beyond geology, and new interdisciplinary horizons for the social sciences, education, philosophy, the humanities, and geoethics (Wallenhorst and Wulf 2023; Renn 2021; Bohle et al. 2025; Colombo 2026).
title: The Anthropocene Debates: geology, humanities, and interdisciplinary perspectives

description: Before geomaterials become “hard” rocks, they commonly pass through stages in which they behave as soft-matter systems, such as complex fluids, gels, colloids, liquid crystals, and foams. During these stages, they can be regarded as geological soft matter, which commonly occurs during lithification, crystallization and deformation. The initiation of such soft-matter behaviour is highly sensitive to the surrounding physicochemical environment, leading to the formation of striking patterns and complex structures. Understanding how these structures form and evolve remains a major challenge in the Earth sciences. Examples include soft-sediment deformation structures such as load casts and flame structures; mineral dendrites; concretions and chemical banding; crack patterns such as septaria, mud cracks and lava polygons; and dissolution–precipitation forms such as travertine dams, scallops and stalactites. Other examples include patterns associated with microbial mats, such as stromatolitic structures, together with botryoidal and spherulitic textures, as well as hydro-geomorphological patterns such as channel networks and dunes, and vegetation patterns. The physics underlying these patterns, which evolve progressively during the soft-matter stage, commonly involves complex non-equilibrium processes governed by self-organization and self-assembly. These processes allow complex spatiotemporal patterns to emerge from simple rules, while making the underlying physicochemical mechanisms difficult to infer from the pattern alone. Exploring such physical laws and establishing a geological soft-matter paradigm would not only provide an excellent opportunity to study pattern formation itself, but also help develop analogues for understanding geological processes in Earth’s history and potentially on other planets. In this session, we discuss the potential application of the soft-matter paradigm to geological evolution research. We invite contributions that aim to deepen our understanding of complex patterns across scales in natural and experimental systems, investigating the physicochemical processes that generate them, through field observations, experimental work, theoretical modelling, and computational simulations. Contributions involving advanced quantification, conceptual advances, quantitative model development and modelling are warmly welcome.
title: Pattern formation in geological soft matter: initiation, evolution and mechanisms

description: This session explores the need, challenges, opportunities, drawbacks, and obstacles in applying and explaining the special world of compositional data spaces. Compositional data is a special type of non-negative data that carries relevant information in the ratios among the variables rather than in the actual data values. Considering the metric of compositional data may conflict with familiar geoscientific approaches: single chemical elements or mineralogical concentrations as proxies for environmental changes, counts of individuals as indicators of ecological states, etc. Felix Chayes (1960) and John Aitchison (1981) began to establish a parallel universe of statistical methods beyond normality and linearity to gain sustainable insights into Compositional Data Analysis (CoDA) in the geosciences. Since then, the geoscientific community has expanded the range of methods. However, even in the era of rapidly expanding big data methods, sustainable CoDA remains underrepresented in recent research. We welcome contributions from all disciplines to answer the following questions: (i) How does CoDA transform our view of the earth? (ii) How can we gain new sustainable insights by applying CoDA? (iii) How can CodA increase the scalability of numeric models? (iv) How to deal with zeros and missing data? (vi) How to deal with low-count compositions? (v) How should we convincingly communicate CoDA? This session addresses researchers from all quantitative fields to exchange ideas and foster interdisciplinary collaboration.
title: When Numbers Change Meaning: How Compositional Data Analysis Transforms Our View of the Earth

description: Essential Variables (EVs) provide a common framework for characterising key components of the Earth system, but their potential extends beyond observation and monitoring. This session explores how EV frameworks can connect heterogeneous observing systems, from Research Infrastructures (RIs) such as ICOS and ACTRIS, to satellite data and models, and support the transformation of essential observations into actionable climate information. European Environmental Research Infrastructures (ENVRI) are a key part of this integration layer. Beyond providing observations, RIs contribute long-term stewardship, calibration and quality assurance, standards, provenance, data and access services, computational environments and increasingly integrated information services. Together with satellites and models, these capabilities provide operational foundations for connecting observations across domains and scales. We focus on interfaces where integration remains difficult: • EV frameworks and harmonisation: ECVs, EOVs, EBVs; definitions, metadata, provenance and harmonisation across domains, RIs and satellite data. • Interoperability and integration: FAIR and semantic interoperability, machine-actionable data, persistent identifiers, and integration of RI, satellite, model and other environmental observations. • Scale and uncertainty: Integration across spatial and temporal scales; uncertainty, consistency, traceability and fitness-for-purpose. • Infrastructures enabling integration: Stewardship, quality assurance, access services, data spaces, digital twins, cloud/HPC environments, knowledge graphs and other technical and organisational architectures. • Translation into climate services and decision support: From Analysis-Ready Data to Action-Ready Information; co-creation with users and communities; and applications in adaptation, mitigation, risk management and policy. The session will examine the pathway from EV frameworks and European observing infrastructures to regional and local climate information, climate services and decision support. We welcome contributions demonstrating how RIs, satellite data and models can work together as an integrated infrastructure, and how this can translate observations into meaningful information for climate adaptation, mitigation, environmental management and policy support.
title: From Essential to Actionable: Linking Research Infrastructures, Earth Observations and Climate Services

description: Rotational ground motions have emerged as an important complementary observable in seismology, driven by advances in the development of rotational seismometers and independent six-component measurement systems. The growing availability of these sensors is making it increasingly possible to measure the complete six-component seismic wavefield generated not only by earthquakes, but also by ambient and anthropogenic sources, providing new opportunities to investigate wavefield properties and their interaction with buildings and critical infrastructure. Sensitive to spatial gradients of the wavefield, rotational measurements carry information that is fundamentally different from conventional translational measurements. They therefore offer new opportunities to characterize seismic wavefields, resolve small-scale subsurface heterogeneities, develop more complete descriptions of earthquake ground motion, and improve our understanding of how seismic waves couple with infrastructure and contribute to structural response and damage. Beyond traditional seismology, rotational observations are increasingly being explored for seismic monitoring, rapid characterization of earthquake effects, structural health monitoring, and earthquake engineering. Together, these developments open new possibilities for integrating rotational observations across computational seismology, geophysics, and engineering. This interdisciplinary session brings together researchers working on the observation, instrumentation, modelling, and application of rotational ground motions. We welcome contributions focused on the development of rotation-measuring instruments and independent six-component sensors; observations of earthquake- and ambient-noise-induced rotations; theoretical and numerical modelling of rotational wavefields; full-waveform inversion; computational seismology; seismic source and wave-propagation studies; near-field and strong motion observations; seismic monitoring and event characterization; and applications to structural health monitoring, earthquake engineering, and infrastructure resilience. We particularly encourage contributions presenting new experiments and field deployments using emerging rotational sensors, analyses of corresponding datasets, novel computational approaches, and interdisciplinary applications of rotational ground-motion measurements.
title: Rotational Ground Motions: Harnessing Six-Component Wavefields from Earthquake Science to Infrastructure Monitoring

description: Archaeometry, while a broad discipline, is an important area of geoscience research, often seeking to not only utilise existing methodologies, but also pioneer new methods or approaches which often have interdisciplinary applications. Recent advances in the field across many sub-disciplines such as pigment research, conservation, paleoclimate reconstructions, mineral magnetism and dating have resulted in high-impact publications, and new insights into our understanding of the past. The interdisciplinary nature of archaeometry often means those working on novel, or interesting applications of geoscience methods can miss the opportunity to benefit from the knowledge of others working at the forefront of methods development in the field. This session aims to bring together researchers working on novel methods or applications of methods to discuss recent advances in provenance studies, conservation, paleoclimate reconstructions and dating. We particularly welcome contributions addressing geoscience applications in pigment and materials research. We invite contributions where geoscience methods are used to answer archaeological questions, in particular new applications, innovative approaches and novel methods are especially welcome. The session will provide a forum to bring together those working at the forefront of their field, bringing together those bridging archaeometry and geoscience to exchange ideas, compare approaches, identify common challenges and foster new opportunities for collaborations.
title: Geoscience methods and applications in Archaeometry

description: This session addresses the challenge of consistently combining terrestrial and marine datasets referenced to different vertical reference surfaces, a fundamental requirement for, among other applications, effective coastal-zone management and robust coastal-hazard assessment. This includes the integration of terrain elevations, bathymetric data, and/or sea-level data, including model-derived water levels, as well as the realization and unification of the vertical reference surfaces to which these datasets are referenced. We welcome contributions proposing strategies for land–sea vertical reference integration across scales, from global to local, as well as studies applying and evaluating such strategies. Contributions are also invited on the realization of height and depth reference surfaces, including (marine) geoid and chart datum models, height-system unification, and the transfer of vertical datums across the land–sea interface.
title: Bridging Land and Sea: Vertical Reference Integration across Geodesy, Hydrography, and Coastal Oceanography

description: The Antarctic continent contains approximately 10% of Earth's least understood continental crust, much of it hidden beneath the Antarctic Ice Sheet. Yet this concealed lithosphere exerts a fundamental influence on geothermal heat flow, subglacial hydrology, sediment and nutrient fluxes, ice-sheet behaviour, ocean productivity, and climate feedbacks. Understanding Antarctica therefore requires a truly interdisciplinary perspective that links solid Earth processes with the cryosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere and atmosphere. This session provides a forum for the newly approved SCAR Scientific Research Programme Antarctic Geosphere Evolution (AGE), which aims to advance understanding of Antarctica's four-dimensional lithospheric evolution and its interactions with Earth-system processes. We welcome contributions spanning geological, geophysical, geochemical, biological and modelling approaches, particularly studies that bridge traditional disciplinary boundaries. Topics may include, but are not limited to: • Antarctic lithospheric architecture and tectonic evolution • Geodynamics, mantle structure and geothermal heat flow • Lithosphere-cryosphere coupling and ice-sheet dynamics • Subglacial hydrology and groundwater systems • Sediment, dust and nutrient fluxes from Antarctica to the Southern Ocean • Provenance studies and reconstruction of the hidden Antarctic continent • Interactions between geological processes, marine productivity and biogeochemical cycles • Integration of geological, geophysical and geochemical datasets • Integration of Antarctica’s components in full-plate reconstructions and computational tectonics. The session particularly encourages studies that develop new connections between disciplines and improve understanding of how Antarctica's lithosphere influences the wider Earth system across spatial and temporal scales.
title: Antarctic Geosphere Evolution (AGE): Linking Lithosphere, Ice Sheets, Oceans, Ecosystems and Climate

description: Social-science and humanities (SSH) research is crucial for informing ambitious, effective, just and societally acceptable climate action. This session highlights how SSH insights on social metabolism, labor transitions, perceptions and societal readiness, institutional dynamics, justice, needs and capabilities, and power relations can enrich and reshape diverse modeling approaches. We aim to provide a platform for interdisciplinary work that broadens what models and scenarios can represent, clarifies their limits, and strengthens connections across methods and disciplines. We welcome contributions that: integrate SSH concepts and methods into integrated assessment models (IAMs), energy–economy–environment models, energy-system models, or other analytical frameworks; use empirical, qualitative or participatory approaches to inform model assumptions, structures, constraints and scenario design; engage with normative dimensions such as fairness, feasibility, responsibility and societal acceptance, including in emerging areas such as carbon dioxide removal and other climate-response strategies; connect justice questions to marginalized or disadvantaged communities, particularly in the Global South; examine how governance, institutions, finance, law, power relations, and material and human needs shape transition pathways; investigate social outcomes of modeled scenarios, including distributional, labor, health and wellbeing implications; and explore how new data, methods and technologies can address, or reproduce, gaps in whose experiences and priorities are represented in climate analysis. We particularly encourage work engaging with distributive, procedural, recognitional, transitional and other dimensions of justice, as well as studies that provide meaningful two-way connections between social science and modeling communities. Contributions need not themselves be modeling studies where they provide empirical, conceptual or normative insights that can inform how climate and energy scenarios are developed, evaluated or interpreted. By convening these perspectives, the session seeks to advance interdisciplinary approaches that make climate and energy modeling more relevant, inclusive and transparent about both what it represents and what lies beyond its scope.
title: Advancing Justice and Social Science Integration in Climate Modeling

description: The session deals with scientific concepts and empirical studies in the natural and social sciences and humanities that address the societal pressures on the Earth system or the impacts of Earth system changes on societies in the context of the Anthropocene. It involves inter- and transdisciplinary approaches for a better understanding of (i) key interlinkages, feedbacks and natural and social tipping points, (ii) normative views of habitability such as planetary boundaries and social justice, and (iii) transformative capacities to preserve or regain habitability. Explicit account is taken of the complexity, dynamics and uncertainties of the underlying Earth system processes, as well as of associated social, economic and political developments across spatial and temporal scales. The aim is to explore the potential of deeper integration of the different research strands with their ontological and epistemological knowledge and empirical evidence for the advancement of Anthropocene research. Contributions can be on topics ranging from anthropogenic pressures on Earth system compartments such as climate, biodiversity, water, soil and land and/or their impacts on settlements, infrastructure, livelihood, food security and human health with secondary effects on poverty, inequality, and migration. Selected guiding questions are: What additional knowledge and methods are needed to more appropriately describe key interlinkages between the Earth system and societies shaping the Anthropocene? Are the political and social responses to this global challenge necessarily global and if not, how is decision-making and power best devolved to local levels where flexible community resilience might be fostered? What natural and social sciences and humanities’ evidence is needed as reference to further negotiate and agree on the future habitability of the planet for human societies and all wild species? What science communication and education can facilitate the transfer of actionable knowledge and strengthen societal and mental capacities for sustainability transformations without destroying the hope for a liveable future? Approaches from all related disciplines and studies from around the world will be considered. (Continuation of Session ITS3.2/SSP1.8 at EGU26 as second edition of an EGU session series)
title: Navigating the Anthropocene towards habitability: linking research on Earth system processes and societal dynamics, values and policies

description: We welcome contributions that address a range of environmental and societal effects of nuclear war.
