Areas of interest include, but are not limited to: - Radioactive contamination -Radioactive fallout and long-range transport -Effects on supply chains and infrastructure -Nuclear detonations in space and EMP attacks -Nuclear winter and climatic disruption -Fires and blast effects -Smoke transport and aerosol plume dynamics -Impacts on the hydrological cycle and oceans -Impacts on ecological systems and ecosystem services -The use of science to contribute to reduction of nuclear threats.
title: Environmental and societal effects of nuclear war

description: The growing scientific and policy focus on tipping points in the Earth system reflects their potential for profound physical and socio-economic consequences. If crossed, tipping points could trigger abrupt changes that are effectively irreversible on human timescales. Continued Global Warming is predicted to drive major changes across the North Atlantic, pushing key components of the climate system towards potential critical thresholds and abrupt reorganisation. Yet, the nonlinear nature of these systems means that future change is difficult to observe, model, predict, and govern. Early Warning Systems (EWS) have emerged as a potential method of translating our understanding of abrupt changes in the climate and their impacts into useful and actionable information for relevant stakeholders and decision makers. Important questions remain around how best to inform and govern the response to North Atlantic tipping and what information can be robustly provided considering deep uncertainty. To address these challenges, this session aims to bring together interdisciplinary perspectives to inform the co-design of EWS that can support tipping point governance. We welcome contributions from observations, modelling, impact studies, and governance. We have particular interest in modern approaches able to inform governance and response, including under deep uncertainty. Our primary focus is on North Atlantic tipping elements, including the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, Subpolar Gyre and Greenland Ice Sheet. Studies of other tipping elements and their interactions are also welcome. This session builds on themes being explored by the UK Advanced Research and Invention Agency (ARIA) Forecasting Tipping Points programme.
title: Informing Early Warning, Response, and Governance of Tipping Points and Abrupt Changes in the North Atlantic

description: Plastic pollution is ubiquitous in terrestrial, freshwater, and marine ecosystems. Reliable data on plastic abundance and fluxes are crucial to study its sources, sinks, transport dynamics, and impact. Furthermore, long-term and large-scale monitoring is required to design, implement, and assess plastic pollution prevention and reduction measures. In this session we invite contributions that present recent advances in plastic pollution monitoring across the entire Geosphere (atmosphere, land surface, soil, rivers, estuaries, oceans and beyond). Presentations may focus on: • Novel monitoring methods, including advanced techniques (e.g. remote sensing, multi/hyperspectral cameras, acoustic sensors, artificial intelligence); • Monitoring strategies, including large-scale and long-term efforts, and citizen science approaches; • All plastic size ranges, from nano to macro; • Baseline studies to assess current plastic pollution levels; • Long-term trends or recent discoveries based on plastic monitoring data. With this session we aim to bring together scientists that work on novel approaches to provide reliable data on environmental plastic pollution.
title: Advances in plastic pollution monitoring across the Geosphere

description: Landscapes are shaped by geomorphic processes, but life also shapes landscapes. Interactions and feedbacks between organisms, ecosystems and geomorphic processes structure many dynamic environments, including rivers, coasts, hillslopes, aeolian and deglaciating landscapes. Yet, many biogeomorphic feedbacks remain poorly understood and quantified, in particular their mechanisms, strength and thresholds. As these landscapes are increasingly affected by climate and land-use change, understanding how biota influence geomorphic processes—and vice versa—is becoming increasingly important. Improved understanding can support nature-based solutions (NbS) and geoheritage conservation and contribute to the conservation of geodiversity and biodiversity, as well as the maintenance of ecosystem functions and services. Our session brings together research on interactions between plants, animals, ecosystem processes and geomorphic processes, landforms and materials. We particularly seek to connect researchers working in environment-specific communities, including fluvial, coastal, aeolian and hillslope geomorphology, and provide a forum to explore common biogeomorphic processes and feedbacks across environments. We welcome research spanning functional traits and individual organisms to ecosystems and landscapes, from mountain environments to the sea. By bringing together studies from different environmental settings, we aim to identify common principles, context-dependent contrasts and transferable insights in biogeomorphology, and foster synergies between research communities. Topics may include, but are not limited to: • biogeomorphic processes, rates and feedbacks; • the role of plant and other organisms’ traits in geomorphic processes; • biota as ecosystem engineers, landform creators and landscape shapers; • biogeomorphic feedbacks under climate and land-use change; • applications of biogeomorphology for nature-based solutions, hazard mitigation and geoheritage conservation Innovative approaches—including field monitoring, laboratory and flume experiments, remote sensing, artificial intelligence, numerical and statistical modelling, and combinations thereof—are warmly welcomed, especially when providing new insights into interactions between life and landscape, resolving previously inaccessible interactions or pushing scalar boundaries.
title: Biogeomorphology: Life-landscape feedbacks from the mountains to the sea

description: Globally, landscapes are starting to dynamically respond to human-accelerated climate change hazards. Whilst in the past it was often possible to use geotechnical solutions to control natural landscape dynamics, such as using nature-based or engineered solutions to control river morphology, reduce coastal erosion and flood risks and reduce landslide hazards, these methods are increasingly unviable. As climate change impacts accelerate there will be growing economic, social or physical limits to continued use of ever more expensive geotechnical solutions. Managing many of our landscapes using geotechnical solutions will achieve hard adaptation limits. This session welcomes papers that explore the potentialities of hard physical adaptation limits and the impacts of these for our societies which are built assuming a relatively ‘fixed’ landscape. We welcome papers that can demonstrate how many nature-based solutions work against rather than with natural landscape responses to environmental factors such as sea level rise, increased river flows (leading to avulsions), increased rainfall triggering landslides more frequently and/or drought conditions driving more widespread wildfires reducing landscape stability. Papers exploring some of the wicked problems that arise from increasingly dynamic landscapes, including release of wastes, graves and buildings into the landscape are also sought.
title: Dynamic landscape responses to climate change: identifying physical adaptation limits to geotechnical solutions

description: Freshwater systems, societies and ecosystems are often studied separately, yet they are deeply intertwined parts of complex social-ecological systems. Advancing a holistic understanding of these systems is essential to addressing many grand challenges of the Anthropocene, such as ensuring water security, biodiversity conservation, and climate change mitigation and adaptation. This session invites a broad range of submissions that study the dynamics of freshwater social-ecological systems. These may include socio-hydrological, ecohydrological, social-ecological, or other approaches that share an interest in investigating the properties of complex adaptive systems (eg., thresholds, resilience, emergent behaviour, path dependence, cross-scale effects). We invite empirical, model-based, and theoretical contributions, which may include, but are not limited to: - Network analysis, agent-based modelling, and system dynamics studies that represent feedbacks between hydrological processes and human behaviour such as decision-making and governance - Machine learning and remote sensing applications to detect system change, map risks, and anticipate regime shifts - Analysis or modelling of tipping points and cross-scale teleconnections (for example, virtual water trade) in human-freshwater systems - Research on how ethics, power, justice, and values shape, and are shaped by, interactions between infrastructure, policy, and biophysical systems, including transdisciplinary work co-produced with water users, communities, and decision-makers This session's overarching aim is to bring together diverse communities (hydrologists, ecologists, data scientists, social scientists, and sustainability scientists) into an interdisciplinary dialogue about the complex interactions between freshwater, society, and ecosystems. We especially welcome contributions showing how understanding these interactions can inform freshwater management to advance broader social and sustainability goals.
title: Freshwater social-ecological systems: feedbacks, thresholds, resilience, and sustainability from local to global scales

description: Understanding and responding to Europe’s climate risks requires sustained investment in science, from fundamental research and the development of research talent to long-term observations, advanced analytical capabilities and world-class research infrastructures. Climate risks are increasingly interconnected across ecosystems, food systems, human health, infrastructure, and the economy and finance, highlighting the need for robust knowledge, data and research capabilities to understand their interactions and strengthen climate resilience. Across the Horizon Europe programming period, Pillar I – Excellent Science has contributed to this knowledge base through frontier research supported by the European Research Council (ERC), researcher training, mobility and interdisciplinary collaboration through the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions (MSCA), and the development, access and integration of European Research Infrastructures (RIs). The session welcomes contributions on how frontier science, research talent and research infrastructures provide the knowledge, data, methods and scientific capabilities needed to address these risks areas and interactions among them, including compound, cascading and cross-border risks. Research highlighting risks associated with heat, drought, floods, wildfires and changes affecting marine and terrestrial environments are particularly encouraged. By bringing together researchers, projects and infrastructures supported across the different components of Horizon Europe Pillar I, the session aims to connect complementary expertise and capabilities and explore how Excellent Science can provide the knowledge, people, observations and research capacity needed to better understand Europe’s interconnected climate risks and strengthen the scientific foundations for a climate-resilient Europe.
title: Excellent Science for Climate Resilience: Connecting Frontier Research, People and Research Infrastructures across Horizon Europe Pillar I

description: The Geological Time Scale (GTS) is the result of centuries of observation, curation, and quantification of the stratigraphic record. The forthcoming iteration of the GTS, GTS2030, aims to begin the process of moving the GTS towards a broader audience, connecting domain scientists, data resources, and community organizations to develop a new modality of open science GTS construction. This session invites geochronologists, paleontologists, stratigraphers, astrochronologists, age modelers, data scientists, programmers, users of the Geologic Time Scale, anyone else interested in the next iteration of the GTS to submit an abstract. Best practices for open science, FAIR data system for the GTS are also welcome. This session is organized by the International Subcommission on Timescale Calibration (ISTC) of the International Commission on Stratigraphy (ICS).
title: Moving the Geologic Time Scale (GTS) into an Open Science Ecosystem

description: Digital geoscience depends on combining Earth observations, in situ measurements, model output, and digital twins across domains and scales. Yet differences in grids, data formats, computing environments, and access conditions can make results difficult to compare and reproduce. This session explores how open, interoperable workflows can bridge these gaps. The Pangeo community and its open-source ecosystem support scalable analysis from laptops to HPC and cloud systems. A unified, standardized data infrastructure based on Discrete Global Grid Systems (DGGS) could provide a common spatial framework for Earth observations and model outputs that currently use heterogeneous grids. Combined with cloud-native formats, such a framework can reduce repeated, ad hoc data transformations and make their provenance easier to trace. This creates opportunities for analysis-ready data and reproducible, trustworthy AI, while enabling tests of computational efficiency. Earth system digital twins and federated data platforms offer settings to test integration of observations, simulations, and user applications across domains and scales. We welcome methodological advances and applied studies from atmosphere, climate, ocean, land, biodiversity, and natural hazards research. Topics include: Cross-domain fusion of observations, simulations, and digital-twin outputs DGGS-based indexing, regridding, and analysis across spatial and temporal scales Scalable, reproducible, and FAIR workflows using open-source tools (Xarray, Iris, Dask, Jupyter, Kerchunk, VirtualiZarr, Intake) alongside open standards and formats (STAC, Zarr, Parquet, GeoParquet) Interoperable data access and processing across HPC, cloud, and federated infrastructures AI/ML workflows with traceable data preparation, validation, uncertainty assessment, and evaluation of computational efficiency Executable notebooks, workflow portability, sustainable computing, and practical barriers to reuse Contributions may focus on Pangeo, DGGS, digital twins, or their combination. Studies using Pangeo tools alone to build reproducible, FAIR, and community-driven workflows in any domain of Earth or environmental science are equally welcome. We especially encourage work that shows how a method developed in one geoscience domain can be adapted, evaluated, and reused in another.
title: Pangeo and DGGS: Enabling FAIR, Open, and Reusable Workflows for Transdisciplinary Digital Earth Science

description: Water management in Europe has often relied on emergency response, reacting to floods, droughts and scarcity once they occur. Three recent EU policy developments mark a shift in this framing: the Nature Restoration Law (2024), the EU Water Resilience Strategy (2025), and the Competitiveness Compass 2025). Together they treat water and landscapes not only as risks to manage, but as protected natural infrastructure that contributes to ecosystem health and a sustainable economy. This session invites contributions that move beyond reactive risk management toward proactive, systemic resilience: landscapes and catchments designed to absorb shocks, restore ecological function, and generate long-term value. We welcome studies addressing how catchments, rivers, cities, and rural landscapes can be reimagined as resilient systems considering binding restoration targets. Relevant approaches include nature-based solutions, water reuse and circularity, digital twins for landscape and catchment planning, and governance models that align water security with economic strategy. Of particular interest are creative, cross-disciplinary approaches connecting hydrology, ecological restoration, landscape design, engineering, and policy: how can we design landscapes that are simultaneously flood-resilient, drought-resilient, ecologically restored, and economically productive? Contributions may range from local to continental scale, and include case studies, modelling work, policy analysis, or nature-based interventions, connecting risk science, legal restoration requirements, economic sustainability, and long-term resilience planning.
title: Restoring the Water Cycle: Resilient Landscapes between Policy and Practice

description: Considerable progress has been made in modelling multi-hazard and systemic climate and natural hazard risk, including the interactions, cascading effects, and feedbacks through which climate-related risks propagate across interconnected systems. However, stronger links are needed between these advances in risk assessment and the emerging discourses and approaches to systemic risk governance. In particular, approaches to governance need to reflect the distinctive characteristics of systemic risk while responding to diverse stakeholder perceptions, knowledge, capacities, and needs. This interdisciplinary and transdisciplinary session aims to bridge systemic risk assessment, modelling, communication, and governance. We invite presentations and posters addressing three interconnected questions: 1. How can multi-hazard and systemic risks be assessed and communicated in ways that are scientifically robust, decision-relevant, and appropriate to the needs and perceptions of different stakeholders? 2. How do systemic risks propagate across interconnected infrastructure, economic, environmental, and social systems, and how can these dynamics, including cascading impacts, feedbacks, and potential tipping points, be simulated and assessed? 3. What science-based governance frameworks and discourses can translate systemic risk knowledge into effective climate change adaptation, disaster risk reduction, and progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals? In particular, how might systemic risk governance be organised around and combine instrumental, reflective, participatory, and epistemological governance discourses? By bringing together perspectives from hazard risk science, modelling, governance, policy, and practice, the session seeks to advance a more integrated understanding of how knowledge about climate-related systemic risk can inform actionable and legitimate governance responses. We will actively seek to enhance Equality, Diversity, and Inclusion (EDI) in the composition and conduct of the session.
divisions: Impacts of Climate and Weather in an Inter- and Transdisciplinary context
title: Integrating Assessment and Governance of Climate Related Systemic Risk

description: Climate change, biodiversity loss, pollution, natural hazards and other forms of environmental change present challenges not only for understanding Earth systems, but also for how environmental knowledge is produced, interpreted and shared. Across the Earth and environmental sciences, researchers are increasingly collaborating with artists and creative practitioners to develop new ways of engaging with environmental processes, data, places and communities. Art-science collaboration can extend beyond communicating completed scientific findings. Creative practices may contribute to observation and sensing, working with environmental data, visualisation and representation, field-based inquiry, interpretation of uncertainty and change, participatory research, and engagement with place-based and experiential knowledge. At the same time, a growing range of projects provides practical experience of how such collaborations work in different research and environmental contexts. This session brings together empirical case studies, methodological contributions and critical reflections on art-science collaboration in Earth and environmental research. We welcome contributions from across the geosciences and environmental sciences, together with collaborating artists, creative practitioners, and humanities and social science researchers, particularly addressing: (1) art-science collaborations concerning climate, water, biodiversity and ecosystems, pollution, landscapes, natural hazards and other Earth and environmental processes; (2) creative and arts-based approaches to environmental observation, fieldwork, sensing, mapping, visualisation, sonification, environmental data, modelling and interpretation; (3) methods combining scientific observations and evidence with local, Indigenous, experiential or other forms of knowledge; (4) participatory and place-based approaches involving scientists, artists, communities and other partners; (5) methodological and comparative studies examining how creative practices can be integrated into different stages of Earth and environmental research; (6) different models of collaboration, including artist residencies, field-based collaborations, museums and cultural institutions, research programmes, laboratories and community partnerships.
title: Art-science collaboration in Earth and environmental research: methods, case studies and lessons

description: Geology does not only shape the physical environment in which societies develop. Rocks, landforms, geological and hydrological processes, water bodies and other abiotic features also influence how people perceive, use, interpret and culturally appropriate their surroundings. Through these interactions, geodiversity becomes embedded in cultural landscapes, local identities, traditions, beliefs, myths and other forms of tangible and intangible heritage. Cultural geology – also developed in some scholarly traditions under the term Culture Geology – provides an interdisciplinary framework for exploring relationships between geological environments and human societies, while geomythology examines how geological phenomena, extreme events and landscape features are interpreted, remembered and transmitted through myths, legends and oral traditions. Together, these approaches reveal dimensions of geodiversity and geoheritage that may remain difficult to capture through purely geoscientific assessment. Building on the concept of mythogenic landscapes, we invite contributions examining how abiotic features and processes act as culture-shaping factors. Geological, geomorphological and hydrological characteristics can influence myths and imaginaries, settlement patterns, sacred and monumental landscapes, cultural practices, architecture, material culture, the use of geological materials, place names, local knowledge, and perceptions of environmental change and natural hazards. Conversely, cultural interpretations may influence how geological features are valued, protected and incorporated into heritage. Particular attention will be given to intangible geoheritage, geocultural heritage, geomythology, geofolklore, hydromythology, Indigenous and local knowledge, cultural perceptions of geological materials, geological materials in architecture and archaeological heritage, collective memory of geological processes and extreme events, toponymy, geoconservation, geoeducation, geotourism and public engagement. We welcome studies combining geosciences with archaeology, history, anthropology, folklore studies, ethnography, cultural geography and heritage studies. The session aims to bring together geoscientists and scholars from the humanities and social sciences to develop a holistic understanding of relationships between people and the abiotic environment and of how cultural meanings contribute to the recognition, interpretation and protection of geoheritage.
title: Cultural Geology and Geomythology: Exploring the Human Meanings of Geodiversity and Geoheritage

description: In 2009, a consortium of Icelandic geothermal companies known as the Iceland Deep Drilling Project drilled a well (IDDP-1) into Landsvirkjun’s (National Power Company of Iceland) geothermal field within Krafla Caldera. After 2000 m of drilling they encountered magma, as evidenced by quenched rhyolitic glass. This opened the opportunity to access shallow magma at a known location on an actively utilized geothermal field. The Krafla Magma Testbed is the endeavour to establish a magma observation and experimentation platform at depth. This platform will allow us to learn about magmatic process in-situ, how they interact with the host rock and surrounding hydrothermal system, and how they react to perturbations, either as part of energy extraction or even perhaps as part of a hazard mitigation programme. In preparation for accessing near-surface magma there remains a lot of previous and ongoing research that needs to be brought together, as well as research and development challenges that remain to be solved. This session invites contributions related to the Krafla Magma Testbed, and could consist of details of the science plan, previous and ongoing work in understanding the Krafla caldera and geothermal field, as well as work from other volcanic systems that has relevance to near-surface magmatic processes, magma drilling, near-magma subsurface conditions (e.g. temperature gradients, fluid flow and geochemistry, geomechanics and rheology, magma-hydrothermal interaction), subsurface magma modelling, detection and monitoring of near-surface magma bodies, instrumentation of high-temperature wells, deep geothermal energy, volcano monitoring, etc. This list is not exhaustive but gives an indication of the kinds of topics being sought to stimulate exchange and discussions regarding the existing scientific knowledge about this environment, the outstanding scientific needs to access it and the unique opportunities that accessing it could bring to science.
title: In-situ magma observation and experimentation – the Krafla Magma Testbed

description: Understanding earthquake generation processes requires an integrated approach that combines dense observational networks, advanced numerical modeling, and cross-disciplinary collaboration. Recent developments in near-fault monitoring—including dense seismic networks and arrays, Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) systems, high-resolution GNSS, and machine learning detection techniques—provide unprecedented observation scale to investigate fault behavior, rupture initiation, and seismic hazard. This session aims to highlight the central role of Near-Fault Observatories (NFOs) and present innovative approaches for characterizing both natural and induced earthquakes, using multiparameter datasets and advanced data processing techniques. By integrating seismology, geodesy, geochemistry, and environmental monitoring, participants will explore how integrated observations improve our understanding of stress accumulation, rupture propagation, aseismic slip, postseismic deformation, enhancement of seismic catalogs and fluid migration along active fault zones. Deciphering fault mechanics and earthquake dynamics is essential for robust seismic hazard assessment and risk mitigation. Near-Fault Observatories and dense real-time monitoring infrastructures enable high-resolution tracking of fault processes in close proximity to earthquake sources, facilitating the development of physical models and next-generation early warning systems. We invite contributions that demonstrate the following: • Innovative NFO & Near-Field Monitoring Techniques: Development and application of novel strategies for collecting and analyzing data from dense seismic networks/arrays, DAS, low-cost GNSS, geochemical sensors, and satellite remote sensing. • Data Integration and Analysis: Application of machine learning, automated detection pipelines, real-time processing, and multiparameter data assimilation to enhance earthquake characterization. • Fault Process Studies: Investigation of rupture initiation, propagation, aseismic slip, postseismic deformation, fluid migration, and induced seismicity captured by near-fault instrumentation. • Modeling and Simulation: Development of physics-based models for earthquake rupture dynamics and hazard assessment calibrated by high-density observational data.
title: Investigating Seismic Dynamics with Near-Fault Observatories (NFOs) and Dense Multidisciplinary Infrastructures

description: Geothermal energy, hydrogen storage, carbon capture and storage (CCS) and critical raw materials all play a vital role in the energy transition and in securing Europe's strategic resources. Exploration and monitoring of these resources and infrastructures require affordable, reliable, and scalable geophysical methods to reduce subsurface uncertainty, de-risk drilling, and ensure safe and sustainable operation. In recent years, passive seismic imaging has emerged as a cost-effective exploration tool, particularly valuable in complex geological settings and at depths beyond the reach of conventional active methods. These approaches are increasingly demonstrating their potential not only for geothermal and subsurface storage applications, but also for mining exploration. This session invites contributions that advance passive seismic methodology and modeling for applications to subsurface imaging, as well as case studies showcasing applications to geothermal energy, hydrogen storage, CCS and critical raw material exploration. We particularly encourage studies highlighting integration of passive seismic techniques into industrial exploration workflows, and contributions spanning ambient-noise and/or earthquake-based approaches.
title: Passive seismic methods for subsurface imaging applied to the energy transition

description: This session will cover applied and theoretical aspects of geophysical imaging, modelling and inversion using active- and passive-source seismic measurements as well as other geophysical techniques (e.g., gravity, magnetic, electromagnetic) to investigate properties of the Earth’s lithosphere and asthenosphere, and explore the processes involved. We invite contributions focused on methodological developments, theoretical aspects, and applications. Studies across the scales and disciplines are particularly welcome. Among others, the session may cover the following topics: - Active- and passive-source imaging - Full waveform inversion developments and applications - Advancements and case studies in 2D and 3D imaging - DAS imaging - Interferometry and Marchenko imaging - Seismic attenuation and anisotropy - Developments and applications of multi-scale and multi-parameter inversion - Joint inversion of seismic and complementary geophysical data
title: Imaging, modelling and inversion to explore the Earth’s lithosphere and asthenosphere

description: Recent advances in the experimental quantification and numerical modelling of effects of surface geology on earthquake ground motion include efforts to use seismic ambient noise for estimating site response. Despite all developments, we still do not know how to determine site amplification for real earthquakes based on ambient noise characteristics in a simple way avoiding the inversion of underground structure. In fact, there is still no clear evidence that this is even possible. This uncertainty is closely linked to the fundamental differences between the seismic wavefields of earthquakes and ambient noise. It is therefore important to better understand a) the earthquake ground motion in local surface sedimentary and topographic structures, b) seismic ambient noise in these structures, and c) characteristics of seismic ambient noise that could suggest, identify or even quantify a potential effect of surface geology on earthquake ground motion. Numerical modelling can very much help to understand both earthquake ground motion and seismic ambient noise. Whereas more modelling was focused on the earthquake ground motion, only relatively limited work has been done on the numerical modelling of ambient noise: at both low frequencies (microseisms) and high frequencies (microtremor). Therefore, we still do not sufficiently understand the relation between earthquake motion and seismic noise in local surface structure, what quantitative information can be reliably extracted from noise measurements, and which processing techniques are most appropriate. Thus, we welcome contributions on a) site effects, b) seismic ambient noise in local surface structures, c) linking earthquake ground motion with seismic ambient noise in relation to site response. All kinds of approaches can be considered: instrumental measurements with sparse or dense arrays, advanced processing, theoretical or numerical modelling of earthquake ground motion and/or seismic ambient noise. Studies could concern sites with various dimensionalities (1D, 2D, 3D, with or without random material heterogeneities) and various underground and surface geometry (including topography). Examples of apparent inconsistencies between noise measurements and instrumental earthquake site response are also welcome to gather as complete as possible picture of the issues which are still ahead.
title: Analysis and modelling of site effects of earthquakes and seismic ambient noise

description: Following the success of last year’s edition, we are delighted to bring this session back to EGU2027 to keep the community up to date about the most recent advances in inclusion studies! Understanding the processes shaping our planet is the main goal of Geosciences. Fluid, melt and mineral inclusions offer an invaluable contribution, allowing to directly study unreachable portions of Earth’s interior. Besides constraining pressure, temperature and oxygen fugacity conditions at the time of their formation, inclusions can provide innumerable geochemical information, shedding light on fluid and melt sources, chemistry, physical state, migration and interactions occurring from sedimentary and magmatic environments to orogenic belts, subduction zones and deep into Earth’s mantle. The recent development of high-resolution analytical techniques, such as Raman microspectroscopy, microthermometry, scanning and transmission electron microscopy, X-ray and electron diffraction, microtomography, microfluorescence and mass spectroscopy, has allowed to obtain an unprecedented level of details from micro- to nano-scale, highlighting features never observed so far and opening new scenarios in Earth’s dynamics. Contributions on innovative studies about fluid, melt and mineral inclusions and relationships with their host mineral phases are welcome from any field of Geosciences, spanning from magmatism, metamorphism and deep mantle dynamics to palaeoclimatology and sedimentary processes, oil & gas and ore deposits. Works presenting innovative and advanced tools to investigate natural samples, as well as experimental studies, are appreciated. Early career researchers are strongly encouraged to present their contributions.
title: - Looking into the unreachable: Inclusions as snapshots into Earth processes, from the crust to the deep mantle and beyond

description: The rapid advancement in spectroscopic techniques at micro- and nanoscale offers new methods of investigation in the broad field of mineralogy and open new frontiers in a wide range of geoscience studies. Spectroscopies are crucial for interpreting a complicated range of behaviour and are often the only means to explore microscopic and rare minerals and mineral inclusions, as well as materials behaviour in extreme conditions. This session will explore advances in spectroscopic methods for investigating solid, melt, and fluid inclusions in minerals and any other geological materials. The session will bring together both theoretically, experimentally oriented and naturalist scientists, providing them with an opportunity to share ideas, discuss methods and learn from one another. Particular emphasis will be placed on correlative and in situ workflows, latest improvements, and the integration of spectroscopic data with other techniques. Studies addressing methodological developments, analytical challenges, cultural heritage, geological applications, and interpretations of crustal, magmatic, hydrothermal, metamorphic, deep Earth and planetary processes are welcome.
title: The application of spectroscopic methods to minerals, and solids and fluid inclusions.

description: Geochronology provides the temporal framework for the study of geologic processes, allowing us to quantify the timing, rates, and durations of the processes that shape our planet. Improvements on well-established techniques, in conjunction with new methodologies and capabilities, continue to provide greater levels of detail and complexity in geochronological investigations. Consequently, geochronological studies are blooming in a variety of fields and in many cases could revolutionize our understanding of fundamental natural processes. With this session, we aim to provide a platform to discuss 1) advances in a broad spectrum of geochronological methods (sample preparation, analytical techniques, innovative data reduction strategies, and interpretational and modelling approaches) and 2) applications of such methods to a variety of problems covering a multitude of temporal and spatial scales across the broader Earth Sciences. We particularly encourage presentations of novel and unconventional applications or attempts to develop new geochronometers.
title: Advances in geochronology: from the traditional to the avant-garde

description: Crystal-scale observations of rock microstructures and textures provide a fundamental basis for understanding the petrogenesis of igneous, metamorphic and mineralised rocks. Petrography remains at the heart of petrological investigation: it provides the observations to develop new hypotheses and the context needed to interpret increasingly sophisticated textural, geochemical, and computational datasets. This session celebrates the value of detailed petrographic observations and highlights how traditional and modern datasets can be combined to reconstruct geological processes across a wide range of spatial and temporal scales. We invite contributions applying textural and microstructural approaches to igneous, metamorphic, and mineralised systems, with particular emphasis on studies that place petrography and microstructural observations at the centre of geological interpretation. This may include contributions that combine traditional (e.g., optical microscopy, universal stage) and modern (e.g., EBSD, X-Ray-Tomography and -Ptychography, chemical mapping, XMapTools) methods, as well as submissions focused on advances in quantitative petrography, 3D and 4D imaging, and numerical models of microstructural and/or textural evolution.
title: The modern petrographer: integrating traditional and novel approaches to reconstruct geological processes

description: Mineralogy is the cornerstone of many disciplines and is used to solve a wide range of questions in geoscience. This broad session offers the opportunity to explore the diversity of methods and approaches used to study minerals, and how minerals behave and evolve in their many contexts. Also, we will address issues that involve the use and development of techniques and the relevant ab initio simulations beyond current applications in metamorphic and magmatic petrology applied to the Earth and other planetary bodies. We welcome contributions to all aspects of mineralogy, including environmental, soil science, metamorphic, plutonic, deep Earth, planetary, applied mineralogy, and so on. All approaches are welcome: analytical, experimental and theoretical.
title: Solving geoscience problems using mineralogy

description: The transport sector, comprising road traffic, shipping and aviation, is a significant contributor to global warming and has detrimental effects on air quality. The combustion of fossil fuels emits gases and particles that alter the chemical composition of the atmosphere. In addition to CO₂, non-CO₂ effects (NOx, contrails, aerosols, and aerosol-cloud interactions) are also important, some of which have warming and others cooling effects on the climate. Driven by growing demand, the contribution of aviation to climate change is expected to increase, and emissions from road traffic and shipping may also rise depending on evolving mobility patterns and technological development. It is therefore crucial to develop and implement measures that reduce the climate footprint of transport. Mitigation options include alternative fuels such as electricity and hydrogen, technological improvements such as exhaust after-treatment systems, and operational measures such as optimized routing. A change in the share of demand between transport modes (modal shift) can complement these technical and operational measures. Assessing the effects of such measures with numerical atmospheric models relies heavily on state-of-the-art emission inventories. Providing information on the uncertainties in emission data is essential for a reliable assessment of air quality and climate effects; these uncertainties further interact with those associated with the representation of physical, chemical, and dynamical processes in atmospheric models. The objective of this session is to bring together the community that develops transport emission inventories with the community that uses them. The session has two aims: first, to establish a shared understanding of the requirements for, and uncertainties in, transport emission inventories; second, to review the latest research on the non-CO₂ and air-quality effects of transport emissions. The overarching goal is to reduce the uncertainties in the assessment of the climate and air-quality impacts of the transport sector. Contributions are welcome on topics ranging from measurement campaigns and modelling studies to strategies for reducing the environmental impact of transport.
title: Towards sustainable road traffic, shipping and aviation: from emissions to climate and air quality effects

description: Significant uncertainties remain in our understanding of Carbon Dioxide (CO2) and Methane (CH4) fluxes across land, ocean, and atmosphere at both regional and global scales. Remote sensing of CO2 and CH4 offers great potential to enhance our understanding of the natural carbon cycle and to monitor anthropogenic emissions. Recent advances in CO2 and CH4 remote sensing technologies, spanning spaceborne, airborne, and ground-based platforms, have delivered unprecedented accuracy and coverage. Furthermore, next-generation platforms such as CO2M, Merlin, TANGO, and CO2Image promise to further enhance observational capabilities. When integrated with ground-based observation networks and modeling tools, these space-based observations can significantly improve our understanding of the carbon cycle from local to global scales. This session invites contributions on all aspects of CO2 and CH4 remote sensing, including current missions (e.g., GOSAT/2/GW, OCO-2/3, S5P/S5, IASI-NG, Carbon Mapper, MicroCarb, GHGSat), upcoming and planned missions (e.g., CO2M, Merlin, TANGO), as well as ground-based networks (e.g., TCCON and COCCON), airborne platforms, and other remote sensing instruments. We welcome contributions on advances in retrieval techniques, instrument concepts, and validation activities, with an emphasis on interpreting observations related to natural fluxes and anthropogenic emissions.
title: Remote Sensing of Carbon Dioxide and Methane from Space

description: Globally, wildfires are intensifying and becoming more frequent, significantly altering the atmospheric composition due to the emitted smoke aerosol and fire-related gaseous emissions. Smoke particles interact with radiation and cloud microphysics, as well as affecting on the biosphere and human health. Extreme wildfires that trigger the formation of pyrocumulonimbus clouds can inject smoke aerosols into the stratosphere, where they can have long-lasting climate effects similar to those of volcanic eruptions. Increasingly frequent climate extremes and wildfires, such as those experienced in the summer of 2026, and shifting patterns of wildfires change atmospheric smoke distributions. Thus, it is crucial to understand the interconnected processes from smoke formation to its impacts. The aim of this interdivisional session is therefore to bring together scientists from different disciplines to explore the impact of wildfire smoke and co-emitted aerosol particles, such as bioaerosols and dust, on atmospheric processes, air quality, and biosphere dynamics. Possible contributions include, but are not limited to: • Characterization of the emission, transport, and deposition processes of smoke and its interaction with other aerosol particles • Interactions of smoke and related aerosol particles with atmosphere, radiation, clouds, and climate including large-scale effects • Relation between vegetation, burning conditions, and smoke properties • Chemical composition and atmospheric ageing of smoke particles • Modelling, remote sensing, and field and laboratory studies of all processes from smoke formation to its atmospheric impacts • Impacts of wildfire emissions on terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems • Health effects of smoke By integrating research from atmospheric science, chemical analysis, combustion physics, vegetation ecology, and other disciplines, we aim to clarify the complex relationships between wildfires, smoke formation, transport, and ageing, and their effects on the environment.
title: Wildfire smoke and its interactions with the atmosphere, biosphere and climate

description: Light Absorbing Carbonaceous aerosols (LACs), including black carbon and brown carbon, are major components of atmospheric particulate matter and play a critical role in Earth’s radiative balance, air quality, climate and health burden. Their complex sources, chemical transformation, and transport create substantial challenges for accurately quantifying their environmental impacts and developing effective mitigation strategies. This session aims to bring together observational, modeling and interdisciplinary research on carbonaceous aerosols from local to global scales. We welcome studies investigating emission sources and drivers, including anthropogenic (fossil fuel combustion, biomass burning, industrial emissions fossil-fuel combustion, residential combustion, transportation and agricultural burning) and natural processes (wildfires, biogenic volatile organic compound oxidation). Contributions addressing source apportionment, emission inventories, chemical and physical characterization, optical properties, atmospheric lifetimes, ageing and transformation are particularly encouraged. The session will also highlight advances in ground-based, airborne and satellite remote sensing, as well as innovative measurement techniques for characterizing LAC abundance, composition and optical properties. We also invite studies that integrate observations with atmospheric models, data assimilation, machine learning and multi-platform datasets to improve understanding of these carbonaceous aerosol variability and trends. The central focus is on the carbonaceous aerosols, climate and health nexus. Contributions addressing radiative effects, aerosol–cloud interactions, health risks (exposure assessment, epidemiological linkages, and attributable disease burden), environmental inequalities and climate-air quality interactions are encouraged. We also welcome research examining emission-control strategies and the translation of atmospheric science into evidence based air quality and climate policy, while integrating Clean-air regulatory frameworks, targeted reduction strategies (e.g., short-lived climate pollutants), and climate-air quality co-benefit evaluations. We aim to connect aerosol sources and processes with observations, impacts and policy applications, the session seeks to foster collaboration among researchers of all career stages across atmospheric chemistry, aerosol science, remote sensing, climate science, health research and policy communities.
title: Light Absorbing Carbonaceous Aerosols: From Observations to Chemistry, Climate–Health and Policy Nexus

description: Satellite, ground-based, and other observational platforms, together with chemical transport models, have greatly advanced our ability to characterize atmospheric composition and air quality from local to global scales. Recent advances in polar-orbiting and geostationary satellite sensors, ground-based networks, and field campaigns are providing unprecedented observations of aerosols, reactive trace gases, and greenhouse gases with improved spatial, temporal, and spectral resolution. These complementary observing systems offer new opportunities to characterize diurnal variability, extreme pollution events, emission sources, and transboundary transport, while improving our understanding of human exposure to air pollution and its associated health impacts. At the same time, advances in artificial intelligence (AI), data fusion, and atmospheric modeling are creating new opportunities to integrate satellite observations, ground-based measurements, meteorological data, and chemical transport models. These approaches enable high-resolution and gap-free characterization of atmospheric composition, support near-real-time monitoring and forecasting, and improve assessments of air pollution exposure, radiative effects, emissions, and health impacts. This session invites contributions that advance our understanding of atmospheric composition, air quality, and health through observations, modeling, data integration, and emerging computational approaches. We particularly welcome studies using satellite and ground-based observations, field measurements, chemical transport models, AI and machine learning, multi-source data fusion, and novel approaches for air pollution monitoring, exposure assessment, and environmental health applications.
title: Advances in Atmospheric Composition, Air Quality, and Health

description: The interactions between aerosols, climate, weather, and society are among the large uncertainties of current atmospheric research. Mineral dust is an important natural source of aerosol with significant implications on radiation, cloud microphysics, atmospheric chemistry, and the carbon cycle via the fertilization of marine and terrestrial ecosystems. Dust impacts snow and ice albedo and can accelerate glacier melt. In addition, properties of dust deposited in sediments and ice cores are important (paleo-)climate indicators. This interdivisional session -- building bridges between the EGU divisions AS, CL, CR, SSP, BG and GM -- had its first edition in 2004 and it is open to contributions dealing with: (1) measurements and theoretical concepts of all aspects of the dust cycle (emission, transport, deposition, size distribution, particle characteristics), (2) numerical simulations (physical or machine learning) of dust on global, regional, and local scales (3) meteorological conditions for dust storms, (4) interactions of dust with clouds and radiation, (5) influence of dust on atmospheric chemistry, (6) fertilization of ecosystems through dust deposition, (7) interactions with the biosphere, cryosphere, and hydrosphere, (8) any study using dust as a (paleo-)climate indicator, including sediment archives in loess, ice cores, lake sediments, ocean sediments and dunes, (9) impacts of dust on climate and climate change, and associated feedbacks and uncertainties, (10) implications of dust for health, transport, energy systems, agriculture, infrastructure, etc. We especially encourage the submission of papers that integrate different disciplines and/or address the modelling of past, present, and future climates.
title: Aeolian dust: initiator, player, and recorder of environmental change

description: Climate change is taking place at all levels of the atmosphere, from the surface to the edge of space. It is well-known that increasing greenhouse gas concentrations, in particular CO2, cause cooling and contraction throughout the middle and upper atmosphere. In the middle atmosphere, stratospheric ozone depletion and subsequent recovery play an important role as well, and interactions with circulation changes are still being disentangled. There are still considerable unknowns regarding long-term changes in atmospheric dynamics, including winds, tides, planetary waves, gravity waves, and large-scale residual circulations. These can also be related to considerable spatial variations in long-term trends in for example temperature or ionospheric quantities, as well as dependencies of trends on season and local time. In the ionosphere, additional spatial variations and seasonal/local time dependencies arise from long-term changes in the Earth’s magnetic field, which can also interact with variability and changes in atmospheric dynamics. Building a consistent pattern of long-term change across different atmospheric layers, regions, seasons and local times is therefore a fundamental challenge, which is important to address, given the connections with climate change near the surface and impacts of upper atmospheric changes on space operations and sustainability. This session welcomes studies that contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of all aspects of long-term changes in the stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere, and ionosphere, as well as their broader impacts, from surface weather to space operations.
title: Long-term changes in the middle and upper atmosphere and their broader impacts

description: Marine aerosols are a major source of uncertainty in climate forcing estimates because marine clouds are highly sensitive to the cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) and ice nucleating particles (INP) provided by these aerosols. Over the remote oceans, CCN and INP populations are shaped by primary sea spray and secondary formation, and are increasingly influenced by transported dust, smoke, and anthropogenic pollution. Marine aerosols are also vertically coupled, but this coupling remains poorly quantified: the free troposphere delivers aerosols down into the marine boundary layer, while the marine boundary layer feeds particles and precursors back aloft. Constraining the resulting climate impacts requires ambient observations, laboratory experiments and modelling across scales to be brought together. This session brings together work on the sources, formation processes and impacts of marine aerosols across the full depth of the marine atmosphere - from the boundary layer to the free troposphere - and across primary, secondary and transported origins. We welcome observations from diverse platforms, alongside laboratory experiments and modelling from regional to global scales. Studies that connect emission and formation processes to cloud and climate response are particularly encouraged. Topics of interest include, but are not limited to: • Primary marine aerosol: production mechanisms, fluxes, size distribution, composition, CCN/INP activity • Secondary marine aerosol: iodine, sulfur, ammonia, amine and organic emissions and mechanisms, their chemical transformation and new particle formation • Transported aerosols: dust, smoke, anthropogenic and volcanic plumes over the ocean, their fates and impacts • Vertical coupling: entrainment, convective transport and detrainment, aerosol and precursor exchange between the marine boundary layer and free troposphere • Marine aerosol-cloud interactions: CCN/INP control of clouds; cloud processing and wet removal of aerosols; radiative and precipitation responses • Perturbations of the marine background: shipping emissions and fuel-sulfur regulation, and proposed interventions such as marine cloud brightening • Climate response and model evaluation: marine aerosol radiative effects and feedbacks, the pre-industrial baseline and future projections, and representation of marine aerosol in Earth system models
title: Aerosols and their impacts in the marine environment

description: Atmospheric radicals (OH, HO₂, RO₂, NO₃ and halogen oxides) control the oxidation of trace gases, drive the formation of secondary pollutants such as ozone, and influence climate. Their sources, such as HCHO, HONO and ClNO₂, and their chemical fate determine how primary pollutants are transformed, so understanding them is central to addressing regional air pollution and climate change. Yet radicals remain among the hardest species to study. Their concentrations are extremely low, they react very quickly, and the reaction networks they initiate are highly complex. This session brings together experimentalists and modellers working on radical chemistry across laboratory, chamber and field settings. We invite contributions on the development of techniques for detecting radicals, their precursors and intermediate species, and on the adaptation of instruments to ground-based, mobile, shipborne, airborne and other platforms. We also welcome work on quality assurance, including calibration procedures and inter-comparison of different techniques, as well as on model development, from new reactions and mechanisms to revised model configurations and uncertainty analysis. Finally, we encourage studies that apply radical measurements and modelling in field and chamber experiments.
title: Atmospheric Radicals: Measurement, Modelling and Their Role in Air Quality and Climate

description: Loess deposits cover large areas of the Earth and host dense populations and major infrastructure worldwide. Although widely known as a terrestrial paleoclimate archive, loess is above all a problematic geomaterial: its open metastable micro-fabric, high porosity and water sensitivity make it prone to liquefaction, subsidence, erosion, and catastrophic landsliding under intense rainfall, irrigation, water-table rise, human induced loading and vibrations, or seismic shaking. Climate change and rapid land use transformation are altering the drivers of these processes, making the hazard non-stationary. Developing hazard mitigation and sustainable engineered solutions requires a better understanding of loess behavior across multiple scales – from fabric dynamics at the micro-scale to to slope- and landscape-scale failure. This remains the central open problem, and it is one that no single discipline can solve. This session brings together geologists, geomorphologists, geotechnical engineers and disaster risk experts. It also fosters discussions with experts in machine learning and AI to better understand opportunities for connecting information across the scales. We welcome contributions on, but not limited to: • Micro- to nano-scale characterisation: advanced imaging (CT, SEM, NMR), pore-network and fabric evolution, inter-particle bonding and cementation, physico-chemical controls, and their upscaling within unsaturated soil mechanics. • Geomorphology and erosion dynamics: aeolian deposition and provenance, landscape evolution, gully initiation and headcut retreat, sediment connectivity, and land-use or vegetation-restoration effects. • Upscaling and heterogeneity: developing tools to connect information and insights across the scales. • Geotechnical behaviour and geohazards: wetting-induced collapse, static and seismic liquefaction, failure mechanisms and runout of loess landslides, monitoring, modelling and early warning, including InSAR, UAV and LiDAR approaches. • Engineering solutions and risk mitigation: soil stabilisation and improvement, infrastructure design on collapsible ground, eco-engineering and nature-based solutions, and risk-informed prevention strategies. We particularly encourage novel experimental techniques, multi-scale and coupled modelling, and case studies from loess regions worldwide, to build a genuinely comparative and global understanding of loess systems and sustainable methods to mitigate the impact of loess geohazards.
title: Loess Systems: Micro-to-Macro Dynamics, Geohazards, and Engineering Solutions

description: Hydroclimatic extremes are increasingly recognized as interconnected environmental and societal hazard than isolated episodes of water availability and scarcity. Their impacts can propagate through hydrological systems and ecosystems, alter water availability and quality, affect agricultural productivity and influence human health and well-being. This session will explore the mechanisms and cascading pathways through which drought and related hydroclimatic extremes generate risks across water, ecosystems, and society. The session will bring together emerging approaches for understanding and characterizing different forms of drought, including long-term conventional droughts- meteorological, Agricultural, Hydrological, Ecological, and Socio-economic droughts as well as rapidly developing Flash Droughts and their potential transitions to flood conditions. Contributions addressing drought characteristics, drought-to-flood transitions, underlying drivers and mechanisms, detection and identification techniques, monitoring and prediction, and changes under future climate change are particularly encouraged. This session welcomes studies investigating the impacts of drought and associated hydroclimatic extremes on water resources and water quality, ecosystems, agricultural productivity, and human health, as well as their interactions, compound effects and cascading risks. Studies focusing on drought dynamics and impacts in data-scarce regions are particularly encouraged. Interdisciplinary research employing remote sensing observations, modelling, artificial intelligence, and other emerging methodologies, including assessments of drought and drought-to-flood transitions under climate change and future projections. By bringing together researchers from climate science, natural hazards, hydrology, environmental sciences, ecology, agriculture, and health, the session aims to advance an integrated understanding of drought dynamics, rapid hydroclimatic transitions, cascading impacts, and associated risks. It further seeks to foster advances in monitoring, prediction, early warning, adaptation, and resilience to evolving hydroclimatic extremes.
title: Hydroclimatic Extremes and Cascading Impacts: From Water Scarcity to Water Quality, Ecosystems and Human Health

description: The polar regions are experiencing rapid and profound environmental changes, with the Arctic warming at nearly four times the global average. Aerosol-cloud interactions remain one of the largest sources of uncertainty in climate models, particularly in these fragile and rapidly evolving environments. Mixed-phase clouds, biogeochemical processes in the ocean and sea ice, and atmospheric dynamics all contribute to complex feedbacks that modulate Earth's radiative balance, influence weather systems, and drive climate change. This session, inspired by the goals of initiatives such as QuiESCENT (Quantifying the Indirect Effect: from Sources to Climate Effects of Natural and Transported aerosol in the Arctic), CATCH (Cryosphere and ATmospheric CHemistry), CIce2Clouds (Coupling of ocean-ice-atmosphere processes: from sea-Ice biogeochemistry to aerosols and Clouds), BEPSII (Biogeochemical exchanges at Sea Ice Interfaces), and PICAASO (Partnerships for Investigations of Clouds and the biogeochemistry of the Atmosphere in Antarctica end the Southern Ocean) aims to foster interdisciplinary collaboration by bringing together researchers studying aerosols, clouds, ocean–ice biogeochemistry, and their coupled interactions in both the Arctic and Antarctic. We seek to bridge disciplinary gaps to advance our understanding of polar climate systems. We invite contributions that address the following key topics: - Aerosol-cloud interactions: Their influence on cloud microphysics, radiative properties, and precipitation patterns in polar environments, including the contrasting effects of anthropogenic pollution and natural aerosols. - Biogeochemical cycling: Marine and terrestrial sources of aerosols, including sea salt, mineral dust, biological particles, black carbon, and organic aerosols, and their feedbacks with atmospheric components. - Boundary layer dynamics: The role of atmospheric and oceanic boundary layer processes in shaping aerosol and cloud properties, as well as their impact on boundary layer mixing and local pollution processing. - Observational and modeling advances: Innovations in field campaigns, remote sensing, laboratory experiments, and modeling frameworks to improve the representation of polar aerosol–cloud–ocean–ice systems in climate models. - Climate feedbacks and projections: Implications of polar aerosol–cloud interactions for climate model performance and global climate predictions, with a focus on reducing uncertainties in projections.
title: Bridging Disciplines: Interactions Between Polar Aerosols, Clouds, Sea Ice, and Oceans in a Changing Climate

description: Black carbon, brown carbon, and mineral dust—collectively known as light-absorbing aerosols (LAA)—are key drivers of climate. Their influence spans the atmosphere, land (e.g., snow and ice albedo), and water (e.g., oceans and lakes) systems. Major uncertainties remain around their emissions, physical-chemical properties, and mixing states. The estimates of LAA effective radiative forcing in earth system models differ by over two-fold globally. To address this, we need enhanced observations and improved model representations of LAA spatial distribution, microphysical features, and lifecycle evolution. Such progress would reconcile conflicting data and ensure accurate aerosol treatment in climate models. We welcome contributions covering: (a) LAA characterization, transformations, and removal processes; (b)multi-platform observational analysis, field campaign experiments on LAA; (c) relationships among LAA chemical, microphysical, and optical attributes; (d) numerical modelling of LAA across scales; (e) evaluation of LAA radiative forcing and climatic effects; and (f) AI and data-driven techniques for studying LAA-relevant processes.
title: Light-absorbing Aerosols in the Earth System: Properties, Processes, and Impacts

description: Bioaerosols influence public health, climate dynamics and economy. Up to 30% of the global population now suffers from pollen allergies and asthma, a burden that has steadily intensified over recent decades and costs an estimated €50–150 billion annually to the public health system. Beyond human health, pollen and fungal spores also impair agricultural and forestry productivity, reducing crop yields and forest vitality. These challenges are further compounded by climate change, as rising temperatures and elevated CO₂ levels alter the life cycles of fungi and plants, leading to intensified pollen and spore emissions. Accurate quantification of bioaerosols in different regions around the globe with markedly different emission patterns is therefore critical across a broad spectrum of research domains, including cloud-aerosol interactions and climate feedback, or public health responses to allergenic species. In response to these demands, bioaerosol monitoring is undergoing a paradigm shift that builds upon recent advances in novel automatic bioaerosol measurement techniques, including in situ monitoring, DNA-based and omics techniques and remote sensing, gradually replacing traditional manual methods. Nevertheless, significant technical challenges remain. Real-time methods with high temporal resolution often suffer from limited discriminatory power, whereas offline techniques provide rich taxonomic and physiological details but lack temporal resolution and struggle to yield absolute quantitative atmospheric concentrations. Furthermore, the emergence of this high throughput and taxonomically resolved techniques paves the way to advancing current modelling and forecasting capabilities for aeroallergens and raises further challenges in producing climatological time series that allow for assessing long term trends in bioaerosol concentrations and quantifying their response to climate change. This session seeks to bridge these gaps by uniting interdisciplinary expertise in bioaerosol research. We invite contributions on novel detection methods and laboratory and field validation, indoor and outdoor ambient observations, chemical composition detection, model development and forecasting, as well as exposure assessment and associated health impacts, including impacts of bioaerosol-air pollution interactions on all the above. Our goal is to foster cross-cutting dialogue that advances both fundamental understanding and practical monitoring capabilities.
title: Modern bioaerosol research: detection, characterisation, modelling and impacts

description: Short-lived greenhouse gases (GHG), including methane (CH4) and ozone (O3), are important contributors to global warming. Unlike long-lived GHGs, their tropospheric abundance is strongly influenced by reactive processes and depends on complex photochemical formation and removal pathways and the availability of precursors and reactants. Additionally, CH4 and O3 are photochemically coupled in the troposphere: the hydroxyl (OH) radical, whose production is largely driven by sunlight, is the dominant atmospheric sink of CH4, while CH4 oxidation contributes to O3 formation and impacts atmospheric oxidation capacity. This session focuses on the photochemical sources, sinks and mechanisms governing short-lived GHGs in the troposphere, with a particular emphasis on CH4 and O3, their precursors and key reactants. Relevant topics include, but are not limited to: the chemistry of CH4 and O3 and their interactions with nitrogen oxides (NOx), volatile organic compounds (VOC), hydroxyl (OH) and peroxy (HO2, RO2) radicals, carbon monoxide (CO), and halogen species (Cl, Br, I). The goal of this session is to discuss how photochemical pathways affect the abundance and spatio-temporal distribution of short-lived GHGs, associated uncertainties and challenges, and their future climate implications. We welcome contributions from observational, laboratory, and modeling studies across the entire troposphere, including innovative measurement technologies, advances in global modeling and other novel methodological approaches. Submissions may address photochemical mechanisms and reaction pathways, tropospheric oxidation capacity, ozone formation sensitivity, methane lifetime, regional and global long-term trends, precursor emission changes, and the broader impacts of short-lived GHGs on climate and human health, both now and in the future.
title: The role of tropospheric photochemistry in climate change

description: Indoor air quality is vital to human health, as people spend most of their time indoors, including at home and in the workplace. While indoor activities such as cooking or cleaning elevate indoor pollution levels, outdoor pollutants simultaneously enter buildings through windows, doors, ventilation, or structural leaks. Conversely, pollutants generated indoors, such as volatile organic compounds or particulate matter, exit through these same pathways, contributing to urban air pollution. Moreover, the indoor processing of primary pollutants differs significantly from outdoor dynamics (e.g., oxidants and surface interactions). This divergence adds complexity to how pollutants transform during transport and produce secondary pollutants, such as secondary organic aerosols and ozone. Understanding this dynamic is essential for developing effective mitigation strategies and informing policy. It requires integrated insights into emission sources, chemical transformation, indoor-outdoor exchange mechanisms, and the influence of occupant behaviour. This session invites contributions from laboratory/chamber experiments, indoor and outdoor field observations (including both lived-in and model-house environments), and modelling studies that advance our knowledge of the indoor-outdoor air pollution interface. We particularly encourage submissions addressing indoor emission sources, pollutant transport, transformation, and exposure assessments.
title: Indoor and Outdoor Air Pollution Interface: Emissions, Transport, Transformation, and Exposure

description: Understanding the complex physical and chemical transformations of biogenic and anthropogenic emissions is essential for predicting their effects on air quality and climate. This session focuses on investigations ranging from fundamental molecular-level mechanisms to complete chemical mechanisms that drive and explain these large-scale atmospheric processes. We welcome contributions that bridge the gap between microscopic processes and macroscopic atmospheric phenomena, spanning gas-phase kinetics, multiphase chemistry, and the nanophysics that drives aerosol forcing. Topics of interest include: 1) computational and theoretical advances, including quantum chemistry, molecular dynamics simulations, and machine learning; 2) experimental insights from laboratory, atmospheric simulation chamber, and field studies; and 3) the application of novel experimental techniques and the use of research infrastructures (such as ACTRIS, ICOS, and IAGOS) for detailed process studies.
title: Multiscale investigations into atmospheric processes: theory, simulation, and observation

description: The atmosphere integrates surface–atmosphere exchange across spatial and temporal scales. Monitoring and interpreting atmospheric greenhouse gases (GHGs), such as carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane (CH4), therefore provide fundamental information on carbon fluxes from natural and anthropogenic sources and their links to energy and water cycling. Combining observations with process-based and data-driven modelling can constrain poorly understood processes, particularly in the terrestrial biosphere, and reveal the mechanisms and climatic drivers governing GHG exchange and carbon–climate feedbacks. Such process-level understanding is essential for predicting how these feedbacks will evolve in a changing climate. Machine-learning (ML) approaches provide additional opportunities to extract information from increasingly diverse and extensive datasets. This session focuses on top-down, bottom-up, and hybrid modelling frameworks that investigate GHG exchange using observational platforms such as surface and ecosystem networks (e.g. ICOS Atmosphere and Ecosystem, FLUXNET, NOAA), aircraft campaigns (e.g. MAGIC and COMET), and active and passive remote-sensing missions (e.g. ECOSTRESS, OCO-2/3, TROPOMI, and GOSAT). We particularly welcome studies that combine data sources not traditionally used together to constrain GHG fluxes and the underlying processes. Contributions may explore how the integration of diverse observations with process-based models, machine learning, or novel data-assimilation approaches can identify climatic controls, improve process representation, and advance understanding of carbon–climate feedbacks.
title: Understanding greenhouse gas exchange and carbon–climate feedbacks using in situ observations, remote sensing and machine learning

description: Methane is a potent short-lived climate forcer, and rapid mitigation measures are crucial for meeting climate targets and limiting currently expected temperature overshoots. This session will explore these methane mitigation measures, spanning emissions reduction approaches, novel point-source oxidation technologies, and potential atmospheric methane removal approaches. We invite contributions covering: - Assessment of methane emission reduction approaches - Novel and emerging methane mitigation approaches, including emissions destruction and atmospheric removal - Measurement and verification of mitigation effectiveness - The role of methane mitigation in future climate scenarios
title: Methane Mitigation: from Point Source Emissions to Global Sinks

description: Aircraft emit a mix of gases and particles in the Earth’s atmosphere, near the surface and at altitude, up to 12 km. Aviation emissions degrade air quality in the vicinity of airports and globally, and contribute to climate change through pathways that are specific to emissions released at altitude, including but not limited to NOx-induced ozone, methane and stratospheric water vapour changes, and aerosol–radiation and aerosol–cloud interactions. These impacts remain uncertain, while the sector continues to grow at ~5% every year. At the same time, the atmospheric implications of mitigation options, including Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) and hydrogen, are also not well understood, despite their high policy relevance. This specialised session synthesises measurement and modelling contributions towards better understanding the present and future impacts of aviation emissions on atmospheric composition, air quality and climate, alongside the substantial recent progress on contrail research. We invite contributions on: - the characterisation and quantification of gaseous and particulate emissions from current and future fuels, engines and combustor technologies, including ultrafine particles (volatile and non-volatile), lubrication oil and emerging or unregulated pollutants, based on laboratory, engine test-cell, airport and in-flight measurements as well as emission models and inventories; - the atmospheric fate of these emissions: plume processing, transport pathways, chemistry, aerosol microphysics and removal processes; - their air quality effects near airports and at regional and global scales, and the associated exposure and health implications; - their non-CO2 climate effects through ozone, methane, water vapour and aerosol–radiation and aerosol–cloud interactions, including feedbacks, metrics and uncertainty assessment; - the atmospheric implications of mitigation options, including fuel composition, sustainable aviation fuels, hydrogen and electrified propulsion, engine technology and operational measures. We hope that these contributions will bring the community together and spark fruitful discussions and collaborations towards an improved understanding of aviation’s growing impacts on the atmosphere.
title: Aircraft emissions and their air quality and non-CO2 climate impacts

description: This session is organized for the third time at EGU General Assemblies and reflects the recent emerging trends of atmospheric monitoring: (i) realizing multi-instrument synergy retrieval and (ii) bridging three branches of atmospheric research (modelling, in situ measurements, and remote sensing). This session encourages discussions that explore the synergies of complimentary observations, such as synergies of passive imagery with active vertical profiling of the atmosphere, synergies of observations in different spectral ranges and at different time and/or spatial scales, and synergies of satellite observations with sub-orbital observations and chemical transport model simulations. Synergy is important because the quality of measurements cannot be radically improved once the instruments have been deployed, but algorithms can continuously evolve and notably improve results with data fusion and optimization of the joint sensitivity of multi-instrument datasets.
