The the session especially welcomes the ides and demonstrations of synergy methods and Interdisciplinary applications using novel observations from the , EPS-SG, MTG, PACE, Copernicus Sentinels, EarthCARE and other recent and forthcoming advanced satellite missions (e.g., CO2M) as well as field campaigns. The session also invites presentations that demonstrate the benefits of collaboration amongst the three core fields of atmospheric aerosol studies outlined in the Models, In situ, and Remote sensing of Aerosols (MIRA) international working group, which was formed to facilitate collaborations and improve discussions amongst these fields of study and across regional boundaries. For this year, presentations relevant to coordinated campaigns, including the forthcoming NASA/ESA experiment CoSENSE, which bring together ground-based and airborne remote sensing and in situ measurements, satellite observations and atmospheric modelling for EarthCARE Cal/Val and scientific exploitation, are particularly welcome. More information can be found at https://science.larc.nasa.gov/mira-wg/.
title: Enhancement of atmosphere characterization using synergy of multi-instrument remote sensing observations and bridging with transport models and in situ measurements (e.g. MIRA).

description: Reliable greenhouse gas (GHG) observations (e.g. CO2, CH4, N2O) and complementary chemical and isotopic tracer measurements (e.g. δ13C(CO2), δ18O(CO2), δ13C(CH4), δ2H(CH4), as well as radioactive tracers e.g. radon, 14CH4, 14CO2) are critical for tracking emissions, detecting changes in atmospheric composition, understanding sources and sinks, and informing effective climate policy. As GHG mitigation strategies and reduction targets increasingly rely on precise, long-term data, it is essential to ensure that measurements are accurate and comparable across time and space. Metrology, the science of measurement, plays a vital role in this process by providing standardised calibration methods, uncertainty assessment, and traceability to international reference standards and scales. While metrology has traditionally been applied in controlled laboratory settings, its principles are increasingly critical to real world, in situ atmospheric observations, where long-term consistency, cross-network comparability, and data integrity are key. Additionally, emerging measurement platforms including UAVs, mobile laboratories, and low-cost sensor networks present new calibration challenges that require innovative metrological approaches. Strengthening the connection between metrology and in situ atmospheric observations is key to building globally consistent datasets that support climate research, emissions verification, and international reporting. This session aims to foster cross-disciplinary dialogue and highlight advances that improve the comparability of GHG and tracer measurements across spatial and temporal scales. We invite contributions that explore novel or improved calibration strategies, measurement and analytical strategies, uncertainty quantification, interlaboratory comparisons, and traceability chains for GHGs, chemical, stable isotope, and radioactive tracers. Of particular interest are studies that address harmonisation between measurement networks, improvements in temporal and spatial resolution, and integration with satellite data or modelling frameworks.
title: Greenhouse gas and tracer observations: calibration, harmonisation, and cross-network consistency

description: Over the last years, more and more satellite data on tropospheric composition have become available and are now being used in numerous applications. In this session, we aim to bring together reports on new or improved data products and their validation, as well as studies using satellite data for applications in tropospheric chemistry, emission inversions and air quality. This includes both studies on trace gases and aerosols. We welcome presentations based on studies analysing data from current and future satellite missions, including the geostationary GEMS, TEMPO and Sentinel-4 platforms and the recent S5, IRS, IASI-NG and 3MI instruments. Topics also include the inter-comparisons of different remote sensing measurements dedicated to tropospheric chemistry sounding and/or analyses with ground-based measurements and chemical transport models.
title: Satellite observations of tropospheric composition and pollution, analyses with models and applications

description: Atmospheric aerosols influence cloud formation and Earth's radiative balance by acting as cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) and ice nucleating particles (INPs). Among the diverse aerosol population, biological and biogenetic particles, including bacteria, fungal spores, pollen, plant debris, marine organic matter, and their molecular fragments, have emerged as disproportionately efficient nuclei, capable of initiating ice formation at temperatures far warmer than mineral dust or other inorganic aerosols. Despite growing recognition of their importance, the sources, atmospheric transport, transformation, and ice- or cloud-nucleating mechanisms of these particles remain incompletely understood, limiting their representation in cloud microphysics and climate models. This session invites contributions that advance understanding of the origin, composition, and atmospheric processing of biological and biogenetic aerosols and their role as CCN and INPs. We welcome studies spanning laboratory investigations of nucleation mechanisms, field observations and sampling campaigns, novel detection and characterization techniques, and modeling efforts that quantify the climatic relevance of bio-aerosols across scales. Contributions addressing the coupling between terrestrial and marine ecosystems and atmospheric ice/cloud nucleation, as well as the impact of a changing climate and land use on bio-aerosol emissions, are particularly encouraged. By bringing together atmospheric scientists, microbiologists, and modelers, this session aims to foster interdisciplinary dialogue.
title: Aerosols, cloud condensation nuclei, and ice nucleating particles: the particular role of biological and biogenetic particles

description: The composition of the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere (UTLS) plays a key role in the climate system, influencing radiation, atmospheric chemistry, and dynamics. Recent advances in observations and modeling are providing new insights into the processes governing the variability and long-term evolution of this region. The session focuses on topics related to UTLS dynamics, transport, and chemical processes that determine atmospheric composition and its implications for radiation and climate across a range of spatial and temporal scales. We encourage contributions based on in situ and remote-sensing observations from recent and ongoing field campaigns as well as on models of varying complexity, ranging from comprehensive chemistry–climate models to idealized and conceptual approaches. Especially, we welcome studies connecting observational datasets with process-level understanding or model evaluation.
title: Dynamics and chemistry of the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere (UTLS)

description: In recent years, microplastics and nanoplastics have become recognised as ubiquitous atmospheric pollutants. However, many open questions remain regarding emissions, transport and deposition of microplastics and nanoplastics, along with atmospheric processes that determined their fate. In this session we welcome contributions from observational, laboratory and modelling studies that advance the field of airborne microplastics and nanoplastics research, including: - Sampling and analysis of airborne micro- and nanoplastics - Atmospheric microplastics and nanoplastics and their interactions with different environmental compartments (oceans, land and the cryosphere) - Contributions of soils, roads and other terrestrial sources to the atmospheric micro- and nanoplastic burden - Ocean-atmosphere exchange of microplastics and nanoplastics - Microplastics and nanoplastics in the cryosphere - Interactions between micro- and nanoplastics and other sources of aerosol - Interactions between microplastics, nanoplastics, radiation and clouds - Airborne microplastics as vectors for chemical and pathogen transport - Indoor, outdoor, urban, rural and remote microplastics and nanoplastics (measurements, observations, modelling) - Toxicological and exposure studies related to airborne micro- and nanoplastics - Degradation of macro-, micro- and nanoplastics in real and simulated atmospheric conditions - Airborne sources and sinks of micro- and nanoplastics (measurements and modelling)
title: Atmospheric microplastics and nanoplastics

description: Aerosols significantly influence Earth’s climate, atmospheric chemistry, and air quality through their direct interactions with radiation and their effects on cloud formation, properties, lifetime, and precipitation. Aerosol-cloud interactions are particularly important in marine, high-altitude, remote, and extreme environments, including the Himalayas, and the Polar regions, where unique atmospheric conditions provide valuable insights into global climate and atmospheric processes. Understanding how aerosols form, grow, and transform; act as cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) and ice-nucleating particles (INPs); interact with clouds and radiation; and are ultimately removed from the atmosphere is essential for improving climate models and reducing uncertainties in climate predictions. Despite their importance, aerosol properties, sources, and transformation processes in these environments remain poorly constrained. Observational data are limited because of logistical challenges, harsh conditions, and restricted accessibility. This session aims to address these knowledge gaps by bringing together observational and modelling studies from marine environments, high-altitude regions, remote continental environments including Amazon Tall Tower Observatory, and extreme environments: including the Himalayas, the Arctic, and Antarctica. We invite contributions addressing: • Light-absorbing aerosols, including black carbon (BC), brown carbon (BrC), and mineral dust; • Aerosol-cloud interactions and the properties of CCN and INPs; • Microphysical properties and mixing state; • New particle formation, growth processes, and formation pathways; • Source apportionment of aerosols; • Results from recent field campaigns involving ground-based, shipborne, aircraft, and measurements from autonomous platforms; • Emerging observational techniques and research infrastructure, including uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs), balloon-borne sensors, and automated ground-based systems that enable high-resolution measurements under extreme conditions; • The physical and chemical properties of aerosols and their precursors, including the roles of different chemical species in regional and global atmospheric processes; and • Interactions at air-sea and air-snow interfaces and their relationships with meteorological and chemical processes.
title: Advances in Aerosol Observations Across Marine, High-Altitude, Remote Continental, and Extreme Environments: Sources, Transformations, and Climate Interactions

description: Volcanic aerosol clouds from major tropical eruptions cause periods of strong surface cooling in the historical climate record and are dominant influences within decadal surface temperature trends. Advancing our understanding of the influence of volcanoes on climate relies upon better knowledge of: (i) the radiative forcings of past eruptions and the microphysical, chemical and dynamical processes which affect the evolution of stratospheric aerosol properties and (ii) the response mechanisms governing post-eruption climate variability and their dependency on the climate state at the time of the eruption. This can only be achieved by combining information from satellite and in-situ observations of recent eruptions, stratospheric aerosol and climate modelling activities, and reconstructions of past volcanic histories and post-eruption climate state from proxies. In recent years the smoke from intense wildfires in North America and Australia has also been an important component of the stratospheric aerosol layer, the presence of organic aerosol and meteoric particles in background conditions now also firmly established. This session seeks presentations from research aimed at better understanding the stratospheric aerosol layer, its volcanic perturbations and the associated impacts on climate through the post-industrial period (1750-present) and also those further back in the historical record. Observational and model studies on the stratosphere and climate impacts from the 2022 eruption of Hunga Tonga are also especially welcomed. We also welcome contributions to understand the societal impacts of volcanic eruptions and the human responses to them. Contributions addressing volcanic influences on atmospheric composition, such as changes in stratospheric water vapour, ozone and other trace gases are also encouraged. The session aims to bring together research contributing to several current international co-ordinated activities: SPARC-SSiRC, CMIP7-VolMIP, CMIP7-PMIP, and PAGES-VICS.
title: Volcano-climate impacts and the stratospheric aerosol layer

description: Atmospheric science research provokes and reacts to policy, and the two fields remain intertwined to the present. Air quality and climate hazards endanger exposed communities, and compounding exposures often harm public health, deepen inequality, and erode resilience, prompting policymakers to act. Evidence-informed action designed to improve air quality can create co-benefits for climate mitigation and simultaneously address health and environmental injustice challenges. This session calls for research seeking to understand how mitigation and adaptation actions to air pollution and climate change could influence atmospheric chemistry and dynamics in the present and future and how these actions could affect health and equality. We welcome abstracts that leverage remote sensing, statistical and earth system modeling, ground-based observations, machine-learning approaches, and policy analysis to test how well policies improve air quality and reduce climate change, health harms, and environmental injustices. We also seek novel atmospheric science research identifying where policy is needed.
title: Atmospheric Science for Action: Linking Air Quality, Climate, Health, Equity, and Policy

description: Atmospherically produced cosmogenic nuclides provide unique tracers connecting processes in the atmosphere with those operating at Earth’s surface. Their application requires understanding not only cosmogenic production but also how these nuclides are transported through the atmosphere and delivered to terrestrial and marine environments. Atmospheric circulation, aerosol transport, precipitation, and scavenging can modify depositional fluxes and thereby influence signals recorded in soils, sediments, ice, and other environmental archives. Recent advances in atmospheric modelling increasingly allow this chain from production to deposition to be quantified for cosmogenic nuclides such as ¹⁰Be and ³⁶Cl. Physics-based production functions can be coupled with atmospheric transport and deposition models to predict spatially and temporally resolved fluxes, which can be tested against observational records. Multi-nuclide approaches may further help distinguish variations in production from those arising during atmospheric transport and deposition. Improved constraints on cosmogenic-nuclide deposition are particularly important for quantitative applications at Earth’s surface. Meteoric ¹⁰Be and ¹⁰Be/⁹Be, for example, are used to quantify soil residence times, sediment transport, weathering, erosion, and catchment-wide denudation, while other cosmogenic nuclides provide complementary constraints on surface processes. Linking atmospheric models to such applications can provide spatially resolved depositional flux estimates and improve the interpretation of cosmogenic-nuclide inventories and ratios in landscapes. This session aims to bring together communities working on cosmogenic-nuclide production, atmospheric transport and deposition, environmental archives, and Earth-surface applications. We welcome contributions on production and transport models, aerosol interactions and scavenging, deposition, model downscaling and validation, as well as studies linking atmospheric modelling with soil and sediment dynamics, weathering and denudation, landscape evolution, and landform dating. Contributions from ice-core, lacustrine, and marine archives and multi-nuclide studies are equally welcome. By connecting these perspectives, the session seeks to advance our understanding of how cosmogenic signals are transferred from the atmosphere to Earth’s surface and used quantitatively to investigate Earth-surface processes.
title: Understanding atmospheric transport and deposition of cosmogenic nuclides for tracing Earth surface processes

description: Remote sensing of clouds and aerosols is of central importance when studying processes and changes in the climate system. The new space-borne generation of active sensors (e.g. EarthCare), passive multi-angular polarimeters (e.g. PACE/SPEX, PACE/HARP-2, 3MI, CO2M, MAP) together with single-viewing instruments (e.g. hyperspectral Sentinel 5P/5/4, OLCI and SLSTR on Sentinel 3) will take the characterisation of aerosols and clouds to a new level. This will significantly improve our understanding of physical and chemical processes in the atmosphere, particularly aerosol-cloud interactions, and climate and radiation studies. Nevertheless, there are still many challenges and unsolved problems in remote sensing algorithms and their applications. The aim of this session is to discuss current developments, challenges and opportunities in the characterisation of aerosols and clouds, in the study of aerosol-cloud interactions and their long-term effects, using ground-based, airborne and spaceborne active and passive remote sensing systems. We invite submissions of theoretical, methodological and empirical studies to advance the field of aerosol/cloud remote sensing, and to improve our understanding of aerosol-cloud interactions and their effect on the climate.
title: Remote sensing of aerosol and clouds

description: Microorganisms (i.e. bacteria, archaea, fungi, and protists) as well as viruses and macromolecules are ubiquitous in the atmosphere. They originate from surfaces including terrestrial, aquatic, marine, cryospheric, and built environments, and redistribute across large spatial and temporal scales. The continuous exchange of biological material by atmospheric transport provides an important but still poorly understood link between distant ecosystems and habitats. Once airborne, microbial cells are exposed to temperature fluctuations, radiation, oxidants, and limited availability of water and nutrients. These conditions can affect their survival, biological functioning, potential infectivity and virulence, as well as their physical characteristics, with important implications for microbial and viral dispersal, gene flow, and for the ability of microorganisms to establish and spread in new environments. Microorganisms, viruses, and microbially-produced macromolecules can also influence atmospheric and Earth-system processes. Biological particles and macromolecules can act as cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) and ice-nucleating particles (INP), affecting cloud formation, precipitation, and potentially the climate. Microbial activity may also affect atmospheric chemical budgets and biogeochemical cycles. Finally, dry and wet deposition returns airborne microorganisms, viruses, and macromolecules to soils, vegetation, water, and ice impacting microbial distribution across these environments. Thus, the atmosphere is as an important interface connecting microbial communities and biogeochemical cycles across ecosystems. This session aims to bring together researchers from microbiology, atmospheric science, biogeochemistry, climate science, One Health, and related disciplines to advance our understanding of atmospheric microorganisms, their interaction with the atmosphere, and their various effects. We welcome contributions addressing (I) microbial survival, activity, and interactions; (II) atmospheric stress responses and microbial evolution; (III) airborne pathogens, infectivity, virulence, and antimicrobial resistance; (IV) emission, transport, transformation, and deposition; (V) biological ice-nucleating particles and cloud–microbe interactions; (VI) microbial contributions to atmospheric chemistry and biogeochemical cycling; and (VII) the consequences of atmospheric microorganisms and viruses for ecosystems, agriculture, climate, and human and animal health.
title: The atmospheric microbiome: from microbial processes to Earth-system impacts

description: Clouds play an important role in the Polar climate due to their interaction with radiation and their role in the hydrological cycle linking poleward water vapour transport with precipitation. Cloud and precipitation properties depend on the atmospheric dynamics and moisture sources and transport, as well as on aerosol particles, which can act as cloud condensation and ice nuclei. These processes are complex and are not well represented in the models. While measurements of cloud and precipitation microphysical properties in the Arctic and Southern Ocean/Antarctic regions are challenging, they are highly needed to evaluate and improve cloud processes representation in the models used for polar and global climate and cryosphere projections. This session aims at bringing together researchers using observational and/or modeling approaches (at various scales) to improve our understanding of polar tropospheric clouds, precipitation, and related mechanisms and impacts. Contributions are invited on various relevant processes including (but not limited to): - Drivers of cloud/precipitation microphysics at high latitudes, - Sources of cloud nuclei both at local and long range, - Linkages of polar clouds/precipitation to the moisture sources and transport, including extreme transport events (e.g., atmospheric rivers, moisture intrusions), - Relationship of moisture/cloud/precipitation processes to the atmospheric dynamics, ranging from synoptic and meso-scale processes to teleconnections and climate indices, - Interactions between clouds and radiation, including impacts on the surface energy balance, - Impacts that the clouds/precipitation in the Polar Regions have on the polar and global climate system, surface mass and energy balance, sea ice and ecosystems. Papers including new methodologies specific to polar regions are encouraged, such as (i) improving polar cloud/precipitation parameterizations in atmospheric models, moisture transport events detection and attribution methods specifically in the high latitudes, and (ii) advancing observations of polar clouds and precipitation. This year, we would particularly like to emphasize new observational activities and opportunities linked to Antarctica InSync, including in-situ, remote-sensing and autonomous observations.
title: Clouds, moisture, and precipitation in the Polar Regions: Sources, processes and impacts

description: The wave of the Information Technology revolution is propelling us into a new era of research in atmospheric and environmental sciences. New techniques, including Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning (AI/ML) are enabling a deeper understanding of complex atmospheric and environmental systems, as well as the interactions among weather/climate, air quality, public health, and socioeconomic factors. Meanwhile, the unprecedented growth in both the volume and dimensionality of diverse and heterogeneous data is creating new opportunities while challenging conventional research paradigms for data integration, analysis, and interpretation. These emerging techniques are therefore becoming increasingly central to addressing the scientific challenges of this new era and supporting science-based policymaking in response to evolving environmental and societal challenges. In this session, we welcome submissions addressing the latest advances in emerging techniques applied to all aspects of atmospheric, climate, and environmental sciences, including but not limited to: - Applications of AI/ML and other emerging techniques for: • Advancing our understanding of the complex Earth system, especially the underlying mechanisms of weather/climate systems, atmospheric environmental systems, and their interactions • Facilitating faster and more accurate weather/climate/air quality modeling and forecasting, especially for extreme weather events, climate change, and air pollution episodes • Providing new insights into the mechanisms of atmospheric chemistry and physics • Improving air pollution tracing and source attribution • Supporting policymakers in making decisions that promote environmental sustainability (e.g., considering interactions among extreme weather, climate change, air quality, socioeconomic factors, and public health - The adaptation and development of AI/ML and other emerging techniques through: • Explainable AI (XAI) • Hybrid methods (e.g., hybrid ML, physics-integrated ML) • Multi-source heterogeneous data fusion and mining • Transfer learning • Advanced modeling frameworks We believe that exchanges across research fields could help break down the limitations of disciplinary thinking and enabling technological innovations. Therefore, contributions from fields other than atmospheric, climate, and environmental sciences are also encouraged.
title: Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning (AI/ML) in Atmospheric, Climate, and Environmental Sciences: Application and Development

description: The "Advanced Spectroscopic Measurement Techniques and Applications for Atmospheric Science" session focuses on the development of novel spectroscopic methods and instrumentation and their use in atmospheric applications. These applications target measurements of concentrations and optical properties of atmospheric constituents, physical properties of the atmosphere, as well as the study of atmospheric processes in laboratories, atmospheric simulation chambers, and field deployments. The session aims to be a forum for sharing information on the state-of-the-art and emerging developments in atmospheric sensing using spectroscopic methods. Topics include developments, demonstrations and early applications of novel spectroscopic methods and instruments from the UV to THz spectral regions for measuring atmospheric aerosols, isotopologues, air pollutants, greenhouse gases and trace gases, as well as spectroscopic measurements of meteorological variables. Spectroscopic methods include high sensitivity and selectivity spectroscopy (such as frequency comb spectroscopy, cavity-enhanced absorption/Raman spectroscopies, photoacoustic & photothermal spectroscopies), low-cost optical sensors, heterodyne radiometry, imaging spectroscopy, and wildfire detection and characterization. Applications include laboratory and simulation chamber demonstrations, vertical concentration profiles and flux measurements. Submissions are also encouraged on novel adaptations of instruments to mobile platforms (e.g., vehicles, in backpacks, UAVs, ships and balloons) and on new spectral data analysis tools (including deep learning spectroscopy). Contributions from scientists and engineers in academic and scientific institutes, regulatory agencies, and commercial companies are welcomed.
title: Advanced Spectroscopic Measurement Techniques and Applications for Atmospheric Science

description: The recent revolution of data-driven forecasting systems based on artificial intelligence (AI) has opened new research possibilities in weather forecasting, climate science, and various other areas. At the same time, many open questions remain–such as how to properly evaluate the model outputs in terms of generalizability under climate change, whether models extrapolate to unseen extremes, and to what extent they are consistent with physical principles. This session focuses on new scientific approaches emerging from this AI revolution, limitations of current models, and strategies to overcome them. We encourage submissions that explore a wide range of topics, including evaluations of outputs and comparisons to numerical models, technical advancements in initial condition optimization or model fine-tuning, novel techniques from explainable AI, and other relevant studies. Bringing together experts from AI, climate sciences, statistics, and applied math will foster interdisciplinary collaborations and guide scientific progress in this quickly evolving field of research.
title: AI for Weather and Climate Extremes: Opportunities and Challenges

description: Understanding and reducing uncertainty in atmospheric and Earth system models requires effective ways to explore model behaviour, compare different models and connect simulations with observations. Key challenges include identifying the processes that cause model uncertainty, distinguishing uncertain parameters from differences in model structure, and establishing whether observational constraints remain robust across models. This session brings together modelling, observational and statistical communities developing methods and applications that address these challenges. We welcome both single-model and multi-model studies, including perturbed parameter ensembles, coordinated model experiments and model intercomparison projects. Topics include: Ensemble design, sensitivity analysis and attribution of uncertainty within and across models. Statistical and machine-learning emulation of individual models and multi-model ensembles, including approaches that capture shared behaviour and model-specific differences. Bayesian calibration, history matching, model weighting, and emergent or process-based observational constraints. Joint use of multiple observations, accounting for observational uncertainty, model dependence and structural differences. Evaluation of how uncertainties propagate across coupled model components and how coupling alters relationships between model variables and observations. Diagnosing structural model deficiencies using model–observation comparisons to guide model development. Designing observations and model experiments to improve constraints on climate uncertainty. Applications across atmospheric composition, clouds, physical atmospheric processes and their coupling with other Earth system components are encouraged, from regional to global scales. We particularly welcome studies investigating whether constraints derived from one model remain informative across other models, and whether improved agreement with observations leads to more reliable climate projections.
title: Constraining atmospheric model uncertainty: ensembles, emulation and observations across models

description: Air pollution remains a critical global challenge, disproportionately impacting vulnerable communities in low- and middle-income countries. Weak policies, fragmented institutions, limited financial and computational resources, and lack of comprehensive monitoring infrastructure hinder effective air quality (AQ) management. Accessible and affordable AQ sensors (low-cost sensor systems, LCS) offer a promising solution by enabling dense spatial networks, rapid deployment, citizen engagement, and integration with other data sources. Yet, persistent challenges remain around data quality, calibration, standardisation, integration with regulatory frameworks, long-term sustainability, and equitable access. Addressing these issues requires strong local capacity-building and international collaboration. This session will showcase best practices in using LCS for AQ monitoring. We will explore case studies where LCS enhance air quality monitoring products (integrating satellite with air sensor information), verify air quality forecasting systems, and support public health and community monitoring initiatives, particularly, but not limited, to resource-limited settings. This session promotes cutting-edge research, case studies, performance evaluations, standardisation efforts, mobile measurements and best practices for using air sensors in air quality monitoring, incl. indoor air quality. These aspects will help to enhance air quality monitoring capabilities and foster strong local and international collaboration. It will also explore strategies for sustainable practices that empower communities and ensure equitable partnerships.
title: Low-cost air quality sensors: challenges, opportunities, and collaborative strategies across the world

description: Fluids play a fundamental role in Earth’s dynamic systems. Magmatism and metamorphism require the presence of fluids. As fluids are carriers of materials through the different levels of our planet, their global cycles efficiently transfer elements from the surface to the deep interior through subduction zones. Volatiles and other incompatible elements significantly contribute to the well-being and sustainability of life. While major uncertainties remain, advances in multi-disciplinary approaches continue to reveal how fluids exert a profound influence on planetary-scale processes. This session brings together scientists investigating fluids and melts, focusing on the full spectrum of volatile and elemental cycles, and how they interact with the surrounding rocks at all scales. We welcome contributions from petrology, geochemistry, and related disciplines, drawing on natural samples, experiments, and modelling. Topics of interest include: i) role of fluids in magmatic, metamorphic and metasomatic processes; ii) deep volatile cycles of H₂O, CO₂, halogens and sulfur; iii ) COHNS fluids and silicate melts role in volatile mobilization and transfer during subduction; iv) physical and chemical properties of volatiles in melts and fluids; v) volatile storage and release in the lithospheric mantle; vi) petrological studies of fluid-rock interactions.
title: No fluids no party: fluids as key to understanding deep processes in the Earth

description: Metal ore deposits, such as porphyry Cu–Au systems, orogenic Au deposits, volcanogenic massive sulfide deposits, and alkaline and carbonatite REE–HFSE systems, form through complex processes involving the transport of metals from source regions, followed by their concentration and deposition in the crust. Understanding ore-forming processes and their associated dynamics is crucial for assessing economic potential and guiding exploration strategies. Across these diverse systems, fluid–rock interactions play a fundamental role in ore formation. They control the formation of ore minerals and the mobilization of metals from source zones to depositional sites, and they leave diagnostic records that help decipher how metals are transported and concentrated. At nano- and microscales, physical patterns in ore deposits, including dendritic structures, banding, fractures, mineral replacement textures, growth patterns and deformation features, provide fundamental records of fluid–rock interaction processes. At meso- to macroscales, these interactions manifest as hydrothermal alteration zones characterized by systematic mineral replacement, overgrowth and mineral zoning. The spatial and temporal organization of these patterns records the physicochemical evolution of ore-forming environments. Concurrently, the chemical reactions that drive ore formation control mineral dissolution and precipitation, as well as the redistribution of ore-forming components. These processes are recorded petrologically as elemental transfer and exchange during fluid–rock interactions, which collectively contribute to the formation of ore deposits. Such observations provide key constraints for thermodynamic and kinetic simulations of fluid–rock interaction processes, thereby deepening our understanding of the underlying mechanisms. Moreover, recent advances in machine-learning techniques have significantly enhanced geochemical quantification and helped uncover hidden physicochemical relationships during the spatiotemporal evolution of ore minerals and deposits. In this session, we invite multidisciplinary contributions that investigate ore deposits and their associated formation dynamics using fieldwork, microstructural and petrographic analyses, geochemistry, machine-learning techniques, and thermodynamic and numerical modelling. Case studies of economic ore deposits are also warmly welcomed.
title: Formation of metal ore deposits during fluid–rock interactions: from physical patterns and chemical reactions to numerical modelling

description: Economic ore deposits are the result of complex, multi-stage geological processes that operate from the scale of mantle and crustal source regions to the scale of individual mineral grains, structures, and ore shoots. Building an ore deposit requires a fertile source, efficient metal mobilization, focused transport through melts or fluids, effective depositional traps, post-ore preservation or upgrading, and, ultimately, a detectable geological footprint. Understanding this complete pathway is essential for both advancing ore deposit science and improving exploration strategies for raw materials. This session invites contributions that investigate any stage of the mineral system pathway, from metal source to final economic concentration. We welcome studies on metal fertility in mantle, magmatic, metamorphic, sedimentary, and crustal reservoirs; the generation and evolution of ore-forming melts, fluids, brines, or hydrocarbons; and the physical and chemical mechanisms that transport and focus metals. Contributions addressing the triggers of ore deposition, including cooling, boiling, fluid mixing, phase separation, wall-rock reaction, redox change, pressure fluctuations, deformation, and permeability evolution, are especially encouraged. The session also emphasizes the later history of ore deposits, including remobilization, metamorphic modification, deformation, weathering, supergene enrichment, burial, erosion, and long-term preservation. These processes can enhance, obscure, or destroy economic mineralization and strongly influence the modern expression of ore systems. Studies that connect primary ore-forming mechanisms with present-day exploration footprints are therefore highly relevant. We encourage multidisciplinary and cross-commodity contributions that integrate field geology, structural geology, petrology, geochemistry, isotope studies, thermodynamic and numerical modelling, experimental work, geophysics, remote sensing, data science, and mineral prospectivity analysis. The session welcomes research on a broad range of deposit types, such as porphyry, skarn, epithermal systems, VMS, sediment-hosted base-metal, magmatic Ni-Cu-PGE and beyond. By bringing together studies from different commodities, tectonic environments, and methodological approaches, this session aims to develop an integrated understanding of how economic ore deposits are built, modified, and preserved.
title: Understanding Mineral Systems - Fertility, Transport, Deposition, Preservation, and Discovery

description: Scientists and researchers are more and more finding new ways to present their work to a broad audience. This includes presenting data through a diverse array of visual forms, from conventional graphs and maps to interactive web applications, physical models, art installations, and other forms of tangible media. These approaches to data visualisation can make complex datasets and systems more accessible and approachable to a wider audience. Oftentimes they can reveal patterns that are difficult to see in raw data and they provide new ways of communicating scientific results to both specialised and general audiences. At the same time, the choice of which specific visual medium is used influences what can be shown, what is emphasised, and how the data are interpreted. This session invites contributions exploring the use of physical and digital media to visualise scientific data. We welcome work that showcases data visualisation in unique ways including, but not limited to; maps, interactive visualisations, virtual and augmented environments, physical or tactile representations, and artistic approaches. Contributions may focus on the development of new techniques, the application of existing approaches to scientific problems or data, or reflections on how different visual forms affect the interpretation and communication of scientific data and research. We particularly encourage contributions that consider the relationship between the data, the medium through which they are presented, and the people using or experiencing the visualisation. Examples from all scientific disciplines supported by EGU are welcome, as are approaches that cross the boundaries between scientific visualisation, design, art, and public engagement. And we particularly encourage contributions from underrepresented groups and countries.
title: Data Visualization through Physical and Digital Media

description: A surprising visual can make us pause, notice a pattern, or ask a question we had never considered. How can we bring that potential into the way we explore and communicate data? This session invites creative, unconventional, still-in-the-works, and carefully crafted approaches to data visualisation. We are interested in work that combines imagination with clarity: visuals that reveal relationships, communicate uncertainty, tell compelling stories, and invite audiences to explore. Contributions may address scientific discovery, education, public engagement, or decision-making at the interface of environment and society. We welcome experiments with visual storytelling, animation, interactive exploration, hand-drawn graphics, physical data objects, immersive experiences, and combinations of visualisation with sound or touch. How can familiar datasets take unfamiliar forms? When does playful design deepen understanding? How can we make complex information accessible while preserving its nuance? Scientists, designers, artists, educators, and communicators are invited to share methods, examples, collaborations, and lessons from experiments (including those that did not work as expected). We aim to inspire new ways of seeing data and offer practical ideas participants can bring into their own research and communication.
title: Seeing Differently: Creative Data Visualisation

description: Art makes use of materials of geological origin: stones, pigments, mortars, metals, etc.; geology, in turn, has been depicted in various ways in art throughout art history; geosciences present their observations and discoveries in a visual form that can be regarded as an artistic expression. The entanglements of art and natural sciences are multiple, bidirectional, and have given rise to hybrid fields of research: Technical Art History, considering the materiality of artworks; archaeometry exploiting the intrinsic information contained in the artistic matter to trace back its origin and fates; Eco-critical art history, which draws on the environmental dimension of works of art – such as historical landscape painting – to critically explore the history of the environment and its changes. In this session, we aim for a rich and diverse transdisciplinary dialogue of colleagues with multiple backgrounds and thus welcome a broad range of contributions in fields such as: - Geosciences in artistic representation, e.g. as sources to study environmental changes, as indicators of the evolution of symbolic and scientific perception of geological objects and phenomena, natural hazards, etc. - Artwork materials and their transformations over time as physical/chemical repositories or archives of environmental history, including air, water and soil pollution (e.g. stone degradation in urban areas) - Geomaterials (stone, pigments, metals, precious stones) used in works of art (sculptures, metal objects, paintings, jewellery, etc.) and their intrinsic properties as an indicator of provenance or as a criterion of authenticity; the conservation issues specific to these materials. - Artistic production and networks in geological landscapes with indigenous/local artistic use of geomaterials, artist migration to geo-resource-rich regions, transport of geomaterials to artistic centres, artistic geomaterials as indicators of power and prestige…
title: Art and Geosciences

description: Time is a fundamental dimension of ore deposit formation. Economic mineral systems are built through a sequence of events involving source activation, magma or fluid generation, metal mobilization, transport, deposition, overprinting, upgrading, preservation, and exposure. Determining when these processes occurred, how long they lasted, and how they relate to tectonic, magmatic, metamorphic, sedimentary, and climatic events is essential for understanding why some systems become economic while others remain barren. This session focuses on the geochronology and temporal evolution of ore-forming systems. We invite contributions that use radiometric dating, isotope geochemistry, petrochronology, mineral chemistry, diffusion modelling, geochronological method development, and integrated field relationships to constrain the timing, duration, tempo, and recurrence of mineralization. Contributions may address both direct dating of ore and alteration minerals and indirect constraints from associated magmatism, metamorphism, deformation, basin evolution, hydrothermal alteration, weathering, or supergene enrichment. A key aim of the session is to link absolute ages with geological processes. We particularly encourage studies that investigate the duration of hydrothermal systems, pulsed versus continuous mineralization, time gaps between magmatism and ore formation, rates of metal accumulation, temporal links between tectonics and fluid flow, and the timing of remobilization or upgrading events. Studies comparing fertile and barren systems, or integrating geochronology with exploration models, are especially welcome. By bringing together specialists in ore geology, geochronology, isotope geochemistry, structural geology, petrology, and exploration, this session aims to improve our understanding of how timing controls the construction, modification, preservation, and discovery of economic ore deposits.
title: Time Matters - Geochronology, Duration, Rates, and Temporal Controls on Mineralization

description: The Earth system evolves through the interplay of processes operating over vastly different temporal and spatial scales. Short-lived perturbations such as earthquakes, mineral phase transformations, and changes in plate kinematics trigger cascades of coupled physical and chemical processes whose effects propagate far beyond the initiating event, ultimately shaping long-term geological evolution. Convergent plate boundaries provide exceptional natural laboratories because they encompass an unparalleled diversity of coupled processes, including subduction, fluid and chemical fluxes, magmatism, deformation, mountain building, and erosion. Together, high-resolution geological and geophysical observations and advances in experimental, analytical, and numerical approaches provide an unprecedented opportunity to investigate how transient and episodic processes interact across scales to shape the evolution of convergent plate boundaries. This session welcomes contributions from geodynamics, tectonics, mineralogy, petrology, geochemistry, geophysics, seismology, magmatic systems, sedimentology, and related disciplines. We particularly encourage interdisciplinary studies that integrate observations, experiments, and modelling to identify the mechanisms through which transient processes couple across scales, thereby linking short-lived, instrumentally observable perturbations to long-term dynamic evolution.
title: From transients to geodynamics: Multi-scale coupling at convergent plate boundaries

description: The lithospheric mantle varies markedly in thickness, composition, thermal structure and redox state. These differences reflect its initial formation conditions and subsequent modification by partial melting, metasomatism and tectonic reworking. The resulting chemical and physical heterogeneities can persist over geological time, recording past tectonic processes while influencing subsequent mantle melting and magma generation. The architecture and composition of the lithospheric mantle control the generation, transport and evolution of mantle-derived magmas, as well as the mobilisation of volatiles and ore-forming elements that contribute to the metallogenic productivity of the crust. At convergent margins, a diverse range of fluids and melts released from the mantle wedge can generate significant chemical and redox heterogeneity in the overlying sub-arc lithosphere. These heterogeneities may persist through later tectonic events and influence arc magmatic activity. At divergent margins and in intraplate settings, lithospheric heating and thinning, asthenosphere–lithosphere interaction and inherited metasomatic domains can generate contrasting magma compositions and volatile fluxes. Comparisons among these tectonic settings provide an opportunity to determine how geodynamic environments, lithospheric architecture and mantle inheritance influence partial melting and the chemical/mass transfer from the mantle towards the surface. Key questions include how: (i) the lithospheric mantle forms and evolves through geological time; (ii) compositional, metasomatic and redox heterogeneity is generated and preserved; and (iii) this inherited structure influences subsequent mantle melting, magma chemistry, volatile transfer and associated mineralisation. This session brings together contributions from mantle petrology, mineralogy and geochemistry; experimental petrology and thermodynamic modelling; and geophysical and geodynamic studies that constrain lithospheric architecture and mantle processes. By integrating these approaches, we aim to better understand how the formation, architecture and modification of the lithospheric mantle control magmatism, volatile cycling and metallogeny through geological time.
title: Lithospheric Mantle Controls on Magmatism, Volatile Cycling and Metallogeny

description: Trans-lithospheric plumbing systems provide a framework for understanding how melts are generated, transported, modified and stored across the mantle-crust continuum, linking deep magmatic processes to their volcanic and plutonic expressions. The architecture and evolution of these systems control how mantle-derived melts interact with the lithosphere, undergo differentiation and mixing, and ultimately feed crustal reservoirs and volcanic systems, including their metal endowment. Investigating their deep roots and connectivity is therefore essential for reconstructing the spatial and temporal evolution of magmatism and for understanding the relationships between igneous processes in the mantle and the crust, as well as the interaction of volcanic systems with the atmosphere. This session thus invites contributions addressing the architecture, dynamics and evolution of trans-lithospheric active or fossil plumbing systems from mantle melting to magma transport, crustal storage, differentiation and eruption. We particularly welcome multidisciplinary studies integrating geophysical, geochemical, petrological, structural or numerical modelling perspectives that investigate the connections between deep and shallow magmatic processes and provide new perspectives on the volcano-plutonic link and associated volcano hazards.
title: Trans-lithospheric magma plumbing systems as windows into volcano-plutonic links

description: Earth’s mantle is compositionally heterogeneous, recording planetary differentiation, core formation, and exchange among deep and surface reservoirs. Understanding its present structure and long-term evolution requires integrating geochemical observations with geophysical constraints. This session welcomes contributions from geochemistry, petrology, mineralogy, geophysics, and geodynamic modelling to investigate mantle composition, heterogeneity, and evolution. Topics include the formation, preservation, and recycling of mantle and crustal reservoirs, evidence for core - mantle interaction, early differentiation, mantle melting as well as links between mantle dynamics and surface processes. We particularly encourage the introduction of new analytical approaches, innovative use of geochemical and geophysical databases, numerical modelling, data-driven methods, and interdisciplinary studies. The session seeks to foster interdisciplinary discussion of how chemical, isotopic, petrological, and geophysical evidence can be jointly used to develop more robust models for the present-day mantle and its evolution through Earth's history.
title: Geochemical and Geophysical Constraints on Mantle–Core–Crust Interaction

description: Minerals, melts, and fluids play critical roles in geological processes across a wide range of spatial and temporal scales. Together, they govern the storage and transport of heat and mass and affect planetary evolution, especially on Earth. The stability of these materials is controlled, in part, by pressure and temperature. At the same time, these intensive parameters influence the physical and chemical behaviour of these materials, such as density, rheology, reactivity, and transport properties. Seemingly, these physicochemical properties influence how minerals, melts, and fluids interact with one another and thus their roles in various geological processes. For instance, such interactions drive metamorphism, magmatism, hydrothermal circulation, and the formation of valuable mineral deposits in the crust. They also influence the mechanical behaviour of rocks, affecting deformation, faulting, and earthquake generation. At deep Earth, mineral-melt-fluid interactions regulate element mobility, mantle metasomatism, volatile recycling, and chemical differentiation. The migration of such fluids and melts can link deep planetary interiors to shallower regions. Nevertheless, their stagnation or pooling can concentrate heat and influence the chemical reactions. Understanding the behaviour and interactions of minerals, melts, and fluids under high-pressure-temperature conditions is therefore paramount for constraining geologic processes from the atomic to planetary scale. This session invites contributions which examine the behaviour and interactions of minerals, melts, and fluids across a wide range of conditions relevant to planetary interiors and the implications for geological processes. We welcome a broad range of studies, including those from experiments, computational simulations and modelling, and analyses of natural samples.
title: Interaction of minerals, melts and fluids in the dynamic Earth

description: The Earth's mantle is a chemically heterogeneous system whose compositional variability both records and drives the planet's evolution. From depleted and enriched domains produced by melt extraction to recycled crustal materials introduced by subduction, mantle heterogeneities serve simultaneously as tracers of deep processes and as active agents controlling melting, buoyancy, and rheology. A central question remains: how do these heterogeneities evolve from their generation in the deep mantle to the geochemical, physical, and tectonic signatures observed in volcanic rocks and at the surface? Addressing this question requires integrating petrological and geochemical observations of mantle rocks and melts with geophysical imaging, experimental constraints, and geodynamic modelling. We welcome studies that connect deep and shallow observations across spatial and temporal scales, from metasomatic overprints in lithospheric peridotites to the volatile and isotopic signatures of volcanic products. Contributions combining petrological and geochemical constraints with geophysical observations and geodynamic models, as well as those addressing feedbacks between mantle composition, mantle flow, melting, and lithospheric deformation, are particularly encouraged. The session focuses on innovative research, observational and field studies, experimental and theoretical advances aimed at understanding the generation, preservation, modification and transport of chemical heterogeneities in the mantle and their consequences for mantle dynamics, magmatism and lithospheric evolution. We welcome contributions from a broad range of disciplines, including mantle petrology and geochemistry, isotope geochemistry, experimental petrology, mineral physics, seismology and tomography, volcanology, geodynamics, thermodynamic modelling and numerical simulations. The session also specifically welcomes contributions from Early Career Scientists.
title: Mantle heterogeneities: origins, evolution and tectono-volcanic expressions

description: Deep Earth hydrogen plays an important role in the structural evolution of our planet. This session focuses on the origin, speciation, and abundance of hydrogen in the Earth's deep interior, and its profound physical and chemical impacts on host minerals. We invite contributions exploring how deep hydrogen influences mineral phase transitions, rheology, electrical conductivity, and elastic wave velocities. Particular attention will be given to the role of hydrogen in shaping key deep Earth structures and interfaces, including the mantle transition zone, core–mantle boundary, and related discontinuities. We welcome interdisciplinary studies integrating high-pressure and high-temperature experiments, first-principles calculations, geophysical observations, and geochemical tracers. By bringing together diverse perspectives, this session aims to advance our understanding of deep hydrogen cycling, its incorporation mechanisms, and broader geodynamic and geophysical consequences.
title: Physical and Chemical Effects of Deep Earth Hydrogen

description: The Solar System encompasses planetary bodies with substantially different compositions, structures, and evolutionary histories. The discovery of more than 6000 exoplanets has further expanded this diversity. Understanding the physical and chemical response of planetary materials is therefore essential for reconstructing planetary formation and long-term evolution and, ultimately, assessing the conditions that shape planetary habitability. Planetary materials experience conditions ranging from the cold surfaces to hot magma oceans and the extreme pressures of super-Earth interiors. No single approach spans this full range. We therefore invite work that brings experiments, calculations, natural sample analysis, and planetary observations into dialogue. This session aims to connect material-scale processes and properties with planetary-scale questions, including the origin of compositional diversity, planetary differentiation, and subsequent thermal and chemical evolution. We welcome studies on crystallization and melting; magma degassing and volatile storage; chemical partitioning; and structural and transport properties of planetary materials. Contributions may span terrestrial planets and icy moons in the Solar System, as well as exoplanets such as super-Earths and large water-rich worlds.
title: Planetary Materials Across the Solar System and Beyond

description: The Archean Eon records the formation of Earth’s earliest continental crust, the establishment of fundamental geodynamic processes, and the emergence of life. Yet the timing and nature of Archean tectonics and the conditions of crustal metamorphism, remain poorly constrained. Although the ancient rock record is fragmentary, Archean cratons preserve evidence from mineral to regional scales, offering a rare window into these processes. We seek studies that provide new constraints on Archean crustal growth and stabilization, metamorphic processes, and the evolution of the lithosphere. We invite contributions investigating the metamorphic and tectonic evolution of Archean terranes through petrology, in situ petrochronology, thermodynamic modelling, geochronology, geochemistry, geophysics and geodynamic modelling. We particularly welcome studies integrating multiple approaches at different scales. Together, these perspectives can help unravel the processes that shaped the early Earth.
title: Old rocks, new ideas: New perspectives in Archean studies

description: The increasing volume, diversity, and complexity of volcanological datasets are creating new opportunities for Machine Learning and computational approaches to extract information, identify patterns, and characterize changes in volcanic systems. This session welcomes contributions aimed at identifying transitions in volcanic state, characterizing unrest and eruptive processes, and developing automated and near-real-time monitoring and forecasting systems, as well as studies addressing the evaluation, comparison, interpretability, robustness, and transferability of ML models across different datasets and volcanic systems. We particularly encourage contributions from volcanologists, data scientists, and monitoring communities that bridge innovative computational methodologies with sustainable data practices, promoting reproducible and reusable ML workflows and data products. Datasets, derived products, workflows, and computational outputs are encouraged to adhere to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable) and open data principles. By sharing these through dedicated research infrastructures and services, such as EPOS, their accessibility, interoperability, and reuse are enhanced for the broader volcanological community.
title: From multiparametric data to volcanic state characterization and monitoring through Machine Learning algorithms.

description: The rapid advancement of Earth System prediction relies on a critical feedback loop: the better understanding of the physical processes, the innovation of predictive algorithms, and their successful integration into real-time operational forecasting models. While scientific research continuously uncovers novel physical mechanisms and develops advanced parameterizations across atmospheric, oceanic, wave, sea-ice, and terrestrial systems, the rapid rise of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) is transforming Earth System prediction. Operational centers worldwide are now actively rethinking their core infrastructures, navigating how to establish an optimal blend of classical physics-based models, pure data-driven architectures, and physics-informed hybrid systems. Transitioning both cutting-edge physics and novel AI/ML models into a 24/7 operational production environment presents formidable hurdles. Ensuring that new algorithms run stably, satisfy stringent wall-clock limits, respect physical conservation laws, and deliver verifiable skill improvements across coupled domains requires extensive engineering. Operational centers must frequently retune parameterizations, re-engineer data assimilation interfaces, or develop bespoke hybrid coupling strategies. Conversely, operational implementation often exposes critical knowledge gaps—such as physical representation limitations or AI vulnerabilities during rare, extreme events—that demand further fundamental research. Due to the fast-paced nature of operational environments, these vital engineering strategies, diagnostic methodologies, and practical "tricks of the trade" are rarely documented in peer-reviewed literature. This session provides a dedicated, collaborative platform for physical modelers, AI/ML researchers, software engineers, and operational practitioners to share their implementation experiences, failure modes, and practical solutions. By fostering an open dialogue on operationalizing conventional, hybrid, and data-driven Earth System Models, we aim to accelerate the Research-to-Operations (R2O) and Operations-to-Research (O2R) pathways and strengthen cross-agency collaboration across all scales.
title: Behind the Forecast: Challenges and Strategies for Operational Earth System Models and Hybrid AI/ML Systems

description: Healthy soils underpin food production, climate resilience and wider ecosystem functioning, yet more than 60% of European soils are considered degraded. The period around 2027 brings two important opportunities to reshape the relationship between soil science, policy and practice. First, the forthcoming reform of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) for the post-2027 period creates an opportunity to strengthen incentives for sustainable soil management. Second, the EU Mission Soil will be moving from experimentation towards the wider implementation and upscaling of Living Labs, accelerating the co-production and application of knowledge on sustainable soil management. Realising the potential of these initiatives will depend on much more than generating new scientific evidence. Effective soil stewardship requires sustained exchange between scientists, policymakers, farmers, advisers and the wider agri-food sector. Yet these relationships are often fragmented by differences in language, priorities, evidence, experience and perceptions of what constitutes credible knowledge. This session will examine how knowledge about soils is produced, interpreted, exchanged and acted upon across this diverse community. It will explore how soil scientists can better understand the knowledge needs, perspectives and decision-making contexts of different stakeholders, while recognising farmers, practitioners and policymakers as producers of knowledge in their own right. We invite participants from across the knowledge chain to come together to ask a deceptively simple question: how do we know what we know? Through dialogue across disciplines and sectors, the session aims to identify practical ways to strengthen bidirectional knowledge exchange and build a more collaborative pathway towards sustainable European soils.
title: SSS Special Programme Group Session: Co-producing Soil Knowledge for Sustainable European Soils

description: Soil erosion has been traditionally divided into sheet, rill, and gully erosion. Rills and gullies concentrate overland flow, leading to a significantly increased flow erosivity. These forms of concentrated flow erosion, both above and below ground, represent an important sediment source within watersheds and produce sizeable economic losses (e.g. reduced crop yields, reservoir sedimentation). Moreover, rills and gullies are effective links for transferring runoff, sediment and pollutants. Despite their relevance, the physical mechanisms that constitute concentrated flow erosion remain poorly understood. This session aims to address this research gap and will focus on recent studies aiming to better understand the process of rill and gully erosion, with the ultimate aim of developing predictive tools and effective management strategies. As such we welcome contributions on: monitoring and measurement techniques; the factors and processes controlling rill, piping and gully erosion; modelling approaches; restoration and control; and the role of piping, rills and gullies in hydrological and sediment connectivity.
title: Gully and rill erosion: recent advancements and novel approaches

description: Soil health is the capacity of soil to function as an ecosystem, providing means to sustain productivity and maintain environmental quality. In the EU alone, 60% of the soils are degraded due to both global change factors (warming, extreme weather events, elevated CO2 levels, droughts, floods, etc.) and human activity (intensive agriculture, land-use change, industrial processes, etc.). Initial modifications of the physical and chemical soil properties, can have dramatic effects on soil biota, which is an important driver of ecosystem services. We invite contributions from field, laboratory and modeling studies focused on biological soil health descriptors or indicators, such as microbial respiration, enzyme activities, diversity and functions of soil (micro)organisms and other parameters affected by global change and human activities. This session welcomes contributions on soil health assessment methods, with a focus on biological soil fertility and the ecosystem services provided by soils. We particularly encourage abstracts that explore soil health across temporal and spatial scales, from micro-level to global perspectives.
title: Soil health under global change and human activities

description: Soil biodiversity is increasingly recognized as a key component of soil health, yet current assessment frameworks often focus on a limited range of biological groups or isolated ecosystem functions. While these specific groups can provide valuable indicators of soil conditions, they may not fully capture the complexity of soil processes and multitrophic interactions that underpin ecosystem functioning. Integrating microorganisms, soil fauna, and their interactions across trophic levels into robust and operational soil health indicators remains a major scientific and practical challenge. This session aims to promote a holistic perspective on soil health indicators derived from soil biodiversity across different trophic groups and methodological approaches. We encourage contributions exploring how information from individual soil organisms groups or integrative multi-trophic approaches can improve indicators related to key soil processes such as carbon and nutrient cycling, soil structure formation, and ecosystem stability under environmental change. Particular attention will be given to studies testing existing or novel biodiversity-based indicators and their applicability across different environmental contexts. The session invites interdisciplinary experimental, observational, and modelling approaches across scales, with particular interest in studies that bridge soil biodiversity research with development and application of soil health monitoring frameworks, implementation of operational indicators in restoration practices, nature-based solutions, and environmental policy. Contributions from researchers working on specific organismal groups are equally welcome, provided they connect to broader multi-trophic or integrative frameworks.
title: Integrating soil life into soil health assessment and management

description: Sustainable agricultural practices are sought to be implemented across Europe and worldwide to improve soil nutrient cycling processes which includes nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) and to reduce loss of nutrients through leaching, surface runoff and gaseous emissions. Indeed, EU targets have been set to improve nutrient use efficiencies (NUE) by 50% by 2030. A key aspect in achieving such a goal is to improve soil carbon (C) stocks and soil organic matter (SOM). It is assumed that by reversing the widespread loss of soil C in Europe’s soils, nutrient-use efficiencies may be improved through the betterment of soil multi-functionality. Soil microbiota will play key role in sustainable plant nutrient supply as they are key drivers in making soil nutrients N and P plant available, while at the same time immobilise excess N and P that is at risk of loss to ground- and surface-waters. Increasing soil C stocks sustainably can be achieved by including organic materials of waste origin from the circular economy model. This will reduce linear economy dependencies and engage the circular economy for the sustainable supply of not only C, but also vital plant nutrients N and P. This session aims to advance our limited understanding of the relationships between soil C and the microbial activities in soil that decide whether plant nutrients N and P are made available or are immobilized. Optimization these processes would allow to improve NUE by more targeted supply of plant nutrients through microbial activities, while at the same time excess nutrients can be prevented from leaching into the ground water by microbial immobilization. The use of circular economy fertilizers with substantial C content may provide multiple benefits by reducing the need for non-renewable linear economy fertilizers while at the same time promote microbial driven NUE. Further research in soil stoichiometry, microbial driven NUE and circular economy fertilization is needed to make the gains in sustainable agriculture that is needed in Europe and the rest of the world.
title: Soil stoichiometry management to improve soil microbiota driven nutrient use efficiencies for sustainable agriculture

description: Microbial metabolism is the engine of key soil functions, including nutrient cycling, carbon transformation, and plant growth promotion. Their metabolism and growth rely on C and energy as well as nutrients (e.g., N and P) and electron acceptors (O2, NO3, etc. ... or C itself). Microbial death processes close the loop to return biomass to non-living soil organic matter as necromass, changing its original quality. This coupled, dynamic system can be investigated at different scales (nm to km) and from diverse perspectives, leveraging concepts of carbon use efficiency (CUE), microbial ecophysiology, thermodynamics, and ecological stoichiometry. This session integrates experimental and modelling insights to elucidate how soil microbial metabolism drive energy and matter flows, taking account of their interactions with other organisms, dependency on environmental conditions, and the implications for soil functions. We welcome new insights into soil microbial metabolism, growth and death, across the diverse transformations and interactions that these involve. Topics of interest include cutting-edge characterization of microbial activity and turnover (e.g., isotope tracing, calorimetry, metagenomics), microbial ecophysiology and stoichiometry, physiological responses to (micro)environmental changes (e.g. metabolomics), carbon and energy-use efficiency, alongside approaches to understand microbial functional responses (e.g. dynamic modelling, artificial intelligence). We aim to stimulate interdisciplinary discussions to advance our understanding of soil biology at scales from the mechanistic understanding of biogeochemical processes to global change. We are excited to welcome Christina Kaiser as our invited speaker in 2027.
title: Metabolism and turnover of soil microorganisms: Experiments and models to decipher element cycling and soil function

description: Biogeochemical activity in soil is concentrated in hotspots created by living roots, decomposing residues, fungal networks, soil fauna, biopores, aggregates and mineral surfaces. These domains are not fixed. They emerge, overlap, shift between oxic and anoxic states, and can persist after the original plant input has ceased. The central challenge is no longer only to locate hotspots. We also need to explain how they develop, what triggers functional shifts, and when brief hot moments leave lasting effects on soils and plants. This session focuses on feedbacks among plant inputs, microbial physiology and succession, and the physical and chemical soil environment. We welcome experimental and modelling studies of the rhizosphere, detritusphere, biopores, aggregates and other soil microhabitats, including links among them. How do root exudates, litter and microbial residues regulate carbon and nutrient flows? How do soil structure, water, oxygen and redox cycles control microbial growth, enzyme activity, priming and greenhouse-gas formation? How do plant development and root death, day–night cycles, wetting and drying, climate extremes, pollution and management reshape hotspot resistance, recovery and legacy effects? We particularly encourage spatially and temporally resolved work using enzyme and chemical imaging, microsensors, isotope tracing, tomography, microfluidics, single-cell methods, metabolomics, multi-omics or synthetic communities. Process-based and data-driven models that connect hotspot dynamics with root systems, soil profiles, fields and ecosystems are equally welcome. Contributions from agricultural, forest, grassland, wetland and restored soils are invited. Together, these contributions will help explain when short-lived, local interactions lead to persistent changes in carbon storage, nutrient availability, soil structure, greenhouse-gas emissions, plant health and ecosystem resilience.
title: Plant–soil–microbe interactions in dynamic soil hotspots: From hot moments to lasting legacies

description: Soil organic matter is chemically diverse and continuously transforms, presenting a matrix whose composition and reactivity regulate key soil processes. The chemical composition of SOM determines whether compounds are rapidly transformed, persist through mineral association, fuel microbial activity, or participate in nutrient cycling, but these relationships are highly context-dependent and can vary with environmental conditions, land-use, and soil properties. This session brings together research exploring how the chemical complexity of SOM controls its transformation, persistence, and function, bridging molecular-scale processes and soil and ecosystem biogeochemistry. Studies investigating the composition, accessibility, and reactivity of SOM and dissolved organic matter using spectroscopic, isotopic, molecular, and fractionation approaches, as well as research linking SOM chemistry to microbial transformation, mineral–organic interactions, aggregation, nutrient cycling, and carbon stabilization are welcome. We encourage contributions on particulate and mineral-associated organic matter, microbial necromass, mineral surface interactions, organo-mineral associations, and molecular biomarkers that reveal SOM composition and reactivity across scales.
title: Chemical complexity and reactivity of soil organic matter: from molecular composition to ecosystem function

description: Global change—including climate warming, altered precipitation, land-use intensification, and changing nutrient inputs—is reshaping ecosystems worldwide, with profound consequences for soil carbon and nutrient cycling. Microbial communities are the key engines of these cycles, ultimately determining whether soils act as sinks or sources. Building a better understanding of how microbial communities, activity and physiology respond to diverse aspects of Global change is crucial to predict biogeochemical processes across temporal and spatial scales. This session highlights research that integrates microbial physiology and diversity into our understanding of soil biogeochemistry under global change. Contributions range from controlled studies with microbial isolates to ecosystem-level assessments across diverse climates, employing flux quantification techniques and advanced approaches such as omics, isotope tracing, microscopy, and spectroscopy. We feature empirical and theoretical studies addressing soil microbial resistance, resilience, and adaptation to single and multi-factorial climatic disturbances, as well as research on the interactions between soil microorganisms, plants and fauna. Join us to exchange ideas, share new findings, and discuss how linking soil microbes to ecosystem processes can improve our predictions of ecological responses in a rapidly changing world.
title: Microbial responses to global change: from physiology to ecosystem feedbacks
