description: Soil, as a highly heterogeneous environment, comprises a myriad of microhabitats hosting an unparalleled biodiversity, ranging from microbiota to plant roots. Several physical and chemical parameters define the soil microhabitat: the geometry of the pore space, notably its connectivity, the water distribution at the microscale and the nature, distribution and association of organic compounds within the soil mineral matrix (organo-mineral associations, soil aggregates). Variations in these parameters result in micro-gradients in oxygen, moisture, nutrients and organic compounds, acting as ecological filters for soil biota, usually promoting the co-existence of contrasting ecological strategies. In addition, the soil microhabitat exerts significant constraints on the mobility of the soil biota, with major consequences for the interactions between soil organisms and repercussions on soil functioning. Finally, microhabitats are highly variable in time, being constantly re-modelled by numerous factors such as the alternation of wet and dry cycles, the activity of the soil biota, especially plant roots and ecosystem engineers and the input of fresh organic matter. In this session we would like to invite contributions on: (i) deciphering the main drivers of the formation and spatiotemporal variability of the soil microhabitats, such as the release of EPS, the formation of biopores, etc., (ii) quantifying the role of the soil microhabitat in determining soil ecology, through field and experimental (microcosms, control of matric potential, isotopic tracing, etc.) approaches, (iii) describing the physico-chemical properties of the soil microhabitats, notably by developing novel tools (µCT, NanoSIMS, microscopy, etc.) rebuilding artificial microhabitats for experimental reproducible works (Soil chips, etc.). and (iv) modeling approaches that aims to capture soil functioning within the heterogeneous soil matrix. Finally, studies assessing the variability in soil activity within the soil matrix, notably focusing on microbial molecular analysis are also welcome.
title: The soil microhabitat: characterization and driving role in soil ecology

description: Over the Earth’s history, microorganisms have evolved distinct ecological strategies to capture resources, grow, tolerate stress and interact with other micro- and macroorganisms. These so-called life-history strategies emerge from combinations of physiological traits that are shaped by local environmental conditions and biotic interactions. Viewing soil microbial communities from this angle is an opportunity to move beyond taxonomic patterns and broad classifications towards a deeper understanding of how functionally diverse taxa co-exist and, ultimately, how they influence ecosystem processes such as carbon and nitrogen cycling. This session examines how microbial traits, functional groups and community assembly shape nutrient and biogeochemical cycling, ecosystem processes and resilience to natural and anthropogenic disturbance. Of particular interest are studies testing trait-based and life-history frameworks, identifying shifts in microbial strategies across environmental gradients or land-use changes. Contributions regarding individual microorganisms to complex communities, combining experimental, genomic or modelling approaches, are encouraged.
title: Soil microbial life-history strategies: from traits to ecosystem processes

description: Soil is the largest terrestrial pool of carbon. Consequently, soil organic carbon (SOC) and soil inorganic carbon (SIC) are the main indicators of soil health, fertility, and biodiversity. Effective monitoring and modeling of SOC and SIC stocks are necessary to understand their dynamics and identify chances for sustainable management, and are crucial to define the soil health status, its dynamics and impact. Modeling techniques of soil traits, and especially the stable C fraction, are thus essential for scaling up data and predicting future changes, but monitoring at spatiotemporal levels and on the soil profile in agroecosystem and natural system is still an important challenge. Soil carbon storage and dynamics, and soil health can greatly be affected by land cover and management, including clear-cutting, soil sealing, and agricultural intensification, especially tillage, application of fertilisers and residues, use of active ingredients, and reduction of the diversification. In addition, climate change, and especially the variation in temperature and precipitation patterns, can modify the dynamics of soil carbon, through a effect on soil moisture regime and microbial activity, with scarcely predictable effects on soil health and nutrient availability for crops, animals, and microbes. Nutrient availability regulates C decomposition and stabilization, thereby tightly linking nutrient cycles with soil dynamics of C and other elements, with special emphasis to N. Tools such as isotopic tracers, lysimeter studies, and digital monitoring platforms provide new insights into nutrient fluxes and their interactions with soil carbon pools. This session addresses the dynamics of SOC, SIC, and nutrients in agroecosystems, and definition and application of soil health, and investigates innovative monitoring and modelling strategies for optimizing soil carbon and nutrient management, and predict soil health depending on the management, and finally support decision-making in natural and agroecosystems. Contributions that integrate monitoring and modelling of nutrient–carbon interactions and that highlight their implications for sustainable soil management are particularly welcome
title: Soil health, carbon and nutrient monitoring, modelling and uptake in natural and agroecosystems

description: Microbial life in soil is highly heterogeneous in space and time. Microbial activity hotspots are localized in the rhizosphere, detritusphere, biopores, hyphosphere, and aggregate surfaces. Although these hotspots occupy only a fraction of the soil volume and may persist for limited periods, they dominate carbon and nutrient transformations and thereby exert a major influence on soil functioning. This session aims to bring together studies focused on microbial life and biogeochemical processes in soil hotspots across spatial and temporal scales. We invite contributions addressing: (i) the formation, persistence, and turnover of microbial hotspots and the biotic and abiotic factors controlling them; (ii) microbial activity, interactions, community composition, and functional traits within hotspots; (iii) the contribution of hotspots to cycles of carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and other elements and to soil organic matter dynamics; (iv) responses of microbial hotspots to environmental change and disturbances; and (v) new experimental, imaging, molecular, isotopic, and modelling approaches for identifying hotspots, quantifying their activity, and linking microscale processes to soil- and ecosystem-scale functions.
title: Hotspots of Microbial Life in Soil

description: Soil microorganisms allocate carbon (C) and energy not only to growth but also to maintenance and other non-growth processes, including cellular repair and stress tolerance, dormancy, storage, and the production of extracellular enzymes and polymeric substances. How microorganisms partition resources among these growth and non-growth pathways determines whether C is respired, released to the extracellular environment, or retained in biomass, with consequences for necromass formation and the persistence of soil organic matter. Yet, the energetic costs and trade-offs underlying this partitioning remain poorly quantified and are not fully reflected in common metrics like the microbial carbon use efficiency (CUE). Thermodynamic approaches offer a complementary mechanistic framework, with the potential to constrain and predict metabolic responses even in complex systems where individual processes cannot be fully resolved. This session explores microbial C and energy allocation as a mechanistic link between microbial physiology and soil C persistence, from single cells to the ecosystem scale. We welcome experimental, theoretical and modelling contributions on microbial maintenance and non-growth metabolism, carbon and energy use efficiency, microbial responses to environmental change (e.g., warming, drought, land-use change), and implications for C stabilization. We particularly encourage studies applying or combining methods to quantify microbial C and energy use, such as isotope tracing, calorespirometry, thermodynamic approaches, and process-based modelling. By connecting microbial ecology and physiology with soil biogeochemistry, we aim to advance a bioenergetic understanding of how microbial metabolism regulates the fate of soil C and to explore how thermodynamic constraints can improve the mechanistic basis of predictive models.
title: Beyond Growth: Microbial Carbon and Energy Use in Soils

description: Soil erosion is a major threat to the global soil functions that sustain life on land, and substantial research has been devoted to understanding, predicting, and controlling erosion processes. Yet there appears to be a discrepancy between the (perceived) gravity of soil erosion and recent scientific activity in the field. Models have become the primary epistemic tool in erosion science, despite a continued overreliance on 1960s empirics now masked by computational prowess. Meanwhile, we struggle to measure lateral soil fluxes beyond small plots, and implementing erosion control measures remains a major societal challenge. These issues point towards a reliability crisis that, left unchecked, risks eroding the credibility of the research field. In this session, we want to co-create future(s) for erosion science by rethinking where we want to go as a scientific field and how we get there through the choices we make today. As such, we welcome a wide range of contributions, from critical perspectives to applied research. We invite submissions addressing, but not limited to, the following subjects: - New or improved approaches to measuring and modelling soil erosion; - Impacts of erosion on soil health, soil functions and ecosystem services; - Interactions between climate change, land-use change, and soil change in shaping soil erosion and its dynamics; - Evidence-based soil conservation—particularly approaches that integrate soil conservation into broader landscape management perspective; - Translating (uncertain) modelled erosion rates into risk assessments for policymakers and managers; - New or improved methods for calibrating and testing soil erosion models—particularly approaches that increase model falsifiability and/or that report case studies of model invalidation (if you have “bad” results, we want to hear about it!) - We expressly encourage contributions that provide broader, critical perspectives on soil-erosion research and point towards a direction forward.
title: The future(s) of soil erosion science

description: The contribution of soil organisms to ecosystem service provision remains poorly quantified. Indeed, soil fauna shape soil hydrology and biogeochemical cycling through bioturbation, pore formation, faeces production, vertical redistribution of organic matter and mucus secretion. While providing ecosystem services, such as erosion control, nutrient cycling and carbon sequestration, their activity can also generate disservices, for example by stimulating greenhouse gas emissions. This session aims to bring together researchers investigating how the functional diversity of soil macro- and meso-fauna shapes soil processes and ecosystem services across scales, from individual species at microscale to communities at ecosystem scale. We particularly encourage contributions that use of measurable functional traits and bioturbation activities to quantify faunal effects on soil functioning. We invite studies addressing how soil fauna by pore formation, faeces production and vertical mixing influences soil organic carbon storage, water infiltration and retention, nutrient cycling and other ecosystem functions. Moreover, the session will address the challenge of scaling faunal effects from controlled experiments to field conditions. We welcome approaches combining community composition, functional diversity, bioturbation measurements and soil properties with observations of ecosystem services across contrasting environments. Studies from both temperate and tropical systems are welcome to explore how environmental context modifies the relationships between soil fauna activity and ecosystem service provision. We also invite contributions addressing the representation of faunal activity in soil carbon and water dynamic models, the development of indicators of fauna-mediated ecosystem functioning, or the quantitative and spatial assessment of ecosystem services provided by soil fauna. By bringing together soil ecologists, biogeochemists, soil physicists, modellers and ecosystem-service researchers, the session seeks to advance a mechanistic and quantitative understanding of how soil fauna communities contribute to soil functioning. Linking measurable organismal functions to ecosystem services will provide a basis for incorporating soil biodiversity into ecosystem assessments, soil process models and sustainable land-management strategies.
title: Functional diversity of soil fauna: linking soil processes to ecosystem services

description: Soils host the largest reservoir of biodiversity on Earth, sustaining an intricate food web that spans from viruses and microbes to protists, nematodes, microarthropods, and other soil fauna. Together, these organisms regulate several soil functions with direct consequences for plant, animal, and human health. However, soil biodiversity remains comparatively understudied relative to aboveground biodiversity, and important taxonomic, spatial, and temporal gaps still limit our capacity to understand and predict how soil communities respond to global change. In recent years, soil biodiversity has risen rapidly on both the scientific and political agenda, reflected in a surge of high-impact publications and in policy developments such as the EU Soil Monitoring Law. At the same time, soil biodiversity faces mounting pressures from land-use intensification, climate change, conventional agricultural management, and the spread of emerging pollutants and other anthropogenic contaminants. This session aims to bring together researchers working across the full spectrum of soil biodiversity research, from fundamental ecology to applied and methodological innovation. We welcome contributions addressing (but not limited to): - Patterns, drivers, and dynamics of soil biodiversity across different taxa and across spatial and temporal scales, including responses to climate and land-use changes. - Impacts of agricultural practices (i.e., tillage, fertilization, etc) on soil biota and soil health, including the transition towards sustainable, solar energy, regenerative, and smart agricultural management. - Effects of metals and emerging pollutants (microplastics, antibiotics, pesticides, PFAS, etc) on soil organisms and ecosystem functioning. - Soil biodiversity–ecosystem functions relationships. - Novel methodological and technological approaches for characterising soil biodiversity, including molecular/genomic tools, automated/high-throughput organism identification, remote sensing and UAV-based approaches, machine learning or integrative modelling frameworks. - Smart and precision agriculture approaches that integrate soil biodiversity monitoring into decision-making for sustainable land management. - Soil biodiversity as a nature-based solution for restoration, climate mitigation, and sustainable land management. Also, their link with policy, monitoring frameworks, and soil health indicators.
title: Soil biodiversity in a changing world: from genes to soil fauna, threats, and smart sustainable management

description: How soil fauna are sampled shapes what we know about them. Soil cores, extraction funnels, pitfall and pan traps, hand sorting and DNA-based approaches each capture a different fraction of the community, with different biases, costs and impacts, which limits comparability across studies. New technologies, including smart and automated traps, in situ and non-destructive detection, low-cost open-source devices and DNA-oriented sample collection, promise more scalable and reproducible sampling, but need validation and standardisation. Robust, comparable methods are also needed to support soil monitoring under Directive (EU) 2025/2360, which requires scientifically validated methods without prescribing taxa. This session focuses on the sampling step: how soil animals are collected, extracted, preserved and documented. We welcome contributions on (i) sampling design and effort optimisation; (ii) comparison of extraction and trapping methods and preservatives; (iii) smart, automated and robotic sampling devices; (iv) in situ and non-destructive detection (imaging, tomography, acoustics, sensors); (v) low-cost, open and citizen-science tools; (vi) DNA-oriented collection and preservation, including non-destructive recovery from trap fluids; (vii) ethical, low-impact and non-lethal sampling; (viii) standardisation, ring tests, reference materials and FAIR metadata; and (ix) transferability across soils, climates and land uses. Method comparisons and negative results are especially welcome. This session is dedicated to the memory of Prof. Dr. Vittorio Parisi, author of the QBS-ar index (2001), who showed how a simple, standardised sampling-to-index workflow can make soil microarthropods a practical tool for assessing soil quality.
title: Beyond the soil core: innovative, standardised and scalable sampling of soil fauna

description: Soils harbor a highly diverse spatial organization that shapes biogeochemical processes and ecosystem functions across scales. For example, these span from microbial habitats, organic and mineral surfaces, detritusphere and rhizosphere to soil aggregate structures and chemical gradients shaped by pedogenic and anthropogenic processes, all influencing the transformation and persistence of organic matter, nutrients other elements. In this session, we invite diverse empirical, synthesis, and modeling studies that address how biological, physical, and chemical hotspots and hot moments shape soil organic matter dynamics, soil biogeochemistry and ecosystem functions. This includes studies that resolve biogeochemical hotspots across spatial and temporal scales to elucidate the mechanisms controlling soil organic matter storage, persistence, and vulnerability. We welcome contributions integrating diverse biological, physical, and geochemical perspectives, from targeted experiments and high-resolution observations to long-term studies, large-scale syntheses, and integrative modeling. Emerging approaches that combine novel analytical or computational methods, including AI and machine learning, with experimental and observational data are particularly welcome. We aim to bring these perspectives together to advance a cross-scale understanding of how soil heterogeneity and architecture shape organic matter dynamics and ecosystem functions.
title: Cross-scale mechanisms of soil organic matter dynamics: From biogeochemical hotspots to ecosystem functions

description: Carbon can persist in the environment for a few years to millennia, depending on the mechanisms that stabilise it. Persistence is increasingly understood not as an intrinsic property of a particular molecular makeup, but as an emerging quality reflective of the physical, mineralogical, microbial and environmental context in which carbon resides. Resolving these controls across the diversity of carbon pools is fundamental to predicting how ecosystem carbon stocks will respond to climate and land-use change over time. This session focuses on the processes that determine the durability of carbon across terrestrial systems. We welcome contributions on the stabilisation of soil organic carbon, including the divergent turnover of mineral-associated (MAOM) and particulate (POM) organic matter and the roles of mineral surfaces, aggregate occlusion and microbial processing; the long-term stability of pyrogenic and biochar carbon; the fate of inorganic carbon generated by silicate weathering, including dissolved inorganic carbon and pedogenic carbonate; and the redox- and moisture-controlled preservation of carbon in peatlands and wetlands, where the balance of aerobic and anaerobic decomposition affects carbon accumulation and loss. We invite studies that utilise field observation, manipulative experiments, isotopic and radiocarbon tracing, spectroscopy, modelling, or novel approaches to illuminate the timescales of carbon persistence and its vulnerability to disturbance. Insights that unify understanding across these otherwise separately studied pools are especially encouraged.
title: Mechanisms and timescales of carbon persistence in soils

description: Soils are the largest terrestrial carbon reservoir, and enhancing the long-term persistence of soil organic matter (SOM) is a key strategy for mitigating atmospheric CO₂ concentrations. Yet, the mechanisms that govern SOM stabilization—and the interventions that might enhance it—remain among the most complex and debated challenges in soil science. Recent advances have deepened our understanding of SOM fractionation and protection mechanisms, particularly the role of mineral-associated organic matter (MAOM), particulate organic matter (POM), and occluded POM (oPOM). Insights into the biotic and abiotic pathways leading to MAOM formation have expanded significantly, alongside the development of new-generation soil models that incorporate these processes into SOM turnover estimates. At the same time, emerging evidence underscores the complex and context-dependent nature of the soil mineral–microbe–vegetation interface. In particular, studies beyond temperate systems reveal that organo-mineral interactions are more dynamic than previously assumed, and that POM can persist for centuries in certain ecosystems or soil horizons. These findings challenge conventional assumptions and highlight the need for tailored management strategies. This session invites contributions that explore SOM dynamics across scales—from molecular mechanisms and microbial processes to ecosystem-level patterns and global models. We welcome studies that introduce novel insights, challenge established paradigms, or provide robust confirmations of existing theories. Whether your work is based on field observations, laboratory experiments, or computational modeling, we are eager to hear how it advances our understanding of SOM persistence and informs practical applications, from land management to climate policy. We particularly encourage early career scientists to participate, including those with preliminary findings or innovative conceptual approaches. If your research touches on any aspect of SOM formation, transformation, or stabilization, join us for a lively and interdisciplinary discussion.
title: Soil Organic Matter Dynamics Across Scales: From Molecular Insights to Ecosystem behavior

description: The interaction of the carbon cycle and other biogenic elements in the soil determines the overall biogeochemical stability and productivity of terrestrial ecosystems. Transformations among C and N, P, S, Ca, Mg, Fe, and Al are closely coupled through organic matter turnover, mineral weathering, sorption and desorption, complexation, precipitation and dissolution, and redox reactions; these processes regulate element availability, mobility, retention, and losses. This session brings together studies investigating the coupled biogeochemistry of carbon, nutrients, and major elements across soils and ecosystems. We welcome research addressing element interactions at molecular, mineral, microscale, and ecosystem levels, using spectroscopic, isotopic, molecular, and modeling approaches. We particularly encourage contributions linking elemental coupling with mineral–organic interactions, such as C-Fe, C-Ca, and C-Al; microbial processes governing C-N-P cycling in soil; nutrient availability for plants and interactions in the plant-soil-microorganism system; weathering; organic matter transformation under redox dynamics; and responses of C and nutrient cycling to environmental change and soil management.
title: Coupled biogeochemistry of carbon, nutrients, and major elements in soils

description: Soil organic matter (SOM) is the largest terrestrial organic carbon pool and a key lever for climate regulation, yet the mechanisms governing its dynamics and long-term persistence across contrasting scales remain debated. A paradigm shift over the last two decades has moved the field from viewing SOC persistence primarily as a function of intrinsic molecular recalcitrance towards a framework in which physical organization and microbial accessibility control turnover times. Resolving how carbon moves from fresh inputs through particulate (POM) to mineral-associated organic matter (MAOM), and where and why it is stabilized or lost, across ecosystems and along the soil–regolith profile, requires integrated, multi-proxy approaches combining methods from soil science, biogeochemistry and isotope geochemistry. This session aims to bring together researchers working along the full SOC continuum and adopting multidisciplinary approaches to disentangle the formation and fate of SOC by investigating SOM chemistry, mineral soil characteristics, physical organization and mineralogy. We invite studies that (i) investigate SOC persistence across contrasting spatial and temporal scales; (ii) trace SOM formation and transformation using classical and non-traditional molecular and isotopic approaches; (iii) apply emerging non-traditional methods, including stable isotope systems of mineral elements, to trace mineral transformation and organo-mineral interactions along the critical-zone profile; and (iv) use models across contrasting scales to integrate data generated by different approaches. We particularly encourage studies combining these complementary approaches to constrain mechanisms of long-term SOC preservation, including studies of Quaternary archives such as loess–paleosol sequences. By bringing together communities from different disciplines, the session seeks to advance a unified, process-based understanding of SOC dynamics by integrating short-term turnover with long-term stabilization. Such an integrated perspective is essential for assessing the persistence of carbon across contrasting soil types and climates and its responses to environmental change, and for underpinning robust climate and land-management strategies. We particularly encourage submissions from early-career researchers and under-represented regions, and invite contributions that could form the basis of a topical collection in Biogeosciences or SOIL.
title: Tracing the Fate of Soil Carbon: From Rapid Turnover to Long-Term Persistence

description: Soils represent a major terrestrial store of both organic and inorganic carbon. At present soils are a net carbon sink, and building soil carbon stocks holds a potential to contribute to achieving net zero carbon. Furthermore, the accrual, stability, and cycling of carbon is fundamental to the productivity and resilience of soil systems, and preserving or even increasing soil carbon stocks is critical for allowing sustainable agricultural crop production. Avenues for organic carbon sequestration in soils include plant-based inputs, the addition of pyrogenic carbon (biochar), and addition of composts or other additives such as manures and soil conditioners provided additionality and leakage effects are considered. Enhanced silicate weathering may hold significant potential for building up inorganic carbon stocks, while inputs from bedrock, and mediation by land use changes such as afforestation, may also increase inorganic soil carbon stocks. This session seeks to explore how soil carbon stocks can be increased so as to simultaneously enhance agricultural productivity, mitigate negative repercussions of changing environmental conditions, and contribute to achieving carbon neutrality. In addition to organic carbon, focus will be given to inorganic carbon pools in agroecosystems and their response to management practices such as fertilisation, irrigation, liming, or other mineral additions. Alongside this, advances in methods for monitoring and modelling rates of soil carbon loss or carbon sequestration in soils will be discussed, including approaches to quantify and characterise organic and inorganic carbon in calcareous soils. We welcome contributions exploring methods of increasing both organic and inorganic carbon stocks, and studies exploring the storage, stability, and cycling of carbon within soil systems. Early career researchers are strongly encouraged to apply, and we seek submissions considering empirical, modelling, or meta-analytical approaches.
title: Carbon sequestration in soils: organic and inorganic mechanisms of increasing soil carbon stocks as a pathway to net zero and improved soil functioning

description: Plastic pollution in soils is a global issue of growing concern for scientific communities and the public alike. Soils are a major sink for plastics, with agricultural land ranking among the most polluted land-use categories. Despite this, significant knowledge gaps remain concerning the analysis of plastic in soil, its sources, and its fate. This session seeks to bridge these knowledge gaps, which is an essential step towards improving risk assessments, informing policies, guiding agricultural practices and industrial strategies to mitigate plastic pollution and its environmental impact. We welcome contributions from observational, monitoring, laboratory, and modelling studies from urban settings, agroecosystems, and soil interfaces between different environmental compartments, covering all scales from nano- to macroplastics, with a focus on: • Detection of plastics in soil systems: methods for sampling, detection, and quantifying plastic pollution in soils. • Distribution and source apportionment: monitoring efforts and source apportionment, spatio-temporal patterns • Transport dynamics of plastics: transport of plastics and their co-transport with other contaminants from soil to other environmental compartments. • Degradation of plastic in soil: physical and chemical degradation, photodegradation, biodegradation, additive leaching, and the sorption processes of other chemicals. • Impact of plastic on soil ecosystems: physical and chemical interactions between soil and plastic particles, ecotoxicological effects of plastics and/or their leached additives on soil properties, soil health, plant growth and soil fauna. • Economic and policy perspectives: economic drivers for agricultural plastic use, designing solutions, and supporting policies and regulations for reducing and sustainably managing agricultural plastics. Research related to, but not explicitly listed above, may also be considered.
title: Plastics in soils - where do we stand?

description: Soils have been identified as a major sink for plastics which has led to increasing concerns for essential soil ecosystem services. However, we still lack an in-depth understanding of transport processes and the fate of macro-, micro-, and nanoplastics in the terrestrial environment. In this session, we invite contributions that present empirical, monitoring, and modelling studies for all scales of plastic pollution and soil systems, advancing our mechanistic understanding of transport and fate in the terrestrial environment. This includes but is not limited to urban settings, agroecosystems, and soil interfaces between different environmental compartments. Presentations may focus on: • Experimental studies at different scales (lab, mesocosm, field, etc.) advancing our process-based understanding of transport and transformation processes • Monitoring efforts to understand source attribution and quantification of spatiotemporal trends in inputs, releases, and transfers • Models addressing fate and transport processes within terrestrial environments and their interfaces, such as connected aquatic and atmospheric systems • Human behaviour, littering and littering dynamics, urban drainage systems, and solutions We welcome interdisciplinary research, including contributions from the social sciences.
title: Buried and beyond: Transport and fate of micro- and macroplastic in soil systems

description: Soil ecosystems provide essential services, including nutrient cycling, water filtration, carbon sequestration, and habitat provision. However, industrial activities, intensive agriculture, mining, urbanization, and waste disposal have led to widespread accumulation of contaminants in soils globally. From legacy pollutants such as potentially toxic elements and persistent organic pollutants to contaminants of emerging concern, soil contamination poses a growing threat to terrestrial biodiversity and agricultural productivity. While extensive research has documented contaminant concentrations in soils, significant knowledge gaps remain regarding how pollutants alter fundamental belowground ecosystem processes and soil functioning, thereby affecting major processes on an ecosystem level. Contaminant mixtures, dynamic environmental conditions, and climate change stressors alter contaminant bioavailability, bioaccumulation pathways, and ecotoxicological impacts on microbial communities, soil fauna and vegetation. Furthermore, developing scalable, cost-effective, and ecologically sound remediation and management strategies requires a deep mechanistic understanding of soil-pollutant interactions and physiological responses of plants. This session aims to bring together contributions from all aspects of soil pollution research, including methodological advances focused on the sources, distribution, ecological impacts, and sustainable management of soil pollutants. We encourage interdisciplinary contributions that link physical and chemical pollutant characterization with plant responses, ecosystem function assessment, and novel remediation frameworks. Studies on the effects of soil pollution on ecosystem processes and biogeochemical cycles (e.g., carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus dynamics) under pollution pressure are especially welcome, as are novel insights into processes governing bioavailability, trophic transfer, and soil-to-plant contaminant accumulation. We welcome presentations of laboratory and field research results as well as theoretical studies. We intend to bring together scientists from multiple disciplines. We especially encourage young researchers to submit their contributions.
title: Advances in Soil Pollution Research: Ecosystem Processes, Functioning and Management

description: Soil contamination encompasses a wide range of inorganic and organic pollutants, including metals and metalloids, petroleum hydrocarbons, pesticides and other persistent organic contaminants, as well as emerging contaminants such as per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) and microplastics. The coexistence of multiple contaminants can increase the complexity of remediation and requires approaches capable of addressing contaminant-specific behaviour while supporting the recovery of soil functions. Nature-based solutions (NbS) are increasingly being explored as sustainable approaches for the remediation and restoration of contaminated soils. These include the application of organic, mineral and engineered amendments, phytoremediation and plant-assisted remediation, microbial and bioremediation processes, as well as combinations of these strategies. Their effectiveness depends on the interactions between contaminants, soil properties, amendments, plants and microorganisms, and may involve contaminant immobilization, transformation, degradation, uptake or changes in bioavailability and mobility. This session aims to bring together research addressing the application and development of nature-based approaches for the remediation of soils affected by a broad range of contaminants, from metals and metalloids to conventional organic pollutants and emerging contaminants such as PFAS and microplastics. Contributions addressing single or multiple contaminants, contaminant mixtures, soil–plant–microorganism interactions, amendment-based remediation, phytoremediation, bioremediation and integrated approaches are particularly welcome. We also encourage contributions evaluating the long-term performance, mechanisms, scalability and environmental sustainability of nature-based remediation strategies, as well as their capacity to reduce contaminant risks and contribute to the recovery of soil functions. Interdisciplinary studies connecting contaminant biogeochemistry, soil science, environmental microbiology, plant science and remediation engineering are especially encouraged.
title: Advancing nature-based remediation of soils contaminated with conventional and emerging contaminants

description: Soil contamination by potentially hazardous substances (e.g. metals, metalloids, radionuclides, organic compounds and emerging contaminants) is one of the major environmental challenges affecting soil and plant health, ecosystem services, food production and sustainable land management, as well as promoting other forms of soil degradation (e.g. erosion, salinisation and loss of organic matter and biodiversity). Understanding the extent and effects of soil contamination is essential for developing sustainable land management and remediation strategies. Although several remediation approaches have been investigated, particularly on a laboratory and greenhouse scale, their long-term effectiveness and sustainability in real field conditions are largely unknown. The success of remediation should be evaluated based on the removal or immobilisation of contaminants, as well as the recovery of soil properties, biological activity, biodiversity and ecosystem services. This session focus on the transition to soil remediation at medium- and long-term soil recovery, with a particular emphasis on assessing and monitoring recovery processes. The aim is to bring together interdisciplinary research addressing contaminant removal, immobilisation and dynamics, environmental risk reduction, recovery of soil functions, soil–plant–microorganism interactions, ecosystem services and overall soil health, as well as legal frameworks, limitations of remediation strategies, and sustainability assessment of remediation strategies. The session provides an opportunity to present studies and establish new partnerships with the aim of developing multidisciplinary strategies to contribute to the assessment and remediation of contaminated sites.
title: Beyond remediation: tracking soil recovery and ecosystem functioning in contaminated landscapes

description: Understanding how magma is generated, stored, transferred, mobilised, and ultimately transported toward the surface is central to deciphering volcanic behaviour and thus to improve the assessment of volcanic hazard. The trans-crustal evolution of magmas, and the associated variation in their rheological properties, exert a fundamental influence on magma remobilisation and on the timing, magnitude, and style of volcanic activity. Reconstructing how magma properties evolve through time is therefore essential for understanding the processes that regulate volcanic activity and for interpreting monitoring signals recorded at the surface. In this framework, the petrological and geochemical record preserved in crystals, melts, and volcanic products provides a unique window into trans-crustal magmatic processes, revealing the physical and chemical evolution of magmatic systems from long-term storage to the final stages preceding eruption. These observations can be combined with field observations, experiments, numerical models, geophysical and monitoring data to constrain where, when, and how magmatic systems become eruptible. This session aims to bring together studies investigating the pathways from magma generation and storage to mobilisation, ascent, and eruption. We particularly encourage petrological, volcanological, geochemical and geophysical contributions that constrain the architecture of magma plumbing systems, the processes and timescales of magma evolution and migration, their link with eruptive activity, and explore how petrological and geochemical observations can improve our understanding of pre- and syn-eruptive dynamics. Relevant approaches include field observations, mineral and melt chemistry, diffusion chronometry, thermobarometry, melt and fluid inclusions, isotope and trace-element geochemistry, experimental petrology, thermodynamic and kinetic modelling, numerical simulations, and textural and rheological investigations. Contributions integrating petrological information with geophysical, geodetic, or monitoring datasets are particularly encouraged. We also welcome emerging approaches, including automated mineral and textural analysis, machine learning, data-driven modelling, and high-resolution analytical techniques.
title: Pathways to eruption: tracking magma dynamics beneath volcanoes

description: Soil degradation poses a critical threat to global environment, ecosystem services, and agricultural sustainability. Natural and agricultural systems are increasingly vulnerable to severe degradation processes—including desertification, soil erosion, salinisation, and chemical pollution—driven by the combined pressures of climate change and anthropogenic activity. Shifting precipitation regimes and rising average temperatures disrupt the soil water balance, intensifying water deficits, nutrient losses, and increasing soil salinity. Concurrently, unsustainable land management, deforestation, intensive cultivation, and the overapplication of agrochemicals accelerate physical and chemical disturbances that impair overall soil quality and biodiversity. This session convenes research—from long-term field observation plots to advanced remote and proximal sensing—to systematically examine the mechanisms, impacts, and indicators of soil degradation, resistance, and resilience across diverse land uses and environmental contexts. We welcome contributions that quantify how land-use dynamics drive the depletion of critical soil functional properties and evaluate spatial and temporal trends in soil health. In parallel, the session explores innovative, evidence-based soil conservation strategies designed to halt and reverse soil degradation. Key topics include sustainable management practices such as conservation agriculture, agroforestry, organic amendments, targeted erosion control, and soil salinity management. We place strong emphasis on how these practices restore soil structure, improve water retention, and foster biological activity, thereby enhancing ecosystem capacity to buffer extreme weather events. Finally, we highlight the integration of long-term observational data with policy frameworks and participatory stakeholder approaches. By bridging observational science with sustainable soil management, this session aims to advance available approaches for long-term soil conservation, agricultural productivity, and overall soil functionality.
title: Soil Degradation and Resilience Under Global Change: Causes, Impacts, and Conservation Strategies

description: Glaciers and volcanoes interact in several ways. Volcanic and geothermal activity can alter the dynamics or mass balance of glaciers, and glaciers can influence the frequency and mechanisms of volcanic eruptions, resulting in the construction of distinct glaciovolcanic landforms. However, because of the remoteness of many glaciovolcanic environments, these interactions remain understudied. In these complex settings, hazards associated with glacier-volcano interaction can vary from lava flows to volcanic ash fall, lahars, landslides, pyroclastic density currents, or glacial outburst floods. These can happen consecutively or simultaneously and have devastating impacts on society, as well as affect glaciers, rivers and the atmosphere. As glaciological and volcanological processes generate concurring signals, the challenge is to study, understand and ultimately discriminate these potentially coexisting signals. We wish to fully include geophysical observations of current and recent events with geological observations and interpretations of deposits of past events. Glaciovolcanoes also often preserve a unique record of the glacial or non-glacial eruptive environment that is capable of significantly advancing our knowledge of how Earth's climate system evolves. We invite contributions focused on ice-covered volcanoes from anywhere on Earth and other planets that: • improve the understanding of signals generated by ice-covered volcanoes; • analyse glaciovolcanic eruptions, deposits or landforms; • deal with the mitigation of hazards associated with ice-covered volcanoes; • study the volcanic impacts on glaciers and vice versa; • address climate and environmental change through glaciovolcanic studies. Research on recent glaciovolcanic activity is especially welcomed. This includes geological observations e.g. of deposits in the field or remote-sensing data, together with experimental and modelling approaches. We aim to bring together scientists from volcanology, glaciology, seismology, geodesy, hydrology, geomorphology and atmospheric science to enable a broad discussion and interaction.
title: Volcano–glacier interactions on Earth and beyond

description: Agrogeophysics applies geophysical methods such as electrical resistivity tomography, electromagnetic induction, ground-penetrating radar, seismic and other techniques, across platforms ranging from hand-held instruments and ground-based systems to drone- and satellite-borne sensors, to characterise spatial and temporal patterns and processes in the soil-water-plant continuum that are relevant for agronomic management. Being minimally invasive, spatially exhaustive, multi-scale and repeatable in time, these methods give access to information of states and processes in agroecosystems that conventional point-based monitoring cannot provide, and they are increasingly used to support sustainable, water-efficient and climate-resilient farming. This session brings together contributions that monitor, map or model soil and plant properties and states of agronomic relevance, including texture and structure, salinity, compaction, water content and fluxes, rooting depth and root-zone dynamics, soil organic carbon, drainage and irrigation performance; develop and apply proximal or remote sensing approaches to soil-water-plant interactions; bridge the scale gap between laboratory, plot, field, farm and landscape; establish and test pedophysical relationships linking sensed properties to soil and plant variables of interest; fuse geophysical data with agronomic, soil sampling, remote sensing and yield data; integrate geophysical observations into hydrological, crop and root-water-uptake models, data assimilation schemes or digital twins; exploit machine learning and other data-driven tools for acquisition design, inversion, interpretation and upscaling. We particularly welcome work on operational use in real farming systems, benchmark datasets and open data and software, uncertainty quantification, and the translation of geophysical information into decision support, advisory services and soil monitoring policy.
title: Agrogeophysics: sensing soil-water-plant interactions to support sustainable agricultural management

description: Soil health is fundamental to crop productivity, ecosystem vitality, water regulation, carbon storage, nutrient supply, and the resilience of terrestrial ecosystems to multiple stressors. Yet soils are increasingly exposed to dynamic pressures associated with climate change, including drought, heatwaves, flooding, rapid rewetting, and shifting seasonal patterns. These stressors can alter soil functioning gradually or abruptly, with consequences for biological activity, plant performance, soil structure, and the capacity of soils to resist and recover from disturbance. Because many of these responses are mediated by soil microorganisms and their interactions with plants and the soil matrix, understanding soil health under climate stress requires linking processes across scales and scientific domains – from microbial habitats to fields and landscapes. This session aims to bring together research that advances the concept, assessment, and management of soil health in a changing and increasingly dynamic environment. We welcome contributions that address how soil health and soil multifunctionality respond to climatic variability and extremes, and how resilience can be understood, monitored, and sustained across spatial and temporal scales. Particular emphasis is placed on the role of soil biota, especially microorganisms, as drivers and indicators of soil health, as well as on plant-soil-microorganism interactions that shape resistance, recovery, and long-term functionality of soils. We invite experimental, observational, and modelling studies that contribute to a more integrative understanding of soil health, including the development of indicators, resilience concepts, monitoring approaches, and management strategies. Topics may include soil health under climate extremes, biological indicators of soil functioning, plant-soil-microorganism interactions, recovery after disturbance, scaling from soil microsites to landscapes, and links between soil health, ecosystem services, and sustainable land use. Contributions that connect fundamental mechanisms with applied assessment and land management are especially encouraged. By connecting perspectives from soil and plant sciences, microbiology and biogeochemistry to landscape-scale processes, this session will provide a platform to discuss how soil health can be defined, measured, and strengthened under the increasing pressures of global change.
title: Soil health in a dynamic world - from microbes to landscapes

description: This session offers an opportunity to present studies or professional works regarding irrigated agriculture, either with disciplinary or multidisciplinary approaches, to promote resilience at different spatial scales, mainly when water and soil are limiting factors. It explores scientific, technological, and managerial breakthroughs aimed at transforming irrigated agriculture in a changing climate in the following areas: • Traditional, novel, and transitional technologies for irrigation management, control and practical application. • Digital irrigation: application of satellite UAV, and thermal imaging for ET estimation, crop stress detection, and yield forecasting. • Precision Irrigation: application of sensor networks, artificial intelligence, big data in irrigation scheduling. • Clime adaptation: strategies for mitigating heatwaves, prolonged droughts, and soil salinization in irrigated systems. • Safety in non-conventional water resources (treated wastewater, desalinated water, and brackish resources) in agricultural systems. • Improving the integration of climate change scenarios and weather forecasts into agro-hydrological models and decision support systems to improve decisions in irrigation management and safe surface water-groundwater interactions. • Water- Food-Energy-Ecosystem (WEFE) Nexus for evaluation of: energy footprint, carbon trade-offs, and environmental flows associated with modern irrigation systems.
title: Irrigated Agriculture Under Climate Extremes: Innovative Water Management, Soil Resilience, and the Water -Energy- Food Nexus

description: The session deals with the documentation and modelling of the tectonic, deformation and geodetic features of any type of volcanic area, on Earth and in the Solar System. The focus is on advancing our understanding on any type of deformation of active and non-active volcanoes, on the associated behaviours, and the implications for hazards. We welcome contributions based on results from fieldwork, remote-sensing studies, geodetic and geophysical measurements, analytical, analogue and numerical simulations, and laboratory studies of volcanic rocks. Studies may be focused at the regional scale, investigating the tectonic setting responsible for and controlling volcanic activity, both along divergent and convergent plate boundaries, as well in intraplate settings. At a more local scale, all types of surface deformation in volcanic areas are of interest, such as elastic inflation and deflation, or anelastic processes, including caldera and flank collapses. Deeper, sub-volcanic deformation studies, concerning the emplacement of intrusions, as sills, dikes and laccoliths, are most welcome. We also particularly welcome geophysical data aimed at understanding magmatic processes during volcano unrest. These include geodetic studies obtained mainly through GPS and InSAR, as well as at their modelling to imagine sources. The session includes, but is not restricted to, the following topics: • volcanism and regional tectonics; • formation of magma chambers, laccoliths, and other intrusions; • dyke and sill propagation, emplacement, and arrest; • earthquakes and eruptions; • caldera collapse, resurgence, and unrest; • flank collapse; • volcano deformation monitoring; • volcano deformation and hazard mitigation; • volcano unrest; • mechanical properties of rocks in volcanic areas.
title: Volcanic processes: tectonics, deformation, geodesy, unrest

description: The availability of plant nutrients is governed by interacting chemical, physical, and biological processes within the soil–soil solution–plant continuum. Understanding these processes is essential for assessing soil fertility, optimising fertiliser requirements, and evaluating the environmental risks associated with nutrient losses and contamination. Conventional extraction methods used to estimate plant-available nutrient fractions often provide only a static snapshotof soil nutrient availability and may not deliver the level of accuracy and detail on soil fertility required for effective nutrient managemant in modern intensive agriculture aimed at achieving high crop yields. More accurate assessment of dynamic nutrient availability is equally important in organic farming, where crop nutrition depends strongly on the mobilisation and cycling of soil nutrient reserves. This session will focus on the processes controlling the release of nutrients from the soil matrix into the soil solution, their sorption and desorption at soil particle surfaces, diffusion and transport, and subsequent uptake by plant roots. Contributions examining the effects of soil texture, pore structure, mineralogical composition, pH, and organic matter content on the mobility and bioavailability of phosphorus, potassium, magnesium, sulphur, and micronutrients are particularly encouraged. The session will also address the release of mineral nutrients during organic matter decomposition. This includes microbial mineralisation, enzyme-mediated decomposition, rhizosphere processes, and the effects of root exudates on the cycling and availability of phosphorus, sulphur, and micronutrients. We welcome laboratory and field studies, as well as experimental, theoretical, and modelling approaches. Contributions that integrate processes across the soil–soil solution–plant continuum, connect nutrient pools with fluxes and plant uptake, or develop improved approaches for assessing dynamic nutrient availability are especially encouraged. By bringing together soil and plant scientists, biochemists, microbiologists modellers, this session will advance our understanding of nutrient dynamics within soils and nutrient transfer from soil to plants, thereby enabling more accurate assessments of soil nutrient status, fertiliser requirements, and associated environmental risks.
title: Dynamics of plant nutrients in the soil–soil solution–plant continuum: Roles of organic matter decomposition, biochemical processes, pH, and soil texture

description: Magma composition, eruptive frequency, and tectonic context are highly variable features of volcanoes. Within such contexts, volcanic volatiles play a key role in magma transport, and impact on the style and timing of volcanic eruptions. Gas chemical and isotopic compositions may change over time, reflecting variations in the magmatic feeding systems of volcanoes. As the magma rises from depth, the decreasing pressure allows volatile species to partition into the gas phase. Bubbles form, grow, and coalesce, and gases start to flow through the vesciculated magma. Eventually, fluid and gases reach the surface and are released into the atmosphere through soil degassing, fumarolic vents, or bubbling through a water surface, forming large plumes or explosive eruption columns. Volcanic emissions can also have significant impacts on the terrestrial environment, atmospheric composition, climate, and human health at various temporal and spatial scales. For instance, sulfur dioxide emissions can cause acid rain and influence aerosol formation, and if an eruption column reaches the stratosphere, it causes global dimming and a lowering of the Earth’s surface temperatures that may last for years. Similarly, halogens can dramatically affect proximal ecosystems, influence the oxidation capacity of the troposphere, and alter the stratospheric ozone layer. Understanding the physicochemical processes underlying volcanic eruptions has improved tremendously through major advances in computational and analytical capabilities, instrumentation and monitoring networks, thereby improving the ability to reduce volcanic hazards. This session focuses on all aspects of volcanic volatile degassing in the Earth’s system through case studies and theoretical and multidisciplinary approaches. We invite contributions discussing how novel measurement techniques, field measurements, direct and remote ground and space-based observations, and modeling studies of volcanic degassing can provide new insights into volcanic and atmospheric processes at local and global scales. Finally, but significantly, we strongly encourage critical contributions that offer alternative explanations and viewpoints, willingness to consider new ideas supported by evidence, and with the potential to improve the ability to forecast eruptions.
title: Volcanic degassing

description: Spatial soil information is fundamental for environmental modelling and land management. Spatial representation (maps) of soil attributes (both laterally and vertically) and of soil-landscape processes are needed at a scale appropriate for environmental management. The challenge is to develop explicit, quantitative, and spatially realistic models of the soil-landscape continuum. Modern advances in soil sensing, geospatial technologies, and spatial statistics are enabling exciting opportunities to efficiently create more consistent, detailed, and accurate soil maps while providing information about the related uncertainty. The production of high-quality soil maps is a key issue because it enables stakeholders (e.g. farmers, planners, other scientists) to understand the variation of soils at the landscape, field, and sub-field scales. They can be used as input in environmental models, such as hydrological, climate or vegetation productivity (crop models) addressing the uncertainty in the soil layers and its impact in the environmental modelling. When the products of digital soil mapping are integrated within other environmental models it enables assessment and mapping of soil functions to support sustainable management. We welcome presentations that 1) demonstrate the implementation and use of digital soil maps in different disciplines such as agricultural (e.g. crops, food production) and environmental (e.g. element cycles, water, climate) modelling 2) advance the tools of digital soil mapping 3) investigate the philosophy and strategies of digital soil mapping at different scales and for different purposes. We also welcome contributions reporting the state of the art of soil property prediction from hyperspectral satellites, especially focusing on quantitative estimations making use of data-driven approaches such as machine learning, and physically based modelling or the integration of both.
title: Digital Soil Mapping and Assessment using Pedometrics approaches and remote sensing

description: The explosivity of a volcanic eruption reflects the processes which occur as magma ascends from the Earth's interior towards the surface. Investigating the processes and timescales that control the physical, chemical and rheological evolution of magma within volcanic reservoirs and conduits is essential to provide insight into eruptive style, and, consequently, into volcanic hazard assessment and mitigation. Magmatic processes, such as crystallisation, magma mixing and degassing, control magma differentiation and rheology, which in turn influence the remobilisation of crystal mushes, magma storage within the crust, the formation of eruptible magma, ascent dynamics, magma fragmentation and, ultimately, eruptive behaviour. Analysis of the textural, chemical and isotopic characteristics of eruptive products can constrain pre- and syn-eruptive conditions and processes, in order to investigate the dynamics of magma storage, ascent and emplacement. Analytical and field observations, laboratory experiments, and numerical modelling are fundamental tools for investigating pre- and syn-eruptive processes and magma rheology, and for understanding the volcanic system and eruptive dynamics. This information can support petrological monitoring approaches, where geochemical and textural analysis of erupted products can provide real-time data over evolving eruptive episodes and important insight for mitigating the risks associated with volcanic activity. In this session, we welcome petrological, experimental, geophysical and volcanological studies that investigate pre- and syn-eruptive conditions, magma rheology and the dynamics of magmatic processes within magma reservoirs, volcanic conduits and during emplacement through analytical, experimental, and numerical-based approaches. Contributions that investigate the hazards associated with volcanic activity, including petrological monitoring approaches, and interdisciplinary works that consider the close and complex interplay between magmatic processes, conduit dynamics and eruptive behaviour are encouraged.
title: Understanding the physico-chemical processes of magma storage and ascent: Implications for eruptive behaviour and volcanic hazards

description: Wildfires are a global phenomenon with significant environmental, social, and economic impacts. These impacts are expected to intensify due to climate change, land abandonment, inadequate land management and planning factors that further drive land degradation and reduce the provision of ecosystem services. This growing threat calls for urgent scientific attention to better understand the effects of wildfires on ecosystems and to develop integrated tools for land management before and after fires. Such efforts are essential for reducing vulnerability to wildfires and mitigating their impacts. However, this challenge extends beyond the scientific community, requiring the active involvement of stakeholders and policy-makers worldwide, as fundamental resources, such as water, soil, raw materials, and habitats, are at risk. This session invites contributions from researchers studying the effects of wildfires on ecosystems, covering the full spectrum from prevention to post-fire recovery. We welcome laboratory, field, and modelling studies on the following topics: i. Prescribed and/or experimental fires ii. Fire severity and burn severity iii. Fire effects on vegetation, soil, and water iv. Post-fire hydrological and erosive responses v. Post-fire management and mitigation vi. Socio-economic aspects of pre- and post-fire land management vii. Fire risk assessment and modelling
title: Managing wildfires in a changing world

description: Volcanoes are inherently complex and dynamic geological systems capable of generating and distributing vast volumes of sediment to surrounding environments, influencing the evolution of sedimentary systems during their lifetimes and beyond. These processes result in primary volcaniclastic deposits generated directly by volcanic mechanisms, such as pyroclastic density currents and tephra fallout, as well as a wide spectrum of secondary volcaniclastic and volcanic epiclastic deposits produced by the reworking and redeposition of eruption-fed material through lahars, debris avalanches, fluvial activity, and marine sedimentation. These interactions operate across terrestrial and marine environments and over a wide range of spatial and temporal scales, shaping landscapes, sediment routing systems, and basin evolution. The resulting deposits and sedimentary successions preserve valuable records of volcanic activity, environmental change, and landscape response during eruptive and inter-eruptive periods. Understanding the origin, transport and emplacement mechanisms of these diverse deposits is therefore fundamental for accurately reconstructing accumulation histories in modern and ancient volcano-sedimentary systems, and for assessing future hazards and their potential economic and societal impacts. This interdisciplinary session invites contributions addressing all aspects of volcano-sedimentary processes and their geological records, from field-based studies to experimental and numerical modelling approaches.
title: Volcano-sedimentary systems: From volcanic processes to sedimentary records

description: Many political bodies set targets to promote specific land management practices. One of the most ambitious sustainability benchmarks in modern agriculture is the EU's Farm to Fork Strategy, which aims to increase the proportion of organic agricultural land to 25% by 2030. Organic farming and other promoted practices (e.g. agroecology, agroforestry and regenerative farming) aim to make soil and land use more sustainable while still allowing for the production of healthy food at competitive levels. These practices are also frequently associated with climate change mitigation and/or adaptation, as well as the promotion of soil fertility and biodiversity. Crop and soil management practices are key drivers that affect soil and agroecosystem functioning, as well as ecosystem services such as food, fodder and fiber production. However, the long-term effects of specific management practices on soil properties (e.g. soil organic carbon and nutrient stocks, soil as a habitat for biota, or physical soil degradation), or agrobiodiversity-related indicators (e.g. the availability of feed for pollinators and wild flora that is beneficial for crops), are partly unknown and more difficult to assess. This session invites contributions that study the effects of different crop and soil management practices, or land use options, on soil fertility, crop performance, the multifunctionality of agroecosystems, and floral and faunal agrobiodiversity. The session will facilitate interdisciplinary exchange between academia, agricultural practice, nature conservation, and society. We particularly invite contributions focusing on the following: > Organic farming > Conservation agriculture, reduced or no tillage > Regenerative farming > Agroforestry > Crop diversification > Agroecology > Ethnobotany > Biodiversit
title: Organic farming and agroecology: land management for soil fertility, biodiversity and sustainable agri-food systems

description: Climate extremes and unsustainable development are increasingly disrupting soil and water dynamics. Heavy rainfall, prolonged droughts, and human pressures are reshaping water and sediment flows, accelerating land degradation, and threatening food and water security. Addressing these challenges requires continuous monitoring and innovative data integration across various spatial and temporal scales. In this context, sensing technologies offer unprecedented opportunities to monitor the Earth’s surface and understand its processes, especially when they're enhanced by Artificial Intelligence (AI) and advanced computational tools to enhance predictive capability and pattern recognition. These geodata-driven approaches can also support decision-making for diverse stakeholders, for example by helping smallholder farmers manage risk and build resilience. This session invites contributions that push the boundaries of how we observe, measure, and monitor soil and/or soil-water dynamics. We are looking to showcase and discuss research that spans a wide range of scales, from local plots to global systems, and employs a variety of sensing techniques, from proximal sensors (i.e., in-field and machinery sensors) to remote sensing (i.e., UAVs, airborne systems, and satellites). We also welcome studies that explore the fusion of diverse geospatial datasets (e.g., soil sensors, LiDAR, photogrammetry, and satellite imagery) to gain a more holistic, multi-scale understanding of these processes. This also includes research that uses sensed data as input for modelling and/or aim at predict future scenarios under changing conditions. This session is open to, but not limited to, the following topics and application fields (e.g., agriculture, forestry, urban development, and mountain environments): Advanced proximal sensing and ground-based monitoring • Remote sensing, UAV, airborne, and satellite remote sensing of soil and water investigations • Fusion and integration of multi-source geospatial data • AI and machine learning for soil and water analysis • Novel monitoring workflows, protocols, and open-source tools • Linking sensing data with process-based or distributed models • Critical evaluations of opportunities and limitations of emerging technologies • Translating sensing and modeling into decision-support frameworks Interdisciplinary contributions are more then welcome, as well as the participation of early career scientists (ECS).
title: Monitoring Soil and Water in the Era of Global Change

description: This session aims to bring together scientists from a range of disciplines, including geophysics, and igneous and metamorphic petrology, to develop an understanding of the physical processes involved in the emplacement of magma bodies in the crust. The mechanisms by which space is made are very poorly understood, with models ranging from those invoking ductile flow of the country rock (e.g. diapiric emplacement) to those involving brittle behaviour (e.g. stacking of sheets). A critical dimension to the problem concerns the nature of the environment into which the magma is emplaced. This may range from coherent, cool, continental crust to a pre-existing trans-crustal mush column, with thermally matured or evolving crustal conditions. The contrasting host rock rheologies of these two end-members can result in very different emplacement mechanisms, showing that understanding magma emplacement requires not only examining the intrusions themselves, but also their mechanical, in addition to thermal and chemical, interactions with the surrounding crust. We welcome contributions from field studies, theoretical/numerical models, phase petrological, microstructural and palaeomagnetic observation, and experimental research, that capture essential features of the deformational, chemical and thermal evolution as magmas are emplaced.
title: The physics of magma intrusion: testing the paradigms

description: The agri-environmental sciences offer endless possibilities for the application of Interpretable Machine Learning methods.These methods can aid in evaluating mechanistic assumptions or in revealing unforeseen connections between variables. Covering different spatial and temporal scales and linking between them, scientists have proposed and used a wide variety of IML models, each with their unique demands regarding data, statistical analysis and interpretation of results. To gain an appreciation of this range, this session invites contributions involving interpretable Machine Learning and xAI applications in the agri-environmental and forestry sciences. The applied models may cover different a-priori assumptions, data requirements, spatial and temporal scales, and methods of statistical analysis. The rationale of their choice should be communicated clearly to give (early career) scientists methodological inspiration for their own pursuits.
title: Interpretable Machine Learning for Agri-Environmental Systems: Models and Insights

description: There is a demand to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and increase soil organic carbon in the agricultural sector to mitigate climate change. Further, there is an interest in improving soil health to improve productivity and resilience of crop- and grasslands. Different EU initiative/programs (e.g. GreenDeal; EU Soil strategy for 2030, 4 per mille, Soil Mission) underpin the relevance and political interest in these topics. Therefore, applicable solutions for agriculture are required to achieve one or some of these targets. Due to the complexity and heterogeneity of the processes generic solution can have locally diverse impacts and optimum solution might differ based on local conditions. Clear advice for farmers requires an excellent data basis for impacts of management practices under diverse conditions and low uncertainty. Therefore, a better understanding about the impacts of smart agricultural solution in the field is required to improve the understanding of the variety of options. The objective of the session is to provide an overview about available options to improve agriculture to mitigate climate change by reducing emissions or increasing soil organic carbon. Beside climate change mitigation, farmers have a major interest in improving soil health to increase the resilience of the system, improve the quality of the products or increase yield. Therefore, we invite applications for studies, which analyse management practice changes for climate change mitigation options, including their impacts to the wider agricultural system. This includes studies using field or laboratory measurements, or modelling, in croplands or grasslands, in organic or conventional systems. Studies that include multiple aspects of the agricultural system are of most interest, although studies that focus on one of these aspects are also welcome.
title: Climate smart agriculture to reduce emissions and improve soil organic carbon

description: Agricultural systems are increasingly challenged to maintain soil health and ecosystem functioning while reducing external inputs, nutrient losses and environmental impacts. Integrated crop–livestock systems offer opportunities to reconnect nutrient and carbon flows between crops, plants, animals and soils, with livestock manures and other organic resources playing a central role in closing biogeochemical cycles. However, these systems also involve complex interactions and trade-offs affecting soil processes, nutrient availability, carbon dynamics, greenhouse gas emissions, biodiversity and the resilience of agroecosystems under global change. This session invites contributions exploring the interactions between soils, plants and livestock across integrated and circular agroecosystems. We welcome studies addressing soil physical, chemical and biological processes; carbon and nutrient cycling; soil organic matter and soil health; manure and organic amendment dynamics; greenhouse gas emissions; microbial and soil biodiversity; and the effects of management on ecosystem functions and resilience. We particularly encourage contributions that investigate how plant–livestock integration and circular management can support agroecological transitions, including approaches that reconnect livestock-derived nutrients with plant production and soil functioning across croplands, grasslands, pastures and mixed farming systems. Experimental, modelling and long-term observational studies are welcome, as well as research examining trade-offs, synergies and system-level outcomes under changing climate and management conditions.
title: Soil–plant-livestock interactions in circular agroecosystems: processes, functions and resilience under global change

description: Agroforestry systems (AFS) – land-use systems in which woody perennials are deliberately integrated with crops and/or livestock on the same land-management unit, following a specific spatial arrangement or temporal sequence – are increasingly promoted as a Nature-Based Solution for resilient and climate-adapted agricultural systems. Through the synergistic interaction of trees and herbaceous components, AFS deliver a wide range of ecosystem services (ES), including provisioning, regulating, supporting, and cultural services. The latter are closely linked to traditional agricultural landscapes, some recognized as FAO GIAHS (Globally Important Agricultural Heritage Systems). Despite their well-documented benefits, the adoption and conservation of AFS remain challenged by rapid global change, including climate change, rural depopulation, agricultural intensification, and the erosion of traditional knowledge. AFS are complex systems that are challenging to study and implement. Only a few models simulate their biophysical processes, and available approaches are often data-intensive or poorly suited to their intended purpose. Experimental studies are also difficult to generalize, as results often depend on highly site-specific conditions and interactions. This complexity creates ambiguity in the definition of AFS, hindering their recognition in agricultural and environmental legislation. In this context, the session aims to bring together researchers and practitioners to advance hybrid knowledge on AFS worldwide and support their practical implementation. We welcome contributions that: - Assess ES of AFS across different scales; - Evaluate the vulnerability of AFS under current and future scenarios, and their potential to contribute to climate change mitigation and adaptation; - Design innovative practices to improve the efficiency, productivity and sustainability of AFS; - Investigate processes linked to the inclusion of trees in croplands and/or pastures through experimental or modelling approaches; - Discuss barriers – technical, economic, governance-related – that hamper the successful implementation of AFS; - Showcase transdisciplinary approaches involving stakeholder engagement and co-creation in AFS; - Highlight understudied traditional AFS and the value of traditional ecological knowledge. The session is organized within the Shared Innovations for Mediterranean Agroforestry Systems (SHARE) project, part of the PRIMA Programme supported by the EU.
title: Ecosystem services in agroforestry: challenges and opportunities in a changing world

description: Soil management practices strive to balance outcomes across soils, climates, landscapes, or management histories. A management practice can enhance soil health, carbon storage, nutrient retention, or crop productivity in one context, but generate limited, neutral, or even undesirable soil changes in another. Understanding these context dependencies is therefore essential for determining when, where, and why management practices succeed.
