This session focuses on the mechanisms, interactions, and boundary conditions that determine desirable soil management outcomes across spatial and temporal scales. We particularly welcome studies examining interactions among beneficial management practices, including cover crops, crop rotations, reduced tillage, residue management, and organic amendments, and their interactions with soil properties, landscape position, weather and climate extremes, and management legacies. We especially encourage multi-factor and mechanistic research addressing synergies and trade-offs among soil carbon and nitrogen dynamics, water availability and retention, soil health, greenhouse gas emissions, crop productivity, and ecosystem services. By bringing together researchers across diverse fields including soil science, biogeochemistry, agronomy, ecology, and environmental sciences, this session aims to identify the drivers of when and where soil management delivers benefits and to support evidence-based, site-tailored strategies for sustainable agriculture.
title: From Outcomes to Practices: When, Where, and Why Soil Management Works

description: Agriculture is pivotal in the European economy and the global food supply. Europe is a significant producer of diverse crops, contributing significantly to feeding the world's population. The quality and characteristics of agricultural products are closely linked to the specific environmental conditions in which they are grown. These environmental factors, including climate, soil, and water, can vary significantly across regions and are increasingly influenced by the challenges of climate change. Understanding the spatial and temporal variability of environmental factors is crucial for managing and preserving agricultural landscapes and adapting to climate change's current and future impacts. This requires a deep understanding of plants’ mechanisms for acclimation, keeping in mind that functional traits (e.g., phenology,etc.) can be indicators and proxies of plant status, plasticity and resilience. Moreover, it involves applied research and technological innovation in agriculture, including the use of sensors to monitor environmental variables, remote sensing and drones for crop monitoring, predictive models for yield and disease, and advanced methods to study nutrient cycles and soil health. Furthermore, growing public awareness of the importance of ecosystem health and sustainability has led to adopting quantitative approaches to understand the link between agricultural practices and ecosystem services, which are crucial for achieving long-term environmental goals. Agroecological approaches, such as cover cropping, organic amendments, and integrated pest management, are being increasingly adopted to enhance biodiversity, soil health, water and nutrient retention, and resilience to climate change. On these bases, the session will delve into: - Quantifying and Spatially Modeling Environmental Factors: Examining the complex interplay of climate, soil, and water and their influence on plant growth, yield, and quality. - Agricultural Resilience to Climate Change: Exploring the adaptability of agricultural systems in the face of a changing climate and identifying strategies for adaptation and mitigation. - Sustainable Agricultural Practices and Ecosystem Services: Analyzing the impact of diverse agricultural practices on soil and water quality, biodiversity, and related ecosystem services. - Precision Agriculture and Technological Innovation: Utilizing advanced technologies to optimize resource use, improve crop management, and enhance sustainability.
title: Adaptation and resilience in agriculture: addressing climate change with science and technology

description: Machine learning (ML) is increasingly used in soil science to predict soil properties, biogeochemical processes, water and solute transport, greenhouse gas emissions, and environmental risks across spatial and temporal scales. However, high predictive accuracy does not necessarily guarantee reliable scientific inference or robust extrapolation. Data leakage, inappropriate data splitting, limited representativeness of training data, poor uncertainty characterization, and a lack of process consistency can substantially undermine model reliability when ML is transferred across soils, sites, regions, or environmental conditions. This session focuses on the development and application of trustworthy and process-informed machine learning for soil science. We aim to bring together researchers working at the interface of soil science, environmental modeling, hydrology, biogeochemistry, and artificial intelligence to discuss how domain knowledge and physical, chemical, and biological processes can be integrated with data-driven approaches. We particularly welcome contributions addressing: (1) rigorous model evaluation and data-splitting strategies that match intended extrapolation targets; (2) data leakage, distribution shifts, domain adaptation, and cross-site or cross-region generalization; (3) uncertainty quantification, interpretability, explainability, and causal inference; (4) hybrid and process-informed ML integrating mechanistic models, physical constraints, or scientific knowledge; (5) physics-informed and theory-guided learning for soil processes; (6) multi-scale learning from laboratory experiments to field, regional, and global applications; and (7) reproducible benchmarks, open datasets, and emerging foundation-model approaches for soil and environmental sciences. The session seeks to move soil ML beyond purely accuracy-driven prediction toward models that are scientifically consistent, interpretable, transferable, and trustworthy. We especially encourage studies that critically examine when and why machine-learning models succeed or fail, and how combining mechanistic understanding with modern AI can improve both prediction and scientific discovery in soil systems.
title: Trustworthy and process-informed machine learning for soil science

description: Observations are the cornerstone of understanding hydrological processes, providing data for model development and validation. However, integrating monitoring strategies and measurement tools with data analysis and modelling remains a major challenge in vadose zone hydrology. This session brings together experimentalists, modelers, and data scientists working on innovative approaches for observing and simulating vadose zone processes, with emphasis on observation–model links across scales, from laboratory and plot experiments to field, catchment, regional, and continental applications. Advances in remote sensing, high-performance computing, artificial intelligence, digital twins, and the Internet of Things offer new opportunities to address these challenges. Integrating observations and models can improve quantification of water and solute fluxes, characterization of soil hydraulic properties, process identification, and assessment of responses to environmental change, including droughts, heatwaves, land-use change, soil degradation, salinization, erosion, contamination, and agricultural and water-management practices, while reducing predictive uncertainty. We welcome contributions addressing: • Innovative observations and monitoring technologies: laboratory and field methods, sensor networks, remote and proximal sensing, geophysics, environmental tracers, and measurements of soil water, energy, solute fluxes, and soil physical, hydraulic, and biogeochemical properties. • Multi-scale data integration and analytics: data fusion and assimilation, uncertainty analysis, artificial intelligence and machine learning, and analysis of large, heterogeneous, high-frequency datasets. • Vadose zone modelling: process-based, data-driven, and hybrid approaches; parameterization and validation; inverse modelling; model–data integration; upscaling and downscaling; uncertainty quantification. • Applications under environmental change: vadose zone responses to droughts, heatwaves, climate variability and change, land-use change, irrigation and agricultural management, soil degradation, salinization, erosion, contamination, and other natural or anthropogenic disturbances. • Emerging challenges and research frontiers: digital twins, interoperable monitoring infrastructures, high-performance computing, cross-scale and cross-environment transferability, and new strategies for linking observations with predictive models.
title: Measuring and modeling vadose zone processes across spatial and temporal scales: challenges and perspectives

description: Recent advances in sensing, machine learning and process modeling have expanded on what is possible within Pedometrics, a branch of research at the interface of soil science and data science. However, many methodological challenges remain. This session focuses on methodological advances that improve the reliability, reproducibility and pedological soundness of digital soil mapping, spectroscopy and spectral transfer functions, pedo-transfer functions or other predictive statistical applications in soil science. We specifically invite contributions that address the underlying statistical, computational and conceptual tools needed to 1) produce pedologically consistent multi-property, multi-depth, multi-timepoint soil maps, 2) create suitable sampling designs for current state-of-the-art mapping approaches, 3) provide physically or chemically meaningful pedo-transfer functions, 4) quantify and propagate uncertainty in space–time and for multivariate outcomes, 5) provide methods for up- and downscaling (change-of-support) and realistic aggregation of uncertainties, 6) contribute to explainable machine learning and robust soil science-informed model diagnostics, and 7) integrate mechanistic soil process knowledge with data-driven algorithms into so-called hybrid approaches or soil science informed machine learning. The session welcomes contributions that develop, compare, or benchmark novel approaches or present (open) software implementations that strengthen the foundations of pedometrics and enable robust and reproducible frameworks. We welcome developments towards all kinds of applications such as global to local soil health monitoring, soil function assessments or for farm level and forest management. The session aims to bring together statisticians, process modelers, computer scientists and pedologists to discuss methodological solutions that are general, reproducible and transferable across regions and applications.
title: Innovations in Pedometrics: Solving challenges towards reliable spatio-temporal soil mapping, spectro- and pedo-transfer functions

description: Seismic and infrasound observations are essential for monitoring and understanding volcanic systems, providing complementary constraints on subsurface dynamics, eruptive processes, and atmospheric interactions. However, the interpretation of these data is challenging: volcanic heterogeneity, steep topography, and atmospheric variability significantly distort both seismic and acoustic signals, while diverse source mechanisms—from magma migration to explosive eruptions to surface flow activity —produce a wide range of waveforms that remain difficult to understand comprehensively. Numerical and physics-based modelling provides a crucial framework for disentangling these effects and linking observations to underlying volcanic processes. These complexities demand high-resolution imaging, advanced source inversion strategies, and integrated analyses that leverage both seismic and acoustic datasets. This session invites contributions from researchers in volcano seismology, infrasound, and related fields, focusing on (i) seismicity and infrasound catalogues and their spatio-temporal evolution, (ii) wave propagation, scattering, and atmospheric effects, (iii) high-resolution imaging of volcanic structures, (iv) joint seismic–acoustic source inversions, and (v) time-lapse monitoring and forecasting. We particularly welcome approaches that extract robust information from sparse or incomplete datasets, as is often the case for remote or poorly instrumented volcanoes. Studies on geothermal analogues, novel instrumentation, and emerging analysis methodologies (e.g., machine learning) are also welcome. By fostering cross-disciplinary dialogue between seismologists, acoustic specialists, and numerical modellers, this session aims to highlight recent advances and key challenges in characterizing volcanic processes and improving hazard assessment
title: Volcano Seismology and Acoustics

description: Population growth and expanding infrastructure mean the impacts of volcanic eruptions are expected to increase. Ongoing unrest or eruptive activity at Etna, Campi Flegrei, on Iceland’s Reykjanes Peninsula, and Tenerife, highlight the potential threats of eruptions in Europe and the need to strengthen volcanic risk reduction efforts on local to regional scales. Effective volcanic risk reduction requires robust risk assessment that integrates the multiple volcanic hazards, as well as the exposure and vulnerability of people and assets. This session invites contributions that advance volcanic hazard/risk assessment and risk reduction, including eruption forecasting, probabilistic hazard assessment, multiple-hazard management, assessment of exposure and vulnerability, impact and loss modelling, volcanic damage and impact assessments, multi-hazard and cascading risk, dynamic and probabilistic risk assessment, and approaches for evaluating resilience. We particularly welcome submissions that address emerging challenges, exploring the multi-hazard nature of volcanic environments and its increasing interactions with the climate and other hazards, as well as quantifying the dynamic nature of exposure and vulnerability during crises, especially in spatially limited environments like volcanic islands. We welcome stakeholder engagement and community-based risk reduction approaches, including successful examples of communication and coordination among stakeholders and with at-risk communities, as well as approaches that strengthen resilience. Contributions exploring volcanic hazard and risk management and the translation of scientific understanding into actionable insights for preparedness, mitigation, response, and risk reduction are encouraged. This session is co-sponsored by the IAVCEI Commission on Volcanic Hazard and Risk (CVHR).
title: Volcanic risk assessment and reduction: advances in quantifying volcanic hazard, vulnerability, impacts, and resilience

description: Since the early days of soil science, protocols for fractioning of soil organic matter exist to better understand and describe the composition or turnover in soils. This remains a hotly debated topic, largely due to the persistent challenge of achieving meaningful measurements of soil carbon quality to better capture the persistence and vulnerability of carbon in soils. Unlike other soil parameters that are comparatively more straightforward to measure, the mechanisms conferring the persistence of soil organic matter in soils are far harder to isolate and quantify, and no single method will and can capture all of them simultaneously. Chemistry, density, size, thermal stability and many more intrinsic properties are used to separate soil carbon in operationally defined pools to be able to understand its (potential) persistence or functioning. For instance, by size and mechanical stability fractionation, aggregates and very stable pseudosands can be obtained for further analysis of physically protected organic matter. Moreover, a plethora of chemical and physical fractionation schemes exist to extract microbial or fungal parts to estimate their biomass, or density fractionation is applied to soils to separate particulate and mineral-associated organic matter. Despite a methodological diversity, a persistent difficulty lies in reconciling operationally defined fractions shaped by the extraction method itself with functionally meaningful, biologically or biogeochemically relevant pools in soil. This session invites contributions focussing on methods to fractionate soil carbon in functional pools, from highly sophisticated, to novel or classical methods . We particularly welcome efforts to link laboratory-based fractions to computational modelling frameworks. Contributions that go beyond successful stories are especially encouraged: we invite submissions that reflect on fractioning not yielding the expected trends, and the exploration of the reasons behind this lacking link.
title: The good, the bad and the labile: How (not) to fractionate the soil carbon pool

description: Effective management of soil and water resources is fundamental to sustainable development, ecosystem resilience, and human well-being. Connectivity provides a powerful framework for understanding the transfer of water, sediment, nutrients, and associated materials across heterogeneous landscapes and their responses to climate variability, extreme events, land-use change, and human interventions. In particular, hydrological and sediment connectivity link landscape structure with hydro-geomorphic processes and provide an important basis for understanding watershed responses to environmental change. Recent advances in field monitoring, remote sensing, geomorphometric analysis, process-based modelling, and data-driven approaches have improved our ability to quantify connectivity across spatial and temporal scales. However, challenges remain in translating connectivity assessment into process understanding, predictive capability, and effective management. Key questions include where and when critical source–pathway–sink linkages emerge, how connectivity changes under natural and anthropogenic disturbances, and how interventions can enhance desirable connectivity or promote strategic disconnectivity. This session invites studies developing and applying connectivity-based approaches for sustainable watershed management. We welcome contributions addressing hydrological, sediment, geomorphic, and related ecological connectivity using field observations, experiments, remote sensing, geomorphometric indices, process-based models, and data-driven or machine-learning approaches. Studies focusing on temporal dynamics, cross-scale interactions, extreme events, land-use and climate change, and structural–functional connectivity are particularly encouraged. The session also promotes the application of connectivity concepts to nature-based solutions and watershed restoration, including vegetation restoration, riparian management, and soil and water conservation measures. By bridging process understanding, monitoring, prediction, and management, we aim to clarify where, when, and how connectivity can be managed to reduce soil erosion and sediment-related risks, enhance watershed resilience, and support sustainable soil and water resource management.
title: Advancing connectivity-based approaches for sustainable watershed management: processes, prediction, and nature-based solutions

description: Earth Observation provides essential insights into volcanic processes, supporting the detection and interpretation of unrest, the monitoring of eruptive activity, and volcanic hazard assessment. Integrating these observations with ground-based measurements and advanced computational methods offers new opportunities to improve our understanding of volcanic systems and strengthen forecasting capabilities. This session brings together contributions at the interface of Earth Observation (EO), volcanology, and computational innovation. We welcome studies using radar, optical, thermal, and multispectral or hyperspectral observations, particularly those integrating complementary datasets to investigate surface deformation, thermal anomalies, gas emissions, and volcanic deposits. Contributions may address the full range from methodological developments to operational monitoring and forecasting applications. A central focus is the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) in extracting information from complex datasets, identifying patterns and anomalies, and supporting predictive modeling. We encourage approaches that combine data-driven methods with physical understanding, including physics-informed learning, data assimilation, and statistical and probabilistic frameworks, with attention to uncertainty, interpretability, and robustness. The session also welcomes emerging quantum and quantum-inspired approaches, including Quantum-AI and Quantum-ML, that seek to complement established methods in EO and volcanology. Topics of interest include hybrid classical–quantum workflows and the exploration of computational challenges associated with high-dimensional data, nonlinear processes, and complex optimization problems.
title: Advancing Volcano Monitoring and Forecasting: Earth Observation and Innovative Computational Approaches

description: Volcanic eruptions are spectacular manifestations of natural forces that dynamically shape our planet. Their impacts spread from the geosphere to the hydrosphere and the atmosphere with the potential to have severe consequences at global scale. Within the volcanological community, forecasting volcanic eruptions remains a primary goal in volcanic hazards and risk mitigation. Over the past decades, the quantity and resolution of observations and the quality of monitoring resources have steadily increased, providing a wealth of data on the underlying physical processes that drive volcanic eruptions. Novel technological advancements have significantly broadened both the spatial coverage and frequency bandwidth of geochemical and geophysical observations at active volcanoes. By integrating multi-parametric data from both ground and space, scientists now gain an unprecedented vision of the surface manifestations of mass transport beneath volcanoes as well as the internal structure from static and functional imaging techniques. This enables the detection and tracking of subtle signals of volcanic unrest prior to eruption, even at remote or inaccessible volcanoes. These advancements have been accompanied by new models and processing techniques including with artificial intelligence and machine learning, leading to innovative paradigms for the interpretation and inversion of observational data (geophysical, geochemical, geological). Within this context, this session aims to convene a multidisciplinary audience for discussing the most recent innovations in monitoring tools and to present observations, methods, and models that enhance our understanding of volcanic processes fostering our capabilities in volcanic early warnings and risk reduction.
title: Monitoring active volcanoes

description: The implementation of the Soil Monitoring Law (SML) requires harmonized and operational monitoring systems capable of assessing soil condition, identifying degradation processes, and supporting sustainable soil management across Europe. Building on existing national and regional monitoring programmes, this session aims to showcase practical approaches, tools, and experiences that facilitate the transition from soil monitoring to evidence-based decision making. We invite contributions addressing the development and application of soil health indicators, monitoring networks, assessment frameworks, and innovative technologies, including remote and proximal sensing, digital soil mapping, modelling approaches, and sensor-based monitoring. Particular attention will be given to methods for harmonizing and integrating datasets, establishing common assessment criteria, and supporting reporting and policy implementation across multiple governance levels. The session will also highlight how monitoring information can support sustainable land management, soil restoration, climate and biodiversity policies, and stakeholder engagement, fostering the effective implementation of the Soil Monitoring Law and the protection of soil resources across Europe.
title: Implementing the soil monitoring: indicators, monitoring networks and practical applications

description: Over the past decade, soil organic carbon has gained unprecedented prominence in international and European policy, from the launch of the “4 per 1000” Initiative to the EU Carbon Removals and Carbon Farming Certification Framework, Soil Monitoring and Resilience Directive and Mission “A Soil Deal for Europe”. This session will address three complementary questions. First, what has actually changed? Contributions are invited to assess the effects of these initiatives on research agendas, stakeholder involvement, monitoring systems and land-management practices. Second, what knowledge is now needed for credible public action? Contributions could examine how scientific knowledge on soil carbon can inform policy design, target-setting, implementation and evaluation, while considering trade-offs with other soil-health objectives. Third, how can this knowledge become effectively usable? The session will welcome analyses of how evidence has been mobilized in the design and implementation of soil and climate policies, which institutional and collective arrangements have facilitated—or hindered—its use, and what lessons have been learnt.
title: From soil carbon ambitions to credible public action: what has changed, and what knowledge is now needed?

description: Volcanic eruptions can perturb the atmosphere and climate across a wide range of spatial and temporal scales. The stratospheric injection of sulfur dioxide and the subsequent formation and transport of sulfate aerosols can affect the Earth’s radiative balance, atmospheric circulation, and the coupled atmosphere-ocean system. This constitutes a complex scenario that continues to present important open questions, calling for advanced modeling, computational, and observational approaches. This session focuses on strategies that combine physical and data-driven modeling, multi-source data, and real-time monitoring to enhance our ability to detect, quantify, model and predict the climate impacts of volcanic activity. We therefore welcome contributions addressing volcano-climate interactions from a broad range of perspectives, including physical modeling, satellite observations, in situ measurements, and paleo records. Particular emphasis is placed on approaches aimed at quantifying short- and long-term effects, identifying eruption-induced anomalies and patterns, and exploiting advanced technologies, including machine learning and emerging computational methods. Case studies of recent or historical major eruptions are also encouraged.
title: Volcano-climate interactions: Observations, Modeling, and Impacts

description: Hydrothermal alteration influences physical and chemical properties of volcanic rocks, fluid migration, and evolution of volcanic and magmatic-hydrothermal systems. The circulation of hot magmatic fluids dissolves primary minerals, reorganises soluble elements, and precipitates secondary alteration assemblages. Such alteration processes record important information for understanding ancient and modern systems, and change physical and mechanical rock properties in ways that influence magma and fluid migration pathways, eruption styles (e.g., phreatic eruptions), flank stability, and resources. Despite its importance, alteration can often be treated simplistically due to paucity in quantitative understanding of its spatio-temporal distribution. Recent advances have enabled characterisation of alteration minerals and processes across space and time, integrating remote sensing and geophysical methods, mineralogical and geochemical constraints; mechanical property measurements; and data-driven models that couple fluid flow, reaction, and deformation. This session thus invites contributions from remote sensing, geochemistry, mineralogy, geophysics, rock physics, and modelling that advance our understanding of alteration in magmatic-hydrothermal systems, and the implications of this alteration for volcanic hazards. We encourage diverse contributions, especially those integrating multiple disciplines: ground, satellite, drone and airborne remote sensing (multi and hyperspectral, thermal, SAR, LiDAR), time-series monitoring, structural studies, fluid-rock interaction processes, mineralogical evolution, experimental simulations, geochemical modelling, geophysical mapping (ERT, MT and others), rock physics and mechanics, field to laboratory studies, scaling from sample to edifice, phreatic/phreatomagmatic explosions, fluid migration, flank instability and collapse, and computational modelling. Through this session we aim to establish a shared framework linking alteration across disciplines and outcomes in different volcanic settings, and to promote the gradual standardisation of approaches and understanding of hydrothermal alterations, its impact on volcanic systems, and distribution across time and space. We also foster collaborations to improve our ability to identify and evaluate critical developments driven by hydrothermal processes that may lead to instability, flank failure or triggered explosions.
title: Hydrothermal alteration in volcanic settings: An interdisciplinary approach

description: Monitoring volcanic processes for early detection and/or timely identification of hazardous phenomena relies on the integration of field observations, remote sensing data and numerical models. This session is dedicated to exploring open questions in the understanding, modelling, and forecasting of volcanic processes and associated hazards. We welcome inter-, cross-, and multi-disciplinary research spanning field observations, satellite remote sensing, physico-mathematical formulations, probabilistic forecasting, data assimilation and fusion, and the development and application of advanced numerical methods. Particular emphasis is placed on approaches that link traditional volcano monitoring with advances in computational science, statistical analysis, Machine Learning (ML), and Artificial Intelligence (AI). The session aims to promote scientific exchange on the challenges and opportunities associated with the comprehension of complex volcanic systems and translating multidisciplinary observations into improved modelling and hazard assessment. Contributions are encouraged, but not limited, to address the following objectives: (i) advancing the understanding of volcanic processes and their spatio-temporal dynamics; (ii) developing innovative approaches for the monitoring, modelling, and forecasting of volcanic phenomena; (iii) assessing model performance and robustness through validation against real-world case studies, analytical solutions, and laboratory experiments; (iv) quantifying uncertainty propagation in forward modelling, including sensitivity analysis, and inverse modelling, including optimization and calibration; (v) exploring the potential of AI- and ML-based methods for integrating and processing heterogeneous, multidisciplinary datasets to enhance volcanic hazard assessment, risk reduction, mitigation strategies, and decision-support applications. Finally, the session seeks to bring the community together to incentive scientific debate and inspire future directions on volcanic risk mitigation, infrastructural resilience, and societal impacts in active volcanic regions.
title: Advances in Understanding, Monitoring and Forecasting Volcanic Processes and Hazards

description: Geoscientific studies are essential for the imaging of buried archaeological sites and for identifying internal structure and condition of historic buildings. They provide important information on the properties, weathering, and degradation of building materials (natural stone, bricks, mortars, ceramics, concrete), as well as on moisture and fluid transport. Geoscientific methods can also be used to evaluate the dynamic properties and structural response of historic structures and to reconstruct their deterioration and damage history, including the identification and interpretation of earthquake-related damage. Such approaches contribute to understanding the long-term evolution of archaeological and built heritage and support the planning and evaluation of conservation and restoration measures. This session welcomes contributions showcasing the application of geosciences to the following topics: (i) properties, provenance, production, use, and durability of historical materials; (ii) weathering processes, micro-fracturing, structural decay, and reconstruction of deterioration and damage processes ; (iii) fluid transport, propagation of evaporation fronts, and salt crystallization mechanics in porous media; (iv) high-resolution, non-destructive testing and monitoring including the assessment of dynamic properties and structural response; (v) imaging and identification of buried archaeological sites; (vi) impact of environmental variables, microclimatic fluctuations, and climate change on porous geomaterials outdoors, indoors, underground, or underwater; (vii) identification and reconstruction of earthquake-induced damage and its integration with archaeoseismological investigations; (viii) integration of theoretical geomorphological concepts into practical strategies, adaptation measures, and materials for conservation and restoration; (ix) hardware/software design for collecting and processing compositional, structural, dynamic, and environmental databases.
title: Cultural heritage – a geoscientific perspective

description: Despite unprecedented scientific understanding of the environmental system, translating environmental science knowledge into sustained societal action remains a major challenge. More than a decade after Stoknes (2014) described this as a psychological paradox, ecological crises are intensifying while environmental protection continues to compete with other societal priorities. Science communication research has shown that communicating more scientific facts, more clearly or more frequently, is not sufficient on its own. Environmental science communication is consequently undergoing experimentation and transformation. Alongside established approaches, researchers are exploring storytelling, emotions, humor, aesthetics, identities, popular culture, participatory practices and novel visual formats. Digital platforms have accelerated these developments, creating spaces where scientific knowledge intersects with internet culture, entertainment, influencer practices and vernacular communication. Innovative approaches are also emerging beyond social media, including through museums, art-science initiatives, journalism and innovative institutional communication. These developments raise questions about how environmental science communication is changing. How are communicators adapting to changing media environments and audiences? Which actors and practices are driving innovation? How are emotions, identities, aesthetics, humour and storytelling incorporated into environmental communication, and how do these approaches interact with traditional information-centred models? How are scientific institutions and researchers responding? This session invites contributions studying and engaging with emerging forms of environmental science communication. We particularly welcome interdisciplinary research connecting environmental science with communication studies, social sciences, humanities, arts and design. Topics may include: • novel approaches to communicating environmental science; • emotions, identities, aesthetics, storytelling and humor; • visual, creative and artistic approaches; • social media, short-form video and influencers; • popular culture, memes and entertainment; • participatory approaches; • communication targeting younger audiences; • institutional responses to changing communication environments; • critical perspectives on the ethics and power relations of environmental communication;
title: Innovation and creativity in environmental science communication

description: Climate projections, reanalyses and Earth observation products are increasingly available, but their spatial resolution, biases, uncertainties and limited connection to sector-specific needs often constrain their direct use in societal risk and impact assessments. At the same time, advances in artificial intelligence, statistical modelling and data integration offer new opportunities to translate climate information into actionable indicators of hazards, exposure, vulnerability and risk. This session invites inter- and transdisciplinary contributions that connect high-resolution climate information with impacts on human health, agriculture and food systems, water resources and vulnerable populations. Relevant topics include statistical and machine-learning downscaling; integration of climate, environmental, health and socioeconomic data; satellite-derived exposure indicators; climate-sensitive health outcomes; crop and hydrological impact modelling; extreme, compound and cascading risks; vulnerability mapping; uncertainty propagation; early-warning systems; and the co-development of climate services and adaptation strategies. We particularly welcome studies that evaluate whether climate information is fit for its intended societal application, connect methods and evidence across disciplines, compare alternative modelling or data-integration approaches, and address challenges faced by data-scarce and highly vulnerable regions. Contributions that address the needs of, collaborate with, or generate relevant information for public-health agencies, agricultural and water-management organizations, education systems, humanitarian actors, local communities and policy stakeholders are especially encouraged.
title: High-Resolution Climate Information for Societal Risk Assessment: Health, Food Systems, Water Resources, and Community Vulnerability

description: The Water–Food–Land nexus represents a complex and interconnected system in which changes in water availability, agricultural production, land use, and ecosystem dynamics influence one another across spatial and temporal scales. Addressing these interconnected challenges requires integrated approaches that can capture both local variations and broader regional and global patterns. This session explores the emerging role of GeoAI (Geospatial Artificial Intelligence) and multi-scale Earth Observation (EO) in understanding, monitoring, and managing the Water–Food–Land nexus. Advances in satellite remote sensing, cloud computing, geospatial analytics, machine learning, and AI are enabling the integration of diverse Earth observation datasets to generate timely and actionable information. The session will highlight innovative approaches for monitoring water resources, crop and vegetation dynamics, land-use and land-cover change, drought and environmental stress, and the interactions among these systems. Particular emphasis will be placed on multi-scale analysis, data fusion, AI-driven modelling, and decision-support frameworks that can bridge field-level observations with landscape, regional, and global assessments. By bringing together researchers, practitioners, and policymakers, the session aims to showcase how GeoAI and Earth Observation can support sustainable resource management, climate resilience, food and water security, and evidence-based planning within the interconnected Water–Food–Land nexus.
title: GeoAI and Multi-scale Earth Observation for the Water–Food–Land Nexus

description: Moving to a low carbon economy to fight climate change will require the constructions and operations of multiples large renewable energy and critical mineral mining projects, which often include extensive supportive infrastructures across large geographic areas. As such, these projects will have long-lasting and far-reaching impacts on the host ecosystems, the watersheds and the communities. Across the world, these projects are more likely to be developed in rural and remote areas where biophysical systems have had limited anthropogenic impacts. These new projects will bring a suite of impacts to theses socio-ecological systems that can be hard to quantify and, therefore, mitigate. To support a green, just and equitable transition, natural and social scientists across a broad range of disciplines must come together to develop innovative cumulative assessments methods, frameworks, and indicators. This is imperative to support science-based impact assessments and policies across the globe. In this session, we invite participant to submit their work related to natural project development, impact assessments, and large-scale modelling of cumulative impacts. We especially are interested in bringing together participants from different areas of the world to showcase their research in their particular context.
title: Cumulative impacts at large scales: modelling for a green, just and equitable transition

description: Metal sulphides (such as pyrite FeS2, chalcopyrite CuFeS2, or galena PbS) play a central role in the global sulphur and iron cycles and link the geosphere, biosphere, and hydrosphere. They serve both as sinks for sulphur and metals under oxygen-free conditions and as significant sources of acid and dissolved metals when exposed to oxygen. They regulate the Earth's long-term oxygen concentration, bind toxic heavy metals, and play a key role in bio-geo-chemical processes. This session encourages contributions from scientists investigating metal sulphides across a range of physico-bio-geo-chemical conditions in various earth science disciplines, including but not limited to paleoenvironmental reconstructions, nuclear waste storage, ore deposit formation or acid mine drainage. Our aim is to foster intradisciplinary knowledge transfer between different research areas and approaches, including geochemical field studies, in-situ and laboratory investigations of rocks and formations as well as numerical simulation studies within the given context. Along with this multidisciplinary poster session, the GeoPanel (GP) "Metal sulphides: Key to Earth and Engines of Human History" is organized which will focus on some general aspects. The scientific in-depth discussion of metal sulphides is planned here.
title: Sulphides: Key to Earth and Engines of Human History

description: The growing global demand for Critical Raw Materials (CRMs) is expected to further intensify extractive activities. Securing a resilient and reliable supply of CRMs will require the identification and development of new and alternative resources, including their recovery as by-products of conventional mining operations and from the reprocessing of extractive waste (EW). In this context, the development of more efficient, cleaner, and innovative approaches for the extraction and recovery of CRMs from both primary and secondary resources will be crucial. CRMs production, from exploration and extraction to processing and waste management, can generate significant environmental pressures, including landscape alteration, land-use degradation, and soil and water contamination. These environmental pressures are closely interconnected with social and economic challenges, but also create new opportunities throughout the supply chain, particularly in relation to the valorization and management of EW facilities. A sustainable CRMs supply therefore requires a responsible and integrated approach. This session welcomes contributions addressing, but not limited to, the following topics: • Exploration and extraction of CRMs from primary mineral resources. • Recovery of CRMs as by-products of conventional mineral exploitation. • Revalorization of EW facilities as secondary sources of CRMs. • Technological innovations for the exploration, extraction, processing, and reprocessing of minerals from primary deposits and EW. • Advances in sampling and characterization methodologies for minerals and EW to improve resource assessment and environmental impact evaluation. • Multiscale exploration of CRMs through innovative sensing technologies, automation, and modelling of primary and secondary resources. • Environmental aspects and challenges associated with CRMs supply chain. • Environmental and geotechnical innovations for addressing the challenges posed by EW facilities. • The role of regulatory frameworks in promoting innovative approaches and supporting responsible production and CRMs recovery. • Contributions of economists, social scientists, legal scholars, psychologists, and policymakers to addressing the social and economic challenges associated with new and reactivated mining activities and to fostering a responsible and socially accepted mining sector. • Applications of artificial intelligence and machine learning throughout the mining life cycle.
title: Critical Raw Materials from Primary and Secondary Resources: Innovative Approaches for a Responsible Supply

description: Machine learning (ML) methods have emerged as powerful tools to tackle various challenges in ocean science, encompassing physical oceanography, biogeochemistry, and sea ice research. This session aims to explore the application of ML methods in ocean science, with a focus on advancing our understanding and addressing key challenges in the field. Our objective is to foster discussions, share recent advancements, and explore future directions in the field of ML methods for ocean science. A wide range of machine learning techniques can be considered including supervised or unsupervised learning, interpretable techniques, and physics-informed and generative models. The applications to be addressed span both observational and modelling approaches. Observational approaches include for example: - Identifying patterns and features in oceanic fields - Filling observational gaps of in-situ or satellite observations - Inferring unobserved variables or unobserved scales - Automating quality control of data Modelling approaches can address (but are not restricted to): - Designing new parameterization schemes in ocean models - Emulating partially or completely ocean models - Parameter tuning and model uncertainty - Agentic AI The session also welcomes submissions at the interface between modelling and observations, such as data assimilation, data-model fusion, or bias correction. Researchers and practitioners working in the domain of ocean science, as well as those interested in the application of ML methods, are encouraged to attend and participate in this session.
title: Machine Learning for Ocean Science

description: Solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) and hyperspectral sensing offer complementary perspectives on vegetation physiology, biochemistry and structure. Connecting these observations with ecosystem processes presents opportunities to improve assessments of photosynthesis, vegetation stress and productivity in terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems for climate change adaptation and mitigation. We welcome contributions on SIF and hyperspectral sensing across leaf, canopy, landscape and global scales. Topics of interest include, but are not limited to. (1) Remote and proximal sensing observations. Advances in satellite SIF and imaging spectroscopy, retrieval algorithms, atmospheric correction, cal&val, cross-sensor harmonization, and integration with ground and airborne data. (2) Radiative transfer modelling. Simulation and interpretation of SIF and reflectance; effects of canopy structure, spectral reabsorption and scattering, and illumination and viewing geometry; and coupling with photosynthesis and land-surface models. (3) Machine learning and model-data fusion. Retrieval of vegetation properties, fusion of SIF and hyperspectral data, integration with ecosystem models, hybrid modelling, uncertainty, and transferability across ecosystems. (4) Vegetation traits and ecosystem processes. Estimation of plant pigments, water content and other functional traits; relationships among SIF, photosynthetic efficiency and gross primary productivity. (5) Natural or managed ecosystem applications. Monitoring crop phenotyping, yield and precision agriculture. Assessment of forest functional diversity, canopy condition, photosynthesis and carbon uptake. Detection of disturbance, recovery, and disease impacts. Monitoring phytoplankton photosynthetic activity and aquatic productivity. (6) Integration across sensors and scales. Combining SIF and hyperspectral observations with thermal, microwave, LiDAR and ecosystem flux measurements, as well as atmospheric CO₂ and carbonyl sulfide (OCS) observations, to connect vegetation structure and function with carbon and water cycling. (7) Climate resilience, mitigation and adaptation. Linking stress indicators with hazard exposure and ecosystem vulnerability to assess risks to productivity and ecosystem function; quantifying resistance, recovery time and legacy effects; evaluating adaptation outcomes under climate extremes; and assessing implications for carbon uptake and climate change mitigation.
title: Solar-induced fluorescence and hyperspectral remote sensing: linking vegetation traits, photosynthesis and ecosystem responses across scales

description: In this session I suggest discussing why the critical minerals matter in energy transitions and how the petroleum engineer, or geoscientist, is able to transfer to the mineral sector smoothly. Moreover, what explanation is still difficult? Is it the dataset issue or the spare module? Then explore what the basic, medium, and generative AI applications have done and what is still needed. What about the limitation of them not only on prediction accuracy or geological realism but also on uncertainty interpretation
title: AI for Critical Mineral Exploration, Characterization, and Sustainable Resource Development

description: Background: Fast technological advances and the targets set for energy transition drive the increasing demand for Critical Raw Materials (CRMs). These trends cause fundamental dependencies on a secure raw material supply, and highlight the limitations and vulnerabilities of relying predominantly on primary raw material extraction. Given the projected growth in demand in the upcoming years, primary resources alone are unlikely to sustainably meet future raw material needs, increasing the importance of recovery of valuable materials from secondary sources to strengthen the supply chains. Consequently, circular concepts have gained increasing importance in order to close material loops, reduce dependence on primary resources and mitigate global supply risks. In this context, developing smarter and more efficient methods and technologies for the detection and monitoring of secondary raw materials will be essential to improve material recovery and support their reliable reintegration into material supply chains. Objectives: In this session, we welcome contributions with focus on novel technologies and workflows such as: - Sensor-based detection, identification and characterisation of CRMs, polymers, REEs, semiconductors and other valuable materials in complex and heterogeneous waste streams; - Imaging, spectroscopic, and multimodal sensing approaches for continuous digitalisation and material identification; - AI-based workflows and advanced data processing approaches for multisensor fusion, process optimisation, and automated decision-marking in secondary raw material recover/monitoring of stocks and flow; - Chemical, physical, and density-based methods for material separation and recovery, including pre-treatment workflows designed to improve the separability and recovery of materials from complex streams; - Applications targeting recovery of materials from complex waste streams such as: re-mining and secondary resources including mine waste and tailings, end-of-life vehicle (ELV), waste from electric and electronic equipment (WEEE).
title: Towards sustainable raw material cycles: methods and technologies for an efficient characterisation, digitalisation and monitoring of secondary raw materials

description: The Asia-Pacific region encompasses an extraordinary diversity of geological, environmental, climatic, oceanographic, and ecological systems, while also facing many of the world's most significant Earth and environmental sustainability challenges. This session welcomes contributions from across the full spectrum of disciplines represented at EGU, showcasing research conducted in, relevant to, or led from the Asia-Pacific region. Hosted through the EGU27 Perth Regional Hub and running throughout the week of the General Assembly, the session provides a dedicated opportunity for researchers from across the Asia-Pacific region to participate in person in this global conference. It aims both to highlight the breadth and excellence of geoscience research in the region and to strengthen engagement by enabling participation from researchers who may not be able to travel to Europe and/or have limited timezone access to the online sessions in Vienna. Contributions may address regional challenges such as climate change, natural hazards, water resources, ecosystems, oceans, energy, or mineral resources, but are not limited to these themes. We particularly encourage interdisciplinary studies and contributions that advance understanding of Earth and environmental systems within the Asia-Pacific context. Presentations will be organised into thematic sessions across the week, bringing together related topics from the Earth, environmental, and planetary sciences to promote scientific exchange, foster new collaborations, and strengthen connections between the Asia-Pacific and global geoscience communities.
title: Earth and Environmental Science in and from the Asia-Pacific Region

description: Microorganisms (bacteria and archaea) are widely suggested to influence the formation of minerals. But how do we know? Is the evidence for microbial involvement in mineral formation truly robust in every case? The mechanisms by which microorganisms may affect mineral formation are diverse: do they simply alter their environment through metabolic activity, driving the surrounding fluid to supersaturation with respect to a particular mineral phase? Or can they mediate the nucleation and growth of a mineral that is already supersaturated in the fluid but whose formation is kinetically inhibited? And how might these different processes manifest in the sedimentary record? These controversial questions call for an open and unbiased debate. This Geopanel provides a forum for such a discussion from a multidisciplinary perspective, bringing together panellists representing mineralogical, geochemical, microbiological and sedimentological viewpoints. The aim is not to promote a particular interpretation, but to critically examine the evidence, clarify the mechanisms involved, and develop a more differentiated understanding of the role of microorganisms in mineral formation — helping the field to build a stronger scientific foundation.
title: Panel discussion on small organisms: can bacteria influence mineral precipitation?

description: There have been enormous advances in the use of earth observation technology for water quality monitoring over most recent years. However, despite these developments the technology is rarely used in national or regional water quality monitoring programmes. A recent report of the European Commission Joint Research Centre (Attila et al. 2025) highlighted that only 3 of the 22 European countries from which EO experts responded to a survey are currently using earth observation data to report on the Water Framework Directive. Obstacles preventing a wider implementation that were identified in the survey include: - A lack of common guidelines on how to utilize EO for WFD reporting, - Legal issues regarding EO application in the current WFD monitoring guidelines, and - A lack of information about EO tools This corresponds to the eight bottlenecks for progress in the application of Copernicus services in operational monitoring, which were identified by the Water-ForCE consortium in a Roadmap (Water-ForCE, 2024). The roadmap also set out seven recommendations to help close these bottlenecks. The proposed session will give an overview on the Water-ForCE roadmap, the current status of implementation of its recommendations and the road ahead. Besides Water-ForCE, other networks that actively promote the implementation of earth observation in water quality monitoring include the UNESCO-IHP International Initiative on Water Quality and GEO Aquawatch. Both are open and collaborative networks, giving the scientific community an opportunity for participation. Complementing the Water-ForCE roadmap, a global indicator for lakes based on earth observation data, which was developed in the context of the UN Sustainable Development Goals, will also be introduced.
title: Water-ForCE in action – applying remote sensing technology in operational water quality monitoring
